title: Approaching the Mystery: Faith, Reason and Authority
desc: How to approach the Trinity: belief and understanding, truths above reason, the authority of Scripture, tradition, creeds and Fathers, and rules for interpreting Scripture in doctrinal dispute.

topics.title: How should the mystery of the Trinity be approached: by faith, reason, or inquiry?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Trinity is known by revelation and held by faith rather than discovered or settled by unaided reason. Owen, Warfield, Hilary and Bickersteth appeal to Scripture and the Spirit's revealing work, Augustine to the purifying of the heart by faith and love, and Waterland to Scripture together with the consensus of the Church over fourteen to sixteen centuries. Augustine's one answer recorded as 'Yes' on natural reason in fact argues only that reason's divine attributes apply to the whole Trinity and to each Person, and so do not show the Trinity. They differ on what reason and inquiry may do once faith is given. Augustine encourages continued 'faith seeking understanding' through prayer and analogies such as lover, loved and love, and Warfield credits reason with showing the doctrine's consistency and superiority to an abstract monad. Hilary insists that faith is not 'devoid of reason' and must actively refute heretical arguments, while Waterland lets reason interpret revelation and concedes that only a real demonstration, which he says the opponents lack, could outweigh Scripture and the Fathers. By contrast, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose and Irenaeus discourage inquiry into God's essence: Gregory treats it as idle and a source of heresy, though he defends conceptual terms against Eunomius, Ambrose urges praise instead of questioning, and Irenaeus prefers simple belief and love to subtle questions; Bickersteth and Waterland likewise stress that ordinary believers need not explain the 'how' before believing.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
refs.quote: since we desire to understand the eternity, and equality, and unity of the Trinity, as much as is permitted us, but ought to believe before we understand

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: the doctrine of the Trinity is purely a revealed doctrine. That is to say, it embodies a truth which has never been discovered, and is indiscoverable, by natural reason.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: will leave God the Word, Who was in the beginning, below itself, just as it has left below it all other things, and itself comes to be in Him in Whom God the Word was not

ans.text:
Start with faith, let Scripture lead, and then use your mind fully and humbly to understand what you already believe. Faith, reason and inquiry are not rivals here. They work in a certain order, and the order matters.

First, faith comes first because the Trinity is something we could never have worked out for ourselves. By looking at creation, people can see that there is a God who is powerful, wise and good. Paul says as much in Romans 1:20. But nothing in nature tells us that this one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. No amount of clever thinking reached that truth on its own. We know it only because God has shown it to us. Jesus says in Matthew 11:27 that "no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." When Peter confessed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus told him that "flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but My Father in heaven" (Matthew 16:17). Paul makes the same point in 1 Corinthians 2:11: "no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God." So the Trinity is not a theory we invent. It is a gift we receive.

That means the Bible is where we begin. In Scripture we meet one God, who alone is to be worshipped. We also meet the Father who sends, the Son who is with God and is God (John 1:1), and the Holy Spirit who is spoken of as God. Jesus sends his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice that it is one name, and three are named. Before we try to explain anything, we hold on to what God has said. There is one God. The Father is not the Son. The Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. Each is fully God. And they are equal in everything that makes God God.

Does reason have any place, then? Yes, a real and honorable one. God gave us minds so that we would seek him. Reason helps us read the Bible carefully, compare passage with passage, and see what a text truly says. The Bereans in Acts 17:11 were praised for examining the Scriptures to test what they heard. Reason can also show that the doctrine is not a contradiction. Christians do not say God is one and three in the same way. He is one in his being, meaning what he is. He is three in persons, meaning who he is. And reason can answer objections and expose bad arguments.

But reason must serve as a helper, not sit as the judge. Here is the danger. If I decide beforehand what God can and cannot be, based on what I know of created things, I have made my small mind the measure of God. That is like a child measuring the ocean with a teacup and declaring that anything the cup cannot hold must not exist. God says in Isaiah 55:9, "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts." It should not surprise us that God's own inner life is beyond us. We cannot even fully explain how our own minds work, or many things in the physical world. We can know for certain that God is, and know truly what he has told us about himself, without grasping completely what he is.

This is why humility is the right posture. A believer does not need to explain how the Father, Son and Spirit are one God before trusting it. The first Christians were baptized into that name and worshipped Jesus as Lord long before anyone wrote careful explanations. Many of us believe both that God knows everything ahead of time and that we make real choices, without knowing exactly how the two fit. Faith rests on God's word, not on our ability to picture it.

Inquiry, then, is welcome, as long as it grows out of faith rather than replacing it. Asking questions about the Trinity is not doubt or disloyalty. It is love wanting to know its Beloved better. "Seek His face always," says Psalm 105:4. The person who should worry us is not the one still searching, but the one who claims to have figured God out completely. Paul, after years with Christ, said he had not yet attained it all but pressed on (Philippians 3:12). He also tells us that "now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12). We will be learning about God forever, and gladly.

This kind of seeking is also a matter of the heart, not only the head. Scripture says that without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11:6), and that God is love (1 John 4:8). We come to know a loving God by loving him, praying, worshipping and obeying, not merely by debating. A proud or careless heart will twist even true ideas. A humble heart, washed by grace, sees more clearly. So it is wise to begin by remembering who we are before God: creatures and forgiven sinners, invited to know him because he chose to make himself known.

One more practical point. When a doctrine is this deep, it is wise to be cautious about our own private conclusions. If my reading of Scripture leads me somewhere almost no believer has gone before, I should suspect my reading before I suspect the whole church's. That is simple modesty. Christians do weigh this differently. Some give great weight to what believers have confessed together across the centuries, reasoning that one person is more likely to err than the whole church. Others stress that every teaching must still be tested afresh by Scripture, since Scripture alone is God's own word. Both agree that the Bible is the source, and that a new idea about God deserves extra caution.

So approach the Trinity the way you would approach a great and holy friend. Listen first to what he says about himself. Believe him. Then think hard, ask good questions, and keep seeking, knowing that the answers you find will lead you not to pride but to worship.

topics.title: In what sense is the Trinity a mystery, and can what is incomprehensible be rationally believed?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Trinity, and especially the manner of the Son's generation, exceeds human comprehension, and that this is no reason to reject it. Hilary, Augustine, Athanasius, Irenaeus and Gregory of Nyssa ground this in the weakness of the creature before God, in God as the only fit witness to himself, and in analogies from nature and from our own minds that we also cannot understand. Gregory and Athanasius add that one should hold the received faith, or keep silent and believe, even when argument fails. Owen and Waterland argue more formally. Owen distinguishes what is above reason from what is against it, and the true reason of things from the maimed reason of individual men. Waterland insists that a mystery must be intelligible and free of real contradiction, that faith reaches exactly as far as our general and confused ideas reach, and that anti-Trinitarian objections prove too much, since they would equally overthrow eternity and omnipresence. Emphases also differ: Augustine stresses sin, the enigmatic character of the image, and the bodily imagination as causes of the difficulty, with full sight reserved for the life of bliss; Edwards and Bickersteth stress fuller scriptural revelation, Edwards holding that it multiplies the mysteries we see while making knowledge clearer, and Bickersteth that Scripture answers every rational objection.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Why then so unequal and partial, with respect to the Trinity, the case being exactly the same? why may not the thing be true, though the Mannmr, or modus of it, be above comprehension!

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: the least intimation of a truth by divine revelation will make me embrace it, although it should be contrary to the reason of all the Socinians in the world

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: If we assume that an event did not happen, because we cannot discover how it was done, we make the limits of our understanding into the limits of reality.

ans.text:
The Trinity is a mystery because it is true and has been made known to us, yet it is too deep for our minds to take in completely. That does not make belief in it unreasonable. Believing something we cannot fully understand is very different from believing something we can see is false.

In the Bible, a "mystery" is not a riddle or a puzzle we are told not to think about. It is something God has revealed that we could never have worked out alone. Paul writes in 1 Timothy 3:16, "By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great," and goes on to speak of Christ, who "appeared in the flesh." The mystery has been told out loud. We know it. But what we know is so large that we cannot get to the bottom of it. It is like standing on the shore of the ocean: you really do see the sea, but you do not see all of it.

That is the sense in which the Trinity is a mystery. Scripture makes certain things plain. There is one God. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. The three are not one person wearing three masks, because they speak to one another, love one another and send one another. We can know and say these things clearly. What we cannot do is picture or explain how one God exists as three persons. We know that it is so. We do not know how it is so.

It helps to separate two kinds of claims. Some claims are against reason. They contradict themselves, like a square circle, or saying there is one God and three Gods in exactly the same sense. Other claims are above reason. They are not contradictory, but they reach beyond what our minds can measure. The Trinity belongs to the second kind. The church does not say God is one and three in the same respect. It says God is one in his being, or "essence" (what God is), and three in persons (who God is: Father, Son and Spirit). That may stretch our minds past their limits, but it does not ask them to accept nonsense.

Why should we expect God to be beyond us? Think about what we are. We are small, created beings, and our minds are damaged by sin. God is the Creator of everything, infinite and eternal. The Lord says in Isaiah 55:9, "As the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts." If we could fit God neatly inside our heads, he would be no bigger than our heads. A God we could fully explain would be a God we had made up. That God is beyond our understanding is just what we should expect if he is real.

We already live with this in ordinary life. Jesus speaks in Mark 4 of a farmer who scatters seed. Night and day the seed sprouts and grows, though the farmer does not know how. Nobody refuses to plant a garden because they cannot explain the mystery of life inside a seed. We cannot even explain our own minds: how thoughts arise, how we remember, how we pass life on to our children. We are sure these things happen while understanding very little of how. It would be strange to demand of God a clarity we cannot find even in ourselves.

The same goes for the Son being "begotten" of the Father. To be begotten means to come from someone as their true offspring, sharing their nature, the way a child shares the humanity of its parent. Scripture calls Jesus the Father's one and only Son, who was with God in the beginning and is God (John 1:1, 1:18). We are not told how this eternal sonship works, and we should not imagine it as a birth in time, or as anything bodily. When Jesus turned water into wine at Cana, the servants knew the wine was real, though they could not say how it got there. Not knowing how something happened is no reason to deny that it happened. Jesus says in Matthew 11:27, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." Some depths of God are known only to God. Moses put it simply: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us" (Deuteronomy 29:29). We hold on to what is revealed and do not invent the rest.

Part of our difficulty is that we tend to think in pictures. We imagine God the way we imagine objects, where three things are always more than one thing. So we wonder how Father, Son and Spirit together could be no "more God" than any one of them. But God does not have size or parts. He is not a substance that can be divided into pieces or added up. When our imagination tries to draw a diagram of the Trinity, it will always get it wrong. That is not because the truth is confused. It is because the tool is too small for the job.

So is faith opposed to reason here? No. Reason tells us that it is wise to trust a witness who knows more than we do and who has shown himself trustworthy. Only God fully knows himself, so only God can tell us truly who he is. He has spoken in Scripture and above all in his Son. To believe him is not to switch off our minds. It is to use them well, by recognizing their limits and listening to the one who has none. Faith does not refuse reason's help. It simply follows God further than reason alone could walk.

Two misunderstandings are worth avoiding. One is to think that "mystery" means we know nothing, so anything goes. That is not true. The Bible's teaching about God is clear enough to be confessed, defended and sung. The other is to think that if we cannot explain something, we must reject it. That makes our own understanding the measure of everything that is real, which is a strange position for a creature to take toward its Creator. If someone believes the Trinity is a genuine contradiction, the fair thing is to show it. Otherwise the real question is simply whether the Bible teaches it.

It is also true that the more God reveals, the more mystery we see. The New Testament tells us far more about Father, Son and Spirit than the Old, and in doing so it opens up even greater depths. This is not a failure. It is what happens when finite people are shown more of an infinite God.

For now, Paul says in 1 Corinthians 13:12, "we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face." Our partial knowledge is real knowledge, enough to trust, love and worship the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The right response to this mystery is not suspicion but wonder. With Paul we can say, "O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" (Romans 11:33). We believe what God has shown us, keep seeking to understand it through prayer and study and faithful living, and are content to let God be greater than our grasp.

topics.title: Can the Trinity be known or proven by reason and created things?
topics.cmp: Augustine is the most optimistic: citing Romans and the Book of Wisdom, he holds that the Trinity can be known in part through created things, which bear traces of unity, form and order, and especially through the mind's memory, understanding and will as an enduring image. He adds that this image is unequal and more divided than the Trinity itself, and that reason reaches only 'as far as possible' alongside Scripture. Owen agrees modestly that creation offers resemblances of a Trinity in unity, but uses this only to rebut the charge that the doctrine is contrary to reason, while denying that philosophy without Christ yields any true spiritual knowledge of God. Warfield, by contrast, rejects every attempted rational proof: the self-representation argument of Keckermann and Lessing leads to pantheism, Richard of St. Victor's argument from love abuses figurative language, and the self-consciousness argument yields two Gods and no Spirit; he also denies that pagan triads are analogues or sources, while still allowing Augustine's lover-loved-love as a sympathetic analogy rather than a proof. Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary stress the limits of knowledge from a different side: Gregory argues that knowing the Maker does not reveal a work's substance, and Hilary holds that human terms for God fall short, so that worship takes the place of definition. Waterland defends non-scriptural terms such as perichoresis only as answers to speculative objections, not as reason's grounds for the doctrine.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.quote: it is now our business to demonstrate not only to believers, by authority of divine Scripture, but also to such as understand, by some kind of reason, if we can

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: It is obvious that arguments like this prove too much. If God’s representation of Himself, to be perfect, must possess the same kind of reality that He Himself possesses, it does not seem easy to deny that His representations of everything else must possess objective reality.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: There is so great an intimation made of such an expression and resemblance of a Trinity in unity in the very works of the creation

ans.text:
No. Reason and the created world can tell us a great deal about God, but they cannot discover or prove that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. We know that only because God has shown it to us, above all by sending his Son and his Spirit, and by telling us so in the Bible. Once we know it, though, reason and creation can help us think about it. They can also show us that the Trinity is not nonsense.

Start with what creation can teach. Paul says in Romans 1:20 that "God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship." Look at the stars, or a newborn child, and you can rightly conclude that there is a wise and powerful Maker. But notice what Paul lists: God's power and his divine nature. He does not say that creation reveals the inner life of God. A painting tells you the painter is skilled. It does not tell you who is in the painter's family.

The Trinity is exactly that kind of inner, personal knowledge. Jesus says in Matthew 11:27 that "no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." John 1:18 says that no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is himself God, "has made Him known." Paul adds in 1 Corinthians 2 that only the Spirit of God knows the deep things of God, just as only your own spirit knows your private thoughts. If the Father, Son and Spirit are known only by the Son and the Spirit making them known, then no amount of clever thinking can get there on its own. God's people learned that God is three-in-one through events, not through argument. The Son became man. He prayed to his Father. He promised and poured out the Spirit. He sent his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19).

Over the centuries, thoughtful Christians have tried to build proofs anyway, and the attempts are worth looking at honestly. One argument goes like this. God knows himself perfectly, and a perfect picture of himself must be a real second person. But God also knows everything else perfectly. By the same logic, every idea in God's mind would have to be a real, eternal being alongside him. That would blur God and the world together. Another argument says that a mind thinking about itself must split into two. But you can think about yourself without becoming two people, and there is no reason God cannot do the same. And even if the argument worked, it would give us two, not three.

A more appealing argument comes from love. God is love (1 John 4:8), and love needs someone to love, so God must be more than one person. This is beautiful, and it fits what the Bible reveals. As a proof, though, it falls short. It is not obvious that God's own perfect being could not be a worthy object of his own perfect love. Arguments that try to show why there must be exactly three tend to feel forced. So these are good ways of pondering what God has revealed, not ways of proving it.

What about the hints of the Trinity that many have noticed in creation? People have pointed to the way a single human mind remembers, understands and loves. That is one mind with three distinct activities. Others have pointed to a lover, the beloved, and the love between them. Some Christians have been quite hopeful about these "traces" and have spent long effort tracing them. Others are more cautious, worried that they can mislead. Both groups agree on the main point. These pictures help a believer who already knows the truth from Scripture. They do not lead an unbeliever to it. And every picture limps. Your memory, understanding and love belong to one person and can be stronger or weaker than one another. The Father, Son and Spirit are three persons, always fully equal, and yet one God more perfectly united than any human mind. The likeness is real but faint, like a reflection in a dim mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Still, these reflections do something useful. People sometimes say the Trinity is irrational. Yet we find unity and threeness woven together in our own minds and in the world, so it is unreasonable to call the idea absurd. The Trinity is above reason, in the sense that we could never have worked it out. It is not against reason, as if it were a contradiction. We do not say God is one and three in the same sense. He is one God, one in his being or "essence," meaning what he is. He is three persons, the Father, the Son and the Spirit, meaning who he is.

Finally, some claim Christians borrowed the Trinity from pagan religions that had groups of three gods, such as the Egyptian father, mother and son, or the Hindu trio of creator, preserver and destroyer. Look closely and the resemblance disappears. Those are three separate gods, or a divine family modeled on human families, or one force passing through different phases. Some reflect little more than a habit of counting in threes. The Bible's teaching is something else entirely. There is only one God, and the earliest Christians were Jews who would rather die than worship more than one. That one God is eternally Father, Son and Spirit. The doctrine did not come from the myths around the church. It came from what God did in Jesus Christ and what he said in his Word.

So we come to the Trinity as children receiving a gift, not as detectives solving a puzzle. Reason and creation can help us admire it, explain it and defend it. Only God's own self-revelation can give it to us.

topics.title: How is the doctrine of the Trinity established, expounded and defended?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the doctrine of the Trinity rests on revelation rather than on unaided reason. Owen, Waterland, Bickersteth and Hilary each make Scripture the rule, and Irenaeus warns against speculating on what Scripture leaves undeclared, such as the manner of the Son's generation. Their grounds and emphases differ. Owen treats terms like essence and person as derivative deductions with no original weight, and he reduces what must be proved to a few scriptural propositions. Warfield likewise lists three elements (one God; Father, Son and Spirit each God; each a distinct person), but he stresses that the church's formulations faithfully aim to do justice to the New Testament's composite fact. Waterland argues epistemologically that no a priori philosophical maxim can judge what Scripture reveals. Bickersteth argues from the shared divine names, attributes and acts and from the one baptismal Name, and he gives creeds positive value for stability, though only when proved from Scripture. Gregory of Nyssa insists on keeping the divinely handed-down names Father, Son and Holy Ghost against philosophical substitutes, appealing to tradition and the councils as well as the Lord's words. Hilary, by contrast, grants that the Church may under necessity make pronouncements beyond Scripture's explicit words to fix the meaning of the baptismal Names against heretics, though he does so reluctantly.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: And yet if those had been the more appropriate names, the Truth Himself would not have been at a loss to discover them, nor those men either, on whom successively devolved the preaching of the mystery

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: if combined with assertions that God is one, we find Three revealed in Scripture to whom the same names, attributes, and acts are ascribed, the same so far as a personal distinction allows; if we look vainly for any fourth Divine one

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: the sum of this revelation in this matter is, that God is one; — that this one God is Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; — that the Father is the Father of the Son; and the Son, the Son of the Father

ans.text:
The doctrine of the Trinity is established from the Bible, explained with careful words that help us say clearly what the Bible teaches, and defended by showing that those words faithfully match Scripture. Scripture comes first and has the final say. Creeds, reasoning and special terms all serve it, never the other way round.

It helps to see what the Bible actually needs to show. The doctrine of the Trinity is not a long list of complicated claims. At its heart it says three things. First, there is only one God. Second, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. Third, the Father, the Son and the Spirit are truly distinct from one another. The Father is not the Son, and neither is the Spirit. If Scripture teaches all three of these, the doctrine stands. Everything else is an effort to hold them together without letting go of any of them.

The Bible does teach each one. Israel's great confession is "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and the New Testament never backs away from it. Yet John opens his Gospel by saying that "the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Thomas falls before the risen Jesus and calls him "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). When Ananias lies to the Holy Spirit, Peter tells him he has lied to God (Acts 5:3-4). The same names, the same powers and the same works that belong to God alone are given to the Son and to the Spirit. Still, the three are never blurred together. The Father speaks to the Son, the Son prays to the Father, and the Son promises to send the Spirit. And Jesus tells his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice that he says one name, yet three are named. Put these threads side by side and the Trinity is not something added to the Bible. It is what you find when you take all of the Bible seriously at once.

What about words like "Trinity," "person" and "essence," which you will not find in Scripture? These are tools for explaining, not new sources of truth. "Essence" or "being" means what God is: his one divine nature. "Person" means who: the Father, the Son and the Spirit, each a real "I" who can speak to the others. So we say God is one in what he is and three in who he is. "Trinity" is simply a single word for "three-in-one." These terms carry no weight on their own. If the Bible's teaching is true, the words follow naturally, and believers have no reason to object to them. If the Bible did not teach it, no one would bother defending the words. This is why it is a mistake, when someone challenges the Trinity, to argue first about technical vocabulary. Start with what God has said. The vocabulary comes second.

That also explains why we keep to the names God himself gave: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Some people have tried to swap these for abstract labels like "the First Being" and "a second Being." But Jesus handed us these names, and they say things the abstractions miss. A father and a son share the same nature, and "Spirit" points to God's own breath and life. We should not trade the names God chose for ones we find more convenient.

Creeds work in a similar way. A creed is a short, shared summary of what the church believes the Bible teaches. Creeds are a real gift. They give stability, they guard against drifting with every new idea, and they help ordinary Christians know what matters most. But a creed earns our trust because it can be shown from Scripture. The church teaches, and the Bible proves. Christians differ somewhat on how much weight creeds carry. Some see the early creeds as a reliable, Spirit-guided reading of Scripture that is binding on the church. Others accept the same creeds but stress that they are always open to testing by the Bible, which alone is without error. Both sides agree on the great creeds about the Trinity, and both agree that they stand or fall with Scripture. Like the Bereans in Acts 17:11, we check what we are taught against the Scriptures.

Where does reason fit? Reason is God's gift, and we need it to read the Bible carefully, to notice how passages fit together, and to show that the Trinity does not contradict itself. Saying one God in three persons is not the same as saying one God and three Gods, or one person and three persons. But reason alone could never have discovered the Trinity. We only know it because God has made himself known. Nor can reason sit as judge over God and announce ahead of time what is or is not possible for him. God knows his own nature far better than we do. The right question is not "Could God be like this?" but "Has God told us he is like this?" Humility and prayer belong to this study. We ask the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures to help us understand them as they were meant.

Is it right, then, to say things about God in words the Bible does not use? Yes, as long as we are saying the same thing the Bible says, only more plainly. This has sometimes been necessary. People have used the biblical words "Son" or "Spirit" while emptying them of their meaning. For example, some have called Jesus "Son of God" while denying that he is truly God. When that happens, the church has to spell out what the words mean so that the truth is not lost. That is not adding to Scripture. It is guarding it.

There is a limit, though. The Bible tells us that the Son is begotten of the Father, which means he shares the Father's very nature as a son shares his father's. It does not tell us how this happens, and we should not invent answers. "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us" (Deuteronomy 29:29). We "know in part" (1 Corinthians 13:12). So the faithful way to approach the Trinity is to believe all that God has shown us, explain it as clearly as we can, defend it from his Word, and then stop where Scripture stops, in worship rather than speculation.

topics.title: How does Scripture reveal the Trinity?
topics.cmp: Bickersteth and Warfield agree that Scripture's lack of a formal, compact Trinitarian statement does not weaken the doctrine, but they explain it on different grounds. Bickersteth appeals to God's providential method: Scripture's variety parallels nature. He argues that a single explicit article might not have silenced doubt and could have bred a careless, 'petrified orthodoxy,' whereas comparing scattered references exercises the mind and improves the heart, with the framing of creeds left to the Church. Warfield's explanation is historical: the Trinity was revealed in deed, in the incarnation of the Son and the outpouring of the Spirit, so it was already the common possession of Christians, and the occasional, practical New Testament writings presuppose it and allude to it with an unstudied naturalness that makes their testimony more impressive, while still stating it explicitly when occasion arises. Warfield alone treats the Old Testament, holding that it may legitimately be read in the New Testament's light as a dimly lit room whose contents are revealed and perfected, not corrected. On the doctrine's effect on our knowledge of God, Edwards stresses that the fuller New Testament revelation makes God both better known and more visibly mysterious and incomprehensible, whereas Warfield emphasizes that, though difficult in itself, the Trinity eases rather than burdens the intellect by resolving difficulties in conceiving an infinite, loving, self-conscious God.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: Thus the Old Testament revelation of God is not corrected by the fuller revelation which follows it, but only perfected, extended and enlarged.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: the simple rule of our faith in the One living and true God – Father Son and Spirit, the source of creation, redemption, and sanctification, – is marked out with a precision that he who runs may read.

refs.author: Jonathan Edwards
refs.quote: what the New Testament has revealed, tho it has more opened to our view the nature of God, yet it has increased the number of visible mysteries

ans.text:
Scripture reveals the Trinity less by giving us a definition than by telling us what God has done. In sending his Son and pouring out his Spirit, God showed us who he is: one God, who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Bible records and explains that self-revelation from beginning to end.

It helps to see that the revelation came first in events, and only then in writing. The Son of God became a man, lived among us, died, and rose again. After he ascended, the Holy Spirit was poured out at Pentecost and came to live in believers. People who walked with Jesus and then received the Spirit found that they had met God himself in each. The New Testament is the record of what they saw and experienced, and their reflection on it. In that sense the Trinity is not an idea someone worked out at a desk. It is what God showed us when he came to save us.

The Old Testament prepares for this. Its great confession is that God is one: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The New Testament never takes that back. Jesus himself quotes it (Mark 12:29). But the Old Testament also holds hints that God's oneness is richer than a simple, solitary unit. God says, "Let Us make man in Our image" (Genesis 1:26). The Spirit of God moves over the waters and later fills prophets and kings. The Word of the LORD comes and acts. A mysterious figure called the Angel of the LORD speaks as God. In Psalm 110:1 the LORD speaks to one David calls "my Lord." The prophets promise a child who will be called "Mighty God" (Isaiah 9:6).

Is it fair to read these passages in the light of Christ, or is that reading later ideas back into them? Think of a room that is fully furnished but dimly lit. When someone turns on the light, nothing new is added to the room. You simply see what was there all along. Jesus himself taught his disciples to read the Old Testament this way, explaining what all the Scriptures said about him (Luke 24:27). So the New Testament does not correct the Old Testament's picture of God, as if Israel had believed in the wrong God. It fills that picture out. The same God is now seen more clearly.

In the New Testament, the Trinity is everywhere assumed and sometimes stated outright. At Jesus' baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father's voice says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:16-17). Jesus sends his followers out "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice that he says "name," singular, yet names three. Paul closes a letter with a blessing: "May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all" (2 Corinthians 13:14). John opens his Gospel by saying the Word was with God and the Word was God (John 1:1). Paul describes salvation as the Father sending his Son, and then sending "the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, 'Abba, Father!'" (Galatians 4:6).

What is striking is how casually the apostles speak this way. They are not usually trying to prove the Trinity. They mention Father, Son, and Spirit side by side while talking about spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:4-6), prayer, holiness, or the plan of salvation (Ephesians 1:3-14). That tells us something important. The early Christians already believed this. It was part of the air they breathed, so the writers could take it for granted. Their letters were written to meet practical needs in real churches, not to serve as textbooks. Evidence given offhand like this is, if anything, more convincing than a formal argument. It shows the Trinity was the settled background of all their thinking about God.

Some ask why God did not simply give us one clear sentence, perhaps spoken by Jesus, that sets out the whole doctrine. We should be humble here, because God does not always tell us his reasons. But we can see some wisdom in the way he did it. The Bible is like a landscape rather than a list. Its stories, laws, songs, prophecies, and letters all work together, and the truth about God runs through all of them. If we had one neat formula, many people might memorize it and never read the rest. Their faith could become a dry slogan that never touched the heart. Instead, God invites us to search the Scriptures, compare passage with passage, and meet him as he really acted in history. That kind of study shapes both mind and heart.

Would a single explicit verse have ended the arguments? Probably not. Any such verse could be disputed like any other: people could question its wording, its translation, or whether it was original. In fact, some older English Bibles include a line in 1 John 5:7 that states the Trinity very directly, but it is missing from the earliest manuscripts, and most scholars agree it was added later. Its absence does not weaken the doctrine at all, because the teaching rests on the whole sweep of Scripture, not one proof text. And the Bible already has statements as plain as John 1:1, yet some people still are not persuaded. In the end, true faith is a gift of God, not merely the result of winning an argument (1 Corinthians 2:14).

This also answers a common worry: that because the word "Trinity" is not in the Bible, the doctrine must be a later invention. The word is a summary, the way "the Bible" is not a word found in the Bible either. When the church later wrote creeds, it was not adding to Scripture. It was stating carefully, in guarded words, what Scripture already teaches: there is one God; the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God; and they are truly distinct from one another. The creeds are fences that keep us from wandering away from what the Bible says.

Finally, does this fuller revelation make God easier or harder to understand? In a way, both. We know far more about God after Christ and Pentecost than before. And yet the more we see, the more wonderful and beyond us he appears. That is what we should expect of the true God. But the Trinity is not just a puzzle added to our faith. It actually helps us. If God were a single, solitary person, whom did he love before he made the world? Scripture says "God is love" (1 John 4:8). The Trinity shows us how that can be true from all eternity: the Father loves the Son in the Spirit (John 17:24). Once we see God this way, we find in him not a lonely power but a living fellowship of love, into which, through Christ and by the Spirit, he welcomes us.

topics.title: On what authority does the doctrine rest: Scripture, tradition, the Fathers, or the Church?
topics.cmp: All the authors treat Scripture as authoritative, but they differ on what stands beside it. Basil gives unwritten apostolic tradition, handed down "in a mystery," the same force as written teaching, and he faults those who demand written proof alone. Irenaeus makes the apostles' teaching, preserved in the apostolic churches through bishops like Polycarp, the place to find the truth against late-arising heresies. Waterland, by contrast, denies the Church's infallibility and ranks the Fathers as inferior, collateral proof: they are historical evidence of what the Church believed, attested as well as the canon, and a strong presumption about how to interpret Scripture, yet they cannot settle articles of faith on their own. Augustine subordinates every theologian's writings to canonical Scripture, to be corrected only by the divine text or unanswerable reason. Warfield argues that the doctrine is biblical because it lies in Scripture "in solution," while Gregory of Nyssa emphasizes the spiritual sense beneath Scripture's letter rather than any external authority.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: The doctrine of the Trinity lies in Scripture in solution; when it is crystallized from its solvent it does not cease to be Scriptural, but only comes into clearer view.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: We do not appeal to the ancients, as if we could not maintain our ground, from Scripture and reason, against all opposers: this has been done over and over.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Against those who say that it is not right to rank the…
refs.quote: they clamour for written proof, and reject as worthless the unwritten tradition of the Fathers.

ans.text:
The doctrine of the Trinity rests on God's own revelation. That revelation was given through Jesus Christ and handed on by his apostles, and we meet it most surely in the written Scriptures. The church, its early teachers and its creeds do not add to that revelation. They serve as witnesses and guides who help us read it rightly.

Start with where the authority comes from. Jesus sent his apostles with his own authority. He told them in Luke 10:16, "Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me." So the question is never simply what a church leader thinks. It is what the apostles received from Christ and passed on. Jude 3 calls this "the faith entrusted once for all to the saints." Nothing new can be added to it, and Paul warns in Galatians 1:8 that even an angel preaching a different gospel should be refused.

The New Testament is the apostles' teaching in written form. That is why Paul can say in 2 Timothy 3:16 that "all Scripture is God-breathed." Scripture is the one place where we can be certain we are hearing God speak without human error mixed in. When the Bereans heard Paul himself preach, Acts 17:11 praises them for "examining the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true." If an apostle's preaching could be checked against Scripture, so can any later teacher's.

Some people object that the word "Trinity" is not in the Bible, so the doctrine must come from the church rather than from Scripture. But a teaching can be fully biblical without using a biblical word. The Bible says there is only one God. It also calls the Father God, the Son God, and the Spirit God, and it shows them as distinct from one another. Jesus sends his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), one name shared by three. The doctrine of the Trinity simply gathers these scattered threads and states plainly what they add up to. Putting the Bible's teaching into a summary is not leaving the Bible. It is taking all of it seriously at once.

So where do the early Christian writers and the creeds fit in? Think of them as witnesses. If you want to know what a group of people believed long ago, you read the books they left behind. The writings of the early church show us how the first generations, some of them taught by people who knew the apostles, understood the faith. They confessed Jesus as truly God and worshiped the Father, Son and Spirit together. That is real evidence. It tells us the Trinity was not invented centuries later at a council. The councils put into careful words what the church had already believed and prayed.

This witness has weight, though it is not infallible. Early teachers were godly but fallible people. They sometimes expressed themselves clumsily before the church had worked out clearer language, and they sometimes made mistakes. We do not believe something just because an ancient writer said it. We believe what God says in Scripture. Any human teacher, ancient or modern, is to be corrected by the plain teaching of Scripture and by sound reasoning, not by someone's personal preference or cleverness.

Still, there is wisdom in listening to the church across the ages. When believers in every place and generation have read the Bible the same way on a central matter, a brand-new reading that contradicts them all should make us cautious. That is especially so when the new reading depends on setting aside parts of Scripture that do not fit. Modern readers are no smarter than ancient ones, and we are further from the apostles' time. False teachings also tend to have a clear starting date and a founder. The true faith goes back to the beginning. And it is worth remembering that we recognize which books belong in the Bible partly through this same long testimony of the church. Throwing out that witness entirely would weaken the very thing we lean on to know our Bible.

Here sincere Christians do disagree about how these pieces relate. Some hold that Scripture alone is the final and only infallible authority. In their view the church's tradition and creeds are valuable but always answerable to the Bible. Their main reason is that only Scripture is described as God-breathed, and the Bible itself models testing all teaching by it. Others hold that the apostles handed on the faith both in writing and by word of mouth. In their view Scripture and this living tradition belong together, faithfully guarded and interpreted by the church's teachers. They point to 2 Thessalonians 2:15, where Paul says to "stand firm and cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter." They also point to 1 Timothy 3:15, which calls the church "the pillar and foundation of the truth." On the doctrine of the Trinity itself, though, these Christians stand together. They agree that it is the faith of the Bible and of the church from the start.

What should an ordinary believer do when teachers disagree? Go back to Scripture first, and read it whole rather than picking out favorite verses. Listen humbly to how Christians through the centuries have understood it, especially in the creeds that churches everywhere still confess. Be wary of anyone who claims the church got the basics wrong for nearly two thousand years. Pray for understanding, because these are deep things about God that our minds can only partly grasp. Our confidence does not finally rest on any human teacher. It rests on God, who has made himself known as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

topics.title: What is the true apostolic faith, and how is it known and kept?
topics.cmp: Each author answers a different question here, so they rarely address the same point directly, but several converge on faith as dependent on God's initiative rather than human reasoning. Hilary grounds true faith in God as its own Author and Witness through self-revelation, in deliberate contrast to philosophy. Gregory of Nyssa likewise sets faith above knowledge, arguing from Abraham's history that faith alone unites the soul with God's incomprehensible nature and is counted for righteousness. Novatian, by contrast, states the content of faith according to the Rule of truth (the Father as almighty Creator) and supports it partly from the ordered works of creation, an argument from the visible world that Hilary and Gregory do not use. Augustine stresses why faith is needed: every good, and final blessedness in enjoying God forever, comes from God alone. Irenaeus answers how faith is kept: by apostolic tradition and the Spirit writing salvation on the heart, even without written Scriptures. Owen's answer concerns God's forbearance in Christ, which seeks the sinner's recovery and full forgiveness, rather than faith itself.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Novatian, with the View of Treating of the Trinity, Sets…
refs.quote: The Rule of truth requires that we should first of all things believe on God the Father and Lord Omnipotent; that is, the absolutely perfect Founder of all things

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: [She believes] in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: who pervert the truth, darken the light, divide the indivisible, rend the scatheless, dissolve the perfect unity

ans.text:
The true apostolic faith is the one message about God that the apostles received from Jesus Christ and handed on to the church. It names one God, the Father almighty, who made all things. It names his Son Jesus Christ, who became man to save us, and the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets and now lives in God's people. We know this faith because God himself has made it known, and we keep it by holding on to what was given, not by inventing something new.

Start with where faith comes from. We could never work out the truth about God by our own cleverness, any more than a character in a novel could work out the author's life story from inside the book. God has to tell us about himself, and he has. Faith rests on his own word. He is both the one who speaks and the one who vouches for what is said. That is why faith is not a guess or a leap in the dark. It is trust in a God who has spoken and shown himself, above all in his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2).

This also explains why faith, and not cleverness, is how we come near to God. Scripture says that "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (Romans 4:3). Abraham did not understand everything about God. He trusted him. Knowledge can only grasp what is already in front of it. Faith reaches toward what God has promised but we cannot yet see. Hebrews 11:1 calls faith "the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see." Every good thing we need, and above all the goodness that makes us right with God and leads to everlasting joy with him, comes from God alone. Faith is the hand that receives it.

Next, what does this faith actually say? From the start it has had a clear shape, and that shape is threefold. Jesus sent his followers out to make disciples, "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice that it says one name, not three names, yet Father, Son and Spirit are each named. The apostles taught one God, the Father, Maker of heaven and earth and everything in them. They taught one Lord, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who truly became human, died for our sins, rose again and will return. And they taught the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets and is given to all who believe. Paul sums up the gospel he received and passed on "as of first importance": Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The early creeds that churches still say together are simply short summaries of this same message.

This faith is fixed. Jude urges believers "to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints" (Jude 3). "Once for all" means it was given whole. We are not waiting for a new edition. A gifted preacher can explain the faith more fully and more beautifully than a plain one. But no one can add to its substance, and a less able teacher does not shrink it. Think of a family heirloom. One person polishes it well and another only dusts it, but neither of them makes a different object. No student is greater than the Master, and the faith belongs to him. Paul warns that even if an angel from heaven brought a different gospel from the one first preached, it must be rejected (Galatians 1:8).

How is this faith known today? The apostles' teaching was written down in the Scriptures, which are "God-breathed" (2 Timothy 3:16). Scripture is the standard by which every teaching is tested. When we want to show that something is part of the faith, we show it from the Bible itself. We do not appeal to someone's private insight. It is worth remembering, though, that the faith is not only for people with books and libraries. For centuries many believers could not read. Yet they knew and held the same faith, written on their hearts by the Spirit through preaching, baptism, prayer and worship. They held it so firmly that they would not even listen to teaching that contradicted it. The faith is simple enough for a child to confess and deep enough that no scholar ever exhausts it.

Sincere Christians do differ on how Scripture relates to the church's ongoing teaching and tradition. Some hold that Scripture alone is the final authority over every church teaching. Their reason is that only Scripture is directly God-breathed, and traditions can drift. Others hold that the church's living tradition and teaching office stand alongside Scripture as its trustworthy interpreter. Their reason is that the apostles handed on the faith by word of mouth as well as in writing. Yet all of them agree on the heart of the matter. The faith in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, came from the apostles, is witnessed in Scripture, and is not ours to change.

How is this faith kept? The first Christians "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching" (Acts 2:42), and that is still how it is done. We keep it by reading and hearing Scripture, by being baptized into the name of the Father, Son and Spirit, by confessing the faith together, and by trusting the Holy Spirit, who guards what has been entrusted to us. We do not keep it alone. Paul speaks of "one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all" (Ephesians 4:5-6). The faith belongs to the whole church, and we hold it together.

That shared confession is one of the marks of the true church. Across every century and continent, Christians have received the same God the Father, the same Son who became flesh for our salvation, and the same gift of the Spirit. Teachings that break from this are usually newer, and they tend to splinter into many competing versions. Some teachings say, for example, that the Son is a lesser kind of being than the Father. These may sound like they protect God's oneness, but they actually divide him. They split the one God into unequal parts and try to fit the infinite God into our small categories. The true faith confesses Father, Son and Spirit as one God, undivided.

A few gentle cautions may help. Holding the apostolic faith does not mean every Christian must agree on every secondary question. It means standing together on the core that God has revealed. Nor does it mean switching off our minds. We think hard about the faith so that we can understand it, explain it and enjoy it, but we think inside it, not above it. And this faith is not cold doctrine. It is the path to the deepest happiness there is. One day we will see the God we now trust. Then we will want nothing evil, lack nothing good, and enjoy him forever, with the certainty that this joy will never end.

topics.title: What rules govern the interpretation of Scripture in Trinitarian disputes?
topics.cmp: The authors broadly agree that Trinitarian disputes are lost by misreading Scripture rather than by any fault in Scripture: Augustine places the blame on readers, Irenaeus and Hilary insist that words be read in their proper order, connection and circumstances rather than as isolated phrases, and Irenaeus requires obscure passages to be settled by clear ones. Athanasius and Basil add specific linguistic cautions: comparative 'as' marks likeness in some respect, not equality, and prepositions carry no fixed technical sense. Athanasius also offers an overall scope, Scripture's double account of Christ as eternal Son and as incarnate, by which to read every passage. They differ plainly on literal versus figurative reading. Owen demands submission to the plain and obvious sense and calls allegorizing the Trinitarian texts irrational, and he holds that valid consequences of Scripture are themselves revealed. Gregory of Nyssa, by contrast, argues that Proverbs 8 is false if taken literally and so requires a hidden sense, while Novatian treats anthropomorphisms as accommodation to the people's capacity and Irenaeus reads the Levitical food laws figuratively. They also point to different guides when interpretation is contested: Irenaeus names the presbyters in apostolic succession, Waterland the consensus of the earliest Fathers when texts seem evenly matched, and Owen a special unction from Christ beyond knowing the letter. Augustine, unlike Irenaeus's insistence on a single rule of truth, welcomes several interpretations of a text so long as none contradicts sound doctrine.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: it contains a double account of the Saviour; that He was ever God, and is the Son, being the Father’s Word and Radiance and Wisdom; and that afterwards for us He took flesh of a Virgin, Mary Bearer of God, and was made man.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: For how far soever the lines be drawn and extended, from truth nothing can follow and ensue but what is true also; and that in the same kind of truth with that which it is derived and deduced from.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: a reasonable man will not receive any passage cited from this book, be it never so clear and intelligible at first sight, without examination and inspection; for assuredly there is some mystical contemplation underlying even those passages which seem manifest.

ans.text:
There is no secret code for reading the Bible about the Trinity. There are a handful of sensible, Bible-taught habits that keep readers from twisting it. Christians have leaned on these habits since the earliest debates about who Jesus is. Most of them are simply what careful readers do with any important book. A few come from the Bible's own example.

The first rule is to let the clear passages explain the unclear ones, and never the reverse. You cannot settle one puzzle by appealing to another puzzle. A dark parable, a line of poetry or a hard prophecy should not become the foundation of a teaching about God. Those foundations are laid by plain statements. Scripture plainly says there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). It plainly calls the Word God (John 1:1). It plainly says the Father, Son and Holy Spirit share one name (Matthew 28:19). A difficult verse should be read in a way that fits these, not used to overturn them. If everyone built doctrine on whatever obscure text they liked best, there would be as many religions as readers.

The second rule is to keep verses in their setting. A verse means what it means in its own context: who is speaking, to whom, and why. Think of a mosaic of a king made from precious stones. Someone could pry the stones loose and rearrange them into the picture of a dog. Then he could insist it is still the king's portrait because every stone is genuine. False teaching often works this way. It quotes real Bible words, but in an order and connection the Bible never gave them. Using the Bible's vocabulary does not make a system biblical. Peter warns that some parts of Paul's letters are hard to understand, and that the ignorant and unstable distort them, as they do the rest of the Scriptures (2 Peter 3:16).

The third rule is that what Scripture plainly implies is as true as what it states outright. Jesus himself reasons this way. Arguing with those who denied the resurrection, he points to God's words, "I am the God of Abraham," and draws the conclusion that the dead live (Matthew 22:31-32). The text did not say "there is a resurrection" in so many words, yet Jesus held his opponents responsible for what followed from it. In the same way, the Bible may not use the word "Trinity." But it teaches that there is one God. It also teaches that the Father is God, the Son is God and the Spirit is God, and that they are distinct from one another. If all of that is true, then they are one in being and three in person. Truth can only lead to truth, so a conclusion drawn rightly from revelation carries the authority of revelation.

The fourth rule is to know when the Bible speaks in pictures and when it speaks plainly. Scripture often uses human language about God. It speaks of his arm, his eyes, his regret, his coming down to see. God stoops to speak in ways we can grasp. The limits belong to us, not to him. Some books are also poetic by design. Proverbs opens by saying it will help readers understand proverbs, parables and riddles (Proverbs 1:6). So when Wisdom speaks in Proverbs 8 about being with the LORD at the beginning, we should not read it like a lab report. It cannot be used to prove that the Son is a created being.

The opposite mistake is just as dangerous. Some people call every clear statement about Christ's divinity a mere figure of speech. If "the Word was God" and "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30) can be waved away as metaphors, then nothing written can be pinned down at all. A good reader looks for the kind of writing each passage is. He does not turn plain statements into symbols just because their meaning is uncomfortable.

The fifth rule is to pay attention to how comparisons work. When Jesus says, "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36), he is not saying we become equal to God. He is giving us a pattern to imitate in our own creaturely way. When he compares himself to Jonah (Matthew 12:40), the likeness lies only in the three days. Jonah was not the Savior. So when Jesus prays that his disciples may be one as he and the Father are one (John 17:11), it does not follow that his oneness with the Father is only the kind of unity believers share. Words like "as" and "like" draw a parallel in some respect. They do not make two things identical. The same goes for small words like "from," "through" and "in." Scripture uses them freely as the occasion requires. They are not technical terms that rank the persons of the Trinity.

The sixth rule, and perhaps the most important, is to remember that the Bible speaks of Christ in two ways. He is eternally God the Son, the Father's Word and Wisdom. And for our sake he became truly human, born of Mary. Paul describes the one who was in the form of God taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5-8). Some verses speak of Jesus in his divine glory. Others speak of him in his humble human life: tired, hungry, growing in wisdom, saying "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). Both kinds are true of the one Christ. Many misreadings come from taking the second kind and forgetting the first. Christians may offer more than one explanation of a hard verse, as long as none of them makes the Son less than truly God.

This rule is not imposed on the Bible from outside. Jesus taught that the whole Old Testament points to him. On the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he explained what was written in all the Scriptures about himself (Luke 24:27). Prophecies were often riddles until they were fulfilled. Afterward, in the light of the cross and resurrection, they became clear.

What about when two readings of a verse seem evenly matched? Many Christians find help in how the earliest believers, those closest to the apostles, understood the faith they had received. Christians weigh this differently. Some give the church's long, shared reading real authority as a guide to interpretation. Others insist Scripture alone is the final judge, and treat early witnesses as valuable but correctable. Both sides agree that the Bible remains the rule. They also agree that a reading no faithful Christian ever held should make us very cautious.

That leads to the question of blame. If people who deny the Trinity quote the Bible, is the Bible at fault? No. A clear map is not to blame when someone holds it upside down. The fault lies with the reader, as Peter says, not with the Scripture. The Bible is so trustworthy that error can often be answered from the very passages its defenders appeal to.

Finally, right method is necessary but not enough. Knowing the words of a doctrine is not the same as knowing Christ. Paul says the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). John tells believers that they have an anointing from the Holy One (1 John 2:20). So we read carefully, humbly and prayerfully. We ask the same Spirit who inspired the Scriptures to open our eyes to the Son they reveal.

topics.title: How should Scripture's signs, figures and types be understood?
topics.cmp: Each question here was answered by a single author, so the authors never disagree on the same point. They do share an assumption: Scripture's signs and figures point past their surface to a spiritual or Christological meaning, and taking the letter alone is inadequate or even dangerous. Augustine works most theoretically, classing enigma as an obscure species of allegory and explaining the desire to know a sign's meaning from the mind's partial knowledge. He also offers a detailed Christological reading of Moses' rod as Christ's death and the whole Christ rising with the Church. Gregory of Nyssa grounds figurative reading in Paul's teaching that the Lord is the Spirit, and he argues that names like Curse, Sin or Leopard must be taken through conception, because read literally they would be blasphemous. Basil stresses God's teaching purpose, saying types and shadows gradually train weak eyes for the full light, while Owen (hyssop as Christ's promises) and Ambrose (Peter's threefold vision as signifying the Trinity, linked to baptism's threefold confession) apply typology to particular details rather than setting out a theory of it.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Of the Term ‘Enigma,’ And of Tropical Modes of Speech.
refs.quote: so every enigma is an allegory, but every allegory is not an enigma. What then is an allegory, but a trope wherein one thing is understood from another?

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: If the bodily veil of the words were removed, that which remains is Lord and life and Spirit, according to the teaching of the great Paul, and according to the words of the Gospel also.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and…
refs.quote: Just so the Law, having a shadow of things to come, and the typical teaching of the prophets, which is a dark utterance of the truth, have been devised means to train the eyes of the heart

ans.text:
Scripture's signs, figures and types should be read as real pointers that God built into his Word, most of them pointing to Christ. We read them with joy and care: we let the plain teaching of the Bible steer us, and we never let a picture overrule what the Bible says clearly.

The Bible itself teaches us to read this way. After his resurrection Jesus walked with two disciples, and "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself" (Luke 24:27). He took the bronze snake Moses raised in the wilderness as a picture of his own cross: "Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up" (John 3:14). Paul calls Adam "a pattern of the One to come" (Romans 5:14). He says the rock that gave Israel water "was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Hebrews calls the law "only a shadow of the good things to come" (Hebrews 10:1). A "type" is exactly this: a real person, event or object in Israel's history that God shaped to foreshadow something greater. It is a bit like a sketch an artist makes before painting the full picture.

Why did God speak this way at first? Think of someone who has been in a dark room for a long time. If you threw open the curtains at noon, they would be dazzled. It is kinder to let their eyes adjust. God dealt gently with his people in the same way. Through the sacrifices, the temple, the priests and the festivals, he trained their hearts to understand forgiveness, holiness and atonement. Then he showed the full light in his Son. The shadows were not mistakes. They were God's patient teaching.

Scripture also uses many figures of speech, and some are plain while others are dark. Paul's comparison in 1 Thessalonians 5, about not sleeping but staying awake and sober, is easy to grasp. Other sayings are riddles, like Proverbs 30:15 with the leech and its daughters. Some stay hidden until they are explained, as Paul explains Abraham's two sons as two covenants in Galatians 4. When we meet a saying like that, we sense that it means something we cannot yet see, and that sense is good. It stirs us to dig deeper, pray, and compare Scripture with Scripture.

Figures matter especially when the Bible speaks about God and Christ. Christ is called a Lion and a Lamb. Paul says God "made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf" (2 Corinthians 5:21), and that Christ became "a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). Read in a flat, literal way, some of these would sound shocking or even blasphemous. Read as figures, each one fixes our attention on a single truth. The lion speaks of his strength and kingship. The lamb speaks of his sacrifice. "Made sin" means he took our guilt and its penalty, not that he did anything wrong. The question to ask of any figure is: what point is this picture making?

Paul says the letter alone "kills, but the Spirit gives life," and that when someone turns to the Lord the veil is taken away (2 Corinthians 3:6, 16-17). He does not mean the words or the history are unimportant. He means that reading the Old Testament without Christ is like reading through a veil. When we turn to him, we see what it was about all along: the living Lord, who gives life by his Spirit. Jesus said, "The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life" (John 6:63).

What about readings that find the Trinity in threes, such as Peter's vision in Acts 10, which came three times? Some Christians have seen echoes of the Trinity in patterns like this. They point to that vision, to the threefold "Holy, holy, holy" of Isaiah 6, to Abraham's three visitors in Genesis 18, and to Peter's three affirmations of love after his three denials. Many believers find these echoes fitting and devotionally rich, because the one God who is Father, Son and Spirit is the author of all Scripture. Others are more cautious. They note that Acts explains the vision itself: God was teaching Peter not to call unclean what God has made clean, and that he shows no favoritism (Acts 10:15, 34-35). They also note that repetition in the Bible often simply signals that something is certain and urgent, as Joseph said of Pharaoh's doubled dream (Genesis 41:32).

A wise path holds both concerns together. The doctrine of the Trinity does not rest on number patterns. It rests on clear teaching. Jesus sends his disciples to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). The New Testament also plainly speaks of each as God while insisting there is one God. Once that is firmly in place, it is not wrong to notice that threefold patterns can call it to mind, much as baptism has often included a threefold confession of faith. But such readings are best offered as reflections, not as proofs.

So a few simple guidelines help. Start with the plain meaning of the passage in its setting. Let clearer passages explain darker ones. Look for Christ, because he is the center of the whole Bible. Never draw from a figure a teaching that contradicts what Scripture says plainly, and do not build a doctrine on a picture alone. Hold your more creative readings humbly. Finally, remember that even now "we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror" (1 Corinthians 13:12). The signs are given to lead us onward, until one day we see face to face the One they all point to.

topics.title: Why does the doctrine of the Trinity matter, and why keep it rather than Arian or Sabellian alternatives?
topics.cmp: Warfield and Waterland agree that neither Arianism nor Sabellianism can replace the doctrine of the Trinity, but they argue differently. Warfield appeals to Scripture together with the Christian consciousness of salvation, which kept searching the Scriptures until a valid Trinitarian formulation satisfied it. Waterland argues comparatively and cautiously: unanswered difficulties do not justify abandoning a well-grounded doctrine, one of the three schemes must be true, the rivals face greater difficulties, and only a strict demonstration could outweigh Scripture, the judgment of the primitive Church, and centuries of worship paid to Christ. Basil takes a different angle, defending the importance of precise theological terms on the ground that even tiny words like Yea and Nay can separate truth from falsehood, while Augustine alone addresses how the Trinity is known and loved: not as the number three but as God, loved now only by believing, with faith giving way to sight when God is seen face to face.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: Neither the Sabellian nor the Arian construction could meet and satisfy the data of the consciousness of salvation, any more than either could meet and satisfy the data of the Scriptural revelation.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
refs.quote: We love then in the Trinity, that it is God: but we never saw or knew any other God, because God is One; He alone whom we have not yet seen, and whom we love by believing.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Prefatory remarks on the need of exact investigation of…
refs.quote: what term in theology is so small but that the effect of its weight in the scales according as it be rightly or wrongly used is not great?

ans.text:
The Trinity matters because it is the truth about who God is, and because the God who saves us is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Every simpler alternative ends up losing either the real God or the real Savior.

The church confesses one God in three persons. There is one divine being, one "essence" (what God is), and three persons who share it fully: the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. They are not three gods, and they are not one person under three names. Christians did not invent this to make things complicated. They were driven to it by the Bible and by their own experience of being saved.

The two main alternatives each try to make God easier to grasp. One, often called the Arian view, says the Son is the first and greatest thing God ever made. He is glorious, but he is a creature. The other, often called the Sabellian view, says there is only one divine person who appears in three roles: Father in creation, Son in redemption, Spirit in the church. It is like one actor wearing three masks.

The first view cannot fit what Scripture says about Jesus. John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and John 1:3 says that through him all things were made. Something that made all things cannot itself be one of the things made. Thomas falls before the risen Jesus and calls him "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28), and Jesus accepts it. Hebrews 1:6 has the angels worshiping the Son. The Bible is fierce about worshiping God alone. So if the Son were only a creature, the church's worship of him would be idolatry. And Isaiah 43:11 says that the Lord alone is Savior. A creature, however exalted, cannot be the one who saves us.

The second view cannot fit the Bible either. At Jesus' baptism, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:17). That is not one actor changing costumes. The Son prays to the Father, is sent by the Father, and speaks of "the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). Real love and conversation pass between them. This is part of why Scripture can say "God is love" (1 John 4:8). Before there was any world to love, the Father loved the Son in the Spirit.

Ordinary Christian experience points the same way. Galatians 4:6 says God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, "Abba, Father!" When you pray, you come to the Father, through the Son who died for you, by the Spirit who moves you to pray. Take away the true divinity of the Son or the Spirit, and that prayer is no longer meeting God himself. Merge the three into one person, and the Son is no longer standing beside you as your go-between with the Father. Believers have long sensed that both alternatives leave the gospel hollow. That is why they kept searching the Scriptures until they could say clearly what they found there.

Some people think the arguments over this were fussing about words. But small words can carry huge weight. A single "yes" or "no" can be the difference between truth and a lie. The early debates turned on whether the Son is the same in being as the Father or only like him, and that small difference decides whether Jesus is God or a creature.
