Jesus himself said that not the smallest letter of God's word would pass away. So we should take care with the words we use about God.

It is true that the Trinity raises questions we cannot fully answer. How can three be one without being three gods? We should be honest about that. But you can have good reason to believe something without being able to answer every objection. Think of a doctor who trusts a treatment that works even though some of its workings are not yet understood. The real choice is not between a doctrine with difficulties and one without them. It is between this teaching and the alternatives. Those alternatives have far greater problems: they contradict plain passages of Scripture, and they make Christian worship either idolatrous or confused.

The church has confessed this faith from its earliest centuries and has worshiped Jesus as God all along. Before anyone asks us to stop worshiping Christ, they would need a truly overwhelming proof. Clever objections are not enough. No such proof has ever been given.

It also helps to remember what we actually love in the Trinity. It is not the number three. Anyone can hold up three fingers. What we love is that the Trinity is God: the Father who gave his Son, the Son who gave himself, the Spirit who gives us new life. We do not yet see this God with our eyes, so for now we love him by trusting what he has shown us.

That will not always be so. Paul says that now we see only a dim reflection, as in a mirror, but then we shall see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Faith is for the journey. One day it will give way to sight, and we will behold the very God we now believe in. Holding fast to the Trinity now is how we keep our eyes on the right God until that day.

title: Knowing God and His Incomprehensibility
desc: Whether and how God can be known through creation, reason, revelation and Christ, and the limits of the finite mind before the infinite divine essence.

topics.title: How can God be known: through creation, reason, or only through Christ and revelation?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that God's essence exceeds human comprehension and that full or saving knowledge of God comes through the Son and revelation. They differ sharply on how much creation and reason can yield. Irenaeus and Gregory of Nyssa grant a real natural knowledge: Irenaeus says implanted reason gives all creatures a perception that there is one God, as subjects know an unseen emperor, and Gregory says creation's order shows God's eternal power and godhead (Romans 1). Yet both bound it tightly. Irenaeus insists no one knows God without the Son and the Word. Gregory, with Novatian, argues that names and works signify God's operations, not his essence, so that knowing God's incomprehensibility is itself a kind of knowledge. Augustine is similarly apophatic (God is good without quality, great without quantity), but he alone stresses rising by the mind to eternal, unchangeable truth and by love and humility, and he distinguishes knowledge (scientia) of Christ's temporal acts from wisdom (sapientia) about the eternal Word, both reached in the one Christ. Owen goes furthest: creation shows God's power, goodness, wisdom and all-sufficiency but not his patience. Worldly wisdom, the bare letter of Scripture, and God's attributes considered apart from Christ give no saving or comforting knowledge and even produce terror or hardening, so all such knowledge lies only in Christ. Hippolytus grounds knowledge of the Trinity in Scripture alone rather than human reasoning. Waterland adds that technical Trinitarian terms add no new knowledge without new revelation.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For the Son is the knowledge of the Father; but the knowledge of the Son is in the Father, and has been revealed through the Son

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Here the soul makes an advance beyond the attainment of its natural capacities, is taught more than it had dreamed concerning God. For it learns that its Creator is God of God; it hears that the Word is God and was with God in the beginning.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: The design of these terms is not to enlarge our views, or to add any thing to our stock of ideas; but to secure the plain fundamental truth, that Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are all strictly divine

ans.text:
God can be known through all three, but not in the same way or to the same depth: creation and reason show us that God is, and something of what he is like, while only God's own word, above all in Jesus Christ, shows us who he truly is and how sinners can come home to him.

Start with creation. The Bible says plainly that the world points to its Maker. "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands" (Psalm 19:1). Paul goes further in Romans 1:20: God's "eternal power and divine nature" have been clearly seen, "being understood from His workmanship." Think of walking into a beautifully built house. You don't meet the builder, but you know someone skilled, careful and generous made it. In the same way, the order, beauty and sheer existence of the world tell us that it did not come from nowhere. Someone powerful, wise and good stands behind it. Paul made this case to people in Athens who had no Bible (Acts 17:24-28), and conscience adds its own witness, since people everywhere sense that some things are truly right and wrong (Romans 2:14-15).

Reason helps too, especially by clearing away wrong ideas. One of the most useful things the mind can learn is what God is not. He is not the sun, not the sky, not a very large person, not a mighty angel, not anything that changes or wears out. He is not good the way we are good, by borrowing goodness from somewhere else. He is goodness itself, so he can never become more or less good. Even our failure to grasp God fully teaches us something true: that he is greater than our minds can hold. That is not ignorance. It is a real kind of knowledge, the knowledge that we are dealing with the infinite God.

But there are limits. Seeing what someone does is not the same as knowing them. Watching leaves blow about tells you there is wind, but not what wind is. Creation tells us there is a mighty and wise Creator, but it cannot tell us his name, his heart toward sinners, or that he is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. No sunset or argument would ever lead you to the Trinity. That truth is known only because God has told us, chiefly by sending his Son and his Spirit.

There is a deeper problem as well. Romans 1 does not end with people happily learning about God from nature. It says they knew God but "neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him" (Romans 1:21). Sin bends our use of what we know. And even what we see clearly does not comfort us on its own. If you learn that God is holy and just, and you know you are not, that knowledge makes you want to hide, like Adam in the garden. If you see that God is patient, you may simply take advantage of it. Nature cannot tell a guilty person how to approach God in peace.

That is why the Bible points us to Christ. "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). Jesus says in John 14:6, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me." And in Matthew 11:27 he says that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Paul says that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). In Jesus we see God's justice, holiness, mercy and patience not as threats but as working together for our good. At the cross, sin is truly judged and sinners are truly forgiven. That is something creation could never show. It is wonderful to build a beautiful house, but even more wonderful to take a ruined one and restore it to greater glory than before. Redemption shows God's wisdom even more brightly than creation does.

The Holy Spirit is needed too. Paul says that only the Spirit of God knows the thoughts of God, and that the Spirit reveals them to us (1 Corinthians 2:10-12). The same God who said "Let light shine out of darkness" shines in our hearts "to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6). So knowing God truly is a gift of the whole Trinity: the Father makes himself known, through the Son, by the Spirit. Even our faith and love toward God are his gifts, not our achievements.

Sincere Christians have differed on how much reason can do on its own. Some hold that careful thinking can actually prove that God exists and work out some of his attributes, because Romans 1 says these things are "clearly seen." Others stress that sin so clouds the mind that such reasoning rarely leads anyone to God without his word, because the same chapter says people suppress the truth. Both sides agree on the main point: nature leaves us without excuse, but only Christ, made known in Scripture by the Spirit, leaves us with hope.

So don't set these against each other. Enjoy creation as a real window onto God's glory. Use your mind to think rightly about him. But come to know him as Father, and to know him as your God and your joy, by looking to Jesus. True wisdom, in the end, is not just knowing facts about God. It is trusting and worshiping him.

topics.title: Can the finite mind comprehend or rightly speak of the infinite God?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the finite mind cannot comprehend or define God's essence: Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Novatian, Augustine, Irenaeus and Bickersteth each say no, and Hilary and Gregory (with Novatian's argument that a God who could be conceived would be smaller than the mind containing Him) press this most insistently. Their grounds differ. Hilary argues from the limits of a created, dependent, time-bound reason and from God's indivisibility. Gregory argues from infinity (the unlimited cannot be comprehended or named), from our ignorance of our own soul and of the created order, from God's silence about His essence in the creed, and from the insurmountable gap between created and uncreated natures, which even angels cannot cross. This last point serves his polemic against the Eunomian claim to grasp the essence in a single term. Irenaeus and Bickersteth stress instead that God has made Himself knowable, so real but limited knowledge is available: that He is Creator, or what is sufficient for salvation. Novatian and Ambrose likewise allow knowledge of the invisible through visible works (Romans 1) and through careful analogy, provided it is not carnal, and Hilary similarly permits analogy only as a clue. Augustine's emphasis is distinctive: the mind must be purified and must hold by faith before it can understand, it is the best place to seek an image of the Trinity, and even speech that applies properly to God is admitted only hesitantly. Owen, Bickersteth and Gregory (on divine names that say what God is not, and Abraham's unknowing) direct the inquirer to reverent adoration, prayer, and adherence to Scripture's revelation rather than speculative scrutiny.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: it is not possible that that which is by nature infinite should be comprehended in any conception expressed by words

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For that which is “of” [ex] any one is either of his substance or of his power. Of his substance, as the Son, Who says: “I came forth of the Mouth of the Most High;” as the Spirit, “Who proceedeth from the Father;”

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: however far the limited mind of man might strain in the hazardous effort to define Him, the gap was not lessened between the finite nature which struggled and the boundless infinity that lay beyond its ken

ans.text:
No human mind can ever take the full measure of God, yet we can know Him truly and speak of Him rightly, because He has chosen to make Himself known. Both halves of that answer matter. If we forget the first, we shrink God down to our size. If we forget the second, we fall into a fog where nothing certain can be said about Him at all.

It helps to separate two ideas: comprehending and knowing. To comprehend something is to get your arms all the way around it, to grasp it completely, with nothing left over. To know something is to have a real and accurate grasp of it, even if only in part. A child can truly know the ocean by wading in it, feeling the waves and tasting the salt, without ever comprehending the ocean. Our knowledge of God is like that, only more so. What we know is real, but He is always more.

The Bible makes this clear. "Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised; His greatness is unsearchable" (Psalm 145:3). Through Isaiah, God says, "For My thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways My ways... For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways" (Isaiah 55:8-9). Paul, after pages of careful teaching in Romans, does not end with a neat summary. He breaks into praise at the depth of God's wisdom and knowledge, and confesses that His judgments cannot be searched out and His ways cannot be traced (Romans 11:33). Paul knew a great deal about God. That knowledge led him to wonder, not to a sense of having mastered his subject.

Why must it be so? God is infinite, without limits of any kind. We are finite. We had a beginning, we depend on Him for every breath, and our minds have edges. Whatever fits completely inside a limited mind must itself be limited. If we could hold God entirely in our thoughts or pin Him down in a definition, He would be smaller than our thoughts, and so would not be God. The gap between Creator and creature is not one that study or cleverness can close, because it is not a matter of how far we have gone but of what we are.

A simple exercise in humility helps here. We cannot even fully explain ourselves. How does your mind relate to your body? What exactly is a thought? Why do joy and grief live side by side in one heart? If we are a mystery to ourselves, we should not be surprised that the One who made us is beyond our grasp. Even the angels, who see far more than we do, cover their faces before Him.

But here is the good news. God has not left us guessing. Moses told Israel, "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever" (Deuteronomy 29:29). God has spoken in creation, in His word, and above all in His Son. "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). Jesus says that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him (Matthew 11:27). So our knowledge of God does not rest on our climbing up to Him. It rests on His coming down to us. That is why it can be both limited and completely trustworthy.

What about our words? When we call God good, wise, faithful, or Father, are we speaking accurately, or only making rough guesses? The church's answer is that these words are true of God, but God is these things in a fuller and higher way than any creature. When we say God is wise, we do not mean He is wise the way a clever grandmother is wise, only bigger. We mean that real wisdom is found in Him perfectly, and every bit of wisdom in creatures is a small reflection of His. In fact, the direction runs the other way from what we might assume. Paul says every family in heaven and on earth takes its name from the Father (Ephesians 3:14-15). God is not called Father because He resembles human fathers. Human fathers are called fathers because, at their best, they faintly resemble Him. Our words point truly, like a finger pointing at the moon. The finger is not the moon, but it is pointing at the right thing.

Thoughtful Christians have weighed this a little differently. Some stress that our words must keep the same core meaning when applied to God, or else Scripture would tell us nothing we could understand. Others stress that every word must be stretched and purified when used of God, or else we will picture Him as a larger version of ourselves. Both sides are guarding something real. Together they remind us that God's words about Himself are both genuinely meaningful and never exhaustive.

This matters especially when we come to the Trinity. Scripture teaches that there is one God, and that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each fully God, yet are not three gods. We cannot picture how this works, and every comparison we reach for falls short somewhere. That is not a sign that the teaching is confused. It is exactly what we should expect when finite minds meet the infinite God. A mystery is not a contradiction. It is a truth that goes deeper than we can see to the bottom of. The right question is not "Can I fully explain this?" but "What has God said about Himself?" We believe what He reveals, we say what Scripture says, and we refuse to fill in the gaps with clever guesses, especially guesses that make God tidier and smaller.

There is also a warning here. Staring straight at the sun does not help you see more. It blinds you. People who demand to see past what God has shown often end up losing even what they could have seen. The wise path is to receive gratefully what has been given and not grasp at what has not.

Knowing God is also not only a matter of the intellect. Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). Sin clouds our sight. Our hearts, attached to lesser things, tend to picture God in the shape of those things. So growth in knowing God goes hand in hand with faith, repentance, worship, and obedience. God gives light to those who walk in the light they already have.

Finally, our present knowledge is real but partial, and it will not always be this way. "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known" (1 Corinthians 13:12). Even in that day, we will not comprehend God as He comprehends Himself. We will always be creatures. But we will see Him clearly, and our many stumbling words will give way to one unending song of praise. Until then, the proper response to an infinite God is not frustration that we cannot master Him, but joy that He has made Himself known, and worship for the depths that remain.

topics.title: Can God be known from the created world and by natural reason?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Augustine, Hilary and Novatian all affirm that the created world bears witness to its Maker. Irenaeus argues that a made work points to its maker. Augustine holds that the universe proclaims an excellent Creator, perceived by the natural reason God gave us, and he reasons to God's attributes by ranking perfections: the living above the non-living, the unchangeable above the changeable. Hilary likewise reasons from the greatness and beauty of creatures to a Maker beyond all thought, and Novatian adds that all nature and even the unspoken human mind testify to the one God. They differ in how far such knowledge reaches. Augustine is the most confident about natural reason, while Irenaeus says God's immeasurable greatness cannot be known and that he is known instead through his love and his Word to those who obey. Hilary flatly denies that reason, philosophy or virtue can by its own power attain true knowledge of God, citing Moses, who did not know God until God revealed his name from the bush, and so insisting on revealed terms. Gregory of Nyssa takes a narrower, critical line: against Eunomius he rejects reasoning between God's being and his works as circular when both are equally unknown.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For even creation reveals Him who formed it, and the very work made suggests Him who made it, and the world manifests Him who ordered it.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: What Universal Nature Teaches Us Concerning God.
refs.quote: the whole nature of the universe itself which surrounds us, and to which we also belong, proclaims that it has a most excellent Creator, who has given to us a mind and natural reason

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The Creator of great things is supreme in greatness, of beautiful things in beauty. Since the work transcends our thoughts, all thought must be transcended by the Maker.

ans.text:
Yes, the created world really does tell us that God exists and something of what he is like, but it cannot tell us everything we need to know, and it cannot by itself bring us to know him as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Start with what the Bible plainly says. "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands" (Psalm 19:1). Paul goes further in Romans 1:20: "For since the creation of the world God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse." Notice what he says. God himself is invisible, but his power and his godhood can be seen in what he has made. And this is not knowledge kept for scholars. Paul says it is plain enough that no one can claim ignorance.

The reasoning behind this is simple. A made thing points to a maker. If you find a watch on a beach, you do not suppose the sand assembled it. In the same way, a universe that is ordered, lawful and full of life points beyond itself to someone who made and orders it. When Paul preached to people who had never read the Scriptures, he appealed to exactly this. He told them that God "has not left Himself without testimony" because he sends rain and fruitful seasons and fills people's hearts with food and gladness (Acts 14:17). In Athens he spoke of the God who made the world and everything in it, who gives all people life and breath, so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out and find him, though he is not far from any of us (Acts 17:24-28).

Creation also teaches us something about what God is like, and not only that he is. Think of it this way. Whoever makes great things must be greater than they are. Whoever makes beautiful things must be more beautiful still. The psalmist asks, "He who implants the ear, does He not hear? He who forms the eye, does He not see?" (Psalm 94:9). We can see that something living is greater than something lifeless. Something that thinks is greater than something that does not. Something lasting is greater than something that fades. So the One who made living, thinking creatures must himself be living and wise in the fullest way. He must be unchanging and everlasting, mighty, good and beautiful beyond anything he has made. This is why the Bible treats it as foolish to worship the sun, the stars, the wind or anything else in creation. These things are only signposts. The right response to a glorious sunset is not to bow to the sun but to praise the One who made it.

There is also a witness inside us. Paul says that people who never received God's law still show its demands written on their hearts, with their conscience bearing witness (Romans 2:14-15). Deep down, human beings know they are not their own makers and that they answer to someone. All of creation, from the angels to the seas, honours the one God who made it. And the human heart, even when it will not admit it, is aware of him too.

But there are real limits, and they matter.

First, God is greater than anything we can measure. "Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised; His greatness is unsearchable" (Psalm 145:3). Creation shows us that God is, and that he is mighty and wise. It cannot show us the full depth of who he is, any more than a painting tells you everything about the painter. We see his fingerprints, not his face. Even the beauty we glimpse in the world is far beyond our understanding, and the beauty of the One who made it is greater still.

Second, sin gets in the way. Right after saying that God's power is clearly seen, Paul says that people "suppress the truth by their wickedness" (Romans 1:18). Although they knew God, they did not honour him or give thanks, and their thinking became futile. They turned to idols instead (Romans 1:21-23). So the problem is not that the evidence is weak. The problem is that we do not want to follow where it leads. This is why Paul can say that "the world through its wisdom did not know Him" (1 Corinthians 1:21). Clever reasoning on its own has never brought humanity home to God.

Third, there are things about God that creation simply cannot tell us. Nature can tell you there is a powerful and wise Creator. It cannot tell you his name. It cannot tell you that he forgives sinners, or that he sent his Son to die and rise again. And it cannot tell you that the one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. These truths come only because God chooses to make himself known. Jesus says, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him" (Matthew 11:27). Moses is a good example. He was trained in all the learning of Egypt. Yet he came to know God personally only when God spoke to him from the burning bush and told him his name (Exodus 3). In the same way, we must let God tell us who he is. When we speak about God, especially about the Trinity, we should stay close to the words he has given us in Scripture, and not invent ideas of our own.

Sincere Christians have weighed these points a little differently. Some put great weight on reasoned arguments for God's existence. They point out that the Bible itself appeals to creation and conscience, and that such arguments can clear away obstacles to faith. Others are more cautious. They stress how badly sin bends our thinking, and they note that in Romans 1 the knowledge of God from nature mainly serves to leave people "without excuse." They think that real knowledge of God begins with his word. Both sides agree on the main thing. Creation truly points to God, and saving knowledge of God comes through his revelation in Christ.

Two misunderstandings are worth avoiding. One is to think that because God can be known from nature, we do not really need the Bible or Jesus. A signpost is a good thing, but it is not the destination, and nature cannot tell us how a sinner can be made right with God. The other mistake is to think that the world tells us nothing at all, as if faith had to ignore the evidence around us. The Bible never says that. It invites us to look up at the sky, to consider the rain and the harvest, and to give thanks. As Hebrews 11:3 puts it, by faith we understand that the universe was formed at God's command.

So the believer can enjoy the world with open eyes. The mountains, the stars and the gift of a mind able to wonder at them all speak of a Creator who is great, wise and good. And when we open the Scriptures, we learn that this same Creator is the Father who sent his Son and gives his Spirit, so that we might know him not just as Maker but as our God.

topics.title: Is philosophical knowledge of God superior to Christian faith?
topics.cmp: Augustine and Irenaeus agree that intellectual knowledge of God, however genuine, does not outrank faith and love, and both locate the danger in pride rather than in knowledge itself. Augustine carries most of the topic. Using the image of the homeland seen from afar and the 'ship of wood', he argues that only humble faith in the crucified Mediator carries a person to God. He adds that the philosophers' grasp of God's unchangeable substance gave them no insight into temporal order, the course of the ages, or the resurrection of the flesh, because they did not glorify God (echoing Romans 1) and lacked the angelic revelation granted to the pious fathers. His answers on the mind's judgment of corporeal images, illustrated by an arch at Carthage and the walls of Carthage and Alexandria, show that he grants the mind real access to unchangeable rules of eternal truth above itself, so his complaint is not against rational vision as such. Irenaeus works instead from exegesis of 1 Corinthians 8:1. He insists that Paul does not condemn true knowledge of God but only a pretended knowledge that puffs people up, draws them from God's love, and leads them to posit an imperfect Creator. His target is a specific heretical claim to perfection rather than the pagan philosophers Augustine addresses.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: They are Proud Who Think They are Able, by Their Own…
refs.quote: But of what use is it for the proud man, who on that account is ashamed to embark upon the ship of wood, to behold from afar his country beyond the sea?

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: not that he meant to inveigh against a true knowledge of God, for in that case he would have accused himself

ans.text:
No. Careful thinking can catch real glimpses of God, but it cannot bring anyone home to Him, and it is not a higher road than simple trust in Christ crucified.

The Bible says honest reasoning can learn true things about God. Paul writes that "since the creation of the world God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship" (Romans 1:20). Thoughtful people outside Israel and the church have reasoned that there must be a God who is eternal, who does not change, and on whom everything else depends. Think of how you judge a building beautiful, or an argument sound, or an act unfair. You are measuring things against a standard of truth and goodness that sits above your own mind. You did not invent it and you cannot change it. That points to God, and Christians need not deny it.

But this knowledge has two serious limits.

The first is a limit of content. Reason can work out what God must always be. It cannot work out what God has freely chosen to do. No amount of reflection on an unchanging God will tell you that the Son would become a man, die on a Roman cross, and rise again. It will not tell you that our bodies will be raised and the world made new. These are not timeless truths waiting to be deduced. They are acts of God in history, and promises about a future no one has seen. We can know them only if God tells us, which He did through the prophets and finally through His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). The same goes for the Trinity. That the one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not something we figured out. We know it because God showed Himself in the sending of the Son and the pouring out of the Spirit. On these matters the humble believer who has listened to God's word knows more than the brilliant thinker who has not.

The second limit is deeper. It is a limit of the heart. Paul goes straight on to say that "although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him" (Romans 1:21), and their thinking became dark. Knowing about God is not the same as being reconciled to Him. Picture someone standing on a cliff and seeing, far across the sea, the country where he belongs. He knows it is there. He may describe it well. But he is too proud to step into the plain wooden boat that could carry him across. Another person cannot see the far shore at all. Yet he has climbed into the boat, and the boat is taking him there. That boat is the cross. "For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know Him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe" (1 Corinthians 1:21). The proud thinker sees and stays put. The humble believer trusts and arrives. Jesus defines eternal life as knowing "the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). This is a personal knowing that comes through the Mediator, not through cleverness.

Does this mean Christians should distrust knowledge? Some read Paul's words "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Corinthians 8:1) that way. But Paul was no enemy of knowing God. He prays that believers would grow "in the knowledge of God" (Colossians 1:10). He counts everything loss compared to knowing Christ (Philippians 3:8). He would be condemning himself if he meant all knowledge is bad. His target is a puffed-up kind of knowing. That is the person who thinks his insight puts him above others, or above the God who made him, and who drifts away from love. He adds at once that "the one who loves God is known by God" (1 Corinthians 8:3). True knowledge of God humbles us and draws us into love. False knowledge swells us up and leaves us cold.

So faith is not the poor cousin of philosophy, a crutch for those who cannot think. Nor is faith opposed to thinking. Christians are free, even encouraged, to use their minds to understand what they believe more deeply. But the order matters. We receive God's word in faith, through Christ and His cross, and then we seek to understand. Even then we see only "a dim reflection" for now, waiting for the day we will see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). The greatest mind that refuses the cross is still far from home. The simplest believer who clings to it is already on the way.

topics.title: Can God's existence be demonstrated a priori?
topics.cmp: Whether God's existence as first cause can be proved from prior grounds, and whether necessity of existence can be the cause of God's being.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: The eaistence of ὦ first cause is demonstrable, a priori: as it lies under these terms, it seems reducible to case the second; as being sound without sense. But resolve it into this; There is a cause prior to the first; and then the irepugnancy appears.

ans.text:
No. In the strict sense, God's existence cannot be proved "a priori," because there is nothing prior to God from which such a proof could start. We can, however, reason toward God from the world He has made, and the Bible encourages us to.

The phrase needs a little unpacking. To prove something "a priori" means to prove it from what comes before it: from its causes or grounds. We know why water boils because we know the heat that causes it. To prove something "a posteriori" means to reason backward from its effects. We see smoke and conclude there is a fire. The question is whether God can be proved the first way, by pointing to something that stands behind Him and explains Him.

The Bible's answer is that nothing stands behind God. He is the first cause of everything else. Paul writes, "For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things" (Romans 11:36). When God reveals His name to Moses as "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14), He is telling us that He simply is. He did not receive His being from anyone. If someone claimed to prove the first cause from a cause before it, they would really be saying there is something earlier than the first. That contradicts itself, like talking about the step before the first step.

Some people try a subtler route. They say that God exists because He exists necessarily, as if "necessity" were a deeper ground that explains God and holds Him up. That gets things backward. Necessity is not a thing standing behind God. It describes how God exists: He cannot fail to be, and He depends on nothing. A description belongs to the one it describes. It cannot come before him and cause him. Think of a person's honesty. It describes the person; it did not create them. In the same way, God's necessary existence is a truth about God, not a foundation underneath Him. Scripture says God is not served by human hands "as if He needed anything," and that He "gives everyone life and breath and everything else" (Acts 17:25). He is the ground of all things, and nothing is the ground of Him.

None of this means faith is irrational or that Christians cannot give reasons. The Bible points us to the other kind of reasoning, from effects back to their source. "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands" (Psalm 19:1). Paul says that God's "eternal power and divine nature" have been "clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship" (Romans 1:20). The order, beauty and very existence of the world point to a Maker, as a house points to a builder. These arguments do not put anything above God. They begin with what He has made and rise toward Him.

Sincere Christians have disagreed about some arguments that start from the very idea of God rather than from the world. One example says that a greatest possible being must exist. Some believers find these arguments sound and helpful. They reason that if God is truly the necessary being, careful thought about what that means should show He must exist. Others doubt them. They point out that such arguments can seem to move from our ideas to reality too quickly, and that the Bible usually directs us to creation and to God's own self-revelation. Either way, even the defenders of these arguments do not claim to have found a cause behind God. At most, they claim to have shown from what God is that He cannot fail to be.

This matters for the Trinity as well. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit share the one divine being, and that being depends on nothing outside itself. The Son is "begotten" of the Father, meaning He eternally comes from the Father as a son shares his father's nature. That is not a case of something prior causing God to exist. It is the eternal life of the one God, who has no beginning and no source outside Himself.

So we do not explain God by something greater. We know Him because He has made Himself known, in creation and supremely in His Son. That is why worship, not proof, is the fitting end of our thinking: "Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things" (Revelation 4:11).

topics.title: Can creatures see God, and how can Scripture say both that God was seen and that no one can see Him and live?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Augustine, Hilary and Novatian agree that God in His own nature cannot be seen or grasped by creatures. They also agree that some real knowledge or sight of Him is still possible, but they explain this in different ways. Irenaeus distinguishes respects: in His greatness and glory the incomprehensible Father is unseen, while in His love He is known through His Word and grants Himself to be seen by those who love Him, for what is impossible for men is possible for God. Novatian instead resolves Scripture's tension by distinguishing persons: the God seen by Abraham was the Son, who descends and so is seen, while the Father has never been seen. Hilary, by contrast, treats the Son as equally ineffable with the Father, because an invisible Image is as beyond our grasp as its original. Augustine stresses that knowing God is a matter of the mind, not bodily eyes, and that in this life we see only through a mirror and enigma, namely the image of the Trinity in our own minds, until face-to-face vision after death, which he also links to dying to carnal affections; on the separate point of God's own perception, Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine agree that God does not perceive through divided senses but is at once sight, hearing and understanding.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How the Apostle Says that God is Now Seen by Us Through…
refs.quote: in a glass nothing is discerned but an image. We have endeavored, then, so to do; in order that we might see in some way or other by this image which we are, Him by whom we are made, as by a glass.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For even as the Father is ineffable because He is Unbegotten, so is the Son ineffable because He is the Only-begotten, since the Begotten is the Image of the Unbegotten.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of…
refs.quote: Whence it may be understood that it was not the Father who was seen, seeing that He never was seen; but the Son, who has both been accustomed to descend, and to be seen because He has descended.

ans.text:
Yes, creatures can truly see God, but never in the way we see a tree or a face across the room, and never so fully that we take in all that He is. The Bible holds both truths together. In one sense God is invisible and beyond us. In another He has shown Himself, and He promises that His people will one day see Him face to face.

Start with what God is. Jesus says in John 4:24 that "God is Spirit." He has no body, no size, no shape, no colour. Our eyes are made to see physical things, so they simply have nothing to land on when it comes to God's own being. This is why Paul speaks of God as the one who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see (1 Timothy 6:16). That is not because God is hiding. It is because He is greater than anything eyes were built to see. To know God has always been less like looking and more like coming to understand, trust and love Him with the heart and mind.

The same is true in reverse. When the Bible speaks of "the eyes of the LORD" or His "ear," it is speaking in a picture, the way we would to a child. God does not gather information through separate senses, one thing by sight and another by hearing, and then put it together. He simply knows. All of Him knows all things at once, perfectly and immediately. As Hebrews 4:13 puts it, nothing in all creation is hidden from His sight. We see God dimly and in part; He sees us completely.

So how can Scripture say people saw Him? Abraham welcomed the LORD at his tent (Genesis 18). After wrestling through the night, Jacob said, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared" (Genesis 32:30). Exodus 33:11 says the LORD spoke with Moses face to face, as a man speaks with his friend. Yet a few verses later God tells that same Moses, "you cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live" (Exodus 33:20), and lets him see only His back as He passes by.

The Bible is not contradicting itself here. When God appeared to Abraham or Jacob, He really was present and really was seen, but He showed Himself in a form He chose, fitted to what human beings could bear. It is a little like the sun. You can see sunlight on a field, feel its warmth and know the sun is real and present. But you cannot stare into the sun itself without being blinded. Moses was given real meetings with God, closer than almost anyone. What he could not have in this life was the full, unveiled sight of God's glory.

Many Christians through the centuries have gone a step further. They point to John 1:18: "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known." From this they conclude that when God appeared in the Old Testament, it was the Son, the eternal Word, who came near, since it has always been His role to make the invisible Father known. Others are more cautious. They agree the Son is the one who reveals the Father, but say the Old Testament does not tell us which person of the Trinity appeared each time, and that we should simply say the one God showed Himself. Both views agree on the main point. God made Himself seen without ever ceasing to be the invisible God.

That main point comes to its fullest in Jesus. The Son is called "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). When Philip asked Jesus to show them the Father, Jesus answered, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Even here we should be careful. The disciples' eyes saw a human body. What they came to know through that body was God Himself. The Son is God just as the Father is, so He is just as far beyond our full grasp as the Father. In His divine nature He is no more visible than the Father. But by becoming man He opened a way for us to know God truly. In other words, God remains unknowable in His greatness, but He is truly knowable in His love.

Why, then, can no one see God's face and live? Part of the answer is that we are mortal and sinful, and the full glory of the holy God is more than this frail, fallen life can hold. Isaiah, seeing a vision of the Lord, cried out that he was ruined (Isaiah 6:5). But there is another side to it. To see God fully, we must pass through a kind of death. The old, mortal life has to give way to the resurrection life. Even now, the more truly we come to know God, the more we die to sin and to the pull of the world. And at the end, God will raise us and make us able to see what we cannot see now.

That is the Christian hope. Jesus promises, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). John writes that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, "for we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2). Revelation 22:4 says His servants will see His face.

Paul describes the difference between now and then in 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see only a dim reflection, as in a mirror; but then we will see face to face." Ancient mirrors were polished metal, and the image was real but blurred. In this life we know God through reflections: through Scripture, through creation, through Christ's work in us, even through the way we ourselves were made in His image. These are true glimpses, but they are dim. Then the mirror will be set aside.

One more caution is worth adding. Even in heaven, seeing God face to face will not mean measuring Him or getting to the bottom of Him. God is infinite and we will always be creatures. The sight of God will be clear, real and joyful, but it will never run out. That is not a disappointment. It means there will always be more of God to know and to love.

topics.title: How can we know and love God, and righteousness, without seeing them?
topics.cmp: Augustine supplies nearly every answer on this topic, and his answers agree with one another throughout. We love a righteous man like Paul not for his bodily human nature but for his righteous mind. We love that mind through an unchangeable form of righteousness that we behold within, or above, ourselves in the truth. Even the unrighteous must already know righteousness in this inward, non-bodily way in order to love it and wish to become righteous, yet beholding it does not make anyone righteous; that requires cleaving to the form by love. His grounds are mainly philosophical and introspective: righteousness is a beauty of the mind, invisible to bodily sense, so knowledge of it cannot come from outside. He also draws on Scripture ("owe no man anything but to love one another"), and he ties the whole process to seeing God, in whom the form of righteousness is beheld more clearly the more ardently it is loved. John Owen, answering only whether God's righteousness is known by nature, likewise affirms a natural, universal knowledge of righteousness, but on different grounds and with a different emphasis. He appeals to Scripture (Abraham's "shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" and sinners knowing that evildoers deserve death) and stresses the anxious question of what righteousness can let a person stand before God's judgment, rather than Augustine's account of loving an inward form.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Our Love of the Righteous is Kindled from Love Itself of…
refs.quote: But we do not believe that the ministers of God ought so to live because we have heard it from any one, but because we behold it inwardly within ourselves, or rather above ourselves, in the truth itself.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: This all men are persuaded of, that God is a most righteous God; (that is a natural notion of God which Abraham insisted on, Gen. xviii. 25, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?”)

ans.text:
We can know and love God without seeing Him because He has already made Himself known to us: in the sense of right and wrong He has placed in every heart, and above all in Jesus Christ, His Son, by the Holy Spirit. Faith takes hold of that real, though partial, knowledge, and love grows from it.

Start with a simple truth. We cannot love something we know nothing about. Nobody longs for a food they have never heard of. So when the Bible says, "Though you have not seen Him, you love Him" (1 Peter 1:8), it does not mean we love a blank. It means we love Someone we truly know in part, even though we do not yet see Him with our eyes.

Righteousness, or goodness, helps us see how this works. Think of someone you deeply admire for their goodness, perhaps a godly grandmother now with the Lord, or the apostle Paul. What exactly do you love in them? Not their height or the color of their hair. You love their faithfulness, their honesty, their self-giving love. None of these things can be seen with the eyes. You can see a kind act, but you could never recognize it as kind unless you already had some idea of what kindness is.

Where does that idea come from? Not from memory of something seen, the way you remember a town you once visited. Not from hearsay either, the way you might picture a faraway city you have only read about and perhaps picture it wrongly. When you think about what it means to be fair or faithful, you are not imagining something absent. You are recognizing something true and real, and when someone explains it well, others recognize it too. Paul says that even people without the Bible "show that the work of the Law is written on their hearts" (Romans 2:15). Abraham could appeal to it when he asked, "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25). He knew, and he knew God knew, what "right" means.

That standard of goodness is not something we invented, and it does not change with our moods. Suppose you admired a person and later learned he was a fraud. Your opinion of him changes, but goodness itself has not changed. In fact, your disappointment shows that what you loved all along was the goodness you thought you saw in him. That steady, unchanging goodness is not a thing floating above God. It comes from God Himself, who is good, righteous and true. So every time we love what is truly good, we are already, in a faint way, reaching toward Him.

But seeing what is good does not make us good. Most of us can describe a righteous life far better than we live one. Knowing the shape of goodness is like seeing a mold; you only take its shape if you are pressed into it. We become righteous only by clinging to goodness in love, and the sad truth is that, on our own, we love it too little to be changed. This is why we need the gospel. God does not leave us admiring a standard we cannot reach. Christ, the righteous One, gives Himself to us, and "God's love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us" (Romans 5:5). The Spirit gives us a new love for what we could only admire before.

The same is true of God Himself. We do not see Him face to face yet. "No one has ever seen God," John writes, "but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). Faith is not guessing in the dark. It is trusting what God has shown of Himself, so that He who is believed but not yet seen can be hoped for and loved. And as we love Him more, we come to know Him more clearly and more calmly.

There is a real danger here, and it is worth naming gently. When we love Someone we cannot see, we can easily make up a God to suit ourselves, a picture built from our wishes or fears. Loving that picture is loving something false. That is why our faith must be tied to how God has actually revealed Himself: in Scripture, and supremely in Jesus. The God we love must be the God who is, not the God we would have designed.

John adds a surprising test. "Anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen" (1 John 4:20). Part of the reason is simple: God is love, so the person who will not love the neighbor in front of him is shutting out the very love that God is. "If we love one another, God remains in us" (1 John 4:12). Loving others is not a way of earning a glimpse of God; it is the life of those in whom God already dwells, and it clears the eyes of the heart to know Him better.

Knowing about many things is useful and good, but it can puff us up. Knowledge that serves love builds us up. So we keep learning, keep believing, and keep loving, knowing that our sight is partial for now. As Paul puts it, now we see dimly, as in a mirror, but one day we will see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). The love that begins in faith will end in sight.

topics.title: Must we know God's essence for faith and worship to be valid?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa answers both questions about God's essence and argues that it cannot be known. Worship is still valid, because we know God's glory precisely through reason's failure to comprehend His infinite greatness. Christ's rebuke falls on those who confine God within limited conceptions, not on those who confess His infinity. He supports this from Paul: if God's judgments, ways and promised goods surpass human search, the Godhead itself is all the more unapproachable. Augustine addresses a different but related point, arguing from the example of the virgin birth that faith depends on general notions we truly understand (virgin, birth, a proper name) rather than on unknown particulars such as Mary's face. The two do not contradict each other, but they differ in emphasis: Gregory turns unknowability itself into a form of knowing and a ground of reverence, while Augustine stresses that faith rests on genuinely known generic concepts, so ignorance of details does not make it feigned.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: we know the loftiness of the glory of Him Whom we worship, by the very fact that we are not able by reasoning to comprehend in our thoughts the incomparable character of His greatness

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
refs.quote: It is allowable, then, in this case to say without violation of the faith, perhaps she had such or such a countenance, perhaps she had not: but no one could say without violation of the Christian faith, that perhaps Christ was born of a virgin.

ans.text:
No. Our faith and worship do not depend on fully understanding God's essence, meaning what God is in His very being, deep down. What they depend on is knowing God truly, as He has made Himself known. Those are two different things, and the difference matters.

Think about ordinary life. You warm your hands at a fire, drink water, and step into the sunlight. You use them well every day. Yet very few people could explain what fire or light really is at the deepest level, and even the experts keep finding new puzzles. Someone who simply cooks dinner over a flame is no worse off than a scientist who studies combustion. We know created things as far as we need them for living, and not knowing their inner nature costs us nothing. If that is true of a candle flame, it is far more true of the God who made it.

The Bible is honest about this. Paul ends a long passage on God's plan with a burst of wonder in Romans 11:33. He praises the depth of God's riches, wisdom and knowledge, and says His judgments cannot be searched out and His ways cannot be traced. Think about what that means. If we cannot get to the bottom of God's decisions and His dealings with us, we certainly cannot get to the bottom of God Himself. Paul elsewhere says God dwells in unapproachable light (1 Timothy 6:16). Isaiah 55:9 says His thoughts are higher than ours as the heavens are higher than the earth.

Someone might worry about Jesus' words to the Samaritan woman: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know" (John 4:22). Does that condemn Christians who admit they cannot grasp God's essence? No. Jesus was not faulting people for failing to comprehend the infinite. He was pointing out that the Samaritans had turned away from what God had actually revealed. True worship receives God as He has shown Himself. In fact, confessing that God is greater than our minds can hold is part of knowing Him rightly. The real danger runs the other way. It is shrinking God down to a size we think we have mastered. A god we could fully explain would not be God.

This does not leave our faith vague or guesswork. God has spoken plainly about who He is and what He has done. Our faith rests on things we really do understand. Take the virgin birth. We do not know what Mary looked like, and it makes no difference. But we know what a virgin is and what it means to be born. So we can confess with certainty that Christ was born of a virgin. A believer can shrug about the color of Mary's eyes. No believer can say "perhaps" about the virgin birth itself. The same is true of the Trinity. Scripture tells us clearly that there is one God, and that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each truly God. We cannot picture how this can be, but we know what we are confessing and whom we are worshiping.

This is also why the Bible does not chase questions about God's inner substance. It is not that such questions are forbidden to wonder about. It is that they are not what we need. Moses put it well: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever" (Deuteronomy 29:29). Scripture gives us what we need for life with God. It shows us His character, His promises, His works, and above all His Son.

And that is where real knowledge of God is found. Jesus prays, "Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). This is the knowing of a child who trusts a father. It is not the knowing of a scientist who has taken something apart. We can know God truly, love Him, and worship Him in spirit and truth, while still bowing before a greatness we will never exhaust. Even in eternity we will not run out of reasons to praise Him.

topics.title: Can the human mind comprehend the Son's generation and the mystery of Christ?
topics.cmp: Hilary of Poitiers, Irenaeus of Lyons, Gregory of Nyssa and John Owen all answer no: neither the Son's generation, nor His essence, nor His glory, nor even the power behind His known words and deeds can be grasped by the human mind. Irenaeus and Hilary rest this most directly on Scripture's 'Who shall declare His generation?' and the claim that only the Father and Son know it, with Irenaeus adding that not even angels understand it and turning the point polemically against heretics who 'describe the indescribable.' Owen likewise argues from Scripture (Job 11, Proverbs 30), and he speaks of the Son's glory and majesty rather than His generation. Gregory of Nyssa argues more philosophically: bodily generation offers no common ground for the divine, 'generate' and 'ungenerate' are contradictories with no middle degree, and the Son's essence is known only proportionately through His works. Hilary differs in emphasis from the others: he weighs analogies like the seal, granting them partial use, and insists that devout effort to penetrate the mystery profits the seeker. He also holds that divine study lets believers refute the claim that birth implies prior non-existence, while finally resting in faith in John's words and the bare certainty of the birth.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: no man understands that production, or generation, or calling, or revelation, or by whatever name one may describe His generation, which is in fact altogether indescribable.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The mind of men is powerless with the ordinary resources of unaided reason to grasp the idea of an eternal birth, but they attain by study of things Divine to the apprehension of mysteries which lie beyond the range of common thought.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: In the glory of this majesty he dwells in light inaccessible. We “cannot by searching find out the Almighty unto perfection:

ans.text:
No, not fully. We can truly know that the Son is begotten of the Father, because God has told us so, but how that happens lies beyond what any human mind can take in. The same is true of the glory of Christ and of all He said and did. We can know Him, trust Him and love Him. We cannot get to the bottom of Him.

Start with the word "begotten." When the Bible calls Jesus the Father's "one and only Son" (John 1:14, 3:16), and when the creeds say He is "begotten, not made," they mean that the Son comes from the Father and shares exactly what the Father is. He is not a creature God made, the way a carpenter makes a chair. He is a Son, the way a son has his father's own nature. Hebrews 1:3 puts it this way: "The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature."

This begetting is eternal. It did not happen at some moment long ago. There was never a time when the Father was without His Son. John 1:1 says that "in the beginning" the Word already "was," and was with God, and was God.

That is where our understanding hits a wall. Every birth we have ever seen happens in time. It involves two parents, a body, a pregnancy, growth and change, and a before and after. None of that applies to God. So we cannot reason from ordinary births to the Son's birth, as if it were a bigger version of the same thing.

A common mistake goes like this: "If the Son was born, there must have been a time before He existed." That would be true of us. It is not true of God, who lives outside time. The word "begotten" tells us something true, that the Son is from the Father and of the same nature. But we must leave behind everything in the word that belongs only to creatures.

Jesus Himself marks the limit. In Matthew 11:27 He says, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." The inner life between Father and Son is known fully only to them. We know what they have chosen to show us, and that is real knowledge. But it is not complete knowledge.

Many Christians have also turned to Isaiah 53:8, which older translations rendered "Who shall declare His generation?" In the original setting the verse speaks of the suffering Servant and his descendants, so it is not a direct statement about eternal begetting. Still, the wonder it expresses fits well: who could ever fully explain where He comes from?

It helps to separate two kinds of knowing. Think of standing on a beach. You really do touch the ocean, but you could never hold the whole ocean in your hands. In the same way, we can truly come to know God, but we can never take Him in completely.

This is why every picture of the Son's birth falls short. Christians have compared it to light shining from the sun, or to a seal pressed into wax, which leaves its whole image behind. These pictures help in one way. They show that everything the Father is appears in the Son.

But they also mislead if pushed too far. A seal and the wax are made of different stuff. The seal is stronger and the wax is weaker. Someone has to do the pressing. None of that is true of the Father and the Son, who share one and the same divine nature with no difference in strength or rank. Use the pictures for the one point they make, then let them go.

The same care applies to the words "begotten" and "unbegotten." The Father is unbegotten, meaning He comes from no one. The Son is begotten, meaning He comes from the Father. These two words do not describe the top and middle of a ladder, as though the Son were a halfway being, less than the Father but more than a creature. They are simply opposites, like "asleep" and "awake," with nothing in between. They tell us how Father and Son are related, not that one is more God than the other. The Son is fully God, just as the Father is.

What goes for His origin also goes for His glory. Job 11:7 asks, "Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty?" Proverbs 30:4 asks about God, "What is His name, and what is the name of His Son?" Paul says God dwells in "unapproachable light" (1 Timothy 6:16). He prays that we would know "the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge" (Ephesians 3:19).

Notice that Paul prays for us to know something that surpasses knowledge. We can grow in knowing Christ forever and never come to the end of Him.

The same holds for Christ's earthly life. We know what He did: He turned water into wine, calmed the storm, raised Lazarus, died and rose again. These are real events, not myths. But how the eternal Son became a baby in Mary's womb, or how a word from His mouth stilled the sea, stays beyond us. The facts are clear. The divine power behind them is a mystery.

None of this means faith is vague or that anything goes. Mystery is not contradiction. It is not an excuse to stop thinking either. God has told us plainly that the Son is eternally from the Father, that He is truly God, and that He became truly man for us. Those truths we can confess with confidence. Thinking hard about them is worthwhile, and it deepens our faith even when we never reach the bottom.

What God asks is not that we master the mystery but that we receive it. John 1:18 says, "the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known." We know God because the Son came to show Him to us.

The right response to what is beyond us is not frustration but worship, like Paul's in Romans 11:33: "O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!"

topics.title: How does sin blind the mind to God, and can learning cure it?
topics.cmp: John Owen and Edward Henry Bickersteth agree that sin damages the human capacity to know God. Owen grounds this in the curse for sin: the loss of Adam's original knowledge, the blindness Scripture ascribes to people in their natural state, and the dread of God's presence that came only after the fall through guilt. Bickersteth instead speaks diagnostically, saying the plague of sin impairs our perceptive faculties. He adds that sin is radical and universal, citing the Pauline 'all have sinned', and that the natural heart finds revelations of its own corruption distasteful. On the remedy their emphases differ. Owen argues at length that learning cannot cure the darkness because it is a penal curse that only Christ, made a curse for us, can remove, and that greater ability without Christ only strengthens enmity against God. Bickersteth says nothing about learning and stresses instead the posture of the inquirer: laying aside pride and prejudice to come to God's word humbly as a little child.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: Whatever we come short in of the state of the first man in innocence, whether in loss of good or addition of evil, it is all of the curse for sin.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: to reflect that the plague, the diagnosis of which we would learn, itself impairs our perceptive faculties. Here then, let us humble ourselves as a little child.

ans.text:
Sin darkens the mind toward God the way a cataract clouds an eye: the light is still shining, but we can no longer see it clearly. Learning, however good, cannot remove that cloud. Only God can, through Jesus Christ and by his Spirit.

The Bible does not treat our trouble knowing God as a simple shortage of information. It traces it back to the fall. Adam and Eve walked with God in the garden and knew him without fear or confusion. After they sinned, something broke. They hid. Since then, Scripture describes people in their natural state as being in darkness. Paul says they are "darkened in their understanding and alienated from the life of God" (Ephesians 4:18). Notice what he puts next to each other: darkness of mind and distance from God's life. The darkness is not only a mental weakness. It is part of the curse that sin brought.

This matters because sin is not a small, surface problem. It is not like a stain on one sleeve while the rest of the shirt is clean. It reaches into the heart, where our thinking, wanting and choosing all begin. Jesus says evil thoughts come "out of the heart" (Matthew 15:19). And it reaches everyone: "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). So the very mind we would use to examine God is itself affected by the illness we need cured.

That creates a strange difficulty. Part of what sin damages is our willingness to see the truth. Nobody likes being told they are seriously sick, and the natural heart likes even less being told it is guilty before God. So we tend to resist what God says about us, and we read his word looking for comfort rather than truth. Paul also speaks of a spiritual enemy at work: "the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 4:4). The blindness is real, and we are not neutral observers.

Can education fix this? In one sense, learning is a good gift. Studying languages, history, science and even the Bible's original setting can push back some of the confusion and ignorance that sin brought into the world. Christians should value it. But learning by itself cannot do the deepest work. It can add knowledge to the mind, yet it cannot give a dead heart life toward God or lift a curse. Paul says plainly that "the world through its wisdom did not know Him" (1 Corinthians 1:21), and of the brilliant thinkers who turned from God, "Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools" (Romans 1:22). A very clever person who does not know Christ is just as blind toward God as a simple one. In fact, a sharper mind can simply become better at arguing against him.

Why can only Christ cure it? Because the blindness is part of the penalty for sin, and only the one who bore that penalty can remove it. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). When he took our sin and its punishment on himself, he also dealt with the darkness that came with it. He is "the true Light" coming into the world (John 1:9). And the Holy Spirit applies this light to us. Paul says the natural person cannot understand the things of God's Spirit, "because they are spiritually discerned" (1 Corinthians 2:14). So the healing is the work of the whole Trinity: the Father who said "Let light shine out of darkness" shines in our hearts, "to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6), and the Spirit opens our eyes to see it.

This is why the right way to come to God's truth is with humility. Jesus thanked the Father for hiding these things "from the wise and learned" and revealing them "to little children" (Matthew 11:25). That is not a slight against careful thinking. It means we must lay aside pride and the assumption that we can master God, and come to his word as learners who need his help. A humble child with an open Bible may see more of God than a proud scholar.

That also explains something many believers notice: even people who love God and trust his goodness can feel dread at the thought of standing in his presence. Isaiah, a faithful prophet, cried "Woe is me" when he saw the Lord. This fear comes from sin. Adam had no thought of hiding from God until he had disobeyed. Afterward he said, "I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10). A guilty conscience, together with the knowledge that God is just and does not ignore sin, makes us fear that he has come to bring our wrongs to account.

But the gospel speaks to that dread too. For those in Christ, the guilt has been carried and the curse removed. We still approach God with reverence, because he is holy. Yet the terror of a guilty person before a judge gives way to the trust of a child before a father. As John writes, "perfect love drives out fear" (1 John 4:18). The same Christ who opens blind eyes also takes away the reason to hide.

topics.title: Is God far from us, given that in Him we live and move and have our being?
topics.cmp: The meaning of Acts 17:28 for the mind's dependence on God and whether God, the supreme good, is near or far from those who depend on him for their being.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Trinity in the Mind is the Image of God, in that It…
refs.quote: And therefore it ought to be taken in a more excellent way, and one that is spiritual, not visible, in respect to the mind, which is made after His image.

ans.text:
No. God is not far from any of us, and Paul says exactly that. Speaking to the philosophers of Athens, he tells them that God made people so that they would seek Him and reach out for Him and find Him, "though He is not far from any one of us. 'For in Him we live and move and have our being'" (Acts 17:27–28).

Think about what that sentence claims. It is not only that God is close by, the way a friend might sit in the next room. It is that our very existence hangs on Him at every moment. We did not make ourselves, and we cannot keep ourselves going. If God stopped holding us in being, we would not slowly fade. We would simply not be. Paul says elsewhere, "For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things" (Romans 11:36). Of the Son he writes, "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). The One we depend on that completely cannot be distant.

It helps to see what "in Him" does and does not mean. It is not a statement about physical space, as if God were a vast container and we floated inside Him like fish in water. In a bodily sense we live and move inside the physical world too, and Paul means far more than that. Nor does it mean that we are pieces of God or that God and creation are the same thing. God is the Creator, and we are His creatures. Paul's point is about dependence and presence. God is present to everything He has made, holding it in being, while remaining wholly distinct from it.

This applies most deeply to the human mind. We were made in God's image (Genesis 1:27). Our ability to think, to remember, to understand, and to love is not something we produce on our own. Every true thought we think and every real good we love is given and upheld by Him. God is the highest good, the source of every other good thing. That good is not a faraway prize at the end of a long road. It is the good by which we exist at all. In that sense He is closer to us than our own thoughts.

The whole Trinity is involved in this nearness. The Father is the source of all things. The Son holds all things together. And David asks, "Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence?" (Psalm 139:7). The answer is nowhere. There is no corner of the universe, and no corner of the heart, where God is absent.

Why, then, do we so often feel that God is far away? The distance is real, but it is not a distance of place. It is on our side. Picture someone standing in bright sunlight with their eyes shut. The sun is not far off, yet they see nothing. Our attention is scattered, our desires are bent toward lesser things, and above all our sin breaks fellowship with God. Isaiah tells Israel that their sins had built a barrier between them and their God and hidden His face from them (Isaiah 59:2). God was still present. He was holding them in being even as they turned from Him. What was broken was the friendship.

So Scripture speaks of nearness in two ways. In one sense God is near to everyone, believer and unbeliever alike, because no one exists apart from Him. In another sense people can be "far away" from Him and need to be brought near. That is what Christ has done: "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ" (Ephesians 2:13). Through the Son, and by the Spirit living within us, the God who was always present to us becomes the God we know, trust, and love.

This is both a comfort and an invitation. It is a comfort because you never have to travel to find God. He is already upholding you as you read this. It is an invitation because His nearness calls for an answer. Paul told the Athenians that God placed us where we are so that we would seek Him. James puts it simply: "Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you" (James 4:8). We do not cross a great distance to reach Him. We turn and open our eyes to the One in whom we already live and move and have our being.

title: Divine Names and Theological Language
desc: What names such as God, Lord, Father and Ungenerate signify, whether names come from God or human conception, and the Eunomian dispute over naming the divine essence.

topics.title: Does 'Ungenerate' define God's essence, and can that essence be comprehended?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa supplies nearly all the answers and is consistently negative: 'ungenerate' does not define or name God's essence. It is a privative term or human conception (epinoia) that says only that the Father has no cause or beginning, and the divine nature stays beyond every name and beyond human comprehension. His grounds are mostly logical and philosophical. He argues that negations are secondary, that 'ungenerate' and 'endless' are both needed to express eternity, and that 'simple' and 'ungenerate' are not convertible. He also shows that Eunomius's identification leads to absurdities: Sabellianism, an opposed or non-divine Son, and immortal creatures becoming consubstantial with the Father. He adds analogies (the ant, the heavens, children grasping a sunbeam) and Scripture (Psalm 102, Luke's genealogy, Manoah's angel, 'above every name'), and he repeatedly leans on Basil as his authority. Athanasius agrees in rejecting 'Unoriginate' as a basis for theology, but his emphasis is different. He objects that the word is unscriptural, Greek in origin and ambiguous in sense, so its meaning must be specified before the question can be answered. He prefers 'Father', the name Christ taught, which implies the Son. Gregory, by contrast, is willing to keep 'ungenerate' as a harmless, reverent conception, interchangeable with 'First Cause', and also holds that 'Father' itself conveys ungeneracy. Augustine adds the narrower point that 'begetter' and 'unbegotten' are distinct notions of the Father, the first relative to the Son. Hilary's distinction between definition and conferred description, and Irenaeus's claim that no one with a superior can properly be called God, touch the topic only indirectly and do not take up the ungenerate-essence question.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: if they confine God’s being to the one, their definition of this being will be manifestly imperfect and curtailed by half; it is thought of only by the absence of beginning

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For he who has any superior over him, and is under the power of another, this being never can be called either “God” or “the great King.”

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: the Unoriginate is specified not by contrast to the Son, but to the things which through the Son come to be. And excellently: since God is not as things originated, but is their Creator and Framer through the Son.

ans.text:
No. Calling God "ungenerate" (or "unoriginate") tells us something true, but it does not tell us what God is in his innermost being. That being, which theologians call God's "essence," is far beyond anything our minds can fully take in.

Start with the word itself. To be "generated" or "begotten" means to have your existence from someone else, the way a child has life from a parent. To be "ungenerate" simply means not to have come from anyone. The word does not appear in the Bible, but the idea does. Psalm 90:2 says that "from everlasting to everlasting, You are God." Psalm 102 contrasts the passing world with the Lord, who stays the same and whose years never come to an end. Nothing stands behind God or before him.
