He is the source of everything and has no source himself.

Notice what kind of word this is. It works like "invisible," "immortal," or "tireless." Each tells you what is absent, not what is present. When Paul calls God "immortal" and "invisible" in 1 Timothy 1:17, he is saying that death and visibility do not apply to God. He is not giving a full description of God's nature. If I tell you that a certain house is "not made of brick," you have learned something real. You still do not know what the house is made of, or what it looks like. In the same way, "ungenerate" rules something out: God did not begin, and nothing caused him. It does not lay out his being for inspection.

An everyday comparison helps. Adam had no human father. Seth, his son, did. Being "nobody's son" was true of Adam, but it was not what made him human. If it were, Seth would not have been human at all. Having a father, or not having one, describes how someone stands in relation to others. It does not define what they are.

This is exactly why the question matters for the Trinity. Some once argued that "ungenerate" is the very definition of God. Then, since the Son is begotten of the Father, they concluded that the Son must have a different and lesser nature. The argument sounds tidy, but it rests on a mistake. Being unbegotten is what marks the Father off from the Son. It is not what makes the Father God. The Father is God and has no source. The Son is God and is from the Father. Both share one and the same divine being. John 1:1 says that "the Word was God." Jesus says in John 5:26 that "as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself." The Son receives the very same life the Father has, not a lesser copy. So "unbegotten" and "begotten" name a real distinction between the Persons, the way "father" and "son" do. They do not name two different kinds of being.

In fact the plain biblical name "Father" already carries the idea of being unbegotten. To call him the Father points to the Son he has eternally begotten. It also implies that he comes from no one, since if anything stood above him, that would be the true first source. So we lose nothing by sticking with the Bible's own language. What matters is the truth the words point to, not one particular technical term.

Can God's essence, then, be fully understood? Scripture answers with humility. Psalm 145:3 says God's greatness is unsearchable. 1 Timothy 6:16 says he "dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see." Paul, after pages of careful teaching, breaks out in Romans 11:33 in wonder at how unsearchable God's judgments are. A finite mind cannot hold the infinite God, any more than a cup can hold the ocean. Anyone who claims that one word sums up the whole of God has mistaken his own idea for the living God.

This does not mean we know nothing, or that our words about God are empty. God has truly made himself known. John 1:18 says, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known." Jesus says in Matthew 11:27 that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. We can know God truly, personally and savingly, as John 17:3 describes eternal life. We simply cannot know him exhaustively. It is like knowing a dear friend: you really know them, yet they are always more than you can put into words.

So many names fit God: unbegotten, eternal, immortal, holy, good. Each is a true window onto him. None of them is a fence around him. That should lead us not to clever definitions but to worship of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, the one God who is always greater than our thoughts.

topics.title: Do 'unbegotten' and 'begotten' prove that the Father and Son differ in essence?
topics.cmp: Hilary of Poitiers, Augustine of Hippo, and Gregory of Nyssa all deny that 'unbegotten' and 'begotten' prove a difference of essence between Father and Son. Each grants that the Son does not share the Father's unbegottenness, yet holds that he has the Father's whole nature. They reach this conclusion by different routes. Hilary argues from the nature of birth itself: a true and perfect birth from God can only be God and imparts the whole fulness of the Begetter's nature, since the Son has no other source for his substance. Augustine argues logically that not everything said of God is said according to substance: 'Father', 'begotten', and 'unbegotten' (understood as the denial of a relation, 'not a son') are relative terms and so cannot mark diverse substances. Gregory shares the view that the terms denote a manner of existence rather than nature, and he uses the analogy of the ungenerated Adam and generated Abel as one 'man' along with a theory that names signify properties, not incomprehensible essences; his distinctive emphasis is polemical, as he repeatedly turns Eunomius's own premises (convertible terms, the relation implied by 'Son', the active and the passive sharing one nature, knowing a work from its maker) into reductiones ad absurdum that either make the Son ungenerate or prove him coessential.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: the name Begotten signifies indeed the manner of His origin, but does not make Him different in kind from the Begetter

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: If, that is, the thing that is detected both in the Father and the Son, I mean the singleness of life, is one, the very idea of singleness excluding, as we have said, any variation

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Father and the Son are Together One Wisdom, as One…
refs.quote: they are not therefore not one essence, because the Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father, or because the Father is un-begotten, but the Son is begotten: since by these names only their relative attributes are expressed.

ans.text:
No. 'Unbegotten' and 'begotten' tell us how the Father and the Son are related to each other, not what kind of being each one is. They mark a real distinction between two persons, but not a difference in their divine nature.

First, what the words mean. To 'beget' is to father a child. When Christians say the Son is 'begotten' of the Father, they mean that the Son has his being from the Father, the way a son comes from a father. When they call the Father 'unbegotten,' they mean that nobody gave him his being. He is not from anyone. These are old words, and the second is not even found in the Bible, but they say something true: the Father is the source, and the Son is from the Father.

Some have reasoned like this: the two words are opposites, so the two beings must be opposites too. One must be the true, highest God, and the other a lesser, different kind of being. The argument sounds tidy, but it mixes up two different questions. One question is 'Where does he come from?' The other is 'What is he?'

Think of the first family in Genesis. Adam was not born. God formed him from the dust. His son Seth was born. If we ask where each came from, the answers are opposite: one was born and the other was not. But if we ask what each one is, the answer is the same. Both are fully human. Being born did not make Seth a different kind of creature from his father. Genesis 5:3 even says Adam fathered a son 'in his own likeness, after his own image.' How you came to be is one thing. What you are is another.

Here is another everyday picture. 'He is sitting' and 'he is not sitting' are exact opposites. Yet nobody thinks a man changes into a different kind of thing when he stands up. The opposite words describe his position, not his nature. In the same way, 'begotten' and 'not begotten' describe how each person stands toward the other. They are not a definition of God's being.

In fact, the very names the Bible uses point the other way. 'Father' and 'Son' are relationship words. A father is a father because he has a son, and a son is a son because he has a father. In ordinary life, what a father begets shares his own nature. A man begets a man. He builds a house, but the house is not human. Begetting gives you the same kind. Making gives you a different kind. That is why the church has always said the Son is 'begotten, not made.' If the Son were truly begotten of God, he is God, just as a human son is human.

Scripture makes this clear. 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). The Son is 'the exact representation of His nature' (Hebrews 1:3). He is not a rough copy but the perfect imprint of who the Father is. 'In Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form' (Colossians 2:9). Jesus says, 'For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself' (John 5:26). Notice both halves of that verse. The Son receives this life from the Father. That is what 'begotten' means. Yet what he receives is the same life the Father has, life in himself. Nothing is missing, and nothing new or lesser is added. And Jesus can say, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), and 'Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father' (John 14:9).

There is also a problem with treating 'unbegotten' as the very definition of what God is. Look at what the word actually says. It does not describe something the Father has. It says something he is not: he is not from anyone, he is not a son. You cannot build a whole account of God's nature out of a word that only tells you what someone is not. And our words for God are true but limited. God's being is far beyond what any human label can capture, so we should be careful about cutting the Godhead in two because two words sound opposite.

Scripture also turns the order around. Jesus says, 'No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him' (Matthew 11:27). We do not first get a clear grip on the Father's nature and then measure the Son against it to find him lacking. We come to know the Father through the Son. That only works if the Son truly shares and shows what the Father is.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, 'begotten' does not mean the Son had a beginning, as a human child does. God is eternal, and the Father was never without his Son. The Son's coming from the Father is an eternal relationship, not an event in time. Second, saying the Father and Son share one nature does not mean they are the same person. The difference between begotten and unbegotten is real. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father. The Son is everything the Father is, except being the Father.

So the honest conclusion runs opposite to the argument. The words 'begotten' and 'unbegotten' show that Father and Son are truly distinct persons. But because the Son is truly begotten of the Father, and not made, he shares the Father's own nature. He is true God from true God.

topics.title: What do the names applied to God signify, and can any name express the divine essence?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa dominates this topic and argues consistently that no name, not even "Godhead," "Father," "He Who is," or Christ's titles such as Bread and Way, expresses the divine essence. Names are formed by human conception (epinoia) from God's operations toward us (theos from "beholding") or by negating created conditions, so privative terms like "ungenerate" and "indestructible" say what God is not and ascribe rather than bestow. He grounds this in Scripture (Abraham and Moses not knowing the Name, the name "above every name"), in analogies (marks of recognition, corn as seed, fruit and food), and in philosophical argument against Eunomius (the diversity of languages, contraries, the infinite cannot be bounded by a name). Novatian and Irenaeus agree that God's proper name cannot be expressed: Novatian because what exceeds the intellect exceeds any name's meaning, and Irenaeus because terms like Understanding and Light are fitting but fall short, though Irenaeus also stresses that the many Hebrew titles (Sabaoth, Adonai) all name the one God rather than several powers. A real difference in emphasis appears over "He Who is" (Exodus 3:14): Hilary reads it as teaching that absolute, beginningless being belongs to God, and Waterland holds that "Jehovah" primarily signifies God as necessary, immutable Being itself, rejecting the reading of it as "faithfulness to promises"; Gregory instead insists that Moses is given "the Being" without any name that discloses the essence. Other contributors treat names Christologically rather than epistemologically: Augustine ("made unto us wisdom" in time), Athanasius ("servant," "created"), and Hilary ("brethren") all refer such terms to the incarnation, not the Word's essence, while Ambrose takes "Fire" as pointing to the Spirit's Godhead and Novatian treats "Fire" and "Spirit" as figures adapted to the hearers.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: We are taught the fact of Its existence, while we assert that an appellation of such force as to include the unspeakable and infinite Nature, either does not exist at all, or at any rate is unknown to us.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Thus God has brethren according to His flesh, for the Word became flesh and dwelt amongst us: but the Only-begotten Son, unique as the Only-begotten, has no brethren.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: All these terms happen to be proper to man’s constitution; and such as these do not designate the Essence of the Word, but that He has become man.

ans.text:
No name we have can capture what God is in his very being, yet every name God gives himself in the Bible is true, and each one tells us something real about him. Both halves of that answer matter. Leave out the first and we shrink God to the size of our words. Leave out the second and we are left with a God we cannot know at all.

Start with the limit. Paul says God "lives in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him" (1 Timothy 6:16). God is infinite, and our words are finite. A word draws a line around something so we can point to it, but God has no edges to draw a line around. Trying to hold God in a name is like trying to hold the ocean in your cupped hands. You really do hold seawater, but you do not hold the sea. That is part of what it means that Christ has been given "the name above every name" (Philippians 2:9). His name is not just the top entry on a list of comparable names. He surpasses naming altogether.

So how do God's names work? Mostly they come from what God has shown us of himself: what he does, how he deals with us, and how he differs from everything he made. Think of how you might describe a stranger by his hometown, his age or his job. Each detail is true and helps you recognize him, but none of them is the man himself. In the same way, God is called Creator, Shepherd, King, Judge and Savior. Each name is true, and none is the whole of him.

The names also work in different ways. Some tell us what is in God: he is just, good, wise and loving. Others tell us what is not in God: he is immortal, meaning death cannot touch him, and unchanging, meaning he has no ups and downs or decay. Theologians sometimes call him "uncreated" or "without beginning." These negative names are not weaker than the positive ones. Knowing that God can never fail, fade or die is real and precious knowledge.

One caution helps here. When God has several names, do not picture him divided into parts, with one name for each part. Saying God has no beginning and saying he has no end are not two halves of his life. They describe one endless life, seen first looking back and then looking forward. God is not just in one corner and loving in another. All that he is, he is wholly.

The names were not invented to give God qualities he lacked. When we call God holy, we are not making him holy. We are recognizing what he already is. Our words describe him; they add nothing to him.

What about the special name God revealed to Moses? When Moses asked God's name, God answered, "I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: I AM has sent me to you" (Exodus 3:14). Then he added, "This is My name forever" (Exodus 3:15). The Hebrew name, written with four letters and usually printed "LORD" in English Bibles, is closely tied to this "I AM."

That name points to God as the one who simply is. He does not borrow his existence from anyone. He depends on nothing, and he cannot change. "I, the LORD, do not change," he says in Malachi 3:6. Some have suggested the name mainly means "the one who keeps his promises." God certainly does keep his promises. But the deeper meaning is that he is the ever-living, unchanging God, and that is exactly why his promises can be trusted. A God who could change might fail to keep his word. The God who is "I AM" will not. It is striking that Jesus applied this language to himself: "before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58).

Sincere Christians weigh this name a little differently. Some hold that "I AM" names God's very being more properly than any other name, because it says not what God does but that he is life and being itself. Others stress that even this name points toward God's being without fully containing it. Both sides agree that it is the deepest name God has given, and that God is still greater than our grasp of it.

Can this name be spoken? Over time, out of deep reverence, Jewish readers stopped pronouncing it aloud and said "Lord" instead. That is why its original pronunciation is not certain. "Jehovah" is a later form that blended the name's consonants with the vowels of the Hebrew word for "Lord." "Yahweh" is scholars' best guess at the original. Christians differ on whether to use the name aloud. Some do so gladly. Others follow the long habit of saying "the LORD."

What matters most is plain. God gave his name so that his people could call on him, not so that it would be locked away. "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Romans 10:13). The commandment is not to avoid his name but not to take it in vain. Reverence is about the heart, not only the syllables.

The Bible also gives picture names. "Our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews 12:29) does not mean God is a flame. It shows his blazing holiness, which purifies and judges. Jesus says, "God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth" (John 4:24). That tells us God is not a physical body that can be located, measured or confined. Even here, "spirit" points us toward God rather than defining him completely.

The many names of Christ work the same way. He calls himself the Bread, the Light, the Way, the Door, the Vine and the Good Shepherd. Each describes what he is and does for us: he feeds us, shows us the way, brings us in and holds us together. Think of grain, which can be called seed, harvest or food depending on how you look at it. It is one thing seen from several sides. Christ is one Lord, rich enough to need many names. If each title described his inner nature, he would be a strange mixture of bread, doors and vines. Yet none of these names is empty. Every one is given to teach us.

The names Father, Son and Holy Spirit are especially important. "Father" does not spell out the divine nature. It names a relationship: the Father is Father of the Son. So whenever we confess the Father, we are already confessing the Son, who shares his glory. The Father, Son and Spirit do not need names to know one another. The Son is in the Father, and the Spirit "searches all things, even the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10). The names are given for our sake, not theirs.

Finally, many names do not mean many gods. A man may be husband, father, teacher and neighbor and still be one man. Scripture is firm: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus sends his disciples to baptize "in the name" (one name, not "names") "of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). The one God is known to us as Father, Son and Spirit, and praised under many names.

So we can speak of God with confidence, because his names are true. We should also speak with humility, because he is always more than we can say. The right response to his names is not to think we have mastered him, but to trust him and worship him.

topics.title: What do the names 'Father', 'Son', 'Begotten' and 'Only-begotten' signify?
topics.cmp: Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius and Warfield agree that 'Father' and 'Son' name a real, eternal relation, not a title of creation, adoption or mere dignity, and that this relation entails a shared nature. Augustine treats 'begotten' and 'son' as the same relative term in the category of relation. They ground this differently. Hilary argues that God's own words ('This is My Son') do not deceive and that 'Only-begotten' rules out adoption. Gregory, arguing against Eunomius, insists that the natural sense of the names be kept while passion, time, matter and the created–uncreated pattern are stripped away, and he refuses to let 'Father' collapse into 'Creator.' Athanasius prefers 'Father' to 'Unoriginate' because it names God from the Son rather than from his works, and because a father, unlike a maker, cannot be without his offspring; Irenaeus, for his part, refuses to model the Word's indescribable generation on a human mind uttering a word. Athanasius and Gregory both distinguish 'Only-begotten' (by nature, from the Father) from 'First-born' (said for our sakes), but Gregory ties 'First-born' to the incarnation, while Athanasius relates it more broadly to creation, with the Son stamping his image on it as its archetype. The clearest divergence is Warfield's: Gregory says 'Father' marks the Father as the Son's cause, and Athanasius reads 'Only-begotten' as 'God from God.' Warfield instead reads 'Son' as connoting likeness and equality with no subordination, holds that 'only begotten' may mean only uniqueness, and calls any idea of derivation at most very distant.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Reply is Made to the Cavils of the Heretics in Respect…
refs.quote: with a wonderful blindness, they do not perceive that no one can be said to be begotten except in relation to something. For he is therefore a son because begotten; and because a son, therefore certainly begotten.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: This question must certainly be answered in the negative. Although, no doubt, in many of the instances in which the terms “Father” and “Son” occur, it would be possible to take them of merely economical relations, there ever remain some which are intractable to this treatment

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: will allow to the title ‘Father’ only the meaning that the Only-begotten is not Himself without a source, but derives from That the cause of His being

ans.text:
These four names tell us that the Father and the Son are truly related to each other as father and son, that this relationship has no beginning, and that because the Son comes from the Father in this way, he shares everything the Father is as God. They are not nicknames or polite titles. They are the names God himself uses in the Bible to show us who he is.

Start with what any of us understands when we hear the words father and son. A father is a father of someone. A son is a son of someone. Each name points to the other. And a son is the same kind of being as his father. A human father has a human son, not a statue or a machine. When the Bible calls God 'Father' and Jesus 'Son', that ordinary meaning carries over. The Son is from the Father, and he is of the same nature as the Father. The people who heard Jesus understood this clearly. John 5:18 says that he 'was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.' Jesus did not correct them. Elsewhere he says plainly, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30).

The Bible also teaches that this sonship is eternal, not something that started at Bethlehem. Jesus prays to be glorified with 'the glory I had with You before the world existed' (John 17:5), and he speaks of the Father loving him 'before the foundation of the world' (John 17:24). John's Gospel opens with the Word who 'was' in the beginning and 'was God' (John 1:1), and only then calls him the Son from the Father. If God has always been Father, then he has always had a Son. There was never a time when the Father was alone and later became a father. A builder can exist before he builds anything. But no one is a father without a child. So the name 'Father' itself implies that the Son is just as eternal as he is.

This is where the word 'begotten' comes in. To beget means to father a child, to give rise to someone who shares your own nature. It stands in contrast with making. A carpenter makes a table, and the table is something different from him. A father begets a son, and the son is what the father is. When Christians say the Son is 'begotten, not made', they mean he is not a creature God produced, however exalted. He is God from God, the way light shines from light. Hebrews 1:3 puts it this way: the Son is 'the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature.'

A natural worry follows. Human begetting involves bodies, time, change and a mother. Does calling God 'Father' bring all of that into God? No. The Bible uses words from our world because we have no other words. But we must strip away everything that belongs only to bodies: time, physical process, passion, a before and after. What is left is the heart of the matter: the Son is truly from the Father and truly shares his nature. In the same way, we should not picture the Son coming from the Father like a human thought forming and then being spoken, one step after another. God has no stages. How the Son is eternally from the Father is beyond our understanding. We can say that it is true without pretending to describe how it happens.

'Only-begotten' adds one more point. The Son is the one and only Son of God by nature. Believers are called children of God too, but we become so by adoption and grace. He is Son by who he is. John 1:18 says that 'the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known.' Many modern Bibles, including the one this site uses, translate the Greek word as 'one and only' rather than 'only begotten.' Sincere Christians have discussed which is better. Some argue the word simply means 'unique, one of a kind.' Others answer that in a passage about a Son coming from a Father, uniqueness of birth is exactly what is meant. Either way, the point stands: there is no other Son like him.

The Bible also calls Christ 'firstborn'. He is 'the firstborn over all creation' (Colossians 1:15), 'the firstborn from among the dead' (Colossians 1:18), and 'the firstborn among many brothers' (Romans 8:29). This can sound like it clashes with 'only-begotten'. A firstborn has younger brothers and sisters, while an only child has none. The answer is that the two titles describe him in different respects. 'Only-begotten' speaks of who he is eternally in relation to the Father, and there he has no brothers. 'Firstborn' speaks of his place over creation and what he has done for us. He holds the rank of the heir over all things. By becoming man and rising from the dead, he has made us his brothers and sisters and leads us into God's family. 'Firstborn' does not mean he was the first thing created. It means he is the head and source of the new family he gathers.

Some have tried to replace the name 'Father' with a word like 'Unbegotten' or 'Uncaused', and to call the Son simply 'Begotten', as if the real point were that one is uncaused and the other caused, and so different in nature. But that trade loses the very thing the Bible's names teach. 'Unbegotten' only tells us something the Father is not: he does not come from anyone. It says nothing about a Son at all. 'Father' tells us that he has a Son, that he has always had him, and that the Son shares his nature. The biblical names are richer and truer, and we should keep them.

Can these names be used of the whole Trinity, or of the Father and Son together? In one sense, yes, the word 'Father' can be used more broadly. The one God, Father, Son and Spirit together, creates us, cares for us, and adopts us, so God may be called our Father in that wider sense. But the names in their proper, eternal meaning belong to particular Persons. Only the Father is Father of the Son. Only the Son is begotten. The Spirit is neither Father nor Son. The Father and the Son are not begotten together, and the Son is not his own Father. Keeping these names in their places guards against two mistakes. One is blurring the Persons into one. The other is treating the Son as a lesser being.

So when you pray 'Our Father' or confess Jesus as God's only Son, you are using words God has given to reveal himself truly. The Son is really the Son, eternally from the Father, equal with him, and one God with him. And through this Son, God welcomes us as his children.

topics.title: Do the titles 'God', 'Lord' and 'Almighty' signify God's nature or a relation of dominion?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that a title like 'god' given to a creature does not confer the divine nature: Hilary says Moses was appointed a god to Pharaoh without having God's nature, and Irenaeus holds that prophets, apostles and Christ never properly call any other being God or Lord. They differ sharply on what 'God' itself signifies. Daniel Waterland insists that 'God' and Theotes properly denote the divine substance, with dominion only a secondary notion, while Gregory of Nyssa derives Theos from theasthai ('to see') and says it names one operation of God rather than grasping his substance, though he also allows that 'God' can be used both absolutely and relatively. Waterland's case against Clarke rests on the consensus of Catholic antiquity, on Scripture's rebukes of the prince of Tyre and the Lycaonians, on the absurdity that God would only have become God at creation, and on Clarke's own reading of John 1:1; he concedes that the full Scripture idea of God includes a relative notion of Governor, which is why phrases like 'my God' make sense. On 'Lord' and 'Almighty' the Fathers lean toward relation or dignity: Gregory treats 'Almighty' as relative to a creation that needs ruling and argues, against Eunomius's reading of 2 Corinthians 3:17, that 'Lord' signifies dignity rather than essence; Augustine says God's lordship is not eternal because lord and servant are correlatives; Ambrose, by contrast, stresses that Godhead and Lordship are inseparable and pass between the Persons without change of nature; and Athanasius grounds the Son's lordship in his sonship rather than in mere eternity.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: I maintain that dominion is not the full import of the word God in Seripture ; that it is but a part of the idea, and a small part too; and that, if any person be called God, merely on account

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: is proved to be Lord not so much from His eternity, as in that He is God’s Son; for being the Son, He is inseparable from the Father, and never was there when He was not, but He was always

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: He Who is God is Lord, and He Who is Lord is God, for the Godhead is in the Lordship, and the Lordship is in the Godhead.

ans.text:
The word 'God' names what God is, his very nature, while 'Lord' and 'Almighty' mainly describe his rule over everything he has made. That rule flows out of who he already is. God does not become God by ruling. He rules because he is God.

Take the word 'God' first. Some people have argued that it is only a title of office, like 'king' or 'governor', so that anyone with enough authority could be called a god. The Bible does not use the word that way. When the prince of Tyre claimed to be divine, the Lord answered, 'you are a man and not a god' (Ezekiel 28:2). His problem was not that his kingdom was too small. He was a weak, mortal creature. When the crowd at Lystra tried to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, the apostles protested that they were only human, just like everyone else (Acts 14:11-15). Paul says the Galatians were once 'slaves to those who by nature are not gods' (Galatians 4:8). Being God is a matter of nature: living without beginning, owing your existence to no one, and being infinitely wise, good and powerful. Authority over others follows from that. It does not create it.

There is a simple test. If ruling over creatures were what made God God, what was he before anything was created? He would have become God only on the day he made the world. And if he ever let the world fall back into nothing, he would stop being God. That is absurd. Moses prays, 'from everlasting to everlasting You are God' (Psalm 90:2), and that includes the time before the mountains were born. John says the same of the Son: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). That is before anything was made, so there was nothing yet to rule. The word 'God' there can only mean what the Word is.

We do say 'my God' or 'the God of Israel', and that is right. The Bible's full picture of God includes his care for his people as their protector and ruler. So the word naturally carries a sense of relationship as well. But this no more turns 'God' into a mere job title than calling someone 'my father' means 'father' has nothing to do with real, shared human life.

'Lord' and 'Almighty' work a little differently. 'Lord' speaks of ownership and authority. 'Almighty' in the New Testament translates a word meaning 'ruler of all'. These titles describe God in relation to what he rules. In that sense his lordship over us began when we began. You cannot be Lord over a servant who does not yet exist. This does not mean anything changed in God. When a new family moves in next door, you become their neighbor without anything in you changing. The change is on their side. In the same way, when God created the world, the world began to stand under his rule. God himself stayed exactly as he always was.

The power and majesty behind these titles, however, were never new. God did not gain strength when he made the world. He was always able to do all things. So 'Almighty' names a relationship that began in time, but it rests on a power that is eternal. Heaven's worship holds these together: 'Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come' (Revelation 4:8).

One more thing deepens the meaning of 'Lord'. In most English Bibles, 'LORD' in the Old Testament stands for God's personal name, revealed to Moses as 'I AM'. That name speaks of God's own unending being. So when the New Testament gives Jesus the title 'Lord', it is not handing him a lesser honor. Paul takes a passage from Isaiah, where every knee bows to the LORD alone, and applies it to Jesus (Philippians 2:10-11, echoing Isaiah 45:23). The title still speaks of authority. But Scripture uses it in the place of God's own name. So confessing Jesus as Lord in this full sense means confessing that he shares the very being of the God of Israel.

It also helps to see what 2 Corinthians 3:17, 'the Lord is the Spirit', does not mean. Some have argued that 'Spirit' there means 'essence', so that 'Lord' would be the name of the Son's essence. But Paul goes straight on to speak of 'the Spirit of the Lord', which would then mean 'the essence of the essence'. That makes no sense. In context, Paul is contrasting the life-giving Spirit with the written code that brings death. He is not giving a definition of the word 'Lord'.

These titles belong equally to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. They are not divided up, as if the Father were God and the Son only Lord. Whoever is truly God is Lord, and whoever is Lord in the full sense is God. Thomas shows this when he falls before the risen Jesus and says, 'My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28). Yet there are not three Gods or three Lords. Each Person shares the one divine nature, and so the one divine lordship.

What about the places where Scripture calls others 'gods' or 'lords'? God told Moses he would make him like God to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1). That meant Moses would stand before Pharaoh with God's authority and work wonders by God's power. It did not mean he became divine; elsewhere he is simply called God's faithful servant. Rulers and judges are sometimes called gods because they carry a borrowed authority. Idols and false spirits are called gods only because people treat them that way, though they are not gods by nature. Earthly masters are called lords in an ordinary human sense. In every case the title is borrowed or misused. Only the one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is God and Lord in the full and proper sense.

topics.title: Are names given by God or devised by human conception?
topics.cmp: Covers the dispute with Eunomius over whether names are prior to creation or products of human conception (epinoia), and whether epinoia discovers truth. It also covers Genesis on God 'calling' things by name, Babel, and whether human naming rivals God's authority.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: as being afraid lest, His name not being uttered among creatures as yet unborn, He should be ignorant or forgetful of Himself, through ignorance of His own nature because of His name being unspoken

ans.text:
God made the things of the world, and he gave us minds and voices, but the actual words we use, including most of our words for God, are formed by people using the gifts he gave them. That does not make our language about God made up or untrustworthy. God has also spoken to us in Scripture, and there he takes up ordinary human words and fills them with true meaning about himself.

The question can sound academic, but it once mattered a great deal. Some early teachers argued that God himself coined certain words, especially the word "unbegotten," meaning "never born, without any source." Their reasoning ran like this. If God personally gave the word "unbegotten," it must name his very being, what God is at the deepest level. The Son is "begotten," meaning he comes from the Father the way a son comes from a father. So the Son must be a different kind of being from God. The church saw that this argument quietly turned a word into a weapon against the Son's full divinity. Part of the answer was to look carefully at where names come from.

Start with Genesis. God forms the animals, but he does not label them. "He brought them to the man to see what he would name each one. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name" (Genesis 2:19). Making a thing and naming it are two different acts. The first belongs to God. The second he hands to Adam, as part of the dignity of being made in his image. Naming is not a rival to God's authority. It is a gift he shares, a little like a father who builds a garden and invites his child to name the flowers.

What about Genesis 1:5, where "God called the light 'day'"? The point is not that God spoke a Hebrew word into the void. Light and day are not quite the same thing. Light is what drives out darkness, while a day is a span of time made by light and darkness taking turns. The verse tells us God made and ordered these realities. God makes things that truly exist, and our words follow after, describing what he has made.

Psalm 147:4 says God "calls each one by name," speaking of the stars. This does not mean God invented the star names we use. Many of those names come from pagan myths, and God is not their author. The verse means that God knows every star individually and completely, the way you show you really know someone when you call them by name. Nothing in his creation is a blur to him.

Babel points the same way. In Genesis 11:7 God says, "Come, let Us go down and confuse their language." He confuses a language that already exists. He does not hand out finished dictionaries. Afterward the scattered peoples call the same sky, the same bread, and the same God by different words. The things stay the same for everyone while the names differ, which shows that the words come from us.

So is it right for people to speak of God in words formed by human minds? Yes. God does not need words. He is complete in himself, lacking nothing. Words are for our sake, so we can think, pray, and praise. No single word can capture what God is, so Scripture and the church use many: Creator, Lord, Shepherd, Rock, Holy, Merciful. Each adds something true, the way many photographs taken from different angles together give you a fuller sense of a mountain no single photo can hold.

This also means our thinking about God, when it is humble and guided by Scripture, can discover real truth. Our reasoning is not just a factory for fantasies. It is a gift of God by which we move from what we already know to what follows from it. That is how all honest learning works, and it is how believers have come to understand more of what God has shown.

The most important names come from God's own revelation. When Moses asks God's name, God answers, "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14). Jesus sends his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). These are still words in human languages, but God himself has chosen them to make himself known, so we receive them with special reverence and do not trade them away.

This also settles the old argument about "unbegotten." The idea behind it is true: the Father has no source. But the word itself is not in the Bible, and it was being used to make the Son lesser. So it is wise to say the same truth with the name Jesus gave us, "Father." A father is a father because he has a son. That name points to the Father having no source, and it also binds him to the Son instead of setting them apart. Words serve the truth, and when a word is twisted, we can keep the truth and choose a better word.

In short, God is the Maker of all things. He gave us the gift of naming. He knows every creature by name. And in Scripture he has given us true names for himself, which we may trust even though no name exhausts him.

topics.title: How do names relate to the natures and realities they signify?
topics.cmp: Covers whether names arise from nature or from human choice, how names relate to knowledge of things, and whether several names for one subject signify real distinct properties. It also asks whether different names for angelic ranks imply different natures.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: the general usage of men bears witness to our argument, which does not apply the term “most proper” where the name does not truly agree with the nature.

ans.text:
Names are signs that point to real things, but they do not make those things what they are. A thing's nature comes first. The name comes afterward, as a label we attach so we can think and talk about it. That simple point turns out to matter a great deal when we speak about God.

Start with how naming works among us. In Genesis 2:19, God brings the animals to Adam "to see what he would call each one. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name." God made the animals. Adam named them. The lion was already a lion before anyone said the word. The world's many languages make the same point. A Hebrew speaker and an English speaker use completely different sounds for the sky, yet they look up at the same sky and understand the same thing. If names grew out of things by some law of nature, everyone would use the same words. At Pentecost in Acts 2, people from many nations each heard God's wonders in their own language. The words differed, but the truth they carried did not.

It follows that we do not need a name before we can know something. A child who has never heard the word "fire" still learns quickly that it is hot. Our senses and minds, which God gave us, grasp things directly. Names are markers we add afterward so we can share what we know. We need them because we cannot simply lay our thoughts open to one another. Words are the bridge between one mind and another.

Changing a name does not change the thing. In John 1:42, Jesus tells Simon, "You will be called Cephas," which means Peter, or "rock." The new name carried a promise and a calling. But Simon did not become a different kind of being. He was the same man, now known by a name that pointed to God's purpose for him.

What about the names God uses for Himself and for His world? When God speaks to us in human words, He is stooping down to our level out of love. Think of a mother who talks in simple words to her small child. She is not limited to baby talk. She is meeting the child where the child is. Scripture's words about God are true and trustworthy, but they are God graciously meeting us in our language. They do not mean that God is bound to particular syllables, or that we can capture all of Him in a word.

A single thing can rightly carry several names, and those names are not empty. Each one picks out something real about it. Genesis 1:8 says God called the expanse "sky." Elsewhere the same reality is called the heavens or the firmament, and each word highlights a different feature. We call fire bright and we call it burning. Those are two true things about one fire, not two fires. A man can be a carpenter, a husband and a father all at once, and calling him one does not cancel the others. In the same way, Scripture calls God light, love, the living God, the Rock and the Shepherd. Isaiah 9:6 gives the promised Child many names: "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace." Each name tells us something true, and each applies to the whole of who He is. Having many names does not split God into parts.

This also guards against a faulty way of reasoning. Some have argued that because two names differ, the beings they describe must differ in kind. Some reasoned, for example, that since the Son is "begotten" and the Father is not, the Son must be a lesser sort of being. Here "begotten" means that the Son comes from the Father, as a son from a father, rather than being made. But a difference in names can mark a difference of relationship without any difference of nature. A father and his son are called by different names, yet both are fully human. The Father and the Son are truly distinct. The Father is not the Son. Yet John 1:1 says, "the Word was God," and Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one."

There is a further point. A name is used in its full and proper sense only when it truly fits the nature of the thing. People call a statue of a man "a man," but only loosely. Scripture speaks of so-called gods and idols (1 Corinthians 8:5-6). Paul even says of some people that "their god is their belly" (Philippians 3:19). In those cases the word "god" is used without its real meaning. When the New Testament calls the Son God, it is not using the word loosely the way people speak of idols. It means it in the full sense. If the Son's nature were different from the Father's, the word could not belong to both of them properly. The Bible gives it to both, and to the Spirit, because they share the one divine nature.

Finally, consider the angels. Paul speaks of "thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities" (Colossians 1:16). Some have taken these titles to mean that angels come in different kinds of being. But these names describe what angels do and the rank they hold, much as "mayor" or "judge" names an office, not a different species of human. Scripture shows real order among the heavenly powers, but all of them are created spirits made by God and for God.

So names matter because they point to real things, and God has given us true words about Himself. But the reality always comes before the word. When we speak of God, our words should follow what He has revealed about who He is.

topics.title: How may human words, analogies and technical terms be used of God?
topics.cmp: All five authors agree that human words and analogies may be used of God but fall short of His essence. They differ in which question they press. Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary and Augustine stress the limits. Gregory holds that Scripture reveals no definition of the divine essence and that reasoning from creatures to the transcendent is unreliable. Augustine says categories like place and time apply to God only metaphorically and must not be measured by changeable things. Hilary calls analogies such as human birth real but partial aids to weakness rather than descriptions. Even so, Gregory and Hilary defend material and creaturely illustrations against critics, and Gregory argues ad hominem that Eunomius himself uses physical analogies and concedes divine creation despite human limits. Owen and Waterland, by contrast, defend non-scriptural technical terms: Owen argues they are lawful and even necessary if they convey only Scripture's sense, and that the revealed thing must be settled before its terms; Waterland argues historically that metaphysics entered only to answer heretics, the Arians being the true subtle philosophers.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: But His very essence, as not to be conceived by the human intellect or expressed in words, this it has left untouched as a thing not to be made the subject of curious enquiry, ruling that it be revered in silence

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Philosophy and metaphysics were called in to its assistance; but not till heretics had shewn the way, and made it in a manner necessary for the Catholics to encounter them with their own weapons.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Whatever is Spoken of God According to Substance, is…
refs.quote: But position, and condition, and places, and times, are not said to be in God properly, but metaphorically and through similitudes.

ans.text:
Human words can truly speak about God, because God himself chose to speak to us in human language, but they never capture him fully, so we use them carefully and humbly. That one sentence holds both halves of the answer: our words are real and trustworthy, and our words are limited.

Start with the confidence. The Bible is full of ordinary words used of God: Father, Son, rock, shepherd, light, king. God did not wait for us to invent a heavenly language. He met us in ours. When Jesus calls God "Father," he is not using an empty picture. He is telling us something true. The same goes for the Bible's pictures that are plainly not literal. Psalm 19:1 says, "The heavens declare the glory of God." The sky has no voice, yet it really does tell us something, through its beauty and order. Scripture is not mistaken when it speaks this way. Pictures can carry truth.

Now the humility. God is not one more thing in the world, only bigger. He made everything, and nothing he made is his equal. Isaiah 40:18 asks, in effect, to whom we could possibly compare God. The expected answer is no one. So every comparison we draw from created things is like a finger pointing at the moon. It points in the right direction, but it is not the moon. Analogies help our weakness. They do not define God.

This matters especially for words like place and time. The Bible says God is "in heaven," that he is "enthroned between the cherubim," and that his years never end. These are true, but they are not about God sitting in a spot or growing older. Solomon admits in 1 Kings 8:27 that even the highest heavens cannot contain God, let alone the temple he had built. God is not boxed into a location or carried along by the clock as we are. When Scripture speaks of his dwelling or his years, it is describing his real presence and faithfulness in terms we can grasp.

The same care applies to the words "Father" and "Son." The Bible says the Son is "begotten" of the Father. In everyday life that means a child born from a parent. Applied to God, it keeps what is true in the picture: the Son shares the very nature of the Father, just as a human son is fully human like his father. But it leaves out everything that belongs to our weakness. There is no beginning in time, no mother, no change, no separation, no aging. Human birth gives real but partial light. The rule is simple. Whatever we say of an unchanging, eternal, self-sufficient God must not be measured by things that change, decay and depend on others. We already do this without thinking. Human builders can only shape materials that already exist, yet no one concludes that God cannot truly be Creator. In the same way, the limits of human fathering do not mean God cannot truly have a Son.

What about words that are not in the Bible, like "Trinity," "essence" (what God is, his one divine being), or "person" (who the Father, Son and Spirit each are)? Some sincere believers worry that these words bring in human philosophy and cloud the simple faith. That concern is understandable, but the words are not only allowed. They are often needed. Explaining any Bible verse means putting its meaning into our own words. If we could never do that, we could not even think about Scripture, let alone teach it. Such terms are fine when they say exactly what Scripture says, add nothing to it, and simply sum up what is clearly taught or plainly follows from it. Hebrews 1:3 even calls the Son "the exact representation of His nature," using a Greek word that later became one of these technical terms.

Historically, these words came into use defensively. When people began twisting the Bible with clever arguments, for instance claiming the Son is a lesser, created being, believers needed precise words to show what they did and did not mean. A word like "one in being with the Father" works like a fence around a field. The field is the Bible's teaching. The fence just protects it. And we should get the order right. First comes the question of what Scripture actually teaches: there is one God, and the Father, Son and Spirit are each fully God. If we agree on that, we can talk calmly about the best words to express it. If someone denies it, arguing over vocabulary misses the point.

Some care is wise with popular illustrations. Water as ice, liquid and steam, or a man who is a father, son and husband, can suggest that God is one person wearing three masks. A three-leaf clover can suggest that each person is only a third of God. Comparisons like two people sharing one human nature can help show that the Son and the Father share one nature. But like every illustration they fall short, since God is not three separate beings. Use pictures to help, then let them go.

It also helps to know that Scripture does not hand us a full definition of what God is in himself. 1 Timothy 6:16 says he dwells in unapproachable light. What the Bible asks of us is that we believe God exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him (Hebrews 11:6). It tells us real things about him: his power, his faithfulness, that he never changes, that he has no beginning or limit. But it leaves his innermost being beyond our reach, to be worshiped rather than dissected.

Finally, a word of comfort for careful believers. Not every mistake in speaking about God is equally serious. If someone credits the Father with a work the Bible ties more closely to the Son or the Spirit, that is a slip worth correcting. Still, it says nothing unworthy of God. The real danger is speaking of God as if he were a creature, or making things up about him. Speak of God with the words he has given, use helpful terms and pictures with a light grip, and let every word end in worship.

topics.title: Does God speak with words, and is human language fitting for Him?
topics.cmp: Covers what 'God said' means, whether God or angels use audible words, and whether God's adapting His speech to human languages is worthy of Him.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: can it be that in the case of the immaterial, and intangible, and, as Eunomius says, the Supreme and first Being, there is any need of words to indicate the thought of the Father and to make known His will to the Only-Begotten Son

ans.text:
Yes, God truly speaks, and He really does use human words to reach us, but He does not speak the way we do, with breath, a throat and a mouth. When the Bible says "God said," it tells us something true about God. It does not mean He has a body or that He needed a language before the world existed.

Take the first chapter of Genesis. "And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light" (Genesis 1:3). Who was there to hear? No people, no ears, no air to carry a sound. God did not need to give Himself instructions out loud, any more than you need to say "I will stand up" before you stand. The phrase "God said" is the Bible's way of showing that God's will and God's power are one and the same. He wills it, and it is. There is no struggle and no delay. We show what we want by speaking, so Scripture uses speech as a picture we can grasp. It shows how effortlessly God's will becomes reality.

We already read the Bible this way in other places. Scripture says God sees, hears and smells a pleasing offering, and that He has a strong arm. We rightly understand that God, who is spirit (John 4:24), has no eyes, ears or nose. These are true descriptions of what God does, expressed in terms we know. "God said" works the same way. The Bible even makes the point itself. Psalm 19 says "The heavens declare the glory of God" and "Day after day they pour forth speech," and then adds, "Without speech or language, their voice is not heard." Creation speaks without a sound, by showing God's glory to anyone with eyes to see it. In Exodus 14:15 the LORD asks Moses, "Why are you crying out to Me?" though the story records no words from Moses. The cry of his heart counted as a voice before God.

So what about the words God gave to Moses and the prophets? Those words are truly God's word, not merely human guesses about Him. Hebrews 1:1 says that "in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets." Sometimes God made Himself known in a vision or a dream. Sometimes He planted His message in a prophet's mind. At times He made an audible voice be heard, as at Mount Sinai or at Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:17). Even then, God was not using vocal cords. He was making His will known in a form people could receive. In every case the prophets were moved by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21), and what they wrote down in their own languages is exactly what God meant us to hear.

This matters for the Trinity too. The Father does not need to instruct the Son with sentences, as a boss briefs an employee. The Son shares fully in all that the Father is, so the Father's will is already wholly His. In fact the Son is Himself called "the Word" (John 1:1). He is the Father's perfect self-expression, not someone who has to be talked to. The same holds, in a lesser way, for angels. They are spirits, and they do not need sounds to worship God or understand one another. When Scripture records their words, it does so for our benefit.

Is it beneath God to stoop to Hebrew, Greek or English? Not at all. It is love. A good parent kneels down and speaks a child's language, and that is no loss of dignity. At Pentecost God's Spirit made the good news heard so that each person "heard them speaking his own language" (Acts 2:6). Some worry that human language is too tainted by sin to carry God's truth. But think how far God has come down to us already. The Word became flesh (John 1:14). For our sake the sinless Son was even made "to be sin on our behalf" (2 Corinthians 5:21) and became a curse for us. If He would share our sorrow and bear our sin, He will certainly share our speech, one of the finest gifts He ever gave us.

So we hold two things together. God is far above our words, and no sentence can contain Him. Yet He has truly spoken, in creation, through the prophets and above all in His Son. Because He chose to speak our language, we can trust what He has said and answer Him in our own words.

title: The Divine Nature and Attributes
desc: God's simplicity, immutability, eternity, incorporeality, impassibility, omnipresence and self-sufficiency, and how these bear on Trinitarian doctrine.

topics.title: Is God simple, so that His attributes and names are identical with His essence?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that God is simple and without parts, change or accidents, so His attributes are not things He has apart from Himself. Augustine states this most fully: God's greatness, wisdom, goodness, justice, life and love are His essence, and 'to be' is 'to be wise' and 'to be great.' He argues from the non-participation of the highest good, from contrast with the changeable soul and with bodies, and from the impossibility of even inseparable accidents in God. Irenaeus (against Gnostic emanations), Hilary (no transitions or parts) and Owen (the attributes are essentially one, distinguished only by respects of their exercise, so that vindictive justice is an essential property and not a free act of will) broadly agree. The clearest divergence is over the meaning of the divine names. Augustine says that naming one attribute is naming all. Gregory of Nyssa, arguing against Eunomius from Scripture's many titles and from the analogy of one soul skilled in many sciences, insists that each name keeps its own distinct sense while referring to one simple subject, though he allows that paired affirmative and negative names such as 'Life' and 'unreceptive of death' signify the same thing. Jonathan Edwards departs further, restricting the maxim 'everything in God is God' to real attributes and not mere modalities, and identifying God's understanding and love with the distinct divine Persons; Novatian stresses instead that God surpasses all virtues as their Parent.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: for it will not be possible, if God is essentially Father, to exclude the Son from a relationship to Him thus essential.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of…
refs.quote: And since in the Divine simplicity, to be wise is nothing else than to be, therefore wisdom there is the same as essence.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: as they are all essentially the same in him, and considered only under a different habitude or respect, as they are exerted by acts of his will

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible's God is not built out of parts, and His goodness, wisdom, power and love are not extra qualities attached to Him. They are simply what He is. Christians call this the simplicity of God. Here "simple" does not mean easy to understand. It means not made of pieces, not put together.

Think about how it works with us. A person can exist and still lack wisdom. Later they may gain it, and in old age they may lose some of it. Our goodness, patience and strength come and go, because they are qualities we have, not what we are. God is not like that. He did not become wise, and He cannot become less loving. Scripture does not only say that God has love. It says "God is love" (1 John 4:8) and "God is light; in Him there is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5). Jesus does not just teach the truth or give life. He says, "I am the way and the truth and the life" (John 14:6).

There is a good reason for this. If God were good only by sharing in some goodness outside Himself, that goodness would be bigger and more basic than God. Then it, not He, would be the true highest good. But nothing stands above God. He is not great because He measures up to some standard of greatness. He is the standard. All the goodness we meet in people, in creation and in a kind word is borrowed goodness. It points back to the One who is goodness itself. So Paul says God is not served "as if He needed anything" (Acts 17:25). Nothing is added to Him, because He lacks nothing.

The same goes for God's life. We live by breath, food and a heartbeat we did not make. God's life is not received from anywhere. Jesus says the Father "has life in Himself" (John 5:26). When God told Moses His name, "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14), He showed that He simply is. He depends on nothing. And because He is not assembled from parts, nothing can come apart or change in Him. He is "the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow" (James 1:17).

This brings up a natural question. If God's wisdom just is His goodness, and His goodness just is His power, do all the words we use for God mean the same thing? No. When Scripture calls God just, merciful, patient, holy and almighty, each word tells us something real and different. The names are many because our minds are small. We cannot take God in with one glance, so we come at the one reality from many sides. Picture one person who is a good doctor, a fine musician and a patient teacher. They are still one person, not three people stitched together, yet the three descriptions do not mean the same thing. Or think of sunlight, which lights a room and also warms it. It is one light, though we name its effects differently. Our words for God are true, but they never capture Him fully. They are not compliments that add to His honor, since nothing can be added. They are handholds that help us know and worship Him.

Some names say what God is: good, wise, true. Others say what He is not: invisible, immortal, unchanging, without limits. These "negative" names guard us from shrinking God down to our size. Neither kind divides Him. Other names, like Creator, Lord or Savior, describe how God relates to us and to His world. When God created, the world changed. God did not gain a new part.

Simplicity also helps with a real pastoral worry: is God at war with Himself? In His works, His justice and His mercy can look like two different forces pulling in opposite ways. One punishes sin, the other forgives. But in God they are not rivals. His justice is a good justice, and His goodness is a just goodness. The cross shows this most clearly. There God is both "just and the justifier" of those who believe in Jesus (Romans 3:26). He did not set aside His justice to be merciful. He fulfilled it. That is why we can trust God completely. There is no hidden side of Him that might turn against His promises.

How does this fit with the Trinity? Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not three parts or three slices of God, as if each held a third of the divine nature. That would make God a composite after all. Each person is wholly God, sharing the one undivided being. "The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). What distinguishes the persons is not that they own different pieces. It is how they relate to one another: the Father begets the Son, which means the Son eternally comes from the Father, sharing His very nature as a son shares his father's. The Spirit proceeds, or comes forth, from God. So the Father is not wiser than the Son, nor the Son more loving than the Spirit. The one wisdom and love that God is belongs fully to each.

Sincere Christians have discussed how far to press this teaching. Some stress that God's attributes are truly one in Him and differ only in how we grasp them and in their effects in the world. Others, especially in parts of the Eastern church, distinguish between God's inner being, which is beyond us, and His real activity or "energies," through which He truly makes Himself known and shared. They want to protect both God's mystery and our real fellowship with Him. In more recent times, some have asked whether a fully simple God can respond to prayer and grieve over sin, as Scripture shows. Defenders answer that God's responses flow from His unchanging character, not from new moods arising in Him. In fact, these discussions share a lot of common ground. God is one, not a collection of parts. He depends on nothing. His attributes never conflict.

So when you pray, you are not speaking to a committee of qualities, or to a God who is loving on some days and just on others. You are speaking to the One who is all of His goodness all at once. Everything He says to you comes from the whole of who He is.

topics.title: Is the Trinity compatible with divine simplicity?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the point affirm that God is simple and uncompounded. Irenaeus, Hilary, and Novatian describe this positively: God is wholly mind, light, and will rather than a set of faculties or members. Hilary grounds it in God's changelessness ("I am, and I change not"), and Novatian in God's immortality and indissolubility. Augustine reasons similarly that nothing changeable is simple, so no creature is truly simple and only the unchangeable divine substance is. Gregory of Nyssa alone presses simplicity directly into the Trinitarian question, arguing on philosophical grounds that simplicity admits no degrees: imperfect simplicity would be composite, so the Son and Spirit must be simple in exactly the same sense as the Father. Daniel Waterland takes a markedly different, more defensive and sceptical line: he holds that our idea of simplicity is obscure and drawn from defective metaphysics rather than Scripture, and he turns the objection back on Clarke, whose own supposition of extended parts in God would undercut it, rather than building a positive account of simplicity as the Fathers do.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For who does not know that, to be exact, simplicity in the case of the Holy Trinity admits of no degrees.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: He is a simple, uncompounded Being, without diverse members, and altogether like, and equal to himself, since He is wholly understanding, and wholly spirit, and wholly thought

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Scripture says little of it: we have took it chiefly from metaphysics, which are short and defective.

ans.text:
Yes. The Trinity does not make God a compound being, because the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not three parts that together add up to God. Each is wholly God, and the one God they share is not assembled from pieces.

First, what "divine simplicity" means. It does not mean God is easy to understand. It means God is not made of parts. A car has an engine, wheels and seats. A person has a body, a mind, feelings and habits. Things like that are put together, and what is put together can change, wear out or fall apart. God is not like that. His wisdom, power, goodness and love are not separate compartments inside him, like rooms in a house. He does not have love in the way a person has a mood. The Bible says simply that "God is love" (1 John 4:8) and that "God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5). All that God is, he is wholly and at once. His knowing and his willing do not need to negotiate with each other. He is whole, all the way through.

This is not abstract guesswork. It follows from what Scripture says about God. He is one: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). He does not change (Malachi 3:6; James 1:17). He depends on nothing and no one, since he made all things. A being built from parts would depend on its parts and on whatever holds them together, and it could in principle come apart. The living God cannot. Only God is simple in this full sense. Every creature, even an angel or a human soul, is changeable, and so is in some way composed.

So how can God be three? The key is that the Persons are not slices of a pie or ingredients in a recipe. If the Father were one third of God, the Son another third and the Spirit the last third, then God would indeed be a compound, and none of them would be fully God. The Bible will not allow that. Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). Paul says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). The Son is not a portion of God. He is the whole undivided divine nature, just as the Father is, and just as the Spirit is. There are not three gods and not three pieces of one God. There is one God, wholly present in each Person.

What then makes the Persons distinct, if not different parts? It is how they are related to one another. The Father begets the Son; that is, he eternally gives the Son his very life and being, not by making him the way he makes creatures, but the way a father shares his own nature with a son. The Son is begotten of the Father. The Spirit proceeds, or comes forth, from the Father. Jesus says, "For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). These relations do not add anything to the divine nature, as if the Son had an extra ingredient the Father lacks. They describe who is from whom. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit, yet what each one is, is the one simple God.

Every comparison falls short here, but consider a modest one. When a person speaks a true thought, the word is not a separate thing bolted onto the mind. It is the mind expressing itself. Scripture calls the Son the Word who was with God and was God (John 1:1). In God this is perfect: the Word is not a lesser copy or a fragment of the Father, but the full expression of all that the Father is.

This also answers whether one Person might be "more simple" than another, as though the Father were perfectly whole and the Son and Spirit a little less so. That idea does not work. Simplicity cannot come in degrees. Something that is partly put together is simply put together. To say the Son is less simple would be to say he is made of parts, and so is not truly God. It would also mean picturing God as a subject with qualities added in greater or smaller amounts, more wisdom here and less power there. But there is no more and less in God. The Son is simple in exactly the same sense the Father is, because he has the very same nature. The same goes for the Spirit.

One natural question: did the Son not take a human body, which certainly has parts? Yes. In becoming man he took to himself a real human nature, body and soul. But he did not stop being God, and his divine nature was not changed or divided. The one Person, the Son, now lives in two natures. The human nature is composed, as all creaturely things are. The divine nature remains whole and simple.

Sincere Christians have sometimes differed on how far to press the idea of simplicity. Some have worried that saying God's attributes are all one thing makes it hard to say anything meaningful about him, or that our notions of simplicity come more from philosophy than from the Bible, and so should be held loosely. Others answer that Scripture's teaching that God is one, unchanging and dependent on nothing requires us to deny that he is built from parts, while admitting we cannot fully picture what this means. Either way, Christians across the centuries have agreed on the main point: whatever simplicity means, it cannot be used against the Trinity, because the three Persons are not three components of God.

So the Trinity and God's simplicity belong together. God is not a committee, not a compound and not a patchwork. He is one undivided God, and that one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each wholly God and none a part of God. This is why we can trust him completely: there is nothing in him that could come apart, and nothing in one Person that is missing in another.

topics.title: Do the divine attributes belong equally to Father, Son and Holy Spirit?
topics.cmp: Covers the scriptural evidence that eternity, omniscience and incomprehensibility are ascribed alike to all three Persons.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: No one knoweth the Son save the Father. – Matt. 11:27. Lord, thou knowest all things. – John 21:17.

ans.text:
Yes. Everything that makes God God, such as being eternal, knowing all things, and being beyond our full understanding, belongs fully and equally to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. They do not split these qualities among themselves, and none has more of them than the others. This is because there is only one God, and the three Persons share the one divine nature, or 'essence', which simply means what God is.

Theologians call these qualities 'attributes'. An attribute is not a part of God, like a slice of a pie. It is a true description of who God is. God does not merely have eternity; he is eternal. So if the Son and the Spirit are truly God, and not lesser beings standing next to him, they must be eternal, all-knowing and beyond our grasp just as the Father is. The Bible shows that this is exactly how it speaks about them.

Take eternity first. In Isaiah 44:6 the LORD says, "I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me." That is a claim no creature could make. Yet in Revelation 22:13 the risen Jesus says of himself, "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End." He takes God's own title. John 1:1 tells us the Word already was in the beginning, and the Word was God. The prophet Micah, foretelling the ruler to be born in Bethlehem, says his origins reach back to days of old, to eternity (Micah 5:2). The Spirit is included too. Hebrews 9:14 says that Christ "through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God." The word 'eternal' there is the same word Scripture uses for God himself, the one who has no beginning and no end. The Spirit did not come into being at some point. He always was.

Next, knowledge. When Peter is restored after denying Jesus, he says to him plainly, "Lord, You know all things" (John 21:17). Jesus does not correct him. Paul says that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). And the Spirit, Paul writes, "searches all things, even the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10). Think about that. Only someone with God's own mind could search the depths of God. Isaiah 40:13 asks who has ever directed the Spirit of the LORD or taught him as his counselor, and the answer is no one.

Finally, incomprehensibility. This big word does not mean God cannot be known at all. He has truly made himself known. It means no creature can ever take in the whole of him, the way you cannot pour the ocean into a cup. Jesus says in Matthew 11:27, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." Notice the balance. The Son knows the Father completely, which only God could do. And the Son is known completely only by the Father, which means he is as far beyond our full understanding as the Father is. The Spirit, too, knows the deep things of God that no one else can search out.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, three Persons each being eternal and all-knowing does not give us three Gods. There are not three eternities or three minds side by side. There is one eternal, all-knowing God, and the Father, Son and Spirit are each that one God. What tells the Persons apart is not their qualities but how they relate to one another: the Father is Father of the Son, the Son is Son of the Father, and the Spirit comes from God as the Spirit of both.

Second, someone may ask about Mark 13:32, where Jesus says the Son does not know the day or the hour of his return. Christians have long understood this in light of the incarnation. The eternal Son truly became human, with a real human mind that grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52). He spoke here as the one who had taken on our limits for our sake. That does not cancel what he is as God, any more than his getting tired cancels that he upholds all things.
