Third, it is easy to picture the Father as the 'real' God and the Son and Spirit as somehow junior. The Bible does show an order among them: the Father sends the Son, and the Son and Father send the Spirit. But being sent does not make anyone less divine. The one who is sent is just as eternal, just as wise and just as worthy of worship as the one who sends.

Why does this matter for ordinary faith? Because it means that when you trust Jesus, you are trusting one who knows all things, including you. When the Spirit lives in you, the eternal God himself lives in you. And when you pray to the Father, you come to a God who has no beginning and will never fail. We worship one God, fully known by himself, always beyond us, and yet truly given to us in the Son and the Spirit.

topics.title: How does God's nature transcend creatures, and does He need anything from them?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that God transcends creatures and needs nothing from them, but they come at this from different angles. Irenaeus has the most to say on God's self-sufficiency. Arguing from Scripture (Psalm 50, Isaiah, the prophets) and from the Word's eternal glorifying of the Father, he holds that creation, commandments and sacrifices exist for man's benefit, not God's. He also insists that immortality and life are gifts creatures receive by participation and by God's will, not possessions they have by nature. Hilary reaches the same conclusion about God's not needing creatures by reasoning about God as uncaused Source and Container of all. He adds that God is impassible and not bound by nature's laws. Owen agrees, but grounds the point in the Trinity: the Father's eternal delight in the Son makes His love for the saints wholly free. Augustine stresses the difference between spiritual and bodily being and is the most philosophical in method. He warns against conceiving God by bodily or psychological analogy, and argues that union with a creature makes the creature greater but not God. Gregory of Nyssa focuses on the limits of human language and thought. He says privative terms and God's being 'above every name' show His superiority, that a First Cause can depend on nothing, and that creatures advance endlessly by participation while God lacks no good. Ambrose adds that God alone is sinless by nature. Waterland differs in tone from the rest: on whether divine infinity means infinite spatial extension, he suspends judgment rather than affirming a position, citing the silence of Scripture and the Fathers.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: for he from whom death is not absent is not in his essence immortal. But again; if these terms signify the absence neither of death nor of destruction, either they are applied falsely to the God overall, or else they comprise within themselves some different meaning.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: This Work is Written Against Those Who Sophistically…
refs.quote: For he who thinks, for instance, that God is white or red, is in error; and yet these things are found in the body. Again, he who thinks of God as now forgetting and now remembering, or anything of the same kind, is none the less in error

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: so the soul herself is not life, but partakes in that life bestowed upon her by God.

ans.text:
God does not need anything from us at all, and that is exactly what makes His love for us such good news. He is not one more being in the universe, only bigger and stronger. He is the One who gives every other being its existence, while He Himself received His existence from no one.

Start with the most basic difference. Everything we see once began, and it keeps going only because something outside it keeps it going. You had parents. The sun burns fuel. Even angels were made. God is different. When Moses asked His name, God answered, "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14). He simply is. Psalm 90:2 says that "from everlasting to everlasting" He is God. Nothing caused Him, nothing holds Him up, and nothing can wear Him down. He is the first cause of everything else and is caused by nothing.

This is why Paul could tell the thinkers of Athens that God is not "served by human hands, as if He needed anything," because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything (Acts 17:24-25). Think of a child who buys his father a birthday present with money the father gave him. The father is glad, but he is not made richer. That is our situation before God. In Psalm 50 God tells His people, in effect, that if He were hungry He would not tell them, because every animal in the forest and the whole world already belong to Him. He does not eat the meat of bulls or drink the blood of goats.

So why did God ask for sacrifices, offerings, and obedience? For our sake, not His. The prophets keep saying that what God really wants is faithfulness and mercy, not the animals themselves (Hosea 6:6). His commands are like a doctor's instructions. The doctor gains nothing when you follow them. You gain your health. In the same way, worship, thanksgiving, and obedience are the path by which we receive what we lack: friendship with God and a share in His goodness. When we give, God delights to give back far more. Proverbs 19:17 says that kindness to the poor is a loan to the Lord, and Jesus says that whatever we do for the least of His people we do for Him (Matthew 25:40). Paul asks who has ever given God something first, so that God would owe him repayment (Romans 11:35). No one has. All our giving is a response to His.

Did God make us because He was lonely, or because He wanted more glory? No. Here the Trinity matters. Before the world existed, the Father loved the Son, and the Son glorified the Father, in the fellowship of the Spirit. Jesus speaks of the glory He had with the Father "before the world existed" and says the Father loved Him "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:5, 24). God has never been alone or lacking love. He did not create us to fill an empty space in Himself. He created us so that He would have someone to share His goodness with. That makes His love completely free. He loves you not because He needs you, but because He chooses to. A love like that cannot be used up, and it does not depend on what you can offer in return.

Nor does our being joined to God make God bigger. When two buckets of water are poured together, you get more water. But when a person is united to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:17), only the person grows. We become better, wiser, and more alive, while God remains just as full as He always was. The same is true of goodness. No created mind can make itself good. It becomes good only by turning toward the good that God is. The same is true of life itself. Our souls do not have life on their own. We share in life that God gives. Scripture says the first man "became a living being" when God breathed into him (Genesis 2:7).

This is why Scripture says God "alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light" (1 Timothy 6:16). Angels and human souls will last forever, but only because God wills to keep them in being and gives them that gift. In God, unending life is His very nature. In us, it is something we receive. The Son of God took on our mortal nature so that we could come to share in His deathless life.

Because God is so different from creatures, we have to be careful how we think about Him. Jesus says "God is Spirit" (John 4:24). He has no body, color, or size. He is not tired one day and fresh the next, or forgetful and then reminded. He does not learn things the way we do, through eyes, ears, or reports from others. He simply knows. When the Bible speaks of God's arm or His eyes, it uses pictures from our world to tell us real things about Him: His power, His care, His attention. But we should not imagine Him as a very large human being. In the same way, His "infinity" does not mainly mean that He is spread out very far, like endless space. It means that He has no limits or defects of any kind. He is not hemmed in by place, by time, or even by the laws of nature that He Himself made. Solomon confessed that even the highest heavens cannot contain Him (1 Kings 8:27).

This also explains why so many words for God are negative words: immortal, invisible, unchanging, without sin. These are not empty words. They tell us that God is free of every weakness that marks created things. Every creature, left to itself, can fail and fall. God alone is good and holy by His very nature. Saying what He is not is one way of pointing to how full and perfect He is.

A common worry is that this makes God distant or cold. If He needs nothing, does He care? Sincere Christians have discussed how to speak of God's feelings. Some stress that Scripture's language of God's grief and joy shows that He is truly moved. Others stress that God is never overcome or changed by anything outside Him, as we are, and that this is what makes His love steady and safe. Both sides agree that God's love is real and never fails. His fullness is not coldness. A fountain does not need the people who drink from it, but it pours out water all the same.

Another worry is that if God is beyond understanding, we cannot know Him at all. That is not what Scripture teaches. We can truly know God, because He has made Himself known, above all in Jesus Christ. What we cannot do is grasp Him completely, the way we can understand a machine or define a word. Isaiah 55:9 says His thoughts are higher than ours as the heavens are higher than the earth. Paul, after explaining the gospel at length, ends in wonder at the depth of God's riches, wisdom, and knowledge (Romans 11:33). If the whole world could not hold a full account of God's works (John 21:25), our small minds cannot hold God Himself. That is no loss to His glory. Running out of words is itself a way of praising Him, since He is above every name.

One last point. Everything exists in God, because nothing could exist without Him. But not everyone is with God in friendship. The deepest misery a person can know is to live every moment held up by God while ignoring Him. The God who needs nothing invites us to turn to Him, know Him, and love Him. He does not do this because He would be poorer without us. He does it because we are poor without Him, and He freely wants to make us rich.

topics.title: Is God eternal and unchangeable, beyond time and increase?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that God is eternal and unchangeable: Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Athanasius, Novatian, Ambrose and Irenaeus each deny that the divine nature has a beginning, increase, loss, temporal succession, deliberation over the uncertain, or emptiness. They argue in different ways. Gregory of Nyssa works mainly through philosophical analysis of the creature–Creator contrast: creation is extended through temporal intervals, God contains and surpasses the ages, and God's attributes form one compact whole. He uses this against the Eunomian position, holding that Fatherhood is eternal and that cause and caused in the Godhead involve no before and after. He also argues that "without beginning" and "without end" are not equivalent and cannot both define God's essence without making Him a composite of contradictions, while appealing to Scripture's "I am He that is." Augustine concentrates on how temporal predicates such as "Lord," "refuge" and "Father" can begin to apply to God. He holds that they are relative and that all the change lies in the creature, using the analogy of money becoming a price or pledge, and he stresses God's simultaneous, non-successive knowledge and the identity of eternity, truth and love in God. Athanasius applies immutability against the Arians: a Trinity built by addition could also gain or lose, and creation sets no precedent for God becoming Father. Novatian reasons that anything with a beginning would be inferior to what preceded it, and he links incorruptibility and immortality. Ambrose and Irenaeus contribute narrower points: scriptural marks of Godhead and the certainty of divine counsel for Ambrose, and the denial that God is a vacuity for Irenaeus.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: Since, then, it belongs to the creation to have a beginning, that will be alien from the uncreated nature which belongs to the creation.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For probably it will receive some fresh accession, and so on without limit, since at first and at starting it took its consistence by way of accessions. And so undoubtedly it may decrease on the contrary, for what is added plainly admits of being subtracted.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It…
refs.quote: And this by its drawing near to partake of His nature, truth, and blessedness, yet not by His increasing in His own nature, truth and blessedness.

ans.text:
Yes. God has no beginning and no end, and he does not grow, shrink, improve or wear out. He is always fully what he is. The Bible makes this clear, and it matters for our faith: the God we trust today is exactly the God who made the promises.

Start with eternity. Moses prays in Psalm 90:2, "Before the mountains were born or You brought forth the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting You are God." God did not come into being at some point. If he had, something would have been there before him, and he would not be above all things. Nothing comes before God, so nothing is over him. When he revealed his name to Moses as "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14), he described himself as the one who simply is. He does not borrow his existence from anyone. That is why Hebrews 11:6 says that whoever comes to God must believe that he exists. Real, unborrowed existence is one of the marks of true God.

Eternity means more than lasting a very long time. Our lives are spread out in pieces. We had a yesterday that is gone, and we wait for a tomorrow we do not have yet. God is not like that. He does not lose his past or wait for his future. He has his whole life all at once and fully. Peter says that with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like a day (2 Peter 3:8). Time is something God made along with the world. He is not caught inside it the way we are, any more than an author is trapped on one page of his book.

This also shapes how God knows things. We learn step by step. We notice, remember, and guess about what is coming. God does not pick up new facts as events happen. Through Isaiah he says he declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10). He sees all things, past, present and future, in one complete look. So when Scripture speaks of God's counsel or plans, it does not mean he is anxiously weighing uncertain options. His wisdom is never caught off guard.

Now unchangeableness. God says in Malachi 3:6, "Because I, the LORD, do not change, you descendants of Jacob have not been destroyed." James 1:17 calls him the Father of lights, "with whom there is no change or shifting shadow." Psalm 102 contrasts the heavens, which will wear out like clothing, with God: "You remain the same, and Your years will never end." This is why God is called immortal and incorruptible. Nothing can decay in him, and nothing can be taken from him.

Why can't God grow? To grow, you must lack something you later gain. But God is already complete. Paul told the people of Athens that God is not served by human hands "as if He needed anything" (Acts 17:25). He gives life and breath to everything. He does not receive it. And if God could gain something, he could also lose something. A God who could get better could also get worse. The God of the Bible is not like that. He is perfectly good, wise and strong, and he always has been.

The same is true of God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Father did not become a Father at some point. The Son did not show up later. John 1:1 says the Word was with God in the beginning and was God. Jesus speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5). The Father is the source of the Son, but there was never a time before the Son. Being a father and a son only takes time for us, because we are creatures. In God it is eternal. God is not a group that grew by adding members. He is always the same complete Trinity, with nothing added and nothing lost.

A natural question follows. God made the world at a certain moment. He became our refuge when we fled to him. He became our Father when we were born again (John 1:12). Doesn't that mean God changed? The answer is that the change happens on our side, not his. Think of stepping out of the shade into the sunshine. You are suddenly warm and in the light, but the sun did not change. You moved. Or think of a coin that becomes the price of something when you hand it over. A new word now fits the coin, but the coin itself is the same. In the same way, when a sinner turns to God, the sinner is truly made new. God is now rightly called that person's Father and Lord. But God has not become something he was not. The new name describes a new relationship that began with a change in us. Psalm 90:1 says, "Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations." We came home to him. He did not have to rebuild himself to receive us. Even when we are joined to the Lord and become one spirit with him, we are the ones lifted up to share in his life. He does not become more blessed.

This does not mean God is cold, frozen or unmoved by his people. The unchangeable God acts, speaks, rescues, grieves over sin and rejoices over the repentant. The Bible sometimes speaks of God relenting, as with Nineveh. These passages describe God from our side. When people change their ways, his unchanging justice and mercy meet them differently. His steady character is exactly what makes him responsive in a reliable way. A friend whose love never changes is not lifeless. He is trustworthy. And when the eternal Son became man, he took a real human nature that was born, grew and suffered. Yet he did not stop being God or lose anything of his divine nature. Hebrews 13:8 can still say, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever."

Sincere Christians do differ on some details here. Some today think God lives through time alongside us, moment by moment. They say this makes better sense of the Bible's stories of God responding, and of a real relationship with him. Others hold to the historic teaching that God is beyond the before-and-after of time. They point out that time belongs to creation, that God declares the end from the beginning, and that a God who moves through time would be gaining and losing moments. Both sides agree that God has no beginning or end, never fails or decays, and never goes back on his character or promises.

That is the heart of it, and it is good news. Everything around us changes, and we change too. But the God who loved us in Christ is not having a good day that might turn bad. He is the same faithful God, without beginning, without end, and without a shadow of change.

topics.title: Does God have a body or passions, and how is Scripture's bodily language to be read?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the question agree that God has no body and that Scripture's bodily and emotional language is not to be taken literally. Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary, Novatian and Ambrose all treat members, speech, repentance and similar terms as accommodations to human weakness that point beyond themselves, and Athanasius and Waterland likewise reject anything that would make God bodily, passible or divided into parts. They differ in how they ground and decode this language. Augustine argues from the incorporeal intellect as the best part of human nature and from the identity of God's being with his attributes. Gregory of Nyssa argues philosophically that form and composition entail dissolution, and adds analogies such as speaking to the deaf by signs; he reads speech as signifying God's will and each anthropomorphism as fitted to the hearers' spiritual state. Hilary and Novatian read each member as a real incorporeal power (hand as creative activity, eye as knowledge), with Novatian stressing that God is 'all eye, all ear', whereas Ambrose distinctively takes such terms, like 'Right Hand', as signifying the inseparable oneness of the Trinity. Bickersteth is the outlier in emphasis: rather than treating jealousy as non-literal, he defends it as a perfect, flawless form of a just human jealousy, and Irenaeus applies a related interpretive principle that seeks types or right meaning rather than condemning the text.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: We, more consistently, suppose three Persons equal, in all respects; none of them singly part of God; but every one perfect God.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: since in the Godhead are neither members nor parts, but are expressions of the oneness of the Godhead, that we may believe that it is impossible for either the Son or the Holy Spirit to be separated from God the Father

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: What the Author Entreats from God, What from the Reader.…
refs.quote: What, therefore, we do not find in that which is our own best, we ought not to seek in Him who is far better than that best of ours

ans.text:
No. God does not have a body, and he is not pushed around by moods and feelings the way we are. When the Bible speaks of God's hands, eyes, throne or anger, it is using pictures from our world to tell us true things about a God who is far greater than those pictures.

Start with what Jesus said to the woman at the well: "God is Spirit" (John 4:24). A spirit is not made of physical stuff. It has no size or shape and cannot be weighed, measured or seen. After his resurrection Jesus told his frightened disciples that "a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have" (Luke 24:39). Scripture also calls God "invisible" (1 Timothy 1:17). Solomon, praying at the dedication of the temple, admitted that even the highest heaven cannot contain God, let alone a building (1 Kings 8:27). Something with a body takes up space in one place and not another. God fills all things and is not boxed in anywhere.

Think of it this way. The finest thing in you is not your body but your mind: your power to think, know and love. A thought has no color, no height, no left side and right side. If even the best part of us is not made of parts and pieces, we should not imagine that God, who made us, is built like a statue.

Then why does the Bible talk about God's arm, his fingers, his eyes and his feet? Because God speaks to us in our own language, the way a loving parent stoops to talk to a small child. Each bodily word points to something real in God. His "hand" or "arm" means his power to act, as when he brought Israel out of Egypt. His "eyes" mean that he sees and knows everything. His "ears" mean that he hears every prayer. The Bible itself shows this. In Luke 11:20 Jesus says he drives out demons "by the finger of God," and in Matthew 12:28 the same saying reads "by the Spirit of God." The finger is a picture of God's power at work, not a part of a hand. When Psalm 91 says we may hide under his wings, no one thinks God has feathers. In the same way, God's "throne" and "footstool" (Isaiah 66:1) show his rule over all things, not a chair in the sky.

In fact, God needs no bodily organs at all. We need eyes to see and hands to work because our thoughts accomplish nothing until our bodies carry them out. God's will is effective on its own. He spoke, and it was so. He knows our thoughts before we speak them. You could say he is all eye, all ear and all hand, because nothing limits his seeing, hearing or acting.

What about God's feelings? Scripture speaks of his anger, his compassion, his jealousy, even his "regret." Christians have historically taught that God is "impassible." This word does not mean he is cold or uncaring. It means God is not at the mercy of passions. Nothing outside him can sweep over him, change his mood or make him less than he was. Our emotions rise and fall, often without our consent, and they can twist our judgment. God is not like that. "I, the LORD, do not change," he says in Malachi 3:6.

A helpful picture is sunlight. The same light that hurts sore eyes is a delight to healthy ones. The change is in the eyes, not in the sun. In the same way, God is always perfectly holy and perfectly loving. When we turn from sin, we find him merciful. When we persist in evil, we meet his wrath. The change is in us. His anger is not a flash of temper. It is his settled, holy opposition to evil. His jealousy is not insecure envy. It is the right and pure claim of the One who made us and deserves our whole heart, like a faithful husband's rightful claim on his wife. His love is not weaker for being steady. It is stronger, because it never runs out or wears off.

The Bible gives us a clear example of how to read this kind of language. In 1 Samuel 15:11 God says he regrets making Saul king. Yet only a few verses later, in 1 Samuel 15:29, we are told that the Glory of Israel does not change his mind, because he is not a man. Both statements are true together. The first describes how things look from our side: God's dealings with Saul turned from blessing to judgment. The second tells us what God is like in himself (see also Numbers 23:19). God uses language like this for our good. Warnings of his anger hold sinners back, the picture of his pity keeps the fallen from despair, and his delight encourages those who walk with him.

Sincere Christians do differ on how far to press this. Some today hold that God truly experiences something like emotional responses as events unfold, because the Bible's language about his grief and joy feels so personal and alive. Others hold to the older teaching that God's love, joy and anger are real but are not changes in him, because a God who could be moved or harmed by his creatures would not be the unchanging, all-sufficient God of Scripture. Both sides agree that God is not a cold, distant force. He is the living God who truly loves, truly hates evil, and truly hears.

One last point keeps all this from being misunderstood. God the Son did take a real human body when he became man in Jesus Christ. He was hungry and tired, he wept, and he suffered and died on the cross. This does not mean God's divine nature has a body. The eternal Son, who is fully God, added to himself a true human nature, and in that human nature he truly suffered for us. That is the wonder of the gospel. The God who has no body took one so that he could save us in it.

So when you read about God's strong arm, his watchful eyes or his burning anger, take these words seriously. They tell you the truth about him. But let them lift your mind upward, to a God who is greater than every picture, and who has drawn near to us in Christ.

topics.title: Is God present everywhere without being contained in a place?
topics.cmp: All the authors (Hilary of Poitiers, Novatian, Gregory of Nyssa, Irenaeus of Lyons, Athanasius and Augustine) agree that God is everywhere and confined by no place, containing all things rather than being contained, though they draw different consequences from this. Hilary and Novatian ground it most directly in Scripture, both citing the Psalm's 'heaven, hell, the sea'; Novatian, along with Irenaeus, also reads 'heaven is my throne' against any bodily or local enclosure. Hilary argues from God's being Spirit, infinite and immeasurable, while Gregory of Nyssa argues philosophically from the nature of motion as leaving one place for another. Their applications differ: Novatian uses the point against the Father coming from a place, which he ties to the Sabellian heresy, whereas Gregory uses it to refer the Son's 'going' to His human body. Augustine and Athanasius instead reinterpret spatial language: for Augustine, nearness to God is by likeness and the 'place by me' of Exodus 33 is the Church, and for Athanasius, creatures' distance from God is one of nature, not place.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: There is no space where God is not; space does not exist apart from Him. He is in heaven, in hell, beyond the seas; dwelling in all things and enveloping all.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: And That, Although Scripture Often Changes the Divine…
refs.quote: when the feet it is unfolded that He fills all things, and that there is not any place where God is not.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and…
refs.quote: For approach to God is not by intervals of place, but by likeness, and withdrawal from Him is by unlikeness.

ans.text:
Yes. God is present everywhere, all at once, and no place can hold Him in. Solomon understood this when he dedicated the temple in Jerusalem. He prayed, "Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You" (1 Kings 8:27), and he added that this house he had built could hardly do so either.

The Bible says this in many ways. In Jeremiah 23:24 the Lord asks, "Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?" In Isaiah 66:1 He says, "Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool." That is not a picture of a giant sitting on a chair. It is a way of saying that the whole universe is like furniture in His presence. If all of creation cannot box Him in, a building or a mountain certainly cannot. Psalm 139 makes it personal. The writer asks where he could go to get away from God's Spirit. He answers that if he went up to the heavens, God is there. If he went down to the grave, God is there. If he fled to the far side of the sea, God's hand would still guide and hold him.

It helps to see why this is so. Things that are made, like rocks, bodies and planets, take up space. They are here and not there. God is not a made thing. Jesus says in John 4:24 that "God is Spirit." God has no body that could be in one spot and absent from another. He made space itself, so He is not one more object sitting inside it. A better way to say it is that God holds all things, rather than being held by anything. Paul told the people of Athens that God "is not far from any one of us," because "in Him we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:27-28).

One common misunderstanding is to picture God spread out through the universe like air, with a little of Him here and a little over there. That is not the teaching. God has no parts to divide up. All of God is fully present wherever He is, and He is everywhere. He is fully with a believer praying in a hospital room, and just as fully with another on the other side of the world.

A second misunderstanding goes the other way. God being everywhere does not mean God is the same thing as the world, or that the trees and stars are part of God. He fills creation without being mixed into it, the way an author is present on every page of his book without becoming paper and ink.

Then why does the Bible speak of God being "in heaven," or dwelling in the temple, or "coming down" to see something? These are real ways God made Himself known. They are not limits on where He is. When Scripture says God was present in the temple, it means He chose to meet His people there and to show His glory and favor there. It does not mean He was missing from the rest of the world. When God is said to "come down" or "go up," the words describe something God does, such as judging, rescuing or revealing Himself. They do not describe Him traveling across a distance. There is nowhere He is not already.

The same is true when we think about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Father does not send the Son from one region of space to another. When the Son became a man, His human body truly walked from Galilee to Jerusalem and truly ascended. Yet as God, the Son never stopped upholding all things everywhere (Colossians 1:17). When Jesus said, "I am going to the Father," His human nature was really going. His divine nature had nowhere to go that it did not already fill. Likewise, the Spirit's coming to live in believers is a new and special way of being present to bless and change them. It is not God arriving from somewhere far away.

This raises a fair question. If God is everywhere, what does the Bible mean when it speaks of people being near to God or far from Him? It does not mean miles. Isaiah 59:2 says it is our sins that have separated us from God. The distance is a distance of heart, will and character, not of space. A person can sit in church a few feet from the communion table and be far from God. Someone else can be in a prison cell and be very near Him. Notice too that even rebels are never out of God's sight or beyond His reach. He is present to them as their Judge, even when He is not present to them as their Friend.

So we come near to God by turning to Him in faith and being made more like Him. We drift from Him by becoming unlike Him. That is why the New Testament speaks of being renewed in the image of our Creator, and why James 4:8 urges, "Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you." We do not travel toward Him with our feet. We come with trust, repentance and love, through Christ.

This teaching is both a comfort and a challenge. It is a comfort because no believer is ever alone, and no place is too remote or too dark for God to be there. It is a challenge because nothing is hidden from Him, and there is no corner where we can do what we like out of His sight. The God who fills heaven and earth is closer to us than our own breath, and He calls us to be near Him in heart as well.

topics.title: How do God's knowledge, will and creative action work without change or succession?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary agree that God's knowledge and will involve no change, learning or succession. Augustine grounds this in the priority of God's knowledge, in his Word, over the things made, so creatures exist because he knows them. Gregory argues from the simplicity and omnipotence of the divine nature that will, power and effect coincide without any interval, using the analogies of the shipbuilder and of light kindled with fire. Hilary holds that creation's preparation is co-eternal in God's counsel though carried out in an ordered sequence. On scriptural texts that seem to imply change ('Now I know', God's 'thoughts', 'tells the number of the stars'), all three read them as language suited to human understanding, but by different routes: Augustine treats them as a figure naming the cause by its effect (God made Abraham know his own faith), Hilary as God declaring knowledge he already had when the occasion arrives, and Gregory as accommodation to our way of counting. Irenaeus and Edwards stress something else: Irenaeus that God's providence fixes the number and measure of every thing and that his works always proceed from reason, which he turns against the Gnostics, and Edwards, unlike the others, ties creation's purpose christologically to the love in Christ, who is divine wisdom, and to providing him an elect spouse.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge…
refs.quote: He does not know them because they are, but they are because He knows them. For He was not ignorant of what He was about to create; therefore He created because He knew; He did not know because He created.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: through His providence every one of them has obtained its nature, and rank, and number, and special quantity, and that nothing whatever either has been or is produced in vain or accidentally

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: It is otherwise with God; for all that we can conceive as in Him is entirely work and action, His will passing over immediately to its object.

ans.text:
God does not learn, change his mind, or work step by step the way we do. He knows all things in one complete and unchanging act of knowing, he wills all things in one eternal purpose, and the world unfolds in time exactly as he has always known and intended it. Things change; God does not.

Start with how we know things. We find out about the world by looking, asking and counting. Our knowledge comes after the thing. If a tree falls in the yard, the tree falls first, and then we learn about it. With God it runs the other way. Things are not known by God because they exist. They exist because God knows them and wills them. An architect has the house in mind before a single brick is laid. The house comes from the plan, not the plan from the house. God is like that, only far more so. He does not merely plan the shape of things. He gives them their very being.

This is why nothing about creatures ever adds to God's knowledge. When something comes into being, God does not gain a new fact. He knew it fully before, and he knows it the same way after. Psalm 147:5 says, "His understanding has no limit." Hebrews 4:13 says, "Nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight." David marvels in Psalm 139 that all his days were written in God's book before one of them came to be. In Isaiah 46:10 God says, "I declare the end from the beginning." God does not wait to see how things turn out.

But what about verses that sound as if God learns? After Abraham is ready to offer Isaac, the angel of the Lord says in Genesis 22:12, "for now I know that you fear God." Did God find something out that day? No. Years earlier, Genesis 15:6 says, "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness." God already knew Abraham's heart. The "now" marks the moment when that faith was shown and openly declared. Abraham himself came to know how firm his faith was, and God gave him a public witness to it. When a teacher says to a student who has just passed a hard exam, "Now I know you've got it," she may have known all along. The exam made it plain for everyone, including the student.

Scripture often speaks this way. It says God "remembers," though he never forgets. It says God "came down to see" a city, though nothing is hidden from him. It speaks of God's "thoughts," though he does not puzzle things out or turn ideas over as we do. Psalm 147:4 says God "determines the number of the stars," but God does not count them one by one to find out how many there are. These are ways of speaking that come down to our level, so we can grasp something true. The point of the stars is that if God knows even what is too vast for us to count, nothing in our lives escapes him. The same is true of verses that say God "relented" or "regretted." They show God truly responding to people as they turn from sin or fall into it. Yet his response was never a surprise to him. It was part of his good purpose from the start.

God's will works the same way. We often want what we do not have, or get what we did not want. Our wishing and our having are far apart. God is not like that. He is not first able to act and then later acting, like a carpenter who has a skill and only uses it when he picks up his tools. His will is not a sudden urge that rises in him. It is as eternal as he is. Psalm 33:9 says, "For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm." Genesis 1 shows this again and again: God speaks, "and it was so." There is no gap or delay between God's purpose and its result. When you light a fire, the light comes with the flame, not after it. Creation is the effect of God's will, just as light is the effect of fire, but God does not have to wait for it.

This does not mean everything happened at once. God's eternal will includes the when as well as the what. He willed from all eternity that the world would begin, that days would follow days, that you would be born in your time and not another. The order of creation in Genesis 1 is real order in the world. Christians understand the six days in different ways, but on any reading the sequence belongs to the things made. It does not mean God paused between acts, ran out of ideas, or had to think of the next step. Psalm 33:6 says, "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth." God did not gather materials or draft rough plans like a human builder. Things that have a beginning in time have no beginning in God's knowledge and power. An author knows the whole story, while the characters live it page by page. The comparison falls short, because God does far more than write a story, but it helps a little.

Here the Trinity comes in. Scripture says God made all things through his Word. John 1:3 says of the Son, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Proverbs 3:19 says, "The LORD founded the earth by wisdom." The New Testament shows that this Word and Wisdom is the eternal Son. Colossians 1:16 says that all things were created through him and for him. So the Father's knowledge of all things is not a list of facts gathered over time. It is held in his eternal Word, who is always with him. Genesis 1 also shows the Spirit hovering over the waters, bringing life and order. Creation is the work of the one God, Father, Son and Spirit, from one unchanging wisdom and love.

That also means God never acts without reason. Nothing is made by accident or in vain. Each thing has its place, its nature and its limits because a wise and good God gave them. And Scripture tells us the deepest reason for it all. The world was made through Christ and for Christ. God's plan was to gather a people in love around his Son, a bride for the Lamb, and the rest of creation serves that loving purpose.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, an unchanging God is not a cold or frozen God. He is not unchanging the way a stone is. He is unchanging because he is perfectly alive, wholly loving and wholly wise all the time, with nothing missing that he must wait for or catch up on. Second, his knowing things ahead of time does not make our choices fake or our prayers useless. Abraham really obeyed. Our prayers are truly heard. God's eternal purpose includes our real choices and real prayers as the means by which he does his will.

This is a great comfort. James 1:17 calls God "the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow." In Malachi 3:6 God says, "I, the LORD, do not change." The God who knew you before you were born will not be surprised by tomorrow. He does not need to learn your needs, rethink his promises, or recover from a setback. What he has purposed in love, he will do.

topics.title: Is God just in His wrath, patience and judgment?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Bickersteth and Owen all affirm that God's judgment is real and just, but they answer different questions and rest on different grounds. Irenaeus locates the justice of reward and punishment in human free choice. He argues from Christ's exhortations, parables and Romans 2 that people could have done otherwise, that good and evil differ objectively, and that unbelievers bring condemnation on themselves while God only foresees and permits it. He also rejects the Stoic-Valentinian claim that God is bound by necessity. Bickersteth does not discuss free will; he defends the literal reality and permanence of God's wrath, arguing from the cumulative witness of every genre of Scripture and from the New Testament's own use of the flood, Sodom and Egypt as warnings, so that the Gospel has not softened God's immutable justice but only delays it in a day of grace. Owen differs in emphasis by distinguishing God's patience in providence apart from Christ from his patience in Christ. Providence gives only an obscure, fearful glimpse of God and serves to leave sinners inexcusable, whereas patience in Christ is covenanted, grounded in atonement, and aims at salvation. On that basis he reads Romans 2:4 more narrowly than Irenaeus's general appeal to Romans 2 as a ground of judgment.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: they who work it shall receive glory and honour, because they have done that which is good when they had it in their power not to do it

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: If it were only one isolated passage, you might urge it was figurative language: but here it is written in history, prophecy, sermon, epistle, vision, – all alike proving that our God is a consuming fire

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: with that revelation of forbearance which we have in Christ, there is also a discovery of the satisfaction of his justice and wrath against sin; so that we need not fear any actings from them to interfere with the works of his patience

ans.text:
Yes. God is perfectly just in everything He does, whether He is holding back His anger, showing patience, or finally judging. Abraham asked the right question long ago: "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25). The whole Bible answers yes.

Start with judgment itself. God's rewards and punishments are just because good and evil are real, and because people really choose. Right and wrong are not just opinions that change from culture to culture. If they were, Jesus could not have said that the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom while the wicked face fire (Matthew 13:41-43). His warnings only make sense if there is a real difference between the two. In the same way, His commands, such as "let your light shine" and "watch," and His parables of faithful and unfaithful servants, all assume that people are answerable for how they respond. Paul puts it plainly in Romans 2:6-8: God will repay each person according to what he has done. He gives life to those who seek glory and honour by doing good, and wrath to those who reject the truth and follow wickedness. No one is punished for something they did not do, and no one is condemned unfairly.

Some people would like to treat God's wrath as a figure of speech, an old way of talking we have outgrown. But this is not one odd verse. It runs through the whole Bible: in history, in the prophets, in the preaching of John the Baptist, in the words of Jesus, in the letters, and in Revelation. Nor did the New Testament soften the Old. It points back to the flood and to Sodom as real warnings for us (2 Peter 2:4-9; Jude 7), and it says, "our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews 12:29). God's wrath is not a bad temper. It is His settled, holy opposition to evil. A God who did not mind cruelty, lies and injustice would not be good.

So why doesn't God judge at once? Because He is patient. Even now He sends rain and harvests to people who ignore Him (Acts 14:17; Matthew 5:45). Paul asks whether we despise the riches of His kindness, tolerance and patience, "not realizing that God's kindness leads you to repentance" (Romans 2:4). Peter says the Lord is patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9). God's delay is not weakness or forgetfulness. It is room to turn back.

But patience is not the same as approval, and it does not last forever. Paul goes straight on to warn that a hard and unrepentant heart is storing up wrath for the day of judgment (Romans 2:5). Think of a parent who gives a child many chances. Each chance is a kindness, but a child who keeps abusing it has less and less excuse. God's kindness in creation and in daily life is real, but on its own it gives only a dim picture of Him. People can see that He is good and that He is angry at sin, yet still be unsure where they stand with Him. Those who keep refusing His kindness are left without excuse (Romans 1:20).

It is in Jesus that God's justice and patience fully meet. How can a just God forgive sinners without pretending sin doesn't matter? At the cross, the Father gave the Son, and the Son freely bore the judgment our sins deserved. Paul says God did this "to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). He also says God had passed over earlier sins in His forbearance, and the cross shows that this patience was never a lowering of His standards. So a believer need not fear that God's justice will one day overrule His mercy. In Christ, justice has been satisfied, and patience becomes a sure promise. The Spirit then works in us to bring us to repentance and faith.

The question also raises two worries. First, is God bound by some law of necessity, as if He "can't do otherwise"? No. God is not the servant of fate or of nature. He is free. He can give everlasting life to mortal people and raise what decays to be imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:53). His justice is not a machine He is trapped in. It is His own holy character.

Second, is God the cause of unbelief? Some verses sound that way. 2 Thessalonians 2:11 speaks of God sending a powerful delusion. But look at the reason given just before: they perish "because they refused the love of the truth that would have saved them" (2 Thessalonians 2:10). They chose falsehood first. God then hands them over to what they wanted, as a judgment (compare Romans 1:24). He is not the author of their sin. He knows ahead of time what people will choose and governs history so that justice is done.

Sincere Christians differ on exactly how God's sovereign choosing fits with human responsibility. Some stress that God's patience toward the world is a real, open invitation to all, because Scripture says He wants everyone to repent. Others stress that God's saving patience is aimed especially at those He is bringing to Himself in Christ, because Scripture also speaks of His purposes as certain and His grace as effective. Both sides agree on the main point: God is never unjust, and no one is condemned except for their own sin.

So God's wrath is just, because evil is real and deserves judgment. His patience is just and kind, because it gives time to turn. And His judgment will be just, because the Judge knows every heart. The right response is not to test His patience, but to receive the mercy He offers in His Son while it is still today.

title: One God: Monotheism and the Trinity
desc: How confessing the Son and Spirit as God fits with there being one God, answering charges of tritheism and readings of texts on the one, only and true God.

topics.title: How can the Son and Spirit be God without there being more than one God?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that confessing the Son and Spirit as God introduces neither a second or third God nor a single Person under several names: Hilary, Hippolytus, Ambrose, Augustine, Novatian, Waterland and Bickersteth all reject the Sabellian or modalist reading, and Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Waterland, Bickersteth and Warfield read texts like 1 Corinthians 8:6 and 'I and the Father are one' as including the Son in the one God while keeping the Persons distinct. They ground the unity differently: Hilary in the Son's true birth as 'One from One', so that God is not solitary; Athanasius in the Son's being proper to the Father's essence, with the sun-and-radiance image and the claim that Old Testament 'one God' texts are aimed at idols; Gregory of Nyssa, Owen and Augustine in one identical essence or nature, with Augustine adding that essential terms are predicated in the singular and that 'person' is an inadequate word; and Waterland in perichoresis and inseparable union, defended largely through the Fathers and against Clarke and Whitby. There is a real tension over the human analogy. Gregory argues that Peter, James and John share one nature and that calling them 'many men' is a loose usage, while Waterland expressly denies that the Persons have a merely specific unity like that of two men, holding that such a view would amount to Tritheism and that the Fathers rejected the illustration of three suns. They also differ on will. Ambrose and Gregory stress one identical will in the Trinity, whereas Bickersteth ascribes a self-determining will to each Person and makes Christ's doing another's will the decisive proof of distinct personality. Novatian alone grounds the Father's remaining the one God in the Son's subjection to him and his referring all authority back to the Father, and he reads the neuter 'one' as concord and association.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: I shall take care that in our assertion of the One true God I give no cover to the Sabellian heresy that the Father is one Person with the Son

refs.author: Hippolytus of Rome
refs.quote: If therefore I acknowledge Christ to be God, He is the Father Himself, if He is indeed God; and Christ suffered, being Himself God; and consequently the Father suffered, for He was the Father Himself.” But the case stands not thus

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: holds fast the word of godliness, if in the Father he sees the Son, without Whom the Father neither is nor is named

ans.text:
The Son and the Spirit are God without there being more than one God because they do not stand beside the Father as extra gods. They share the one and only divine being with Him. The Bible teaches both truths without apology. There is only one God, and the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully that one God.

Start with what the Bible means by one God. Israel's great confession is "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Through Isaiah, God says there is no God besides Him (Isaiah 45:5). Christians have never stepped back from this. We do not believe in a family of gods or a team of divine beings. There is one Creator, one Lord of all, one being who alone deserves worship.

Yet the same Bible says the Son is God. John begins his Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Notice both halves. The Word was "with God," so He is distinct from the Father. And the Word "was God," so He is not a lesser being. Thomas falls before the risen Jesus and calls Him "my Lord and my God" (John 20:28), and Jesus accepts it.

The Bible speaks of the Spirit the same way. When Ananias lies to the Holy Spirit, Peter tells him he has lied not to men but to God (Acts 5:3-4). The Spirit searches the deep things of God, gives life, and dwells in believers as God dwells in His temple.

How do these fit together? Christians use two words to keep things straight. God's "essence" or "being" is what God is: the one divine life, power, wisdom and glory. A "Person" is who God is: Father, Son or Spirit, each a real "I" who can speak to and love the others. So God is one in what He is and three in who He is. One God, three Persons. This is not a contradiction, because we are not saying God is one and three in the same sense.

Paul shows this in 1 Corinthians 8:6. Writing against the many gods of the pagan world, he says: "yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist." Paul is taking Israel's confession, "the LORD is One," and placing Jesus inside it. He even says all things came through Jesus, which is the work of the Creator alone. Some read this verse as if calling the Father "one God" means the Son is not God. But then calling Jesus "one Lord" would mean the Father is not Lord, and no one believes that. Both the Father and the Son stand on the same side of the line, over against the idols.

Why is this not three Gods? Think about three human beings. Peter, James and John share human nature, but each has his own separate body and life. One can be in Jerusalem while another is in Galilee. One can work while another sleeps. Each has his own share of humanity. That is why we count them as three men.

God is not like that. The Father, Son and Spirit do not each own a separate piece of deity. Each is the whole of the one undivided God. They never exist apart, and they never act apart. Jesus says the Son can do nothing by Himself, but whatever the Father does, the Son also does (John 5:19). Creation, salvation and the giving of new life are works of the Father through the Son by the Spirit, every time. The Bible speaks of one Savior and one Creator, not three, because there is only one saving and creating God at work. Jesus can say "Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father" (see John 14:9) because the Father and the Son are not two separate beings. They dwell in one another.

This also guards against an opposite mistake. Some have thought that if God is one, then Father, Son and Spirit must be three names or masks for a single Person, like one actor playing three parts. But the Bible will not allow that. At Jesus' baptism, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven (Matthew 3:16-17). Jesus prays to the Father, is sent by the Father, and says He came to do not His own will but the will of the One who sent Him. A person does not pray to himself or send himself. And when Jesus says "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), He says "are," not "am." There are two, and they are one.

Jesus sums it up when He sends His disciples to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). It is one name, not three names. Yet it is shared by three who are clearly distinct.

This does not weaken God's unity. It shows how rich it is. One God does not mean a lonely God. Before the world existed, the Father loved the Son in the Spirit (John 17:24). That is how Scripture can say "God is love" without making God need creation in order to have someone to love. God's oneness is not the oneness of a single isolated person. It is the perfect, unbreakable oneness of Father, Son and Spirit sharing one life.

Every comparison eventually falls short here, and that is to be expected. God is not one more thing in the world. We cannot fully picture how three Persons share one being. But we can say clearly what the Bible teaches. Do not divide God into three gods. Do not blur the Father, Son and Spirit into one Person. Worship one God: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

topics.title: Does confessing the Son as God mean worshipping two Gods?
topics.cmp: All the authors answer no: confessing and worshipping the Son as God does not make two Gods, and Hilary, Athanasius and Hippolytus equally insist that God is not one solitary Person, so the Father–Son distinction is real. They ground the unity differently. Hilary, by far the most frequent voice, rests it on the Son's perfect birth from the Father's nature (God from God, one nature and one name) and on mutual indwelling. Athanasius and Novatian stress derivation from the one Father as sole Beginning: the Son is no second unbegotten source, so the Monarchy stands, and Athanasius adds that worship of the Son is worship of the Father in Him. Gregory of Nyssa and Basil argue from the absence of any difference of essence or operation, Basil using the analogy of a king and his image; Augustine argues from the 'one spirit' analogy and treats Father and Son as one Beginning of creation; Waterland appeals to perichoresis, Ante-Nicene testimony, and the defence of Athanasius and Origen, and holds that all worship is one, given primarily to the Father and derivatively to the Son. Novatian alone relies chiefly on a retorsion argument from Scripture's 'one Lord' and 'one good', while Owen concludes, from the divine nature being common to all three Persons, that worshipping any one Person is worshipping all three.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: We teach that it is by no confusion of the Two that God is One; we do not rend Him in pieces by preaching a plurality of Gods, nor yet do we profess a distinction only in name.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: Wherefore neither is the Son another God, for He was not procured from without, else were there many, if a godhead be procured foreign from the Father's

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father…
refs.quote: And thus He could not make two Gods, because He did not make two beginnings, seeing that from Him who has no beginning He received the source of His nativity before all time.

ans.text:
No. Christians who call Jesus God are not worshipping a second God beside the Father. They are worshipping the one God, who has made himself known as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

The worry is understandable. The Bible insists on one God. Israel's great confession is "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus repeats it himself in Mark 12:29. Through the prophets God says again and again that there is no other God besides him. So any teaching that adds a second God has left the Bible behind. But the New Testament also plainly calls the Son God. John opens his Gospel with "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Thomas falls before the risen Jesus and calls him "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). The question is how both can be true.

The key is what makes something count as "two." Two gods would mean two separate divine beings, each with its own power, will and life, standing side by side. That is not what the Son is. He is not a being the Father made, or a god who existed independently and then joined forces with him. Scripture calls him the Father's only "begotten" Son. In this teaching, "begotten" means that the Son comes from the Father and shares exactly what the Father is. A father passes his own human nature to his son. In the same way, the Son has the Father's very own divine life, not a copy and not a lesser version. Hebrews 1:3 calls him "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Think of the sun and its light. The light comes from the sun, yet no one says there are two suns. There is one sunlight, shining from its source. So the Son's godhood is not a second godhood. It is the Father's own. That is why Jesus can say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me" (John 14:10).

This also answers the fear of "two first principles," meaning two ultimate starting points of everything. Christians often speak of the Father as the source or fountain of the Son and the Spirit. That does not set up two origins. It does the opposite. The Son is not a second, independent beginning, because everything he is, he has from the Father. So he always points back to the Father as the one source, and the unity of God is kept. Yet this does not make the Son later or smaller. There was never a time when the Father was without his Son, just as the sun was never without its light. The Son is eternal, but not as a second eternal being. He shares the Father's own eternity. And toward creation, Father and Son are not two makers. Paul says there is "one God, the Father, from whom all things came," and "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came" (1 Corinthians 8:6). One work of creation, one Creator, from the Father through the Son.

We must also avoid the opposite mistake. Some, trying to protect God's oneness, have said that Father and Son are simply one person under two names, like one actor playing two roles. The Bible will not allow this. The Word was "with God" as well as God. The Son prays to the Father, is sent by the Father, and is loved by the Father. These are real relationships, not masks. So the church holds both truths together. There are not two Gods, and God is not a solitary person. There is one God, and within that one God the Father and the Son are truly distinct.

What about worship? Is the Father worshipped fully and the Son a little less? No. Jesus says the Father has given judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him" (John 5:23). Since the Son shares the one divine nature, honoring him is honoring the one God. Worshipping the Son takes nothing away from the Father. Paul says that when every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, it is "to the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:11). There is one faith and one worship, given to one God.

Can we pray to or worship just one Person, such as Jesus? Yes, we may speak to him directly. Stephen did as he died, praying "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59), and the earliest Christians called on his name. But we never worship him as if he were a separate god, cut off from the Father and the Spirit. When we come to the Son, we come to the Father who is in him. Jesus says, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). And we can only confess Jesus as Lord by the Holy Spirit. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Even when we address one Person by name, we are worshipping the one God.

Sincere Christians have sometimes weighted these things differently. Some stress the Father as the source, because it shows clearly why there is only one God and not three independent ones. Others are cautious about that language, because they fear it could suggest the Son is somehow lesser. Both sides agree on the heart of the matter. The Son is fully God, equal with the Father, eternally from him, and one God with him.

So when you sing to Christ, pray in his name, or bow before him as Lord, you are not dividing your loyalty between two gods. You are giving your whole heart to the one true God, who has shown his face to us in his Son.

topics.title: In what does the unity of the one God consist?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that God's unity is not that of a single solitary Person: Waterland denies that the Godhead is monoprosopos (equating that with Sabellian singularity), Hilary reads 'Believe in God, believe also in Me' as excluding a solitary God, and Athanasius rejects the Marcellian expansion-and-contraction of the Monad as leading to Sabellianism. Positively, Waterland locates the unity in one shared substance of distinct Persons, citing Hippolytus and Gregory Nazianzen, and he argues against weaker accounts: agreement of mind, Clarke's 'Father governing through Son and Spirit,' and the communication of attributes without substance, the last of which he says leaves either distinct Gods or mere names. Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa ground the unity differently. Augustine argues philosophically, from divine simplicity and the analogy of three rings of one gold, that God is one essence (he prefers 'essence' to 'substance,' with Exodus 3:14 as support) in which the three must stay unconfounded to remain related. Gregory stresses that the Persons are timeless and equal in honour, with no 'before' or 'more honourable'. The remaining answers come at the topic from other angles: Irenaeus explains the many prophetic titles as one God under various aspects, and Athanasius treats the unchangeable unity of Father and Son as a model for human concord.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: it is from thence we discover that God is not μονοπρόσωπος, a single Hypostasis, but that the Father has his coessential and coeternal Son and Holy Spirit always in him and with him.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.place: Excursus C. Introductory to the Fourth Discourse against…
refs.quote: The doctrine of divine dilatation and contraction denies true personal distinctions in the Godhead.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself,…
refs.quote: if they were confounded together as it were by a commingling, they could not be in any way three, neither could they be mutually referred to each other.

ans.text:
God is one because there is one divine being, one single 'what' that God is, and the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each are that one being fully and together. God's oneness is not a matter of there being only one Person. It is not mere teamwork or agreement. It is not one Person wearing three masks. It is that the one undivided life, nature and glory of God belongs wholly to each of the three, who are never separated and never mixed up.

Start where Israel started. Moses heard, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The prophets kept saying it: there is no other God. The Bible gives God many names, like Lord of Hosts, Holy One, Rock and Shepherd. These do not point to several gods. They show the riches of the one God from different sides. Christians have never stepped back from that. The doctrine of the Trinity is not three gods. It is what the one God has shown us about himself.

So what is the 'one' in 'one God'? Theologians use the word 'essence' or 'nature' here. It simply means what a thing is, as opposed to who someone is. When God told Moses, "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14), he named himself by his very being. God does not just have life. He is life itself, without beginning and without needing anything outside himself. Sometimes people call God a 'substance', and that is fine if it just means he is real and solid, not a mere idea. But God is not like a lump of something with qualities stuck onto it, the way a table has a color that could be painted over. God's goodness, wisdom and power are not add-ons. They are what he is. That is why the unity of God is so deep. There are not parts in God to be shared out.

Now comes what only revelation could tell us. This one being is not a lonely, single Person. Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). The word 'one' there is not 'one person', for he says 'I and the Father', two who speak to each other and love each other. In John 14:1 he tells his friends, "You believe in God; believe in Me as well." There are two to believe in, yet not two gods. And when he sends out his disciples, he tells them to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice it is one name, not three names, and yet three who are named. The Father has always had his Son and his Spirit with him. God has never been alone.

It helps to see what this unity is not, because each mistake is easy to slip into.

Some think God's unity means God is one Person who shows up in three roles. He is the Father in creation, the Son at Christmas and the Spirit at Pentecost, like one actor changing costumes, or like something that stretches out and then pulls back in. But then the Son praying to the Father would be a kind of play-acting. The Father's voice at Jesus' baptism, speaking about his beloved Son while the Spirit descends, would make no sense. The three are really distinct, not just phases or faces.

Others say the three are one only because they agree perfectly and work on the same project. That is like a good committee, or a king ruling through his ministers. It is true that the Father, Son and Spirit always will and act as one. But agreement alone would give us three divine beings who get along very well. That is three gods, and Scripture will not allow it. Their perfect agreement flows from their being one God. It does not create it.

Still others say the Father alone is truly God, and he hands down some divine powers to the Son and Spirit, a bit like a rich man lending his authority to servants. But that does not work either. Either the Son has a divinity of his own, which makes a second, lesser god, or he has none at all, which makes him just a name. The Bible's answer is that the Son shares the Father's very being. That is why he can say, in effect, that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9).

This also means there is no ranking inside God, no first-class and second-class divinity. The Father is the source from whom the Son is eternally 'begotten', a word that means he comes forth from the Father as a true Son, sharing his nature, not made like a creature. The Spirit likewise comes from the Father. But 'from' does not mean 'after' or 'less'. There was never a time when the Father was without his Son, or when God was without his Spirit. And nothing in God can be more or less glorious, since all of God is glory. To lift up one Person over another is really to dishonor the one put lower.

One more caution. Being one does not mean being blended. The three are not melted together into a single mix. If they were, there would be no Father to love the Son, no Son to obey and glorify the Father, and no Spirit to bear witness to both. The Bible's picture is of three who are wholly 'in' one another (John 14:10), sharing one life completely while remaining truly themselves.

Finally, this is not just something for the head. In John 17:21 Jesus prays for his people "that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You." We will never be one being as God is one. Jesus holds up his oneness with the Father as a pattern, not an equal. Our love is changeable and easily broken. The love between the Father and the Son never changes and never cracks. That is exactly why it is a safe model. When a church, a marriage or a friendship looks to that unbreakable oneness, it learns what real unity is: distinct persons, wholly given to one another, sharing one life, with no rivalry and no loss of who each one is.

topics.title: Why must God be one, and can there be any God besides the one Creator?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that there can be only one God and no second or lesser deity, but they reach this through different lines of reasoning. Irenaeus, Hilary, Novatian and Gregory of Nyssa argue philosophically from the divine attributes. Irenaeus says many gods would each lack something and so lose the title Omnipotent. Hilary says omnipotence and eternity admit no degrees, which rules out ranks of gods. Novatian argues that the Highest has no equal and that two infinites cannot coexist, since one would contain the other. Gregory turns the argument from infinity against Eunomius: one infinite cannot be greater or less than another, which excludes ranking the Persons. Ambrose and Owen address how the one God can be three Persons without becoming several Gods. Ambrose holds that the divine nature does not admit number and that there is no division of power in God. Owen, more scholastically, holds that each Person is infinite by the one nature, not by personhood, so there are not three infinites and no finite mode of subsisting. Waterland appeals instead to the consensus of the ancients that worshipping a second, inferior God undermines religion. Irenaeus, in a separate argument, insists that obscure passages of Scripture are no reason to seek a God besides the Creator, because the fault lies in our limitation and not in Scripture.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For how can the Unity of the Godhead admit of plurality, seeing that plurality is of numbers, but the Divine Nature does not admit numbers?

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: It is, indeed, difficult to see how a reflecting mind can conceive one infinite to be greater or less than another infinite.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: All divine properties, such as to be infinite is, belong not to the persons on the account of their personality, but on the account of their nature, which is one, for they are all natural properties.

ans.text:
God must be one because the God the Bible reveals is the highest, all-powerful, limitless Creator of everything, and there can only ever be one of those. There is no other God beside him, no rival, no partner, and no lesser god standing below him.

The Bible makes this clear and often. Israel's great confession begins, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Through Isaiah, God says, "I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me" (Isaiah 45:5). Paul repeats it in the New Testament: whatever so-called gods people may worship, "for us there is but one God" (1 Corinthians 8:6). The Bible does not treat this as a matter of preference, as if Israel simply chose one god from many. It says that the others are not gods at all.

Reason points the same way once we think about what the word "God" means. God is not simply a very powerful being. He is the greatest there is, the one from whom everything else comes. But the greatest cannot have an equal. If there were two gods of the same rank, neither would be the highest. Each would just be one of a pair. Having no equal means being alone.

Consider God's power. Scripture calls him the Almighty. Suppose there were several gods, each ruling its own territory, like kings dividing a map. Then each would lack what the others had. None would truly be almighty, because each would be limited by the others. Power shared out among rivals is no longer all-power. And all-power does not come in grades. You cannot be a little bit almighty.

Consider also that God has no limits. God asks in Jeremiah 23:24, "Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?" Solomon confessed that even the highest heavens cannot contain God (1 Kings 8:27). Something without limits leaves no room outside itself for a second thing of the same kind. If God did not hold all things, something bigger would surround him. Then that bigger thing would have the better claim to be God. So there cannot be two limitless gods side by side.

This also rules out a common idea: a supreme God at the top with a smaller, junior god under him who also deserves worship. Some have pictured Jesus that way, as a kind of second-tier divine being. The Bible will not allow it. A god of lower rank would be a creature, and worshipping a creature is idolatry (Romans 1:25). Yet John 1:1 says that the Word, who became flesh in Jesus, "was God." He is not a lesser deity. Through him all things were made (John 1:3), and he receives the worship that belongs to God alone. Either the Son is truly God, the one God, or he must not be worshipped at all. There is no middle category.

That raises a natural question. If the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, are there not three Gods? Or three limitless beings? The church's answer, drawn from Scripture, is no. There is one divine nature, or "essence". That simply means what God is, his very being. The Father, Son and Spirit do not each have their own separate share of it. Each of them is the whole of the one God. Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). And he sends his disciples to baptize "in the name", singular, "of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19).

So when we say each Person is all-powerful and limitless, we are not adding up three infinities. Each Person is limitless because he is God, and the godhead is one. What makes them distinct is not a different portion of power or greatness. It is how they relate to one another: the Father begets, which means he eternally gives the Son his very being, as a father passes on his own nature to a son. The Son is begotten, and the Spirit proceeds. Counting works for things that can be divided up, like three apples or three people standing in a room. The one being of God cannot be divided, so the Persons do not multiply it. There is one power, one glory and one God, known in three Persons. No human comparison captures this perfectly, and we should not pretend it does. But it is not a contradiction. We do not say one God and three Gods. We say one God, who is Father, Son and Spirit.

For the same reason, there is no ranking within God, as if the Father were more God than the Son. One limitless being cannot be greater or smaller than itself. The Son willingly took a servant's place when he became man, and that is real and precious. But in his divine nature he shares fully in the Father's glory (John 17:5).

Finally, some people have been troubled by hard passages in the Bible.
