They have concluded that the Creator described there could not be the true, good God, and so they went looking for another, higher God. Scripture closes that door. It never offers a better God behind the Creator. When we meet passages we cannot fully explain, the problem lies with our limited understanding, not with God or his Word. "The secret things belong to the LORD our God" (Deuteronomy 29:29). The humble response is to trust the one God who made us and has made himself known in his Son, not to invent another.

topics.title: Is the one God of the Shema the whole Trinity?
topics.cmp: All the authors deny that the Shema's confession of one God excludes the Son. They reach that shared conclusion by different routes. Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa identify the one Lord God directly with the Trinity: Augustine says "Lord" there can denote the whole Trinity, and Gregory argues that the Godhead extends through three Persons while the name of the nature stays singular. Bickersteth argues from Hebrew grammar, reading the plural Elohim beside "one Jehovah" as a unity that contains real plurality, where the singular Eloah would have expressed an absolutely solitary unity. Owen speaks of God as prima Veritas considered essentially as the whole Deity, though faith may also rest distinctly on the Father's own testimony. Waterland defends the creed's "not three eternals but one eternal" as coherent by turning Clarke's own hypothesis against him. Hilary, by far the most heavily represented, takes a different line. He grants that the one God "from Whom are all things" is the Father (as Hippolytus also says plainly), but insists that Moses himself teaches "God and God." He holds that the Son is included in the unity by natural birth, and that "See, I am God" is spoken by the Only-begotten, citing Paul's use of the same song. Athanasius adds a historical argument: such declarations were aimed at idolatry, not at the Word. So the authors differ less in their conclusion than in emphasis. Augustine and Gregory locate the one God in the whole Trinity, while Hippolytus and Hilary keep the Father as the one God and include the Son through his birth and through Scripture's testimony.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the…
refs.quote: or God Himself the Trinity, of which one God it is said, “Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and Him only shall thou serve.”

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: they appear to be in the most definite and expressive manner designed to convey the idea, that, notwithstanding a real plurality intimated in the form Elohim, Jehovah is still ONE.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: this is being, and that being; and yet not two beings, but one being: this eternal, and that eternal; and yet not two eternals, but one eternal. I might go on almost the length of an Athanasian Creed.

ans.text:
Yes. When Israel confessed, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4), the one God they were confessing is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together, not the Father alone with the Son and Spirit standing somewhere outside.

This needs some care, because the Bible also often uses the word "God" for the Father in particular. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 8:6 that "for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist." So it is fair to ask whether the one God of the Shema is simply the Father.

Look closely at the rest of that verse. Paul goes on: "And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist." Paul is echoing the Shema itself, which speaks of one God and one Lord. He takes its words and places Jesus inside them. The Father is the one God from whom all things come. The Son is the one Lord through whom all things come. Paul is not adding a second god beside the first. He is showing that the one God Israel confessed has always included the Son. Creation itself proves the point: John 1:3 says all things were made through the Word. No one can be the maker of all things and also be outside the one Creator God.

So why does the Bible so often say "God" when it means the Father? Because the Father is the source within God. The Son is "begotten" of the Father, which means he comes from the Father the way a son shares his father's own nature, except that this has no beginning in time. The Spirit proceeds, or comes forth, from God as well. The Father is first in that order, so it is natural to call him "God" without further explanation. But being the source does not make the Father the only one who is truly God. The Father passes on to the Son everything that makes him God, and holds nothing back. Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one." What is special to the Father is that he is Father, not that he owns divinity by himself.

Jesus himself handled the Shema this way. In Mark 12:29 he names it as the greatest commandment. A few verses later, in Mark 12:35-37, he asks why David, speaking by the Spirit, calls the Messiah "Lord." He is hinting that the one Lord of Israel's confession is bigger than his hearers thought, and that the Messiah belongs within it.

The same is true of the strong Old Testament sayings that there is no other God. In Deuteronomy 32:39 God says there is no God besides him, and Isaiah 45 says the same many times. These words were aimed at idols, the false gods the nations had made up. They were never aimed at God's own Word or Spirit, who were with him from the beginning. Isaiah 45:23 says every knee will bow to the LORD. Paul applies those very words to Jesus in Philippians 2:10-11. Paul did not think the Son was one of the rival gods those verses ruled out. He saw Jesus as the one before whom every knee bows.

A common worry is that saying "the Trinity is the one God" means three gods, or a committee of gods. It does not. There is one divine nature, one being of God, one power, one will, one glory. Father, Son and Spirit are not three parts of God, as if each held a third. Each is fully God, and yet there are not three Gods but one. That is why Jesus tells us to baptize "in the name" of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). He says one name, not three names.

The opposite worry is that this blurs the persons into one. That is not right either. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit. Scripture can speak of the Father as the one God "from whom" all things come and still include the Son and Spirit in the one God we worship. It does both without contradiction.

So when you say the Shema, or when Jesus says "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only," you are not being told to worship the Father and merely admire the Son. The one LORD you love with all your heart, soul and strength is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Christians confess exactly what Israel confessed. We now know more fully who that one God is.

topics.title: Do Scripture's statements about the one, only, true, or alone immortal God exclude the Son and Spirit?
topics.cmp: All the authors (Hilary, Athanasius, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Novatian, Waterland, Owen and Bickersteth) agree that Scripture's exclusive language about the one, only, true God does not shut out the Son, and where the Spirit is discussed, not the Spirit either. Apparent 'Yes' answers, such as Gregory of Nyssa on Isaiah 43:10, Novatian on John 17:3, and Augustine's qualified 'Father alone', reach the same conclusion: the exclusion falls on false gods or on what is 'not the Father', never on a separated Son. They differ in how they ground this. Athanasius, Novatian and Waterland say the exclusive texts target idols and heretical figments, with the Word implied in the One 'as radiance in light'. Hilary stresses that a foreign nature is excluded while the Son shares the one nature by birth, with the Father in him, and he points to the Father's own words 'there is no God beside Thee'. Augustine refers the texts to the one substance of the whole Trinity and even proposes reordering John 17:3. Gregory of Nyssa argues against Eunomius that denying the Son 'proper' or 'real' existence amounts to denying that he exists, and he identifies the Son himself as the 'immortality' and 'light' of 1 Timothy 6:16. Waterland works by dilemma against Clarke and the Arians (if excluded at all, Christ is no God) and by citing the ante-Nicene Fathers. Unlike Augustine, he allows that 'one God' primarily denotes the Father personally, marking priority of order, while including the others. Ambrose argues from the Son and Spirit conferring the same benefit, and Owen exposes the logical fallacy in the syllogism. Bickersteth departs from Augustine on invisibility: he grants that invisibility is the one attribute of the Father not ascribed to Christ, explaining this by Christ's mediating role rather than reading the text of the whole Trinity.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: It is the peculiar characteristic of the Son of God that there is no God beside Him; the peculiar characteristic of God the Father that there is no God apart from Him.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: not so as to exclude the Son from being comprehended in the one God, but in opposition to false Gods only

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: if the Son is God, and whatever is “after” the Father is not God, it is clear that the saying bears witness to the truth that the Son is in the Father, and not after the Father

ans.text:
No. When the Bible calls God the one, only, true, or alone immortal God, it is setting the living God against every false god and every creature, not setting the Father against the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Bible is firm that there is only one God. In Isaiah 45:5 the Lord says, "I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me." Christians have never wanted to soften that. The question is what these strong words are aimed at. In Isaiah the target is plain: the idols of the nations, gods made of wood and metal that cannot save. The point is that nothing else stands beside the Lord as God. That is quite different from saying the Lord has no Son and no Spirit within his own being.

The Bible itself shows that the Son is not shut out by these words. In Isaiah 44:24 the Lord says he alone stretched out the heavens. Yet Hebrews 1:10 takes words spoken to the Lord as Creator in the Psalms and says them to the Son. In Isaiah 45:23, right after declaring there is no other God, the Lord swears that every knee will bow to him. Paul applies that very promise to Jesus in Philippians 2:10-11. If those passages meant "the Father only, and not the Son," the apostles would be giving God's unique honor to someone else. Instead they show that the Son belongs inside the one God those passages describe.

John 17:3 is the verse people raise most often. Jesus prays, "Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent." Jesus is speaking to his Father, so it is natural that he calls him the only true God. The Father truly is that. But notice what Jesus says next. Eternal life is knowing the Father and knowing Jesus Christ. He puts himself right beside the Father as the one we must know in order to live forever. No prophet or angel could say that about himself. Knowing a creature, however great, cannot be eternal life. Only knowing God can be.

The same writer settles the matter in 1 John 5:20. He speaks of knowing "Him who is true" and being "in His Son Jesus Christ," and then says, "He is the true God and eternal life." The title Jesus used of the Father in his prayer, "true God," is used here of the Son. The word "only" in John 17:3 rules out false gods. It does not rule out the Son, who is not a second, rival god but the Son of the one true God, sharing his very nature. Jesus also says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).

A similar pattern appears in 1 Corinthians 8:6: "for us there is but one God, the Father... And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ." Some read this as if the Father were God and Jesus something less. But Paul is quoting the great confession of Israel, "The LORD our God, the LORD is One," and he places Jesus inside it. "Lord" was the name Jewish readers used in place of God's holy name. And Paul says all things came through Jesus. Calling the Father the one God no more makes Jesus less than God than calling Jesus the one Lord makes the Father less than Lord.

The same is true of 1 Timothy 2:5: "For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Here Paul is speaking of Jesus as our go-between, and a mediator must stand on our side as well as God's. So Paul stresses that he is a man. That does not deny that he is also God. It tells us he became one of us to bring us to God.

What about 1 Timothy 1:17 and 6:16, which call God invisible and say he "alone is immortal" and lives "in unapproachable light"? Some take these to mean the Father alone, since Jesus was seen and Jesus died. But neither passage names the Father. They praise the one God as he is in himself. The Son, as God, shares that life. John 1:4 says, "In Him was life," and Jesus says, "I am the way and the truth and the life" (John 14:6). He did not borrow life from outside himself. He is life. When he died, he died in the human nature he took on for us. He did not stop being the living God, and death could not keep him.

It is the same with being invisible. The divine nature of the Son is no more visible than the Father's. What people saw was the Son in human flesh. That is exactly how the invisible God made himself known. As John 1:18 says, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known." Colossians 1:15 calls him "the image of the invisible God." Think of a voice that cannot be seen but can be heard. The Son is the invisible God made known in a way we can grasp.

The Holy Spirit is not excluded either. When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter told him he had lied to God (Acts 5:3-4). Hebrews 9:14 calls him "the eternal Spirit." He shares the same life and glory.

Why then does the Bible so often call the Father "the one God"? Because the Father is the source. The Son is begotten of him, meaning the Son comes eternally from the Father the way a son shares his father's nature, not made like a creature. The Spirit comes from him too. So it is fitting to speak of the Father as God in a special way, as the source of the Son and Spirit. But being the source does not make him the only one who is God. When we speak of the one God, the Son and Spirit are always included with him, never pushed outside.

So when you read that God alone is God, alone is true, alone is immortal, you can read it with full confidence. It is a wall against every idol and every creature. It is not a wall between the Father and his Son and Spirit. The one true God whom we worship is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Knowing him through Jesus Christ is eternal life.

topics.title: Does Isaiah 42:8, 'I will not give my glory to another,' exclude the Son and Spirit?
topics.cmp: Daniel Waterland and Gregory of Nyssa agree that Isaiah 42:8 does not exclude the Son (and, for Waterland, the Spirit) from divine glory, but they argue differently. Waterland takes 'another' to mean creatures or other gods, which the Son and Spirit are not. He adds positive scriptural evidence that the Father himself shares his glory with them: the command to baptize in their names equally with his own, and the order that all honour the Son as they honour the Father. Gregory works instead from the immediate context: the next clause, 'neither My praise to graven images,' shows that 'another' is God's adversary worshipped through idols, so applying it to the Son puts him in the place of God's enemy. Gregory also argues ad hominem that the Only-begotten himself spoke these words through the prophet, as Eunomius admits. On the second question only Waterland answers. He holds that the text rules out a second, subordinate God sharing divine glory, because God's peculiar glory is to be truly God to the exclusion of other gods, and a reading that lets God merely keep 'the greater share' would accommodate pagan polytheism with its supreme god and inferior deities. His two answers there open with opposite one-word labels ('No' and 'Yes'), but both reach the same substantive conclusion: a distinct inferior God sharing divine titles contradicts the text.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: they had given it to none but his own Son, and his Holy Spirit, whom they believed not to be creatures, nor other Gods; and whom himself had given his glory to, by commanding all men to be baptized in their names

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: it is the Only-begotten Himself Who spoke these words by the prophet, as Eunomius himself subsequently confesses when he says, “this is He Who spake by the prophets.”

ans.text:
No. When God says he will not give his glory to another, he is shutting out idols, false gods and creatures, not his own Son and Spirit. Read carefully, the verse actually works against the idea that Jesus is a second, lesser god.

Start with the verse itself. Isaiah 42:8 says, "I am the LORD; that is My name! I will not give My glory to another or My praise to idols." The second half explains the first. The "another" God refuses to honor is the kind of rival people bow to in carved images. Throughout these chapters Isaiah mocks idols made by human hands and insists there is no God besides the LORD. The point is that the one true God will not share his place with anything that is not God.

The Son and the Holy Spirit are not "another" in that sense. They are not rivals, idols or creatures standing outside God. Christians confess that there is one God, eternally Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Son is not a separate being whom God might or might not decide to honor. He shares the one divine nature with the Father, the same "essence" or being. When the Son is glorified, God's glory is not going to someone else. It stays within God.

The New Testament shows this plainly. In John 17:5 Jesus prays, "And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed." No creature could say that. The Son did not receive God's glory as a later gift. He shared it before anything was made. Hebrews 1:3 calls him the radiance of God's glory. Light from the sun is not a second sun. It is the sun's own brightness reaching us.

The Father himself directs that the Son be honored as God. Jesus says in John 5:23 that the Father has done this "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father." Notice the words "just as." That is not a smaller, second-tier honor. In heaven the same worship goes to both: "To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!" (Revelation 5:13). Jesus also sends his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). That is one name shared by three, with no hint that the Son and Spirit are lesser partners. The Spirit too is called "the Spirit of glory and of God" (1 Peter 4:14).

Even Isaiah points this way. Paul takes words the LORD speaks about himself in Isaiah 45:23, that every knee will bow to him, and applies them to Jesus in Philippians 2:10-11. And John 12:41 says that when Isaiah saw the LORD's glory in the temple, he was seeing the glory of Jesus. The same God who says "I will not give My glory to another" is the God revealed in the Son. Just before our verse, in Isaiah 42:1, God speaks of his chosen Servant and says, "I have put My Spirit on Him." The Father, the Servant and the Spirit all appear in the very passage where God guards his glory.

Some have tried a middle path. They say Jesus is divine in a lesser way, a second god under the Father who gets a smaller share of glory. Isaiah 42:8 is exactly what rules that out. God does not say, "I will keep the largest share of my glory." He says he will not give it to another at all. Many ancient religions honored one high god above a crowd of lower gods. The Bible's jealous God refuses that whole arrangement. If Jesus were a lesser god, worshiping him would be the very thing Isaiah forbids. Since Scripture commands us to worship him, he must be the one true God himself, not a junior partner.

So the verse and the Trinity do not pull against each other. God keeps his glory from idols and creatures, and he shares it fully within himself, Father, Son and Spirit. When we worship Jesus and the Spirit, we are not dividing our loyalty. We are giving glory to the one God, just as Isaiah demands.

topics.title: Are there other gods besides the one true God?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Augustine, Waterland and Owen all reach the same conclusion: Scripture's language about other "gods" never sets up a second true deity beside the one God. Their grounds and emphases differ. Irenaeus argues mostly from the reading of particular texts. He takes 2 Corinthians 4:4 as a transposition of words, so that "of this world" describes the unbelievers rather than a god. He reads "all that is called God" in 2 Thessalonians 2:4 as meaning idols, and he notes that Scripture always qualifies idols as "gods of the heathen" or "other gods." From Isaiah and Ezekiel he argues that the Creator is the same God who raises the dead. Augustine agrees on that last point but grounds it differently: resurrection is the same life-giving work the one God does in the womb, only shown in an unusual way. Waterland and Owen work more by analysis of terms than by exegesis of single verses. Waterland holds that Moses, magistrates, angels and idols are called gods only figuratively, because they resemble God in some one respect such as dominion, and he calls any inference to true deity the fallacy of arguing from a qualified sense to an absolute one. Owen holds that "most high" describes God's sovereign rule over all rather than marking him off from lesser gods beneath him.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: To argue from hence, that any of them is properly God, is making the whole of a part ; and reasoning fallaciously, a dicto secundum quid, as the schools speak, ad dictum simpliciter.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For Paul does not say, “the God of this world,” as if recognising any other beyond Him; but he confessed God as indeed God. And he says, “the unbelievers of this world,” because they shall not inherit the future age of incorruption.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.quote: And who is it that restored to the corpses their proper souls when the dead rose again, unless He who gives life to the flesh in the mother’s womb

ans.text:
No. There is only one true God, and the Bible never treats anything else as a real god, whether greater or lesser. The Lord says plainly in Isaiah 45:5, "I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me." Every page of Scripture assumes this, from Israel's daily confession in Deuteronomy 6:4 that the LORD is one, to Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 8:4: "We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one."

Still, the Bible does use the word "god" for other things, and readers sometimes wonder what that means. The key is to notice how the word is used. In ordinary speech we call a talented musician "a legend" or a strict manager "the boss of bosses" without meaning anything literal. Scripture likewise borrows the word "god" in a limited sense, pointing to one small way something resembles God, or to what people wrongly believe about it.

Take idols first. When the Bible speaks of the gods of the nations, it nearly always adds a word that gives the game away. They are "other gods," "gods of the nations," gods made by human hands, gods that will perish. Paul calls them "so-called gods" in 1 Corinthians 8:5. Psalm 96 says that the gods of the nations are idols, while the LORD made the heavens. The word is used only so we know what is being talked about, the way a news report might mention a "self-proclaimed king." Behind the statues there is no divine being at all. Where there is any spiritual power, it is evil spirits, not gods. Deuteronomy 32:17 says Israel "sacrificed to demons, not to God."

The same is true of a passage like 2 Thessalonians 2:4, where the coming "man of lawlessness" sets himself above every so-called god or object of worship. Paul is not suggesting a crowd of real gods for this figure to climb over. He means the false gods people already worship. This rebel wants to replace them all and be worshiped himself. He is a creature grabbing for a place that belongs to God alone.

Next, human beings. God tells Moses in Exodus 7:1 that He has made him like God to Pharaoh. Moses would speak with God's authority and bring God's judgments, but he was still a man. Psalm 82 calls unjust rulers "gods" because they held the power to judge, which is God's work entrusted to them. Then the psalm warns that they will die like mere men. Jesus quotes this psalm in John 10:34-35 to point out that if Scripture could call judges "gods," His enemies had no grounds to charge Him with blasphemy for calling Himself the Son of God. Rulers are called gods in one narrow respect, because they rule. To conclude they are partly divine would be like hearing someone called "King David" and deciding we could just as well say "God David." A resemblance in one point does not make the whole thing true.

Angels belong in the same category. They are mighty, they live in God's presence, and in a few places the original wording groups them with "gods" or "heavenly beings." But they are created servants. When John fell down before an angel in Revelation 22:8-9, the angel stopped him at once and told him to worship God.

What about 2 Corinthians 4:4, where Paul says "the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers"? Most Christians understand this to mean Satan. Jesus calls him "the ruler of this world" in John 12:31. Satan is not a real god. Paul is speaking with sharp irony: the devil acts like a god to those who follow him, but he is a fallen creature already under judgment. Some early readers took the verse differently. They thought Paul meant the true God, who hands over to blindness the unbelievers of this present age. Either way, the verse gives no support to the idea of a second divine power running the world.

Titles like "the Most High God" can also mislead. They sound like the top rank in a ladder of gods. But the title describes God; it does not compare Him with other gods. It means He reigns over everything, with no power above Him or beside Him. It is like calling God "the Almighty." That does not mean there are other, weaker almighties.

This is also why the Bible never divides God's work among different powers. The God who raises the dead is the very same God who gives life in the womb. Paul describes Him as the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that did not exist (Romans 4:17). Creation and resurrection are not jobs for two deities. They are the work of the one Lord of life.

All of this matters for understanding the Trinity. When Christians confess the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, they are not adding gods, as if the Son and the Spirit were junior gods like the "gods" in Psalm 82. Paul holds both truths together in 1 Corinthians 8:6: "yet for us there is but one God, the Father," and "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came." The Son is not a creature honored with a borrowed title. He is the one true God, sharing fully in the one divine nature with the Father and the Spirit. Moses, judges and angels can be called "gods" only by comparison. The Son is God by nature.

So you can read these passages without worry. The Bible's language is rich and sometimes surprising, but its message never wavers. There is one living God, and He alone deserves our trust and worship.

topics.title: Is the doctrine of the Trinity logically coherent, avoiding both tritheism and modalism?
topics.cmp: Waterland, Gregory of Nyssa and Ambrose all deny that the doctrine falls into tritheism or modalism, but most of the answers here are Waterland's, and only on the Sabellian question do two authors answer the same question. Waterland argues the case at length. He says the propositions are only seemingly repugnant, like foreknowledge and future contingents. He distinguishes two senses of 'being': the Persons are three res, yet una res numero, because none exists separately. He locates unity in the Father as sole principle, with a coessential, inseparable Son and Spirit, and he defines tritheism historically as denying that unity of principle or making the Persons separate or alien. He leans heavily on antiquity and Revelation over speculation, and even cites the doctrine's long survival as confirming it is not absurd. Gregory argues polemically against Eunomius: no one in the Church taught that the Father's essence is divided or that he takes on three guises, and the Sabellian charge recoils on Eunomius himself, who, like Sabellius, denies the Son and Spirit a share in the Godhead. So on Sabellianism Waterland answers by contrasting real Persons with Sabellius's merely nominal distinction, while Gregory turns the accusation on the opponent. Ambrose offers no argument, simply asserting that speaking of two Gods or Lords is as profane as speaking of three.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: The belief of three Persons, every one singly God, and all together one God, seems to fall under case the fourth: the ideas are seemingly, not really, repugnant.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For as it is profane to say that there are three Lords or three Gods, so, too, is it utter profanity to speak of two Lords or two Gods

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: we say that it is equally impious and ungodly to call the Lord of the creation a created being and to think that the Father, in that He is, is separated or split up, or departs from Himself, or assumes the guise of three persons, like clay or wax moulded in various shapes

ans.text:
Yes. The Trinity is a mystery beyond our full understanding, but it is not a contradiction. A contradiction would be saying God is one and three in the same sense: one God and three Gods, or one Person and three Persons. Christians have never said that. We confess that God is one in being and three in Persons. He is one "what" and three "whos."

Here "being" or "essence" means what God is: his divine nature, with all his power, wisdom, goodness and life. "Person" means who God is: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, each truly distinct from the others. Each Person is fully God, because each has the whole divine nature, not a third of it. Yet there are not three divine natures, only one, shared completely by all three. So when we say "the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God," we are not counting three Gods. We are saying the same one God is truly known as Father, Son and Spirit.

This is not a puzzle someone invented. It is where the Bible leads. Scripture insists that there is only one God: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Yet John 1:1 says the Word "was with God, and the Word was God." Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one." And he sends his followers to baptize "in the name," singular, "of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Paul holds both truths together in 1 Corinthians 8:6, where there is "one God, the Father" and "one Lord, Jesus Christ," through whom all things came. Christians believe the Trinity because they will not let go of any of these texts.

So why is this not three Gods? It helps to ask what would actually make three Gods. You would need three separate beings, each existing on its own, each with its own independent power. Or you would need three rival sources of everything, or three divine beings of different kinds. Christians have always rejected all of that, and rightly called it false. The Father is the eternal source. The Son is "begotten" of him, which means he comes from the Father's very being, not made like a creature, and has always done so. The Spirit proceeds from the Father, which means he too eternally comes forth from him. The Son and Spirit are not copies or offshoots standing apart from the Father. They share his one being, are never separated from him, and always act together with one will and one power. Three human beings share "human nature," but each is a separate person who can go his own way. The Father, Son and Spirit cannot. That is why the comparison to three people fails. It is also why we do not speak of two Gods or three Gods, but one.

The opposite mistake is to say God is one Person who simply wears three masks, acting as Father at one time, as Son at another, and as Spirit at another. This is often called modalism. It sounds simpler, but the Bible will not allow it. At Jesus' baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven, all at once (Matthew 3:16-17). Jesus prays to the Father, speaks of the glory he had with the Father before the world began (John 17:5), and promises that the Father will send "another Advocate," the Spirit (John 14:16). Someone does not pray to himself, send himself, or call himself "another." The Persons are real and distinct. Their distinctness is not just a matter of names or roles.

Nor does the Church teach that the Father's being is cut into three pieces, or that God shifts shape from one form to another. God does not divide and does not change. All three Persons are fully God, always, together.

Can we picture how this works? Not completely, and we should be honest about that. But being beyond our understanding is different from being against reason. We cannot fully picture how God knows our future choices while we still freely make them, yet Christians rightly believe both. In the same way, we know clearly what we mean when we say each Person is truly God and that God is one. How these fit together in God's own life is deeper than we can see. That is not surprising. We are speaking about the infinite God, and we know him best not by guessing but by what he has shown us of himself in Scripture and in Christ.

So the Trinity holds a careful middle path. It refuses to divide God into three, and it refuses to blur the Father, Son and Spirit into one Person with three names. One God, three Persons. That is not a contradiction. It is the living God the Bible reveals.

topics.title: Does the oneness of God exclude a plurality of divine Persons?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that God's oneness does not exclude a plurality of divine Persons, but each makes the case on different ground. Owen and Bickersteth argue from Scripture itself: Owen holds that the very texts affirming God's oneness (Deut. 6:4, Isa. 44:6, 8) also signal a plurality of persons, while Bickersteth points to the Lamb sharing the Father's throne and receiving equal worship in Revelation. Basil and Gregory of Nyssa instead reason philosophically about number, holding that counting or ordering the Persons is a human device that leaves their nature unchanged. Gregory adds a scriptural illustration (Paul, Silvanus and Timotheus) and stresses that the joined names show the three acting harmoniously toward one end. Waterland, following Tertullian against Praxeas, and Hippolytus, against Noetus, answer specific opponents: Waterland by analysing 'monarchy' as one sole rule that a Son can share, and Hippolytus by insisting that confessing one God is compatible with the 'economy' and by rereading Noetus's own texts as the Father speaking of and to the Son.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: it is nowhere mentioned in the Scripture, but that, either in the words themselves or the context of the place, a plurality of persons in that one sense is intimated

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: Mere numerical rank does not create a different nature: that which we would count in a number remains the same in nature whether we count it or not.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Here, he says, it signifies only one authority ; and he shews that, taken in that sense, it was no just objection against a Trinity of Persons.

ans.text:
No. The Bible's insistence that there is only one God does not rule out the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit being three distinct Persons, because the oneness Scripture teaches is the oneness of the one divine being, not a solitary God who is alone inside himself.

Start with the bedrock. Israel's great confession is, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Christians have never softened this. There are not three Gods, three rulers, or three sources of everything. There is one God, one divine nature, one will, one power, one glory. When Christians say "essence" or "nature," they simply mean what God is. There is only one of that.

But the same Bible that says God is one also shows us, again and again, someone speaking to someone else within that one God. At Jesus' baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and the Father's voice speaks from heaven (Mark 1:10-11). In John 17:5 Jesus prays, "Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed." A person does not pray to himself, or share glory "with" himself. So the Father and the Son are truly distinct. Yet Jesus also says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). Both statements stand. The Son is not a second God beside the Father. He is the one God, together with the Father and the Spirit. A "Person" here means a distinct someone who can say "I" and "You," while "God" names the one being all three fully share.

Notice how often the Bible's own statements of God's oneness carry hints of this. In Isaiah 44:6 the LORD says, "I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me." In Revelation 22:13 Jesus takes that very title for himself: he is the First and the Last. Either there are two "firsts," which is impossible, or the Son shares the one identity of the LORD. Even Deuteronomy's confession names "the LORD" and "our God" and "the LORD" again, and Jesus himself reads Israel's faith as including the Son and the Spirit when he sends his disciples out to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice it is one name, not three names, yet three who bear it.

The book of Revelation paints the same picture in heaven. God sits on his throne. Yet Jesus says he "sat down with My Father on His throne" (Revelation 3:21), and the Lamb is seen in the midst of the throne. All creation then sings, "To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!" (Revelation 5:13). There is one throne and one worship. In a Bible that forbids worshiping anyone but God, the Lamb receives exactly the same praise. The God on the throne is not alone in endless solitude. Within his one life there is the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.

Some have objected that God's "monarchy," his sole rule over all things, means there can only be one Person. But think of a king who shares his throne with his own son and has him carry out his rule. The kingdom is not split in two. It is still one kingdom with one authority, now exercised by the father through the son. God's rule is like that, only more deeply so. The Father, Son, and Spirit do not hold three pieces of power. They share one power and act as one. The Father is the source, from whom the Son is "begotten," which means the Son comes from the Father as a son comes from a father, sharing his very nature, though in God this is eternal and had no beginning. So the one rule and the one source of the Godhead are kept, and the Persons are kept too.

A common misunderstanding goes the other way. Some imagine that the one God simply plays three roles, like one actor wearing three masks, being the Father at one moment, the Son at another, and the Spirit at another. But that cannot explain the Son praying to the Father, the Father sending the Son, or the Son and the Spirit both being present at the same moment as the Father speaks. Those are real relationships between real Persons, not one Person changing costumes.

What about counting them, or always listing them in the same order? Does calling the Spirit "third" make him lesser? No. Counting does not change what things are. If you count three people in a room, the third person is not less human than the first. Paul opens a letter from "Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy" (1 Thessalonians 1:1). They are named in an order, but all three are equally men, joined in one shared work. Numbers are just a tool we use to say "more than one," much like a scale or a ruler. They do not add or subtract anything from what is weighed or measured.

The usual order, Father, Son, and Spirit, does matter. It reflects real relationships: the Son is from the Father, and the Spirit is sent to us from the Father through the Son. But it is an order of relation, not of rank or worth. Scripture itself sometimes shuffles the order, as in 2 Corinthians 13:14, which speaks of "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit." When Jesus says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), he is speaking as the one who took on our humanity and came as the Father's sent servant, not denying the divine nature he shares with the Father.

So the oneness of God and the three Persons are not rivals. The Bible gives us both, often in the same breath. We worship one God, and we come to that one God through the Son, by the Spirit, to the Father. That is not a weakening of the confession that God is one. It is what the one God has shown us about himself.

topics.title: Do names applied to each Person make three Gods, Lords or Holies?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose of Milan, Augustine of Hippo and Hilary of Poitiers agree that names applied to the Persons do not multiply the Godhead. Gregory reasons from the single 'name' of the baptismal formula that any term for the divine Nature belongs equally to all three. Ambrose argues that because Godhead and Lordship are one and the Persons indwell one another, there are neither two or three Lords nor three Holies, citing Christ's saying about serving two lords and 'the Lord thy God is one Lord.' Ambrose also adds scriptural texts showing that things are said to be 'of' the Son and 'of' the Spirit just as they are 'of' the Father. Augustine treats a different side of the question: the relative names Father, Son and Gift are not shared mutually as 'friends' is, so there cannot be three Fathers or three Sons. Hilary, for his part, holds that the Son's birth from God proves him God without undoing the one God, while Warfield shifts from doctrinal argument to historical explanation, attributing the New Testament formula 'God, Lord, Spirit' to the speakers' different relations to Christ rather than to any difference in deity.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: that name should be applied alike to Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, whether it be “the Good” or “the Incorruptible,”

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: So, as we do not say that there are two Lords, when we so style both the Father and the Son, so, too, we do not say that there are three Lords, when we confess the Spirit to be Lord.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three…
refs.quote: But this is not the case in the Trinity, since the Father only is there father; and not Father of two, but of the Son only. Neither are they three Sons, since the Father there is not the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit.

ans.text:
No. When the Bible calls the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each "God," "Lord," or "holy," it is not counting three gods, three lords, or three holy beings. It is describing the one God, whose single nature belongs fully to each of the three.

Start with the name Jesus gave his church. He sent his disciples out "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice the word: name, not names. There is one name because there is one God. Whatever is true of God simply as God, his power, his goodness, his eternity, his holiness, his right to rule, is true of the Father, true of the Son, and true of the Spirit. None of them has a smaller share.

That is why counting works differently here than it does with us. Three people share human nature, and we rightly call them three humans, because each has his own separate piece of humanity. They can be apart from one another, disagree, and outlive one another. God's nature is not like that. It cannot be sliced into portions. The Father does not own one part of the Godhead and the Son another. Each Person is the whole one God, and Jesus can say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and also that he is in the Father and the Father is in him. Where there is one Godhead, there is one Lordship and one holiness, not three stacked side by side.

Take the word "Lord." Israel's great confession was, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus himself warned that no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24), yet he accepted Thomas's worship, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). He was not setting up a second master to compete with the Father. Paul even says of the Spirit, "Now the Lord is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:17). If calling both Father and Son Lord does not make two Lords, calling the Spirit Lord does not make three. There is one rule, one authority, exercised by the one God who is Father, Son, and Spirit.

The same is true of holiness. In Isaiah's vision the angels cry, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts" (Isaiah 6:3). Holiness is not a badge each Person earns separately. It is the very character of God, and that character is one. The Father is holy, the Son is holy, the Spirit is holy, yet there is one Holy One.

There is, however, one kind of name that is not shared, and it is worth seeing why. Words like "Father," "Son," and "Spirit" do not describe what God is but how the three are related to one another. Think of three friends: each is a friend to the others, so we can say "three friends." But in God the relationship names do not run both ways. Only the Father is Father, and he is Father of the Son alone. Only the Son is Son. Only the Spirit is the Spirit, breathed out and given by God. So we never speak of three Fathers or three Sons. The names for God's nature belong to all three equally; the names for their relationships belong to each one alone. Holding those two kinds of names apart keeps us from either merging the Persons together or splitting God into three.

This also helps with a puzzle many readers notice. Jesus usually speaks of "the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit." Paul and most of the apostles more often say "God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit," as in his blessing: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you" (2 Corinthians 13:14). Does calling the Father "God" and Jesus "Lord" put Jesus a step lower?

Not at all. The difference comes from who is speaking. Jesus would not naturally call himself "the Lord"; "the Son" was how he expressed his closeness to the Father and his likeness to him. Paul, on the other hand, was a servant and worshipper of Jesus. Christ was his Lord, so "Lord" became his everyday name for him. And for a Jew like Paul, "Lord" was no small title. It was the word his Bible used for the very name of God. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul takes Israel's confession of the one LORD and opens it up: "for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist." He places Jesus inside the one-God confession, sharing in the making of all things. Paul is not giving a ranked list; he is naming each Person by how he, a saved sinner, knows and worships him.

So when Scripture calls the Father "the one God," it does not make the Son less God. The Son is called the only Son because he is born of the Father, not made, and a son has the same nature as his father. His being from the Father is exactly what shows he is truly God, while God remains one. In the same way, the Bible freely says that we receive things from the Son and from the Spirit as well as from the Father: "From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace" (John 1:16), and whoever sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit (Galatians 6:8).

A common mistake is to picture the Trinity like a committee of three gods who agree with each other, or a family of three who share a last name. Scripture will not let us count that way. Another mistake runs the other direction, treating "Father," "Son," and "Spirit" as three masks worn by one Person. Scripture will not allow that either. The simple rule is this: what God is, he is once, and each Person is all of it; who God is, he is as three, each truly distinct from the others. That is why Christians can worship Jesus as Lord and the Spirit as Lord, and still sing with Israel that the LORD is one.

title: Persons, Essence and Their Distinction
desc: The terms person, substance, hypostasis and essence, real distinction against Sabellian modalism, relative and absolute predication, and the mutual indwelling of the Persons.

topics.title: Are the Father, Son and Holy Spirit really distinct Persons in one undivided substance?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are really distinct and not one Person under several names, and they reject Sabellius, Noetus and Praxeas while holding one God. Augustine, Athanasius, Hilary, Novatian, Hippolytus, Bickersteth and Warfield argue mainly from Scripture: the sending of the Son and Spirit, Christ's prayers and obedience to the Father, the baptism scene, 'another Advocate,' and John 5 and 10:30. Augustine, Owen and Gregory of Nyssa ground the distinction in relations of origin or incommunicable properties, and Hilary says the Son's birth is the only distinction between Father and Son, but they describe the Spirit's origin differently: Owen has the Spirit proceed from both, while Gregory has him come from the Father by means of the Son. On what makes them one they plainly diverge. Novatian, using 1 Corinthians 3:8, and Hippolytus place the oneness in shared mind, agreement, power and disposition, whereas Hilary reads that same text as unity of nature, and Athanasius says unity of agreement is only the creaturely copy of the Son's natural unity with the Father, which he illustrates with the sun and its radiance and with fire and its light. Owen treats the Persons as distinct intelligent, willing agents who know and love one another, while Edwards says they share one understanding, which is the Son; others defend the doctrine against objections in their own ways, with Waterland arguing from patristic history and terminology, and Gregory (on being without degrees), Owen (finite reasoning about the infinite) and Bickersteth (the analogy of white light) using philosophical reasoning and analogy.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How It Was Brought About that the Greeks Speak of Three…
refs.quote: there is both Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit; and that the Son is not the same with the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the same with the Father or the Son

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: The Holy Ghost therefore, cannot be identified or confounded either with the eternal Father, or with his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: but the Holy Spirit is not commingled with the Father and the Son, but is distinct from the Father and from the Son. For the Holy Spirit did not die

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible shows the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as three real and distinct Persons, not three names for one Person, and it also teaches that they are one God whose being is not split or shared out among them. Both truths belong together, and the Christian faith lets go of neither.

Start with the oneness. Scripture is clear that there is only one God: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Christians have never believed in three gods. When the church says the three Persons share one "substance" or "essence," it means they share one and the same divine being: one life, one power, one wisdom, one glory. The Father does not hold one third of God, with the Son and the Spirit holding the rest. Each Person is fully God, and there is still only one God.

Now the distinctness. Some have suggested that God is a single Person who wears three masks. On this view he appears as Father in creation, as Son in Jesus, and as Spirit in the church, the way one actor can play several parts. That idea can sound simple and tidy, but it does not fit what the Bible actually shows.

At Jesus' baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:16-17). That is not one actor changing costumes. All three are present at once, and one speaks to and about another.

The Gospels are full of this kind of real relationship. Jesus prays to the Father, thanks him, obeys him, and says he is going to him. If the Son were simply the Father under another name, those prayers would be a kind of talking to himself. They would teach us nothing true about God.

Jesus speaks of a relationship that existed before the world began. He prays, "And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). He also says the Father loved him before the foundation of the world (John 17:24). Love needs someone who loves and someone who is loved. Before anything was made, the Father and the Son were already together, sharing glory and love.

John's Gospel opens the same way: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Notice both halves. The Word was "with God," so he is distinct. The Word "was God," so he is not a lesser being.

When Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), he holds both truths in one sentence. "I and the Father" names two. "Are one" confesses one God. Had he meant there was only one Person, he could have said "I am the Father." He never says that.

The Holy Spirit is likewise his own Person, not just another name for the Father or the Son. Jesus says he will ask the Father, and the Father "will give you another Advocate" (John 14:16). The Spirit is "another": not the Father who gives, and not the Son who asks. Jesus also commands baptism "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). That is one name, so one God, but three who are named.

The Spirit came down on Jesus at his baptism and on the disciples at Pentecost. Nobody would say the Father came down on Jesus at the Jordan, or that the Son was poured out at Pentecost. And it was the Son who took on a human body and died on the cross, not the Father and not the Spirit.

So what is a divine "Person"? It does not mean a separate being, the way three human beings are three separate people with three separate bodies and lives. In God, a Person is a real someone who fully has the one divine being in his own particular way. Each one can say "I," speak to the others, and love the others. There is one "what" in God (one divine being) and three "whos" (Father, Son and Spirit).

What makes them distinct, if they share everything that makes God God? The Bible's answer is their relationships to one another. The Father is Father because he has a Son. The Son is Son because he is from the Father. Christians often say the Son is "begotten" of the Father, an old word meaning "born of" or "coming from" in a way that shares the same nature. This is not a birth at some point in time. It is an eternal relationship: there was never a moment when the Father was without his Son. The Spirit is distinct from both because he "proceeds," or goes out, from the Father, as Jesus says in John 15:26.

This is the one point on which sincere Christians have disagreed. Many believe the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son together. They point out that he is called "the Spirit of Christ" as well as the Spirit of God, and that Jesus says he will send the Spirit. Others hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, perhaps through the Son. They point to Jesus' own words in John 15:26 and want to keep the Father as the single source within God. Both sides agree on what matters most here: the Spirit is fully God, and he is really distinct from the Father and the Son.

These distinctions are not just about how God acts toward us. Some say God is only one Person on the inside, who simply appears as three when he deals with the world. But the Son was with the Father and loved by him before creation. That means the three are not roles God took on for our sake. They are who God eternally is. His outward works, sending the Son and pouring out the Spirit, show us what was already true within God.

It also helps to see that the three are never separated. Jesus asks, "Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me?" (John 14:10). This does not mean one is tucked inside the other like a box within a box. It means each fully shares the same divine life. Whoever meets the Son meets the very God who is the Father's own, which is why Jesus can say that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father. They are distinct, but they are never apart, never in competition, and never working on separate projects.

Everyday comparisons only go so far here. Water as ice, liquid and steam, or one man who is a father, a son and a husband, both picture one thing in three forms or roles. That is exactly the mistake the Bible rules out. It is better to accept that God is beyond our full understanding than to make him easier to grasp by flattening what he has shown us.

Why does this matter? The gospel depends on it. The Father really sent his Son, and the Son really offered himself to the Father for us. The Spirit really comes to live in us and unite us to Christ. When we pray, we pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. We are drawn into a love that has existed between the three Persons from all eternity. If the Persons were only names, that love would be only a figure of speech. Because they are real, the love is real too, and Paul can bless the church with "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Corinthians 13:14).

topics.title: What terms rightly express three Persons in one God?
topics.cmp: All the authors hold that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God in nature, essence and name, and are really distinct Persons. Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Hilary and Daniel Waterland all reject both tritheism and Sabellian confusion. Augustine does by far the most work on vocabulary, arguing philosophically. Essence is not a genus or species, and nothing of the divine essence exists beyond the Trinity. Absolute predicates such as good, eternal and omnipotent are said of the Trinity in the singular, while Father, Son and Gift are said relatively. 'Person' is used only out of the need to answer 'three what?', since God exceeds speech; Augustine even says 'person' is generic rather than the specific name the case would require, and that 'substance' applies to God only improperly, so the Greek 'three hypostases' and Latin 'three persons' agree in meaning despite Latin unease. Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary instead stress that the scriptural names themselves are real and informative: Hilary says Father and Son imply each other, Gregory says 'Son' alone among Christ's names signifies community of nature and that sharing the names 'Spirit' and 'Holy' properly proves one nature; Ambrose similarly argues that one shared Name implies one Godhead, and Bickersteth that one name of Jehovah holds three. On why we do not say three Gods, Augustine rests on Scripture's 'the Lord thy God is one God', Gregory on the claim that a common nature is never really plural even among men, and Waterland on sameness of substance plus inseparability making one numerical substance, while John Owen defends terms like 'one essence, three subsistences' as revealed because they follow necessarily from Scripture.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: As to the question, whether it shall be called specific or numerical, | am in no pain about it. Neither of the names exactly suits it; nor perhaps any other we can think on.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: The same love which is the Father’s is also the Son’s. For He Himself said: “He that loveth Me shall be loved of My Father, and I will love him.”

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and…
refs.quote: I do affirm, that if essence is a genus, then a single essence has no species; just as, because animal is a genus, a single animal has no species. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three species of one essence.

ans.text:
The church has learned to say that God is one in essence and three in person: one being, who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. These words do not explain God. They are careful fences, chosen to say what the Bible teaches and to keep us from saying what it denies.

Start with the two truths the words have to hold together. Scripture is clear that there is only one God: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). It is just as clear that the Father, the Son and the Spirit are each God, and that they are not the same as one another. The Father sends the Son. The Son prays to the Father. The Spirit is sent in the Son's name. Jesus tells us to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice that it says one name, yet three are named. Christians needed a way to say "one" and "three" without contradicting themselves. They did it by saying God is one in one respect and three in another.

The word for what God is, the "one", is essence. Older writers also used substance or being. Essence simply means what something is. Your essence is human. God's essence is everything that makes God God: eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good, perfectly holy. There is only one of these, so there is only one God.

The word for the "three" is person. Greek-speaking Christians often used another word, hypostasis, which means something like a real, distinct someone who truly stands there. The same word appears in Hebrews 1:3, where the Son is called "the exact representation of His nature." For a while the different words caused confusion. In Latin, "substance" usually meant the same as "essence", so "three substances" sounded like three gods. In Greek, "person" could sound like a mere mask or role. In time Christians saw that both sides meant the same thing. There is one divine being, and within it there are three who are truly distinct from one another, not three faces worn by one actor.

Why say "person"? It is not because the word captures God perfectly. It is because once we confess that there are three, someone fairly asks, "Three what?" We need some answer. "Three gods" is wrong. "Three parts" is wrong. "Three roles" is wrong. "Persons" is the best word we have. It says that the Father, the Son and the Spirit are each a real "who", able to know, love, speak and be spoken to.

The word still has limits. When we say "three persons" about people, we mean three separate beings with three separate lives. That is not what we mean about God. The Father, Son and Spirit do not have three separate divine natures, three wills pulling in different directions, or three separate amounts of power. Our ordinary words fall short of God, and we should hold them humbly.

The word consubstantial, or "of one substance", comes from the creed many churches recite. There the Son is called "of one being with the Father." This answered people who said the Son was only like the Father, a high and glorious creature. "Like" leaves room for a second, lesser being. "Of one substance" means the Son shares the very being of the Father. Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one."

The phrases "of one substance" and "one substance" guard different truths, so we need both. "One substance" stresses that there is only one God. "Of one substance with the Father" stresses that there really is a Son, distinct from the Father, who shares that one being.

This raises a subtle question. Is this oneness like the way three human beings share "humanity"? Peter, James and John all have the same kind of nature, yet they are three men. If the Trinity worked that way, we would have three gods of the same kind, and that is not what the Bible teaches.

The Father, Son and Spirit do not merely share the same kind of being. They are the one and the same God. Divine nature is not a category that the persons are individual examples of. It cannot be split up or multiplied. Some Christians have pointed out that no human term, whether "same kind" or "same individual", fits perfectly. What matters is that the oneness is real and not a figure of speech, and that the persons are still truly distinct.

A picture sometimes helps: three statues cast from one lump of gold. Every picture breaks down somewhere, though, and this one does too. Statues are made of pieces of gold, and the gold is not a person. Take any comparison as a hint, not a model.

These terms also shape how we use other words. Whatever belongs to God's being is said of each person and of God as a whole, in the singular. The Father is almighty, the Son is almighty, the Spirit is almighty, yet there is one Almighty. Each is good, wise and eternal, yet there is one good, wise and eternal God. Jesus can say "I am the truth," and the Spirit is "the Spirit of truth," because truth belongs to the one God they share.

Other words name how the persons relate to one another, and these belong to one person only. Only the Father is Father. Only the Son is Son, begotten of the Father, which means he comes from the Father's own being, not made but eternally from him. Only the Spirit is the Spirit who proceeds and is given as God's gift.

This is why we can pray in the name of all three. In 2 Corinthians 13:14, Paul blesses the church with the grace of Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit. It is one blessing, given by three.

One more caution: God is a Trinity, but not "triple." Three people together are more than one person alone. With God it is not so. The Father alone is not a third of God, and the three together are not "more God" than each one. Each person is the whole, perfect God, and nothing is added by counting them together.

In the end, these words serve worship. They help us say, without falling into error, what Scripture shows us. We know one God, who loves us as the Father who gave his Son, as the Son who gave himself, and as the Spirit poured into our hearts. It is one love, not three.

topics.title: Which things are said of God substantially, and which relatively?
topics.cmp: Augustine's distinction between absolute and relative predication, the reply to the Arian claim that every predicate names God's substance, and whether anything is said of God by accident. Includes related logical points on correlative names and negation.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: He proceeds to refute those arguments which the heretics…
refs.quote: some things are also predicated of Him relatively, i.e. not in respect to Himself, but to something not Himself, as He is called Father in respect to the Son, and Lord in respect to the creature that serveth Him

ans.text:
Some things are said of God as he is in himself, and some are said of him in relation to another. Words like good, wise, almighty, eternal and holy describe what God is. Words like Father, Son, begotten and Lord describe how one stands toward another. Seeing the difference clears up a great deal of confusion about the Trinity.

Start with the first kind. When we call God good, great, wise or eternal, we are not comparing him to anything. We are saying what he is. These words are said of his being, what older writers called his "substance" or "essence," meaning simply what God is. Because the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit share one and the same divine being, these words apply fully to each of them. The Father is almighty, the Son is almighty, and the Spirit is almighty. Yet we do not add them up into three almighties, as if there were three Gods. There is one almighty God. Jesus can say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), because what the Father is, the Son also is.

Now the second kind. "Father" is not a word God uses about himself in isolation. A father is always the father of someone. The Father is called Father because of the Son, and the Son is called Son because of the Father. In the same way, the Spirit is called the Gift because he is given, and given by someone. These words do not name a different kind of being. They name a relationship within the one God. So when the Bible says the Father begets the Son, it tells us how the Father and Son are related. It does not tell us they are made of different stuff.

This matters because a very old argument against the full deity of Christ ran like this. Every word said about God, it claimed, describes his very being. The Father is "unbegotten" and the Son is "begotten." So they must have different beings, and the Son cannot be God in the same sense as the Father. The answer is that the argument proves too much. If every word about God describes his being, then the Bible's statements that the Father and Son are one, and that the Son is equal with God (John 5:18; Philippians 2:6), would prove at once that they share one being. Once we admit that some words describe relationships rather than being, "begotten" and "unbegotten" fall into that group. A difference in relationship is not a difference in nature. A human son is no less human than his father.

Someone might ask whether these relationships are just passing features of God, like a man's suntan or his mood. They are not. In creatures, anything that is not part of what a thing is tends to be something that can come and go. A man can gain or lose weight, learn or forget, and become a father at a certain age. God is not like that. "I, the LORD, do not change" (Malachi 3:6), and with him "there is no change or shifting shadow" (James 1:17). Nothing in God can be gained, lost or worn away. The Father did not become Father one day, and the Son did not begin to be Son. He is the eternal Son, who was with God in the beginning (John 1:1). So the relationships in God are neither his being nor some changeable extra. They are as eternal and unchanging as God himself.

What about things that begin to be said of God at a certain time? God became Creator when there was a world, and Lord of Israel when there was an Israel. He became our refuge when we ran to him. Has God changed? No. The change is on our side. Think of a large rock on a hillside. When a traveler comes and shelters behind it, the rock becomes "his shelter." Nothing happened to the rock. Something happened to the traveler. In the same way, when Scripture says "Lord, You have been our dwelling place" (Psalm 90:1), the newness belongs to the creatures who now stand in relation to God, not to God, who is "from everlasting to everlasting" (Psalm 90:2).

One caution keeps all this in balance. The Father is not merely a relationship, as if he were nothing in himself and only "Father-toward-the-Son." A relationship needs someone who is related. A man must first be a man before he can be anyone's master or friend. So the Father is truly God in himself, and is also Father in relation to the Son. Each of the three is fully someone, not a mere label. That is part of what we mean by calling each a "person."

This also explains how the Son and Spirit can fully have wisdom, life and love without erasing the order among them. Jesus says, "For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). The Son has everything the Father has, including life in himself. But he has it from the Father, as God from God and wisdom from wisdom. The Spirit likewise has it from the one from whom he proceeds. Full equality in being and a real order of relationship go together.

Two smaller points round this out. First, sometimes a relational word has no matching word going the other way, but it is still relational. Scripture calls the Spirit the pledge, or down payment, of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:14). A pledge is always a pledge of something. Yet ordinary language has no neat word for what the pledge belongs to, as "giver" pairs with "gift." That gap is only a matter of how we talk. It does not mean the relationship is missing.

Second, putting "not" or "un-" in front of a word does not change what kind of word it is. "Not near" is still about relationship, and "not white" is still about color. So "unbegotten" is still a word about relationship. It simply says the Father is not from anyone. It does not describe a different divine nature from the Son's.

The practical upshot is simple. When you hear that God is holy, good or eternal, you hear what is true of the Father, the Son and the Spirit alike, the one God. When you hear Father, Son, begotten or sent, you hear about the real, eternal relationships within that one God. Keeping these two ways of speaking straight protects both truths the Bible teaches: there is one God, and the Father, Son and Spirit are truly distinct.

topics.title: What does the mutual indwelling of the Persons mean?
topics.cmp: Hilary of Poitiers and Basil of Caesarea agree that the Father being in the Son and the Son in the Father expresses one shared nature while the Persons stay distinct. Hilary insists this nature is inseparable but not confused, rejects any picture of one body containing another, and grounds the indwelling in the Son's true generation from the Father, citing the Gospels and Christ's own words. Basil states the same unity more briefly, as 'one and one' by distinction of Persons and one by community of nature. Others draw different consequences from Christ's saying: Gregory of Nyssa argues that because the Son has the whole Father in Him, He has the Father's full power, while Irenaeus uses it to argue that whatever bears the Son bears the Father, so only God's own creation could visibly bear His Word. Most of these authors speak only of Father and Son, but Jonathan Edwards explicitly extends the indwelling to all three Persons and frames it with a speculative model of the Son as God's idea of Himself and the Spirit as God's love, whereas Augustine, rather than offering an analogy, applies it to believers, teaching that through the Spirit's gift of love the whole Trinity dwells in them.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: to confess the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father through the unity of an indivisible nature, not confused but inseparable, not intermingled but identical, not conjoined but coexisting

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: In what manner in the confession of the three hypostases…
refs.quote: For the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son; since such as is the latter, such is the former, and such as is the former, such is the latter; and herein is the Unity.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: when the Lord declared, “For I am in the Father, and the Father in Me,”

ans.text:
When Jesus says that He is in the Father and the Father is in Him, He is telling us that the Persons of the Trinity are not three separate beings standing side by side. Each one lives wholly in the others, because they share one and the same divine life. Christians have sometimes used an old Greek word, perichoresis, for this. It simply means a mutual indwelling, or a being-in-one-another.

Jesus speaks this way often in John's Gospel. In John 10:30 He says, "I and the Father are one." A few verses later He says that His works show "that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father" (John 10:38). When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus answers that anyone who has seen Him has seen the Father, and asks, "Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me?" (John 14:9-10). He even says that the Father, dwelling in Him, is the One doing the works.

What does this mean? It helps to start with what it does not mean. It is not like one box sitting inside another, or water poured into a jar. Physical things cannot be inside each other both ways at once. If the jar holds the water, the water does not also hold the jar. God is not made of parts or spread out in space, so we should not picture the Father and the Son as two objects sharing a room. The Son is "in" the Father because they have one and the same nature, or essence. Essence here simply means what God is: His being, His life, His power, His goodness. There is only one of that. The Father does not have one portion of it and the Son another. Each has all of it.

That is why the Son can say the Father is in Him. The Son does not hold a slice of the Father. He holds the whole Father, because He has the whole divine nature. In the same way the Father holds the whole Son. This has a practical result. Whatever the Father is, the Son is too. Whatever the Father can do, the Son can do. That is why Jesus can say in John 5:19 that whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. No one in the Trinity is a lesser helper or a junior partner. Wherever one Person is at work, the others are present and at work too.

Why is this true? The Bible's answer lies in the relationship between the Father and the Son. Scripture calls Jesus the Father's only begotten Son. Begotten means fathered, brought forth from the Father's own being, rather than made from nothing like a creature. A human son receives his father's human nature. The eternal Son receives the Father's divine nature, but completely and without any beginning. He did not start to be the Son at some point. Because He comes from the Father in this way, He is never outside the Father, and the Father is never outside Him. The Son's very existence is to be from the Father and in the Father.

It matters just as much that this indwelling does not blend the Persons into one. The Father does not turn into the Son, and the Son does not dissolve into the Father. The Father is still the one who sends and the Son is still the one who is sent. The Son prays to the Father, and the Father speaks from heaven about the Son. They are truly two Persons, and the Spirit truly a third. Yet they are not divided either. A simple way to hold this together is to say the Persons are distinct but never separate, united but never mixed. They are one in what they are, and distinct in who they are toward one another.

This is true of the Holy Spirit as well, not only of the Father and the Son.
