Paul writes that the Spirit searches even the deep things of God, and that no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:10-11). The Spirit knows God from within, because He is within. Scripture calls Him both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ in the same breath (Romans 8:9). So the Father is in the Son and the Spirit, the Son is in the Father and the Spirit, and the Spirit is in the Father and the Son. Each is wholly present in the others.

This also explains why we speak of one God, not three. Since the three Persons share one undivided being, Christians call God holy, good, almighty, Savior and Judge in the singular. We do not worship three holy ones or three almighty ones, but one holy, almighty God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Finally, this teaching touches our own lives closely. Jesus promises in John 14:23 that if anyone loves Him and keeps His word, the Father will love him, and "We will come to him and make Our home with him." Notice the word "We." Paul says that God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit whom He has given us (Romans 5:5). The Spirit is the one given, but because the Persons are never apart, the gift of the Spirit brings the whole Trinity. Where the Spirit dwells, the Father and the Son dwell too. You never receive one third of God.

In John 17:21 Jesus prays for His people to be one, "as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You," and asks that they may also be in Us. Our share in God is real, but it is not the same as the Persons' share in one another. They are in each other by nature, as the one God. We are in God by grace, as creatures who are adopted, forgiven and made new. We are never turned into God, and we do not lose ourselves in Him. But we are welcomed into the fellowship that the Father, Son and Spirit have always enjoyed. The mutual indwelling of the Trinity is not just a puzzle for the mind. It is the home that God opens to His children.

topics.title: Which Scripture passages show the Persons to be distinct?
topics.cmp: Daniel Waterland and Benjamin B. Warfield both find the Persons distinguished in the Gospel record, but they argue differently. Waterland argues polemically, from the Sabellians' own premise that the divine nature was personally united to the man Christ Jesus: since Christ prays to the Father, is forsaken by him, and says the Father knows what he does not, the Father cannot be the Person united to that humanity, so there must be a distinct divine Son. He qualifies the ignorance texts as ignorance 'in a certain respect.' He also appeals to the Fathers: Tertullian, Hippolytus and Eusebius never used a literal reading of the Son's ignorance against the Sabellians, which he takes to show they did not read those texts that way. Warfield instead points to narrative scenes, the annunciation (Luke 1:35 and Matthew's Immanuel) and the baptism recorded by all four evangelists, where the three Persons appear together and the Deity of each, especially the Son, is emphasized as a deliberate revelation of the Triune God. On a cautionary point of interpretation, Augustine and Athanasius agree in substance that a third-person phrasing does not by itself mark a different person, though Athanasius's answer is headed 'Yes' while Augustine's says 'No.' Each supports this with Scripture's habits of speech (Augustine from the Psalms and Romans 1:3-4, Athanasius from Moses' self-references) but applies it to a different text: Augustine reads 'in the image of God' as the one Trinity, while Athanasius reads Peter's words as meaning the Word and Christ are one through the incarnation.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: it is manifest that the Father and Son are there spoken of, as of two Persons; and one as Anowvng, the other as not knowing, though only in a certain respect

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: Here the Holy Ghost is the active agent in the production of an effect which is also ascribed to the power of the Most High, and the child thus brought into the world is given the great designation of “Son of God.”

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
refs.quote: we are not compelled to understand any other person in the Trinity, but the one and selfsame Trinity itself, who is one God, and after whose image man is made.

ans.text:
The Bible shows that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are distinct Persons in many places. The clearest are the scenes where they act toward one another: one speaks and another is spoken to, one sends and another is sent, one prays and another hears. These passages matter because some have suggested that God is really a single Person who simply shows up in three roles, like one actor changing masks. Scripture does not let us think that way.

Start with the baptism of Jesus, which all four Gospels record. Jesus stands in the Jordan. The Spirit comes down from the opened heavens like a dove and rests on him. A voice from heaven says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:16-17). All three are present at the same moment, each doing something different. The Father speaks, the Son is spoken about, and the Spirit descends. One actor cannot play three parts on the same stage at the same time, especially when one of them is talking to another.

The announcement of Jesus' birth points the same way. The angel tells Mary, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). The Spirit is the one at work. The Most High is the Father whose power overshadows Mary. The child is his Son. Matthew's account adds that this child will save his people from their sins and will be called Immanuel, "God with us" (Matthew 1:21-23). It was fitting that the coming of the Son into the world was also a revealing of the triune God.

Then there are Jesus' prayers. In John 17 he prays at length to his Father. He asks, "Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). That is not a man talking to himself. It is the Son speaking to the Father about a shared glory they had together before creation. John's Gospel opens the same way: "the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). You can only be "with" someone who is not simply yourself. On the cross Jesus cries, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" and at the end, "Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit."

Jesus also counts the Father as a second witness alongside himself. The law said that the testimony of two is valid, and Jesus says he testifies about himself and the Father who sent him also testifies about him (John 8:17-18). If Father and Son were one Person, there would be only one witness, and his argument would fall apart.

The Spirit is distinguished in the same way. Jesus says, "I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate" (John 14:16). Here the Son asks, the Father gives, and the Spirit is sent as "another" helper, someone other than Jesus himself, though fully sharing his work. The command to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19) names all three side by side, under one name.

A harder passage also shows the distinction. Speaking of his return, Jesus says, "about that day or hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (Mark 13:32). Christians have explained this in slightly different ways. Most understand it as Jesus speaking as a true man, in the humble state he willingly took on, rather than meaning that God the Son lacks knowledge. Others stress that it was not his task to reveal that day. But on any reading the verse plainly sets the Son and the Father side by side as two, not one. This points to something deeper. It was the Son, not the Father, who became a man. The Father did not take on flesh, pray, or die. So the one who did must be a real Person who is not the Father, yet is truly God.

It helps to add a word of caution. Not every place where the Bible speaks of God in the third person proves there is another Person. Scripture often talks this way about one and the same subject. Moses writes "as the LORD commanded Moses" about himself, and the Psalms switch freely between speaking about the Lord and speaking to him. So the strongest evidence is not a turn of grammar. It is the real relationships the Bible shows: Father and Son speaking to each other, loving each other, sending and being sent, and the Spirit coming from them to us.

None of this means there are three Gods. The same Bible insists that the Lord is one (Deuteronomy 6:4), and Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). The Persons are distinct, but they are not separate or divided. They share one divine nature, one being of God, while truly relating to one another as Father, Son, and Spirit. The God we worship is not a lonely Person playing roles. He is a living fellowship of love, and through the Son and by the Spirit he welcomes us into it.

topics.title: Are the Son and Spirit only temporary modes or expansions of one God?
topics.cmp: Ambrose and Athanasius agree in rejecting the view that the Son and Spirit are temporary forms or mere names of the one God, but they argue on different grounds. Ambrose argues from the doctrine of God itself: the view collapses the Holy Spirit's distinction and makes God a single being shifting between forms, whereas Father, Son, and Spirit remain unchangeably distinct while sharing one power. Athanasius instead argues by reductio. If the Word withdrew back into the Father, creation, which came to be through the Word's going forth, would cease to exist. He also turns the opponents' own condemnation of the Arians against them, since censuring 'once the Son was not' tacitly concedes that the Son truly exists, which makes their denial of his subsistence worse than the Arian position. Ambrose, alone of the two, explicitly includes the Spirit; Athanasius's answers concern only the Word or Son.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: whereas the distinction between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit always abiding and unchangeable, preserves the Unity of its power.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: if the Monad itself was dilated into a Triad, and that, Father and Son and Holy Ghost, then Father and Son and Spirit prove the same, as Sabellius held

ans.text:
No. The Son and the Holy Spirit are not temporary forms that God puts on for a while and then sets aside, and they are not pieces of the Father that stretched out from him and will one day be pulled back in. The Father, the Son and the Spirit are three real persons who have always been, and always will be, the one God.

Some have pictured God as a single person who, at some point, expanded into three, perhaps to create the world, to become human, or to give the Spirit. When the job is done, the idea goes, the Son and the Spirit fold back into the Father. Others have said that "Son" is just a title God wears for a season, which will be dropped once its purpose is met. These ideas can sound reverent, but they do not match what the Bible shows us, and they collapse under their own weight.

Think about what expanding actually means. A balloon that is blown up is bigger, but it is still the same balloon. Paul once urged the Corinthians to open wide their hearts to him (2 Corinthians 6:11-13). If they did, they would not turn into other people. They would still be the same Corinthians, only more open. In the same way, if the Father simply expanded, the result would not be three persons. It would just be the Father, stretched out. The Son and the Spirit would be names for the Father at different times, not persons who truly relate to one another.

But Scripture shows them relating to one another as real persons. At Jesus' baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:16-17). All three are present at once, and each acts toward the others. Jesus prays to the Father, not to himself. He promises that the Father will send "another Advocate," the Spirit (John 14:16). A person cannot be "another" to himself.

The Bible also says the Son did not begin to exist when he was needed. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Before anything was made, he already was, and he was with God, which means distinct from the Father, though never separate from him. Jesus speaks of "the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). If the Son only appeared later, God would once have been without his Word, his own self-expression. That would make God incomplete, needing to grow into who he is. But God does not change (Malachi 3:6). The Father has always been Father, because he has always had his Son.

There is a practical side to this too. Scripture says all things were made through the Word (John 1:3) and that in him "all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). The world does not just get started by the Son and then run on its own. It is held in being by him moment by moment. If the Son were to withdraw into the Father and stop existing as Son, the creation he upholds would have nothing to rest on. We are only secure because he truly and permanently is.

The same is true of our salvation. Jesus told his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). We are joined to the Son in baptism. If "Son" were only a temporary label, set aside once its work was finished, then what we were baptized into would simply lapse. But the risen Jesus remains our Savior. "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Hebrews 13:8). He "always lives to intercede" for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and of his kingdom "there will be no end" (Luke 1:33).

Some wonder about 1 Corinthians 15:28, where Paul says that at the end the Son will be made subject to the Father, "so that God may be all in all." This does not mean the Son dissolves or disappears. A person who hands over a finished task to someone is still there afterward. Paul is describing Christ completing his saving mission and presenting the redeemed kingdom to the Father. The final picture of Scripture is "the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Revelation 22:1), with the Son still present forever.

So God is not one person changing costumes or swelling and shrinking. He is eternally one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each truly himself and always united. That is good news. The God who made us, saved us and lives in us will never stop being who he has shown himself to be.

topics.title: Does distinguishing the Persons imply composition, inequality or corporeality?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine and Irenaeus all deny that distinguishing the Persons brings composition, inequality or corporeality into God, but each argues on different ground. Gregory works mainly by logical and philosophical analysis against Eunomius. Common and special attributes are 'accompanying conceptions' rather than the essence, as Basil's example of the name 'Peter' shows, so their conjunction does not make the simple, non-quantitative nature composite. He turns the charge back on Eunomius's own 'true Light' and 'unapproachable Light'. He also uses the many incorruptible souls of one essence to show that consubstantiality does not imply bodily corruption, and he calls it profane to rank the Persons like creatures. Augustine concentrates on equality: in a nature without bulk, where to be, to be true and to be great are the same, one Person is as great as two or all three, and his few 'Yes' answers state this same conclusion (each is as great as all together, since perfection cannot increase) rather than a different view. He contrasts this with men, statues and bodies, and he separately offers created signs, including the consecrated bread and wine, as an analogy for signifying without identity. Irenaeus argues from Scripture, reading Paul's 'star differs from star' as a difference in glory only, so that beings derived from the Father's light cannot differ in substance or passibility. This point parallels Gregory's insistence on sameness of nature, though it is aimed at a different opponent.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For our statement does not hereby violate the simplicity of the Godhead, since community and specific difference are not essence, so that the conjunction of these should render the subject composite

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Of the Attributes Assigned by Hilary to Each Person. The…
refs.quote: but in that highest Trinity one is as much as the three together, nor are two anything more than one.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For if “one star differs from another star in glory,” but not in qualities, nor substance, nor in the fact of being passible or impassible

ans.text:
No. Telling the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit apart does not split God into parts, rank one Person above another, or give God a body. Each of those worries comes from picturing God the way we picture things in the world: things with size, made of pieces, that wear out. God is not like that, and once we see why, the objections lose their force.

Start with what the church means by God's "essence." The word simply means what God is: his being, his nature, everything that makes God to be God. The Father, the Son and the Spirit do not each have a share of that nature, the way three people might split a pie. Each is fully God. Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one," and Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the exact representation of His nature." What makes the Persons distinct is not a difference in what they are, but how they stand toward one another. The Father is Father because he has a Son. The Son is Son because he is from the Father. The Spirit is breathed out, or proceeds, from the Father. These are relationships within the one God, not ingredients he is made of.

That answers the first objection, that distinct features must make God composite, meaning built up out of parts. A thing is composite when it has pieces that could, at least in thought, be taken apart, like the wood and nails of a chair. But being "Father" or "Son" is not a piece of God bolted onto the divine nature. It is a way the one undivided God exists in relationship. Even our ordinary speech shows this. When you hear a friend's name, the name points you to that particular person, not to some extra stuff added to human nature. Peter and John are equally human. Their names mark out who each one is, not a different kind of being. In a far higher way, the names Father, Son and Spirit mark out who, not a different what.

Scripture itself speaks this way. John 1:9 calls the Son "the true Light," and 1 Timothy 6:16 says God dwells in "unapproachable light." Both are light. They are one light shining, not two lights of different kinds, and not one light chopped in half. Anyone who calls both Father and Son "light" while also distinguishing them is already admitting that a shared nature and distinct Persons can go together without making God a patchwork.

The second worry is about size. Surely, someone says, three Persons together must be more than one Person alone? With bodies that is true. Three gold coins are worth more than one. Three people fill more space than one. But Jesus teaches that "God is Spirit" (John 4:24). God has no bulk, no volume, no quantity. When we call God "great," we do not mean he is large. We mean he is perfect: perfectly good, wise, true and alive. And perfection cannot be increased by addition. The Father is not partly God, waiting for the Son and Spirit to make up the total. He is wholly God. So is the Son, and so is the Spirit. Put them "together" and you do not get more God. You get the one God, who was already fully present in each. That is why Christians confess one God, not three gods, and not a God who is "triple" the way a three-layer cake is triple.

This also rules out inequality between the Persons. The Son is not a smaller portion of deity, and the Spirit is not a lesser third. Jesus could say, "Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9), because nothing of the Father's divinity is missing in the Son. Paul says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form" (Colossians 2:9). All the fullness, not most of it. When the Bible speaks of the Son obeying or being sent, it is speaking of the order of their relationship and of the Son's humble work as a man for our salvation, not of a lower grade of being.

A third objection uses examples from creation. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15 that the sun, moon and stars differ in splendor, one star from another. Doesn't that show that things coming from one source can differ in their very nature? But Paul is talking about differences in glory among created things, in a passage about the resurrection body. He is not describing different kinds of substance, and he is certainly not describing God. Creatures can differ greatly from one another, as the whole sky differs from one small star. To imagine that kind of gap between the Father and the Son would be to treat God as one more ranked item in creation. The Trinity stands above creation altogether, and the divine nature does not come in higher and lower degrees. Analogies from the world can help us a little, but where they bring in size, rank or pieces, we must leave that part behind.

The last worry runs in two directions. Some say that if the Persons share one essence, they must be identical, just one Person wearing three masks. Others say that if things share one nature, they must be bodily and so able to decay. Neither follows. Sharing a nature does not erase who someone is. Every human being shares one human nature, yet you are not your neighbor. In God, the Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit, even though each is the one God. As for decay, bodies wear out because they are made of parts that can come apart, not because they share a nature with other bodies. Human souls share one nature, yet that does not make them crumble like flesh. And God, who has no parts at all, cannot fall apart. "I, the LORD, do not change" (Malachi 3:6).

It helps to see the difference between sharing God's nature and imitating God's character. We are called to be merciful as our Father is merciful, and by grace believers really do grow in kindness and humility. But that does not make us one with God in nature. We remain creatures who reflect him. The Son and the Spirit do not merely reflect God's goodness. They are God, sharing his very being, and therefore also perfectly one in will and action.

So the Christian can confess, without contradiction, that God is three Persons and one God. The Persons are truly distinct in their relations, yet the divine nature is not divided, not ranked, not made of parts and not bodily. This is hard for our minds because we are so used to thinking in terms of space and quantity. But the difficulty is on our side, not in God. The God who is Spirit is fully present as Father, fully present as Son, and fully present as Holy Spirit, and he is one.

topics.title: If the Son has all that the Father has, why is he not the Father?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Waterland, and Gregory of Nyssa all deny that the Son's full possession of what the Father is makes Him the Father or strips Him of His own existence. Augustine gives the positive ground most directly: the Son is equal to the Father, "Essence of Essence," and the distinction lies solely in the relation of begetting and being begotten, not in essence. Waterland does not name the relation. He argues that the Son can share even the Father's individual attributes, as He shares the individual essence, without being the Father, and he turns the issue polemically: denying this reduces the Son to a creature, so the real question is whether the Son is God at all. Gregory meets a narrower opponent's claim, that the Father's essence draws existence to itself. He refutes it by philosophical reductio, showing that it is either superfluous or unintelligible and ends either in Sabellius's error or in separating the Existent from existence. None of the three answers appeals explicitly to Scripture.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father,…
refs.quote: is altogether that which the Father is, yet is not the Father, because the one is Son, the other is Father

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: On the contrary, I affirm, that he hath the individual attributes of God the Father, as much as he has the individual essence: for otherwise he must be a creature only

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For we too say that He who has all that belongs to His own Father is all that He is, save being Father, and that He who has all that belongs to the Son exhibits in Himself the Son in His completeness, save being Son

ans.text:
The Son has everything the Father has except one thing, which is being the Father. That one exception is not a gap in the Son's nature or a quality he lacks. It is simply the difference between giving and receiving, between the one who begets and the one who is begotten.

Start with what the Bible says the Son shares. Jesus says in John 16:15, "Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine." In his prayer in John 17:10 he says to the Father, "All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine." Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the exact representation of His nature." So the Son is not a smaller or partial copy of God. Whatever makes the Father God, his life, power, wisdom, eternity and glory, belongs to the Son fully. Theologians call this shared divine nature the "essence": what God is.

This is not two sets of divine qualities that happen to match, as if the Father had his own wisdom and the Son a second wisdom just like it. There is one God, so there is one divine wisdom, one power, one life, and the Son has that very wisdom and life. That is why Jesus can say in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one." If the Son had only a lesser, borrowed set of powers, he would be a creature, however exalted. The real question is never whether the Son is a little less than the Father. It is whether he is God or not, and Scripture's answer is that he is.

So why is he not the Father? Because "Father" and "Son" are not names for qualities. They are names for a relationship. To be Father is to be the one from whom the Son comes. To be Son is to be the one who comes from the Father. "Begotten" is the Bible's word for this. It means the Son comes from the Father the way a son shares his father's nature, not the way a craftsman makes a table. Jesus puts it this way in John 5:26: "As the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself." The Son has life in himself, the same divine life, but he has it from the Father. The Father has it from no one.

Think of it this way. Everything that can be given, the Father gives the Son. But the Father cannot give the Son the position of being the Giver, because the Son is the one receiving. That is not a limit on the Father's generosity. It is just what it means for there to be a giving at all. The Son receives everything, and so he is fully God. He receives it, and so he is the Son and not the Father.

An everyday comparison helps a little. A human son has the same human nature as his father. He is just as human, not half human. Yet no one confuses the two, because one is the father and the other the son. The comparison breaks down in important ways. A human father and son are two separate beings, and the father existed before the son. In God there is one being, and the Son is eternal. John 1:1 says that in the beginning "the Word was with God, and the Word was God." There was never a time when the Father was without his Son. Still, the comparison shows the main point. Sharing a whole nature does not erase the difference between parent and child.

Some have objected that if the Son has absolutely everything the Father has, then the Son must also be the Father, and we end up with one person who is both begetter and begotten. The answer is that the objection actually shows the truth it tries to deny. Because the Son has all the Father is, Jesus can say in John 14:9, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father." The Father is fully shown in the Son, while remaining himself. Yet the Son never speaks as if he were the Father. He prays to him, is sent by him, and speaks of the glory he shared "with" him before the world existed (John 17:5). You cannot be with yourself in that way. The Father and the Son are distinct, and they are distinguished only by this relation, not by any difference in what they are.

Two opposite mistakes are worth gently avoiding. One is to think that because the Son comes from the Father, he must be less divine, a sort of second-tier God. Scripture rules this out by giving him everything the Father has. The other mistake is to think that "Father" and "Son" are just two roles or masks worn by one person at different times. Scripture rules this out too, because the Father and the Son love each other, speak to each other, and are present together, as at Jesus' baptism.

So the Son is not the Father, not because something is missing in him, but because he is the Father's beloved Son. He shares the whole of God's nature, and he shares it as the one who receives it eternally from the Father.

topics.title: How do wisdom, understanding and love belong to each Person?
topics.cmp: Augustine and Owen agree that wisdom (and for Owen also will and immensity) is said of God according to the one essence: Augustine argues from divine simplicity, where to be is to be wise, and holds that each Person singly is wisdom yet the three together are one wisdom, not three. Owen likewise holds that such attributes belong to each Person as God, not by that Person's personal property. Augustine sharply separates these essential names from the relative name 'Word,' which, like 'Son,' belongs to the Son alone, so Father and Son are not together one Word. Edwards takes a markedly different approach: he identifies the Son with the divine understanding and the Spirit with the divine love, and says the Spirit has understanding, and the Father is wise and loving, because the other Persons indwell Him, citing Scripture's calling the Son the wisdom, reason and truth of God. This account, in which the Father is wise by His own wisdom, the Son, being in Him, stands in tension with Owen's claim that wisdom is in the Father simply because He is God and not by any personal property. It also differs from Augustine's view that each Person is wisdom by the one essence rather than through a relation to another Person.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Father and the Son are Together One Wisdom, as One…
refs.quote: Whence the Father and Son together are one wisdom, because one essence, and singly wisdom of wisdom, as essence of essence.

refs.author: Jonathan Edwards
refs.quote: The understanding is so in the Spirit that the Spirit may be said to know, as the Spirit of God is truly and perfectly said to know and to search all things, even the deep things of God.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: The wisdom, the understanding of God, the will of God, the immensity of God, is in that person, not as that person, but as the person is God.

ans.text:
Each of the three Persons is fully wise, fully understanding and fully loving, yet there are not three wisdoms or three loves in God but one, because wisdom and love belong to the one God whom all three are.

Start with what the Bible says about God himself. Paul marvels in Romans 11:33, "O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" Wisdom is not something God picked up or holds onto, the way a person gains wisdom with age. God does not have wisdom the way we have a coat. He simply is wise, through and through. To be God and to be wise are, in him, the same thing.

That is the key. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, yet there is one God. The Father, Son and Spirit each have the whole of the one divine being, not a third of it. Whatever belongs to that being, such as wisdom, goodness, power, knowledge and love, belongs fully to each. So the Father is wise, the Son is wise, and the Spirit is wise. But since there is only one divine being, there is only one divine wisdom. They are not three wise beings comparing notes, like a committee. They are one God who knows and loves with one wisdom and one love.

The creed gives a helpful picture when it calls the Son "Light from Light." The Father is light and the Son is light, yet together they are not two lights but one light. In the same way the Son is Wisdom from Wisdom, and the Father and Son together are one wisdom. The Spirit, being God, is that same light and that same wisdom.

Someone may ask why the Bible seems to give wisdom especially to the Son. Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" in 1 Corinthians 1:24, and John calls him the Word in John 1:1. A word is how a mind expresses what it knows, so it fits that the Son is pictured as God's perfect expression of himself. But this does not mean the Father lacks wisdom of his own, or that the Spirit is not wise. It means the Son is wisdom in a particular way: wisdom that comes from the Father, as a son comes from a father.

This shows an important difference between two kinds of words we use about God. Some words describe what God is. "Wise," "good" and "almighty" are like this, and they are true of all three Persons together as one. Other words describe how the Persons stand toward one another. "Father," "Son" and "Word" are like this. A son is always someone's son, and a word is always someone's word. So while the Father and Son together are one wisdom, they are not together one Word, any more than they are together one Son. Only the Son is the Word, because only the Son comes from the Father. The shared words never multiply. The relational words never merge.

What about love and the Spirit? Scripture links the Spirit closely with love. "God is love," says 1 John 4:8, and Romans 5:5 says God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Many Christians have found it fitting to think of the Spirit as the love that flows between the Father and the Son. But this does not make the Spirit a love without a mind, or a mere force. The Bible plainly shows him knowing. In 1 Corinthians 2:10 we read, "The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God," and the next verse says no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. The love of God is never blind love. It is love that sees and knows.

How, then, should we think of each Person having understanding and love? The surest answer is that each has them because each is God. The Father is wise not because he is the Father but because he is God, and the same is true of the Son and the Spirit. Some thoughtful Christians have added a further way of putting it. Jesus says in John 14:10, "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me." Because the Persons dwell completely in one another, the Son, who is God's Wisdom, is never absent from the Father or the Spirit, and the Spirit, who is God's Love, is never absent from the Father or the Son. On this view the Father is never without his Wisdom and the Spirit is never without understanding. This picture is meant to show how closely the Persons share everything. It does not suggest that any Person is lacking on his own. None of them is ever on his own.

Two misunderstandings are worth avoiding. One is to imagine three separate minds that happen to agree, which would make three gods. The other is to think the Persons are only three names for one person playing different roles, which would erase the real Father, Son and Spirit the Bible shows us. The truth lies between. There is one wisdom, one understanding and one love, because there is one God. And that one wisdom and love belongs wholly to the Father, wholly to the Son and wholly to the Spirit, each in his own distinct way.

title: God the Father
desc: The Father as unbegotten source, the eternity of his fatherhood, his invisibility, and how he is known and seen through the Son.

topics.title: What does it mean that the Father alone is unbegotten, the source 'from no one'?
topics.cmp: Novatian, Gregory of Nyssa, and Augustine agree that the Father alone has no source and is the beginning of the Son, but they make the point in different ways. Novatian states it directly: the unborn Father, beyond any beginning, is the beginning of the Son and of creatures, and the born Son reveals him as that beginning. Gregory of Nyssa argues defensively against Eunomius, insisting that Basil's 'from no one' denies any cause and does not assert origin from nonentity; he grounds this in Luke's genealogy, read as a list of fathers ending in God, and adds that 'ungenerate', like 'Father', is a relational name with more than one meaning rather than God's essence. Augustine reaches a similar non-essential conclusion by philosophical analysis, holding that 'Beginning' is said of the Father relatively, toward the Son and toward all things from him, like 'creator' or 'master', and not according to substance. Irenaeus also reads Luke's genealogy, but for a different purpose: for him its backward order shows Christ regenerating and recapitulating Adam and all nations, not the Father's unbegottenness.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father…
refs.quote: For since that is the beginning to other creatures which is unborn,—which God the Father only is, being beyond a beginning of whom He is who was born,—while He who is born of Him reasonably comes from Him who has no beginning

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Father and the Son the Only Beginning (Principium)…
refs.quote: if the begetter is a beginning in relation to that which he begets, the Father is a beginning in relation to the Son, because He begets Him

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: Stealing an expression from its context, from which he drags it, as from its surrounding body, into a naked isolation, he tries to carp at it by worrying the word

ans.text:
To say the Father alone is unbegotten means that he is the one person of the Trinity who comes from no one. He was not born, made, sent, or produced by anyone. He has no source behind him. He is the source.

The word "begotten" is an old word for being fathered, for receiving your life from a parent. The Bible speaks of the Son this way. John calls him the one and only Son who comes from the Father (John 1:14, 18), and Jesus says, "I came from God" (John 8:42). The Holy Spirit also comes from the Father. Jesus calls him the Spirit "who proceeds from the Father" (John 15:26). But Scripture never says the Father comes from anyone. Nobody sends him and nobody begets him. That is all "unbegotten" means. It is a way of saying that the Father has no father.

Luke gives a striking picture of this. His family tree of Jesus runs backward, generation by generation: Jesus was the son of Joseph, as people supposed, the son of Heli, and so on, all the way back. It ends with "the son of Adam, the son of God" (Luke 3:38). Every name in that list points to a father before it. Adam had no human father, so Luke goes straight to God. And then the list stops. There is no one to name before God. The chain of fathers ends in the one who has no father. That is the Father's place within the Trinity too. Every line of origin traces back to him, and with him it comes to rest.

People sometimes misunderstand the phrase "from no one." It does not mean the Father came from nothing, as if he popped into being out of emptiness. It means the opposite. He never came to be at all. He simply is, without cause or beginning. "From everlasting to everlasting, You are God" (Psalm 90:2). Nothing stands behind him, above him, or before him.

This is also why Christians have sometimes called the Father the "beginning" of the Son. This needs care, because it sounds as if the Son had a starting point. He did not. The Son has always been the Son, just as the Father has always been the Father. A father is not a father until he has a child, and God the Father has never been without his Son. So "beginning" here does not mean a first moment in time. It means source. Think of the sun and its light. The light comes from the sun, but there was never a sun that had not yet started shining. Or think of a spring and the stream that flows from it. Jesus puts it this way: "For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). The Son has the very same life as the Father. He has it from the Father, eternally.

Another common mistake is to think that being unbegotten is what makes God God. If that were true, the Son and Spirit, who come from the Father, would be something less than God. But being unbegotten is not a description of what God is made of, so to speak. It describes how the Father stands toward the other two persons. Being someone's son tells you about a man's relationships, not about whether he is fully human. A son is every bit as human as his father. In the same way, the Son is every bit as divine as the Father. "I and the Father are one," Jesus says (John 10:30). The difference between Father and Son is not in their divine nature or glory. The difference is only in who comes from whom.

So the name "Father" carries two truths at once. It says he has no source, and it says he has a Son. Both belong together. A king is someone with no master over him and also someone who rules. In the same way, the Father is the one who comes from no one and the one from whom the Son is eternally born.

The Father is also the beginning of all creation, but in a different way. Paul writes that for us there is "one God, the Father, from whom all things came," and "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came" (1 Corinthians 8:6). Creatures come from the Father by being made out of nothing, through the Son. The Son comes from the Father by being begotten, sharing his own life. One is making, and the other is fathering. That is why the Son is Creator alongside the Father and not a creature.

Sincere Christians agree that the Father is the unbegotten source. They have disagreed over whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son together. Some stress that the Father is the single fountain of the Godhead, since Jesus says the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Others point out that the Spirit is also called the Spirit of the Son (Galatians 4:6) and is sent by the Son, so they see the Son sharing in the Spirit's coming forth. Both sides confess that the Father is the source who is from no one.

For ordinary believers this is more than a puzzle about words. It means that when we pray "Our Father," we come through the Son to the very source of all life and love. Behind the Father there is nothing deeper and no one higher. And he has always been a Father who pours out his life to his Son, and in the Son, to us.

topics.title: Has God always been Father, and is 'Father' a relative name?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary of Poitiers and Augustine all treat 'Father' as a relative name that implies the Son, but they develop the point in different directions. Gregory argues it most fully against Eunomius: 'Father' by its meaning brings the Only-begotten with it, so the Son's eternity cannot be separated from the Father's, while 'ungenerate' carries no such relation. One of his answers is labelled 'No' but makes the same case, saying the Father has neither existence nor name without the Son, as the Powerful cannot be without Power, and appealing to Christ as God's Power and Wisdom. Hilary reasons more briefly that because there is a Father there is a Son, in whom the Father is revealed and who is therefore very God. Augustine agrees that God is called Father relatively, in relation to the Son, as He is called Lord in relation to creatures, but his distinctive concern, which the others do not raise, is that a relative name presupposes substance: the Father must be something in respect to Himself, as a man must exist before he can be called master, or else he would be wise, great and good only through what he begot, and the Son would absurdly be substantial while the Father is merely relative.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: But if the First Father has no cause transcending His own state, and the subsistence of the Son is invariably implied in the title of Father, why do they try to scare us

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Because there is a Father we know that there is a Son; in that Son the Father is manifested to us, and hence our certainty that He is born the Only-begotten and that He is very God.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of…
refs.quote: Wherefore, if the Father also is not something in respect to Himself then there is no one at all that can be spoken of relatively to something.

ans.text:
Yes. God has always been Father, because he has always had a Son. And yes, "Father" is a relational name. It tells us who God is toward the Son, not some separate quality he has on his own.

Start with what the Bible says about the Son. John's Gospel opens, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The Son did not come into being at some point. He was already there "in the beginning." On the night before he died, Jesus prayed, "Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). He also spoke of the Father loving him "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). So before anything was made, there was a Father and a Son, loving each other and sharing glory.

If the Son has always existed as Son, then the Father has always been Father. You cannot have one without the other. A man is not a father until he has a child. But the Son has always been, so there was never a time when God was not yet Father.

This is where the word "begotten" helps. To beget means to bring forth someone who shares your own nature. A carpenter makes a chair, which is a different kind of thing from himself. A father begets a child, who is the same kind of being as himself. The Bible calls Jesus God's "one and only Son" (John 1:18), not something God made. And unlike any human birth, this begetting is not an event that happened on a certain day. It is an eternal relationship: the Father always giving his whole life and being to the Son, and the Son always receiving it.

Some people imagine that God was first just "God" and only later decided to become Father, perhaps at creation or at Bethlehem. Scripture closes off that idea. God does not change. James calls him the Father "with whom there is no change or shifting shadow" (James 1:17). If being Father to such a Son is good, God would never have lacked it. If it were not good, he should never have taken it up. A God who later gained a Son would be a God who once lacked something. The living God has never lacked anything good. At Bethlehem the eternal Son took on human flesh. He did not begin to be the Son there.

Now to the second part of the question. Some words describe what a thing is in itself, like "wise" or "good." Others describe how it stands toward something else, like "teacher," "friend," or "father." "Father" is the second kind. It means "Father of the Son." That is why saying "Father" already brings the Son to mind. John puts it this way: "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father" (1 John 2:23). Jesus taught us to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). These are names that belong together.

This matters, because it shows how three persons can be one God. Whatever is said of God in himself is true of all three alike. The Father is God, wise, good, eternal and almighty. So is the Son. So is the Spirit. Yet there are not three Gods, three wisdoms or three almighties. What tells the persons apart is not a difference in their divine nature. It is their relations to one another. The Father is the one who begets. The Son is the one who is begotten. The Spirit is the one who proceeds.

One caution keeps us from going too far the other way. "Father" is relational, but the Father is not only a relation. A man can only be called a master because he is first a man. In the same way, there must be someone real to stand in a relation. The Father is truly God in his own right. He is not merely a label whose whole reality depends on the Son.

Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). That does not mean the Father would be powerless or foolish on his own. Rather, the Son is the perfect expression of a Father who is himself all-wise and all-powerful. Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Think of light and its brightness. There has never been a light without its shining, yet the light is truly light in itself. The Father and Son are one in being, fully God together, and distinct only in that one is Father and the other is Son.

Two practical points follow. First, when we call God "Father," we are not projecting human fatherhood onto heaven. Paul says every family in heaven and on earth takes its name from the Father (Ephesians 3:14-15). The eternal Father of the Son is the original, and human fathers are faint copies. Second, God is our Father in a different way than he is the Son's. The Son is Son by nature, from all eternity. We become God's children by grace, through being joined to his Son. That is why Jesus could speak of "My Father and your Father" (John 20:17). The love the Father has always had for the Son is the very love into which he now welcomes us.

topics.title: How can the invisible Father be known and seen through the Son?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the invisible Father is known only through the Son, and none thinks God can be seen by natural power or comprehended in his essence. Irenaeus says this repeatedly: the Father is the invisible of the Son, the Son the visible of the Father, and the Father is revealed through the Word from the beginning of history and in the Incarnation. Bickersteth, Gregory of Nyssa and Owen add that saving faith requires belief in the Father through the Son, Owen stressing faith in what God has revealed and fellowship with the Son as Mediator. On the ground of this revelation, Athanasius and Hilary root it in the Son's being of the Father's own essence and nature, so that knowing the Son simply is knowing the Father. Augustine argues similarly from oneness and from the analogy of the word, while Gregory uses the analogy of a mirror's reflection. Novatian, by contrast, grounds it in the Son as image, whose works imitate the Father's, and treats seeing the Son as a training that prepares believers for a future vision of the Father. The sharpest difference is over John 14:7: Novatian reads 'have seen' as a future vision spoken of as already done, while Hilary holds the disciples had already seen the Father's nature in the Son and would now come to know it. Augustine and Ambrose also stress that the Son's divinity itself is not visible, so what was seen was his flesh, held by faith.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: He Proves Also that the Words Spoken to Philip Make…
refs.quote: But if Christ Himself had been the Father, why did He promise as future, a reward which He had already granted and given?

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: it is manifest, therefore, that the Father teaches through the words of the Son, and, though seen of none, speaks to us in the manifestation of the Son, because the Son, by virtue of His perfect birth, possesses all the properties of His Father’s nature

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For assuredly one cannot, by uttering all these phrases that disagree one with another in signification, intend to indicate by incompatible terms that Essence which is simple and uncompounded.

ans.text:
We see the invisible Father by looking at Jesus, because the Son is the perfect image of the Father, sharing everything the Father is. The Gospel of John puts it plainly: "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18).

Start with the problem. The Bible insists that God the Father cannot be seen. Paul describes Him as the one who "lives in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see" (1 Timothy 6:16). This is not because God is shy or far away. It is because He is infinite and we are small. Our eyes, minds and hearts are made for created things. On our own we cannot climb up to God, any more than a cup can hold the ocean. If we are to know Him at all, He must come to us.

That is exactly what He has done in His Son. The New Testament gives the Son several names that each show this from a different angle. He is the Word (John 1:1). A word is how a hidden thought becomes known. You cannot see what is in my mind until I speak, and then my words carry my thought to you. The Son is God's Word in a far deeper sense: He expresses the Father fully, because He is not a sound that passes away but is Himself God. He is also called the Image of God: "The Son is the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). And He is the radiance of God's glory, "the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Light shining from the sun is not a second sun. It is the sun's own brightness reaching us. In the same way, when the Son shines on us, it is the Father's own glory we are meeting.

This is why Jesus could say something astonishing to His disciples. When Philip asked, "Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us," Jesus answered, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:8-9). Philip was not being faithless. He simply had not yet understood what he had been looking at for three years. In the face, words, kindness, holiness and suffering of Jesus, he had been looking at what the Father is like. Paul says the same thing in another way: God has given us "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Why does seeing the Son mean seeing the Father? Because the Son is not a creature who merely resembles God, the way a good portrait resembles a person. He is the Father's own Son, born of the Father before all time. That is what the old word "begotten" means: not made, but coming from the Father and sharing His very being, the way a child shares the nature of a parent, only without any beginning in time. Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). So knowing the Son and knowing the Father are not two separate projects. They are one knowledge. You cannot have one without the other.

Here we should clear up a common misunderstanding. Seeing the Father in the Son does not mean that Jesus simply is the Father wearing a human costume. Jesus prays to the Father, is sent by the Father, and returns to the Father. They are truly distinct persons. The Father is revealed in the Son precisely because the Son is His Son, His perfect image, and not a mask.

A second misunderstanding goes the other way. Some imagine that because Jesus calls Himself "the way" and "the door," knowing Him means we now understand God completely, as though God's inner being were something we could get to the bottom of. But when Jesus says whoever enters through Him "will be saved" and will "find pasture" (John 10:9), He is describing rescue and nourishment, not a full grasp of God. In Jesus we truly know God: His character, His love, His purposes. Yet God remains greater than our minds can contain. We know Him truly without knowing Him exhaustively.

The Son did not begin revealing the Father only at Christmas. All things were made through the Word (John 1:3), so creation itself bears the marks of His wisdom and points to its Maker. Throughout the Old Testament, God spoke through prophets, visions and appearances, and many Christians have understood these as early ways in which the Son was already making the Father known. But people did not recognize God through creation's wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:21). So the Word Himself became flesh, lived among us, died on the cross and rose again. In doing so He showed the Father's heart more clearly than ever, and opened the way back to Him.

This also means the Son is how the help of the unreachable God comes to us. We cannot reach the Father, but the Father reaches us through the Son. Jesus says, "No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6), and "no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him" (Matthew 11:27). This is not a narrowing of God's welcome. It is the door He has opened. When we call on the Son, we are heard by the Father. The reverse is also true: it is the Father who draws us and teaches us to recognize His Son, as when Jesus told Peter that his confession had been revealed by the Father in heaven (Matthew 16:17). John warns that "whoever denies the Son does not have the Father," but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well (1 John 2:23). Believing in a supreme being is not yet the Christian faith. Christians believe in God as Father, and that means believing in His Son.

How, then, do we see the Father today, when we cannot see Jesus with our eyes? By faith, through the Scriptures that show Him to us, and by the Holy Spirit who opens our hearts to recognize Him. Faith is not a lesser kind of knowing. It is trusting what God has truly shown us. When we read how Christ welcomed sinners, wept at a grave and gave His life for us, we are learning, with real certainty, how the Father loves us.

And there is more to come. Jesus promised, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). John adds that when Christ appears, "we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2). What we now see by faith in the Son, we will one day behold face to face. Until then, the way to know the Father is the same as it has always been: look at Jesus.

topics.title: Can the Father be known or confessed apart from the Son and the gospel?
topics.cmp: All five authors answer no: the Father is known only through the Son. They give different grounds. Hilary argues that God is apprehended only through God, so our dependence on the Son for knowing the Father proves the Son is true God. Gregory of Nyssa uses the image of an archetype, which is known exactly only in its image, and he turns this against Eunomius's attempt to bypass the Son and reach the Begetter's being directly. Irenaeus stresses that the infinite Father is invisible to us, so the Son's manifestation is itself the knowledge of the Father, and he uses Matthew 11:27 against the Gnostic claim that the 'Mother' or 'seed' reveals the truth. The clearest difference concerns creation. Athanasius treats creation, rightly contemplated, as a real path: one contemplates the Word who framed it and so begins to apprehend the Father, though Christ still points Philip to Himself rather than to creation. Owen is more restrictive and soteriological. For him creation and providence give only an obscure glimpse that leaves people inexcusable, and God's chief properties, his love and pardoning mercy toward sinners, are revealed only in Christ and the gospel, so that apart from the gospel the Father is known only as wrathful and anything else is an idol.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: God cannot be apprehended except through God; even as also God accepts no worship from us except through God.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For the manifestation of the Son is the knowledge of the Father; for all things are manifested through the Word.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: He that hath not the Son, the same hath not the Father, 1 John ii. 23; and not to have God as a Father, is not to have him at all

ans.text:
No. The Bible teaches that the Father is truly known only through his Son, Jesus Christ, and that the full truth about him, especially his love for sinners, is made known in the gospel.

Jesus says this himself. In Matthew 11:27 he says, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." In John 14:6 he adds, "No one comes to the Father except through Me." When Philip asked to be shown the Father, Jesus did not point him to the sky or the hills. He pointed to himself: "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).

Why should this be so? John 1:18 gives the reason: "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known." The Son is not a messenger standing outside God, passing on secondhand news. He is God himself, sharing the Father's own life from all eternity. That is what Christians mean when they call him "begotten" of the Father. It does not mean he had a beginning. It means he is the Son, the same kind of being as his Father. So when we know the Father through the Son, we are knowing God through God. No angel, prophet, or spiritual teacher could do that, because only the Son knows the Father from the inside.

Doesn't creation tell us about God? Yes, and the Bible makes this clear. Romans 1:20 says God's "eternal power and divine nature" are seen in what he has made, so that people are without excuse. The stars, the seasons, and our own conscience tell us there is a mighty Maker and that we answer to him. But notice what creation shows and what it does not. It shows power, wisdom, and order. It leaves us guilty before a holy God. It cannot tell us that this God will forgive us, or that he wants to welcome us as his children.

There is also a deeper link. The world itself was made through the Son. Colossians 1 calls him "the image of the invisible God" and says all things were created through him and hold together in him. So even the light we glimpse in creation is his light. When we look at creation rightly, with the gospel in hand, we see the fingerprints of the Son who made it, and through him we begin to see the Father.

Think of a painting and a letter. A painting can tell you the artist is gifted. Only a letter in the artist's own words can tell you that he loves you. Creation is the painting. Christ is the Father's own Word to us.

That is why the gospel is such good news. Apart from it, a guilty person who thinks about God mostly meets his holiness and his anger at sin. In the gospel the Father shows his heart. "This is how God's love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him" (1 John 4:9). We learn about God's love for sinners from the cross. We do not learn it from nature.

This also guards against a common mistake. Some people picture the Father as stern and the Son as the kind one who talks him round. But the Bible says the Father sent the Son because he loved the world (John 3:16). The Son does not change the Father's mind about us. He shows us what the Father's heart has always been.

Can someone deny the Son and still have the Father? Scripture answers directly: "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well" (1 John 2:23). Father and Son belong together, like a light and its shining. You cannot keep the sun while refusing its light. A person may sincerely believe in a supreme being and still miss the Father, because the Father has chosen to be known in his Son. This is not a reason for pride on our part. It is a reason to point others gently to Jesus, the only one who can show them the Father.

What about Israel in the Old Testament? God was not unknown to them. He revealed himself to them by name, by covenant, and by promise. At times the prophets even called him Father, meaning the One who created Israel, chose it, and cared for it. Deuteronomy 32:6 asks, "Is He not your Father, your Creator?" and Isaiah prays to God as "our Father." Still, those were glimpses. That God is eternally Father because he has an eternal Son was not yet openly known. Nor was the fact that we can call him "Abba, Father" by the Spirit of that Son (Galatians 4:6).

Sincere Christians weigh this differently. Some stress that Israel did not yet truly worship God as Father, since knowing the Father and knowing the Son go together. Others stress that faithful believers in Israel did know the true God, and they did so through the promised Christ, even if only in shadow. Both sides agree on the key point. Jesus said Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56), and Paul says the rock that followed Israel in the wilderness "was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Whatever Israel truly knew of God, it knew through the Son who was coming.

So the answer is both humbling and hopeful. We cannot climb up to the Father by our own reasoning or by studying nature. But we do not need to, because the Father has come down to us in his Son. Whoever looks to Jesus is not looking away from the Father. He is looking straight at him.

topics.title: How did the Father bear witness to the Son?
topics.cmp: The Father's testimony to the Son despite the Jews never hearing his voice or seeing his form (John 5:36-38), and the purpose of the heavenly voice at the baptism and Transfiguration.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: since, therefore, the working of the Son is the Father’s testimony, it follows of necessity that the same nature was operative in Christ, by which the Father testifies of Him.

ans.text:
The Father bore witness to the Son in three ways: through the works He gave Jesus to do, through His voice from heaven at key moments, and through the Scriptures He had already given. Of these, Jesus pointed above all to His works. In John 5:36 He says that "the works that the Father has given Me to accomplish—the very works I am doing—testify about Me that the Father has sent Me."

This raises a fair question. In the very next breath Jesus tells His opponents, "You have never heard His voice nor seen His form" (John 5:37). So how can He say the Father has testified, if they never heard Him speak?

The answer is that the Father's testimony did not need a booming voice to be real. It was right in front of them. When Jesus healed the lame man, gave sight to the blind, and raised the dead, the Father was speaking. These were not just signs Jesus did on the Father's behalf, the way a messenger carries a letter. Jesus says in John 14:10 that it is "the Father dwelling in Me, performing His works." The Father and the Son act together in one work, because they share one divine life. That is part of what Jesus means in John 10:30 when He says, "I and the Father are one." So the miracles were the Father's own testimony to His Son. They also showed who Jesus is, since no mere creature could do the works of God as his own.

It is also true that the Father did speak aloud. At Jesus' baptism a voice came from heaven: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:17). But this does not contradict John 5:37. That voice came at the Jordan, out in the wilderness. Jesus was speaking to religious leaders in Jerusalem who had not been there. John the Baptist, who did witness it, told others what he had seen (John 1:32-34). Jesus says the testimony of the works is weightier even than John's.

Does this mean His hearers had an excuse? No. Jesus explains why they had not heard the Father: "nor does His word abide in you, because you do not believe the One He sent" (John 5:38). The problem was not that God was silent. It was that they would not receive the Son. The Father had testified openly through the works, and also through the Scriptures, which Jesus says "testify about Me" (John 5:39). Had they believed in Jesus, they would have heard the Father in Him and seen the Father in Him. As Jesus later told Philip, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). The Father's face is shown to us in the Son.

Why, then, did the Father speak from heaven at the baptism at all? Because Jesus truly became a man, with an ordinary human body. People saw a carpenter from Nazareth stepping into the river like everyone else. It would have been easy to see only a man and miss who He really is. The Father's voice made plain that this humble man, who had come to save us, is His own beloved Son. It is the eternal Son, not an adopted one, who had taken on our flesh.

At the Transfiguration the Father said the same words again, but He added a command: "Listen to Him!" (Matthew 17:5). Why add this here? At the baptism, the main human witness was John the Baptist. He was a prophet sent ahead of Jesus, and he already knew who Jesus was. On the mountain, the Father was speaking to the apostles, the men who would carry Jesus' teaching to the world. The command was for them, and through them for us. Moses and Elijah, the great figures of the Law and the Prophets, had just appeared with Jesus. Then they vanished, and the disciples saw only Jesus. The point is clear: God's final word is His Son. As Hebrews 1:1-2 puts it, God spoke in many ways through the prophets, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son.

Peter later wrote that he and the others heard that voice from heaven themselves, while they were with Jesus on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:17-18). We were not there, but we hear that same testimony through the witnesses who were. That is why Christians listen to Jesus through the apostles' teaching in the Bible.

So the Father has not left His Son without witness. He testified by the works He did in and through Jesus, by His spoken word at the Jordan and on the mountain, and by the Scriptures. And He still testifies today. When we trust the Son, we come to know the Father, and His word comes to dwell in us.

topics.title: Do God's visible appearances mean that only the Father is invisible?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus and Augustine agree that the visible appearances of God to the prophets do not mean that only the Father is invisible or that a different, visible God was seen, but they argue against different opponents and on different grounds. Irenaeus answers heretics who would split the God of the prophets from the invisible Father. He grounds his reply in the nature of prophecy: the prophets foretold that God would be seen by men. The God they spoke of is the one God and Father, incomprehensible in His greatness yet letting Himself be seen out of love, and the varied forms of His appearing belong to the deeper understanding of the one faith. Augustine instead rebuts the specific claim that the Father appeared only to a dreaming Daniel while the Son and Spirit appeared to the waking Moses. He relies on scriptural and philosophical reasoning: neither the Word nor the Spirit, nor even a human spirit, is seen with bodily eyes; a sleeping man is still a man, so a dream-appearance would already contradict 'no man hath seen'; and whoever can form bodily likenesses in dreams can form bodily creatures for those awake. Irenaeus stresses the unity and loving self-manifestation of the one God, while Augustine stresses that all such appearances are created signs and that every divine person is invisible in himself.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: they did not, as some allege, [proclaim] that He who was seen by the prophets was a different [God], the Father of all being invisible. Yet this is what those [heretics] declare, who are altogether ignorant of the nature of prophecy.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.quote: When men sleep, are they then not men? Or cannot He, who can fashion the likeness of a body to signify Himself through the visions of dreamers, also fashion that same bodily creature to signify Himself to the eyes of those who are awake?

ans.text:
No. The Bible does not teach that the Father alone is invisible while the Son and the Spirit can be seen. In His own divine nature, God is invisible, and that is equally true of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. When God appeared to people in Scripture, the one true God was making Himself known through something visible. The Father was not hiding behind a lesser, more visible god.

The Bible plainly says God cannot be seen. Paul praises "the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God" (1 Timothy 1:17). Jesus says "God is Spirit" (John 4:24). God tells Moses, "you cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live" (Exodus 33:20). John adds, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18).

Yet the same Bible tells of people who saw God in some way. Abraham met the Lord by the oaks of Mamre. Moses saw the burning bush and spoke with God "face to face." Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up. Daniel saw the Ancient of Days on a throne. And God appeared in different ways to different people.

Some have concluded that there must be two gods: a hidden, unknowable Father, and a lower god who did the appearing. Others, believing in the Trinity, have argued for a milder version. They say the Father is invisible by nature, while the Son and Spirit are visible by nature, so the visions must have been of the Son or Spirit. Both ideas misunderstand what was happening.

Think of it this way. When God appeared as fire, a cloud, a man, or a figure on a throne, He was not showing His bare divine being, as if God simply is fire or has a body. He was taking up something He had made and using it as a sign of His presence. It is like a voice coming through a speaker. The voice is truly the speaker's own, but the device is not the person.

The Son shares the same divine nature as the Father, so the Son is no more "made of" visible stuff than the Father is. The Spirit is just as invisible. When the Spirit came down on Jesus at His baptism, Luke says He came "in bodily form like a dove" (Luke 3:22). The dove was a visible sign, not the Spirit's own nature.

Some have argued from the visions of Moses and Daniel. Daniel saw the Ancient of Days in a dream at night, while Moses saw his visions awake. So, they say, the Father showed Himself only to a sleeper, which supposedly does not count as really seeing Him. But a person who is dreaming is still a person. If "no one has ever seen God" were broken by a dream, it would be broken just the same. And the God who can form a picture of Himself in a sleeper's mind can just as easily form a visible sign for someone who is awake. Being asleep or awake changes how the vision comes. It does not change which God is being seen, or whether His true nature is seen.

The visions also matter because they look forward. Prophecy announces what God will do, and the prophets foretold that God would one day be seen among people. That promise came true in a unique way when the Son became man. He did not merely borrow a shape for a moment. He took a real human body and soul as His own for ever. So Paul calls Him "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). Jesus told Philip that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father (John 14:9). The Son became visible in His human nature, not because His divine nature is more visible than the Father's.

Sincere Christians have differed on one related point. Was it always the Son who appeared in the Old Testament, especially as "the angel of the LORD"? Many have thought so. They point out that the Son is the One who reveals the Father, and that John says Isaiah saw Christ's glory (John 12:41). Others are more cautious. They note that Scripture does not always say which person of the Trinity was at work, and that the one God could make Himself known through a created sign in any of these ways. Either way, both sides agree on what matters most here. The God who appeared is the one true God, and in His own nature He remains invisible.

So the answer is not that the Father is hidden and the others are seen. The whole Trinity is beyond the sight of our eyes. Yet out of love, this same God has made Himself known, through signs to the prophets and finally and fully in Jesus Christ. One day His people will see Him as He is (1 John 3:2).

topics.title: What is proper to the Father, and how do believers relate to him?
topics.cmp: The five authors answer different questions, so they mostly complement rather than contradict one another. Still, a common thread runs through them: the Father is known and approached in relation to the Son. Augustine reasons philosophically about predication and concludes that nothing is said of the Father as such except relative terms (Father, begetter, beginning); everything else is said with or in the Son. Irenaeus, working from Scripture (Peter's confession, Paul's apostleship), likewise binds Father and Son together in a reciprocal revelation: the Son leads to the Father and the Father reveals the Son. On the believer's side the emphases diverge. Owen stresses affective communion, with the Father loving first and requiring love in return. Gregory of Nyssa stresses sacramental means, holding that grace is actually given through the baptismal Names. Athanasius, interpreting Christ's command to be merciful as the Father is, sets a firm limit that none of the others raises: creatures made from nothing cannot become as the Father is, and are sons and gods only by grace, not by nature as the only-begotten Son is.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: What is Said of the Father and Son Together, and What Not.
refs.quote: if nothing is spoken of the Father as such, except that which is spoken of Him in relation to the Son, that is, that He is His father, or begetter, or beginning

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.place: Chapter XIII—Refutation of the opinion, that Paul was the only apostle who had knowledge of the truth
refs.quote: the Son indeed leading them to the Father, but the Father revealing to them the Son.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: When the soul sees God, in his dispensation of love, to be love, to be infinitely lovely and loving, rests upon and delights in him as such, then hath it communion with him in love.

ans.text:
What belongs to the Father alone is his fatherhood: he is the Father of the eternal Son. Almost everything else we say about God, the Father shares fully with the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Father is God, almighty, eternal, wise, holy and good, but so is the Son, and so is the Spirit. There are not three almighties or three Gods, but one God. So if we ask what makes the Father distinct, the answer is not some extra power or a higher rank. It is a relationship. He is the Father of the Son, the one from whom the Son is eternally 'begotten.'

That word needs explaining. To 'beget' means to have a child who shares your own nature, the way a human father has a human son. A builder makes a house, which is something different from himself. A father begets a son, who is the same kind of being as he is. When Christians say the Father begets the Son, they mean the Son is not a creature the Father made.
