He is God from God, sharing the one divine nature. And this begetting did not happen at some moment in the past. There was never a time when the Father was without his Son, because God never changes. John 1:18 calls Jesus 'the one and only Son, who is Himself God,' who is at the Father's side.

So the Father is the source within God: the Son is from him, and the Spirit proceeds from him, while he himself is from no one. Sincere Christians have disagreed on one part of this. Some hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son together. They point out that the Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son (Galatians 4:6), and that Jesus sends the Spirit. Others hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. They point to Jesus' words in John 15:26 about the Spirit who goes out from the Father, and they want to keep the Father as the single source. Both sides agree that the Father, Son and Spirit are equally God.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, 'Father' does not mean older or greater, as if he came first and the Son came later. Jesus says in John 10:30, 'I and the Father are one.' Second, 'Father' is not a statement about God having a body or being male in a biological sense. It tells us about relationship, love and origin. The Father has always loved the Son, and that love is the heart of who he is as Father.

How do we come to know this Father? Not by our own cleverness. The Father and the Son work together to bring us in. Jesus says in Matthew 11:27 that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. So the Son leads us to the Father. But it also works the other way. When Peter confessed that Jesus is the Christ, Jesus told him this was not revealed by flesh and blood but by 'My Father in heaven' (Matthew 16:17). And in John 6:44 Jesus says no one can come to him unless the Father draws him. The Son shows us the Father, and the Father shows us the Son. Paul, too, says he was made an apostle through Jesus Christ and God the Father together (Galatians 1:1). The persons of the Trinity never compete. They act as one.

This is also why Christians are baptized 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19). Note that it says 'name,' not 'names.' There is one God into whom we are baptized. Christians differ on how exactly God gives grace through baptism. But all agree that it is no empty ritual. It marks us as belonging to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, and God is truly at work when it is received in faith.

What kind of relationship does the Father want with us? Above all, he wants love. He does not wait for us to love him first. As 1 John 4:19 says, 'We love because He first loved us.' The Father sent his Son out of love (John 3:16). Through the Son, he adopts us, so that by the Spirit we can call him 'Abba, Father' (Galatians 4:6, Romans 8:15). Communion with the Father means this: we see that he really is love, we trust it, we rest in it, and we love him back with our whole heart. When Jesus taught us to pray 'Our Father in heaven' (Matthew 6:9), he invited us into this same trust. Many believers feel God the Son is kind but the Father is stern. Scripture says the opposite. The Son came because the Father loved us.

But there is an important line here. Jesus is the Son by nature, and he always has been. We become sons and daughters of God by grace, through adoption (Galatians 4:4-7). We are welcomed into the family. We do not become what Jesus is. This matters when we read a command like Luke 6:36: 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.' Does that mean we can become equal to God? No. We are creatures, made from nothing, and we will always depend on God for every breath. We can never become what the Father is.

What the command means is simpler and more beautiful. Look at how the Father treats people. He is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked (Luke 6:35). Then go and do the same, for his sake. A child can copy a father's generosity without ever becoming the father. In the same way, we reflect God's mercy as a mirror reflects the sun. The light is real, but it is borrowed. Our likeness to God is a gift that grows in us, not a claim to his place.

So what is proper to the Father is that he is the eternal Father of the Son, the source of the Son and the Spirit. He is equal to them in every way. And our relationship to him is that of adopted children. Through the Son, we are drawn into the love the Father has always had for his Son. He loves us first, we love him in return, and we learn to show his mercy to others.

title: The Eternal Generation of the Son
desc: How the Son is begotten from the Father's substance rather than made, why this involves no passion, division or act of will, and what generation-analogies can and cannot teach.

topics.title: Is the Son truly the Father's natural Son, begotten rather than made or created?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son is the Father's true, natural Son, begotten from His substance and neither created nor adopted. They also agree that this is a strict either/or: Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa and Waterland all say there is no middle ground between God and creature, and that believers' sonship by grace differs in kind from His. They argue in different ways. Hilary works mainly from the plain wording of Scripture ('This,' 'My,' 'His own' Son, John 20:31, Peter's confession) and holds that the Father's fatherhood and saving faith both depend on a true birth. Athanasius stresses the contrast between Offspring and work, and between coming by nature and coming by will. He adds reductio arguments (an endless series of mediating Words, a barren divine essence), a soteriological point that a creature could not join us to God, and reads 'created' in Proverbs 8 as referring to the Incarnation. Gregory of Nyssa argues mostly against Eunomius, using the logic of relative terms, the exhaustive division of created and uncreated (which he also frames as dominion versus slavery), and Eunomius's own premises. Augustine and Waterland rely more on a formal disjunction of substance, Waterland adding a reading of the ante-Nicene Fathers against Clarke. Bickersteth, Novatian, Hippolytus and Irenaeus give brief exegetical support. There are smaller differences in emphasis. Edwards explains the Father being called simply 'God' partly by His economic office, while Augustine explains it purely by the Father being from no one. Waterland alone allows that an explicit profession of 'eternal generation' could be dispensed with, provided the Word's eternal personal subsistence is held. Gregory alone declines 'product of generation' as a fit name for the Son.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The creation of the world is sufficient evidence to me that Thou art wise; and I am sure that Thy Wisdom, Who is like Thee, must have been begotten from Thyself.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: it regards the preexistent eternity, the “from everlasting” of the Lord, and as such declares him to be the beginning, or origin, or originator, or precisely as we say, the First Cause of the creation of God.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: who is there, who to the God in whom he has put faith, refuses to give credit, when He says, ‘This is My beloved Son,’ on the pretence that He is not a Son, but a creature?

ans.text:
Yes. Jesus Christ is the Father's own Son by nature. He shares the Father's very being, and He was not made, created, or adopted into the family the way we are. This is what the Nicene Creed means when it calls Him "begotten, not made."

To see why this matters, it helps to notice the difference between begetting and making. To "beget" means to father, to give life to offspring of your own kind. When a man fathers a child, the child is human, just as he is. When the same man builds a bench, the bench is something else entirely: wood, shaped by his skill, nothing like him in nature. A son shares what his father is. A product only reflects what its maker can do. So when the Bible calls Jesus God's Son, it is not giving Him an honorary title. It is telling us that He has the same divine nature as the One who begot Him. Everything else, angels and people and stars, was made. The Son was not.

The Bible draws this line clearly. John says that through the Word "all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). If the Son made everything that was ever made, He cannot be one of the made things Himself. He stands on the Creator's side of the line. Hebrews 1:3 says the Son is "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Think of the sun and its light. The light comes from the sun, yet it is not a separate thing the sun built. It is the sun's own brightness shining out, and there was never a sun without its light.

But doesn't the Bible call believers sons of God too? It does, and that is a wonderful truth. Yet Scripture is careful to say how we become God's children. We are adopted. Paul says we have received "the Spirit of adoption," by whom we cry "Abba, Father" (Romans 8:15). God sent His Son "to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:5). We were once outsiders and were brought in by grace. Christ was never brought in. He is the One through whom we are brought in. An adopted child really belongs to the family, but he was born to other parents and received his new name as a gift. The Son was never anything other than the Father's Son, so there was nothing for Him to receive. He is Son of God by nature and became a son of man by mercy. We are sons of men by nature and become sons of God by grace.

Several passages show that Jesus' sonship is in a class by itself. John calls Him "the one and only Son from the Father" (John 1:14). Some translations say "only begotten." Readers have debated the best English for that word, but either way it marks Him as unique, the only Son of His kind. Paul says God "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). That little word "own" carries great weight. Paul's point is the size of God's love. It only works if God gave up His true Son for people who were strangers, not one creature on behalf of other creatures.

When Peter confessed, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," Jesus said this had not been revealed to him "by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven" (Matthew 16:16-17). If "Son of God" only meant a godly man or a favored servant, Peter would not have needed a revelation from heaven to say it.

Jesus' enemies understood this too. They wanted to kill Him because He was "calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God" (John 5:18). They knew He was not claiming a pious title but a real share in God's nature. Jesus did not correct them. He went on to say that the Son does whatever the Father does and deserves the same honor. Later He told Philip, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). No adopted child, however beloved, could say that.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, "begotten" does not mean anything physical, as if God had a body or a wife. It is a picture borrowed from family life, and it teaches one thing above all: like comes from like. Second, it does not mean the Son had a starting point. Human fathers exist before their sons, but God is eternal and unchanging, and He has always been Father. A Father with no Son would not be a Father. So the Son has always been the Son, just as the sun has never been without its light. This is why Christians speak of the Son's eternal begetting. Third, when Colossians 1:15 calls Christ "the firstborn over all creation," it speaks of His rank and inheritance, as the firstborn son held first place in a family. The very next verse explains that in Him all things were created.

Some have tried to find a middle ground: the Son was not made from nothing exactly, but He is still not fully God. But there is no third kind of being between God and creature. Either the Son shares the Father's divine nature, or He was brought into being by God's will like everything else. If He was brought into being, then He is a creature, however glorious, and could change or cease to exist. The Bible does not leave us there. It shows us a Son who made all things, holds them together, and is worshiped as God.

This is not a dry point of theory. If the Son were only a creature, then God would have given something less than Himself to save us. Because Jesus is the Father's own Son, His coming shows us God's own heart, and His gift on the cross is the greatest gift God could give. And because He is Son by nature, He is able to make us sons and daughters by grace.

topics.title: What does it mean that the Son is begotten from the Father's substance?
topics.cmp: All five authors agree that the Son is truly and properly begotten from the Father's own substance, and that this generation neither divides, diminishes nor changes the Father. Hilary of Poitiers and Athanasius both insist that the Father keeps all that He gives the Son. Hilary argues from God's spiritual, indivisible nature: Scripture says a spirit has no flesh or bones, so no severing or loss is possible. He reads 'from Himself' and 'God from God' as excluding both another source and nothingness while keeping Father and Son distinct. Athanasius argues more metaphysically. Nothing external or intermediate is shared: the Son is Himself what is partaken of the Father's essence, so to beget is the same as to be wholly participated. Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine work instead from the divine names. Gregory holds that 'Son' must be taken in its highest sense, which can only be sameness of essence, and he supports kinship of nature from Scripture's example of Seth in Adam's likeness. Augustine stresses that Son, Word and Image are relative terms referring to the Father. Daniel Waterland is the most historical and polemical. He reads the Nicene phrase as aimed chiefly against the Arian 'from nothing', since a Son formed from some other matter was a view no one held, and he infers from it the Son's oneness with the Father in the same undivided, individual substance. He is also the only one who addresses whether generation is by necessity of nature or by the Father's will, answering against Clarke that it is both, so long as 'will' means consent rather than arbitrary choice.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: For, if the Son were ab extra, and independent of the Father ; the alliance, the relation, the unity of the Persons, in the same Godhead, had (upon their principles) been lost, and Ditheism unavoidable.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: it follows that what is partaken is not external, but from the essence of the Father. And as to this again, if it be other than the essence of the Son, an equal extravagance will meet us

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Yet we must not imagine that the Father did not give, because He still possesses, or that He has lost, because He gave to the Son.

ans.text:
To say the Son is begotten from the Father's substance means that the Son shares the Father's own being, the very same divinity, rather than being something God made or something merely like God. The creed puts it in four short phrases: he is "God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made."

Two words need explaining. "Substance" here does not mean a material stuff. It means what God is, his very being or nature, the thing that makes God God. "Begotten" is the Bible's family word. A father begets a son, and a son has the same nature as his father. A man builds a house, but he begets a child. The house is a different kind of thing from the builder. The child is the same kind of thing as the parent. Scripture insists on the second picture for Jesus. John calls him "the one and only Son from the Father" (John 1:14), and says this only Son "is Himself God and is at the Father's side" (John 1:18).

Why add "from the Father's substance"? Because people can use the word "Son" loosely. Christians are called sons of God too, by adoption. Some in the early church said Jesus was the first and greatest thing God made out of nothing, and called him "Son" only as a title of honor. The phrase was added to shut that door. The Son did not come from nothing, as creatures do. Nor was he shaped from some other material, as Adam was formed from dust. The only source left is God himself. He is from the Father, and from nothing else.

This is also why the church confessed the Son to be "of one substance" or "of the same being" with the Father, not merely "of a similar being." A copy can be very like the original and still be a different thing. If the Son were only like God, he would be a second, lesser being beside God, and we would have two gods or a creature we were worshiping. But there is only one God. Since the Son has no nature except the divine nature he receives from the Father, he shares that one nature fully. That is how Jesus can say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and why Hebrews 1:3 calls him "the exact representation of His nature." Paul says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form" (Colossians 2:9). Fullness, not a portion. This also fits the plain sense of the word "likeness" in Scripture. When Adam had Seth "in his own likeness" (Genesis 5:3), Seth was not a statue of Adam. He was a real human being like his father.

Some worry that this sounds as if God were split in two, as if the Father cut off a piece of himself. It does not mean that. Jesus teaches that "God is Spirit" (John 4:24), not a body that can be divided. Think of light shining from the sun, or one candle lighting another. The second flame is truly fire, and the first loses nothing. The Father gives the Son all that he is, yet he still has it all. Jesus says, "Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine" (John 16:15). The Father has not given anything away and become poorer. Nor did the Father stop being himself and turn into the Son. The Son is born from the Father, who goes on being Father. They are truly two persons, Father and Son, and one God.

It also helps to remember that this begetting is eternal. It is not an event that happened at some point before creation. There was never a time when the Father had no Son. The Father is always Father, which means there is always a Son. John 1:1 says the Word already "was" in the beginning, with God, and was God. The names the Bible gives him, Son, Word, Image, Radiance, all point to this living relationship. He is Son of the Father, the Word of the Father, the image of the Father. These names tell us who he is in relation to the Father, and none of them leaves him outside God's own life.

Someone might ask whether the Father begets the Son by choice or by nature. The best answer is both, rightly understood. The Father did not pick the Son the way he chose to create the world, which might not have existed. That would make the Son a creature. Yet the Father is not forced either. It is like God's goodness. God is good by his very nature, and he is also gladly and freely good. In the same way the Father eternally and gladly begets the Son. As Jesus says, "as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). The Son receives life from the Father, but it is the same unending life the Father has.

All of this matters for ordinary faith. If the Son were only a high creature, then meeting Jesus would be meeting someone very close to God, but not God. Because he is from the Father's own being, to know the Son is to know the Father, and to be joined to Christ by the Spirit is to share in the life of God himself. When we worship Jesus, we are not honoring a substitute. We are worshiping the one true God.

topics.title: How is the Son begotten of the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son is truly begotten of the Father and that this generation involves no passion, division or loss in the Father's essence. They argue this in different ways: Athanasius and Hilary use light from light and fire from fire, Hilary also points to the virgin birth, Gregory of Nyssa reasons from human begetting (Adam and Abraham) and spiritual rebirth, and Waterland speaks of 'interior generation.' They differ plainly on the role of the Father's will: Athanasius insists the Son is begotten by nature and not by will or counsel, yet not against the Father's pleasure; Hippolytus flatly says the Father begat the Word 'in his good pleasure, as he willed'; Gregory says the Father's ever-present good will is directed toward the Son, so generation involves will without delay. Augustine and Waterland take a middle line: Augustine turns the 'willingly or unwillingly' dilemma back on the heretic, and Waterland reads 'from the will' as meaning no more than 'God of God,' while denying that the Father's love for the Son is a matter of free choice. They also differ in method and emphasis. Edwards alone builds a philosophical account of the Son as God's perfect idea of Himself, echoed in Augustine's Word as the Father uttering Himself. Hippolytus and Novatian stress that the manner of generation is unknowable, and Bickersteth and Gregory warn that creaturely images such as the sun and its ray are inadequate, with Gregory correcting the image to make the Son 'another sun.'

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: Therefore call not the Son a work of good pleasure; nor bring in the doctrine of Valentinus into the Church; but be He the Living Counsel, and Offspring in truth and nature, as the Radiance from the Light.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Against Eunomius, Saying that the Son of God is the Son,…
refs.quote: demanded of him in turn, whether God the Father was God willingly or unwillingly; in order that if he answered unwillingly, that misery would follow

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: things which are all equally alien from the Divine generation of the Only-begotten: for if any one of these things were admitted, the rest will of necessity all enter with it.

ans.text:
The Son is begotten of the Father in a way unlike any birth we know. The Father eternally shares his whole divine being with the Son. Nothing is cut off, nothing is lost, and there was never a moment when it began. To say the Son is 'begotten' means that he comes from the Father as a true Son, not that he was made or that he started to exist.

The word matters because the Bible gives it to us. John calls Jesus 'the one and only Son from the Father' (John 1:14), and adds that this Son 'is Himself God and is at the Father's side' (John 1:18). Jesus speaks of 'the glory I had with You before the world existed' (John 17:5). Scripture insists that the Son is truly from the Father, and also that he was with the Father before anything was created. 'Begotten' holds both truths together.

Think about the difference between making and begetting. A carpenter makes a table. The table is something other than the carpenter: a different kind of thing, put together at a certain time and place, out of wood he had to gather. When parents have a child, they do not make a different kind of thing. A human being comes from human beings and shares their nature. That is the heart of what 'begotten' tells us. The Son is not a product God built. He shares the Father's own nature. Everything that makes the Father God is fully in the Son, which is why Jesus can say, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). Creation is made. The Son is begotten.

The human comparison only goes so far, though, and we must leave much of it behind. Human birth involves bodies, time, change, a place, a moment of conception, and two people who live separate lives. None of that belongs to God, who is spirit and does not change. The Father did not become a Father at some point. The Son did not grow from small to great or move from not existing to existing. Begetting happened once and finished for us, but for God it has no starting point and no finishing point. Questions like 'When did it begin?' or 'Is it over now?' do not really apply. It is simply the eternal way the Father and the Son are related. As the Father has always been Father, the Son has always been Son. Scripture speaks of the coming ruler 'whose origins are from of old, from the days of eternity' (Micah 5:2).

Some people worry that if the Father gives his nature to the Son, the Father must lose something, as if God were a pie cut into slices. But God's being cannot be divided. Even among us, parents do not become less human by having a child. Light is a better picture, and one the Bible itself uses. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son 'the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature.' A light shines out its brightness without growing dimmer. Its brightness has always been there as long as the light has. Another picture is a thought and the word that expresses it. Your mind brings forth a word without being emptied. This is surely part of why John calls the Son 'the Word' who 'was with God' and 'was God' (John 1:1). The Father gives himself wholly and remains wholly himself. The Son receives everything and lacks nothing. Jesus puts it this way: 'as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself' (John 5:26). The Son does not borrow life the way creatures do. He has the very life of God, received from the Father.

Another question follows. Did the Father decide to have a Son, the way he decided to create the world? Here the church has answered carefully. Creation exists because God freely chose to make it. He could have done otherwise. The Son is different. He belongs to who God is. God did not first exist alone and then deliberate about whether to have a Word and Wisdom, as if he might have stayed without them. The Father is Father by his very nature, just as he is good by his very nature. Yet this does not mean the Son exists against the Father's wishes, or by some force pressing on God. God is not good unwillingly. He is good gladly and wholly. In the same way the Father delights in the Son with complete love: 'the Father loves the Son and shows Him all He does' (John 5:20). The Son's eternal birth is not an accident or a constraint. It is the everlasting overflow of the Father's life and love. It stands even deeper than choice, and it is entirely welcome to him.

Two Bible phrases sometimes confuse people. Psalm 2:7 says, 'You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.' The New Testament applies this to Jesus' resurrection and kingship (Acts 13:33). That is the public showing of who he already is, not the start of his existence. Colossians 1:15 calls him 'the firstborn over all creation.' In the Bible 'firstborn' often means the heir with rank and rights. The very next verse says all things were created through him, so he cannot be one of them.

Sincere Christians who fully believe that the Son is eternal God have discussed how much weight to put on the word 'begotten.' Some point out that the Greek word in John's Gospel may simply mean 'unique' or 'one of a kind,' and they prefer to speak only of the Son's eternal relationship to the Father. Most Christians through the centuries have held that 'begotten' teaches something real. In their view, the names Father and Son, and pictures like radiance and Word, show that the Son eternally comes from the Father while being equal to him. Both sides agree on what matters most: the Son never began, was never created, and is God in the fullest sense.

In the end this is a mystery to adore more than a puzzle to solve. We cannot picture it, because everything we know was born or made in time. But we can understand enough to worship rightly. The Son is not a lesser god or the first creature. He is true God from true God, the Father's own beloved Son, sharing everything the Father is, from all eternity.

topics.title: What do Scriptures such as Psalm 110:3 and John 16:28 teach about the Son's eternal birth?
topics.cmp: On John 16:28, Hilary of Poitiers and Augustine of Hippo read the verse differently. Hilary repeatedly separates 'I went forth from God' (the Son's birth from the Father's nature, which shows He is God) from 'I came from the Father into the world' (His mission or incarnation). He argues from the order of the clauses, from the wording ('came out' rather than 'was sent'), and from the Apostles' response, 'By this we believe that Thou wentest forth from God,' which he takes to answer only the new truth of His divine birth. Augustine instead reads 'I came forth from the Father' as referring to the Son's appearing in the servant form, less than the Father in the creature He took on, and not to His eternal birth. On Psalm 110:3, Athanasius and Hilary agree in substance, though Athanasius's answers are labeled 'No.' His reasoning rejects reading the verse as Christ's birth from Mary: many are born before the star rises, and the 'morning star' is Christ's flesh (Revelation's 'Bright and Morning Star'), so the begetting precedes it. Both argue from parallel anthropomorphisms ('heart' for Athanasius; hands, eyes and heart for Hilary) that 'womb' signals a real begetting from the Father without bodily members. Hilary adds that the image declares the fact of generation, not its manner, and that it rules out the Son being a creature made from nothing.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The Son, therefore, is from the Father, not by His Advent, but by His birth; and love for the Father is only possible to those who believe that the Son is from Him.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to…
refs.quote: What is meant by “I came forth from the Father,” unless this, that I have not appeared in that form in which I am equal to the Father, but otherwise, that is, as less than the Father, in the creature which I have taken upon me?

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: it is plain that the flesh of the Saviour is called ‘the Morning Star,’ which the Offspring from God preceded; so that the sense of the Psalm is this, ‘I have begotten Thee from Myself before Thy appearance in the flesh;’

ans.text:
These passages point past Christmas and past the Son's mission to something deeper. Before Jesus was born of Mary, and before he was sent into the world, he was already the Son, born of the Father in a way that has no beginning. Christians call this the Son's "eternal generation." "Generation" here simply means "being begotten" or "being born from." It is the Bible's way of saying that the Son truly comes from the Father and shares the Father's own nature. He is not made by the Father the way the world was made.

Start with John 16. On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples, "I came from the Father and entered the world. In turn, I will leave the world and go to the Father" (John 16:28). Notice that this is two steps, not one. First, he came from the Father. Then he entered the world. The second step is his coming to us as a man to save us. The first step is more basic. It is where he is from at all. Before he ever arrived among us, he had his very being from the Father.

The disciples' reaction shows they sensed something new. They had heard Jesus say many times that the Father had sent him, and that caused no surprise. Prophets are sent too. But when he spoke this way, they said in effect, "Now you are speaking plainly, and because of this we believe that you came from God" (John 16:29–30). They had grasped that he was not only a messenger with a message from God. He had come out from God himself. Only God can come forth from God in that way. A creature comes from God only in the sense of being made by him. The Son comes from the Father the way a son comes from a father, sharing the same nature. If his origin is God, then what he is, is God.

The rest of John's Gospel agrees. Jesus prays about "the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). John calls him the one and only Son, who is himself God and is at the Father's side (John 1:18). The Word who "became flesh" (John 1:14) was already with God and already was God in the beginning (John 1:1). His birth in Bethlehem was the start of his human life. It was not the start of his existence or of his sonship.

Psalm 110:3 needs a word of explanation, because Bibles read it differently. Most modern translations, including the one this site uses, follow the Hebrew text. In them the verse speaks of the king's people, of holy splendor, and of "the womb of the dawn" and "the dew of Your youth." But the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, which many early Christians read, words the line differently: "from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you." The difference comes from how the Hebrew letters were read and vowelled. Many Christians took that wording as God the Father speaking to his Son. Even in the Hebrew, the psalm is plainly about someone greater than an ordinary king. Jesus himself used its opening verse to show that David's son is also David's Lord (Matthew 22:41–45).

Read the Greek way, the verse makes two points. "Before the morning star" places this birth before creation itself, since the stars were made before any human being. It cannot simply mean Jesus' birth from Mary. Many babies are born before dawn, so that would be nothing special. Some also noticed that Jesus calls himself "the bright Morning Star" (Revelation 22:16), and read the line as "I begot you before you appeared in the flesh." Either way, the point is a birth that comes before time.

Second, "from the womb" does not mean God has a body. God is spirit (John 4:24). Scripture often borrows bodily words to tell us real things about him. It speaks of his hand to show that he truly acts, his eyes to show that he truly sees, and his heart to show that he truly wills. In the same way, "womb" tells us that the Father truly begot the Son from himself, from his own being. He did not produce the Son out of nothing, as he did the world. The picture tells us that the Son truly comes from the Father. It does not tell us how. We should not imagine a process, a moment in time, or any change in God.

That leads to a common misunderstanding. When we hear "begotten," we picture something that starts to exist at a certain point. A human son is younger than his father. But the Father has never been without his Son, just as the sun has never been without its light. The Son is "from" the Father, but there was never a time when he was not. That is why Christians call this birth eternal. It is not an event in the past. It is the never-ending relationship in which the Father is Father and the Son is Son. Micah 5:2 hints at this when it says the ruler from Bethlehem has origins from of old, from ancient days.

Sincere Bible readers have not all read these passages the same way. Some take "I came from the Father" in John 16:28 as describing only his being sent on his mission. They read the whole saying as a picture of his coming down to us and returning to heaven. Others point out that the Son's mission rests on something deeper. He can be sent from the Father because he is first from the Father by nature. Both readings agree that Jesus came to us from the Father's side. The church's historic teaching holds that his coming into the world reveals who he already was.

Why does this matter for ordinary faith? Jesus says the Father loves us "because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God" (John 16:27). Believing that Jesus truly comes from God is not a side issue. If he were only a creature, even the highest one, then in seeing him we would not see God. Because he is the Father's own Son, born of the Father before all ages, we can say with confidence that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). The child in the manger is the eternal Son who came from the Father and entered the world for us.

topics.title: Was the Son begotten by an act of the Father's will or through an intermediate energy?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius and Daniel Waterland all deny that the Son was produced either by an intermediate 'energy' or by a prior act of the Father's will that would place the Father before him. Gregory carries most of the weight, and his target is Eunomius's graded energies. He argues philosophically that an unsubstantial energy cannot produce a substantial Son, and that such an energy would become the Son's real father, push the Son and Spirit down in rank, and leave no foundation for creation through the Word. He uses everyday analogies (fire, sun, the hand) and Scripture's teaching that God's single command produced all things to show that varied works do not imply varied energies. Athanasius argues mainly from Scripture: it never speaks of the Word as being 'by will' and reserves a preceding will for things that once were not. His positive claim is that the Son is himself the Father's living Will and Counsel, so that 'by will' amounts to the Arian 'once He was not.' Gregory, by contrast, stresses that there is no medium between Father and Son and that they are united through identity of will. Waterland, drawing on the Fathers (Athanasius, Nazianzen, Cyril, Augustine), adds a distinction neither of the others draws. The Father begat the Son with his will's approval (volens) but not by a prior choice, and the Arian dilemma can be turned back by asking whether the Father is God willingly.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: The Holy Spirit also according to this sequence will be found not in the third, but in the fifth place, that ‘energy’ which follows the Only-Begotten, and by which the Holy Spirit came into existence necessarily intervening between them.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: that Word must surely be the living Will of the Father, and an essential energy, and a real Word, in whom all things both consist and are excellently governed

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: The Father bégat his Son, either nolens or volens ; against his will or with his will: it could not be against his will, that is absurd ; therefore it must be with his wll ; therefore that act of the will was precedent to the Son’s existence

ans.text:
Neither. The Son was not produced by a decision the Father made beforehand, and no go-between power stood between them to bring him about. The Son is begotten of the Father's own nature, directly and eternally, with nothing in between.

It helps to know what "begotten" means. To beget is to give rise to offspring who share your own nature. A carpenter makes a table, which is a different kind of thing from himself. A father begets a child, who is human just as he is. When the Bible calls Jesus the Father's "only begotten" or "one and only" Son (John 1:14, 3:16), it is telling us that the Son is not something God made. He comes from the Father the way a son comes from a father, and so he has the same divine nature. Hebrews 1:3 puts it beautifully: "The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Radiance is not added to a light later, and nothing stands between a light and its shining. Where the light is, the shining is.

Some people have reasoned this way. Either the Father begot the Son against his will, which is unthinkable, or he did it by his will. And if by his will, then the choosing came first and the Son came afterward, so the Son must be lower and later. The answer is that this mixes up two different things. The Father is not unwilling about his Son. He loves and delights in him: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). But delighting in something is not the same as deciding, at some earlier moment, to make it. God is good, but he did not first decide to become good. Goodness is simply what he is, and he is glad to be so. In the same way, the Father has never been without his Son. He fully embraces the Son's existence, but the Son does not depend on a choice that came before him.

There is also no "before" here to speak of. Before and after belong to time, and the Son is the one through whom time and the ages were made. John 1:1-3 says, "In the beginning was the Word," and "Through Him all things were made." Notice the word "was." When everything else began, the Word already was. If the Son had come about by a decision made at some earlier point, there would have been a moment when the Father was not yet a Father, and a moment when the one through whom all things were made did not yet exist. Scripture never speaks that way.

In fact, the Bible ties God's will and choosing to created things, the things that once did not exist and then were brought into being. Revelation 4:11 praises God because he created all things, and they exist by his will. The Son, however, is never described in Scripture as existing "by will" or as being made. He is described as the Word who was with God and was God, the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and the one through whom and for whom all things were created (Colossians 1:16). God's will for creation is carried out through his Son. So the Son cannot be just another result of that will. Otherwise we would need yet another Word, standing behind the Son, through whom the Son was made, and Scripture knows of no such thing.

Others suggested a kind of middle step. On this view, an activity or energy flowed out from the Father and produced the Son, the way a craftsman's tool cuts out a shape. But think about where that leads. If some power coming out from the Father produced the Son, then that power, and not the Father himself, would really be the Son's source. The Son would be a son in name only, more like a product of a tool than a child of his Father. And if that in-between power is not a real, living thing in its own right, it could not give real being to anyone. Something that has no substance cannot produce someone who truly and fully exists. The whole picture would also push the Son down the ladder, into third place behind the Father and his energy, and the Spirit even further. Yet Jesus says plainly, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me" (John 14:10-11). There is no room for anything to stand in between.

Some have also argued that because the Son and the Spirit are different from each other, they must have been produced by different powers of different strength, which would make them unequal. But even in creation that reasoning fails. God spoke one word of command, and out came light and darkness, sea and land, stars, animals and people, all wonderfully different. Variety in what results does not mean a ranking of powers behind it. And God's nature cannot be ranked against itself in any case. God is perfectly and unchangeably good. Nothing can limit his goodness, and nothing above him forces anything on him. So the Son and the Spirit are not lesser copies with a smaller share of goodness or power.

A few misunderstandings are worth gently clearing up. "Begotten" does not mean that the Son had a beginning, as human children do. It describes a relationship, not a starting date. Saying the Son is not "by will" does not mean the Father was forced, or that something outside God compelled him. It means the Son belongs to who God is, rather than to what God decided to make. And calling the Son the "firstborn over all creation" (Colossians 1:15) does not make him the first creature. As the very next verse explains, all things were created through him. The title speaks of his rank as heir and Lord over creation.

This matters for ordinary faith. If the Son were the product of a choice or of some go-between power, then in Jesus we would meet something less than God himself. But Jesus says, "As the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). This giving is not a gift handed over at some point in time. It is the eternal life of the Father, shared fully with the Son from all eternity. So when we look to Jesus, we are not looking at a messenger produced at a distance. We are seeing the Father's own Son, true God from true God, with nothing standing between him and the Father.

topics.title: Does the Son's generation involve passion, division, emission or diminishment?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son's (or Word's) generation from the Father involves no passion, division, separation or diminishment, and that the Son shares the Father's impassibility, perfection and unalterableness. Their grounds differ with their opponents. Athanasius argues from divine simplicity and immateriality, and from the scriptural titles Word, Wisdom and Radiance. He also uses analogies from creatures, such as radiance from light and reason from mind, to show that offspring can come forth without parts or passion. Gregory of Nyssa answers Eunomius by insisting that the immaterial must be judged by its own properties. He separates the carnal sense of "Son" from the bare relation to the begetter. He points to the passionless virgin birth to show that even bodily birth need not involve passion, and he rejects any measuring of the Son by the quantity of a productive power. Irenaeus, writing against Valentinian emanation, argues more philosophically: emission would require a space more ancient than God and would make God compound. He also reasons that consubstantial offspring must be as impassible and knowing as their source, or else the Father himself would suffer. Hilary simply affirms from revelation that "God of God" is not contrary to reason. Waterland, speaking historically, adds that the Fathers' images (light from light, sun and rays, fountain and streams) were chosen precisely because they show sameness of nature, signifying consubstantiality.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: for He is not composed of parts, but being impassible and simple, He is impassibly and indivisibly Father of the Son.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For if a man, or a bull, or any other of those things which are generated by the flesh, is not free from passion in generating or being generated, what has this to do with that Nature which is without passion and without corruption?

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Nor yet did my soul perceive anything contrary to reason in God of God, since He was revealed as having been in the beginning God with God.

ans.text:
No. When Christians say the Son is "begotten" of the Father, they mean something far higher than human birth, and none of the things that go with human birth apply: no process or change in God, no splitting of God into pieces, no part of God sent away from Him, and no loss to the Father or shortfall in the Son.

A few words first. To be "begotten" means to come from a parent and share the parent's own nature, as a child shares human nature with its father. That is why the Bible calls Jesus the Son. It tells us He is not a creature God made but someone who comes from the Father and is truly what the Father is. Older Christian writing sometimes uses the word "passion" here. It does not mean strong feeling. It means being acted on, going through a process, or changing. To say God is "impassible" is to say He is not pushed around, worn down or altered the way created things are.

Human begetting involves all sorts of things that do not belong in God. A human father acts at a moment in time. His body is involved, and he gives up something material of himself. The child then exists separately from him, starts small and weak, and grows. All this happens because we are bodily, changing, limited creatures. God is not. He is spirit, as Jesus says in John 4:24. He has no body to divide and no parts to give away. He does not change. In Malachi 3:6 the Lord says, "I the LORD do not change." So when Scripture uses the word Son, we keep what the word is meant to teach, a true relationship and a shared nature. We leave behind what belongs only to bodies.

Jesus made this kind of distinction Himself. When Nicodemus took "born again" in a fleshly sense, Jesus answered in John 3:6, "Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit." If even being born of the Spirit is unlike bodily birth, how much more is the eternal begetting of the Son by the Father.

The Bible also gives other names for the Son that guard against wrong pictures. He is the Word (John 1:1). A word or thought comes from a mind without the mind being cut in pieces or losing anything. Hebrews 1:3 calls Him "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Light shines from its source without the source being divided or dimmed, and the source is never without its shining. Think too of one candle lighting another. The first flame loses nothing, and the second is the same kind of fire. No picture is perfect. A word can be forgotten and a candle can go out. But together these images show how one can truly come from another with no tearing, no draining and no difference in kind.

Some imagine the Son being "emitted" from God, like a ray sent out into space until it stands at a distance from Him. That cannot be right. There is no space outside God that existed before Him to receive anything. And the Son is never separated from the Father. Jesus says in John 14:10, "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me," and in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one." The Son comes from the Father and is still in the Father. The Father gives the Son His own life and nature without letting go of it. As John 5:26 puts it, the Father has granted the Son to have life in Himself, just as the Father has life in Himself.

This also means the Son is not a smaller or dimmer copy. A perfect Father does not beget an imperfect Son. A Son who shares the Father's very nature has everything that nature is: wisdom, power, eternity and unchangeableness. Jesus says in John 16:15, "Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine," and Colossians 2:9 says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells." If the Son lacked the Father's knowledge or could change for the worse, He would not be the exact representation of the Father at all. That is why Christians confess Him as "God from God, Light from Light." He knows the Father perfectly, as Matthew 11:27 says, and He is unchanging. Hebrews 13:8 says He is "the same yesterday and today and forever."

Nor is this begetting an event that happened once and was over, as if there was a time when the Son was not yet. John 1:1-2 says the Word was in the beginning with God, and was God. The Father has always been Father, and the Son has always been Son.

One point can cause confusion. Doesn't the Bible say Jesus wept, suffered and died? Yes, and truly. But that belongs to His becoming man. The eternal Son took a real human nature and in it He hungered, suffered and died for us. That is a different matter from His eternal coming forth from the Father. In His divine nature, as He comes from the Father, nothing is suffered, lost or diminished.

There is nothing unreasonable in this. Even the birth of Jesus from Mary was no ordinary human birth, since He was conceived by the Holy Spirit. If God could bring about a human birth beyond the usual way of things, we should not be surprised that the Son's eternal birth from the Father is beyond anything we know. We cannot picture it fully. But Scripture tells us enough to say what it is not. The Father gives all that He is to the Son, loses nothing, and stays undivided. The Son receives all and lacks nothing. So when we worship Jesus, we are not worshiping a piece of God or a lesser copy of God, but God the Son, one with the Father.

topics.title: Can human or bodily generation serve as an analogy for the Son's birth?
topics.cmp: Hilary of Poitiers and Gregory of Nyssa agree that human generation cannot serve as an exact model for the Son's birth, and that the divine generation is nonetheless real. Hilary treats human analogies as a ladder toward God's majesty, setting aside intercourse, conception, time and travail, and he insists that God's immutability and incorporeality, rightly part of the Church's faith, do not rule out a true birth of God from God. Gregory makes the parallel point through the meaning of words, drawing on Scripture's symbolic language for God: shared names like 'Father' carry meanings as different as God is from man. Their emphases differ. Hilary counsels being content with the fact of the birth and appeals to the Law and the Prophets against Arian reasoning. Gregory instead argues dialectically against Eunomius, turning the logic of natural generation against him: if Eunomius models the Son's generation on animal generation, offspring share their parent's nature, so the Son cannot be inferior. Gregory also objects to making ungeneracy the Father's sole defining character.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: They use the fact, true in itself, that God is immutable and incorporeal, as an argument against the birth of the Son from Him.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: for such productions are of the same type as their progenitors: whereas he assigns to the members of his succession strange and uninherited qualities

ans.text:
Human birth can help us understand the Son's birth only in part. It shows us something true, but it can never be an exact model, because God is not a creature and does not have a body.

When the Bible calls Jesus the Father's "one and only Son" (John 1:14), it is telling us something real. The old word "begotten" simply means "born from" or "fathered." The church has always confessed that the Son is begotten of the Father before all ages. This does not mean he was made. It means he comes from the Father in a way no creature does.

So what does human birth get right? Think about what we see in ordinary life. A human child is fully human, just like its parents. Puppies are dogs, not cats. Living things bring forth offspring of their own kind. This is exactly the point the Bible makes about the Son. He shares the Father's very nature, or "essence," which means what God is. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." A son is not a lesser kind of thing than his father. So anyone who uses the word "Son" and then makes Jesus a lower, different sort of being has broken the very picture he is using. If the comparison to birth teaches anything, it teaches that the Son is fully God, as the Father is.

Then what does human birth get wrong? Almost everything else. A human birth involves a body, a mother, conception, nine months of waiting, pain in labor, and a moment when the child begins to exist. The child later separates from the parent, grows up, and may outlive him. The father existed before the child did, and he changed by becoming a father. None of this belongs to God. Jesus says in John 4:24, "God is Spirit." He has no body to divide. He does not change (Malachi 3:6). He does not live inside time, waiting for things to happen. So the Father did not "become" a Father at some point, and there was never a time when the Son was not. The Son's birth is eternal. The Father has always been the Father, and the Son has always been the Son.

Jesus himself gave us the key to this when he spoke with Nicodemus. Nicodemus heard about being "born again" and pictured a grown man going back into his mother's womb. Jesus corrected him: "Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit" (John 3:6). A spiritual birth must not be judged by the rules of a bodily one. If that is true of our new birth, it is even more true of the Son's eternal birth from the Father. It is a mistake to take something that belongs only to bodies, like having a beginning or being split off, and charge it against God, who has no body.

It also helps to notice how the Bible uses words for God. Scripture speaks of God's "arm," his "eyes," and his "house." No one thinks God has muscles or a building with rooms. These words sound human, but their meaning is lifted up to fit who God is. The same goes for "Father" and "Son." The words are true, but they mean far more when used of God. In fact, Paul suggests the order runs the other way. He speaks of "the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name" (Ephesians 3:14–15). God's fatherhood is the original. Human fathers are the small copy, not the pattern.

This is also why the Bible gives us other pictures alongside birth. The Son is called the Word of God (John 1:1). A word comes from a mind without cutting the mind in half or taking time to form. He is also the radiance of God's glory (Hebrews 1:3). Light shines from the sun as long as the sun exists, and the light is never separated from it. No single picture says everything. Together they guard each other. Birth shows that the Son has the same nature as the Father. Word and light show that this birth is spiritual, eternal, and without division.

There are two opposite mistakes to avoid. One is to press the human picture too far and conclude that the Son must have had a beginning, or must be smaller or later than the Father. The other is to decide that, because the picture is imperfect, the Son is not really a Son at all and the word is just a figure of speech. The Bible rules out both. The Son is truly born of the Father, and that birth is unlike any birth we know.

In the end, human comparisons are like a ladder. They help us climb a little way toward the truth, but they do not reach all the way into God's life. God reminds us, "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways" (Isaiah 55:8). We can say with confidence what Scripture says: the Son is truly from the Father, fully God, and eternal. How that happens in God's inner life, we gladly leave as a mystery to worship rather than a puzzle to solve.

topics.title: Does what originates from a source share the same nature as that source?
topics.cmp: Hilary of Poitiers, Irenaeus of Lyons, and Gregory of Nyssa all affirm that what originates from a source shares its nature, but they reach this by different routes and for different purposes. Hilary argues from the concept of birth itself: equality is the absence of difference, and true birth can only yield an undifferentiated nature, so it alone grounds the Son's equality with the Father. Irenaeus uses the principle polemically against the Valentinians, arguing that emanated products must be like their producer and one another, and that what proceeds from an inseparable union must itself stay united, as water with moisture or fire with heat; on this basis he reduces their system to absurdity, with Bythus a vacuum and the Æons without substance. Gregory argues from natural and human analogies to show what does not break sameness of nature: wine differs in qualities from the vine's moisture yet is the same substance, and Adam (moulded) and Abel (begotten) differ in manner of origin yet share one definition of being. He then applies this to the Father and Son, whereas Irenaeus's answers stay with refuting Gnostic emanations and do not speak directly of the Trinity.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: And this is the only possible origin of true equality; birth can only bring into existence a nature equal to its origin.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: if it proceeded from the same source [as they did], it must be similar in nature to Him who produced it, as well as to those along with whom it was produced.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: so that in substance the two are the same, but are distinguished by qualitative differences.

ans.text:
When we speak of true begetting, yes. What comes from a source by birth shares the nature of that source, and this is the heart of what Christians mean when they call Jesus the Son of God.

Think about what begetting means in ordinary life. To beget is to father a child, to pass on your own kind of life. A man does not father a statue or a cat. He fathers a human being. Genesis 5:3 tells us that Adam had a son in his own likeness, after his own image. What is born shares the nature of the one it is born from. Making is different. A carpenter makes a table, but the table is not a carpenter. What you make can be very unlike you. What you beget is your own kind.

This is why the Bible's language about the Son matters so much. Scripture does not say that God made a very great being and then called him his Son. It says the Word was with God in the beginning and "the Word was God" (John 1:1). Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Light that shines from the sun is not a different kind of thing from the sun's light. In Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). Jesus says that "as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). The Son receives from the Father, but what he receives is the Father's own life, not a lesser copy. So the church confesses that the Son is "of one being" with the Father. "Essence" or "being" here simply means what God is. The Father is God, and the Son is God in exactly the same sense.

Someone might object that the Father and the Son came to be in different ways. The Father is from no one, and the Son is from the Father. Doesn't a different origin mean a different nature? Not at all. Adam was formed from the dust, and his son Abel was born of a mother. They came into being in very different ways, yet both were fully human. How someone comes to be does not change what they are. In the same way, the Father being the source and the Son being begotten tells us how they are related to each other. It does not make one more God than the other.

The reverse mistake is also worth avoiding. Some have argued that likeness depends only on the manner of birth. But if that were so, every creature born in the same way would resemble every other, and a mouse would be like an elephant. What decides the nature is not the method but the source. A child is human because he comes from humans. The Son is divine because he comes from God.

Nor does sharing a nature mean the Son differs from the Father in some lesser way, as wine differs in taste from the sap of the vine while still being the same stuff. The Son is not God with a few qualities missing. He is all that the Father is, except being the Father. That is why Jesus can say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and why seeing him is seeing the Father.

Here every human picture reaches its limit. A human father and son are two separate people, and the father exists before the son. In God it is not so. The Son is not a second god alongside the Father. There is one God, and the Son shares the one divine being itself, not merely the same kind of being. And the Father was never without his Son. The Son is eternally begotten. There was never a time when he was not. A sun never exists without its radiance. In the same way, God has always been Father, and so the Son has always been.

The same truth applies to the Holy Spirit. Jesus speaks of "the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father" (John 15:26). The Spirit is not begotten as the Son is, but he too comes forth from God and shares God's own nature. Christians have disagreed about whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son. One side stresses that Jesus names the Father as the source. The other points out that the Spirit is also called the Spirit of the Son and is sent by him. But both agree on the main point. Whatever comes forth from God within God is fully God.

This is good news, not just a puzzle. If the Son were only a made thing, then in Jesus we would meet something less than God. Because he is begotten and not made, sharing the Father's very nature, in Jesus we meet God himself.

title: The Son's Eternity and Pre-existence
desc: Whether there was when the Son was not, his co-eternity and immutability, eternal Sonship, and his existence before the incarnation and creation.

topics.title: Is the Son eternal, or was there a time when he was not?
topics.cmp: All the authors (Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius, Augustine, Basil, Novatian, Ambrose, Irenaeus, Waterland, Owen, Bickersteth, Warfield) agree that the Son is eternal and that there was no time when he was not, and most rest this on the correlation of Father and Son (an eternal Father requires an eternal Son), on the Son's being God's Word, Wisdom, Power, Life and Truth, which God was never without, and on the radiance-and-light analogy. Several also argue from God's immutability and perfection (Athanasius, Gregory, Hilary, Ambrose) and from Scripture's 'was,' 'ever' and 'I am' (Athanasius, Gregory, Owen, Bickersteth, Waterland on Proverbs 8 and Psalm 90). Their emphases differ: Gregory argues most philosophically against Eunomius, holding that the divine nature has no interval or extension and that the Father is prior only by causation, a point Novatian puts as priority of origin; Hilary stresses that birth is not beginning, so that 'before his birth' simply does not apply to the Son, and that the birth exceeds understanding; Waterland works historically and linguistically, insisting that 'eternal' and 'before all ages' be taken strictly against Clarke and reading ante-Nicene talk of a 'temporal generation' as a manifestation of an already existing Word. They handle some points differently: on the Father's will, Athanasius denies that any will precedes the Son, Gregory allows a will simultaneous with its object, and Waterland calls the generation natural and necessary. Augustine approves the wisdom argument while flagging a difficulty in it, and Waterland grants that the Word's eternity alone does not strictly prove eternal sonship. Only Edwards offers an account of how the Son is begotten, as God's reflex act of self-knowledge.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: we have always maintained the birth existing out of time

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: points by the force of this mode of expression to the truth that He is conceived as being both from Him and with Him

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Son, According to the Apostle, is the Power and…
refs.quote: If the Son of God is the power and wisdom of God, and God was never without power and wisdom, then the Son is co-eternal with God the Father

ans.text:
The Son is eternal. There was never a moment, and never a "before time," when the Father existed without him. He has always been the Son, just as the Father has always been the Father.

The question usually comes from the word "begotten," or "born." The Bible calls Jesus the Father's one and only Son, and the creeds say he is "begotten of the Father." In ordinary life a son is born after his father already exists, and before that the son did not exist. So it seems natural to reason that if the Son is begotten, he must have had a starting point. But that reasoning carries human limits over to God. A human father has a beginning and lives in time, so his child's birth happens at a moment in time. God the Father has no beginning and is not inside time at all. When Christians say the Son is "begotten," they mean that he comes from the Father and shares the Father's very nature, the way a son shares his father's nature. He is not a thing the Father made. And because the Father he comes from is eternal, his coming from the Father is eternal too. Being from the Father tells us where the Son comes from. It does not tell us when, because there is no "when" in God.

The Bible gives us a picture that helps. Hebrews 1:3 says, "The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Think of the sun and its light. The light comes from the sun, not the other way round. Yet as long as there has been a sun, it has been shining. There was never a sun sitting in the sky dark, waiting to start giving light. In the same way, the Son comes from the Father, yet the Father was never without his radiance. Every comparison falls short of God, but this one shows that coming from something does not have to mean coming after it.

Scripture speaks plainly about the Son's eternity. John opens his Gospel with "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). At the very beginning, the Word already was. John then adds, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). If the Son himself had been made, he would be one of the "all things," and he would have had to make himself, which is nonsense. He stands on the Creator's side of the line, not the creature's. Jesus also speaks of "the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5), and of the Father's love for him "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). In John 8:58 he says, "before Abraham was born, I am!" He does not say "I was," as if he were simply older than Abraham. He uses the timeless "I am," echoing the name God gave himself at the burning bush. Paul says, "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). Long before, the prophet Micah foretold a ruler from Bethlehem whose "origins are of old, from the days of eternity" (Micah 5:2).

There is also a simple line of reasoning about God himself. God does not change ("I, the LORD, do not change," Malachi 3:6). If the Son had a beginning, then God was once not a Father and later became one. He would have gained something he did not have before, and that is a change in God. The names "Father" and "Son" belong together. You cannot be a father without a child. So if God is truly and eternally Father, then there has always been a Son. Scripture also calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the Word of God. To say there was a time without the Son would be to say there was a time when God had no Word and no Wisdom. No Christian wants to say that.

So the Son is eternal in the same way the Father is. He has no beginning and no end, and his life is not measured out in years. There is still a real order between them. The Father is the source, and the Son is from the Father. The Father sends, and the Son is sent. But this is an order of relationship, not of time, just as the light is from the sun without being younger than it.

A few passages are sometimes used to argue that the Son had a beginning. Colossians 1:15 calls him "the firstborn over all creation." In the Bible, "firstborn" often means the one with the rank and inheritance of the heir. That is why the very next verses say that all things were created through him and for him. He is over creation, not part of it. Proverbs 8:22, where Wisdom says the Lord brought her forth at the beginning of his way, is also raised. That chapter is a poem about God's wisdom. Christians read it in different ways, but it cannot be made to contradict the clear teaching that the Word was God in the beginning and that everything was made through him. Others point to verses where Jesus grows, learns or is called a servant. These belong to his becoming man at a point in history, born of Mary. The eternal Son took on a human life that did have a beginning, but he himself did not begin then.

One other mistake goes the opposite way. Some have pictured the "Son" as only a role or mode that the one God took up for a season, like an actor's mask, set aside once the job is done. But in the Gospels the Son speaks to the Father, prays to him, and is loved by him before the world began. That is a real relationship between two persons, not one person changing costumes. And "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Hebrews 13:8). He is not a passing phase.

This matters for our faith. If the Son were a creature, however great, then in him we would meet something less than God. Because he is eternal and fully God, when we see Jesus we truly see the Father (John 14:9). The love that saves us is the same love the Father and Son have shared from all eternity.

topics.title: Is the Father prior to the Son in time?
topics.cmp: All the authors deny that the Father precedes the Son in time. Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, Waterland, Athanasius and Novatian all hold that any priority of the Father is one of cause or order, not of duration. Gregory of Nyssa gives by far the fullest argument, and it is mainly philosophical and dialectical: an interval would give the Father a beginning, an infinite interval is incoherent, divine simplicity excludes being first Ungenerate and later Father, and making the Son later than the ages he made is absurd. He also appeals to Scripture's names for the Son as Life, Light and Truth. Basil shares Gregory's argument from the Son as Maker of the ages and from the mutual relation of Father and Son. Athanasius, by contrast, stresses that human begetting is no model for divine generation and treats the question of whether the Son 'was before His generation' as meaningless, illustrating this with the sun and its radiance; Hilary explains why human birth, unlike divine, implies prior non-existence. Novatian argues from John 8:58 that Christ must be God to exist before Abraham, and Waterland argues historically that Novatian and the pre-Nicene writers allowed the Son's subordination but not a denial of his coeternity.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: when Novatian speaks afterwards of the Father’s being precedent to the Son, he can mean it only in order of nature, not in respect of duration.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: let it suffice on the ground of causation only to conceive of the Father as before the Son; and let not the Father’s life be thought of as a separate and peculiar one before the generation of the Son

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: creates not as man creates, but yet creates as God, it is plain that He begets also not as men beget, but begets as God.

ans.text:
No. There was never a moment when the Father existed and the Son did not. The Father comes 'first' only in the sense that the Son comes from Him, as light comes from its source, not in the sense that the Father was around for a while before the Son arrived.

The question is natural. Jesus calls God His Father, and among us fathers are always older than their sons. A man lives for years before his child is born. So it can seem obvious that God the Father must have existed before the Son. But the Bible points us firmly the other way, and once we see why, the picture of a 'before' and 'after' inside God falls apart.

Start with how John opens his Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). John does not say the Word came to be at the beginning. He says the Word already was. However far back you go, the Son is already there, with God. John adds that "through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Hebrews says the same: it is through the Son that God "made the universe" (Hebrews 1:2).

Think about what that means. Time itself is part of what God made. Days, years and ages are part of creation, not something God lives inside. If the Son made all things, He made time too. So it makes no sense to say there was a time before the Son. That would make the Son younger than the very ages He created, like saying a clockmaker is newer than the clocks he built.

Jesus speaks this way about Himself. He says, "before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58). He does not say 'I was,' as if He were simply very old. He uses the language of timeless being. On the night before He died He prays, "glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). Paul says plainly that "He is before all things" (Colossians 1:17). If He is before all things, nothing comes before Him, not even a stretch of time in which the Father was alone.

The word 'Father' itself points the same way. No one is a father without a child. If God is eternally the Father, as Scripture assumes, then He has eternally had a Son. If there was once no Son, then God was once not a Father and only became one later. That would mean God changed and gained something new, but the Bible presents God as unchanging (Malachi 3:6; James 1:17). God is not built out of parts that can be older or newer than each other. He does not grow into being Father. He simply is Father, always.

So in what sense is the Father 'first'? In the sense of source, or order. The Son is 'begotten' of the Father. That word means He comes from the Father and shares the Father's very nature, the way a child shares the nature of a parent, and unlike something that is made, which is different from its maker. Jesus says, "as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). The Son receives His life from the Father. The Father never receives from the Son. That is a real order: the Father is the fountain, the Son flows from Him. But it is an order of relationship, not of time.

A common picture helps here. Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory" (Hebrews 1:3). The light shining from the sun comes from the sun, not the other way around. Yet the sun has never existed without shining. The moment there is a sun, there is sunlight. In the same way, the Son comes from the Father, but the Father has never been without His Son. Like every comparison, this one limps. The sun is a created thing that once began. God never began at all. But it shows how one thing can come from another without coming after it.

This also answers the objection from human birth. When a human child is born, there was a yesterday when he did not exist. He comes from parents who were living before him, in a world that was already running. None of that applies to God. God does not need materials to create the way a builder does. He does not sit in a place the way we do. So He does not beget the way we beget. Human fatherhood happens in time because we are creatures in time. God's fatherhood is eternal because God is eternal. Asking 'when' the Son was begotten, or what the Father was doing before, treats the Son as something outside the Father, made at a certain date. The Bible treats Him as the Father's own Word, as much a part of who God is as a person's thoughts are part of his mind.

There is a further problem with putting the Father before the Son. If the Father existed for some stretch before the Son, that stretch had to have a definite length, bounded by the Father at one end and the Son at the other. Measured backward, that would give the Father's own life a starting point too. Making the Son a latecomer ends up making the Father a latecomer as well, and then neither is truly eternal. The Prophet speaks of the coming ruler "whose origins are from of old, from the days of eternity" (Micah 5:2). Scripture calls the Son the Life and the Light. To say there was a time when Life did not live, or Light did not shine, is a contradiction.

Two misunderstandings are worth avoiding. First, saying the Father and Son are equally eternal does not mean they are two independent gods who simply happen to coexist. The Son really does come from the Father. That is why He is called Son and not brother. Second, saying the Son comes from the Father does not make Him a creature or a lesser kind of God.
