When Jesus says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), Christians have understood this in terms of His becoming a servant for us and of the Father being the source within God. It has not been taken to mean the Son is a later or lesser being. Some have stressed the Son's humble role more, and others His equality more, but the church's historic faith has held both together. The Son is "God from God, Light from Light," fully God, and He has never not been.

So the honest answer is that the Father is before the Son only as a fountain is 'before' its stream: as the source, never as an earlier time. From all eternity the Father has loved the Son, and the Son has been with the Father. When we worship Jesus, we are not worshiping someone who was added to God at some point. We are worshiping the eternal Son, who was with God in the beginning and is God.

topics.title: Is the Son eternal and unchangeable like the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son is eternal and unchangeable like the Father and that change belongs to creatures, not to God, but they reach this by different routes. Athanasius argues most directly for the Son: because the Son is proper to the Father's unalterable essence, he must share that unalterability. He meets the Arian reading of 'loving righteousness' by pointing out that Scripture says the same of the Father, and he adds a soteriological reason: the second Adam had to be unalterable to undo the first Adam's fall. Novatian, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary argue more philosophically about the divine nature as such. Novatian says being born or made is itself a change, Gregory says perfect fulness admits neither addition nor loss, and Hilary says a nature capable of progress could never be perfect. On the Son specifically, Gregory refutes Theognostus by showing that what exists for the sake of another is worth less than it, while Hilary uses 'the Word was with God' and the Son's unique comparability to God. Augustine stresses the contrast between creatures and the Word or Wisdom. He uses the changeable but invisible soul as an analogy, extends unchangeability to God's will, counsel and to the Spirit, and alone develops how changeable souls can share in unchangeable wisdom; Irenaeus similarly sets God, ever the same, against man, who grows toward him.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: He Who is absent when we seek for His origin in time is present all the while with the Creator of time.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: for things originate, being from nothing, and not being before their origination, because, in truth, they come to be after not being, have a nature which is changeable; but the Son, being from the Father, and proper to His essence, is unchangeable

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: if the Lord also exists on account of the world, and not all things on account of Him, the whole of the things for the sake of which they say He exists, would be more valuable than the Lord.

ans.text:
Yes. The Son has always existed, and in his divine nature he cannot change, just as the Father cannot. He did not begin, he does not grow, and he will never fade. Hebrews 13:8 puts it simply: "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever."

Start with eternity. John's Gospel opens with the words "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Notice that John does not say the Word came to be in the beginning. He says the Word already *was*. Whenever you try to go back to a starting point for the Son, you find he is already there, and already "with God." He is not a lonely, free-floating being outside of time. He has always been with the Father, sharing his life. Jesus speaks the same way about himself: "before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58). He also prays about "the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5).

Now, unchangeableness. Theologians sometimes call this "immutability," which just means "not able to change." God says through the prophet, "I, the LORD, do not change" (Malachi 3:6). The letter to the Hebrews takes a psalm about God and applies it directly to the Son. Speaking of the heavens and the earth, it says, "They will perish, but You remain," and "You remain the same, and Your years will never end" (Hebrews 1:10-12). The whole universe will wear out like old clothing, but the Son will not.

Why is the Son unchangeable when everything else changes? Think about what change is. When something changes, it either gains something it lacked or loses something it had. Creatures change all the time because we came from nothing. We once did not exist, then we began. We grow, learn, age and decline. Even our thoughts and moods shift from hour to hour. That is not a flaw in us. It is simply what it means to be a creature.

God is different. He is not a creature, and he did not begin, so there was never a moment when he was missing something. He is already complete in every good thing. A perfect God cannot get better, because he would have to have been less than perfect before. He cannot get worse, because loss would be a kind of slow dying, and God is life itself. The Son is not a creature made by the Father. He is the Father's own Son, sharing the very same divine nature. So whatever is true of the Father's nature is true of his: eternal, complete, unchanging.

This also guards against an old mistake. Some have imagined that God first made the Son as a kind of tool, a first creature he could use to make the rest of the world. But Scripture says all things were created "through Him and for Him," and "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16-17). The world exists for the Son's sake, not the Son for the world's sake. A tool is always worth less than the job it serves. The Son is not the world's instrument; he is its Lord and its goal.

The Son's will is just as steady as his nature. Hebrews 1:9 says of him, "You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness." Someone might ask whether this means the Son had to struggle, choosing good over evil the way we do, perhaps able to fall the other way. But Scripture says the same kind of thing about the Father, who loves what is right and hates what is evil. Nobody concludes from this that the Father might drift into sin. Such words describe God as a just judge. Being holy by nature, he delights in what is good and turns away from what is wicked. It is not a tug-of-war inside him. The Son is free, but his freedom is the freedom of perfect goodness, not the shakiness of a will that might go either way.

A thoughtful reader will ask: did the Son not change when he became a man? The Gospels tell us Jesus grew "in wisdom and stature" (Luke 2:52), got tired, wept, suffered and died. All of that is true, and it matters a great deal. But when "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14), the Son did not stop being God or turn his divine nature into something else. He took a real human nature to himself and added it to who he already was. In that human nature he truly grew, hungered and suffered. In his divine nature he remained what he had always been. Think of a king who puts on a servant's clothes and works beside his servants. He really does the servant's work. But he does not stop being the king.

This is good news for us. The first man, Adam, was changeable. He turned away from God, and sin and death spread to all of us. Christ came as a new Adam. He took our weak, changeable human nature, yet he himself could not be turned aside from God. So the tempter's attack failed against him. His faithfulness now reaches all who belong to him, just as Adam's failure once reached everyone. Our rescue does not rest on a Savior who might have wavered. It rests on one who is always the same.

There is one more question here. If God never changes, how can he care for a world that changes constantly? How can Proverbs picture God's Wisdom "delighting" in humanity, as if something new had been added to him? God's joy in his creation is not a new feeling he lacked before. He rejoices in what he has made because he sees in it the reflection of his Son, his own image, in whom he has always delighted. And his unchanging wisdom is not far from us. The Son "upholds all things by His powerful word" (Hebrews 1:3). Because every changing thing was made through him, he never abandons any of it. He is present to every moment of time without being carried along by time.

That is where our hope lies. We are changeable, but we are not shut out from the One who does not change. Through Christ, our restless and shifting lives can share in God's steady wisdom and goodness. We can be changed, slowly and truly, into his likeness. We are the ones who move toward God, and he never stops giving to us. Because the Son does not change, his promises do not change, his love does not cool, and the ground under our feet will hold.

topics.title: Did the Son exist as a distinct Person before his incarnation and before creation?
topics.cmp: All the authors—Hilary, Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Athanasius, Novatian, Owen and Waterland—agree that the Son existed as the Word with the Father before his birth from Mary and before creation, and they reject the view that he began as a mere man (Hilary against Hebion, Owen against the Socinians, Paul of Samosata and Photinus). Most rely on the same Johannine texts, especially John 1:1-3 and John 17:5, but they put them to different uses. Novatian argues from 17:5 that one must exist to possess glory and rejects the 'predestination' gloss as an addition to Scripture that would make Christ inferior to men. Hilary reads the same verse as a return to the unity of the divine nature. Hilary and Owen add Proverbs 8 and the Psalms, and Owen alone stresses that John 1 expounds Genesis 1:1. The arguments beyond Scripture vary: Athanasius reasons that the ages were made through the Word, so there were no times before him, that the patriarchs could only have known the Father through the Son, and that the 'Son' and 'Word' texts must be read alike as eternal; Owen argues that a being prior to all creatures must be the Creator rather than a creature; Irenaeus argues that a Word beginning under Tiberius would charge God with neglect, and he ties pre-existence to the Word's constant presence with mankind and to recapitulation; Hippolytus notes that the Son's offering of his flesh to the Father shows he is distinct from the Father. Waterland differs in focus, arguing historically from the Fathers (Irenaeus, Novatian, Theophilus, Athenagoras) that the pre-existent Word was eternally generated and was already a Person, not a mere attribute, before his 'procession.'

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Let Hebion try to sap the faith, who allows the Son of God no life before the Virgin’s womb, and sees in Him the Word only after His life as flesh had begun.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: he censures those who pretended to ascribe any beginning to the nativity of the Word; which is in effect asserting an eternal prolation, or generation

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For I have shown that the Son of God did not then begin to exist, being with the Father from the beginning; but when He became incarnate, and was made man, He commenced afresh the long line of human beings

ans.text:
Yes. The one we know as Jesus did not begin to exist in Mary's womb. As the eternal Son of God, he was already alive, already a distinct Person, and already sharing the Father's glory before Bethlehem, before Abraham, and before the world itself was made.

The clearest place to start is the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). John goes on to say that this Word "became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). The Word, then, is not a new person who appeared at Christmas. He is someone who already was, and who then took on a human life. John also says, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Whoever makes the world must be there before the world. A builder exists before the house.

Jesus speaks about himself the same way. He says, "I have come down from heaven, not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me" (John 6:38), and "I came from the Father and entered the world" (John 16:28). You cannot come from somewhere you have never been. When his opponents mocked him for claiming to know Abraham, he answered, "Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58). He does not say "I was," as if he were merely very old. He says "I am," echoing the name God gave himself at the burning bush, the name of one who simply is, with no beginning.

Most moving of all is his prayer the night before he died: "And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). A little later he adds that the Father loved him "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). Here we see two Persons, the Father and the Son, in a relationship of love and shared glory before anything was created. That is why we say the Son existed as a distinct Person. He was not just an idea in the Father's mind or a quality the Father had, the way a person has wisdom or a voice. You cannot love a mere quality, and a quality cannot pray to be given back the glory it once had.

Paul teaches the same thing. He says Christ, "existing in the form of God," emptied himself, "taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness" (Philippians 2:6-7). Someone must already exist in order to take on something new. He writes that God "sent His Son, born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4). The Son was sent; he was not produced by the sending. And he says of Christ, "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). The prophet Micah, foretelling the ruler to be born in Bethlehem, speaks of one whose origins are from of old, from ancient times (Micah 5:2).

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up.

Some have said that Christ "existed" before the world only in God's plan, the way all of us were known to God before we were born. But that is not what the texts say. Jesus does not say he was planned to have glory. He says he had it, with the Father, in the Father's presence. If the Son pre-existed only as a plan, he would be no different from Abraham or from us, and his words about coming down from heaven would mean nothing special. Yet Scripture sets him above every creature, even the angels (Hebrews 1).

Others ask whether Jesus' human body or human nature existed in heaven beforehand. It did not. His human body and soul began in Mary's womb by the work of the Holy Spirit. What came down from heaven was the eternal Son himself, who then took a real human nature as his own. That is why he can be called "Son of Man" even when speaking of coming from heaven: it is one and the same Person who was in heaven as God and who now lives on earth as a man. Some ancient copies of John 3:13 even add that the Son of Man "is in heaven" while speaking on earth. Many modern translations leave those words out, but the truth behind them is clear elsewhere. The Son did not stop being God, present everywhere, when he became man. He took on our nature without leaving his own behind. How this can be is beyond our full understanding. But we can see that Scripture teaches it, even if we cannot picture it.

Finally, does pre-existence by itself prove that the Son is God? Not on its own. Angels existed before Jesus was born, and they are creatures. But the Son's pre-existence is of a different kind. He did not exist merely before Mary. He existed before creation itself, and creation was made through him. Time and the ages are part of what was made, and Hebrews says God made the universe through the Son (Hebrews 1:2). So there was never a "time" before the Son. If he is the one through whom everything that has a beginning was made, he cannot himself be one of those things. That places him on the Creator's side of the line, not the creature's. This is why Christians confess that he is eternally the Son of the Father. "Begotten" here means that he is truly from the Father, sharing the Father's own nature, the way a son shares his father's nature. But it does not mean he had a starting point. There was never a moment when the Father was without his Son.

This matters deeply for our faith. At Christmas we do not celebrate a good man whom God later lifted up. We celebrate the eternal Son, who shared the Father's glory before the world began and who freely came down to be one of us. The love that sent him was not a new idea in God. It is the love that has always been between the Father and the Son, now opened up to us.

topics.title: Is the second Person eternally the Son and eternally personal?
topics.cmp: Athanasius and Hilary agree that the second Person was Son before the incarnation. Athanasius argues at length that sonship cannot be caused by the flesh or by the union, and that what Scripture says of the Son (knowing and revealing the Father, being in his bosom) must have been true before the incarnation. He also argues that the Old Testament speaks of the Son and of men as sons for the true Son's sake, and that making God Father only later would introduce change into God. Hilary grounds the same conclusion more briefly in Paul's teaching that all things were made through him, so his creating work before time shows he already existed as Son. Hippolytus differs plainly: the pre-incarnate Word was perfect Word and only-begotten but not yet perfect Son, called Son in anticipation of what he would become, and manifested as one perfect Son only as incarnate. Waterland, writing on a related but distinct question, judges that confessing an eternal, distinct, consubstantial Word while referring sonship to creation and incarnation is tolerable, but he recommends eternal generation as the safer, more generally approved and ancient expression.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: Next, if He is first Word and then Son, it will appear that He knew the Father afterwards, not before; for not as being Word does He know Him, but as Son.

refs.author: Hippolytus of Rome
refs.quote: For neither was the Word, prior to incarnation and when by Himself, yet perfect Son, although He was perfect Word, only-begotten.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: let him who holds the Son to have become Son in time and by His Incarnation, learn that through Him are all things and we through Him, and that His timeless Infinity was creating all things before time was

ans.text:
Yes. The one we know as Jesus did not become God's Son at Bethlehem, and he was never merely an idea or power in God's mind that later turned into a person. He has always been the Son of the Father, and he has always been a living, personal 'someone' who knows and loves the Father.

Start with how the New Testament speaks about his coming. Paul writes that 'when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman' (Galatians 4:4). John says that God 'sent His one and only Son into the world' (1 John 4:9). You cannot send a son who does not yet exist as a son. The wording assumes that before he was born of Mary he was already the Son, living with the Father, and was then sent on a mission.

The Bible also gives the Son, by that name, a part in creation. Hebrews 1:2 says God has spoken to us 'by His Son,' through whom 'He made the universe.' Colossians 1 speaks of 'the Son He loves' and then says that in Him all things were created. Creation came long before the manger, so the Son was there at the very beginning.

The Son's own words point the same way. In his prayer in John 17 Jesus asks the Father to glorify him with the glory he had with the Father 'before the world existed,' and he says, 'You loved Me before the foundation of the world' (John 17:5, 24). This is a Son speaking to his Father about a shared life before anything was made. And love needs persons. A thought or a quality cannot love or be loved. Someone has to be there to receive it. So the Son was not only eternal but eternally personal, a real partner in the Father's love.

It helps to see that 'Word' and 'Son' are two names for the same person, not two stages of his life. John opens his Gospel by saying, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). A few verses later he calls this same Word 'the one and only Son' who is at the Father's side and has made Him known (John 1:18). 'Word' tells us he is the one who perfectly expresses and reveals God. 'Son' tells us he shares the Father's own nature and stands in a loving relationship with him. Both are true of him always.

This matters for what we believe about the Father too. If there was a time when the Son was not yet Son, then there was a time when the Father was not yet Father. God would have changed, becoming something he had not been before. But Scripture presents God as unchanging. 'Father' is not a title God picked up along the way. It names who he has always been, because he has always had his Son.

The word 'begotten,' which Christians have long used of the Son, can sound as if he had a starting point. It does not mean that here. It means that the Son comes from the Father the way a son shares his father's very nature, not the way a craftsman makes a table. He is not made or created. And because the Father is eternal, the Son's coming from the Father has no beginning either. A common picture is the sun and its light. As long as the sun has been shining, its light has been streaming from it. There was never a sun without its light.

Some readers point to verses like Psalm 2:7, 'You are My Son; today I have become Your Father,' or Romans 1:4, where Jesus is 'declared' to be the Son of God by his resurrection. These verses speak about the Son being publicly shown and enthroned in his saving work. In Acts 13:33 Paul applies the psalm to the resurrection. To be declared Son is not the same as beginning to be Son. A king's son does not become his father's son on coronation day. He is crowned because he already is the son.

In fact the Old Testament already hints at the Son. Psalm 2 and Psalm 110 speak of one whom God addresses as his own and seats at his right hand, and Proverbs 30:4 asks of God, 'What is His name, and what is the name of His Son?' Jesus also says that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him (Matthew 11:27). Yet God made himself known to Abraham, Moses and the prophets. That knowledge came through the Son, who was already there to reveal the Father.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. The first is the idea that the Word was at first simply God's inner reason or plan, something like a thought in his head, and became a distinct person only when God spoke at creation. Some early Christian writers used language that can sound this way, describing the Word as first 'within' God and then 'going forth.' Read carefully, they usually meant that one and the same Son was first hidden with the Father and later revealed in his works, not that a person came into being where before there was only an idea. In any case, the Bible's own picture is clear. The Word was 'with God' in the beginning, in a face-to-face relationship, and was loved before the world began. He was never a mere thought.

The second concerns a disagreement among sincere, Bible-believing Christians. Some have held that the Word is fully and eternally God and a distinct person, but that the title 'Son' properly belongs to him only from his human birth. They point out that Luke 1:35 links being called 'the Son of God' to the virgin birth, and they worry that 'Son' might suggest he is lesser or later than the Father. Most Christians throughout history, however, have held that he is eternally the Son. They note that verses about the Son being sent and creating the world, and his own words about the glory and love he shared with the Father, only make sense if he was Son before he came. They also point out that among humans a son is fully equal in nature to his father, so 'Son' implies equality, not inferiority. Those who prefer 'eternal Word' still confess the same divine person, so the gap is smaller than it may seem. Even so, the eternal sonship view follows the Bible's language more closely and better protects the truth that God has always been Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

So when we pray 'Our Father' through Jesus, we are invited into a relationship that did not begin in time. The Son has always been at the Father's side, loved by him and sharing his life. At the incarnation he did not become something new to God. He came to bring us into the love he has always known.

topics.title: Is the Word of God eternal, or did he have a beginning?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Word is eternal and uncreated rather than a being with a beginning. Augustine and Owen argue that the Word existed before all creation because all things were made through him, and Owen adds that nothing can precede all creatures except God's eternal nature. Irenaeus makes a similar contrast between the Word, who always co-existed with God, and man, who has a beginning. Athanasius draws on the widest range of grounds: the analogies of the sun and its radiance and the fountain and its stream, the claim that God is always Father and always Maker and so must always have his proper Word, the contrast between created 'becoming' and the Word's 'was', and a reading of the Bible's 'became' and 'made' passages as referring to the Incarnation. On John 1:1, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa and Owen give different accounts of 'the beginning', while Athanasius sides with Gregory. For Hilary it is the datable beginning of creation, which the Word's 'was' already exceeds; for Owen it marks existence before all creation, which amounts to eternity; for Gregory and Athanasius it signifies the Father himself, in whom the Son is without beginning and inseparably co-eternal.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: it follows that the Word is from Him and is ever co-existent with Him, through whom also the Father caused that all things which were not should be.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own…
refs.quote: Since, “in the beginning,” the Word was not made, but “the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and all things were made by Him;” neither had all things been made by Him, unless He had Himself been before all things and not made.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For thou, O man, art not an uncreated being, nor didst thou always co-exist with God, as did His own Word

ans.text:
The Word of God never had a beginning. He has always existed with the Father, as fully God as the Father is, and he is not a creature that God made at some point, however early or however exalted.

The clearest place to see this is the opening of John's Gospel. John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The words echo Genesis 1:1, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." Genesis tells us what God made at the beginning. John tells us who was already there. Notice the verb. John does not say the Word came to be in the beginning, or was made in the beginning. He says the Word *was*. Push your thinking back as far as you like, to the first moment of creation or before it, and the Word is already there. There is no point at which you can say, "Before this, the Word did not exist."

John then makes the point sharper. Verse 3 says, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Think about what that means. If the Word were a created thing, he would have had to make himself, which is impossible. John draws a single line through all of reality. On one side is everything that was made. On the other side is the One through whom it was all made. The Word stands on God's side of that line, not ours. Paul says the same in Colossians 1:16-17: all things were created through him and for him, and "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together."

Jesus speaks this way about himself. In John 17:5 he prays, "Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed." In John 8:58 he says, "Before Abraham was born, I am!" He does not say "I was," as if he were merely very old. He uses the language of a present that has no beginning, the language God uses of himself when he tells Moses, "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14). The prophet Micah, foretelling the ruler to be born in Bethlehem, says his origins are from of old, from the days of eternity (Micah 5:2).

There is also a simple line of reasoning behind this. The Bible calls the Word God's own Son. The church has used the word "begotten" for this. It means that the Son comes from the Father the way a child shares the nature of a parent. He is not made from some other material. But God is not like a human father, who exists for years before his child does. God never changes and is never incomplete. If the Son is truly the Father's own Son, then the Father has always been Father, and the Son has always been with him. Think of the sun and its light. As long as the sun has been shining, its light has been shining from it. The light comes from the sun, but it is never "younger" than the sun. The comparison is imperfect, as all comparisons with God are. Still, it shows that coming from someone does not have to mean coming after them.

The same goes for God as Creator. Scripture says God made the world through his Word and Wisdom. If that Word once did not exist, then God was once without his own Word and Wisdom. That would be a God who later gained something he lacked, and that is not the God of the Bible.

What about verses that say the Word "became" something, or was "made"? The key is John 1:14: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us." The One who always *was* (verse 1) at a certain point in history *became* a man (verse 14). He did not begin to exist in Mary's womb. He began to be human there. So when Scripture says he was "born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4), "made in human likeness" (Philippians 2:7), "became" superior to the angels (Hebrews 1:4), or was "made both Lord and Christ" (Acts 2:36), it is speaking about what he took on and accomplished as the incarnate Savior. It is not speaking about the origin of his divine being. A good rule for reading the Bible here is to ask whether a verse is speaking of the Son as he eternally is with the Father, or of the Son as he came among us for our salvation.

Some people stumble over Colossians 1:15, where the Son is called "the firstborn over all creation." In the Bible "firstborn" often means the one with the rank and inheritance of the heir. In Psalm 89:27 God says of David's line, "I will appoint him as My firstborn," though David was the youngest son. The very next verse in Colossians explains why the Son holds this place: because all things were created through him. That puts him above creation, not inside it.

One more question sometimes follows. If the Word is eternal, must the world he made also be eternal? No. The Maker and the things he makes are different. Creation has a beginning. Time itself belongs to the created world. But the One through whom the ages were made has no beginning, and nothing true of creatures, such as having a starting point, can be carried over to him.

This matters deeply for our faith. When we look at Jesus, we are not looking at God's finest creature or a go-between who stands halfway between God and us. We are looking at God himself, the eternal Word who was with the Father before the world existed. He came near and took on our flesh, so that people who had a beginning could be given everlasting life in him.

topics.title: Does Scripture teach that the Son is eternal like the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the Son's eternity affirm it, but they argue from different texts and by different means. Bickersteth and Waterland both set the Old and New Testament phrases used of the Father beside those used of Christ (Mic. 5:2, Rev. 1:17, Ps. 90:2, Prov. 8:22-23). Bickersteth moves from shared eternity to the Son's Deity, since one from everlasting must be God and there are not two Gods. Waterland presses a polemical parity argument against the Arians: whoever denies that these phrases prove the Son's coeternity must equally leave the Father's eternity unproven, even granting that the Hebrew word can mean limited duration. Gregory of Nyssa argues instead from the grammar of Scripture's unqualified present tense, the Son "is" in the Father and in his bosom with no "once" or "when", and adds a philosophical point that excellence is always present in its fountain. Athanasius reasons from Proverbs 8:30 that since the Father always rejoiced and did not draw his joy from outside himself, the Wisdom he delighted in always existed and is proper to his essence, not made from nothing. Owen reads the same verse quite differently: he takes the Father's delight chiefly as delight in the Son's love for humanity and their redemption rather than in the Son as the image of the Father's perfections, and he does not use the passage to argue for the Son's eternity.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: Bethlehem was the predicted birthplace into our world of One “whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.”

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: the proof of the Son’s eternity stands upon the same foot, in Seripture, with the proof of the Mather’s ; and is expressed in as strong words.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: the Scripture which declares that the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son, without adding to the phrase “once” or “when” or “then,” but testifying His eternity by this affirmative and unqualified utterance.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible speaks of the Son's eternity in the very same language it uses for the Father's, so that what is true of one in this respect is true of the other. There was never a time when the Father existed and the Son did not.

Start with the opening of John's Gospel. 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). Notice the verb. John does not say the Word came into being at the beginning. He says the Word already was. Go back as far as you like, to the very first moment of anything, and the Word is already there. John then adds that 'through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made' (John 1:3). That leaves only two groups: things that were made, and the One through whom they were made. The Son is not in the first group. If he had been made, he would have had to make himself, which is nonsense.

Jesus speaks the same way about himself. He prays, 'Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed' (John 17:5). He tells his opponents, 'before Abraham was born, I am!' (John 8:58). He does not say 'I was,' as a very old person might. He says 'I am,' the language of one who simply exists without beginning, echoing the name God gave himself at the burning bush. His hearers understood the claim, which is why they picked up stones.

John 1:18 makes a related point. It describes the one and only Son, who is himself God, as being at the Father's side (older translations say 'in the bosom of the Father'). Again the wording is 'is,' not 'came to be.' The picture is of a closeness that simply belongs to who the Son is. Elsewhere Jesus says he is in the Father and the Father is in him (John 14:10). Scripture never adds 'from a certain time' or 'once he was made.' It states the relationship plainly, as something that always holds.

Now set texts about the Father beside texts about the Son. Of God it is said, 'from everlasting to everlasting You are God' (Psalm 90:2). In Isaiah the Lord says, 'I am the first and I am the last' (Isaiah 44:6), as a mark that sets him apart from every false god. Yet the risen Jesus says, 'I am the First and the Last' (Revelation 1:17), and again, 'I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End' (Revelation 22:13). Hebrews takes a psalm addressed to God, which says that the earth and heavens will wear out like clothing but God remains and his years never end, and applies it directly to the Son (Hebrews 1:10-12). The same chapter says to the Son, 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever' (Hebrews 1:8). The prophet Micah, foretelling the ruler to be born in Bethlehem, says his origins are 'from the days of eternity' (Micah 5:2). The child born in a stable had no beginning as the Son of God.

Someone may object that the Hebrew words translated 'everlasting' or 'of old' can sometimes mean only a very long time, such as an ancient age. That is true of the words on their own. But this objection proves too much. The Old Testament uses these same words for the eternity of the Father. If they cannot show that the Son is eternal, they cannot show that the Father is eternal either. When God chooses the very phrases he uses for his own endless life and then uses them of his Son, the natural lesson is that the Son shares that life. And the New Testament removes any doubt by speaking of the Son as existing before all things and before the world itself (Colossians 1:17; John 17:5).

Proverbs 8 needs a little care. There, Wisdom speaks as a person, saying she was with the Lord before the mountains and the seas, beside him as he made the world, his delight day by day, rejoicing before him always (Proverbs 8:22-30). The Hebrew word in verse 30 can mean a master craftsman, or one brought up and cared for at someone's side. Christians have long read this passage in the light of Christ, whom Paul calls 'the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24). Proverbs is poetry, so we should not build the whole doctrine on it. But read with the rest of Scripture it makes a beautiful point. God was never without his wisdom. He was never without the one in whom he delights. His joy did not come to him from outside, at some later date. If the Father always rejoiced in his Wisdom, then that Wisdom always existed. The passage ends with Wisdom delighting in the human race (verse 31), a hint that the Son's love for us and his purpose to save us also reach back before time.

Some have pointed to verse 22, where some translations say the Lord 'created' Wisdom, to argue that the Son had a beginning. Others translate the word as 'possessed' or 'brought forth,' and both readings are possible in the Hebrew. In any case, a poetic picture of God's wisdom cannot overturn the plain statements that the Son made all things and existed before the world. Whatever the verse means, it cannot mean that God was once without wisdom.

A few words also cause confusion. When the Bible calls Jesus the 'only begotten' or 'one and only' Son, it does not mean he began to exist the way a human child does. 'Begotten' describes a relationship: the Son is from the Father and shares his very nature, as a son shares the nature of his father, but without any starting point. A helpful comparison is the sun and its light. As long as the sun shines, its light shines with it. You never have the sun first and the light later. Hebrews 1:3 uses this picture, calling the Son 'the radiance of God's glory.' Likewise, 'firstborn over all creation' (Colossians 1:15) speaks of rank and inheritance, the place of honor, not of being the first thing God made. The very next verse says all things were created through him.

Why does this matter? Only God is from everlasting. The Bible never treats eternity as something a creature can have from the start. So when Scripture gives the Son the eternity of God, it is telling us he is God, not a lesser being made before everything else. And since there is only one God, the Son is not a second God beside the Father but one with him. This is why the church has confessed the Son as eternally begotten of the Father, God from God, of one being with the Father.

For ordinary believers this is deeply comforting. The One who died for you is not a newcomer to God's love, nor a go-between who was once a stranger to it. He has been at the Father's side forever. 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever' (Hebrews 13:8). When you trust him, you are resting on someone who had no beginning and will have no end.

topics.title: Has Christ always been Lord and King, or did he become so at some point?
topics.cmp: Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa agree that the Psalms' language of the Son being 'set' or 'established' as King marks neither the beginning of his existence nor the beginning of his reign. Athanasius reads Psalm 2:6 and 8:6 through the incarnation: the everlasting King and Word let his kingdom 'shine in a human way' upon Sion to redeem humanity and bring it under the Father's Kingdom, and he was set over works that already existed and needed restoring. Gregory gives two accounts. In one, he argues from the logic of the commands themselves: 'Be thou Lord' is not a command to something non-existent to come into being but a grant of rule over the disobedient to one who already is, so 'establishment' means advance to dignity rather than the forming of his essence. In the other, he reads David with an eye to the dispensation, in which the Lord's humiliation to the estate of a servant was taken up into the majesty of his Kingdom. That second reading comes close to Athanasius's incarnational and redemptive emphasis, while the first is a more distinctively conceptual argument about what the wording can and cannot imply.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For He ever was and is, as Son, so also Lord and Sovereign of all, being like in all things to the Father, and having all that is the Father’s

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: As, then, the establishment of His kingdom does not signify the formation of His essence, but the advance to His dignity, and He Who bids Him “be Lord” does not command that which is non-existent to come into being

ans.text:
Christ has always been Lord and King. He did not start to exist when he was crowned, and he did not earn a throne he lacked. What happened in time was that the eternal King took on our human nature, won back a rebel world, and was openly installed as its ruler in that human nature.

The question comes from verses that sound like a beginning. In Psalm 2:6 God says, "I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain." Psalm 8:6 speaks of someone being made ruler over the works of God's hands, and Hebrews 2 applies that to Jesus. Psalm 110 has God telling the Messiah to sit at His right hand and to "rule in the midst of Your enemies." Most striking of all, Peter tells the crowd at Pentecost that "God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ" (Acts 2:36). If he was made Lord, was there a time when he was not?

The rest of Scripture says no. The Son shared the Father's glory "before the world existed" (John 17:5). All things were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:16; John 1:3). A creature cannot be the one through whom every creature was made. Hebrews 1:8 speaks to the Son with the words "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever." A throne that lasts forever was never a newly built one. Jesus could say, "before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58). And Psalm 110:1 itself has David calling the Messiah "my Lord" a thousand years before Bethlehem. You cannot call someone your Lord if he has not yet become one.

There is a simple reason this must be so. The Son is truly God, of one being with the Father. Being God includes being sovereign over all things. Jesus says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). If the Father is King, so is the Son. A Son who only gained his lordship later would not be fully like his Father. He would be a promoted creature.

So what do the "installed" and "made" verses mean? The key is the incarnation, God the Son becoming a human being. The eternal Son added a real human nature to himself. In that human nature he lived as a servant, humbled himself, and died on the cross (Philippians 2:6-8). "Therefore," Paul says, God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name above every name (Philippians 2:9). What was raised and crowned was the man Christ Jesus, our human nature in him. The Son did not gain a rank he lacked as God. Instead, a human being now sits on the throne of the universe, and that human being is the eternal Son. When Peter says God "made" him Lord, he is speaking of what happened to Jesus as the crucified and risen man. He is not describing the start of the Son's existence or of his divine rule.

Something else truly began, too. That was the open display of his rule, and its reach over a world in revolt. Before the cross, humanity had rebelled. The King's rule was real, but it was rejected. By his death and resurrection he redeemed his people and broke the power of sin and death. After rising he could say, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me" (Matthew 28:18). Psalm 110 makes the same point. He is told to rule "in the midst of Your enemies." That does not call into existence someone who was not there. It sends an existing King to bring rebels back under his reign.

Think of a rightful king whose country has been taken over by rebels. He leaves the safety of his palace, lives among the people in disguise, and suffers at their hands. Then he defeats the usurper and is crowned before everyone in the capital. That coronation day is a real event, and something new happens. But no one there would say he only became king that day. The crowning shows publicly what was always his right, and it extends his rule over those who had refused it.

There are two easy mistakes to avoid. One is to think Jesus was an ordinary man who was promoted to divine status as a reward for his obedience. Scripture's verses about his eternal glory and his role in creation rule that out. The other mistake is to treat his exaltation as mere theatre, as if nothing really changed at Easter and the Ascension. Something did change. Our human nature, in him, now reigns at the Father's right hand. And the kingdom has broken into a rebel world and is spreading until every knee bows.

So when we confess that Jesus is Lord, we are honoring both truths. He is the eternal Son, who has always been the King of all things. He is also the crucified and risen man whom the Father has openly enthroned for our salvation.

topics.title: Does the Son's eternity make him unbegotten, unoriginate or self-existent?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius and Daniel Waterland all hold that the Son's eternity does not make him ungenerate or self-existent: he is eternal yet begotten, deriving his being from the Father. Gregory argues mainly from the relational meaning of 'Son,' which inseparably implies the Father and so excludes ungeneracy. He then distinguishes senses of 'unoriginate': the Son is not unoriginate as having no cause, but he is unoriginate as being above creation, time and sequence. Athanasius makes a similar point against Asterius: if 'unoriginate' means 'not a work but existing always,' the Son must be called unoriginate as the Father is. Waterland goes much further in conceptual analysis. He separates eternity, necessary existence and self-existence. He argues that eternity implies necessary existence, against Clarke, but that necessary existence does not entail self-existence. He also treats unbegottenness as a relative personal character of the Father rather than an essential attribute, citing Augustine. For support he draws on philosophical precedent (Aristotle and the Platonists on eternal emanation), analogies such as the sun and its light, logical critique (equivocation on 'principium'), and patristic witnesses (Novatian, Alexander of Alexandria). Unlike the Greek Fathers, Waterland is willing to call necessary existence a kind of 'self-existence' common to Father and Son if the term is taken that way, and he restricts 'not unoriginate' to the Son's order as second Person rather than any dependence or temporal beginning.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: in confessing His ‘coming from the Father’ he has banished all ideas of Ungeneracy as regards the Only-begotten; and there will be then no danger in pronouncing Him Eternal and yet not Ungenerate.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: You argue that, if the Son be eternal, he is necessarily existing; which I allow: and if necessarily existing, then self-ewistent ; which I ‘deny; and you cannot prove.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: then they must constantly be told that the Son as well as the Father must in this sense be called unoriginate. For He is neither in the number of things originated, nor a work, but has ever been with the Father

ans.text:
The Son is eternal, but that does not make him unbegotten or his own source. He has always existed, yet he has always existed as the Son, receiving his life from the Father. To see why both are true, we need to keep apart some ideas that are easy to blur together.

Start with what the Bible says plainly. The Son never began. John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." When anything else had a beginning, the Word already was. Jesus speaks of "the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5), and he says, "before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58). There was never a moment when the Father was without his Son.

The Bible is just as clear that the Son is from the Father. That is what the name "Son" means. Jesus says in John 5:26, "For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself." The Son has the very same life the Father has, fully and in himself, but he has it as given by the Father. The church's word for this is "begotten." It means the Son comes forth from the Father's own being, not as something made, the way a builder makes a house, but as one who shares the Father's nature, the way a child shares a parent's nature. "Unbegotten" means the opposite: having life from no one at all. Only the Father is unbegotten.

The common mistake is to think that "eternal" and "unbegotten" must go together, so that if the Son has no beginning he can't have a source either. But having no beginning in time is one thing, and having no source is another. Think of the sun and its light. The light comes from the sun, not the other way round. Yet if the sun had always been shining, its light would always have been there too. There would never be a moment of sun without light. The light would be as old as the sun and still be from the sun. The Bible uses this very picture when it calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory" (Hebrews 1:3). Or think of a mind that never stops thinking. Its thought comes from the mind, yet the mind was never without it. In the same way, the Son is from the Father without ever coming after him.

The opposite mistake runs the other direction. Some have argued that because the Father is the source of the Son, the Son must have started at some point. But "source" does not have to mean "earlier." The sun is the source of its light without existing first and making light later. To say the Father is the Son's source tells us about their relationship, who is from whom, not about any time when the Son was missing.

So may we call the Son "unoriginate," without origin? It depends on what we mean. If we mean he is not created, not a product of God's work, never began in time, and stands above all created order, then yes, the Son is unoriginate just as truly as the Father. "Through Him all things were made" (John 1:3), and "He is before all things" (Colossians 1:17). The one through whom time and creation came to be cannot himself be part of time and creation. But if "unoriginate" means having no source at all, being the fountain from which the others flow, then that belongs to the Father alone. In that one sense the Son is not unoriginate. He is second in order, not because he is less or later, but because he is the Son and not the Father.

Does this make the Son depend on the Father the way we depend on God? No. Creatures exist because God chose to make them, and he could have chosen otherwise. The Son is not like that. The Father did not decide to have a Son the way he decided to make a world. The Father is never without the Son, any more than the sun is without its light. God cannot fail to exist, and neither can the Son, because he shares the one divine life. The Son is never cut off from the Father, never a separate being leaning on him from outside. He is one with him (John 10:30).

That helps with the word "self-existent." If it means "existing necessarily, uncreated, having the fullness of divine life in himself," then it fits the Son as fully as the Father, because those things belong to what God is, and the Son is truly God. If it means "existing from no one," then it belongs only to the Father, because it describes how the Father stands toward the Son, not what kind of being God is. Being unbegotten is not an extra piece of divinity that the Father has and the Son lacks. It is simply what makes the Father the Father, just as being begotten is what makes the Son the Son. Both are equally God.

Sincere Christians have used the language here a little differently. Some are happy to say the Son is "God of himself," meaning his divine nature is not a lesser, borrowed copy but the very same uncreated being as the Father's. Others avoid that phrase, wanting to protect the truth that the Son receives everything from the Father. On the substance they agree. As God, the Son lacks nothing and depends on no one's choice. As Son, he is eternally from the Father.

So the Son is eternal, without beginning and without end, uncreated, and fully God. He is also begotten, eternally from the Father. Both truths are held together in the Son's own name. He is the eternal Son of an eternal Father.

title: The Full Deity of the Son
desc: Scriptural and theological proofs that the Son is true God by nature and consubstantial with the Father, not a creature, adopted son or god by title.

topics.title: Is the Son truly and fully God, equal with the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors who answer agree that the Son is truly God and not a creature or lesser deity: Irenaeus, Novatian, Athanasius, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, Ambrose, Augustine, Owen, Waterland and Bickersteth each affirm this, and Basil and Athanasius read the session at the right hand as equality, not lower rank. Their grounds differ: Novatian, Owen and Bickersteth argue from Scripture's ascription to Christ of prerogatives reserved to God, such as forgiving sins, omnipresence, searching hearts and receiving worship; Athanasius, Hilary and Gregory of Nyssa rely more on reasoning about true generation, the Son as perfect image of the Father's essence, the divine simplicity that excludes 'more and less', and the claim that whatever is God is true God; Waterland argues mainly from the Fathers (Novatian, Tertullian, Athanasius) against Clarke's subordinationist readings, and Gregory of Nyssa adds that apostolic tradition puts the burden of proof on the innovators. Warfield, alone, cautions that a perfect image is not by that fact itself God, since it lacks the objective reality of Deity, which tempers the image argument used by Athanasius and Hilary. On particular texts they plainly diverge: Hilary reads John 16:15 ('All things that the Father hath are mine') as the shared divine nature, while Owen reads it as mediatorial grace; Owen reads Matthew 11:27 as the committing of grace, while Irenaeus reads it as showing the Father is Creator; Hilary takes the 'rock' of Matthew 16:18 to be Peter's confession, Owen Christ himself. On the cry of dereliction, Athanasius says it was spoken as from a man while the Word stayed impassible, Hilary denies both weakness in the Word and a Word departing from a separate man and sees an assurance of true death, and Augustine reads it as a mystery of our inner man's death to sin. On 1 Thessalonians 3:12-13, Ambrose and Basil agree that the 'Lord' is the Holy Spirit.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.place: Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St
refs.quote: For that according to John relates His original, effectual, and glorious generation from the Father, thus declaring, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: He Skilfully Replies to a Passage Which the Heretics…
refs.quote: Therefore if He plainly testifies that He is the Son of God, and not the Father, it is an instance of great temerity and excessive madness to stir up a controversy of divinity and religion

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: If they honour him not as they honour the Father, they are, of all men, the most unworthy.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible teaches that Jesus Christ, the eternal Son, is God in the full and true sense. He is not a lesser god, not a highly honored creature, and not a good man whom God adopted. He is equal with the Father in every way that makes God God: in power, knowledge, eternity, glory and worthiness of worship. There is only one God, and the Son shares completely in that one divine being. He remains a distinct person from the Father, but he is not a second or smaller God.

Start with how the New Testament speaks of him. John opens his Gospel this way: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word was "with God", so he is distinct from the Father. And the Word "was God", so he shares God's own nature. John then tells us that this Word became flesh and lived among us (John 1:14). The same John ends his Gospel with Thomas falling before the risen Jesus and saying, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). Jesus does not correct him. He accepts it. In his first letter John says of Jesus Christ, "He is the true God and eternal life" (1 John 5:20). Paul says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). The letter to the Hebrews applies to the Son words spoken to God in the Psalms: "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever" (Hebrews 1:8).

Someone might ask whether Jesus could be called "God" in a looser, lesser sense, the way we might call a powerful ruler godlike. The Bible leaves no room for that. Something either has the nature of God or it does not, much as a flame either is real fire or is not fire at all. There is no halfway kind of God. The Bible insists there is only one God and that he will not share his glory with another (Isaiah 42:8). So if Scripture calls the Son God and gives him God's glory, he must be true God. Otherwise the Bible would be setting up a rival to God.

The case goes beyond titles. Jesus does what only God can do and has what only God has. Scripture says God alone knows every human heart (1 Kings 8:39). Yet John tells us Jesus did not need anyone to tell him about people, because he knew what was in them (John 2:24-25). In Revelation the risen Christ says that all the churches will know he is the one who searches minds and hearts (Revelation 2:23). Nothing is hidden from him. He sees through every pretense, and he notices every sigh of a sorry and humble heart. That is comforting as well as searching.

He also forgives sins against God (Mark 2:5-7). His critics rightly said only God can do that. He made all things (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). He holds all things together (Colossians 1:17). He will raise the dead and sit as judge of every nation (John 5:21-22; Matthew 25:31-32). A creature cannot do any of these things.

Worship settles the matter most plainly. In Scripture, worship belongs to God alone. Angels and apostles refuse it when people offer it to them (Acts 10:25-26; Revelation 22:8-9). Yet Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). Notice the words "just as": not less than the Father, but the same honor. In Revelation 5, every creature in heaven and on earth gives the Lamb the same praise and glory it gives to the one on the throne. The first Christians prayed to Jesus, called on his name, and trusted him with their eternal souls. You may rightly respect and imitate a godly person. You may never put your ultimate trust in a creature. Christ is the one in whom we are called to trust completely.

The New Testament also joins Christ's name with the Father's in its most solemn moments. Believers are baptized "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). The word is "name", singular. Paul's letters open with grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, as one source of blessing. He ends 2 Corinthians by asking for the grace of Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit for his readers. Imagine putting the name of a mere man, even a great apostle, alongside God's name in a blessing like that. It would blur the infinite gap between Creator and creature. The apostles would never have done it unless they knew the Son shares the Godhead.

Jesus speaks of this oneness himself. "I and the Father are one," he says (John 10:30). His hearers understood him to be claiming to be God, and they picked up stones. He also says, "Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine" (John 16:15). Sincere Christians read that verse in two ways. Some take it mainly to mean that everything belonging to God's nature, such as power, eternity and glory, belongs equally to the Son. Others take it to mean the blessings of salvation that the Father planned and the Son won, which the Spirit now gives to believers. Either way, the Son owns what the Father has, without lack, and the Spirit takes from it to give to us.

Some people object that the Bible also uses lofty language for believers. Christians are called children of God. They will "share in the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4). They can be "filled with all the fullness of God" (Ephesians 3:19). Jesus even quotes a psalm that calls human judges "gods" (John 10:34). Does this mean the high words about Jesus are no stronger than the words about us?

They are much stronger. Most of what is said about Christ is never said of believers at all. No believer is called the Creator, the eternal Word, or the one who searches all hearts. No believer is to be worshiped. And where similar words are used, there is a vast difference. Our privileges are given to us, and they come from Christ. They are also limited by the fact that we are creatures. His glory is his own, and it has no beginning. We are made children of God by adoption. He is the Son by nature. Our high calling is the fruit of his coming down to us, not proof that he is only one of us.

What about passages that seem to place Jesus below the Father? Jesus sits "at the right hand" of God (Hebrews 1:3). In the Bible, the right hand is the place of equal honor and shared rule, not a lower seat. God does not have a physical body with a left and a right side. It is picture language for sharing the throne. When Jesus says, "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), he is speaking as the one who took on human nature and came as the Father's servant to save us. Paul explains that the Son, "existing in the form of God", humbled himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death (Philippians 2:6-8). As a man and as our Savior, he gladly placed himself under the Father. As God, he is equal with the Father. Both are true of the one Lord Jesus.

The same truth helps with Jesus' cry from the cross: "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46). This does not mean the Son stopped being God. It does not mean the Trinity was torn apart, or that a divine power left a mere man behind. Jesus is one person, truly God and truly man, and he really suffered and died in his human nature. He was quoting Psalm 22, which begins in anguish but ends in victory and praise. His cry showed that his suffering and death were real, and that he truly bore the weight of our sin. Christians describe the depth of that moment in different ways. Some stress that he experienced the Father's judgment against sin in our place. Others stress that the Father's love for the Son never broke, even then. Both agree that he was not abandoned in the sense of being defeated. The earth shook, the temple curtain tore, and a Roman soldier confessed, "Truly this was the Son of God" (Matthew 27:54). Three days later the Father raised him and seated him in glory.

Why does all this matter for an ordinary believer? Only God can save. If Jesus were less than God, his death could not carry the weight of the world's sin. His word could not be fully trusted, and our worship of him would be idolatry. Because he is true God, we meet God himself when we meet Jesus. As he told Philip, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). We can worship him without fear of honoring him too highly. And we can rest our whole lives on him, because the one who loved us and gave himself for us is the Lord of all.

topics.title: Is the Son God by nature and of one substance with the Father, rather than by title, adoption or promotion?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son is God by nature and of one substance with the Father, not by participation, grace, adoption or mere unity of will, and all who address Romans 9:5 (Hippolytus, Hilary, Irenaeus, Owen, Bickersteth) read it as calling Christ God over all. They argue in different ways: Athanasius and Hilary work mainly from Scripture, with Athanasius pointing to the Son's giving of the Spirit and his possession of all the Father has, and Hilary insisting that true birth transmits the begetter's whole nature and that the unity is natural, not one of will, a point he even supports from the sacrament; Gregory of Nyssa argues more philosophically against Eunomius, from goodness as a property of nature, from the infinite admitting no more or less, from like operations to like nature, and from the analogy of a seal; Augustine relies on the distinction between relation and substance and between the form of God and the form of a servant, together with the image of light from light; Novatian and Edwards reason, respectively, from Christ being both Son of man and Son of God and from the Son as God's perfect idea of himself. Daniel Waterland argues chiefly from the Fathers against Clarke, claiming that the ante-Nicene writers held consubstantiality, that unity of principle and sameness of nature are jointly required, and that no middle ground exists between God and creature. They differ on how the Son's derivation relates to equality: Hilary and Waterland accept that generation gives the Son a secondary place as to origin while denying any inferiority of nature, whereas Warfield treats the Nicene language of generation as a leftover of subordinationist Logos-Christology that the principle of equality must push aside. They also apply Baruch 3:35-37 differently: Hilary takes 'This is our God' as Christ himself seen on earth, while Hippolytus applies it to the Father and identifies the Son with the 'Jacob' and 'Israel' who received knowledge from him and appeared among men.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Unity of principle and sameness of nature together might make two Persons one God, (according to the unanimous opinion of the ancients,) but not either of them alone.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For the creatures are hallowed by the Holy Spirit; but the Son, in that He is not hallowed by the Spirit, but on the contrary Himself the Giver of it to all, is therefore no creature, but true Son of the Father.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: that in the case of the Life-giving Power good does not reside in It essentially, but is imparted to it only, it will become impossible to call it properly good

ans.text:
Yes. The Son is God in exactly the same way the Father is God. He is not God by courtesy, by adoption, or by promotion. He shares the one divine nature with the Father, completely and from all eternity.

The Bible makes this clear. John opens his Gospel with these words: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The Word is "with God," so he is distinct from the Father. Yet he "was God," and already was in the beginning. Nothing here suggests he became God later or was given the title as an honor. Paul says the same when he speaks of Christ's human descent from Israel's patriarchs and then calls him the one "who is God over all, forever worthy of praise" (Romans 9:5). Hebrews calls the Son "the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3), and Colossians says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). That is not a partial or borrowed divinity. It is all of it.

When Christians say the Son is "of one substance" or "of one essence" with the Father, they mean the Son is what the Father is. "Essence" or "substance" simply means the basic reality of a thing, what makes it the kind of thing it is. The Son is not just similar to God, as a good copy resembles the original. He is the same God. This does not mean God is split in half, like a pie cut into slices. The whole divine nature belongs to the Father, and the whole divine nature belongs to the Son. There is still only one God.

The Bible's own word for the Son points the same way. He is the Father's Son, "the One and Only from the Father" (John 1:14). Christians often say the Son is "begotten," an old word that means born of or fathered by, as opposed to made. Think about how birth works. A dog has puppies, not kittens. Parents pass on their own nature to their children. Something you make, like a house or a table, can be quite different from you. Something born of you shares your nature. So when Scripture insists that Jesus is truly God's Son, and not merely God's handiwork, it is telling us that he has God's own nature. Of course his birth from the Father is not like ours. It did not happen at some moment in time, and it involves no body and no change in God. The Son has always been the Father's Son. But the comparison holds on the key point. Birth does not produce something of a lesser kind.

Some have suggested that Jesus was an ordinary man, or a high created being, whom God adopted as his Son. Perhaps this happened at his baptism, when the Spirit came on him. Or perhaps God raised him to divine rank after his resurrection and gave him all authority. But the New Testament tells the story the other way round. Paul says that Christ, "existing in the form of God," humbled himself, took the nature of a servant, and died on a cross (Philippians 2:6–8). Only after that did God exalt him. His exaltation changed his situation, from humiliation to glory. It did not change what he is. His poverty and death did not make him less than God, and his rising and reigning did not make him more. And in any case, a creature cannot be turned into God. God is uncreated and has no beginning. Anything that began to exist cannot become something that never began. The Word was God "in the beginning," before any exaltation took place.

Others have said that the Father and the Son are one only in purpose, the way a believer can be one with God through love and obedience. Jesus does pray that his followers would be one "as We are one" (John 17:22). But our unity is a reflection of his. It is not the same thing. We become one with God by grace, and through Christ. The Son is one with the Father by nature. That is why, when Jesus said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), his hearers picked up stones. They understood that he was claiming to be God, not just claiming to agree with God. Earlier they had wanted to kill him because he was "making Himself equal with God" (John 5:18). And when he said, "before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58), he took on his lips the very name God gave himself at the burning bush.

There is a simple reason why a borrowed divinity will not do. Picture an iron bar in a fire. It glows and gives off heat, but it is still iron. Take it out and it cools down. If the Son were good, wise, or holy only because he received these things from outside himself, he would be like that bar. In himself he would be something less than God, and he could in principle lose what he had. But Scripture presents the Son as the source of life, light and grace, the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3–4). No one can give what he does not have. The Son gives divine life because divine life is his own.

Some people meet the Old Testament figure called "the Angel of the LORD" and conclude that the Son was a heavenly messenger, not God. Many Christians have seen in this figure an appearance of the Son before he became man. But notice what happens at the burning bush. The angel appears in the flames, and then the one who speaks from the bush says, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:2–6). "Angel" means messenger, someone sent. It describes a task, not a kind of being. The Son can be sent by the Father and still be God by nature.

A last objection runs like this. If the Father and the Son share exactly the same nature, then either there are two independent Gods, each with no source, or else God somehow fathers himself. Neither follows. The Father is the source and the Son is from the Father. That difference is real, and it is exactly what the names Father and Son express. But having a source does not mean having a lesser nature. Think of the first man and his son. One was formed directly by God and the other was born of a father, yet both were fully and equally human. Where someone comes from does not change what he is. In the same way, the Son is from the Father but is no less God. And no one is his own father. The Father begets and the Son is begotten. They are two distinct persons with one divine nature.

This is why Christians have always worshiped Jesus, and not simply admired him. If he were God only in name, worshiping him would be idolatry. Because he truly is God, of one being with the Father, we can trust that when we see him, we see the Father (John 14:9). And when he saves us, it is God himself who has come to save.

topics.title: Is the Son a creature or the uncreated God?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son is not a creature but true, uncreated God sharing the divine nature. Athanasius, who answers most of the questions, argues chiefly from the structure of the faith and from Scripture: an originated Son would make the Triad alien to itself and produce two Gods and two faiths. He also points out that the Son judges rather than being judged, that the Song of the Three Children omits the Word from the works that praise, and that Hebrews sets the Son above the angels. Hilary of Poitiers grounds the point in Peter's revealed confession and in exegesis (Bethel, Romans 8), and Ambrose and John Owen argue from what only God can do, namely giving life and bearing the sins of the elect. Bickersteth, by contrast, simply sets Scripture's divine titles beside the same titles given to Christ. Gregory of Nyssa leans more on philosophical distinctions (uncreated versus created being, compound versus common essence, the incomparability every creature has) to rebut Eunomius, while agreeing with Athanasius on reading Psalm 102. Augustine and Irenaeus speak less to the creature question directly: Augustine reads 'God of God' as teaching co-eternity and explains the fittingness of the Son's death against demonic pride, and Irenaeus calls the Son the 'measure' in whom the unmeasurable Father is comprehended and made known.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: the Triad is not originated; but there is an eternal and one Godhead in a Triad, and there is one Glory of the Holy Triad. And you presume to divide it into different natures

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: even the knowledge that we must not imagine a false Christ, a creature made out of nothing, but must confess Him the Son of God, truly possessed of the Divine nature.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: King of kings, and Lord of lords. – Rev. 19:16. His dominion is an everlasting dominion ... and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed. – Dan. 7:14.

ans.text:
The Son is not a creature. He is the uncreated God, who has always existed with the Father and who made everything else that exists. The Bible draws one basic line through all of reality: on one side stands God the Creator, and on the other side stands everything he has made. The Son stands on God's side of that line.

Start with how John opens his Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). John does not say the Word came to be in the beginning. He says the Word already was. Two verses later he adds, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Think about that carefully. If the Son were himself a made thing, he would have had to make himself, which is impossible. John puts every created thing on one side and the Word on the other, as the one through whom they came to be. Paul says the same: "in Him all things were created" and "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16-17).

The letter to the Hebrews makes the point in a striking way. It takes Psalm 102, a psalm about the Lord who made heaven and earth, and says it is spoken of the Son. The heavens and the earth, the psalm says, will wear out like old clothes: "They will perish, but You remain... You remain the same, and Your years will never end" (Hebrews 1:10-12). That psalm sets the unchanging God apart from all changing creatures. Hebrews puts the Son on the unchanging side. That is why the same letter can say, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Hebrews 13:8). Creatures have a beginning, they grow, and they can change for better or worse. The Son does not. He has no beginning to his being.

Look too at what the Son does. Jesus says that "just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes" (John 5:21). Giving life is God's own work. A creature can receive life, but it cannot be the source of life. Jesus goes on to say that the Father has given all judgment to the Son, "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:22-23). Only God judges every human heart, and only God may be honored as God is honored. The Bible fiercely forbids worshiping any creature (Romans 1:25). Yet the Son receives the same honor as the Father. Either Scripture contradicts itself, or the Son is truly God.

Some people try to split the difference. They say the Son is the highest and first of all creatures, a kind of lesser god, made before the world and then used to make the rest. But this does not hold together. It would leave us with two Gods: one who is uncreated and one who was made. It would also mean worshiping a creature alongside the Creator. The Bible knows only one God. Calling someone God while also saying he once did not exist is a contradiction. A "created god" is not God at all.
