It also matters for our salvation. Hebrews 1 shows that the Son is greater than the angels. That is because the work he came to do could not be done by any created being, however holy. To bear the sins of the world, to defeat death, and to bring us back to God, the Savior had to be God himself, who took on our flesh. A mere creature would have been crushed under that weight. And a creature who needed God's gift of life could never give that life to us. If the Son were a creature, he would share our need, not meet it.

When Peter confessed, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," Jesus said that "flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but My Father in heaven" (Matthew 16:16-17). Peter had heard Jesus call God his Father many times, so the title itself was not news. What the Father opened Peter's eyes to was who Jesus truly is: the Son who shares the Father's own divine life.

A few phrases can sound as if the Son was made, so it helps to explain them. Scripture and the creeds call the Son "begotten" of the Father. To beget means to bring forth someone of the same kind as yourself, not to manufacture something different. A man begets a son, who is human like him. He builds a house, which is not. So the Son is God from God, sharing the Father's very nature, and he is not a product the Father built. And this begetting is eternal. There was never a time when the Father was without his Son, just as there is no sun without its light. When Paul calls Christ "the firstborn over all creation" (Colossians 1:15), he means rank and inheritance, as the firstborn was the heir. He does not mean Christ was the first thing made. The very next verse says all things were created in him.

The New Testament also says the Son became a man, grew, learned, and died. That is all true. But it describes the human nature he took on for our sake, not a change in his divine nature. He stayed what he always was, and he became what he was not, so that we might share in his life.

So Christians worship the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit as the one true God. We do not honor a great creature, but the eternal Lord who made us, who came to save us, and who will judge the world.

topics.title: Do the divine works, attributes and honours Scripture gives the Son prove that he is God?
topics.cmp:
All the authors answer yes: the works, attributes and honours Scripture gives the Son show that he is God. None of them dissents. They differ mainly in the kind of argument they use and in the opponent they face.

Novatian, Augustine and Hilary argue that only God can do certain things, so the one who does them is God. For Novatian these are creating the heavenly powers, granting eternal life and giving to the Paraclete. For Augustine it is giving the Spirit. For Hilary it is calming the sea and foreknowing the betrayal, from which he infers the Son's nature by birth. Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa and Basil instead reason from the Son's unity with the Father's Lordship, glory, throne and goodness. Gregory, for example, argues that the same glory means the same nature, and that denying the Son is good amounts to calling him evil. Irenaeus has a different aim: he uses Christ's fulfilment of the Old Testament and his quoting of it to show that Christ's Father is the God of the law and the prophets.

Among the later writers, Bickersteth builds a systematic case from Scripture. He sets texts that reserve to Jehovah alone the searching of hearts, forgiveness, vengeance, worship and ultimate trust beside texts that ascribe the same to Christ. From this he presses a dilemma on the Unitarians: either they trust a creature, which is idolatry, or they refuse the only Saviour. Waterland reaches the same conclusion through philosophical rebuttal of Arian distinctions. He denies that there is a 'limited infinity' or a finite exercise of omniscience, and he insists the Son is properly Creator. Owen chiefly refutes Socinian incoherence and dwells devotionally on the eternity and unchangeableness of Christ's love.

A few points of difference in nuance and confidence stand out. Ambrose refers 'that rock was Christ' to Christ's flesh rather than his Godhead. Bickersteth adds that the arguments alone cannot win heartfelt assent without the Holy Spirit. His two answers on ultimate trust are also recorded with opposite opening words, 'yes' and 'no', although both argue the same conclusion, that the trust given to Christ implies his deity.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: learn that these are the true works of Him Who sojourned for thee in the flesh,

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: but He is Lord of all, because He is one with the Father’s Lordship; and the creation is all in bondage, since it is external to the Oneness of the Father

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Had he not been what they took him for, he should have rejected that worship, as the angel in the Revelations rejected the worship which St. John would have offered him.

ans.text:
Yes. When the Bible gives Jesus the works only God can do, the qualities only God has, and the honour only God may receive, it is telling us plainly that the Son is God. These are not loose compliments. The Old Testament draws a hard line between the Creator and everything he made, and the New Testament keeps putting Jesus on the Creator's side of that line.

Start with that line. Scripture says again and again that human beings are like grass: here today, gone tomorrow, limited in knowledge and power, and often untrustworthy. God alone is eternal, all-knowing and almighty. So the prophets warn us not to put our final hope in princes or in any mere human being, but in the Lord alone (Psalm 146:3-5; Jeremiah 17:5-7). God also says he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). Keep that in mind as we look at what is said about Jesus.

First, creation. Isaiah says the Lord alone stretched out the heavens. Yet John says of the Word, who became flesh in Jesus, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Paul adds that in him all things were created, "things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities" (Colossians 1:16). Think about what that means. If the Son made everything that was ever made, he cannot himself be one of the made things. And if he made even the angels, who existed long before any human being, he is far more than a great man or a high angel. The one who builds the house is greater than the house.

Some people say the Father did the real creating and simply used the Son, like a carpenter uses a hammer. But a hammer does not plan, choose or give life. John calls the Son the Word, and God's Word is not like our words, which do nothing until our hands get to work. God's Word is living and powerful. When the Father creates "through" the Son, it is the one God acting, with the Son sharing fully in the work.

Second, upholding. Creation did not just happen once and then run by itself. It needs to be held in being every moment. Scripture says the Son is "upholding all things by His powerful word" (Hebrews 1:3), and that "in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). No creature could carry the whole universe. Every creature is itself being carried.

Third, his qualities. God is everywhere. Jesus promises, "where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them" (Matthew 18:20), and "I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (Matthew 28:20). He promises to be present with all his people, in every place and every century at once. God alone knows the heart. Yet Jesus knew what was in every person (John 2:24-25). Peter could say to him, "Lord, You know all things" (John 21:17). And the risen Christ says, "I am the One who searches minds and hearts" (Revelation 2:23). God never changes. Hebrews 1:10-12 takes a psalm about the unchanging Creator, who remains while the heavens wear out like clothing, and applies it straight to the Son. So Hebrews 13:8 can say, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever." That has a warm side too. His love for his people does not rise and fall the way ours does. Whom he loves, he loves to the end (John 13:1).

Fourth, his works among us. When Jesus told a paralysed man, "your sins are forgiven," the onlookers objected, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (Mark 2:5-7). They were right about the principle. I can forgive what you did to me, but only God can forgive sin as such, because every sin is finally against him. Jesus did not correct them. Instead he healed the man to prove he had that authority. He also claims the final judgment of every human being. "The Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22). To judge the whole world fairly, you must see every heart and weigh every deed in history. In the Old Testament the Lord says vengeance belongs to him alone. Yet Paul says it is the Lord Jesus who will be revealed from heaven in blazing fire to repay those who reject God (2 Thessalonians 1:7-8). He comes "in the glory of His Father" (Matthew 16:27). That is not a lesser, borrowed glory. It is the very glory that belongs to God. And Jesus gives the Holy Spirit. John the Baptist said Jesus would baptise with the Holy Spirit (John 1:33). Jesus himself promised to send the Spirit from the Father (John 15:26). A creature can receive God's Spirit. Only God can pour him out.

Fifth, trust and worship. This may be the clearest test of all. Jesus says, "You believe in God; believe in Me as well" (John 14:1). He asks for the same faith we owe to God. Try a simple experiment. Take the passages that call us to trust Christ for our salvation, to rejoice in him, to give him glory forever. Put in the name of Moses, or the archangel Michael, or the martyr Stephen. It sounds wrong at once. In fact it would be idolatry, putting our ultimate confidence in someone who is not God. Yet with Jesus, Scripture commands it.

The same is true of worship. When the apostle John fell down before an angel, the angel stopped him and said, in effect, "Don't! I am a fellow servant. Worship God" (Revelation 22:8-9). Peter refused worship from Cornelius in the same way (Acts 10:25-26). But Jesus accepted worship. When Thomas said to him, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28), Jesus did not rebuke him. Hebrews says, "Let all God's angels worship Him" (Hebrews 1:6). In Revelation 5 all creation gives blessing and honour to the Lamb along with the One on the throne. Jesus himself says the Father wants "all [to] honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). Not almost as much, but just as.

The Father adds his own witness. At Jesus' baptism, and again on the mountain of the Transfiguration, a voice from heaven said, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!" (Matthew 17:5). Notice the words. "This" points to the very person standing there. "My Son" means truly his Son, not a son in some loose sense. "Listen to Him" tells us to trust what Jesus says about himself. Jesus also pointed to his own works as evidence. He said they were meant to show "that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father" (John 10:38). Just before that he had said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). The works, the voice from heaven and Jesus' own words all agree.

A few questions often come up here. Couldn't God simply hand these powers over to a very great creature? Some things God does share with his servants. Prophets worked miracles, and apostles announced forgiveness in his name. But they always did so as servants, pointing away from themselves. Jesus acts in his own name and with his own authority: "But I say to you." And some things cannot be handed over at all. A creature cannot create everything, be everywhere, hold up the universe, or rightly receive worship. To give a creature what belongs only to God would break God's own word that he will not share his glory.

Doesn't this mean there are two Gods? No. The Bible is firm that there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). The point is that the Son shares the one being of God with the Father. That is why the same works, qualities and honours belong to both. The Father and the Son are not two Gods competing for glory. They are the one God, eternally Father and Son.

What about the times Jesus seems limited? He grew tired, prayed, and said even the Son did not know the day or hour (Mark 13:32). The church has always read these passages in light of the incarnation. The eternal Son truly became man and freely took on human limits for our sake. When the Gospels show him hungry, weak or not knowing, they show him in his real humanity. When they show him forgiving sins, stilling storms and receiving worship, they show him as God. Both are true of the one Lord Jesus.

So the evidence is not a single proof text but a whole pattern. Scripture gathers around Jesus everything that marks out the one true God, and it calls us to trust him, love him and worship him without reserve. That is exactly what Christians do when they confess that the Son is "true God from true God."

topics.title: Do Christ's miracles and power over death prove his divinity?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the question agree that Christ's works point to his divinity. Novatian argues most directly and syllogistically: immortality is the fruit of divinity, faith in a mere man is accursed, and raising one's own body is beyond any man. He also reads Isaiah 35's signs of God's coming as fulfilled in Christ. Bickersteth uses a similar Scripture-matching method, setting the Psalm's 'the Lord makes the storm a calm' beside Jesus rebuking the sea. On John 10:18, Athanasius, Hilary, Augustine and Novatian all take the power to lay down and take up his life as proper to God, not to men who die by necessity. Hilary is distinctive in insisting that it is the one God-man who does this, that God the Word did not die, and that the glory is referred to the Father's command. Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa differ slightly on John 2:19: Augustine reads the 'temple' as Christ's body, appealing to the evangelist's gloss and the sign of Jonah, while Gregory takes it as the union of soul and body broken in death. Not every author treats miracles as sufficient proof on their own. Hilary says heretics confess all the miracles and still perish without confessing the Son's generation. Augustine explains that magicians also work wonders, through fallen angels by God's permission, as with Pharaoh's magicians who failed at the lice. Irenaeus defends the reality of the miracles against the Carpocratian claim of mere appearance, grounding this in prophecy and in the disciples' continuing real miracles, and Bickersteth answers that believers' 'greater works' are done only through faith in Christ.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
refs.quote: For every man is mortal; and immortality cannot be from that which is mortal. Therefore from Christ, as a mortal man, immortality cannot arise.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For man dies, not by his own power, but by necessity of nature and against his will; but the Lord, being Himself immortal, but having a mortal flesh, had power, as God, to become separate from the body and to take it again

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: By the power to take His soul again and to raise the Temple up, He declares Himself God, and the Resurrection His own work: yet He refers all to the authority of His Father’s command.

ans.text:
Yes, but not simply because they were amazing. What sets Jesus' miracles apart is how he did them and what they claimed. Above all, he holds power over his own death, something no mere creature could ever have.

Start with the miracles themselves. Other people in the Bible did wonders. Moses parted the sea, Elijah raised a widow's son, and the apostles healed the sick. So a miracle on its own does not make someone God. Look at the difference, though. Moses stretched out his staff at God's command. Elijah prayed and waited. Peter told the crowd not to stare at him as if he had healed a lame man by his own power, but to see that it was done in the name of Jesus (Acts 3:12-16). Jesus never acts that way. He does not pray, "Lord, heal this man." He simply says, "I say to you, get up." He forgives sins on his own authority and proves it by healing (Mark 2:5-12). The servants point away from themselves to God. Jesus speaks as the one in charge.

Scripture also ties certain works to God alone, and Jesus does those very works. The Psalms praise the Lord as the one who calms the storm and hushes the waves (Psalm 107:29). In Mark 4 Jesus stands up in the boat, rebukes the wind, and tells the sea to be still, and there is a great calm. The frightened disciples ask, "Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?" The Old Testament has already answered that question. In the same way, Isaiah 35 promises that when "your God will come," the blind will see, the deaf will hear, the lame will leap, and the mute will shout for joy. When John the Baptist asked whether Jesus was the one, Jesus pointed to exactly these signs (Matthew 11:4-5). He was saying, in effect, that the coming Isaiah promised is happening now, in me.

The clearest sign is his power over death. Every human being dies because we must. Death comes for us whether we want it or not. Jesus says something no one else could say: "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again" (John 10:18). Earlier he told his enemies, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again." John explains that he meant the temple of his body (John 2:19-21). A dead man cannot raise himself. That Jesus could promise to do it, and then did, shows that the one who died was more than a man.

He also gives life to others. "I am the resurrection and the life," he says in John 11:25. In John 8:51 he says that whoever keeps his word will never see death. Think about what that means. A mortal man cannot hand out immortality any more than an empty cup can fill another. Only someone who has life in himself can give it away. The Bible also warns against putting our final trust in mere human beings (Jeremiah 17:5). Yet Jesus calls us to trust him for eternal life. That would be dangerous advice if he were only a man. It is good news because he is God the Son.

This raises a fair question. Does this mean God died? Not in the sense that God's divine nature stopped living. God cannot die. Jesus is one person who is both truly God and truly man. When he died, it was a real human death: his human soul and body were separated. But the one who died is the eternal Son, who took a human body and soul precisely so he could die for us. And as God he raised that body again. So we can rightly say "the Son of God died for me," while understanding that he died in his human nature, not in his divinity. Notice too that Jesus adds, "This charge I have received from My Father." The Bible also says the Father raised him and the Spirit gave him life (Acts 2:24; Romans 8:11). This is not a contradiction. Father, Son and Spirit act together as the one God. The Son does not act apart from the Father but in perfect union with him.

What about magicians and false wonders? Pharaoh's magicians copied some of Moses' signs. Jesus himself warned that false messiahs would perform great signs to deceive (Matthew 24:24). So how do true miracles differ? First, any power evil spirits have is borrowed and limited. God permits it and can stop it at will. When Pharaoh's magicians could not produce even gnats, they had to admit, "This is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:19). Second, Scripture tests a wonder by where it leads. A sign that draws people away from the true God is false, however impressive (Deuteronomy 13:1-3). Jesus' works always lead to the Father, show his goodness, and fulfill what the prophets foretold. Third, his miracles were not illusions or tricks. They really happened, in public, before friends and enemies, and the empty tomb could not be explained away. No deceiver has ever conquered death.

Jesus told his followers they would do "greater works" than his (John 14:12). Does that weaken the case? No. In the same breath he says these works come to "whoever believes in Me" and happen because he is going to the Father. Their power flows from him. A river may water more fields than its source, but it is still the spring that gives the water.

One caution is worth adding. Being impressed by Jesus' miracles is not the same as faith. Crowds enjoyed the bread and then walked away, and even demons knew who he was. The miracles are signs, like road signs pointing beyond themselves. John says he wrote them down "so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God" (John 20:31). The goal is not just to admire what Jesus did, but to confess who he is. He is the eternal Son, equal with the Father, who laid down his life for us and took it up again.

topics.title: Do the titles 'God' and 'Lord' and particular texts in Scripture prove Christ is the supreme God?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Scripture's titles 'God' and 'Lord' mark Christ as truly God by nature, not by an honorary or nominal title like the one given to Moses, idols or men. Their grounds differ. Waterland reasons logically and philologically: every nominal god is excluded, so Christ must be the one Supreme God, and he appeals to the arthrous ὁ Θεός and to Ante-Nicene usage. Bickersteth relies on word statistics for Kyrios, Greek article construction and the apostle's inspired interpretation of Old Testament texts. Gregory of Nyssa argues that God, being truthful, never gives names that do not match a thing's nature, though he allows that titles like Shepherd and Physician are relative to creatures; Hilary stresses that the qualified grants to Moses ('to Pharaoh', 'I have said') differ in kind from the unqualified 'was God' of John 1:1. Novatian, by contrast, puts the Moses contrast in terms of degree, so that if Moses gains the name in limited measure, Christ gains it far more, and Hippolytus likewise speaks of Christ as 'appointed' Almighty by the Father, whereas Waterland stresses coessentiality and Hilary refers Christ's having a God to his birth from the Virgin (Waterland follows this but also allows a reading in terms of the Son's subordination as begotten). Real differences also appear in method and exegesis: Owen holds that each proof text suffices on its own and freely cites Acts 20:28, as Gregory of Nyssa cites 1 Timothy 3:16, while Bickersteth deliberately sets these textually disputed passages aside and rests on the cumulative weight of many texts; and on Romans 1:20 Athanasius refers both 'power' and 'Godhead' to the Son, while Ambrose assigns 'eternal power' to the Son and 'Godhead' to the Holy Spirit.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: But since all are excluded, as hath been before shewn, except the one Supreme God, it is very manifest, that he is the same with the one Supreme God. Not the same Person with the Father, as you groundlessly object to us, but another Person in the same Godhead

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: To reject Him is to neglect the glory of the only God; is not, then, His glory the glory of the only God, if to receive Him steadfastly was to seek the glory of the only God?

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For the Lord did not then fashion Himself to be God, nor indeed is a made God conceivable, but He manifested it by the works

ans.text:
Yes. The New Testament calls Jesus 'God' and 'Lord' in the full sense: not as a courtesy title, but as a statement of who he is. He is the one true God, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The case does not hang on one or two verses. It rests on many passages that all point the same way.

Start with the plainest texts. John opens his Gospel this way: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). Near the end of the same Gospel, Thomas sees the risen Jesus and cries out, 'My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28). John has framed his whole book between these two sentences. Then Hebrews 1 applies a psalm to the Son. God says to him, 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever' (Hebrews 1:8). A few verses later it applies another psalm to him, one that praises the Lord for laying the foundations of the earth and outlasting the heavens. Paul speaks of 'the glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ' (Titus 2:13). He also describes Christ as 'God over all, forever worthy of praise' (Romans 9:5). And John ends his first letter by saying of God's Son Jesus Christ, 'He is the true God and eternal life' (1 John 5:20). At the start of that letter, John had already called Jesus 'the eternal life' that was with the Father (1 John 1:2).

Someone may object that the Bible sometimes calls humans 'gods.' God made Moses like God to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1). A psalm addresses rulers with 'I have said, You are gods' (Psalm 82:6). Doesn't that make the title cheap? Look at how those cases are worded. Moses is 'like God' only 'to Pharaoh.' He stood in God's place as God's spokesman before one king, for a time. He was never worshiped and never called Lord of all. The rulers in the psalm are called gods because they judged on God's behalf. The very next verse says they will die like men. In each case the title is limited, borrowed, and handed out by someone else.

Nothing like that is said of the Son. The Word did not become God at some point. He 'was God' in the beginning. He is not God to one person, but God over all. He is not a judge who will die like men. His throne lasts forever, and he made the world. The God of truth does not hand out grand names that mean nothing. He calls things what they are.

The word 'Lord' works the same way. In everyday Greek it could simply mean 'sir' or 'master.' A few New Testament verses use it like that. But the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which the apostles used, put this same word in place of God's own holy name. That name appears in English Bibles as 'the LORD.' The apostles then took Old Testament verses about the LORD and applied them directly to Jesus. Joel promises that whoever calls on the name of the LORD will be saved. Paul quotes that promise about Jesus: 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' (Romans 10:13). In Isaiah 45, God swears that every knee will bow to him alone. Paul says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus and confess that he is Lord (Philippians 2:10-11). So when Christians confess 'Jesus is Lord,' they are giving him the name that belongs to God alone.

What Jesus accepted matters just as much. Faithful servants of God refuse worship. Peter stopped Cornelius from bowing to him (Acts 10:25-26). An angel told John not to worship him (Revelation 22:8-9). Jesus did the opposite with Thomas. He received the confession 'my God' and called it believing. Scripture even commands, 'Let all God's angels worship Him' (Hebrews 1:6). Jesus said that all should 'honor the Son just as they honor the Father' (John 5:23). The Bible forbids worshiping anyone but the one true God. So if the Son may rightly be worshiped, he cannot be a lesser, honorary god. He must be that one God.

At the same time, this does not mean there are two Gods, or that the Son is the Father under another name. Notice that John 1:1 says both things together: the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The Son is a distinct person from the Father. Yet he shares fully in the one being, or nature, of God. 'Essence' means just that: what God is. So when Jesus speaks of seeking the glory that comes from the only God (John 5:44), he is not shutting himself out. Rejecting him is exactly how his hearers were failing to seek that glory.

Honesty requires admitting that some of these verses are debated. Sincere Bible readers argue over grammar or punctuation. Does Titus 2:13 mean 'our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,' or 'the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ'? Should Romans 9:5 end with a separate blessing of God the Father? Does 'He' in 1 John 5:20 point to the Son or to the Father? Ancient copies also differ in a few places, such as 1 Timothy 3:16 and Acts 20:28. Many careful scholars still think the readings that call Christ God are the most natural. Christians can weigh such questions calmly, because the teaching does not depend on any one of them.

The evidence is less like a chain, which breaks at its weakest link, and more like a rope woven from many strands. Jesus is given God's names. He does God's works: creating, sustaining all things, forgiving sins, raising the dead, and judging the world. He has God's qualities, such as being eternal. He receives the worship that belongs only to God. His name is joined with the Father's in blessing and in baptism. Set aside any single verse you are unsure of, and the conclusion still stands firm. Jesus Christ is not an honorary god. He is, as Thomas said, our Lord and our God.

topics.title: How does Christ's unique Sonship differ from the adoptive sonship of believers?
topics.cmp: Athanasius, Hilary, and Bickersteth agree that Christ's Sonship is natural and unique while believers' sonship is adoptive, and none allows believers equality with the Only-begotten. They argue it differently. Athanasius reasons philosophically from nature: a natural son is offspring of the parent's essence and one with him, whereas men are first creatures and only afterward sons by grace, receiving the Spirit of the Son, and so can lose that grace. He adds Scripture (Psalm 86:16, John's 'become' children) and the analogy of Aaron putting on priestly garments. Hilary makes a parallel case that adoptive sonship is imputed rather than real, but places more weight on Peter's confession as the revealed faith on which the Church is founded, and treats Christ's brotherhood with us as belonging only to his humanity as Mediator. Bickersteth argues exegetically that shared phrasing in Scripture (John 15:9, 'all things are possible') proves no equality. Owen differs in emphasis: rather than guarding the distinction, he dwells on the privileges believers share with Christ through adoption (his name, co-heirship, likeness, sufferings, kingdom) and on their loving obedience, while Irenaeus uses Peter's confession for a different point, that the suffering Son of man is the same as Christ the Son of God.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: But in truth neither we are Word or Wisdom, nor is He creature or work; else why are we all sprung from one, and He the Only Word?

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: In the mystery of the Mediatorship let Him be at once very man and very God, Himself God of God, but having a common Father and God with us in that community by which He is our brother.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: He is urging his disciples as defectible beings, by the plea of the infinite fullness of his love towards them, infinite so far as regarded himself, to abide in that love from which without him they would assuredly fall

ans.text:
Jesus is God's Son by nature, forever, while we become God's children by grace, through adoption. The word "son" is shared, but the reality behind it is very different. He is the one and only Son who has always been the Father's own. We are creatures whom God, in love, brings into His family and calls His children.

It helps to think about how a family works. A child born to parents shares their nature from the start. He has never been anything other than their son. An adopted child is just as loved and just as truly part of the family. But there was a time before the adoption, when the child belonged to someone else and had no claim on the name. Adoption is a gift given from outside. Birth is a bond that comes from within.

Scripture uses both pictures, and it keeps them distinct. John calls Jesus "the one and only Son" (John 1:14, 18). Older translations say "only-begotten." To be begotten means to come from the Father the way a child comes from a parent, sharing the same nature, rather than being made the way a craftsman makes a chair. That is why John can say in the same breath that this Son "is Himself God" (John 1:18). The Son did not start out as something else and later get promoted. He was with God in the beginning and was God (John 1:1).

Now see how John speaks about us. To all who received Christ, "He gave the right to become children of God" (John 1:12). Notice the words "gave" and "become." We are not God's children by nature. We are first creatures, made by God. Then, by His kindness, we are brought into His family. Paul says the same thing plainly in Galatians 4:4-6. God sent His Son "that we might receive our adoption as sons." Then He sent "the Spirit of His Son into our hearts," so that we cry, "Abba, Father!" The Son was sent. We receive adoption. We share in sonship only because we are joined to the one who is Son already.

Jesus Himself kept this difference. After His resurrection He told Mary Magdalene, "I am ascending to My Father and your Father" (John 20:17). He did not say "our Father," as if He and the disciples stood in exactly the same place. God is Father to Him in one way and to us in another. His enemies understood this. In John 5:18 they wanted to kill Him because He called God His own Father, "making Himself equal with God." No ordinary believer could say "Father" in that sense.

This is why Peter's confession matters so much. When Jesus asked who He was, Peter answered, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16). Peter could have stopped at "the Christ," the promised King. That would already have been a great deal. But he went further and spoke about who Jesus is in His very being. Jesus said this did not come from flesh and blood but was revealed by His Father in heaven (Matthew 16:17). He then said He would build His church on this confession. Peter was not calling Jesus a remarkable man whom God had honored with a title. He was confessing the same truth the Father spoke from heaven: "This is My beloved Son."

Psalm 86 offers a helpful picture of where we stand. In verse 16 David prays for God to turn to him, give strength to His servant, and save "the son of Your maidservant." David speaks as one born into God's household as a servant, someone who needs mercy and rescue. Many Christians have long seen in this a picture of the difference. We are like the children of the household servants. We need strength and salvation to be given to us. The true Son has the Father's own strength as His by right. He does not need to be saved. He is the one who saves.

Some common confusions are worth clearing up. One is the idea that because Scripture calls angels, Israel, and believers "sons of God," Jesus must be a son in the same way, only greater in degree. But the same word can carry very different weight. Jesus says, "With God all things are possible," and also, "All things are possible to the one who believes." No one concludes from this that believers are all-powerful. In the same way, sharing the word "son" does not make our sonship the same as His. Hebrews makes the point directly: "To which of the angels did God ever say: You are My Son?" (Hebrews 1:5). If He were a son only in the way we are, He would be one son among many. Instead He is the only one.

Another confusion is the idea that Jesus was a good man whom God adopted as His Son, perhaps at His baptism. But the voice at the baptism did not make Jesus the Son. It announced who He already was. The Son existed before He took on flesh. He came down to us. He was not raised up from among us.

A third worry is that calling our sonship "adoption" makes it second-rate or flimsy. It does not. Our adoption is real and secure because it rests on Him. Because the Son truly became one of us, He is "not ashamed to call them brothers" (Hebrews 2:11). He is "the firstborn among many brothers" (Romans 8:29). We share His name, His inheritance, and even His sufferings, and one day we will share His glory. As a man, He stands beside us as our brother. As God, He stands above us as our Lord. No believer ever becomes equal to Him in His divine nature.

So the difference is the difference between the source and the gift. He is the Son by nature, and through Him we become sons and daughters by grace. Everything we have as God's children we have only because He is God's Son in a way we never will be. That should humble us, and it should also give us great joy. The Father's own Son has made room for us at His table.

topics.title: Do words like 'made', 'created', 'servant' or 'Saviour' imply the Son is a creature?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that creaturely or humble terms ('servant', 'made', 'created', 'became', 'Saviour', 'Physician') do not make the Son a creature, and the dominant strategy, shared by Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary, is to refer such language to the Incarnation and economy rather than to the Word's eternal essence, especially on Acts 2:36, Hebrews 1:4 and Hebrews 3:2. They differ in the arguments they lean on. Athanasius relies heavily on scriptural parallels from ordinary usage (Solomon as David's 'servant', Isaac's 'I have made him thy lord', Job's sons 'coming to be'), and he adds a distinctive alternative: that 'made' said of a true Offspring may simply mean 'begat', or 'manifested' (Acts 2:36), or 'trustworthy' rather than 'believing' (Hebrews 3:2). Gregory of Nyssa argues more from the logic of names and from close grammar: work versus son, the reductio that frogs and dogs would be 'sons', the demonstrative 'this Jesus whom ye crucified', and word order. He also answers Eunomius's charges that this reading implies 'two Christs' or a second self-emptying. He frames the 'making' as the transformation of the lowly humanity into Lord and Christ, where Athanasius treats it as the manifestation of a lordship the Word always had. Hilary dates scriptural 'creation' language to the saving dispensation. Augustine, more permissively, allows that unclear passages may safely be read under either rule. Waterland, Irenaeus, Bickersteth and Basil contribute narrower points: Waterland on the ineffable Father–Son relation and on worship, Irenaeus on how Christ is Saviour, salutary and salvation, Bickersteth on Christ as Author of salvation, and Basil on humble titles revealing power and love rather than lowering his dignity.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: it follows, surely, that He Who is truly Son is Son, and is confessed to be God by reason of His being of the very nature of Him that begat Him.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: But this enefable relation is not that of a creature to his Creator; but of a Son to a Father, of the same nature with him. This may be styled meffable: the other cannot, in any true or just sense.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: This was not the birth of the divinity, but the creating of the flesh; the new Man taking the title of the race, and being created according to God Who was born before the ages.

ans.text:
No. When the Bible uses humble words about Jesus, such as being "made" Lord, "appointed," or taking the form of a "servant," it is describing what the eternal Son became for us when he became a man. It is not describing a beginning to his existence as God.

The key to these passages is something the Bible says plainly at the start of John's Gospel. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). A few verses later we read, "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). So there are two true things to say about Jesus. He always was God. And at a point in history he became something he had not been before, a real human being. Many puzzling verses become clear once we ask which of these two the verse is talking about.

Paul puts it this way in Philippians 2:6-7. Christ was "existing in the form of God," yet he "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness." Notice the order. He was first in the form of God. Then he took on the form of a servant. The servant language does not tell us he was a creature from the start. It tells us how low the Creator was willing to stoop. A king who puts on work clothes and serves his people is still the king.

Take Acts 2:36, where Peter says, "God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ!" Look closely at what Peter is talking about. He speaks of "this Jesus," using his human name. He speaks of the one "whom you crucified," and it was his human body that hung on the cross. Just before this, Peter has described Jesus being raised and exalted to God's right hand. The point is not that God created the Son's divine nature. The point is that the man the crowd rejected and killed has now been raised and openly installed as Lord and Messiah. The humble one has been lifted high.

Also notice that Peter does not say God made him exist. He says God made him Lord and Christ. Those are words about rank and authority. When David was anointed king, he did not start being a man that day. He was given a new role. In the same way, Jesus, who already was who he was, was publicly given the rule over all things as the risen Saviour of his people. As God, the Son always reigned. As a man, he now reigns over us as the one who won our redemption on the cross.

The word "made" is used this way elsewhere too. Paul says, "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf" (2 Corinthians 5:21). No Christian thinks the Son became sinful by nature. Everyone sees that this is about what happened at the cross, where he carried our sin. If "made" there refers to his saving work and not his inner being, it is fair to read Acts 2:36 the same way.

Hebrews 3:2 says Jesus was faithful to the one who appointed him. The Greek word behind "appointed" can also mean "made," so some have argued that the Son must be a made thing. But the verse is about Jesus as "the apostle and high priest of our confession" (Hebrews 3:1). Hebrews has just explained how he became our high priest. He shared in our flesh and blood and was "made like His brothers in every way" (Hebrews 2:14-17). He was appointed to that office as one of us. Some Christians also point out that the Bible uses "made" or "became" loosely, even of parents having children, so the word need not mean "created" at all. Either way, the verse does not teach that the Son's divine nature was manufactured.

Hebrews 1:4 says the Son "became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs." Again the setting matters. That same chapter says the Son made the universe and holds it up by his word (Hebrews 1:2-3). It calls him God: "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever" (Hebrews 1:8). It says that he laid the foundations of the earth (Hebrews 1:10). Angels are servants who were made. The Son is the Maker who sits on the throne. So when he "became" superior to them, it means that the one who humbled himself below them for a while, by becoming man and dying, has now been exalted far above them. That is how chapter 2 explains it.

What about the title "Saviour"? Far from making Jesus a creature, this title points the other way. In the Old Testament, God says, "I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me" (Isaiah 43:11). The New Testament gladly gives that title to Jesus and even speaks of "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" (Titus 2:13). He saves us because he is God come to rescue us. He saves us as one of us, because he truly became man.

There is a simple rule of thumb here. The Bible never says the Son was made as God, or that the Word was a creature. In fact it says the opposite: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). If he made everything that was made, he cannot be one of the things that were made. So when you meet humble words about Jesus, read them as the story of the Creator stepping down into his creation. He became a servant, was made like us, and was raised up as Lord and Christ.

This matters for our faith. If the Son were only a high creature, his humility would be no great wonder. A creature serving is simply doing its duty. But the Bible's good news is that God himself, without ceasing to be God, came down to serve and save us. The humble words do not shrink him. They show us how great his love is.

topics.title: Does Psalm 82 ('Ye are gods') show that Christ is called God only as men are?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Athanasius, Hilary and Novatian all deny that Psalm 82 reduces Christ to God only in the sense that men are called gods. Each holds that Christ is God in a way the psalm's 'gods' are not. Their grounds differ. Athanasius argues from participation: men are gods only by grace, through sharing in the Word by the Spirit, whereas Christ is the one participated in and is one in essence with the Father. Irenaeus reads the psalm in terms of adoption and the Church: God (the Son) stands among the adopted, while 'ye shall die like men' points to human weakness and to those who refuse adoption, and no son of Adam is called God absolutely as Christ is. Hilary works from Christ's own use of the verse in John's Gospel, treating it as a rebuttal of the blasphemy charge that leads to His claim, as the one sanctified and sent, to be Son by nature and birth. Novatian argues a fortiori from Psalm 82:1: if those Christ judges and rebukes are called gods, much more is the one who stands among them and overcomes the prince of wickedness.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: other beings, to whom He said, ‘I said ye are Gods,’ had this grace from the Father, only by participation of the Word, through the Spirit.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: if other men may use this name without blasphemy, there can obviously be no blasphemy in its use by the Man Whom the Father has sanctified

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.place: Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God
refs.quote: He [here] refers to the Father and the Son, and those who have received the adoption; but these are the Church.

ans.text:
No. When Jesus quoted the words "You are gods" from Psalm 82, he was not saying that he is God only in the loose way that some human beings were once called gods. He was using the psalm to show how weak his opponents' charge was, and then pointing to something far greater about himself.

Start with the psalm. Psalm 82 pictures God standing in a heavenly courtroom: "God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the gods." He rebukes these "gods" for judging unjustly and favoring the wicked, and commands them to defend the weak and the fatherless. Then he says, "I have said, 'You are gods; you are all sons of the Most High.' But like mortals you will die." Christians have understood these "gods" in slightly different ways. Many see them as human rulers and judges. Others see them as heavenly powers behind earthly rulers. But Jesus himself points to what matters. They are called gods because the word of God came to them. They were given a share of God's authority to judge on his behalf. The title was on loan. They were not gods by nature, and the psalm reminds them that they will die like anyone else.

Now look at John 10. Jesus had just said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). The crowd picked up stones, because they understood him to be claiming to be God, though he was a man. Jesus answered by quoting Psalm 82. His reasoning runs from the lesser to the greater. If Scripture, which "cannot be broken," could call mere men "gods" because God's word came to them, how can it be blasphemy for the One whom the Father set apart and sent into the world to call himself the Son of God?

Notice what Jesus does and does not say. He does not say, "Calm down, I only mean what the psalm means." He puts himself in a different class. They were people to whom the word of God came. He is the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world. That means he was with the Father before he came. John's Gospel opens by telling us who he is: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The judges in the psalm received the word. Jesus is the Word.

The crowd did not hear him as backing down, either. He went straight on to say that the Father is in him and he is in the Father, and they tried again to seize him (John 10:38-39). His answer took away the charge of blasphemy without taking back the claim.

This helps us see the difference between being called god by gift and being God by nature. The Bible does speak of God raising human beings to great dignity. Believers are adopted as God's children and cry "Abba, Father" (Romans 8:15). Peter even says we come to share in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). But in every case we are receivers. We share in God's life only because God gives it to us through his Son and by his Spirit. The Son is not one more receiver. He is the one we share in, the source of the gift. Think of the moon and the sun. The moon can shine brightly, but all its light is borrowed. The sun gives light. The Son does not borrow his godhood from the Father the way we borrow ours. He shares the Father's very being from all eternity. So Thomas could fall before the risen Jesus and say, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28), and Jesus accepted it. No judge in Psalm 82 could have rightly received that.

The psalm actually points the same way. The "gods" in it are judged, rebuked, and told they will die. Jesus is the one who gives eternal life to his sheep, so that no one can snatch them out of his hand or his Father's hand (John 10:28-29). Those who die like mortals cannot give life that never ends. Only God can.

So two mistakes should be avoided. One is to think Jesus lowered himself to the level of the psalm's "gods," as if he were only a very godly man with a high title. The other is to think that because believers are called sons of God, we will one day become gods in the same way Jesus is God. Neither is true. By grace we are brought into God's family and made like Christ. But Christ is God's eternal Son by nature, the true God who came among us so that we could share in his life.

title: The Son's Equality and Texts of Subordination
desc: Whether the Son's being sent, obeying, receiving, praying, not knowing the day, or the Father being greater make him inferior, and how order differs from inequality.

topics.title: Is the Son inferior or subordinate to the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors deny that the Son is inferior to the Father in nature, power, glory or honour. Hilary, Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, Ambrose, Augustine, Waterland, Bickersteth and Owen all rest this on John 5 (the Son does whatever the Father does, and is honoured as the Father is), on the Son's possessing all that the Father has, and on his being the perfect Image. Where they differ is in what, if anything, they let 'subordination' mean. Augustine, joined by Bickersteth, Owen and Warfield, refers the texts of inferiority (John 14:28, the sending, the prayers, 'not mine to give') chiefly to the form of a servant, the mediatorial office, or the Incarnation. Augustine insists that, apart from the assumed humanity, sending implies only that the Son is from the Father. Hilary and Athanasius, by contrast, also read 'the Father is greater' as the Father's prerogative as Begetter and Giver. Waterland makes a subordination of order or origin, with the Father as head and fountain and the Son 'God of God', the centre of his case, and he appeals heavily to the pre-Nicene Fathers to separate it from Arian inferiority of nature. Novatian similarly stresses that the Son's power is delivered by the Father and that his obedience shows the Father as the one source. On obedience there is a real divergence. Gregory of Nyssa confines it strictly to the Incarnation, says the Son created by his own sovereign authority, and calls the Father's priority one of cause only, not of time. Hilary, while calling the subjection an event of the Dispensation, speaks of the Son's eternal allegiance and of the Father as the Son's God. Warfield doubts that the New Testament gives compelling evidence of any eternal subordination in modes of subsistence, suggesting the subordination in operation may rest on a voluntary Covenant of Redemption. Beyond Scripture, Augustine argues from divine simplicity that the attributes are inseparable, so equality in one means equality in all. Gregory argues that what is generated shares the nature of its source and that sameness of attributes shows sameness of nature. Waterland relies on logical rebuttal of Clarke and appeal to the Fathers.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: But that God, the Son of God, Born of God the Father…
refs.quote: Thus making Himself obedient to His Father in all things, although He also is God, yet He shows the one God the Father by His obedience, from whom also He drew His beginning.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: He pays to the Father the tribute of obedience to the will of Him Who sent Him, but the obedience of humility does not dissolve the unity of His nature: He becomes obedient unto death, but, after death, He is above every name

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: Or because these Beings are to be thought of as of greater or less extent, the smaller included within and surrounded by the larger, like casks put one inside the other, inasmuch as he detects degrees of size within Beings that are illimitable?

ans.text:
No. The Son is not a lesser God or a lower kind of being. He shares the one nature of God fully with the Father, with the same power, the same glory, and the same right to worship. Yet the Bible does contain sayings that sound lowly, such as Jesus saying that the Father is greater than he is. Those sayings are true and important. They just do not mean what they might seem to mean at first glance.

Start with the plain claims. John opens his Gospel with "the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Paul says that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form" (Colossians 2:9). Jesus also says the Father has given judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). No creature could rightly receive the same honor as God. So whatever the lowly sayings mean, they cannot mean that the Son is less than God.

How, then, do we read the lowly sayings? Two keys open nearly all of them.

The first key is that the Son became a man. Paul writes that Christ, "existing in the form of God," did not cling to his equality with God. Instead he "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6-7). He did not stop being God. He added to himself a real human life, with a human body, a human mind, and a human will, and he lived it in humility and obedience. As a man he grew tired, prayed, wept, learned obedience, and died. In that servant's role the Father truly is greater. So when Jesus, on the night before the cross, says, "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), he speaks as the one who has come down and is about to return to the Father's glory. Notice that he says this to comfort his friends: they should rejoice that he is going home. The same Jesus who says "the Father is greater than I" also says "I and the Father are one." Both are true, because he is both truly God and truly man.

The second key is that the Son is from the Father. Even before he became a man, the Son is called "Son" because his life comes from the Father. The word "begotten" means just this. A father begets a son who shares his own nature, unlike making a statue, which is a different thing from its maker. The Son is not made. He is eternally from the Father, and so he has everything the Father has. That gives a real order within God: the Father sends, the Son is sent. The Father gives, the Son receives. But order is not the same as rank. A son is not less human than his father because he comes from his father. In the same way, the Son is not less divine because his divine life is from the Father. Some see the word "greater" in John 14:28 partly in this light. The Father is the source, the one who gives. But the gift he gives is his whole self, held back in nothing.

This helps with another saying that troubles people. Jesus says, "the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it" (John 5:19). Read on, though: "For whatever the Father does, the Son also does." Jesus said this right after his opponents accused him of "making Himself equal with God" (John 5:18). He does not back away from the claim. He strengthens it. The Son cannot act apart from the Father, because they are never apart. It is not that he lacks strength. In the same way, truth "cannot" lie. That is not weakness but perfection. And the Son does everything the Father does, which only God could say.

The Son's being "sent" works the same way. Being sent shows where the Son comes from, not that he is lower. If I send a message by my own word, my word is not less than I am. It is me reaching out. When the Father sends the Son into the world, it is God himself coming to save us.

Sincere Christians do differ on one finer point. Some believe that the Son, while fully equal in nature, also eternally and willingly defers to the Father within the life of God. They point to how often Scripture describes the Son as sent and as doing the Father's will. Others answer that God has one will, shared by Father, Son, and Spirit. On this view, the Son's obedience belongs to his mission as the incarnate Son, carried out in his human will. They also point out that eternal obedience is hard to separate from inequality. Both sides agree on what matters most: the Son is not a lesser being, and he deserves the same worship as the Father.

So the lowly sayings are not embarrassments to explain away. They are the footprints of love. The Son, equal with the Father in every way, came down to serve, to obey, and to die for us. The humility we see in Jesus does not show that he is less than God. It shows us what God is like.

topics.title: How does order among the Persons differ from inequality, and in what sense is the Father 'greater'?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius, John Owen and Ambrose all deny that the Persons differ in degree, honour or rank, and they agree that 'greater and less' cannot be taken in a material or quantitative sense. Their arguments differ. Gregory argues mainly from the infinity and perfection of the divine nature: the infinite cannot be 'less,' a 'more honourable' necessarily implies a 'less honourable,' and size would make God a compound body subject to dissolution. Athanasius and Ambrose answer specific scriptural or figurative objections by forbidding bodily readings. Athanasius appeals to the immaterial images of Light and Radiance, and Ambrose to the images of 'hand' and 'finger,' which he says show the inseparable oneness of divine power. Owen instead uses a logical point, exposing an equivocation between 'God' as nature and 'God' as person. Only Gregory says positively what order there is: a natural order in which the Persons are distinct as Persons yet united in being. None of the answers given explains directly in what sense the Father is called 'greater'; Athanasius takes the phrase only as the objectors' premise.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: cannot be regarded as in any way a ‘less,’ although this teacher of heresy attempt to curtail its infinitude by introducing the idea of degrees

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: who think God to be material, and understand not what is ‘True Father’ and ‘True Son,’ nor ‘Light Invisible’ and ‘Eternal,’ and Its ‘Radiance Invisible,’

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: The collusion of this sophism consists in that expression, “be God” and “that God.” In the first place the nature of God is intended; in the latter, a singular person.

ans.text:
Order among the Father, Son and Holy Spirit is about where each Person comes from and how they relate to one another; inequality would be about one having less of God's nature than another, and the Bible teaches order without inequality. When Jesus says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), he is not saying he is a lesser God.

Start with the order. Christians have always named the Persons in a set sequence: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, as Jesus does in Matthew 28:19. That sequence is not random. The Father is from no one. The Son is "begotten" of the Father, a Bible word meaning he comes forth from the Father as a son from a father, sharing the same nature, not made the way a carpenter makes a table. The Spirit "proceeds" from the Father (John 15:26). So there is a real order of origin, and it shows up in how God works. We usually see the Father sending, the Son coming and carrying out the Father's plan, and the Spirit applying that work to us. These relations are what make the Father the Father, the Son the Son, and the Spirit the Spirit, so the three are never blurred into one Person.

Order, though, does not mean rank. Think of a human father and son. The father comes first, and the son comes from him, but the son is not any less human. He has the whole of human nature, not a smaller share. In God it is even stronger, because God's nature cannot be divided at all. Whatever makes God God, his power, wisdom, goodness, glory and eternity, the Son has completely. Jesus says, "Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine" (John 16:15), and "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Paul writes that in Christ "all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form" (Colossians 2:9). The same is true of the Spirit, who searches "the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10) and is never treated as a creature.

This is why there can be no degrees of honour among them. Among people, we give more honour to those who have more worth or authority. But God is infinite and perfect. You cannot have a slightly less infinite God or a partly perfect God. To call one Person "more honourable" would mean calling another "less honourable," and that would make him less than fully God. Jesus rules this out directly: the Father has given judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). Not almost as much, but just as much. Christians therefore worship the Father, Son and Spirit together with one and the same worship.

So what does "the Father is greater than I" mean? Christians have given two main answers, and they fit together. First, Jesus is speaking as the one who "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7). The eternal Son, without ceasing to be God, became truly human. As a man on the road to the cross, he was lower than the Father, and in that sense the Father was greater. The same Jesus could also say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), because he is both God and man. Second, many Christians add that even apart from the incarnation the Father can be called "greater" as the source: the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son. That is "greater" in the sense of being first in the order of origin, not greater in nature, power or glory. A spring is the source of a stream, yet the water is the same water.

In recent times some sincere Christians have also spoken of the Son's eternal submission to the Father's authority, pointing to verses like 1 Corinthians 11:3 and 15:28. Others answer that God has one will, so the Son's obedience belongs to his saving mission as the one who became man, not to some built-in rank in God. Both sides agree on what matters most: the Son is fully and equally God.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. "Greater" and "less" in God are not about size, like a big box and a small box. God has no body or parts. So when Jesus says the Father is in him and he is in the Father (John 14:10), we should not picture something larger fitting inside something smaller. It is a way of describing perfect unity, like light and its brightness, which are never apart (Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory"). In the same way, when the Bible calls the Spirit "the finger of God" (compare Luke 11:20 with Matthew 12:28), it is not making the Spirit a minor part of a divine body. The picture shows that God acts with one undivided power.

The heart of it is simple. The Father is first, the Son is from the Father, and the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Yet each is fully God, there is one God, and we owe each the same love, trust and worship.

topics.title: What is the sending of the Son, and why is the Son sent but not the Father?
topics.cmp: Augustine supplies most of the answers. He defines the Son's mission as his origin from the Father being made known, or as his being 'made of a woman' (Gal 4:4). He distinguishes a visible sending in the incarnation from an invisible sending to the rational soul. He holds that only one who is from another can be sent, so the Father, being from no one, is never sent, while the inseparable operation of Father, Son and Spirit means the Son also sends himself. Novatian and Hippolytus agree that the Son, not the Father, is sent, but they argue differently: Novatian reasons from Christ's own sayings that one who is sanctified and sent cannot be the sender, which proves the Son a second person, and Hippolytus argues that the visible Word alone is sent (citing Jeremiah and Peter). Augustine instead grounds the asymmetry in the order of origin, and he places the visibility in the Son's assumed human form, insisting that the sending was a joint work and that sayings like 'Neither came I of myself' refer to the servant form. Irenaeus widens the Word's revealing work beyond the incarnation to creation, the law and the prophets. Hilary, Basil and Augustine all deny that the Father's speaking or 'commandment' to the Son is a temporal, bodily order. Hilary stresses divine simplicity, Basil a timeless transmission of will like a mirror image, and Augustine identifies the commandment with the Word himself.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Sender and the Sent Equal. Why the Son is Said to Be…
refs.quote: For as to be born, in respect to the Son, means to be from the Father; so to be sent, in respect to the Son, means to be known to be from the Father.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Moreover, Against the Sabellians He Proves that the…
refs.quote: Or when he finds it placed side by side with others: “Moreover, in your law it is written that the witness of two is true. I bear witness of myself, and the Father who sent me beareth witness of me?”

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: We have established this point to exclude the idea that after silence God spoke to the Son, or after ignorance the Son began to know.

ans.text:
When the Bible says the Father sent the Son, it means that the eternal Son, who was always with the Father, came among us as a man to save us, and in doing so showed the world that he comes from the Father. The Son is sent and the Father is not because sending follows the way they are related: the Son is from the Father, but the Father is from no one.

Start with what sending cannot mean. When a manager sends an employee across town, the employee leaves one place and arrives at another where he was not before. The Son is not like that. As God he is everywhere. John says of him, "He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him. He came to His own" (John 1:10–11). So he was sent to a place where he already was. His coming was not a change of address. It was a new way of being present: God the Son took a human body and soul and lived among us where we could see, hear and touch him.

Paul puts it simply: "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4). Notice how the sending and the birth are joined. The Son's mission is his becoming man of the virgin Mary, and all that he did in that human life, his teaching, his death and his rising. He was the Son from all eternity. In Bethlehem he was sent.

There is a second, quieter way Scripture speaks of the Son coming. He comes to dwell in the hearts of those who believe and to make himself known to them (John 14:23; Ephesians 3:17). That coming is not seen with the eyes, but it is just as real.

Why was he sent? Jesus himself answers: "For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him" (John 3:17). John adds that God showed his love by sending his Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins (1 John 4:9–10). The sending of the Son shows us both how great God's love is and how badly we needed it. He came to cleanse us and bring us back to God, so that we might know him and hold fast to him.

Why, then, is the Son sent and never the Father? Scripture speaks of the Son being sent and of the Holy Spirit being sent, but it never says the Father was sent. The reason lies in who they are. The Son is "begotten" of the Father, which means he has his being from the Father as a son comes from a father, though without any beginning in time, since the Father was never without his Son. The Father, by contrast, is not from anyone. Sending matches this order. The one who is from another is the one sent. The one who is from no one sends. So when the Son is sent, the world learns something true about God from all eternity: this Son comes from the Father. Jesus says, "I have come here from God. I have not come on My own, but He sent Me" (John 8:42).

There is also a plainer reason. It was the Son, not the Father, who became man. The human nature born of Mary belongs to the Son alone. So it fits to call the one who appeared in the flesh the one sent, and the one who did not appear the sender. This is why Jesus can say, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9), and yet still speak of the Father as another who sent him. The Son is not the Father wearing a different mask. When Jesus says the Father "sanctified and sent" him into the world (John 10:36), he shows they are two persons. No one sends himself and receives himself in that way.

Does being sent make the Son less than the Father? It is easy to think so, because among us the one who sends is usually the boss. But Scripture will not let us picture it that way. The Father, Son and Spirit have one will and work as one. The Bible says the Father gave up his Son for us (Romans 8:32), and also that the Son "loved me and gave Himself up for me" (Galatians 2:20). Jesus says no one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). So the Son was not pushed into a task he did not choose. In a real sense the Son shares in his own sending. The coming of the Son into the flesh was the work of the whole Trinity together. Yet it was the Son alone who became flesh, and he did so as the one who comes from the Father. Sender and sent are equal, just as Father and Son are equal, because they are one God (John 10:30).

When Jesus says things like "I have not come on My own" or that he does nothing by himself, he is not admitting weakness. Part of this is the voice of his true humanity, for he really did live as a servant (Philippians 2:7). And even as God, he is saying that he is not a second, independent source. Everything he has and does comes from the Father, perfectly and completely. Jesus says the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself does (John 5:19–20).

That helps us read the places where Jesus speaks of the Father's "command." He says the Father who sent him told him what to say, and that the Father's command is eternal life (John 12:49–50). This is not like an officer barking orders at a junior soldier, or like the Son waiting to be told something he did not know. The Father's will is shared with the Son fully and eternally, the way a mirror holds the whole image at once rather than piece by piece. The Son is himself the Word of the Father and the eternal life the Father gives, so the Father's "command" and the Son agree perfectly.

The same is true of the times the Father spoke from heaven, at Jesus' baptism or before his death. These voices were not the Father catching up the Son on news. Jesus says, "This voice was not for My benefit, but yours" (John 12:30). God put them into human words for our sake. Likewise, the Father did not suddenly decide in time to send the Son. The plan was in God's eternal wisdom. What happened in time was the Son appearing among us, born of a woman when the time was full.

So the sending of the Son is good news in two ways. It tells us who God is: a Father who eternally has a Son, equal to himself, who comes from him. And it tells us what God has done: in love, Father, Son and Spirit together brought the Son among us as one of us, to save the world.

topics.title: Is the Son a servant by nature, or equal to the Father in honour and worship?
topics.cmp: All the authors deny that the Son is a servant by nature or in any way beneath the Father, and they affirm his equality in honour and in the giving of blessing. They reach this conclusion by different routes. Gregory of Nyssa argues mainly by reductio. A slave-Son would leave worship in a double enormity, would be ignorant of the Father's counsels, would be subject to fear, and would even drag the Father, who is wholly in the Son, into servitude. Gregory also holds that divine lordship belongs to God by nature and that a simple nature does not change. Basil likewise reasons philosophically: place cannot be predicated of incorporeal beings, and spatial subordination dishonours the Father as well. Basil adds a qualification the others do not stress: the Son's saving work is voluntary yet always according to the Father's will. Bickersteth, Warfield and Athanasius rely chiefly on Scripture, especially the Pauline salutations joining Father and Son as givers of grace. Even here their emphasis differs. Bickersteth and Warfield read these texts as showing the two as coequal or joint sources: in Bickersteth's words they are 'equally able to grant' and the river of Revelation 22:1 flows 'coordinately' from both. Athanasius instead stresses that the grace is one and single, given by the Father through and in the Son, citing Paul's 'may He direct', not 'they'. Edwards adds a distinctive pneumatological explanation: the Spirit goes unnamed in the salutations because he is himself the grace given. Waterland takes yet another line. From Matthew 4:10 he argues that worship belongs to God alone, so it is excluded from every other being and not only from evil spirits or those claiming supremacy. He also holds that over-honouring and under-honouring the Son are both faults, but not equal ones.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what…
refs.quote: We must not, however, regard the œconomy through the Son as a compulsory and subordinate ministration resulting from the low estate of a slave, but rather the voluntary solicitude working effectually for His own creation in goodness and in pity

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: either he will despise his fellow-slave and deny the faith, having shaken off the yoke of the lordship of Christ, or he will bow before the slave, and, turning away from the self-determining nature that owns no Lord over it, will in a manner worship himself instead of God

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: We must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ. – 2 Cor. 5:10.

ans.text:
The Son is not a servant by nature. He is fully equal to the Father, and he rightly receives the same honour and worship that we give the Father. When the Bible speaks of him serving, it is describing something he chose to do for us, not what he is in himself.

The clearest place to begin is Philippians 2. Paul says that Christ, "existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant." Notice the order. First he was in the form of God, sharing God's own nature. Then he took on the form of a servant by becoming human. Being a servant was something he took up, the way a king might put on a workman's clothes to serve his people. The clothes are real, and the service is real, but they do not change who the king is.

This matters because everything Jesus does in saving us flows from love, not from compulsion. A slave works because he must. The Son came because he willed to, in perfect agreement with the Father. Jesus says no one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). He is never acting outside the Father's will, yet he is never dragged along by it either. Father and Son want the same thing.

Jesus himself makes the point that a servant is outside his master's confidence. In John 15:15 he says that "a servant does not understand what his master is doing." But the Son knows everything the Father does. He says the Father shows him all that he himself is doing (John 5:20), and he prays, "All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine" (John 17:10). Someone who shares everything the Father has, and knows everything the Father does, cannot be a servant underneath him. And if the Son were a slave by nature, then the Father, who is completely one with him, would be bound up with slavery too, which makes no sense at all.

The Bible also shows the Son receiving the honour that belongs only to God. When Satan asked Jesus to bow down, Jesus answered from Scripture: "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only" (Matthew 4:10). Satan did not even claim to be supreme. Jesus refused simply because worship belongs to God alone. Yet Hebrews 1:6 says of the Son, "Let all God's angels worship Him." And Jesus says plainly that the Father has given all judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him" (John 5:23). Not a lesser honour, not a slightly reduced version, but the same honour.

Think about what the alternative would mean. If Jesus were a servant by nature, he would be our fellow servant. Then we would face a bad choice. Either we would refuse to worship him and so reject him as Lord, or we would bow down to a fellow creature, which Scripture forbids. The New Testament never puts us in that bind, because it never treats him as a creature. It calls him Lord in the full sense that God is Lord.

The Son also does what the Old Testament says only God does. Abraham calls God "the Judge of all the earth" (Genesis 18:25). Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). The final Judge of every human heart is not a servant waiting for instructions.

The same equality shows up in ordinary-looking verses. Paul opens his letters by wishing "grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." No apostle would ever write "grace and peace from God and from Peter." Grace is something only God can give.
