By naming the Father and the Son together as its source, Paul treats them as one fountain of blessing. It is not two separate gifts from two separate givers, but one grace from the Father given through the Son. The very end of the Bible pictures this too: the river of the water of life flows "from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Revelation 22:1). It is one throne, shared. And in Revelation 5:13 every creature gives praise and honour and glory to the One on the throne and to the Lamb together.

Someone may ask about Jesus sitting at the Father's right hand. Does that put him in a lower seat, beside and slightly beneath the Father? Not at all. God is spirit and fills all things, so he does not sit higher or lower in space. In the Bible, the right hand is the place of highest honour and shared rule. To sit at the king's right hand is to reign with him. And if we pictured the Father literally seated above the Son, we would be shrinking the Father too, as if he were a body in a room. Belittling the Son always ends up belittling the Father, as Jesus warned.

There is a real ordering in how the Father and Son relate. The Father sends and the Son is sent; the Son delights to do his Father's will. Sincere Christians have discussed how far that ordering goes. Some hold that the Son's obedience belongs only to his mission as a man, since he took the form of a servant for our sake. Others believe the pattern of the Father sending and the Son coming reflects something true of their eternal relationship, while insisting just as firmly that the Son is equal in nature, power and glory. Both sides agree on the point that matters here: the Son is not a servant by nature, and he is to be honoured exactly as the Father is.

So when we worship Jesus, we are not over-honouring a great servant of God. We are giving God what is his. The one who washed the disciples' feet is the Lord of glory, and his humility is the humility of God himself.

topics.title: Does Christ's apparent ignorance, including of the day and hour, show that the Son is not fully God?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Mark 13:32 and Christ's questions in the Gospels do not show that the Son lacks full Godhead, but they explain the 'ignorance' differently. Athanasius, Ambrose, Bickersteth and Waterland refer it to Christ's human nature: as man he did not know, while as Word he knew all things. Their grounds vary: Athanasius points to the omission of the Spirit, Christ's 'ye know not' rather than 'I know not', Acts 1:7, and Paul's 'I know not' in 2 Corinthians 12:2; Ambrose argues from the Spirit's omission; Bickersteth cites Luke 2:52 and Christ's prophetic commission; Waterland draws on Luke 2:52, Tertullian, and the claim that neither Catholics nor Sabellians ever read the text as limiting the Son's divine knowledge. Hilary, though he once also assigns the words to the human nature, mainly treats the ignorance as a feigned economy of concealment rather than real ignorance, resting on Colossians 2:3, the Son as Author of the times, and the Father's love that withholds nothing. Augustine reads 'not know' as an idiom for not making known, and Irenaeus says Christ spoke so that we would learn the Father is above all and leave lofty questions to God; Waterland glosses Irenaeus, and notes that Basil, as giving the Father a 'preference' as the underived source of the Son's knowledge, not as knowing more.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: So that the question, with Irenzeus, is not why the Father is superior in knowledge ; but why, since Father and Son are equally knowing, our Saviour makes such a declaration as gave the preference to the Father.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: acknowledge to what you ought to refer it that He said that the Son knew not. For as man He could [in His human nature] be numbered with creatures Who were created.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The fact that the Father alone knows, is no proof that the Son is ignorant: He says that He does not know, that others may not know: that the Father alone knows, to shew that He Himself also knows.

ans.text:
No. When Jesus says that not even the Son knows the day or hour, He is not admitting that He is less than God. He is speaking as the man He truly became, and as the one sent to tell us only what we need to know. The whole Bible, and this very passage, show that the Son shares the Father's knowledge in full.

Start with who Jesus is. The eternal Son of God did not stop being God when He was born in Bethlehem. He added a real human nature to Himself: a human body, and a human mind and soul. He is one person, but He is both truly God and truly man. So some things are true of Him as God, and other things are true of Him as man. As God He never gets tired, yet as man He fell asleep in a boat. As God He cannot die, yet as man He died on the cross. In the same way, as God He knows all things, yet as man He had a human mind that learned and grew.

The Bible says this openly. Luke 2:52 tells us that "Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man." A human mind grows. Eternal divine wisdom cannot, because it is already complete. So when Mark 13:32 says "no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father," the most natural reading is that Jesus is speaking of Himself as man. He took on our real limits, just as He took on our hunger and thirst, so that He could stand fully with us.

Now look at what Scripture says about the Son's knowledge. John 1:3 says of Him, "Through Him all things were made." That includes time itself and every season of history. It would be strange for the one who made the days not to know His own day. And it is His day, the day of His own return as Judge. Colossians 2:3 says that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." Not some of them, but all. In Matthew 11:27 Jesus says, "no one knows the Father except the Son." Think about that. If the Son knows the infinite God perfectly, He can hardly fail to know the date of an event in the world God made. Knowing the greater surely includes knowing the lesser.

The Gospels also show Jesus knowing what no mere man could know. He read people's thoughts. John tells us He knew from the beginning who would not believe and who would betray Him (John 6:64). Near the end of His ministry the disciples told Him they could see that He knew all things, and after the resurrection Peter said the same (John 16:30; 21:17). Jesus did not correct them.

There is a quiet clue in Mark 13:32 itself. Jesus lists the angels and the Son, but He does not say that the Holy Spirit is ignorant of the day. Scripture says the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God (1 Corinthians 2:10). Yet Jesus says the Spirit will take what belongs to the Son and make it known (John 16:14-15). If the Spirit knows, the Son, from whom the Spirit receives, knows too. This points again to Jesus speaking about His human role, not His divine being.

What about the many questions Jesus asks in the Gospels? He asks where Lazarus has been laid (John 11:34). He asks who touched Him in the crowd. He asks Philip where they can buy bread. Asking a question does not prove ignorance. Teachers and parents ask questions they already know the answer to all the time. John tells us plainly about the bread: Jesus asked this to test Philip, because He already knew what He was going to do (John 6:6). And the one who was about to call Lazarus back from death certainly knew where his body lay. His questions show that He spoke and lived as a real man among us. They draw out faith, teach, and invite people into what He is doing.

The Bible also uses a common way of speaking. Sometimes "I do not know" means "this is not mine to tell you." A government official asked about a sealed matter may say "I can't tell you," or even "that's above my pay grade," while knowing perfectly well. Jesus came as a prophet, sent by the Father to deliver a message. The date of the end was not part of the message He was sent to deliver. So He could truthfully say that, as the one sent, He did not know it so as to reveal it.

Why does He say "only the Father"? Not because the Father knows more. The Father is the source within God. The Son is eternally "begotten" of the Father. That word means He comes from the Father the way light comes from the sun, sharing the same divine life rather than being made. Everything the Son has, including His knowledge, He has from the Father, fully and equally. So it is fitting for the Son, especially while living among us as a servant, to point every secret back to the Father. That is a model of humility for us, not a confession of weakness.

Sincere Christians have explained this in slightly different ways. Many hold that Jesus' human mind really did not have this knowledge during His earthly life, because He truly shared our limits. They point to Luke 2:52 and the fact that He emptied Himself to take the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). Others stress that even as man He was so closely united to God that He knew it but was not commissioned to reveal it, so His words meant "it is not for me to tell." They point to the many places where He knows hidden things. Both views agree on the main point: as God, the Son knows the day fully, and He was not lying or pretending. What He said was true of Him in the way He meant it.

Finally, why is the day hidden at all? Jesus tells us right after this verse: "Be on your guard and stay alert! For you do not know when the appointed time will come" (Mark 13:33). If we knew the date, we might grow careless until it drew near, or become fixated on calculating it. Before His ascension He told the disciples, "It is not for you to know the times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority" (Acts 1:7). He gave us the signs we need so we will not be caught off guard, but He kept back the date for our good. That is love, not ignorance. It keeps us faithful and watchful every day, ready for the return of the Lord who knows exactly when He is coming.

topics.title: Does the Son know all that the Father knows?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son knows all that the Father knows and is truly omniscient. Most of them, especially Athanasius, Hilary, Warfield and Bickersteth, ground this in the exclusive mutual knowledge of Father and Son in Matthew 11:27. They differ in how they explain that knowledge. Augustine and Hilary stress that the Son has His knowing from the Father by nature, through His birth, as He has His being: Augustine says that in God knowing and being are one, so the Father knows by begetting and the Son by being born, while Hilary denies that the Son learns by question and answer. Bickersteth argues from Scripture's language of incomprehensibility ('past finding out', 'unsearchable') and from the Good Shepherd's need to know all His sheep, and he sets the Son's infinite knowledge apart from the saints' finite or future perfected knowledge. Waterland argues against a merely 'relative omniscience' as no omniscience at all, and Hilary argues that nothing made through Christ can lie outside His knowledge.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: The Son then knew, as knowing all things, and knowing His own Father, than which knowledge nothing can be greater or more perfect.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father,…
refs.quote: He knows all that the Father knows; but to Him to know, as to be, is from the Father, for to know and to be is there one

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Each has perfect and complete knowledge of the Other. Therefore, since no one knoweth the Father save the Son, let our thoughts of the Father be at one with the thoughts of the Son

ans.text:
Yes. The Son knows everything the Father knows, fully and perfectly, because he shares the very same divine nature. He did not gain this knowledge by study or by asking. It belongs to him as God, just as it belongs to the Father.

The clearest place to start is Matthew 11:27. Jesus says, "All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." Think about what Jesus is claiming. The Father is infinite. To know him completely you would need an infinite mind. Jesus says he knows the Father in exactly that way, and that only the Father knows him in return. Their knowledge of each other is mutual and matched. No creature could say that. An angel or the wisest saint knows God only in part, and only because God shows himself. The Son knows the Father the way the Father knows himself. Jesus says the same thing in John 10:15: "just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father." There is no greater knowledge than knowing God himself fully, so one who knows the Father completely knows all things.

Notice also the other half of the verse. The Son is not only the knower of God but the one who makes God known. The disciples come to know the Father because the Son chooses to reveal him. Their knowledge is real, but it is a gift, limited, and given to "little children" (Matthew 11:25). The Son's knowledge is the source; theirs is the stream. This is why Paul can say that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). The disciples came to the same conclusion: "Lord, You know all things" (John 21:17).

This also means the Son is as far beyond our understanding as the Father is. Scripture says God's ways are beyond tracing out (Romans 11:33). Paul uses the same kind of language for "the unsearchable riches of Christ" (Ephesians 3:8). And Jesus himself says no one knows the Son except the Father. The Son is not a smaller, more graspable version of God. He is God, just as deep and just as infinite.

Someone might ask: if the Son is "from" the Father, does he get his knowledge from the Father the way a student learns from a teacher? The Bible does say the Father "shows Him all He does" (John 5:20). But this is not question and answer, or moving from not knowing to knowing. Here is a helpful way to think about it. The Son is called "begotten," which means he has his being from the Father eternally, the way a child has the same nature as a parent, though with no beginning in time. In God, knowing is not something added on top of being. God's knowledge is simply God himself. So when the Son eternally receives the whole divine nature from the Father, he receives all of the Father's knowledge with it. He knows everything the Father knows, and he has that knowing from the Father, just as he has his life from the Father. The order is real; the inequality is not.

Two verses often trouble readers here. Luke 2:52 says "Jesus grew in wisdom and stature," and in Mark 13:32 Jesus says that about the day or hour of his return "no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father." How can the all-knowing Son grow, or not know something? The key is that the eternal Son truly became a man. He took a real human mind, which learned things as a boy learns, step by step. As God he knows all things; in his humanity, which he took on in humility for our sake, he lived within human limits. Christians have explained Mark 13:32 in slightly different ways. Many say Jesus is speaking of what he knew in his human mind. Others say that, as the servant sent on his mission, he was not giving out that knowledge as part of his task, much as a messenger might say "I don't know" about something it is not his place to reveal. Both views agree on the main point: this verse describes the humble state the Son entered, not a gap in what he is as God.

So you can trust Jesus completely when he tells you about the Father. No one has ever known God as he does, because he is God the Son, who shares the Father's nature and therefore his perfect knowledge. When you want to know what the Father is like, you look to the Son, who alone can show him to you.

topics.title: When Scripture says the Father 'gave' the Son power, glory, life or authority, did the Son lack them?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Father's 'giving' to the Son implies no lack in the Son, but they explain the language in two different ways. Athanasius and Waterland read many such texts as spoken of Christ's human nature: Athanasius says receiving and needing belong to the flesh, and that the Word received so the gift might abide securely for humanity, unlike Adam who lost it. Waterland, arguing from Scripture's witness to Christ as Creator and Preserver and from catholic antiquity, says the post-resurrection power of Matthew 28:18 was given to the God-Man in his exalted human nature, while the Word was always Lord. Hilary, Augustine and Ambrose instead read 'gave' (especially John 5:26) as referring to the Son's eternal begetting. Augustine argues that the Son is identical with what he has, so giving life means begetting the Son who is life; Hilary grounds the same point in God's simple, non-composite nature ('Living from Living'), and Ambrose stresses begetting rather than adoption and natural love rather than bounty. Distinct emphases include Athanasius's further claim that receiving-language guards against Sabellianism by marking the Son as distinct from the Father, Gregory of Nyssa's insistence that 'God over all' (Romans 9:5) belongs to the Son, and Augustine's appeal to the indivisible working of Father and Son in subjecting all things.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: wherefore do we consider the Giver as receiver, and the Dispenser to others do we suspect to be in need, and divide the Word from the Father as imperfect and needy, while we strip human nature of grace?

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: how easy it is to account for our Lord’s having all power given him, after his resurrection ; given him in respect of his human nature, which was never so high exalted, nor assumed into such power and privilege, till that time

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The Son draws His life from that Father Who truly has life; the Only begotten from the Unbegotten, Offspring from Parent, Living from Living.

ans.text:
No. When the Bible says the Father gave the Son power, glory, life or authority, it never means there was a time when the Son went without them. These texts describe one of two things. Some describe what the eternal Son received in his human nature when he became man. Others describe how the Son has everything from the Father, simply because he is the Father's Son. Neither means the Son was ever lacking or second-rate.

Start with what the Son always had. John opens his Gospel by saying the Word was with God and was God, that all things were made through him, and that "in Him was life" (John 1:1-4). Paul says that in Christ all things were created, in heaven and on earth, and that in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:16-17). Someone who made the universe and keeps it running is not waiting to be handed authority over it. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed, "Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). That is glory he already shared, not glory he hoped to earn. Paul even calls him the one "who is God over all" (Romans 9:5). Christ is not one of the "all things" beneath God. He is the God who is over them.

We also see Jesus using divine authority long before Easter. He forgave sins, which only God can do, and he did it so that we would know "the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (Mark 2:10). He calmed storms, cast out demons, and raised the dead. He did not wait for permission to become powerful. He already was.

So why does Scripture speak of him being given things? The first reason is that the Son truly became a man. A man is a creature, and creatures receive. When the eternal Son took on our flesh, he humbled himself, as Philippians 2 describes. He was hungry, tired, and weak. He suffered and died. Then God raised him and "exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names" (Philippians 2:9). After the resurrection Jesus said, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me" (Matthew 28:18). This is the reward and exaltation of his human nature. The man Christ Jesus, who had walked the road of humiliation, was raised to share the honour the Son had always had as God. He received as man what he had always possessed as God.

This matters for us. When a mere human receives a gift, he can lose it, as Adam did. But when our human nature received glory and authority in the person of God's own Son, the gift was made secure. Because Jesus is one of us and also God, what he received as man is held firmly on our behalf. His exaltation is the guarantee of ours.

The second reason goes deeper, and it explains texts like John 5:26: "For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself." This is not about the Son's humanity only. It speaks of how the Son relates to the Father from all eternity. The Bible calls Jesus the Father's "only begotten" Son. "Begotten" simply means that he comes from the Father the way a child comes from a parent. It does not mean he was made, and it does not mean he had a beginning. The Father has always been Father, so the Son has always been Son.

In that light, the Father "granting" the Son life does not mean there was first a lifeless Son who later got life added to him. It means the Father eternally shares his own life with the Son. The giving is the begetting. Notice the exact words. The Son has life "in Himself," just as the Father does. It is not borrowed life, or a smaller copy. It is the very same divine life, fully the Son's own. Think of a flame that lights another flame. The second fire is no less fire than the first, and it burns by its own heat. The comparison is imperfect, because there was never a moment before the second flame was lit. But it shows how something can be received and still be fully and truly possessed.

One more thing helps here. A creature is one thing and has other things. You are a person, and you have life, strength, and knowledge, which you could lose. God is not put together like that. God does not merely have life. He is life. So when the Father gives the Son life, he is not handing over a possession. He is eternally begetting a Son who is life itself. That is why Jesus could say, "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25).

Why, then, does the Bible use the language of giving at all, if the Son never lacked anything? Because it protects an important truth. The Son has everything the Father has. If Scripture only said that, we might conclude the Son simply is the Father under another name. Words like "given" and "received" remind us that the Son is not the Father. He is the Father's Son, who has all that he has from the Father, eternally and fully. The language shows the order of their relationship, not a gap in rank or worth.

It also helps to see that the Father and Son act together. Paul says the Father put all things under Christ's feet (Ephesians 1:22), but he also says Christ has "the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself" (Philippians 3:21). There is no contradiction. What the Father does, the Son does with him. The Father's giving is never the Son's needing.

So when you read that the Father gave the Son glory, life, or authority, read it in one of two ways. Either it speaks of the man Jesus being raised and honoured for our sake, or it speaks of the eternal Son receiving all things from the Father by being his Son. In neither case did the Son ever lack anything. He is the giver of life to the world because he has always had life in himself.

topics.title: Does the Son share the Father's authority in judgment and the kingdom?
topics.cmp: Hilary, Augustine, and Irenaeus answer different questions here, but Hilary and Augustine converge on one point: sayings that seem to reserve something to the Father do not lessen the Son's share in divine authority. They ground it differently. Hilary argues from the distinction of Persons: fixing the day is kept to the Father to mark His unbegotten authority against the Sabellians, not to make the Son lower in divinity. He then uses Colossians 2:2-3 to argue that the Son is not ignorant of the day, since all the treasures of knowledge are in Him, hidden but not lacking. Augustine instead stresses unity of working: what the Father prepares the Son also prepares, because in the Trinity the one substance works indivisibly. Irenaeus does not take up the question of shared prerogative at all; he presents Christ as the mediator through whom the righteous, by seeing the Lord in the kingdom, gradually grow accustomed to sharing in the Father's glory.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: It is to demonstrate against the Sabellian heretics that the Father’s authority is without birth or beginning, that this prerogative of unbegotten authority is not granted to the Son

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and…
refs.quote: But that which is prepared by His Father is prepared also by the Son Himself, because He and the Father are one.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: the righteous shall reign in the earth, waxing stronger by the sight of the Lord: and through Him they shall become accustomed to partake in the glory of God the Father

ans.text:
Yes. The Son shares fully in the Father's authority to judge and to rule. Some verses speak of the Father keeping certain things to Himself. These show how the Father and the Son relate to each other. They do not show that the Son has less power or less right to reign.

Start with what Jesus says most plainly. In John 5:22-23 He says that the Father judges no one but has assigned all judgment to the Son, "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father." That is a remarkable claim. In the Old Testament, judging the whole world belongs to God alone. Here all of it is placed in the Son's hands. The reason given is that the Son should receive the same honor as the Father. No mere creature, however exalted, could be given that.

Someone may ask why judgment is "given" to the Son if He is truly God. The Bible's answer is that the Father and the Son are one God, but they are not the same person. The Father is the source. The Son is "begotten" of Him, meaning He eternally comes from the Father the way a son comes from a father, sharing the same nature. So everything the Son has, He has from the Father. That includes His life (John 5:26) and His authority. But receiving everything is not the same as having less. A son who inherits his father's whole estate is not poorer than his father. The Son receives all, not part. Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30).

John 5:27 adds a striking detail. The Father has given the Son authority to execute judgment "because He is the Son of Man." Jesus then says, "Do not be amazed at this," and speaks of the hour when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out. We might have expected Him to say "because He is the Son of God."

The point seems to be this. On the last day everyone must stand before the Judge, both the righteous and the wicked, and everyone must be able to see Him. The God who is spirit cannot be seen by sinful eyes. But the Son has become a man. He will come in a real, risen human body, the same Jesus who lived and died among us (Acts 17:31; Matthew 25:31). So the world will be judged by God, yet by God in a human face. And He is a Judge who knows our life from the inside. This does not make His authority merely human. The same voice that raises the dead is the voice of God.

What about Matthew 20:23? There the mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit at Jesus' right and left in His kingdom. Jesus answers that this is not His to grant. Those places belong to those for whom His Father has prepared them.

This does not mean the Son is shut out of the decision. Elsewhere Jesus says, "I am going there to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2). The Father and the Son never act apart from each other. What one does, the other does too, because they share one will and one power (John 5:19). In that moment Jesus was turning the disciples away from scrambling for rank. He pointed them to the cup of suffering and to the Father's gracious plan. He was not denying His own part in it.

Something similar applies to the timing of the last day. Jesus says the Father has fixed the times by His own authority (Acts 1:7). He even says that no one knows the day or hour, "not even the Son" (Mark 13:32).

Christians have understood this in two main ways. One is that Jesus speaks here as a man, within the limits He freely accepted when He became one of us. Another is that His mission did not include revealing the day, so He did not make it known. Either way, the Bible insists that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).

Calling the time the Father's decision honors the Father as the source from whom all things flow. It does not make the Son a lesser God.

Finally, 1 Corinthians 15:24-28 says that at the end Christ will hand over the kingdom to God the Father. Some have taken this to mean the Son's rule is temporary. But the angel told Mary, "His kingdom will never end" (Luke 1:33). At the very end of the Bible we still see "the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Revelation 22:3).

The handing over is best understood as Christ completing His saving work. As our Mediator, He defeats every enemy, including death, and brings the redeemed people home to the Father. He does not step down. Rather, through Him we are brought to share in the Father's glory.

So the Father and the Son do not compete for the throne. The Son reigns and judges with the full authority of God. He has that authority from the Father, and He uses it for the Father's glory. For believers this is deeply comforting. The One who will judge us is the One who died for us. Because He is truly God, His verdict is final.

topics.title: Do Christ's sayings of dependence mean the Son lacks his own divine power and will?
topics.cmp: Hilary, Basil and Bickersteth agree that Christ's sayings of dependence do not mean the Son lacks his own divine power or will. Hilary and Basil ground this in the union of the Son's will with the Father's: Hilary appeals to their one nature received through the birth, so that the Son truly acts and freely wills (citing 'quickeneth whom He will' and 'Father, I will') while all he does is the Father's will, and Basil says the language shows his will joined in indissoluble union with the Father's rather than any lack of initiative. Bickersteth instead resolves the sayings by distinguishing Christ's two natures: as man he depended wholly on the Father, worked miracles by faith, and had his will subjected to the Father's, while as God his will was self-existent, free and efficacious. Irenaeus and Novatian put the stress on the Son carrying out the Father's will: Irenaeus calls him the Father's hand in creation, so that there is no other creator than the one God, and Novatian states flatly that the Son does nothing by his own will or determination but obeys the Father as minister of his will, pointing to the one God the Father. This sits in clear tension with Hilary's and Bickersteth's insistence on the Son's own free will, although Hilary also grants that the Son acts 'not of Himself' because the Father abides in him.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Through the birth the nature of God is abiding in the Son, and does that which He Himself does. What He does God does, but what God does in Him, He Himself does

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what…
refs.quote: it is not because He lacks deliberate purpose or power of initiation, nor yet because He has to wait for the preconcerted key-note, that he employs language of this kind. His object is to make it plain that His own will is connected in indissoluble union with the Father.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: His will, therefore, as man, was subjected to that of his Father: as God, was ever in perfect harmony with his Father’s will, but was self-existent, free, efficacious.

ans.text:
No. When Jesus says he can do nothing by himself, he is not confessing weakness. He is telling us that he and the Father are so completely one that the Son never acts as a rival or a freelancer. The same Gospel that records these sayings also shows the Son willing, choosing, and acting with full divine power.

Start with the sayings themselves. In John 5:19 Jesus says, "the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it." He goes straight on: "For whatever the Father does, the Son also does." Think about how large a claim that is. No creature could say he does everything God does. The Father raises the dead, creates, judges and gives life. Jesus says he does all of that too. So "nothing by Himself" cannot mean "I have little power." It means "I never act apart from the Father." Two verses later he says, "just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes" (John 5:21). That is a will of his own, exercising a power that belongs only to God.

The same holds for John 6:38, where Jesus says he came down from heaven "not to do My own will, but to do the will of Him who sent Me." Some read this as if the Son had private wishes that he had to set aside. The point is the opposite. The Son does not have a separate agenda that competes with the Father's. Notice what the Father's will is in the next verses: that the Son lose none of those given to him and raise them up at the last day. Then, in his prayer in John 17:24, Jesus says, "Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am." The Father wills that believers have eternal life with Christ. The Son wills exactly the same. It is one purpose, held freely by both.

This is why the church has said that Father, Son and Holy Spirit share one divine nature, or "essence": one being, what God is. Because the will belongs to the nature, there is one divine will, not three. It is not that the Son has no will. He has the very will of God, fully and freely as his own, just as the Father has it. Jesus puts it simply: "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). When the Son acts, the Father is at work in him. "The Father who dwells in Me is doing His work," he says in John 14:10. And when the Father acts, it is through the Son. These are not two workers splitting a job. They are one God acting, with the Son acting in his own way as Son.

That last phrase matters. The Son is "begotten" of the Father, which means he eternally receives his being from the Father, the way a son comes from a father, but without any beginning and without being made. So whatever the Son has, he has from the Father, including his power and will. When Jesus says he speaks and acts "from the Father," he is pointing to this relationship. Receiving all things from the Father does not make him less than the Father, any more than a flame lit from another flame is less truly fire. It simply shows where he comes from.

It also helps to remember who is speaking in the Gospels. The eternal Son became a real man. He took a full human nature, including a human mind and a human will. As a man he lived in complete trust and obedience toward his Father, praying, depending, submitting. In Gethsemane we hear that human will bending to God: "yet not My will, but Yours be done" (Luke 22:42). Some of Jesus' sayings of dependence speak from this side of who he is. They show us what a perfectly faithful human life looks like. They do not cancel his deity. They show that God the Son truly became one of us.

At the same time, the Gospels keep showing his divine freedom. When a leper says, "if You are willing, You can make me clean," Jesus answers, "I am willing. Be clean!" (Matthew 8:3). He reveals the Father "to those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him" (Matthew 11:27). And of his own life he says, "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord" (John 10:18). Someone who simply carries out orders he did not choose does not speak like this.

Think, too, about John 8:29: "He has not left Me alone, because I always do what pleases Him." If the Son were only a tool moved by the Father, it would make no sense to say he pleases the Father by what he does. A tool pleases no one. Jesus pleases the Father because he really acts and really wills, and what he wills is always what the Father wills. His saying that he does nothing by himself and his saying that he always pleases the Father fit together only if both describe the same thing: perfect unity, not lack of power.

Christians do discuss one related question. Some believe there is an eternal order in which the Son, while fully equal, always acts in a way that fits his being from the Father, and they see a hint of this in his being "sent." Others hold that the language of obedience belongs only to his life as a man, since in God there is one will and so nothing to obey. Both sides agree on what matters most here. The Son is fully God, with all divine power, and he shares the one divine will freely and completely.

So when you read "I can do nothing by Myself," do not hear "I am weak." Hear "I am never apart from my Father." The Son's dependence is the dependence of perfect love and perfect oneness. And it is good news. It means that when Jesus says "I am willing" to a sinner who comes to him, he is not guessing at what God wants. He is God, willing our good.

topics.title: Does Christ's praying, or prayer through Christ, show that the Son is inferior?
topics.cmp: Waterland, Augustine and Hilary all deny that Christ's praying or our praying through him makes the Son inferior to the Father, but each rests the denial on a different ground. Waterland and Augustine both appeal to Christ's mediatorial role: Waterland says prayer goes through the Son because of his particular office as Mediator, and points to the ancient Church's practice of praying directly to him and joining him with the Father in doxologies; Augustine says the Son intercedes as man while remaining equal in the one Godhead. Hilary, reading the Lazarus account in John, argues instead that Christ's prayer was not a real petition for help at all but a teaching gesture made for the crowd's belief. Owen does not take up the question of inferiority directly. He describes the distinct roles the Father and Christ play in prayer, the Father as fountain of blessings and Christ as their procurer by mediation and purchase, which fits with Waterland's and Augustine's focus on mediation, though it is not argued as a defence of equality.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: as the Son stands to us under the particular character of Mediator, besides what he is in common with the Father, our prayers, igenerally, are to be

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In What Manner Christ Wills that All Shall Be One in…
refs.quote: equal to the Father through the unity of the Godhead, and partaker with us by the taking upon Him of humanity, interceding for us with the Father in that He was man,

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: He prayed then for us, that we may know Him to be the Son; the words of prayer availed Him nothing, but He said them for the advancement of our faith. He was not in want of help, but we of teaching.

ans.text:
No. Jesus' praying, and our praying through him, do not make the Son less than the Father. They show what he became and what he does for us, not a lower rank in who he is.

Start with who Jesus is. The Bible teaches that the Son is fully God, sharing the one divine nature, or "essence," with the Father. Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one." In John 17:5 he prays for the glory he had with the Father "before the world existed." Yet the eternal Son also became a real human being. Philippians 2:6-8 says that though he existed in the form of God, he took the form of a servant and humbled himself. So in Jesus we meet one person who is both truly God and truly man.

That is the key to his prayers. A true human life includes prayer. Human beings depend on God, give thanks, ask, and trust. When the Son took on our humanity, he took on that life of prayer too, and he lived it perfectly. When Jesus kneels in Gethsemane or prays through the night, we are seeing the Son living as a man before his Father. This is not God the Son dropping to a lower level of deity. It is the Son really sharing our condition. He does not stop being God by praying, just as he does not stop being human by working miracles.

Jesus' own words make this plain. At Lazarus' tomb he prays aloud. Then he explains why: "I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me" (John 11:42). He did not pray because he lacked the power to raise Lazarus. He prayed so that the crowd would see that his work and the Father's work are one. The prayer was not help for him. It was teaching for us. Notice too that in his prayers Jesus never hides that he is God. In the very same chapters he claims oneness with the Father and a glory shared with him before creation.

The same goes for his ongoing prayers for us. Hebrews 7:25 says he "always lives to intercede" for those who come to God through him. And 1 Timothy 2:5 calls him the "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." A mediator is a go-between who brings two parties together. Jesus can do this because he belongs fully to both sides. He is God, so he can bring God to us. He is man, so he can represent us before God. His pleading for us is the work of a Savior who died and rose for us. It is not the begging of an inferior. A loving older brother who speaks up for his siblings before their father is not less a son than the father is a father.

What about our praying "through" Jesus or "in his name"? The New Testament usually directs prayer to the Father through the Son. Paul writes, "I thank my God through Jesus Christ" (Romans 1:8). To pray in Jesus' name does not mean adding a phrase at the end. It means coming to the Father with all our hope resting on what Jesus has done. The Father is the source of every blessing we ask for. The Son is the one who won those blessings for us by his life, death and resurrection. We come through him because he is our way in, not because he is a lesser God.

This pattern was never meant to keep honor from the Son. Jesus himself says the Father has given him the work of judging "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). Prayer is also offered directly to Jesus in the Bible. Jesus tells his disciples, "If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it" (John 14:14). Stephen, as he died, prayed, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). The first Christians were known as people who "call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 1:2). And in heaven's worship, praise goes up together "to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb" (Revelation 5:13). Worship that belongs only to God is given to the Son alongside the Father.

So it is right to pray to the Father through the Son, and it is also right to pray to the Son himself and to worship him with the Father and the Spirit. The usual pattern reflects the Son's role as our mediator. It does not lower his rank. When you hear Jesus pray, you are not watching a lesser being ask a greater one for help. You are watching the eternal Son, equal with the Father, living our human life and opening the way for us to come home to God.

topics.title: Which particular texts are cited to make the Son less than the Father, and how are they answered?
topics.cmp: Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine and Bickersteth all deny that John 20:17 or the reply to the rich young man makes the Son inferior in divine nature. Their main shared move is to refer such sayings to Christ's assumed humanity or servant-form rather than to His Godhead, and Hilary does the same with the Vine and Husbandman of John 15. They differ in how they develop this. On John 20:17, Hilary stresses that a servant speaks to servants and that the Begotten God shares the Begetter's nature. Gregory gives the text a soteriological reading: Christ as first-fruits and mediator makes the Father our God and Father too, and he attacks Eunomius for equating the Only-begotten with the apostles. On the rich young man, Hilary, Gregory and Bickersteth all say Christ rebuked the questioner's view of Him as merely a human teacher, while Augustine argues that 'one, that is, God' names the whole Trinity, and so includes the Son, not the Father alone. Augustine also allows any interpretation that does not make the Father's substance better than the Son's. Novatian's use of John 15 has a different aim: he cites the sayings to prove that the Son is not the Father, not to answer claims that the Son is inferior.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Jesus Christ was speaking as a man in the form of a servant to men and servants; what difficulty is there then in the idea, that in His human aspect the Father is His Father as ours, in His servant’s nature God is His God as all men’s?

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: sends to His brethren the announcement of Himself not in His divine character, but in that which He shares with us

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: The Lord refused such homage. It was founded on false assumptions. Its acceptance would have strengthened a yet unhumbled self-righteousness. "Why," he asked, "why callest thou me good?" The stress is on the "why".

ans.text:
The texts most often used to make the Son less than the Father are Jesus' words to Mary Magdalene after he rose, "my God and your God" (John 20:17), his reply to the rich young man, "Why do you call Me good?" (Mark 10:18), and his picture of himself as the vine with the Father as the one who tends it (John 15:1). Each, read carefully, fits with the church's confession that the Son is fully God, equal with the Father, and also truly man.

One key unlocks all three. The Bible speaks of Jesus in two ways because he is one person who is both God and man. Paul says that Christ, "existing in the form of God," took "the form of a servant" and was made in human likeness (Philippians 2:6-7). He did not stop being God. He added a real human life to who he already was. So some things are true of him as God, like "In the beginning was the Word... and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Other things are true of him as man: he grew tired, he wept, he prayed, he died. When a verse sounds like it lowers Jesus, the first question is whether he is speaking from the human life he took on for our sake.

Take John 20:17 first. The risen Jesus tells Mary, "go and tell My brothers, 'I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.'" Some reason that if the Father is Jesus' God, Jesus must be a creature like us. But Jesus became a real man, and a real man rightly worships, prays to and obeys God. As man, he can truly call the Father "my God." That says nothing against his divine nature, which was never a servant's nature.

The wording matters too. Jesus does not say "our Father" or "our God," as if he and the disciples stood in exactly the same place. He says "My Father and your Father." He is the Father's Son by nature, from all eternity. We become God's children by adoption, through him. The wonder of the verse is the good news it carries. Jesus calls the disciples "My brothers" (see Hebrews 2:11). By sharing our humanity and rising as the first of a new humanity, he brings us to his Father. Where he has gone, we will follow. And just a few verses later Thomas falls before this same risen Jesus and says, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). Jesus does not correct him. John could hardly have placed a clearer answer next to the verse in question.

Next, "Why do you call Me good?" Jesus replied. "No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18). Some take this as Jesus denying that he is good, or that he is God. But notice what he does not say. He does not say, "No one is good except the Father." He says, "except God." The man had run up and called him "Good Teacher," treating him as a fine rabbi, a good man among good men, and he was sure he could earn eternal life by his own goodness. Jesus' question is a challenge: do you understand what you are saying? If only God is good in the full sense, then either stop calling me good, or realize who is standing in front of you. Elsewhere Jesus calls himself "the good shepherd" (John 10:11). He says, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). He even claims to forgive sins, which only God can do. So he is not refusing the title. He is pointing the man past a shallow compliment to the truth. Christians have explained the verse in slightly different ways, but the church has always held one line: no reading is acceptable that makes the Son less good than the Father. The one God who alone is good is Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Finally, the vine. "I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard" (John 15:1). Some argue that the gardener is plainly greater than the plant he tends. But this is a picture, and it is a picture of Jesus as the one in whom we live. The vine is where the branches are joined, from which they draw life and bear fruit. That describes Jesus as the Word made flesh, the man to whom we are united by faith. By becoming one of us, he became the living stem into which we are grafted. The Father's care for the vine is his care for the incarnate Son and for all who are joined to him. It is not a ranking of the divine nature. This passage, and others like it where Jesus speaks of being sent, of keeping the Father's commands and of hearing from the Father, does show something true. The Son is not the Father. They are two distinct persons, not one person wearing two masks.

It also helps to know that the Bible's language of Father and Son points to how the Son comes from the Father, not to a lower rank. A son is not a lesser kind of being than his father. He shares his father's nature. When the Son is called "begotten," it means he comes from the Father's own being, eternally, as Son. He is not made, like a creature. So the Father can be called the source without making the Son less divine. Jesus says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). Christians have discussed how far the Son's obedience reflects his human life alone, and how far it reflects his eternal relation as Son. Some stress that all such language belongs to his life as man. Others see in it a fitting order between Father and Son that implies no inequality. Both agree on the main point: in power, glory and goodness, the Son is fully equal with the Father.

So these texts do not make the Son less than the Father. They show a Son who is truly God and who, out of love, became truly man. He speaks humbly as one of us so that he can bring us, as his brothers and sisters, to his Father and our Father.

topics.title: Do titles and attributes ascribed to the Father alone place the Son below him?
topics.cmp: Athanasius, Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa all deny that titles or attributes ascribed to the Father alone place the Son below him, but each argues differently. Athanasius reads 'Almighty' and 'Lord of the Powers' as referring to creatures made through the Son, who rules with the Father as his Word and Image. He uses the Johannine principle that dishonouring the Son dishonours the Father, while granting that 'unoriginate' has a pious sense. Augustine argues from the logic of relative predication: 'Father' and 'Son' are reciprocal, not substantial, terms. On 'who alone has immortality' he argues that the Word did not lose immortality by taking flesh, adding the soul's survival and the Spirit's never being incarnate as further evidence that the text cannot mean the Father to the exclusion of the others. Gregory of Nyssa instead turns Eunomius's reasoning against him, arguing that restricting incorruptibility to the Father would make the Son corruptible, and that the Son's capacity to suffer for our salvation would, by Eunomius's own logic, exalt rather than diminish him. Irenaeus addresses a related but distinct question, holding that mortal flesh becomes immortal not by its own nature but by God's power through the Spirit, a point about the believer's resurrection rather than the Son's rank.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: it is quite plain that neither here is the Son reckoned among that all, nor is God called Almighty and Lord with reference to Him, but to those things which through the Son come to be

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: when he asserted incorruptibility of the Father alone, he places all things which are considered after the Father in the category of corruptible, by virtue of opposition to the incorruptible, so as to make out even the Son not to be free from corruption

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Against Those Who Believed the Father Only to Be…
refs.quote: For He did not therefore lose His immortality, because He took mortal flesh; seeing that it could not happen even to the human soul, that it should die with the body

ans.text:
No. When the Bible gives the Father titles like "Almighty" or says that God "alone is immortal," it is not drawing a line between the Father and the Son. It is drawing a line between the one true God and everything else: creatures, idols and so-called gods.

Take the clearest example. Paul praises God as "the blessed and only Sovereign One, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone is immortal" (1 Timothy 6:15–16). Some have read this as if the Son were left out. But in Revelation 17:14 the Lamb, Jesus, is himself called "Lord of lords and King of kings." The same title is given to both. The word "only" works the same way elsewhere. Jude calls Jesus Christ our only Master and Lord (Jude 4), and no one takes that to mean the Father is not Lord. In each case "only" shuts out rivals to God. It does not shut out the persons who are God.

Someone might say, "But the Son died, so surely he is not immortal the way the Father is." The answer lies in who Jesus is. The eternal Son took on a real human body and soul. He truly died in that human nature. Yet he did not stop being God, and as God he did not stop living. John says of the Word through whom all things were made, "In Him was life" (John 1:4). Jesus says the Father has granted the Son "to have life in Himself" (John 5:26). That means life that is his own, not borrowed. Even an ordinary person's soul does not die when the body dies, as Jesus teaches in Matthew 10:28. Much less did the Son's divine life end on the cross. And notice: the Holy Spirit never took flesh at all. So if "immortal" were meant to exclude anyone who is not the Father, it would exclude the Spirit too, which makes no sense. The verse is about God, the whole Godhead, in contrast with mortal creatures.

The same is true of "Almighty." God is almighty over all things, and Scripture says those things were made through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). The Son is not one of the "all things" the Father rules over. He is the one through whom the Father made them and rules them. Hebrews 1:3 says the Son upholds all things by his powerful word. You cannot be among the things being held up and also be the one holding them up.

What about the Father being "unoriginate," that is, having no source? This is true and worth saying. The Father comes from no one. The Son is "begotten" of the Father, which means he comes from the Father the way a son shares his father's nature. He is not made. He shares the very same being. But being begotten is not the same as being created or being smaller. "Father" and "Son" are names of relationship. One is Father because he has a Son, and the other is Son because he has a Father. The names tell us how the persons are related to each other. They do not tell us that one has more of God's nature than the other. A human son is just as human as his father. The eternal Son is just as fully God as his Father. If the word "unoriginate" is used to push the Son down into the ranks of created things, it dishonours the Father too. Jesus warns that "whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him" (John 5:23).

Finally, there is suffering. God in his own nature cannot be harmed, worn down, or made to suffer against his will. Some argue that since the Son suffered and the Father did not, the Son must be lesser. But the Son did not suffer because his divine nature was weak. He suffered because he freely took our nature in order to save us. Had he refused, we would have been left in our misery with no one to raise us up. Being able to come down and rescue is not a mark of weakness. It is a mark of love and power. The cross shows the Son's glory, not his inferiority.

One more thing is worth seeing. Immortality is something we will one day receive. Paul says our mortal bodies will "put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:53). Our flesh will not gain it by its own strength. God will give it as a gift. The Son, by contrast, is not someone who receives immortality from outside himself. He is the one who gives it. He calls himself "the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25). Only one who is truly God can give eternal life to others.

So the titles and qualities the Bible gives to God belong to the Father, and they belong equally to the Son and the Spirit. The Father is the source within the Godhead, but he is not a greater God. There is one God, eternal, immortal and almighty, in three persons.

title: Word, Wisdom, Image and Radiance
desc: The meaning of the Son's titles and the analogies of light, radiance, fountain and inner word for his relation to the Father.

topics.title: What do the Son's titles Word, Wisdom, Radiance and Image mean?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Word, Wisdom, Radiance and Image name a subsisting, eternally begotten Son of the Father's nature, not a passing sound, a property, or a created likeness. Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary rest this chiefly on John 1 ('the Word was God'), while Athanasius argues that a human word is proper to its speaker yet fails as a model because it is many, transient and passible. Augustine works from the inner word of the mind, explaining why the Son is 'Word' rather than 'Thought', and holds that 'Word', like 'Son', is said relatively, so the Father is not himself the Word. There are differences of emphasis. Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa insist that 'Son' and 'Word' are both true by nature and identical in referent: Athanasius argues this against Eusebians and Marcellians and says 'Word' and 'Radiance' guard 'Son' against human notions, while Gregory separates relative names (Son, Word, Wisdom) from dispensational names (vine, shepherd) and allows that the latter may be conceptions (epinoia). Jonathan Edwards alone reads Image and Form as God's perfect idea of himself, while Irenaeus stresses that only the Father's own Word can reveal the Father and uses the Image-likeness principle to refute Marcus's syllabic Word.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: the hearer may not by any means by inattention or feebleness of thought fall into the common understanding of “Word,” so that the Son should be supposed to be the voice of the Father.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The Word is a reality, not a sound, a Being, not a speech, God, not a nonentity.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge…
refs.quote: as our knowledge is unlike that knowledge of God, so is our word also, which is born from our knowledge, unlike that Word of God which is born from the essence of the Father.

ans.text:
They are four different pictures of one and the same Person, the eternal Son of God. Each one shows something true about how he comes from the Father and how he relates to the Father. Each also guards against a mistake we might make if we used only one of them.

Start with the title the others support: Son. When the Bible calls Jesus the Son of God, it means more than a special favorite. A son shares his father's nature: a human son is fully human, just as his father is. So the Son of God has the same divine nature as the Father. Theologians call this being "begotten": coming from the Father, sharing his very being, and not being made. But human sonship also carries ideas that do not fit God. A human son is born at a moment in time, comes after his father, and lives apart from him. The other titles correct those ideas.

Take "Word." John opens his Gospel this way: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Think of how a word comes from a person's mind. It comes out of the mind, yet nothing is cut off from the mind, and the mind is not made smaller. So the Son comes from the Father without the Father being divided or changed. But John is careful that we do not think of a word as a sound that fades once it is spoken. This Word "was" in the beginning. He was "with God," a real Person facing the Father. And he "was God." Our words are many and soon gone. God has one Word, and that Word is living, eternal and fully divine. Through him "all things were made" (John 1:3).

Take "Wisdom." Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). Ask yourself: was there ever a time when God had no wisdom? Of course not. So if the Son is God's Wisdom, there was never a time when the Father was without the Son. This title shows that the Son is eternal, not a later addition.

Take "Radiance." Hebrews 1:3 says the Son "is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Picture the sun and its light. The moment there is a sun, there is shining. The light is not a piece broken off from the sun. It does not come along later, and it is of the same kind as its source. This is the clearest picture the Bible gives of a birth that is eternal, involves no change, and has no separation. The Father has never been without his Radiance.

Take "Image." Paul writes that the Son "is the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). An image here does not mean a cheap copy or a lesser painting. It means a perfect likeness, showing exactly what the original is. That is why Jesus can say, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). This title tells us why the Son is the one who makes God known. No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is God and is at the Father's side, has made him known (John 1:18). Only someone who truly shares God's nature could show us God truly.

Why is the Son named with words that sound like the Father's own qualities: his word, his wisdom, his glory, his likeness? These names show that the Son is not outside the Father, the way a creature is. He belongs to the Father's very life, as closely as your thoughts belong to you. Yet the names do not mean he is only a quality or activity of the Father. John is clear that the Word was "with God," a real Person in relationship. So these titles are relational. The Father is not his own Word or his own Image. The Son is the Word of the Father and the Image of the Father. Together the titles teach two things at once. The Son is one in nature with the Father and never apart from him. He is also truly distinct from the Father, as the one who is begotten.

This also helps with sayings like John 5:19, where the Son does only what he "sees the Father doing." This does not mean the Son is a learner who watches and copies. To "see" the Father is simply to be from the Father, and to share fully and eternally in the Father's life and work.

Two common misunderstandings are worth naming. First, these titles are not in the same class as names like Vine, Door or Shepherd. Those are word-pictures of what Christ does for us. These titles describe who he is in relation to the Father, before and apart from creation. Second, the titles are not four separate beings, or one being wearing four masks. The Word through whom all things were made is the same Son through whom God made the world (Hebrews 1:2). The Wisdom, the Radiance and the Image are one Lord Jesus Christ.

No single picture is enough, and every picture falls short of God. Put together, though, they say something wonderful. The one who came to us in Jesus is God's own eternal Son. He is as close to the Father as a word is to the mind and light is to the sun. And he shows us the Father perfectly.

topics.title: Is the Son truly the Father's own subsisting Word and Wisdom, one and the same Person as the Son?
topics.cmp: Athanasius, Hilary, Augustine and Waterland all hold that the Son is the Father's one, proper, subsisting Word and Wisdom. None of them treats this Wisdom as a mere name, a quality or attribute in the Father, or a second Logos alongside the Son. Athanasius makes the fullest case and argues on several fronts. Philosophically, a Wisdom that is a quality would make God compound, and only another can 'coexist' with God. Scripturally, he cites the bosom of the Father, 'no one knoweth the Father save the Son,' and 'I and the Father are One.' He also appeals to the fathers and even to Asterius' admissions, while denying, against a Sabellian-sounding view, that God is his own Wisdom or his own Father. Hilary reaches the same conclusion through the concept of birth: what has its own existence by birth cannot be a property inhering in another. Augustine differs in emphasis and qualifies the language. 'Word' is a relative name, whereas 'wisdom' is said of God essentially, so that the Son is 'wisdom that is born,' and multiplying attributes does not multiply sons because in God they are one. Waterland's concern is historical, based on the Fathers. He reconciles patristic statements by distinguishing the eternal inward Word from the Word's going forth in creation, and he rejects the Arian 'twofold Logos' as foreign to all antiquity.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: these men introduce, after their private notions, many images and wisdoms and words, and say that the Father’s proper and natural Word is other than the Son, by whom He even made the Son

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For an object, which has by birth an existence of its own, cannot be regarded as a property; a property is necessarily inherent in some being and can have no independent existence.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: the former being only the Father's own proper Word, and no substantial thing; the latter a created substance, directly contrary to all antiquity, which has nothing to countenance any such notion of a twofold Λόγος.

ans.text:
Yes. The Son is not given the names Word and Wisdom as honorary titles. He is the Father's own Word and Wisdom, a real Person who has always been with the Father. And the eternal Word and the Son born of the Father are not two beings but one and the same Person.

Start with how the Bible speaks. John opens his Gospel this way: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). A few verses later he tells us who this Word is: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father" (John 1:14). The Word who was with God in the beginning is the same one John calls the only Son. Paul says the same thing in different words: Christ is "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3).

Why use words like Word and Wisdom at all? Each picture tells us something true. Our words come from our minds and show what we think. In the same way, the Son comes from the Father and makes Him known. Wisdom is how a wise person does things well. The Old Testament says the Lord founded the earth by wisdom, and Proverbs 8 pictures that Wisdom as being beside God when He made the world. The New Testament shows us that this world-making Wisdom is Christ: "Through Him all things were made" (John 1:3). Radiance is the light that shines out from the sun. It is never separate from the sun and never later than it. So the Son is never apart from the Father, and there was never a time when the Father was without Him.

Some have treated these names as mere labels. In that view, Jesus is called Word and Wisdom only because God gave Him a share in some other wisdom that God has in Himself. Scripture knows of no second, hidden Wisdom behind the Son. If there were one, the Son would be just a student of it, and second to it. His names would be borrowed decorations, like a nickname. But the Bible says that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). He does not borrow wisdom. He is the Father's own Wisdom, coming from the Father's very being. That is what "begotten" means here. The Son is not made from outside, the way a carpenter makes a table. He comes from the Father the way a child shares the nature of a parent, except that with God this has no beginning.

A second misunderstanding goes the other way. It treats the Word and Wisdom as simply a quality inside God, the way we might say a man has good sense. On this view the Son is not really a someone. The Bible will not allow this. A quality cannot be "with" God, as John 1:1 says. Nothing keeps company with itself. A quality cannot pray, love, be sent, or become flesh. The Word does all these things. The Word who "was with God" is clearly someone alongside the Father, not a feature of the Father. There is a deeper reason too. God is not built out of parts, as if He were "God plus wisdom plus power." He is simply and wholly God. The Son is not a piece of the Father. He is the Father's living Word, fully God, as the Father is.

A third mistake treats Father and Son as one Person under two names. On this view God is Father in one role and Word in another. But Scripture keeps them clearly distinct while never separating them. The Son speaks to the Father, prays to Him, and speaks of the glory He had with Him "before the world existed" (John 17:5). John says the only Son is "at the Father's side" (John 1:18). No one can be at his own side. They are two Persons. Yet they are so united that Jesus can say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30).

Some have also wondered whether the eternal Word and the Son might be two different things. Perhaps the Word is God's inner reason, and the Son a lesser being made later? The Bible's own wording rules this out. Jesus says, "No one knows the Father except the Son" (Matthew 11:27). He says, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). If the Word were someone other than the Son, then either the Word would not truly know the Father, or Jesus' words would be false. It is the Son who is at the Father's side, and the Son who reveals Him. So the Son is the Word. There is one eternal Word, distinct from the Father, sharing His very nature. This same Word made the world, and in the fullness of time He became a man.

You may come across early Christian writers who seem to speak differently. Some said the Word was always in God. Others said the Word "came forth" when the world was made. These can be read together without contradiction. They describe one and the same Word from two angles. Think of a thought that has always been in someone's mind and is later spoken aloud. The Son has always been with the Father as His eternal Word. At creation He went out to act, and the Father's wisdom became visible in what was made. That was not a new beginning for the Son himself. It was the start of His work in the world.

One last point. The Bible calls Christ both power and wisdom, but that does not mean God has a separate son for each good quality. In God, power, wisdom, goodness and greatness are not separate things stacked together. They are one undivided life, and the one Son has all of it from the Father. Nor should we ask what the Son exists for, as if He were a tool made for a job. We do not ask why the Father exists, and we need not ask why His radiance shines. The Son is the Word simply because He is the Father's own Son. This is good news for us. When we listen to Jesus, we are not hearing a messenger repeating borrowed lines. We are hearing God's own Word, speaking God's own heart.

topics.title: Is the Father wise only through the Son, His begotten Wisdom?
topics.cmp: Augustine dominates this topic, and his answers consistently conclude that the Father is not wise only through the Son. In God to be is to be wise, so if the begotten Wisdom made the Father wise it would give the Father His very being, which Augustine calls absurd. The Father is therefore wisdom Himself, and the Son is wisdom from wisdom as He is light from light, with Father, Son and Spirit being one wisdom and one essence. Augustine grounds this mainly in divine simplicity and the identity of God's essence and attributes, reinforced by analogy (light from light) and a contrast with whiteness as a quality in a body. He keeps Paul's text in 1 Cor 1:24 intact rather than denying or qualifying it, and in some passages he openly treats the opposing hypothesis as a real difficulty, tests its consequences and defers a final answer. Athanasius agrees that God does not become wise by partaking of a wisdom distinct from Himself, but his emphasis differs: he presents the Father as Father of His own Wisdom, an Offspring proper to Him in whom creatures participate, without developing Augustine's essentialist argument that the Father is Himself wisdom.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Augustin Returns to the Question, Whether Each Person of…
refs.quote: in the same manner as light from light, and yet both one light, so we are to understand wisdom of wisdom, and yet both one wisdom; and therefore also one essence

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: God partakes in nothing, but is Himself the Father of His own Wisdom, of which whoso partake are given the name of wise.

ans.text:
No. The Father does not borrow His wisdom from the Son. The Father is wise in Himself, and the Son is wisdom that comes from wisdom, in the same way Christians confess that He is "light from light" and "God from God."

The question comes from a striking verse. Paul writes that to those who are called, Christ is "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). Some have asked whether this means the Son is the Father's wisdom the way a person's intelligence belongs to that person. If so, it might seem that without the Son the Father would be without wisdom.

To see why that is not so, start with what Scripture says about God Himself. We become wise by receiving wisdom from outside ourselves. We learn it, grow in it, and can lose it again through foolishness or old age. God is not like that. No one taught Him. Paul marvels at "the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God" (Romans 11:33) and asks who has ever been His counselor. God does not have wisdom as something added to Him, the way a coat of paint is added to a wall. He simply is wise, through and through. His wisdom is not one thing and His being another. For God, to exist and to be wise are the same.

Now suppose the Father were wise only because of the Son. Then the Son would be giving the Father something essential to who He is. And since being wise is part of what it is to be God, the Son would in effect be making the Father God. That turns things upside down. The Son comes from the Father, not the Father from the Son. The same reasoning would also apply to God's power, goodness and eternity. We would have to say the Father is powerful only through the Son, good only through the Son, eternal only through the Son. Scripture never speaks that way. Paul can simply say "the only wise God" (Romans 16:27).

There is a second problem. If the Son were just the Father's wisdom, like a quality the Father possesses, then the Son would be a feature of the Father rather than a real Son. But the Bible presents the Son as a distinct person who is with God and who is God (John 1:1). He speaks to the Father, loves Him and is sent by Him.

So how should we read 1 Corinthians 1:24? The key is the word "begotten." It means the Son comes from the Father by sharing His very nature, the way a child shares the nature of a parent. He is not made the way a craftsman makes a table, and there was never a time when the Father was without Him. Whatever the Father is, He gives fully to the Son. The Father is wise, so the Son He begets is wise with the very same wisdom.

The sun and its brightness help here, if only a little. The light that shines from the sun is truly the sun's own light, yet the sun is not bright because of the beams that come from it. The beams come from the sun's own brightness. Hebrews 1:3 uses this kind of picture when it calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature."

This does not mean there are two wisdoms, one in the Father and another in the Son. There is one wisdom, just as there is one God. The Father is wisdom, the Son is wisdom, and the Holy Spirit is wisdom, yet they are not three wisdoms but one, because they share one divine being. The Son has this wisdom not from Himself but from the Father. The Father has it from no one.

Why, then, is the Son in particular called the Wisdom of God? Because He is the one in whom the Father expresses Himself and makes Himself known. The Father created all things through Him and saves us through Him. Above all, God's wisdom is shown in the crucified Christ, which looks like foolishness to the world. That is Paul's point in 1 Corinthians 1. He is not explaining where the Father's wisdom comes from. He is telling us where to find it. Christ "has become for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30), and in Him "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3).

So we can hold both truths together without strain. The Father is wise in His own right. The Son is truly the Father's Wisdom, equal to Him and one with Him. When we look to Jesus, we are not looking at a lesser or borrowed wisdom. We are seeing the very wisdom of God, shining out from the Father for our salvation.

topics.title: In what sense is the Son the Image of the Father, and is He one in nature with Him?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son is truly God and one in nature or essence with the Father. Athanasius and Hilary develop this most fully through the idea of Image. Athanasius argues from what a true image requires: if the Son is the Image of the Father's proper substance, he must be true Offspring, unalterable, eternal, and possess all the Father's attributes, so that whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father. Hilary stresses that the Son is a living Image, not a lifeless copy differing in nature, through whom the Father works, speaks and appears; unlike Athanasius he insists that the Son's own real agency is required for natural unity, and he reads titles like 'Angel' as naming office, not nature.
