The others take different angles: Gregory of Nyssa argues from the wording of John 1:1 and separates the Father–Son likeness from man's likeness to God, while Augustine argues from equality of essence and reads Christ's sayings as pointing faith to the Word equal to the Father, not to the assumed creature. Irenaeus treats Image differently, as the pattern after which man was made and which the incarnate Word displayed and restored, whereas Waterland makes the distinct philosophical point that shared authority alone, without unity of substance and origin, does not make one Godhead.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: how can such a one be the Father’s Image, not having the likeness of His unalterableness?

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For the Son is in such a sense the Image, as to be One in kind with the Father, and yet to indicate that the Father is His Origin.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Why This Opinion is to Be Rejected.
refs.quote: if a pious faith teaches us, as it does, that the Son is like the Father after an equality of essence, then that which is made in the likeness of the Son must needs also be made in the likeness of the Father.

ans.text:
The Son is the Image of the Father in the fullest sense possible. He is not a copy or a picture of God but God's own perfect likeness, sharing the very same divine nature. Whatever the Father is, the Son is too, except that the Son is from the Father. So yes, He is one in nature with Him.

The Bible speaks this way more than once. Paul writes in Colossians 1:15, "The Son is the image of the invisible God." Hebrews 1:3 calls Him "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Jesus says it himself in John 14:9: "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father." God cannot be seen, yet in the Son He is fully shown.

It helps to think about what kind of image this is. A portrait of your grandmother may look like her, but it is made of paint and canvas, not flesh and blood. It shows her without being what she is. The Son is not that kind of image. He is a living Image of the living God. Think instead of a son who is the image of his father because he shares his father's nature, not because someone painted him. Even that comparison falls short, because a human son is a separate being. The divine Son shares the one undivided being of God. That is why John 1:1 can say the Word was with God and also that "the Word was God." The Son is not something less than God that resembles Him. He is God, showing God.

This has a clear consequence. If seeing the Son really is seeing the Father, then everything true of the Father must be true of the Son. The Father is eternal, all-powerful, unchanging, Lord and Creator. An image lacking any of these would show us a smaller God and a false picture. So the Son is eternal too, never coming into being. He is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). He does not change, for "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Hebrews 13:8). A changeable Son could not be the true Image of an unchangeable Father.

Some readers stumble over the word "firstborn" in Colossians 1:15. In the Bible it often means the one with the rank and rights of the heir, not simply the first one made. The next verse makes this plain: all things were created through Him. The Creator of all things cannot be one of the things created.

Yet calling Him the Image also tells us something true. The Son is not the Father. An image comes from an original, so the Son's being Image points to the Father as His source. That is what "begotten" means: the Son is from the Father by nature, as a son is from a father, not made from outside like a creature. He is equal in nature and distinct as a person. Both truths stand together.

You might ask: does the Bible not say that we are made in God's image too (Genesis 1:26)? It does, but the likeness is very different. We are creatures who reflect God in limited ways, as a mirror reflects light it does not produce. The Son is the light itself. In fact, the Bible suggests we were made after the pattern of the Son. That likeness was spoiled by sin. When the Son became man, He showed the true image in human flesh. Now He restores it in us, as God's people are "conformed to the image of His Son" (Romans 8:29). The Son is the original Image. We are images of the Image.

This also answers why the Son alone is called the Image of the Father, when faithful saints, apostles and martyrs also become like God. They become like Him by imitation, learning and growing by grace. The Son is like Him by nature. No apostle ever said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), or "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me." No saint is called the Word, the Wisdom, or the only Son of God. Scripture asks, "Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?" (Exodus 15:11). The answer is that no creature is. Only the One who shares God's own nature can be His true Image.

Several objections are worth a gentle answer. First, the Son is "sent" by the Father. Does being sent make Him lower? No. Sending describes the order of the mission: the Father sends and the Son comes. It does not mean a difference in nature. A father may send his son on an errand, and the son is no less human for going. The Son was sent to make the Father known, and He could do that only because He is the Father's perfect Image.

Second, in the Old Testament a figure called "the angel of the LORD" appears to people such as Hagar and Moses. Many Christians have understood this as the Son appearing before He became man. Does the title "angel" mean He is a created spirit? The word simply means "messenger." It names a task, not a nature. The same passages call this messenger God. Hagar names Him "the God who sees me" (Genesis 16:13), and from the burning bush He says, "I am the God of your father" (Exodus 3:6). He is a messenger by role and God by nature.

Third, Jesus says in John 12:44, "Whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me." Is He turning faith away from Himself? Not at all. He is saying that faith in Him never stops at Him alone or at what can be seen of Him. Trusting the Son means trusting the Father, because they are one. The same Jesus says all should "honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). He is no rival drawing worship from the Father. Everything He does glorifies the Father, and whoever honors Him honors the Father too.

Finally, being the Father's Image does not make the Son a mere instrument the Father moves around. His works are truly His own, done freely and in perfect agreement with the Father. That is what you would expect if the two share one nature and one will. When the Son acts, God acts. When He speaks, God speaks. When we look at Jesus, we are not looking at a reflection of a distant God. We are looking at God Himself, made known to us.

topics.title: What do the analogies of light, radiance and fountain teach about the Father and the Son?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the images of light and radiance, sun and rays, and fountain and stream show the Son as inseparable from the Father and co-eternal with Him. Athanasius, Irenaeus, Basil and Gregory of Nyssa each argue that radiance never exists apart from its source or after it, and Waterland reads the Fathers' use of these similitudes, and Athanasius's 'apaugasma', as proof that they held the Son to be uncreated and from the Father's very substance. Athanasius presses the analogy furthest as a positive argument: generation by nature rather than by a prior act of will, oneness of seeing (to see the Son is to see the Father), and receiving all things without ever having lacked them. Gregory of Nyssa, by contrast, stresses the limits of these images: they must be purified of material notions such as dispersion, loss and emission, they supplement the inadequate name 'Son', and what they fall short of is made up by John's prologue, not by the analogy itself. He also uses glory and brightness against Eunomius to rule out any intermediary 'energy' between Father and Son. Hilary differs in emphasis by testing the images critically: he rejects Hieracas's two-flames-from-one-lamp model because it makes the shared substance something outside both Persons and ignores the Son's birth, while defending 'Light from Light' as God born from God, and Irenaeus uses light from light to deny that any part of the one light is older or younger than another.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: So also when the Son is beheld, so is the Father, for He is the Father’s radiance; and thus the Father and the Son are one.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Their bond of union is not, like that of two flames, two wicks of one lamp, something outside Themselves.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: for before the brightness, of course neither was there any glory, for concurrently with the existence of the glory there assuredly beams forth its brightness; and it is impossible in the nature of things that one should be severed from the other

ans.text:
These pictures teach that the Son comes from the Father and yet has always been with Him, sharing everything the Father is, with nothing between them. The Bible uses them because ordinary words like "father" and "son" alone could mislead us. Images of light, radiance and flowing water fill in what a family comparison leaves out.

Start with the clearest example. Hebrews 1:3 says, "The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Think about the sun and its light. The light comes from the sun, not the other way round. Yet there was never a moment when the sun existed and was not yet shining. As long as there is a sun, there is sunlight. A dark sun would not really be a sun at all.

So it is with the Father and the Son. The Son is "from" the Father, which is what the Bible means when it calls Him the Father's only begotten Son. "Begotten" means born from, sharing the same nature, rather than made. But He did not come along later. If there were ever a time when the Son was not, the Father's glory would once have been without its brightness. That is unthinkable for God. To say the Son had a beginning is in the end to say something wrong about the Father too. This is why John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word," not that the Word began at some point.

The image also shows that the Son shares the Father's very being. Sunlight is not a different thing that the sun manufactures. It is the sun's own light streaming out. In the same way the Son is not a product the Father built. He comes from the Father's own being. That is why Christians confess Him as "Light from Light, true God from true God." He is light that comes from light and is just as truly light.

It also explains how seeing the Son is seeing the Father. Whatever sunlight falls on, the sun is lighting up. You meet the sun through its rays. Jesus says in John 14:9, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father," and in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one." When the Son reveals, heals or forgives, it is the Father's own light reaching us through Him. Nothing stands in between, no go-between power or lesser agent. Nothing can come between glory and its brightness, or between a person and their exact likeness.

The pictures help with another question too: did God have to decide to have a Son, as if He weighed it up first? A light does not deliberate about whether to shine. Shining is simply what light is. The Son comes from the Father by the Father's very nature, not by a choice that came before Him. That does not mean the Father is forced or unwilling. Father and Son delight in each other eternally. But the Son is not one of God's projects. He is the Father's own.

The same idea explains verses where the Son "receives" things from the Father. Jesus says in Matthew 11:27, "All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father," and John 3:35 says the Father "has placed all things in His hands." If sunlight could speak and say the sun had given it the whole world to light up, it would not mean it once lacked that. It would mean that everything the sun has belongs to the light as well. The Son has always had all things, and He always has them from the Father.

The fountain and stream make similar points. Psalm 36:9 says to God, "For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light." A spring and the water flowing from it are one water. As long as the spring flows, the stream is there. A light also gives without losing anything. Light a candle from another and the first is not dimmer. The Father gives His whole life to the Son and keeps it fully. Nothing is used up, divided or split off.

Scripture uses other gentle images in the same way. It speaks of fragrance from perfume and of breath from the one who breathes. Perfume is never without its scent. We should take from these only what they mean to teach: the Son is from the Father and always with Him.

These comparisons also have limits, and it helps to know where they break down. Every one of them is taken from the created world, and God is not a physical object. Sunlight spreads out and weakens with distance. Scent fades, breath scatters into the air, and a stream can be cut off from its spring. None of that applies to God. The Son is not a smaller piece of the Father or a dimmer copy of Him. He is not something leaking away from Him. In the physical world, too, a ray is not quite the same as the sun itself. That is why the Bible does not rest everything on one picture. John 1:1 adds plainly that "the Word was God." Whatever the image cannot carry, that statement does.

Some comparisons simply mislead. One old idea pictured the Father and Son as two flames burning from one lamp. That suggests the divine nature is a third thing, like the oil or the wick, that the two of them draw on. But there is nothing behind or beneath the Father and the Son that they share like a fuel supply. Another weak picture is two torches lit one after another. That only tells us one is older than the other, which is exactly what we must not say. When light comes from light, it is one light, and no part of it is older than another.

There is one more misunderstanding to avoid. Someone might hear "radiance" and think the Son is just the Father's glow, a mode or a power of the Father rather than a real person. But John 1:1 also says "the Word was with God." You can only be with someone who is not simply yourself. The Son is truly distinct from the Father, and He talks with Him, loves Him and is sent by Him. He is also truly one with Him in being.

So these images are windows, not cages. They help us see that the Son is from the Father, has always been with the Father, and shares all that the Father is, with nothing between them. Then Scripture's plain words guard us from pressing the pictures too far.

topics.title: Is the Son's light different from or inferior to the Father's light?
topics.cmp: Answers the objection that calling the Father 'Light unapproachable' and the Son 'true Light', or mapping ungenerate and generate onto light, implies a difference of nature.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: Accordingly the unapproachable is identical with the true, because that which is signified by each expression is equally inaccessible to evil.

ans.text:
No. The Son's light is not a lesser or different kind of light from the Father's. It is the same divine light, the one light of the one God, shining from the Father in the Son.

The question comes from two phrases in the Bible. Paul says that God "lives in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see" (1 Timothy 6:16). John says of Jesus that "the true Light who gives light to every man was coming into the world" (John 1:9). Some have argued that these are two kinds of light. On that view the Father's light is lofty and out of reach, and the Son's light is a lower light that comes down to us. But look at what the two words actually mean.

"Unapproachable" means nothing impure or dark can get near it. "True" means it is the real thing, with no falsehood or darkness mixed in. Both words point to the same thing: light that is completely pure and has nothing of its opposite in it. You could swap them and still speak rightly. The Son's light is unapproachable, because no evil can touch it. The Father's light is true, because it is real light all the way through. John sums this up: "God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5). That is true of the Father and of the Son alike.

There is also a problem of consistency. Some have said the Father must be greater because Jesus calls Him "the only true God" (John 17:3). If "true" made the Father greater there, then calling the Son the "true Light" would make the Son greater than the Father. Nobody can make the word "true" raise someone up in one verse and lower someone in another. In fact, Scripture uses the same language of the Son: "He is the true God and eternal life" (1 John 5:20). Jesus also says plainly, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). That is something only God can say.

Someone might push further. The Father is "unbegotten," meaning He comes from no one. The Son is "begotten," meaning He comes eternally from the Father, not made but sharing the Father's own life. So, the argument goes, doesn't the Son's light differ from the Father's in the same way?

Follow that idea to its end and you can see it fails. Begotten and unbegotten are not higher and lower on a scale. They are simple opposites: you either come from another or you don't. If the difference between the Father's light and the Son's light were that kind of either/or, then the Father would be light and the Son would be its opposite. The opposite of light is darkness. No Christian could say the Son is darkness, when Scripture calls Him the light that darkness cannot overcome (John 1:5). So the premise must be wrong. Being begotten tells us where the Son comes from. It does not tell us that He is a different or weaker kind of light.

Hebrews puts it beautifully: the Son "is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Think of the sun and its brightness. The brightness comes from the sun, but it is not a second, dimmer sun. It is the sun's own light, and there was never a sun without its shining. Or think of one candle lighting another. The second flame is just as much fire as the first.

Every picture falls short somewhere. In our world, light weakens the farther it travels from its source. With God there is no distance and no fading. The Son is not light that has traveled away from the Father and lost some brightness on the way. He is the full shining of the Father's own glory. Christians have long confessed Him in just these terms, as Light from Light, true God from true God.

This matters for us. The Father's light is unapproachable to sinners on our own. Yet the Son is that same light, come near. That is why Jesus can say, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). If the Son's light were lesser, we would meet only a lesser god in Him. Because His light is the Father's own light, when we look to Jesus we are seeing God Himself, shining in a way we can bear. And one day, Scripture says, the city of God will need no sun, "because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp" (Revelation 21:23). That is one light, from the Father and the Lamb together.

topics.title: How is the divine Word like and unlike a human word?
topics.cmp: Finds the likeness of the eternal Word in the mind's inner word rather than in outward speech, sounds or letters. It also shows how the divine Word differs from human words, which are formed, unfold in time, can be false, and are not 'essence of essence'.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How Great is the Unlikeness Between Our Word and the…
refs.quote: the great might of that Word is that it cannot lie, because there cannot be there “yea and nay,” but “yea yea, nay nay.”

ans.text:
The Son of God is called "the Word" because he is to the Father something like what a thought is to a mind. But the likeness is to the quiet word inside your head, not the sounds that come out of your mouth. And even that likeness falls short in important ways.

John opens his Gospel this way: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Why would the Bible call the eternal Son a "word"? Think about what happens when you speak. Before you say anything, something is already going on inside you. You know something, and you bring that knowledge into focus as a clear thought. Only then do you put it into sounds, letters or gestures so someone else can share it.

That inner thought is the real word. The sounds are only its servants. Picture a bilingual person who knows that it is raining. The thought is the same whether they say "it's raining" in English or "llueve" in Spanish. They could also just point at the window. The thought itself belongs to no language at all. Think about a city you have visited. Your "word" for it is not the name, spoken or silently rehearsed. It is the picture and understanding of that city you carry in your memory. When you speak, your thought does not leave you. You still have it. The sounds simply help a similar thought form in your listener's mind.

Here is the likeness. Your inner word is born from what you know. It has nothing of its own; it simply expresses that knowledge. If it is a true thought, it matches what you know exactly. In a similar way, the Son comes from the Father. He is the perfect expression of all that the Father is and knows. That is why Scripture calls him "the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3) and "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). It also explains why the Word never "leaves" the Father. He is always "with God" even while he is sent to us.

The word "begotten" fits here. It means "brought forth from" one's own being, as a child comes from a parent, and not made from outside material. A thought is not built out of bricks. It comes from the mind itself. The Son, likewise, is not a creature God made. He comes forth from the Father himself.

When we say God "speaks" through the Word, we do not mean he made noises in heaven. The outward speaking happened when "the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). Jesus' human voice, his actions and his life became the outward "sound" by which God's inner Word reached human beings.

Now for the differences, and they are large. First, our words unfold in time. A sentence has a beginning, a middle and an end. Even our silent thoughts take time to form. The Son is not like that. He did not start as a half-formed idea and then become clear. He was "in the beginning," eternally complete and eternally with the Father. There was never a time when God was without his Word, just as there was never a time when God was without wisdom.

Second, our words are formed by trial and effort. We turn things over in our minds, grope for clarity and gradually settle on what we mean. Before that, our thought is vague and shapeless. The Son was never vague, never "in progress," never something that could have turned out otherwise. He is simply and perfectly equal to the Father from whom he comes.

Third, our words can be false. We can be mistaken without knowing it, or we can lie on purpose. The Word of God can do neither. Jesus says he does nothing on his own but only what he sees the Father doing (John 5:19). He says he speaks what the Father has given him to say. Paul writes that in the Son of God there was never a wavering "Yes" and "No" (2 Corinthians 1:19-20). This is not a weakness, as if the Son lacked some freedom. It is his strength. Being unable to lie is a mark of perfect truth, and Jesus calls himself "the truth" (John 14:6).

Fourth, and most deeply, our thoughts are not our very being. You know many things you could forget tomorrow, and you would still be you. Your thoughts come and go while you remain. So your inner word is something you have, not what you are. In God it is different. God does not merely have knowledge the way we do. His knowing and his being are one and the same. So the Word that comes from the Father's knowledge is not a passing idea. It is fully God, sharing the one divine nature. That is why the church confesses the Son as "God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God." A human thought could never be called that.

One caution is worth adding. This comparison does not mean the Son is just an idea in God's head, or an impersonal force, or a part of God. Scripture shows the Word as a person who is "with God" and who becomes flesh, lives, speaks, dies and rises. The picture of the inner word helps us see how the Son can come from the Father without being created and without being separated from him. It is a mirror, though, not a photograph. It gives a real glimpse, but the reality is far greater than the picture.

So the next time you put a thought into words, remember the comparison. The clear, truthful thought behind your speech is a small, imperfect sign of the eternal Son. He is everything the Father is, perfectly expressed. He was never formed, never fading and never false.

topics.title: In what sense is the Word of God Truth?
topics.cmp: Why the Word is Truth itself and incapable of falsehood, and what 'grace and truth' in John 1:14 signify.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Word of God is in All Things Equal to the Father,…
refs.quote: this Word is truly truth, since whatever is in that knowledge from which it is born is also in itself and whatever is not in that knowledge is not in the Word

ans.text:
The Word of God is Truth in the deepest possible sense: not merely someone who tells the truth, but the one who is the truth, the perfect and unchangeable expression of everything God is and knows. That is why Jesus could say in John 14:6, "I am the way and the truth and the life." He did not say he teaches the truth or points to it. He said he is it.

It helps to think about how our own words work. When we speak, we try to put what is in our minds into words. But our words can go wrong in several ways. Our minds may be mistaken, so we say false things without meaning to. We may lie on purpose. Our words may fall short of what we really mean. And even when we speak truly, things change, and what was true yesterday may not be true tomorrow.

None of this can happen with the Word of God. The Bible calls the Son "the Word" (John 1:1) because he is how God expresses himself. Unlike our words, he is not a partial or rough attempt. Everything in the Father's mind and knowledge is fully present in the Son, and nothing that is not in the Father's knowledge is in the Son. Hebrews 1:3 says the Son is "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." An exact representation leaves nothing out and adds nothing false. And since God never makes mistakes, his perfect self-expression cannot contain a mistake either.

The Word is also unchanging, just as the Father is. Hebrews 13:8 tells us that "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever." Falsehood often creeps in when something shifts and no longer matches reality. But the Word does not shift. He is always exactly what God is, so there is no room for any gap between what he is and what is true.

This is why the Bible can say that it is impossible for God to lie (Hebrews 6:18). This is not a limit on God, as if there were something he wanted to do but could not. It is like saying light cannot be darkness. Being unable to lie is part of his perfection, not a weakness. The Son shares this fully, because he is God from God, equal with the Father in every way.

A common confusion is to think "the Word of God" here simply means the Bible. Scripture is indeed God's word written, and Jesus prays in John 17:17, "Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth." The Bible is true because it comes from God and its whole message points to Christ. But in John 1 "the Word" is a person, the eternal Son, who was with God and was God. The written word is true because it comes from the living Word, who is Truth itself.

It also helps to know that in the Bible "truth" is more than accurate facts. It carries the sense of faithfulness and reliability, something you can lean your whole weight on. When God revealed himself to Moses, he described himself as abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). Jesus being the truth means he is utterly dependable. What he shows us of God is real, and what he promises he will do.

That brings us to John 1:14: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth." A few verses later John adds, "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). These two words fit together beautifully.

"Grace" means God's undeserved kindness. The greatest grace that has ever happened in history is that the eternal Son joined himself to our human nature, becoming one person who is both truly God and truly man. No human being earned this. It was pure gift. Everything Jesus did in time, his birth, his miracles, his death and his rising, belongs to this grace. These are things we can learn about, hear told, and believe.

"Truth" points us to who he is eternally, before and beyond all of that: the very Wisdom and Word of God, the full reality of God himself. Colossians 2:3 says that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge."

What matters most is that it is the same Son who is both. The one who was born in Bethlehem and died on a cross is the very same person who is eternal Truth. This is how God brings us to himself. We cannot climb up to the eternal truth of God by our own power. Our minds are clouded and our hearts are not clean. So the Truth came down to us in grace. When we trust in what he did for us in history, we are forgiven and cleansed, and that cleansing prepares us to know him as he truly and eternally is. Jesus said, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). Faith in the Word made flesh is the road that leads to seeing the glory of the Word who was with God from the beginning.

So when we say the Word is Truth, we mean that in Jesus we are not getting a copy, an approximation, or one opinion about God among many. We are meeting God's own perfect self-expression, who cannot deceive us and will never change, and who came full of grace so that we could share in that truth forever.

topics.title: What do Christ's many names and titles reveal, and how should figurative names be read?
topics.cmp: Only three authors address this topic, and on separate questions, so their answers complement rather than contradict one another. Gregory of Nyssa supplies most of the answers: he holds that the Son's distinctively divine names (Word, Life, Light, Image, Brightness) prove His nature differs from creation, and that the Son was the Existent who spoke to Moses. He also argues that figurative titles like Shepherd, Stone, Axe and Bread are genuinely scriptural, that they name Christ's various benefits toward us rather than define His essence, and that 'first-born' must be read passage by passage, not used to infer His essence. Irenaeus of Lyons, arguing against the heretics, insists from John's Gospel that Word, Only-begotten, Life, Light, Saviour and Christ all name one and the same person rather than distinct beings. Athanasius of Alexandria, on a related point of reading, argues that Scripture's 'as' comparisons with animals signify moral imitation, not change of nature. All three rely chiefly on close reading of Scripture, but they differ in emphasis: Gregory weighs what the names do and do not reveal about the Son's essence, Irenaeus defends the unity of the person named, and Athanasius gives a general rule for reading figurative language.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: then it is clear that He Who is these things is by nature something else besides the creation, which neither is nor is called any of these things.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: since Logos, and Monogenes, and Zoe, and Phōs, and Soter, and Christus, and the Son of God, and He who became incarnate for us, have been proved to be one and the same

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: And He said this, not that we may become in nature beasts of burden, or become serpents and doves; for He hath not so made us Himself, and therefore nature does not allow of it

ans.text:
Christ's many names show us one and the same Lord from many angles. Some tell us who He is with God from all eternity. Others tell us what He does for us. None of the picture-names means that His nature changes into a door, a rock or a loaf of bread.

Start with the fact that they all belong to one person. John's Gospel opens by calling Him the Word, then says that in Him was life, that He is the true Light, that He came to His own, and that "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:1-14). John is not describing a Word, a Life, a Light and a Saviour as four different heavenly beings. He is describing Jesus. Every title in the New Testament points back to the one Son of God who was born of Mary, died and rose again.

Some of these names lift Him clearly above everything that was made. John says that "in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and that all things were made through Him (John 1:1-3). Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Paul calls Him "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). No angel, prophet or created thing is ever spoken of like this. A creature can reflect God's glory the way the moon reflects the sun. Only the Son is the radiance itself.

These names are also chosen with care. A word comes from a mind, yet a mind is never without its thoughts. Light shines from the sun, yet the sun is never without its light. So the Son comes from the Father, yet there was never a time when the Father was without Him. He shares the Father's very nature, which is what "essence" means: what God is. He is not a lesser copy made later.

The name I AM points the same way. When God sent Moses to Israel, He gave His name as "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14). This is the God who simply is, without beginning. Jesus deliberately took that language for Himself: "before Abraham was born, I am!" (John 8:58). His hearers understood exactly what He was claiming, and they picked up stones. Many Christians also believe that when the LORD appeared and spoke to Moses and the patriarchs, it was the Son making the Father known, since "no one has ever seen God" except through Him (John 1:18). Others are more cautious and simply say the one God spoke. Both agree that Jesus is the God of Israel come in the flesh.

The title "firstborn" puzzles many readers, because it can sound as if Christ was the first thing God created. But Scripture uses the word in more than one way, and each passage has to be read on its own terms. In Colossians 1:15-16 He is "the firstborn over all creation," and the very next verse explains why: all things were created in Him and through Him. In the Bible the firstborn son was the heir and held first rank. God even says of David's line, "I will make him My firstborn" (Psalm 89:27), though David was the youngest son. So the word is about rank and inheritance, not about being made. Elsewhere Christ is "the firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18), because He is the first to rise to everlasting life. He is also "the firstborn among many brothers" (Romans 8:29), because by grace we become God's children in Him. These describe His place as Saviour. They do not mean He is a creature like us.

Then there are the picture-names: the Door or Gate, the Good Shepherd, the Vine, the Bread of life, the Rock, the Way. Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep" (John 10:11), and "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6). Paul says of the rock that gave Israel water in the desert, "that rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4).

No one thinks Jesus is made of wood or stone. Scripture often uses ordinary things as pictures. We are told not to be like a stubborn horse or mule (Psalm 32:9), and to be shrewd as snakes and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16). That does not mean we turn into animals. It means we learn from them what to avoid and what to imitate. In the same way, a comparison with Christ teaches us something true about Him without changing what He is.

The picture-names mostly describe what He is to us. He is Light because He drives away our darkness and ignorance. He is Life because He gives eternal life. He is the Way because He brings us from wandering to the Father. He is the Door because through Him we enter and are safe. He is Bread because He feeds our souls, just as the manna fed Israel (John 6:32-35). He is the Rock because we can stand on Him, and the Shepherd because He guides and protects us.

The sheer number of names is itself a lesson. Christ is greater than any one name can hold, so Scripture gives us many, each catching some part of His goodness. Some open a window onto His eternal oneness with the Father. Others show the many ways He gives Himself to us. Taken together they do not describe many beings, or a changing being. They describe one Lord, fully God, who has come near to save us and can be known and trusted under every one of these names.

title: The Son as Creator and Proverbs 8
desc: The Son's role as true Creator and Preserver rather than a created instrument, including Wisdom 'created' in Proverbs 8 and the title 'first-born of all creation'.

topics.title: Is the Son the true Creator with the Father, or a created instrument or first creature?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son is the true Creator with the Father and not a created instrument or first creature. Waterland, Hilary, Owen, Augustine, Novatian and Irenaeus argue mainly from Scripture's ascription of creation to the Word (John 1, Hebrews 1:10, Genesis read alongside John). Waterland and Hilary add that creatorship, or making out of nothing, is the distinguishing mark of the one true God, and Waterland further rests on the unanimous testimony of the ancients and on the Fathers' restriction of worship to the Creator. Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa press reductio arguments against the Arian and Eunomian instrument-theory: an endless regress of mediators, the contradiction of the Maker being counted among the 'all things' he made, the smith's-tools analogy, and the absurdity that the Son would exist for creatures' sake. They differ on 'first-born of all creation' (Colossians 1:15). Gregory refers it wholly to the saving economy and the new creation; Athanasius combines the economy (the Word's condescension) with the Son's otherness from creation; Hilary, Bickersteth and Warfield read it as priority or lordship over all things. Irenaeus stands somewhat apart in emphasis: against Gnostic demiurges he stresses that the Father is the true author working through his own Word, while Waterland explains the Fathers' 'Father commands, Son executes' language as a difference of order and principle, not of power.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: That the Son was and is endowed with creative powers, is plain from these texts, and others which might be added ; and is confirmed by the unanimous suffrage of Catholic antiquity.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the…
refs.quote: For He made all things by His word, which Word we know, by the right rule of faith, to be His only Son.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: It Is, Moreover, Proved by Moses in the Beginning of the…
refs.quote: He shows that none other was then present to God—by whom these works were commanded that they should be made—than He by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made.

ans.text:
The Son is the true Creator together with the Father, not a tool God made first and then used to make everything else. The Bible says plainly that everything that exists was made through Him, which means He stands on the Creator's side of the line between God and creation, not on the creature's side.

Start with the opening of John's Gospel. John 1:1 says the Word was with God and the Word was God. Then verse 3 says, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Think carefully about that sentence. If the Son were himself a made thing, then he would be one of the "all things" and would have had to make himself. That makes no sense. John leaves no gap for the Son to be a creature. Everything that was ever made came through Him, so He Himself was never made.

The rest of the New Testament says the same. Colossians 1:16 says, "For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible... All things were created through Him and for Him." Hebrews 1:2 says God made the universe through the Son. Then Hebrews 1:10 takes words from Psalm 102, a psalm addressed to the LORD, the God of Israel, and applies them directly to the Son: "In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands."

This matters because the Old Testament treats creation as the mark of the one true God. In Isaiah 44:24 the LORD says He made all things and stretched out the heavens by Himself, alone. No angel or helper shared the work. So when the New Testament gives the work of creation to the Son, it is not handing Him a lesser job. It is placing Him inside the identity of the one God. Only God can bring something out of nothing simply by willing it. If the Son does that, He has the power and the nature of God.

The Genesis account fits this. In Genesis 1, God speaks and things come to be: "Let there be light." God creates by His word. John takes up that very picture. He tells us that the Word by which God made the world is a Person, the Son, who was with God in the beginning and who later became flesh. The one who formed the first man from dust is the same one who was born of Mary to make us new.

What about Colossians 1:15, which calls the Son "the firstborn over all creation"? Some have read "firstborn" to mean "first one created." But that is not what the word means in the Bible. "Firstborn" often speaks of rank, inheritance and authority more than birth order. In Psalm 89:27 God says He will make David His firstborn, even though David was the youngest son in his family. The point is supremacy. And Paul explains his own words in the very next verse: the Son is firstborn "for" in Him all things were created. He is first over creation because He is its Maker and heir, not because He is its first product. Had Paul wanted to say "first created," he had a word for that and did not use it. Many Christians also note that Paul calls Christ "the firstborn from among the dead" (Colossians 1:18), which points to His leading the way in the new creation that comes through His resurrection. Either way, the title speaks of His lordship, not His being made.

Someone may also ask about the word "begotten," as in Jesus being the only begotten Son. To beget is to bring forth something of your own kind, the way a father has a son who shares his human nature. To make is to produce something of a different kind, the way a carpenter makes a table. The Son is begotten of the Father, not made. He shares the Father's very being, the way light shares the nature of the fire it shines from. And this is not something that happened at a point in time. God never existed without His Word or His Wisdom. Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). If the Son were created, there would have been a time when God had no wisdom and no word, and then acquired them later. That is unthinkable for the eternal God.

This brings us to Proverbs 8, where Wisdom speaks and says the LORD brought her forth at the beginning of His way, before His works of old, and that she was beside Him like a master workman when He made the world. In the early centuries some used verse 22 to argue that the Son was the first thing God created. Sincere Christians have read this chapter in different ways. Many have seen it as the Son speaking, because the New Testament identifies Christ as God's Wisdom. Those who read it that way have often taken the language of being brought forth as a poetic way of speaking about the Son's eternal coming from the Father, or about the role He would take on for our salvation, not as a statement that He was made. Others read Proverbs 8 first of all as a poem that personifies God's wisdom, a figure of speech, which finds its fullest meaning in Christ but was not meant to give a technical account of His origin. Either way, a poem in Proverbs should not be read against the plain teaching of John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16 that the Son made all things. And the chapter itself says Wisdom was with God before anything else existed, sharing in His work.

A last worry is that the Bible says God created "through" the Son, which might sound like the Father is the real Maker and the Son is just His instrument, like an axe in a woodcutter's hand. But the word "through" does not make the Son lesser. Romans 11:36 says of God Himself, "from Him and through Him and to Him are all things." The Father does not need a tool, as if He could not create on His own. Rather, the Father never acts apart from His own Word, just as you never act apart from your own mind. When God speaks, His Word is always there. 1 Corinthians 8:6 puts it beautifully: there is one God, the Father, from whom all things came, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came. Paul takes the ancient confession that there is one God and one Lord and places both the Father and the Son within it.

So there is an order in how the Father and Son work. All things come from the Father through the Son. But it is the order of a Father and Son who share one nature and one work, not the order of a master and a hired hand. Jesus said that whatever the Father does, the Son also does (John 5:19). The Son is not an assistant who took the Creator's orders. He is the Creator, with the Father and the Spirit.

This is good news. The one who came to save us is not a stranger to our world or a go-between who stands halfway between God and us. He is the one who made us. When He calms the storm, heals the sick, and raises the dead, the Maker is restoring His own handiwork. And because He is God, when we trust and worship Him we are not giving to a creature the honor that belongs to God alone.

topics.title: Is the Son the Preserver and Governor of all things, and does this prove His Godhead?
topics.cmp: Waterland, Bickersteth, Athanasius, Basil and Irenaeus all ascribe the work of creating and sustaining all things to the Son. Waterland argues historically, from the ante-Nicene Fathers who style the Son Creator in the fullest sense, while granting a priority of order in which the Father gives the fiat and the Son executes it. He also argues from Paul that creating proves eternal power and Godhead. Athanasius grounds the same conclusion by contrast: creating belongs to God alone and his proper Word, whereas a mere minister like Moses never brought things into being. Bickersteth gathers Scripture texts to show the Son as Creator, Upholder and supreme Governor, and Basil stresses that he upholds all without time or bodily instruments. Irenaeus extends the Word's work to forming each person in the womb. The authors divide plainly on Proverbs 8:15, 'By me kings reign': Irenaeus takes it as the Word installing earthly rulers, so that rule comes from God and not the devil. Gregory of Nyssa rejects that reading, because it would make Wisdom share the blame of bad kings, and interprets the kings as the poor in spirit and the princes as those who rule their passions.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: A man must be a very stranger to the ancients, who can make any question whether they attributed the work of creation to the Son, as much as to the Father. They ascribed it equally to both

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: to minister is of things originate as of servants, but to frame and to create is of God alone, and of His proper Word and His Wisdom.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: Jesus is the Creator, for “by him (the Son of his love) were all things created that are in heaven and that are in earth, visible and invisible

ans.text:
Yes, the Bible teaches that the Son keeps the whole universe in being and rules over it, and because only God can do that, these works show that He is truly God.

Start with what Scripture says plainly. Hebrews 1:3 describes the Son as "upholding all things by His powerful word." Colossians 1:17 says, "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together." These verses do not only say that the Son made the world long ago. They say He is holding it together right now. If His word stopped sustaining it for a moment, nothing would remain. Every sunrise, every heartbeat, every atom staying in place depends on Him.

Jesus speaks the same way. When He was criticized for healing on the Sabbath, He answered, "My Father is working until now, and I too am working" (John 5:17). God rested from creating on the seventh day, but He has never stopped caring for and governing what He made. Jesus claims to share in that ongoing work. A little later He adds that whatever the Father does, the Son does too (John 5:19). His listeners understood exactly what He meant. They saw that He was making Himself equal with God.

This care reaches down to each one of us. The psalmist praises God because "You knit me together in my mother's womb" (Psalm 139:13), and God tells Jeremiah that He knew him before He formed him in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5). Scripture also says that all things were made through the Son, and without Him nothing was made (John 1:3). So the One who quietly shapes every child before birth is the same One who walked among us. When Jesus made clay and gave sight to the man born blind (John 9), He was doing openly what He had always done in secret: forming and repairing the bodies He had made.

The Son's rule also reaches the rulers of this world. Colossians 1:16 says that thrones, dominions, rulers and authorities were all created through Him and for Him. Jesus says that all authority in heaven and on earth belongs to Him (Matthew 28:18), and Revelation calls Him King of kings and Lord of lords. Paul teaches that there is no authority except what comes from God (Romans 13:1). Put together, these mean that no president, king or government holds power apart from Christ's permission and oversight.

Proverbs 8 raises a question here. Wisdom speaks in that chapter and says, "By me kings reign." Many Christians, from very early on, have heard the voice of the Son in this Wisdom, since the New Testament calls Christ "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). On that reading, the verse teaches that earthly rule comes from God through His Word, not from the devil. Other sincere Christians have been more careful. They note that Proverbs 8 is first of all a poem about wisdom itself. They worry that the verse might seem to make God responsible for every wicked king. So they read the "kings" in a spiritual sense: people who rule their own desires by God's wisdom. Either way, the wider teaching stands on firmer ground in Colossians and Romans. God sets up and removes rulers. He does this without approving their sins, and He holds them to account for how they use His gift.

Why does all this prove that the Son is God? Paul says that God's "eternal power and divine nature" can be clearly seen from what He has made (Romans 1:20). Creating and sustaining a universe is not the kind of task God hands to a helper. The Old Testament insists that the Lord alone stretched out the heavens and made all things by Himself (Isaiah 44:24). If the Son does these things, He is not a second, lesser maker. He is the one God at work.

Someone might ask, "Didn't God use a mere man, Moses, to lead Israel and give the Law? Couldn't He likewise use a created being to run the world?" But there is a real difference. Moses was a messenger and a servant. He carried God's words and obeyed God's commands. He did not call things into existence or keep the stars in their courses. A servant can deliver a message. Only God can make something out of nothing and keep it from falling back into nothing. A created being would itself need to be held up. It could not be the one in whom all things hold together.

Another misunderstanding is that the Son does this slowly or with effort, like a worker with tools. Scripture says He upholds all things by His word. He needs no hands, no machinery and no time to get things done. Creation simply obeys Him, as the wind and waves did on the lake (Mark 4:39).

It also helps to understand the little word "through." When the Bible says all things were made through the Son, it does not mean He is a lesser go-between. Paul uses the same word of God Himself: all things are "from Him and through Him and to Him" (Romans 11:36). The Father, Son and Holy Spirit do not split creation into three jobs. They work as one God. The Father acts through the Son and by the Spirit, so every work of providence is fully the Father's and fully the Son's.

This matters for everyday faith. The Jesus who died for you is the same One holding your life together this very moment. He formed you before you were born. He keeps the world running, and He rules over every ruler. You can trust Him with your life and with the troubles of the world, because He is not a creature doing his best. He is the Lord.

topics.title: What does Scripture show about the Son sharing in the work of creation?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Son, as Word and Wisdom, is a true agent of creation and not a creature. Hilary, Augustine, Ambrose, Athanasius, Irenaeus and Owen all ground this in Scripture: Proverbs 8, John 1, Genesis 1 and its "Let us make," Psalm 33, Colossians and Hebrews. On "Let Us make," Ambrose answers yes, that the Son is joint Maker and therefore worshipped with the Father, while Hilary's answer is recorded as "No," yet his explanation affirms that the One addressed is not alien or powerless but has power to do what is spoken, so in substance he agrees with Ambrose. Hilary and Irenaeus both read the command in Psalm 33 as implying a distinct Word or Mediator who receives the command, and Hilary argues that creation by sheer will alone would leave no office for a Mediator. Athanasius, by contrast, emphasises that creation is referred to the divine Will rather than to a necessary process in the divine Nature, against Sabellius and Marcellus, and he stresses that Scripture distinguishes the Word from the works. Irenaeus and Owen both insist that even angels and heavenly powers received their very being through the Word, Owen against the Socinians and Irenaeus against Gnostic number speculation; Basil adds that every creature, heavenly powers included, is by creation a servant of God; and Irenaeus alone counsels restraint, holding that what God did before creating is not revealed.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: There is with God Wisdom, begotten before the worlds; and not only present with Him, but setting in order, for She was with Him, setting them in order.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: the Father, by saying, “Let Us make,” showed that the Son was to be worshipped with Himself as the Maker of all things.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: Whom, therefore, did He command? The Word, no doubt, “by whom,” he says, “the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of His mouth.”

ans.text:
Scripture shows that the Son was not a spectator at creation, and not a tool in someone else's hand. He made the world together with the Father, and everything that exists, from galaxies to angels, came into being through Him. That places the Son firmly on the Creator's side of the line between God and everything else.

The clearest statement comes at the start of John's Gospel. John calls the Son "the Word" and says the Word was with God and was God. Then he adds: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). John says it twice, once positively and once negatively, so that no gap is left. Nothing exists that the Father made without the Son. If something had been made apart from Him, John's sentence would be false.

Paul makes the same point and leaves no room for exceptions. In Colossians 1:16 he writes that in the Son "all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him." Those "thrones" and "rulers" are the highest powers in the unseen world, the angels. Some have suggested that the Son merely organized the angels or gave them their ranks, while someone else gave them their existence. Paul's words won't bear that. He says they were created through Him. And notice the last phrase: all things exist "for Him." Creation is not only His work. It is His possession and exists for His glory.

Hebrews says the same. God "has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe" (Hebrews 1:2). A few verses later, the writer takes words from Psalm 102 that speak of the LORD and applies them directly to the Son: "In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands" (Hebrews 1:10).

This matters because the Old Testament insists that creating is something only God does. In Isaiah 44:24 the LORD says that He made all things and stretched out the heavens by Himself, alone. So when the New Testament says the Son made all things, it is not giving Him a lesser job alongside God. It is saying He shares in the one work that belongs to God alone. A creature cannot create the universe, because a creature is part of the universe.

Scripture draws this same line between the Maker and the made in other ways too. Hebrews 4:12-13 speaks of the Word of God and says that nothing in all creation is hidden from His sight, and that everything lies open before the One to whom we must give account. Every creature, angels included, is a servant who will answer to Him. He is the Judge they answer to.

With the New Testament as our guide, we can look back at Genesis and see the Son there from the very beginning. Jesus Himself said that Moses wrote about Him (John 5:46). Genesis 1 describes creation again and again with the words "And God said." God does not simply wish the world into being. He speaks. Psalm 33 picks this up: "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made" (Psalm 33:6), and "He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm" (Psalm 33:9). John tells us who that Word is. The speaking of God at creation was not just a sound in the air. It was the eternal Word, the Son, through whom the Father acts. There is a simple logic here too. A command is given to someone who carries it out, and the world could not obey a command before it existed. The Father speaks, and the Son, His living Word, brings it to pass.

Then comes Genesis 1:26: "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness." Christians have long heard in this "Us" a hint of the conversation within God Himself. Some readers explain it as a royal "we," or as God addressing the angels. But the angels are never said to create anything. And human beings are made in God's image, not in the image of angels. In light of John and Colossians, it makes the best sense to hear the Father speaking with the Son and the Spirit. The verse does not present a superior giving orders to a reluctant or powerless helper. It is one shared purpose and one shared act: "Let Us make." Then verse 27 says "So God created man in His own image," singular. Three speak together, yet it is one God who creates.

Proverbs 8 adds a beautiful picture. There Wisdom speaks as a person and describes being present when God set the heavens in place and marked out the foundations of the earth. "I was a skilled craftsman beside Him," Wisdom says, "and I was His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence" (Proverbs 8:30). Christians have read this passage in light of the New Testament, which calls Christ "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24) and the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden (Colossians 2:3). The Psalms say of God's works, "In wisdom You have made them all" (Psalm 104:24).

So the picture is not of a Father working alone while His Son watches. The Son is beside Him, actively shaping and ordering the world, and sharing the Father's joy in what they have made. The same Scriptures that say God made all things in His Wisdom keep Wisdom distinct from the things that were made. Wisdom is the craftsman, not one of the products.

It is worth addressing one worry about Proverbs 8, because some have used it to argue that the Son is a created being. Proverbs 8:22 speaks of the LORD possessing or bringing forth Wisdom at the beginning of His way. This is poetry, and it should not be pressed to say that there was ever a time when God lacked His own Wisdom. God was never without wisdom. The point of the poem is that Wisdom was there before anything else, working alongside the Lord. The clear teaching of John 1, Colossians 1, and Hebrews 1 must guide how we read a poetic passage. Those texts place the Son before all things and say that every created thing came through Him.

Someone might also ask whether the word "through" makes the Son a mere instrument, the way a carpenter uses a hammer. The Bible's language does show an order within God. Paul puts it this way in 1 Corinthians 8:6: there is "one God, the Father, from whom all things came," and "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came." All things come from the Father, through the Son, and, as other passages add, by the Spirit's life-giving breath (Psalm 33:6; Genesis 1:2). But a hammer has no will, no power of its own, and no share in the honor of the finished house. The Son is described as the one who lays the foundations of the earth with His own hands. He is the one all things are made for, and the one who holds all things together (Colossians 1:17). He is not a tool. The "through" describes how the Father and Son work together, not a difference in rank between a real Creator and a lesser assistant.

It also helps to remember that creation was a free, loving choice of God, not something He was forced to do. The Father, Son, and Spirit did not need the world in order to be complete. They made it because they willed to share their goodness. As for what God was doing "before" creation, Scripture is largely silent, and it is wise not to fill that silence with guesses. What it does tell us is enough: the Son was with the Father in the beginning, and the world we live in is His handiwork.

This is why Christians worship Jesus without hesitation. We do not worship the creature. We worship the Creator (Romans 1:25). The One who was born in Bethlehem, who calmed the storm and who died and rose for us, is the same One through whom the stars, the seas, the angels and we ourselves were made. When He came into the world, John says, He came to what was His own (John 1:10-11).

topics.title: What do John's prologue and John 1:3 prove about the Word as Creator?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that John's prologue presents the Word as God and as Creator of absolutely everything, and none limits 'all things' or 'the world' to a lesser sense. On whether John 1:3 admits exceptions, Owen answers 'yes' and Irenaeus 'no', but they mean the same thing: Owen says the clause 'without him nothing was made' gives the 'all' absolute universality, and Irenaeus says no exception is stated, so visible and invisible, temporal and eternal things are all included. Where they differ is in which opponents they answer and how. Owen appeals to John's inspired purpose against Cerinthus and argues from the text that 'the world' that 'knew him not' cannot be the church or the gospel's new creation, as the Socinians claimed. Irenaeus reads the prologue as showing one Father acting through one Word and refutes the Valentinian Ogdoad and the Pleroma reading by pointing to the passage's order and omissions and to the meaning of 'all things'; Bickersteth instead builds a short syllogism linking John 1 with John's naming of Christ as 'the Word of God' elsewhere. Athanasius, Augustine and Gregory of Nyssa focus on the Son as Light against claims that he is light only in a lesser sense: Augustine contrasts illuminated apostles with the uncreated, illuminating Son, Gregory calls Eunomius's argument mere homonymy and also enlists Proverbs' Wisdom, Waterland (citing Augustine) infers that the Son himself was not made, and Hilary, drawing on Colossians, rejects the view that the Son was only a companion at creation.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: To put a stop unto his abominations, all authors agree that John, writing his Gospel, prefixed unto it that plain declaration of the eternal Deity of Christ which it is prefaced withal.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: Christ then, is the Word, Christ is the Creator, Christ is God.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: there is one God, the Father over all, and one Word of God, who is through all, by whom all things have been made

ans.text:
John's opening verses teach two things plainly: the Word, who became the man Jesus Christ, is truly God, and He is the one through whom God made absolutely everything that exists. John does not leave this to hints. He builds it into the first lines of his Gospel so that everything after them is read in that light.

Start with John 1:1: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Each phrase does a job. "In the beginning" echoes Genesis 1:1, when God created the heavens and the earth. When the beginning began, the Word already was. He did not come into being then; He was already there. "With God" means He is distinct from the Father. He is not just another name for the Father. "Was God" means He shares fully in what God is. So in one verse John gives us a real distinction of persons and a real oneness of God. Christians call the Son "the Word" because, just as our words express our minds, the Son perfectly expresses and reveals the Father (John 1:18).

Then comes John 1:3: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." John says the same thing twice, once positively and once negatively, as if closing every door. Positively, all things came through Him. Negatively, not one single made thing came without Him. That second half is there to stop us from carving out exceptions. Nothing is left out, whether it is stars or seas, bodies or souls, angels or the powers of heaven. Paul says the same in Colossians 1:16: in Him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, including thrones and rulers and authorities.

This also tells us something about the Word Himself. If everything that was made was made through Him, then He cannot be one of the made things. Otherwise He would have had to make Himself, or else John's "all things" would really mean "all things except the Word." John draws a clean line through reality: on one side is everything that was made, and on the other side is the one through whom it was made. The Word stands on the Creator's side of that line. That is why He can be called God without lessening the truth that there is only one God.

Some people have tried to soften this. One idea is that the Son was only present at creation, like a helper or bystander, while the Father did the real work. But John says things were made "through Him," not merely "near Him." He is the one through whom the Father acts. Scripture never pictures the Father and Son as two separate builders. The one God creates, the Father through the Son, and Hebrews 1:2 says God made the universe through His Son.

Another idea is that "all things" means only spiritual renewal, the "new creation" that comes when the gospel is preached, so that John is talking about the church, not the physical world. The text will not allow that. John 1:10 says: "He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him." The world that He made is the same world that failed to know Him. But the church is precisely the people who did know Him and confessed Him as the Son of God. So the world He made cannot be the church. It is the ordinary created world, the one He came into when He was born.

Still others in the early centuries claimed that "all things" referred only to a higher realm of spiritual beings, and that our material world was made by some lesser power. They even read hidden lists of heavenly beings into John's words like "Word," "Life," and "Light." But John is not giving a secret code. He is speaking of one Lord. And he insists that the world was made through Him and that He "came to His own" (John 1:11). This earth, with its dust and bodies and history, belongs to Him because He made it. That matters deeply. The physical world is not a mistake or the work of a rival. It is good because the Son made it, and He came to rescue what was His.

John also calls the Word "the true Light who gives light to every man" (John 1:9). Elsewhere Jesus calls His followers "the light of the world," so some have argued that the Son is light only in the same lesser way. But there is a difference between a lamp and the sun. The disciples shine because they have been lit. The Word is the source of light itself, the one who gives light. John ties this Light directly to creation: the Light was in the world, and the world was made through Him. The one who gives light to every person is the same one who made every person.

All of this comes to its high point in John 1:14: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us." The Creator of all things entered His own creation as a man. He did not stop being God; He took on our human nature. That is the wonder of Christmas. The baby in the manger is the one through whom the manger, the stars above it, and the shepherds' very breath were made.

The Old Testament points the same way. Proverbs says that the Lord founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding (Proverbs 3:19), and in Proverbs 8 Wisdom speaks as one who was beside God when He marked out the heavens and the deep. John gives the big picture in one sweeping statement; Proverbs fills in the details, the earth, the sky, the seas. Many Christians have heard in Wisdom's voice an early echo of the Son, and the New Testament calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Believers have sometimes differed over how directly Proverbs 8 describes the Son, since it is poetry that personifies wisdom. But a line like "the LORD brought me forth" (8:22) cannot mean the Son was created, because John has already told us that nothing made was made without Him. Whatever the poem means, it must agree with that.

So John's prologue proves a great deal. The Word existed before anything was made. He is distinct from the Father yet truly God. Everything that has ever been made, visible and invisible, physical and spiritual, came through Him, which means He Himself was never made. And this eternal Creator is the same Jesus who became flesh to live among us and save us. When we trust Christ, we are not trusting a great creature. We are trusting the one who made us.

topics.title: How should Proverbs 8:22 ('The Lord created me a beginning of His ways') be understood of the Son?
topics.cmp: Every author here except Irenaeus reads the Wisdom of Proverbs 8 as the Son, and all of these deny that 'The Lord created me' makes him a creature: Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary, Augustine, Ambrose and Owen (who simply identifies Wisdom with Christ). Irenaeus departs sharply from them all, taking the Wisdom present with God at creation to be the Holy Spirit, distinct from the Word. Among those who deny the Son's creaturehood, the most common answer is that 'created' refers to the Incarnation or the economy: Athanasius, Gregory, Ambrose (the mystery of the assumed body, with the past tense marking what was predestined) and Augustine (the 'form of a servant' as against the 'form of God' that 'begat me') all take this line. Their grounds differ. Athanasius relies heavily on the wording itself ('for the works' rather than 'a work,' the contrast between 'created' and 'begat,' and 'Wisdom built her a house'), argues that consistency requires a figurative reading, and also offers an alternative reading in which 'created' refers to the impress of Wisdom made in the works. Gregory stresses that a proverb is a dark saying and that the surrounding verses become absurd if read literally; he also notes that other translators read 'possessed,' sets the text against John 1:3, and in one answer reads the 'ways' as the beginnings of virtue in human beings. Hilary frames the question as a strict distinction between an eternal birth before all ages and a 'creation' in time for God's ways, with Christ as the Way, and he adds that the text was meant to show the Jews that Christ existed before Mary.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation, He declares by Solomon: “God by Wisdom founded the earth, and by understanding hath He established the heaven.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For, though no works had been created, still ‘the Word’ of God ‘was,’ and ‘the Word was God.’ And His becoming man would not have taken place, had not the need of men become a cause. The Son then is not a creature.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: it is consequently probable that the phrase we are discussing, being written in close connection with them, is not received by prudent men absolutely and without examination.

ans.text:
Proverbs 8:22 does not teach that the Son of God is a creature. Read carefully, and read alongside the rest of the Bible, it fits the church's historic confession that the Son is eternal, uncreated God, the one through whom everything else was made.

Start with what kind of passage this is. Proverbs 8 is poetry. Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling out in the streets, inviting people to learn from her. Then she describes how she was with the Lord before the mountains were shaped, before the springs and the seas, beside Him as He marked out the heavens and the foundations of the earth. The book calls itself a book of proverbs, which means sayings that use pictures and riddles and must be thought through. Much of this chapter cannot be taken in a flat, literal way. So it is unwise to build a doctrine about God's being on one word lifted out of a poem.

Is the Son really in view here? The New Testament gives good reason to think so. Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). John says of the Word, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). That echoes Wisdom's place at God's side in creation. Many Christians read Proverbs 8 as a real foreshadowing of the Son. Others think it is first a poetic picture of God's wisdom, which finds its full meaning in Christ. Some very early Christians even took it of the Holy Spirit. All agree on the main point. God's wisdom is not something God gained at some moment. He has always had it. A God who was ever without His wisdom would not be God.

Now the hard word. Translations of verse 22 differ. Some say the Lord "possessed" Wisdom, some that He "brought her forth," and some that He "created" her. The Hebrew verb most often means to get or to possess. The idea of "creating" came mainly from an ancient Greek translation. That Greek wording was the one early Christians argued over. People who said the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures leaned on it heavily. The church answered them, and the answer still helps.

First, look at the very next verses. Wisdom says that before the hills she was "brought forth," the language of birth. It is not the language of making. A child comes from a parent and shares the parent's nature. A thing that is made, like a table, does not. When the Bible calls the Son "begotten," it means He comes from the Father and is the same kind as the Father. He is not something the Father built. So even within Proverbs 8, the birth language keeps "created" from meaning that Wisdom is one more creature.

Second, notice the purpose in the verse. In the old reading Wisdom is set in place "for" God's works, at the beginning of His ways. Someone brought in for the sake of the works is not simply one of the works. Think of a builder who comes to a house to repair it. He is not part of the house.

Third, and most important, there is a real sense in which the Son was "created." When the eternal Son became man, He took a true human body and soul. That human nature had a beginning, as ours does. "The Word became flesh" (John 1:14). Hebrews 10:5 has Him say to the Father, "a body You prepared for Me." So many Christians have read "He created me" as speaking of the Incarnation. The Son was not made in His divine nature. He was made man for us. And He became the beginning of God's new ways. By His death and resurrection He opened a new road to life for people who had lost their way. He is "the firstborn from among the dead" (Colossians 1:18). Just as we are not God's children by nature but become His children by grace, the Son is not a creature by nature. He became one of us by grace.

This also clears up a common misunderstanding of the word "firstborn." When Colossians 1:15 calls Christ the firstborn over all creation, it means first in rank and heir of everything. It does not mean the first creature, because the next verse says that in Him all things were created. Whoever created all things cannot be one of the things created.

So the safest and most faithful way to read Proverbs 8:22 is this. It is a poem about God's eternal wisdom, which the New Testament shows is fully revealed in the Son. Its word for Wisdom's coming forth must agree with the plain teaching that the Son is Creator, not creature. And if we keep the word "created," it fits best with the Son's becoming man for our salvation. The obscure verse should be read in the light of the clear ones, not the other way around.

topics.title: What does it mean that Christ is called 'first-born of all creation'?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Athanasius and Gregory of Nyssa agree that Christ is 'first-born from the dead' as the one who opens resurrection life for others, but they ground it differently. Irenaeus frames it as an Adam–Christ recapitulation in which Christ regenerates the ancient fathers into God's life, supported by prophetic and dominical texts about reversal. Athanasius and Gregory stress that Christ was first to overcome death by his own act.
