Athanasius explicitly denies that the title means he died before us, locating it instead in his abolishing death and raising his own body. Gregory adds that the titles belong to the incarnate economy rather than Christ's eternal existence, and he extends 'first-born among many brethren' to the new birth of baptism with the Spirit. Hilary alone addresses how the two titles relate: 'first-born of every creature' concerns creation and 'first-born from the dead' concerns the dispensation of the flesh, together giving Christ pre-eminence in all things. This division between creation and economy parallels Gregory's restriction of the titles to the economy, but Hilary keeps the first title tied to the origin and continuance of creation.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For the Lord, having been born “the First-begotten of the dead,” and receiving into His bosom the ancient fathers, has regenerated them into the life of God, He having been made Himself the beginning of those that live

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: not that He died before us, for we had died first; but because having undergone death for us and abolished it, He was the first to rise, as man, for our sakes raising His own Body.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: He becomes the “first-fruits of them that slept” and the “first-born from the dead,” in that He first by His own act loosed the pains of death

ans.text:
When Paul calls Christ the "firstborn over all creation" in Colossians 1:15, he means that the Son holds the rank, rights and rule over everything God has made. He does not mean that the Son was the first thing God made. The title is about authority and inheritance, not about a starting date.

In the Bible, "firstborn" often names a position more than a birth order. The firstborn son was the heir. He carried the family's name, received the double portion, and led the household after the father. So the word came to mean "the one with first place." God calls the whole nation of Israel "My firstborn son" in Exodus 4:22, though Israel was hardly the first nation on earth. In Psalm 89:27 God says of David, "I will appoint him as My firstborn, the most exalted of the kings of the earth." David was the youngest of his brothers, and many kings had reigned before him. "Firstborn" there plainly means "highest in honor."

The verses that follow in Colossians settle the question. Paul does not stop at "firstborn." He explains it at once: "For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible... All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16–17). If all things were created through the Son, the Son cannot be one of those created things. Otherwise he would have had to make himself. Paul places him on the Creator's side of the line, not the creature's. John says the same: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3).

The same verse also calls the Son "the image of the invisible God." He is the one in whom the unseen God is perfectly shown. A mere creature, however great, could not show us God fully.

So we should hear "firstborn over all creation" the way we would hear "heir of the whole estate." The Son is not the first brick in the building. He is the architect, the builder and the owner. Creation exists through him, is held together by him, and is headed toward him as its goal. Elsewhere Scripture speaks of the Son as "begotten" of the Father, which means he shares the Father's own nature, as a son shares his father's. That is very different from being made. A carpenter makes a chair, but a man begets a son, and the son is as human as the father. The Son is eternally from the Father as Son, never a product of the Father's workshop.

A little further on, in Colossians 1:18, Paul uses the word again: Christ is "the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence." This second title belongs to what the Son did after he became man. Others had been brought back to life before Easter, such as Lazarus, but they all died again. Jesus was the first to rise into a new, deathless life, never to die again. He did not simply escape death. He defeated it from the inside and opened a road for others to follow.

That is why Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). The first sheaf of a harvest promised that the rest of the field was coming. Christ's resurrection is the pledge of ours. Adam's sin made him the head of a race that dies. Christ is the head of a new race that lives. Romans 8:29 says God's purpose is that his people be shaped like his Son, "that He might be the firstborn among many brothers." Through him, ordinary believers become God's children and share his inheritance.

The two titles fit together like two halves of one picture. As "firstborn over all creation," the Son is Lord of the first creation, which he made and upholds. As "firstborn from among the dead," he is Lord of the new creation, which he began by his rising. Everything that exists owes its being to him, and everyone who will live forever owes that life to him. In both, Paul says, he has first place "in all things."

So when we read that Christ is the firstborn, we should not picture God making a lesser being before everything else. We should picture the eternal Son, through whom all things came to be. He took our flesh, went down into death for us, and came out the other side as the head of a living family. The title does not shrink him into a creature. It crowns him as heir of everything and leader of all who will rise with him.

topics.title: Can any creature create, and why did creation have to come through the Word?
topics.cmp: Waterland, Athanasius and Augustine agree that creating out of nothing belongs to God alone and that creatures can at most work on what already exists. Their grounds differ. Waterland builds a cumulative case from Scripture's silence about any creature creating, from reason, and from the consensus of ante-Nicene writers. Athanasius argues that if one creature could create, all could, and then the Word would be needless, so the Word who made all things cannot be a creature. Augustine instead offers a metaphysical account: God works from the innermost and highest point of causation, while angels, men and animals only apply causes from without that draw out what God already wove into the elements. Only Waterland takes up the objection that a finite world needs only finite power, answering that it confuses the degree of power with the extent of what it produces. Only Athanasius explains why creation came through the Word, grounding it in the Word's being proper to the Father's essence, like light shining through its radiance, and in the Word's loving condescension to creatures who could not have endured his untempered nature.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For none of things which are brought to be is an efficient cause, but all things were made through the Word: who would not have wrought all things, were He Himself in the number of the creatures.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: creation every where in Scripture looked on as a divine act; not so much as a grain of sand, or a particle of matter, said to be created by an angel, or archangel, or any creature whatever

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Original Cause of All Things is from God.
refs.quote: He only is the creator who is the chief former of these things. Neither can any one be this, unless He with whom primarily rests the measure, number, and weight of all things existing; and He is God the one Creator

ans.text:
No creature can create in the true sense of the word. Only God can bring something into being out of nothing, and the Bible teaches that he did this through his Son, the Word. That is one of the strongest reasons Christians confess that the Son is not a creature but truly God.

It helps to see the difference between making and creating. A carpenter makes a table, but he did not create the wood. A farmer grows wheat, but he did not invent the seed, the soil or the sun. Everything people do works with material that already exists. We shape things, arrange them and combine them. The same is true of the most powerful creatures, including angels. They can act on the world from the outside, but they cannot cause a single thing to exist where nothing was before.

God is different. He does not work on the world from the outside like a craftsman. He gives each thing its very existence, from the inside out. Every power in nature, every seed that grows and every law that holds was first given by him. When a creature does something remarkable, it is only drawing out possibilities God already placed in his world. Hebrews 11:3 says that "the universe was formed by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible." Paul describes God as the one who "calls into being what does not yet exist" (Romans 4:17). That is something only God does.

Scripture is consistent here. It never says that an angel, a prophet or any creature created even a grain of sand. Creation is always God's own work. In Isaiah 44:24 the Lord says he alone stretched out the heavens and spread out the earth by himself. Creation is one of the main ways the Bible tells us who the true God is.

Someone might object that the world is finite, so making it would only take finite power, and a very great creature might have enough. But that misses the point. The question is not how much was made but what kind of act it is. Turning nothing into something, even something tiny, is not a bigger version of what we do. It is a different kind of act altogether. There is no ladder of effort that climbs from shaping clay to calling a world into existence. That is why Paul can say in Romans 1:20 that God's "eternal power and divine nature" are seen in what he has made. If creating needed only creaturely power, creation would tell us nothing about God.

Now look at what the New Testament says about the Son. John 1:3 says of the Word, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Colossians 1:16 says that in him "all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible," and that "all things were created through Him and for Him." If only God can create, and all things were created through the Son, then the Son is not one of the created things. He stands on the Creator's side of the line. Notice too that John says "all things" and "nothing" without him. If the Son were himself a creature, he would have to have been made through himself, which makes no sense.

This also guards against a common misunderstanding. Some picture the Father as the real Creator and the Son as a helper or tool, a kind of super-angel God made first and then used to make everything else. But if one creature could be given the power to create, there would be no reason another couldn't. Then the Son would not be needed at all, and the Bible's strong claim that nothing was made without him would be empty. The Son is not God's instrument standing between God and the world. He is God's own Word, sharing the Father's very being.

Why did creation have to come through the Word? Because the Word belongs to the Father as truly as light belongs to the sun. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." The sun shines on the earth only through its own rays. In the same way the Father does everything through his Son, who is not something added to God from outside. When God acts, he acts through his Word and by his Spirit. That is simply how the one God works.

There is also something tender here. The God who made all things is infinitely great, and creatures are small and fragile. On their own they could never stand before the full brightness of his glory. Yet in love God did not keep his distance. Through the Son he reached down to what did not yet exist, gave it being, and took hold of it so it would not fall back into nothing. Colossians 1:17 says, "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together," and Hebrews 1:3 says he is "upholding all things by His powerful word." When Colossians 1:15 calls him "the firstborn over all creation," it does not mean he was the first thing made. It means he holds first place and rightful rule over all creation, as its maker and keeper.

This bears on Proverbs 8, where Wisdom speaks of being with the Lord before the world began and at his side as he made it. Many Christians have heard in that passage a picture of the Son, and some verses are hard to translate, since the word used of Wisdom at the beginning can be rendered in more than one way. Sincere believers read the chapter somewhat differently. Some see it mainly as poetry about God's wisdom. Others see it as speaking of the Son's role in creation. But since Scripture plainly says nothing was made without the Son, Proverbs 8 cannot be teaching that he was the first creature. God was never without his Wisdom.

So creation itself points us to Christ. Every star and every breath exists because the Father made it through his Son and keeps it in being through him. That is why we can trust him completely. The one who holds us is not a creature like us, but the Lord who made us.

topics.title: What does the healing of the man born blind show about who the Son is?
topics.cmp: Why Christ healed with clay, what this reveals about the Son as the Maker of man, and the rejection of a Gnostic symbolic reading of the miracle.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For that which the artificer, the Word, had omitted to form in the womb, [viz., the blind man’s eyes], He then supplied in public, that the works of God might be manifested in him

ans.text:
The healing of the man born blind shows that Jesus is not only a healer sent from God. He is the Son through whom God made human beings in the first place. The Creator came to finish His own work.

The story is in John 9. Jesus sees a man who has been blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused it. Jesus answers that neither the man nor his parents sinned, "but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him" (John 9:3). Then He says, "While I am in the world, I am the light of the world" (John 9:5). He spits on the ground, makes mud, puts it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam. The man comes back seeing.

Why mud? Jesus did not need it. Elsewhere He healed with a word, even from far away (Matthew 8:8, 13). So when He does something this unusual, it is worth asking what He is showing us.

Think back to the beginning of the Bible. "The LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils" (Genesis 2:7). God shaped the first man from earth, like a potter working clay. Now Jesus takes earth in His hands and shapes sight into a man who never had it. Christians since the earliest centuries have seen the echo. The hands that worked the soil by the pool are the same hands that formed Adam.

This fits what the rest of the New Testament says about the Son. John's Gospel opens by saying of the Word, the Son before He became man, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Paul says the same in Colossians 1:16: all things were created through Him and for Him. The Father made the world, and He made it through the Son. So when the Son heals with clay, He is not borrowing a power that belongs to someone else. He is doing again, in public, what He has always done.

There is a tender side to this too. Psalm 139:13 says that God forms us and knits us together in the womb. This man had come from the womb with eyes that did not work. Something had been left unfinished. Now the same Maker who forms every child supplies what was lacking, in broad daylight, for everyone to see. The man's neighbors were right to be amazed. As he himself said, "Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind" (John 9:32). Only the One who makes eyes can make eyes where there were none.

This matters for how we understand the Trinity. Jesus is not a lesser helper standing between us and a distant Creator. He is the Father's own Son, sharing the Father's work and power. Jesus says, "My Father is working until now, and I am working" (John 5:17), and whatever the Father does, the Son does as well (John 5:19). The Father creates through the Son, and the Son does nothing apart from the Father. When we meet Jesus, we are not meeting a different god from the one who made us. We meet the very hand of the God who made us. We do not need to look for some other, higher maker behind Him.

The story ends this way. When Jesus reveals Himself to the healed man as the Son of Man, the man says, "Lord, I believe," and worships Him (John 9:38). Jesus accepts that worship. A creature would refuse it. The Creator receives it.

It is also worth clearing up one misunderstanding. Some early teachers treated this miracle mainly as a coded picture of secret heavenly events. One version even claimed it showed that a divine being had come into existence blind and ignorant of God the Father. That reading turns the story upside down. In John 9 the blindness belongs to the man, and later to the religious leaders who refuse to see (John 9:39–41). It never belongs to Jesus. The Son is the light of the world. He knows the Father fully, just as the Father knows Him (John 10:15; Matthew 11:27). There is nothing dark or ignorant in Him.

The miracle certainly has deeper meaning. It pictures how Christ opens blind hearts, and the pool's name, Siloam, means "Sent," pointing to Jesus as the One the Father sent (John 9:7). But that meaning grows out of a real event, done to a real man, by a real Savior. It does not replace the event with a hidden myth.

So this healing teaches a simple and wonderful truth. The Jesus who saves us is the same Lord who made us. He knows how we are put together, because He put us together. What is broken in us, He is able to remake.

title: The Holy Spirit's Deity and Personhood
desc: Proofs that the Spirit is a distinct divine Person, coequal and coeternal with the Father and Son, not a creature, servant or impersonal power.

topics.title: Is the Holy Spirit fully God, coequal and coeternal with the Father and the Son?
topics.cmp: All the authors (Ambrose, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Hilary, Novatian, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Owen, Edwards, Bickersteth, Warfield) affirm that the Holy Spirit is fully God, uncreated, coeternal and equal with the Father and the Son, and owed the same faith and worship. They argue for this in different ways. Ambrose piles up scriptural proof-texts and arguments from worship and service, from shared names (Truth, Power, Life, Lord) and from divine works (creation, forgiveness, sanctification, raising the dead). Basil rests on the baptismal formula, rejects 'sub-numeration' and the slave/free categories, prefers saying the Spirit is 'with' rather than 'in' the Father and Son, and appeals to unbroken patristic tradition, including Origen. Gregory of Nyssa argues philosophically against Eunomius from the created/uncreated divide, identity of operations and divine simplicity, while still granting the Spirit a place 'counted after' the Son in order of cause. Augustine and Edwards both ground equality in the Spirit being the love or bond of Father and Son. Augustine also argues that whatever is not a creature is God, and that the divine substance is simple. Owen and Bickersteth stress personhood, the interchange of divine names and works in Scripture, and prayer addressed to the Spirit. Bickersteth explains why direct evidence of worship of the Spirit is less prominent, and Owen distinguishes the Spirit's essential deity from his economic mission, and Warfield reads 'Spirit of God' as God's own innermost life. There are real differences on particular texts and points. Ambrose reads John 4:24 as 'the Spirit is God,' while Hilary denies that it refers specifically to the Holy Spirit. Edwards says Scripture never speaks of the Spirit's love for the Father, the Son or the saints, because the Spirit is that love; Owen, by contrast, urges believers to value 'the love of the Spirit' (Rom 15:30) and the Spirit's own love in comforting them. Irenaeus identifies Wisdom with the Spirit, whereas Augustine and Gregory associate Wisdom with the Son.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: It is plain then that that, from share in which all creation is excluded, is something special and peculiar to uncreated being.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: attributes any one of which would prove his Godhead – are assigned to him; that He is associated in Divine offices with the Father and the Son; that He with them is worshipped and glorified; that He is Jehovah and God

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: That the Son is Very God, of the Same Substance with the…
refs.quote: But if not a creature, then not only God (for men likewise are called gods), but also very God; and therefore absolutely equal with the Father and the Son, and in the unity of the Trinity consubstantial and co-eternal.

ans.text:
Yes. The Holy Spirit is not a lesser helper God sends, and not an impersonal force. He is fully God, equal to the Father and the Son in every way, and he has always existed, just as they have. There are not three Gods. There is one God, and the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully that one God.

The Bible shows this most plainly by speaking of the Spirit in the same breath as God. In Acts 5, Peter tells Ananias that he has lied "to the Holy Spirit." A moment later he says, "You have not lied to men, but to God!" Lying to the Spirit is lying to God, because the Spirit is God.

Paul reasons the same way. In 1 Corinthians 3:16 he asks, "Do you not know that you yourselves are God's temple, and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" A temple is a house for God, and what makes us God's temple is that the Spirit lives in us. In 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 he calls our body "a temple of the Holy Spirit" and then concludes, "Therefore glorify God with your body." The one whose temple we are is God. The Spirit does not live in us as a servant keeping house for someone else. He lives there as the God who owns it.

The Spirit also has qualities that only God has. Hebrews 9:14 calls him "the eternal Spirit," so he had no beginning. Psalm 139 asks where anyone could go to escape God's Spirit, and the answer is nowhere: he is present everywhere. In 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 Paul says the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. Only God knows the depths of God. A created being, however great, could never know God from the inside.

He also does what only God does. In Genesis 1:2 the Spirit of God is hovering over the waters at creation, and Job says that the Spirit of God has made him. The Spirit gives new birth (John 3:5-8) and will raise our mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). He came upon Mary so that the Son of God took on human flesh (Luke 1:35). Creating, giving new life and raising the dead are God's own work.

The Spirit even bears God's own name. In the Old Testament the personal name of God, the LORD, is used for the one who spoke to Isaiah in the temple (Isaiah 6). In Acts 28:25-26 Paul quotes those same words and says the Holy Spirit spoke them. Paul can also say simply, "Now the Lord is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:17).

Most important, Jesus himself puts the Spirit beside the Father and himself. In Matthew 28:19 he sends his followers out "baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Notice it is one "name," not three names. No creature could be placed in that list. Imagine baptizing in the name of the Father, the Son and the angel Gabriel; it would be unthinkable. Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 does the same, joining the grace of Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit.

Some people assume that because the Spirit is usually named third, he must rank third. But the order shows how God has made himself known: the Father sends, the Son comes, the Spirit is poured out. It is not a ladder of importance. Counting things does not change their worth. Saying "one, two, three" does not make the third thing smaller.

Others think of the Spirit as a power or influence, a kind of divine energy. But Scripture speaks of him as someone, not something. He can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30). He speaks and gives directions (Acts 13:2). He gives gifts to each believer "as He determines" (1 Corinthians 12:11). A force does not have feelings, speak or make decisions. A person does.

A related worry is whether the Spirit is spread thin when he is given to millions of believers. He is not. He is not like a cake cut into slices. Each believer receives the one whole Spirit, as much as each can take in, and he loses nothing by giving himself. Only God can be fully present to everyone at once like this.

Because the Spirit is God, he is rightly worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son. Jesus' words that true worshipers worship the Father "in spirit and truth" (John 4:23-24) do not shut the Spirit out of worship. Jesus calls himself the Truth, and no one thinks that worshipping "in truth" means Jesus should not be worshipped. In the same way, worshipping God by the Spirit does not mean the Spirit is outside the worship. When we praise God, we praise the Father, the Son and the Spirit together.

So it is fitting to thank the Spirit, to love him, and to ask him for help. You can ask him to comfort you, to teach you, and to make Christ real to you. You are not speaking to a lesser being or a mere power. You are speaking to the living God, who has made his home in you.

topics.title: Is the Holy Spirit a distinct Person who acts by his own sovereign will?
topics.cmp: All the authors who answer agree that the Holy Spirit is a personal agent who acts freely, and nearly all rest on the same text, 1 Corinthians 12:11 ("dividing to every man severally as he will"), alongside Acts 13:2 on setting apart Barnabas and Saul. They use it for different ends: John Owen and Edward Henry Bickersteth turn it, with ascriptions of mind, knowledge, grief and command, against Socinian or metonymic readings of the Spirit as God's mere power. Owen adds a pastoral emphasis on comfort, joy, peculiar sin against the Spirit (Acts 5:3), and prayer to him, while Bickersteth adds linguistic arguments and insists that evidence alone cannot produce saving belief without prayer. Ambrose of Milan, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil of Caesarea and Irenaeus of Lyons instead use the Spirit's sovereign will to prove he is no creature but above all things and equal in authority with Father and Son. Ambrose argues this from the virgin conception, the Spirit's sanctifying of angels, and the unforgivable blasphemy, Basil from faith in the Son depending on the Spirit, and Irenaeus from the fact that no man can command the prophetic Spirit. Hilary of Poitiers alone distinguishes the Spirit who distributes the gifts from the Spirit in whom they are distributed, and Augustine of Hippo alone warns against calling the Spirit "unbegotten" lest there seem to be two Fathers.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: such things were everywhere ascribed unto him in the Scripture as uncontrollably evidence him to be an intelligent, voluntary agent. This they found so plain and evident, that they could not deny but that he was a person

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: Unitarians axe wont to speak of the Spirit, as an effusion or emanation separate from God, or an influence or power exercised by God. Can you speak of the mind of an effusion?

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: even so the apostle ascribes independent authority to the dignity of the Spirit, when he affirms that He works all in all as He wills

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible presents the Holy Spirit not as a force or an atmosphere but as Someone: a Person who knows, decides, speaks, and acts, and who does so with the freedom and authority that belong to God alone.

Start with the plainest evidence: what the Spirit does. A force can push or warm or light things up, but it cannot think or choose. Scripture says the Spirit does both. Paul writes that "the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10), and that no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Searching and knowing are the acts of a mind. Romans 8:27 even speaks of "the mind of the Spirit," and says he intercedes for believers according to God's will. Praying on someone's behalf is something only a person can do.

The Spirit also has feelings that can be hurt. Paul warns, "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30). You cannot grieve electricity or wind. You can only grieve someone who loves you. In the same way, Peter tells Ananias that he has lied to the Holy Spirit, and in the next breath that he has lied to God (Acts 5:3-4). You cannot lie to a power. You can only lie to a person.

The Spirit speaks, and he speaks as "I." In Acts 13:2, while the church in Antioch was worshiping and fasting, "the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.'" Notice the words: for Me, and I have called. The Spirit claims the missionaries as his own and names the work as his calling. Two verses later Luke says they were "sent out by the Holy Spirit." Earlier, when Peter hesitated about visiting the Gentile Cornelius, the Spirit told him to go without doubting, because "I have sent them" (Acts 10:19-20). Later the Spirit stopped Paul and his companions from preaching in certain regions and steered them elsewhere (Acts 16:6-7). Paul tells the elders of Ephesus that the Holy Spirit made them overseers of the flock (Acts 20:28). Calling, sending, forbidding, appointing: these are the acts of the Lord of the church. And those he sent were not second-class apostles. Paul's calling came from the Father, from Christ, and from the Spirit alike, with one and the same authority.

The clearest statement of his freedom comes in Paul's teaching on spiritual gifts. After listing wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, prophecy and more, Paul says: "All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines" (1 Corinthians 12:11). The Spirit is not a pipe that gifts flow through. He chooses. He gives one gift to one believer and a different gift to another, in the measure he judges best. That is why no Christian can boast about a gift, and why every Christian can ask the Spirit for what is needed and trust his wisdom in what he gives. Jesus pointed to the same freedom when he told Nicodemus that the Spirit's work is like the wind, which blows wherever it wishes (John 3:8). We cannot control it or predict it. We can only receive it.

Jesus himself speaks of the Spirit as a person. He calls him "another Advocate" (John 14:16), someone to stand beside the disciples as Jesus had. He says the Spirit will teach them, remind them of his words, testify about him, convict the world of sin, guide them into truth, and tell them what is to come (John 14:26; 15:26; 16:8-14). These are the activities of a teacher and a witness, not of an influence.

Some people object that the Spirit is simply "the power of God," and that talk of him as a person is a figure of speech. But that does not fit the way the Bible actually talks. Paul prays that believers will overflow with hope "by the power of the Holy Spirit" (Romans 15:13). If the Spirit simply were God's power, that would mean "by the power of the power." The Spirit has power, but he is not merely power. Others are put off by the name "Spirit," because it sounds vague, like breath or atmosphere. But the name is chosen with care. Just as "Son" tells us something true about the second Person, "Spirit" tells us how the third Person works: from within, quietly, dwelling in us and bearing witness with our own spirit that we are God's children (Romans 8:16). The name points to closeness, not to vagueness. It is also why Christians should not call the Spirit "it," even though older English sometimes did because the Greek word for spirit is grammatically neuter. Jesus used a masculine "he" for the Spirit in John 16:13-14.

One more misunderstanding is worth clearing up. Saying the Spirit acts by his own will does not mean he has a separate agenda from the Father and the Son, as if heaven had three competing wills. There is one God, and the Father, Son, and Spirit share one divine life and purpose. Jesus says the Spirit will not speak on his own but will make known what belongs to Christ (John 16:13-14). That is not a sign that the Spirit is a servant obeying orders. It shows the perfect agreement within God. Each Person truly wills and acts, and they never pull against each other. The Spirit's free choices are God's free choices.

That is why the Spirit is named alongside the Father and the Son when believers are baptized "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). It is also why Jesus warns that blasphemy against the Spirit is uniquely serious (Matthew 12:31-32). No one would treat an insult against a creature or an impersonal force that way.

For ordinary Christian life, this changes a great deal. If the Spirit were a force, we would try to tap into it or use it. Because he is a Person, and God himself, we relate to him. We can trust him, listen to him, pray to him, take care not to grieve him, and thank him for every gift he chooses to give. The One who lives in believers is not a something but a Someone, and he is the living God.

topics.title: What do particular Scripture texts teach about the Holy Spirit?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that these texts show the Holy Spirit to be divine and personally distinct. Ambrose, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine and Bickersteth read 2 Corinthians 3:17 as calling the Spirit Lord. Ambrose, Basil, Owen and Gregory take the lie of Ananias as a lie to God, and Augustine and Owen draw the Spirit's deity from 1 Corinthians 12, where God and the Spirit both work all things. Their grounds differ: Ambrose and Basil rely mostly on close contextual inference (for example, the 'third' Lord of 2 Thessalonians 3:5); Owen gives formal reasoning that only God can be sinned against or obeyed; Gregory argues from divine operations such as begetting God's children and seeing hidden things; Bickersteth argues from worship offered to the 'seven Spirits'; and Basil uses analogies of a man's own spirit and a sunbeam. Real differences appear in how unity and distinction are balanced: Hilary, unlike the others, treats 'the Lord is Spirit' and 'the Spirit of the Lord' as different in sense (proprietor and property), and on 2 Corinthians 13:14 Edwards makes grace, love and communion one benefit, the Spirit as the love of Father and Son, while Owen and Warfield stress distinct blessings or fellowship assigned to each Person. Emphases also diverge on John 15:26 and the baptism: Augustine sees the Father as principium of the deity, Hilary the Son's power as Sender, and Warfield personal distinction, while at Christ's baptism Edwards sees the dove as the Father's love to the Son and Ambrose sees the unity of divine operation.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: we have in this plain, unambiguous affirmation a crowning and convincing argument that the Holy Ghost is one with the Father and the Son, – very and Eternal God.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: that the supremacy of His Nature may be shown by the honour implied in lordship, while at the same time he may avoid confusing in his argument the individuality of His Person

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the…
refs.quote: lest any one should think the Son to be signified, and to be called the Spirit on account of His incorporeal substance, has gone on to say, “And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty;”

ans.text:
Read carefully, a handful of passages show us two things about the Holy Spirit at once: he is truly God, and he is a person distinct from the Father and the Son. Neither point rests on one proof text. The same picture keeps appearing from many directions. Let us walk through some of the clearest passages.

Start with 2 Corinthians 3:17: "Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." Paul has just been describing Moses going into the presence of the LORD and taking off the veil that covered his face. Then he says that whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. In the very next breath he tells us who this Lord is: the Spirit. The Lord whom Moses met face to face, the God of Israel, is the one Paul now calls the Spirit. Some have wondered whether Paul means Jesus here. But Paul immediately adds "the Spirit of the Lord," which shows he has the Holy Spirit in view, and he is careful not to simply blur the Spirit with the Son. In the following verse he says we are being changed into Christ's likeness "from glory to glory," and this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit. Only God can remake a human heart, and Paul says the Spirit does exactly that.

Acts 5 makes the point in a sobering way. Ananias and Sapphira sold land, kept back part of the money, and pretended they had given it all. Peter asks Ananias why he let Satan fill his heart "to lie to the Holy Spirit." A moment later he says, "You have not lied to men, but to God." Lying to the Spirit is lying to God. Notice also what this means about the Spirit as a person. You cannot lie to a force or an influence, any more than you can lie to electricity. A lie is told to someone who knows the truth and is wronged by your deceit. The same goes for Ephesians 4:30, where we are told not to grieve the Holy Spirit. Only a person can be grieved.

Hebrews 3 offers a quieter but striking example. The writer quotes Psalm 95, introducing it with the words "as the Holy Spirit says." The psalm goes on to speak of the Israelites who tested and tried "Me" in the wilderness for forty years. In the Old Testament the one who was tested is plainly the LORD himself. Hebrews puts those words in the Spirit's mouth. The Spirit speaks as God and is the God whom Israel provoked. He did not simply inspire the psalm long ago. He "says" it now, speaking to the church today.

Ezekiel 37 shows the Spirit doing what only God does: giving life. The prophet sees a valley of dry bones. Breath enters them, and they stand up alive. God then explains the vision: "I will put My Spirit in you, and you will live." In Hebrew the same word can mean breath, wind, or spirit, and Ezekiel plays on all three. The point is that the life-giving breath that first made Adam a living being, and that will one day raise the dead, is God's own Spirit. This is why Jesus can say in John 3 that we must be born of the Spirit, and why Paul says in Romans 8:11 that the Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to our mortal bodies.

Some early Christians also pointed to the story of Susanna, found in the longer form of Daniel. There God stirs up "the holy spirit" of the young Daniel to defend an innocent woman. Not all Christians count that book as Scripture. Some churches read it as part of the Bible, and others treat it as useful but not inspired. So the teaching should not rest on it. At most it echoes what the accepted books already show: God's Spirit moves in his servants to bring truth and justice.

The "seven spirits" in Revelation puzzle many readers. In Revelation 1:4-5 John wishes his readers grace and peace from the eternal God, "and from the seven spirits before His throne, and from Jesus Christ." Who could stand alongside the Father and Christ as a source of grace? Not angels. Scripture forbids worshiping angels, and John himself is told not to bow to one (Revelation 19:10). Nor would John pray for grace from seven vague powers. The number seven in Revelation stands for completeness. So "the seven spirits" is a picture of the one Holy Spirit in his full, perfect richness. Isaiah 11:2 similarly describes the one Spirit of the LORD resting on the Messiah as the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge and the fear of the LORD. Later the seven spirits are called the seven eyes of the Lamb, "sent out into all the earth" (Revelation 5:6). They belong to God and to Christ, yet they are named separately, "before the throne." So in one image we see the Spirit's deity and his distinctness together.

John 15:26 shows how the three relate to one another. Jesus says the Advocate, the Spirit of truth, will come. Jesus will send him from the Father, the Spirit "goes out from the Father," and he will testify about Jesus. The Spirit is not the Son, since the Son sends him. He is not the Father, since he goes out from the Father. Yet he knows the Son perfectly and bears true witness to him, which only someone who shares God's own knowledge could do (compare 1 Corinthians 2:10-11, where the Spirit searches even the depths of God). The Son sending the Spirit also shows the Son's equality with the Father, because he does what the Father does.

This verse lies behind one of the few long-standing disagreements among Christians about the Trinity. All agree the Spirit comes from the Father. Some say the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son. They point out that he is called "the Spirit of Christ" (Romans 8:9) and is sent by the Son, and they hold that this reflects who God eternally is. Others say he proceeds from the Father alone, and that the Son's sending concerns the Spirit's mission in the world. They stress that Jesus' words in this verse speak of the Spirit going out from the Father, and they want to guard the Father as the one source within God. Both sides confess the Spirit as fully God, equal with the Father and the Son.

At Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:16-17) all three appear together. The Son stands in the water. The Spirit comes down on him like a dove. The Father's voice says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." The dove and the voice say the same thing. The Father loves the Son and gives him the Spirit without measure. The Spirit is not a mere symbol here, and he is not one person changing masks. Three are present at once, acting together in one work.

Paul's letters show the same pattern almost without trying. In 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 he says there are different gifts but the same Spirit, different ministries but the same Lord, and different ways of working but the same God at work in everyone. Gifts, ministries and workings are not really three separate things. Paul simply thinks of every blessing as coming from the Father, the Son and the Spirit together. He closes 2 Corinthians the same way: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all" (13:14). He could have said "the grace, love and fellowship of God." Instead he names three, and he asks for blessing from the Spirit just as from the Father and the Son. No faithful Jew like Paul would pray for blessing from a creature on equal terms with God.

Put these passages side by side and a consistent picture emerges. The Spirit is called Lord. To lie to him is to lie to God. He speaks as the God of Israel. He gives life as only the Creator can. He stands with the Father and the Son as a source of grace. Yet he is never simply another name for the Father or the Son. He is sent, he testifies, he can be grieved, and he works alongside the other two. This is why Christians confess the Holy Spirit as the Lord and giver of life, who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified. When the Spirit is at work in your life, it is not merely God's power touching you from a distance. It is God himself, personally present with you.

topics.title: Is the Holy Spirit a creature or servant?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Ambrose, Basil, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Athanasius and John Owen all deny that the Holy Spirit is a creature or servant, but they argue it on different grounds. Ambrose argues most often and from the most directions: Scripture shows the Spirit as Creator (Job, the virgin birth), as forgiver of sins and so sinless, as knowing God's depths, and as sent to all and filling all, unlike the Seraph. Hilary also relies on the Spirit's searching of God's depths and on apostolic authority against 'mere human reasoning.' Basil stresses Scripture's speaking of the Spirit singly, his natural holiness against the angels' borrowed holiness, the titles of the Spirit, and the inconsistency of confessing and being baptized into one we rank as a slave. Gregory of Nyssa works mainly by refuting Eunomius through close exegesis: Paul's omission of the Spirit from the list of created ranks in Colossians 1:16, the senses of 'subjection,' and the Spirit's unchangeableness. Augustine and Athanasius instead take up texts that seem to subordinate the Spirit, explaining Christ's receiving the Spirit as man and giving it as God, and the Spirit's being 'given' in time as said relatively to creatures; Augustine adds that the temple argument shows we owe the Spirit worship. Owen briefly appeals to the Spirit's divine works and worship, while Edwards differs in focus, identifying the Spirit with God's loving-kindness and delight rather than arguing directly against the Spirit's creaturehood.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: whom all the angels serve, and to whom they are subject

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For he knows not that he is comparing the Spirit of the Father to those servants whom He created.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Against those who assert that the Spirit ought not to be…
refs.quote: Do you call the Spirit a servant? But, it is said, “the servant knoweth not what his Lord doeth,” and yet the Spirit knoweth the things of God, as “the spirit of man that is in him.”

ans.text:
No. The Holy Spirit is not a creature or a servant of God. He is God himself, the third person of the Trinity, equal with the Father and the Son. He is sent, and he is given, but that is very different from being made or being a servant. Some in the early church argued that the Spirit was the highest of the created spirits, a kind of chief angel who carries out God's orders. Christians rejected that view because the Bible keeps placing the Spirit on God's side of the line between Creator and creation.

Start with creation itself. A creature is something God made. But Scripture shows the Spirit doing the making. Elihu says in Job 33:4, "The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life." The psalmist says that when God sends his Spirit, living things are created and the face of the earth is renewed (Psalm 104:30). The Spirit hovers over the waters at the very beginning (Genesis 1:2). Most wonderfully, the Spirit brings about the conception of Jesus in Mary's womb (Luke 1:35). The coming of God's Son into human flesh is the greatest of God's works. The one who brings it about cannot himself be one of the things made. The Creator is not a creature.

Next, think about what the Spirit knows. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 that "the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." He compares it to the way only your own spirit knows your private thoughts. In the same way, only the Spirit of God knows the thoughts of God. No creature, however great, can see into God's inner life like that. A creature can know only what God chooses to show it. The Spirit knows God from the inside, the way you know your own mind. Jesus also says that a servant does not know what his master is doing (John 15:15). Yet the Spirit knows God's deepest purposes. That is not how a servant stands toward his master.

The Spirit also has qualities that belong only to God. He is everywhere at once. David asks where he could go to escape God's Spirit, and the answer is nowhere (Psalm 139:7-8). An angel has to travel from one place to another. The Spirit fills all things. He is called "the eternal Spirit" (Hebrews 9:14), and only God has no beginning. He gives gifts "as He determines" (1 Corinthians 12:11). That is the free choice of a sovereign, not the obedience of someone carrying out orders. He makes people holy and gives new birth (John 3:5-8; Titus 3:5). Only God can make a sinner new.

The apostles speak of him plainly as God. When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter told him that he had not lied to men but to God (Acts 5:3-4). Paul says our bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). He then says, "glorify God with your body." A temple is a house for God, and it would make no sense for Christ's people to be a shrine to a created being. Jesus himself puts the Spirit beside the Father and the Son in baptism: "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice it is one name, not three. No angel is ever named alongside God like that. We are never baptized into Gabriel or Michael.

What about the fact that the Spirit is "sent"? Angels are called ministering spirits sent out to serve God's people (Hebrews 1:14). So doesn't being sent make the Spirit one of them? No. Being sent describes a mission, not a rank. The Son is also sent by the Father (John 3:17), and he is not a creature.

Look also at how differently the sending works. When an angel is sent, he goes to a particular person, leaves one place for another, and does what he is told. When the Spirit is sent, he is poured out on all God's people at once (Acts 2:17). He does not need to move, since he is already everywhere. And he is the one who gives life and power even to the angels. In the same way, the Spirit is called God's "gift." That does not mean he is a thing God hands over, the way a parent hands a child a present. It means God gives himself to us. The change happens in us when we receive him, not in the Spirit.

Some have also stumbled over the phrase "the Spirit of truth" (John 15:26), as if the Spirit belonged to Christ the way a servant belongs to his master. But in that same verse Jesus says the Spirit "proceeds from the Father." Here "proceeds" means he comes forth from the Father's own life. Scripture never says that about anything in creation. Created things are made out of nothing. The Spirit comes forth from God himself. The Bible pictures this as God's breath or Spirit coming from his mouth, which is a way of saying the Spirit is truly God's own and shares his life (Psalm 33:6).

There is one verse the old arguments leaned on heavily, and it is worth a word. Amos 4:13 praises God as the one "who creates the wind." The Hebrew word for "wind" is the same word often translated "spirit." Some older translations also read "thunder" alongside it. So the verse was taken to mean that God created the Holy Spirit. But read the whole verse. Amos is describing God's power over nature: forming mountains, creating the wind, turning dawn to darkness, treading the heights of the earth. He is talking about storms and landscapes, not about the Holy Spirit. Modern translations rightly say "wind."

The same word can also mean the human spirit, the life God puts inside each person (Zechariah 12:1). Either way, the verse is about created wind or created human life. If the Bible meant to teach that the Holy Spirit was made, we would expect it to say so clearly somewhere. It never does.

The Spirit's work in forgiveness and holiness points the same way. Jesus breathed on his disciples, gave them the Holy Spirit, and spoke of sins being forgiven (John 20:22-23). Only God can forgive sin (Mark 2:7). Every creature, even an angel, is able to fall. Satan himself was once a glorious angel. But the Holy Spirit is holy by his very nature. He cannot fall, because his goodness is not borrowed from anyone else. It is his own, as it is the Father's and the Son's.

Why does this matter? If the Spirit were only a creature, then when he lives in us we would be joined to a creature, not to God. But the good news is that through the Spirit, God himself comes to dwell in his people. When the Spirit comforts you, prays for you, and makes you more like Christ, you are not dealing with a go-between. You are in the presence of God. That is why Christians worship and glorify the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son, one God, forever.

topics.title: Do the Spirit's mission and scriptural expressions about him make him subordinate?
topics.cmp: Nearly all the authors deny that the Spirit's mission or the scriptural language about him makes him inferior. Augustine, Ambrose, Owen, Bickersteth and Gregory of Nyssa reach this conclusion by different routes. Augustine reads the sending and the Spirit's 'not speaking of himself' as signifying procession and origin, not inferiority, and insists that works ascribed to one Person belong to the inseparable Trinity. Owen and Bickersteth instead speak of an office or voluntary condescension in the economy of grace, which Owen frames as inequality of office without inequality of nature; Bickersteth adds the human analogy of a senate sending its own member. Ambrose argues from mutual sending, from the Spirit's hearing by unity of substance and natural knowledge, and from Scripture's own correction of creaturely images such as fount and river. Gregory of Nyssa stresses the shared divine attributes and shows that the title Paraclete is applied to Father and Son alike, while Bickersteth and Basil read 'search' and 'who hath directed' as consistent with divine omniscience. The clear dissenter is Novatian, who holds that the Paraclete is less than Christ because he receives from him, and treats that subordination as evidence of Christ's divinity. Hilary, while not asserting inferiority, emphasizes that in worship the Spirit is the means and God the object, so the Gift is distinct from the One adored. Basil, by contrast, reads worship 'in the Spirit' as the Spirit's light revealing the Lord's Godhead.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Of the Sensible Showing of the Holy Spirit, and of the…
refs.quote: not on account of inequality, or imparity, or unlikeness of substance

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: If any object that He is said to be sent by the Father and the Son, and that this mission implies inferiority, we answer that even among men the being sent is by no means always a mark of subordination.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: If, then, the Son and the Spirit send each other, as the Father sends, there is no inferiority of subjection, but a community of power.

ans.text:
No. The ways the Bible speaks about the Holy Spirit's work never make him a lesser being than the Father or the Son. They describe the part he freely takes in saving us, and the way he is related to the Father and the Son. They do not describe a lower rank or a smaller nature. Let's walk through the expressions that most often raise the question.

First, the Spirit is "sent." Jesus promises that the Father will send the Spirit in his name (John 14:26), and that he himself will send the Spirit from the Father (John 15:26). It is easy to assume that whoever is sent must be the junior partner. But think of a group of equals who choose one of their own number to carry out an important task. The one who goes is not inferior to those who stay. He has simply taken on that job. The Bible says the very same thing about the Son: the Father sent him into the world (John 3:17), yet the Son is God (John 1:1). If being sent does not make the Son less than the Father, it does not make the Spirit less either.

The sending also runs in more than one direction. The Spirit himself sends. In Acts 13:2-4 the Holy Spirit calls Barnabas and Saul, and Luke says they were sent out by the Holy Spirit. So the Spirit is not only the one sent but also the one who sends, just as the Father and the Son do. Sending among the three persons shows that they work together with one power. It does not show that one is under another. In the Bible's own teaching, the work the Spirit is sent to do is a work only God can do. He makes dead hearts alive (John 3:5-8), makes us holy, and lives in believers as in a temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). Being sent tells us about a role in the work of salvation, not a lower kind of being.

Christians have long put it this way. There can be an order in what the persons do without any difference in what they are. The Son freely took on the work of Redeemer. The Spirit freely takes on the work of Helper and Comforter. Neither is forced into a lower place. Each acts with the full will that belongs to God.

Second, the Spirit is called the "Comforter" or "Advocate." The Greek word means one called alongside: to help, to plead for someone, to encourage. Some have treated this as a servant's title. But the Bible gives the same title, and the same work, to the Father and the Son. Paul calls the Father "the God of all comfort" (2 Corinthians 1:3). John says "we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One" (1 John 2:1). When Jesus promises "another Advocate" (John 14:16), he is counting himself as the first one. So the title does not set the Spirit apart from the Father and the Son. It is a name he shares with them.

Nor does "another Advocate" mean that Jesus was not enough. Father, Son and Spirit are never separated in what they do. When the Spirit comes, Christ comes with him. Jesus says, "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you" (John 14:18). When Jesus says the Spirit will guide the disciples "into all truth," he is not saying the Spirit knows more than he does. He is not saying the Spirit knows less, either. The truth the Spirit teaches is the truth of Christ.

Third, the Spirit "speaks what He hears." Jesus says the Spirit "will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears" (John 16:13). Does that make him a messenger who repeats orders from above? Compare what Jesus says about himself: "the Son can do nothing by Himself" (John 5:19), and his teaching is not his own but the Father's (John 7:16). These words do not make the Son less than the Father. They show that he comes from the Father and is never acting apart from him. The Spirit's "hearing" means the same thing. He does not speak a private message separate from the Father and the Son. What he says is what the one God says.

This hearing is not like ours. We hear in order to learn something new. God already knows all things, so in him knowing comes before any hearing. Scripture uses the language of hearing so that we will trust that the Spirit knows the Father's mind fully. It even says the Father hears the Son. At Lazarus's tomb Jesus prays, "Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. I knew that You always hear Me" (John 11:41-42). No one thinks this makes the Father obey the Son. Among the persons of the Trinity, "hearing" speaks of perfect unity, not of a servant taking orders.

Fourth, the Spirit "searches all things, even the deep things of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10). This does not mean he is digging out facts he did not know before. Paul explains in the next verse with a comparison. Only a person's own spirit knows his inner thoughts, "So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:11). Your spirit does not have to investigate itself to find out what you are thinking. It simply knows. In the Bible "search" often means thorough, penetrating knowledge rather than step-by-step discovery. The Lord says, "I, the LORD, search the heart" (Jeremiah 17:10), and no one takes that to mean God is learning. So far from making the Spirit smaller, this verse is one of the strongest in Scripture for his deity. Only one who is God could know the depths of God from the inside.

Fifth, believers worship "in the Spirit." Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worshipers "must worship Him in spirit and in truth" (John 4:24). Christians have read "spirit" here in two ways. Some take it to mean the inner, sincere worship of the human heart, as opposed to worship tied to a holy mountain. Others take it as a pointer to the Holy Spirit, by whom we worship. On the second reading, some ask whether being the one "in" whom we worship makes the Spirit a tool rather than God. It does not. Paul says we speak and live "in Christ," and that does not lower Christ. He also says "no one can say, 'Jesus is Lord,' except by the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:3). The Spirit is the one who opens our eyes, unites us to Christ, and brings us to the Father. Light helps us see. But light is not therefore less than what it shows. There is a real distinction here: the Spirit is the one who enables our worship, and he is also, with the Father and the Son, rightly worshiped and glorified.

Finally, the Spirit is pictured as water flowing from a fountain. Jesus says that "streams of living water will flow from within" the one who believes, and John explains that he meant the Spirit (John 7:38-39). Someone might reason that a stream is smaller than its source. But every picture taken from creation falls short of God, and we must not press it where it was never meant to go. Notice, too, that Scripture does not speak of a trickle. It speaks of rivers of living water that never run dry. And a river is the same water as its spring: same nature, same clearness, same life. The picture teaches that the Spirit comes from God and shares God's own life. It does not teach that he is a lesser kind of thing.

While we are speaking of the Spirit coming from the Father, it is fair to mention one point on which sincere Christians have differed. Some hold that the Spirit eternally comes forth from the Father and the Son. They point to Jesus sending the Spirit and to the Spirit being called "the Spirit of Christ" (Romans 8:9). Others hold that he comes forth from the Father alone, and is sent into the world through the Son. They point to John 15:26, which speaks of the Spirit who "goes out from the Father." Both sides agree on the point that matters here. Where the Spirit comes from tells us how he is related to the other persons. It does not make him any less God.

The Bible's wider witness settles the matter. Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:3-4). Believers are baptized into the one name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). The Spirit gives life, knows God's depths, and dwells in his people as God dwells in his temple. The expressions about his being sent, his hearing, his comforting and his searching all describe the humble, generous way God the Holy Spirit works for our salvation. When God stoops to serve us, that shows his love. It does not lower his glory.

topics.title: Do comparisons with creatures undermine the arguments for the Spirit's deity?
topics.cmp: Basil of Caesarea and Ambrose of Milan both reject the claim that comparisons with creatures weaken the case for the Spirit's deity, but they take up different objections and argue differently. Basil answers the appeals to Moses and to created witnesses. He treats faith in Moses and baptism in the cloud and sea as a mere shadow and type. Such a type shares only the name with Christian baptism and, he says, gave no remission of sins, new life, or spiritual gift. He also turns the argument back on the opponents: Scripture joins Moses with the Lord, not with the Spirit, so their reasoning would cheapen faith in God Himself. On heaven, earth and stones being called as witnesses, he argues that this meets a practical need and says nothing about the witness's nature. Ambrose, addressing the Seraph's cleansing of Isaiah's lips, relies instead on a close reading of the text (the coal, not the Seraph, takes away sin) and on a mystical reading of the coal as the Spirit's grace and as Christ. He adds that even if an angel removed sin, it would act only as a minister sent by God, not by its own authority.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Objection that some were baptized unto Moses and…
refs.quote: Our answer is that the faith in the Spirit is the same as the faith in the Father and the Son; and in like manner, too, the baptism. But the faith in Moses and in the cloud is, as it were, in a shadow and type.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Shall take away, he says, and shall purge, not I will take away, but that fire from the altar of God, that is, the grace of the Spirit.

ans.text:
No. When you look closely at each comparison, it actually shows how different the Holy Spirit is from any creature, not how similar.

The question comes up because the Bible shows that the Spirit is God in several ways. We are baptized into His name. We put our faith in Him. Scripture calls on Him as a witness. He forgives and cleanses sin. Some have objected that the Bible says similar things about creatures. Israel was "baptized into Moses." Heaven and earth are called as witnesses. An angel touched Isaiah's lips and took away his guilt. If creatures can do these things, the objection goes, then these things do not prove the Spirit is God. Let's take each one in turn.

Start with Moses. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:2 that the Israelites "were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea." But Paul's point there is that those events were pictures, or "examples," of things to come (1 Corinthians 10:6). Passing through the Red Sea was a shadow of Christian baptism, and a shadow is not the thing itself. A photograph of a meal will not feed you, however much it looks like dinner. The two baptisms share a word, but little else. The sea did not wash away anyone's sins. It did not give new birth. Nobody came out of it united to Christ in His death and resurrection, as Romans 6:3-4 says believers are. Christian baptism is "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). That is one name shared by three, and the Spirit stands in it alongside the Father and the Son. Moses never stands inside God's name like that.

What about believing in Moses? Exodus 14:31 says the people "believed in the LORD and in His servant Moses." Notice who Moses is joined to there. If that verse made faith in the Spirit meaningless, it would make faith in the LORD meaningless too, and no Christian accepts that. Israel trusted Moses as God's chosen messenger. Their trust rested finally on the God who sent him. Moses was also a forerunner of Christ, the true go-between of God and His people. Trusting God's messenger is one thing. Trusting someone as the source of life and holiness is another. Scripture asks us to trust the Spirit in that second way. He gives new birth (John 3:5-6). He makes us God's children (Romans 8:14-16). He raises the dead (Romans 8:11).

Next, the witnesses. Moses called heaven and earth as witnesses against Israel (Deuteronomy 30:19). Joshua even set up a stone and said it had "heard" the covenant (Joshua 24:27). Paul charged Timothy before God, Christ Jesus and the chosen angels (1 Timothy 5:21). When a leader is responsible for people, he calls on whatever witnesses suit the moment, so that the promise can be remembered later. A stone does not become divine by being named as a witness, any more than a wedding guest becomes part of the marriage. Such language tells us about the seriousness of the moment, not about the nature of the witness. The case for the Spirit's deity never rested on the word "witness" alone. It rests on the whole pattern of what Scripture says He is and does. To lie to the Holy Spirit is to lie to God (Acts 5:3-4). He knows the deep things of God as only God can (1 Corinthians 2:10-11). He is everywhere present (Psalm 139:7).

Finally, Isaiah. In Isaiah 6 a seraph, a kind of angel, takes a burning coal from God's altar and touches Isaiah's lips. He says that because of this, Isaiah's guilt is taken away and his sin is atoned for. Does that mean an angel can forgive sin? Look at the details. The seraph does not say "I forgive you." He points to the coal, and the coal came from God's own altar. The angel is a servant carrying out an errand. A mail carrier who delivers a pardon has not pardoned anyone. The cleansing comes from God. Many Christians have seen in that altar fire a picture of the Spirit's purifying work, and of Christ's sacrifice that burns away our sin.

The New Testament adds something striking about that same vision. John says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory (John 12:41). Paul says it was the Holy Spirit who spoke the words Isaiah heard there (Acts 28:25-26). So in Isaiah 6, the angel is the messenger and the Spirit is the Lord on the throne who sends him. The scribes were right that only God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7). Angels and prophets only announce God's forgiveness. The Spirit is never sent as one creature among others. He is the one who sends.

The common thread is simple. Creatures can serve God's purposes and even point to holy things. The Spirit does something different. He shares God's name, does God's own works, and receives the trust and worship that belong to God alone. Holding these side by side does not weaken the case. It shows the difference between servants and the Lord they serve.

topics.title: Can the Holy Spirit be separated from the Father and the Son?
topics.cmp: Ambrose, Basil, and Hilary all deny that the Spirit can be separated from the Father and the Son, but they argue from different starting points. Ambrose draws on the Spirit's procession, his coming and indwelling (where the Spirit is, the Father and Son are), his sealing and divinizing work, and the confession 'Jesus is Lord'. From these he concludes that Father, Son, and Spirit share one nature and that believers are one temple. Basil argues from worship and baptism: severing the Spirit is unsafe and impossible. Using the analogy of light and sight, he presents the Spirit as the one in whom the Son, as Image, is seen and through whom believers rise to the Father as Archetype. Hilary reverses the direction of the argument: because the one Spirit is both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, the Son must share the Father's nature. Owen addresses a different question. He does not argue for inseparability but stresses the Spirit's own will and loving condescension in coming, alongside his being sent, which places a distinctive emphasis on the Spirit's personal agency within the shared economy of salvation.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: The Holy Spirit also, when He proceeds from the Father and the Son, is not separated from the Father nor separated from the Son. For how could He be separated from the Father Who is the Spirit of His mouth?

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is…
refs.quote: If you remain outside the Spirit you will not be able even to worship at all; and on your becoming in Him you will in no wise be able to dissever Him from God;—any more than you will divorce light from visible objects.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: So that there is not only the mission of Christ, but the will of the Spirit, in his coming: "He will come," — his own will is in his work.

ans.text:
No. The Holy Spirit can never be separated from the Father and the Son, because he shares the one life and being of God with them. Where the Spirit is, the Father and the Son are too, and where they are, he is.

This needs a careful word up front. Inseparable does not mean identical. The Father, the Son and the Spirit are truly distinct persons. At Jesus' baptism the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven (Matthew 3:16-17). Three persons are present, but they are never apart. They are distinct, but never divided.

Think first about where the Spirit comes from. Jesus speaks of the Spirit of truth who goes out from the Father (John 15:26). That might sound as if the Spirit leaves the Father, the way a child leaves home. But God is not made of parts, and he is not spread out in space. The Spirit's 'going out' describes how he eternally has his being from the Father. It is not a departure. A river can flow from a spring while remaining one stream of water with it. In a far deeper way, the Spirit comes from the Father without ever being cut off from him.

Christians have sincerely disagreed on one detail here. Many hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son together. They point out that he is called 'the Spirit of Christ' and is sent by the Son. Others hold that he proceeds from the Father alone. They note that Jesus' words in John 15:26 name only the Father as the source, and they see the Son's sending as part of the Spirit's mission to the world. Both sides agree on what matters for this question: the Spirit is never separated from either the Father or the Son.

The same is true of how God works. The Father, Son and Spirit do not split up a job like a team of builders, each working alone on his own section. Every work of God is the work of all three, though each acts in his own way. Paul's blessing shows this: 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you' (2 Corinthians 13:14). It is one blessing from one God.

When the Spirit is 'sent,' this does not make him a servant running errands. Paul says the Spirit gives his gifts to each believer just as he determines (1 Corinthians 12:11). So the Spirit comes by his own will, freely and in love, in full agreement with the Father and the Son who send him. Only God acts with that kind of authority.

The Spirit is also inseparable from God in the way we come to know God. The Spirit opens our eyes to see Jesus, and in Jesus we see the Father. Jesus said, 'Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). And Paul writes that no one can say, 'Jesus is Lord,' except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). Here is an everyday picture. You cannot see a room without light, and the light is seen together with everything it shows you. In the same way, you cannot see the Son without the Spirit, and in seeing the Son you see the Father.

Worship follows the same pattern. 'Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit' (Ephesians 2:18). We do not worship the Father on one occasion, the Son on another, and the Spirit on a third. We worship one God, coming to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. This is also why Jesus commands baptism 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 28:19). It is one name, not three. Leaving the Spirit out of that name would not simplify the faith; it would tear it apart.

Finally, consider what happens in a believer's life. Jesus promises that if anyone loves him, 'My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him' (John 14:23). How do the Father and the Son make their home in us? By the Spirit. Paul moves in a single breath from 'the Spirit of God lives in you,' to 'the Spirit of Christ,' to 'if Christ is in you' (Romans 8:9-10). He does not mean three separate visitors. When the Spirit lives in you, the whole God lives in you. That is why Paul can say, 'you yourselves are God's temple, and God's Spirit dwells in you' (1 Corinthians 3:16). Your body is not a temple to three gods. It is one temple of the one God.

All of this points to one conclusion: the Spirit shares one and the same nature with the Father and the Son. Notice that he is called both 'the Spirit of God' and 'the Spirit of Christ.' He is one Spirit, belonging fully to both. That only makes sense if the Father and the Son are one in being, and if the Spirit is one with them.

No created thing could be bound to God like this. An angel can be sent away from God's presence on an errand, but the Spirit knows the very thoughts of God from the inside (1 Corinthians 2:10-11). He makes us share in God's own life, and only one who is God can give God's life. So the Spirit is not a force God uses, or a lesser helper standing at a distance. He is God himself, present with us, and he brings the Father and the Son with him wherever he goes.

topics.title: What does grieving, resisting or blaspheming the Holy Spirit show about him?
topics.cmp: Only John Owen and Ambrose of Milan address this topic, and they ask different questions of it. Owen does most of the work. He treats Ephesians 4:30's command not to grieve the Spirit as evidence that the Spirit is a person, citing the double article, the sealing work assigned to him, and the fact that grief is a personal affection, whereas 'quenching' concerns his operations. Owen also insists the grief is metaphorical, since sorrow would imply change and weakness in the Spirit's infinite nature, and holds that our sin is no less serious than if he were actually grieved. Ambrose instead draws a deity argument from resistance and blasphemy: Peter's 'who was I that I should resist God?' shows the Spirit's operation is divine, and the unforgivable blasphemy implies no lesser dignity in the Son, whose dignity with the Spirit is 'one and common'; on Ambrose's reading, what can be pardoned is thinking too lightly of Christ's visible body. The two differ in explaining why that sin is unpardonable: Owen grounds it in the Spirit acting in the name of the Father and Son, so that sinning against him sins against the whole love and authority of the Trinity, while Ambrose locates it in denying the Spirit's own majesty and eternal power.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The Spirit is glorified also by it. He is grieved by our disobedience, Eph. iv. 30; and therefore his glory is in our bringing forth fruit. He dwells in us, as in his temple; which is not to be defiled.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Peter, when sent by the Spirit, did not wait for the command of God the Father, but acknowledged that that message was from the Spirit Himself, and the grace that of the Spirit Himself

ans.text:
These warnings show that the Holy Spirit is a real person, not a force, and that he is fully God, so that sinning against him is sinning against God himself.

Start with the simplest point. You cannot grieve electricity. You cannot lie to the wind or insult gravity. Only a person can be grieved, resisted, lied to or insulted. Yet the Bible says all of these things about the Holy Spirit. Paul writes in Ephesians 4:30, "And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption." In the same breath he gives the Spirit a personal work: he is the one who has put his mark of ownership on believers and will keep them until the end. Isaiah says the same about Israel in the wilderness: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit (Isaiah 63:10). The Spirit is someone we relate to, someone who cares how we live.

What grieves him? Paul tells us in the verses around Ephesians 4:30: lying, bitter anger, harsh words, stealing, unforgiveness. The Spirit lives in believers as in a temple (1 Corinthians 6:19). He is at work making us holy, so when we cling to sin he is, so to speak, wounded by a friend. He is also grieved when we look for our joy anywhere but in God, or when we push away the comfort and assurance he offers us because we stubbornly refuse to believe God's promises.
