Does this mean the Spirit suffers hurt the way we do, or that we can damage God? Christians have historically said no. Our sorrow involves loss, surprise, weakness and change, and God, who is perfect and unchanging, does not have those limits. The Bible uses language from our own experience so we can grasp something true: the Spirit is not cold or indifferent toward us. He loves us like the closest friend, and what we do really matters to him. Some believers today prefer to stress that God truly feels, while others stress that he is never at the mercy of his creatures. Both want to guard something real: God's love is genuine, and God is never weak. Either way, the lesson for us is the same. Sin is just as serious as it would be if we were wounding a dear friend, because that is exactly what it is fit to do.

The Bible also speaks of resisting the Spirit. Stephen tells the leaders who were about to stone him, "You always resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51), and he ties this to how their ancestors treated the prophets. The prophets spoke by the Spirit, so rejecting their message was rejecting him. The same is true today when people harden themselves against God's word. Paul also warns, "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 5:19). The Spirit is often pictured as fire, so stifling his work is like pouring water on a flame.

These passages also show that the Spirit is God. When Ananias lied about his gift, Peter said he had lied to the Holy Spirit, and then said, "You have not lied to men, but to God" (Acts 5:3-4). Lying to the Spirit is lying to God. Likewise, when the Spirit fell on the first Gentile believers, Peter said that refusing them would have meant standing in God's way (Acts 11:17). To resist the Spirit's work is to resist God.

That brings us to the hardest saying. Jesus said that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, and even a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, "but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the one to come" (Matthew 12:31-32). Does this mean the Spirit is greater than the Son? No. Father, Son and Spirit are one God, equal in glory. Look at the setting. Jesus had just freed a man from a demon by the power of the Spirit, and some religious leaders, seeing God's work plainly in front of them, called it the work of the devil. Mark explains that Jesus said this "because they were saying, 'He has an unclean spirit'" (Mark 3:30).

So the difference is not about rank but about what is being rejected. Someone might misjudge Jesus at first, seeing only a carpenter from Nazareth, and later repent. Paul was once a blasphemer and persecutor, and he was forgiven. But the Spirit is the one who shows us Christ, convicts us of sin and brings us to repentance. He comes in the name of the Father and the Son, carrying all of God's saving love to us. To look at that clear light, know it is from God, and deliberately call it evil, and to keep doing so, is to shut the only door through which forgiveness comes. It is not that God refuses someone who comes to him in repentance. It is that this hardened rejection refuses to come at all.

This should both warn and comfort. It warns us never to play games with God's truth or harden our hearts when the Spirit is speaking. But if you are troubled and afraid that you have committed this sin, your very worry is a good sign. Those Jesus warned were not anxious about offending God. A heart that still cares, that still wants Christ, is a heart the Spirit is still drawing, and Jesus promises that whoever comes to him he will never drive away (John 6:37).

title: The Spirit's Procession, Names and Mission
desc: How the Spirit proceeds, the Filioque, his names as Love and Gift, his sending and visible appearances, and his work in Christ, believers and the Church.

topics.title: How does the Holy Spirit proceed, and does He proceed from the Son as well as the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the question affirm that the Spirit proceeds from or belongs to the Son as well as the Father, but they ground and qualify this differently. Augustine gives the fullest account: the Spirit proceeds timelessly and at once from both, principally from the Father, because the Son receives from the Father, in being begotten, that the Spirit proceeds from him. Augustine reads Christ's breathing on the disciples as a sign of this and explains John 15:26's mention of the Father alone by the Son's habit of referring what is his own to the Father; Hilary, Ambrose and Bickersteth reach the same conclusion more simply from scriptural titles such as 'Spirit of Christ' and from the Son's sending of the Spirit. Gregory of Nyssa's answer carries a different emphasis: he places the Spirit's origin in the Father as Primal Light while the Spirit shines forth through the Son, and he rejects Eunomius's claim that the Spirit came into being through the Son as an instrument. Owen distinguishes an eternal, hypostatic procession from an economical going forth. Unlike Augustine, he reads John 15:26 chiefly as the economical sending, and he argues from the outward mission (ad extra) to the inward procession (ad intra) and from Christ's step-by-step teaching in John 14-16, while also stressing the covenant ordering of the Father's love and the Son's purchase. Edwards and Waterland work instead from analogy and patristic language: Edwards orders understanding before will, so the Son does not proceed from the Spirit, and Waterland, following Athenagoras, treats the Spirit as a substantial emanation from the Father, like light from fire.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: What It is that Suffices Here to Solve the Question Why…
refs.quote: if He, too, was called a Son, He would certainly be called the Son of both, which is most absurd, since no one is son of two, save of father and mother

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: it is in reference to a peculiar work that he is said to proceed, — namely, to testify of Christ: which cannot be assigned to him in respect of his eternal procession, but of his actual dispensation

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: What shadow of such a notion did he find in Scripture, that he ventures upon this assertion?

ans.text:
The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father eternally, as His breath and His love, not as a second Son. Most Christians have also confessed that He proceeds from the Son, while others hold that He proceeds from the Father alone, perhaps through the Son. To see what this means, it helps to start with the word itself.

In John 15:26 Jesus speaks of "the Spirit of truth who goes out from the Father." That phrase gives us the word "procession." It simply means coming forth from a source. The Father is the source of the Son by "begetting" Him. That is the Bible's family word, which tells us the Son has the very same nature as the Father, as a child shares the nature of a parent. The Father is also the source of the Spirit, but the Bible never calls the Spirit a son or says He is begotten. He is the Spirit, the breath of God. Both come from the Father, but in different ways, and that difference is what makes them two persons and not one.

Why not call the Spirit a second Son? If He were, He would be the Son's brother, and Scripture insists that Jesus is the one and only Son (John 3:16). And if the Spirit came from both Father and Son as a son, the Father and the Son would be like father and mother, which is unthinkable in God. So Scripture keeps two different words, and we should keep them too, even though we cannot fully explain the difference.

Many Christians have found a helpful picture in our own inner life. When you know something, your mind forms a thought or idea of it. That is something like the Son, who is called the Word of God (John 1:1) and the exact image of the Father (Hebrews 1:3). When you know something good, love for it rises up in you. That is something like the Spirit. God eternally knows Himself perfectly, and that perfect self-knowledge is His Word, His Son. He also eternally delights in what He knows. The Father loves the Son, the Son loves the Father, and that shared love and joy is the Spirit. This is why the Spirit is so often linked with love: "God's love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Romans 5:5). On this picture the Son comes first in order, though not in time, because you must know something before you can love it. The Spirit is the bond of love, the shared delight and gift between Father and Son. The picture has limits. In us, thoughts and loves are passing activities. In God, the Word and the Spirit are real persons, each fully God. Still, it shows why there are exactly two ways of coming forth in God, not one and not ten.

This procession is eternal. There was never a time when the Father was without His Son, and never a time when He was without His Spirit. The Spirit does not begin to exist when He is given to believers. If He did, His very being would depend on creatures. Rather, He is eternally the Gift of God, ready to be given, and He is actually given to us in time. A present is still a gift while it sits wrapped, before anyone opens it.

That leads to an important distinction. The Bible speaks both of the Spirit's eternal origin and of His being sent into the world at Pentecost and into our hearts. Some passages, John 15:26 among them, are mainly about this sending, since they tie His coming to a task: "He will testify about Me." But many Christians have reasoned that the way the persons are sent in history reflects who they are eternally. The Father is never sent. The Son is sent by the Father. The Spirit is sent by the Father and by the Son.

Here is where the question about the Son comes in. The New Testament calls the Spirit not only "the Spirit of God" but "the Spirit of Christ" (Romans 8:9) and "the Spirit of His Son" (Galatians 4:6). Jesus says the Father will send the Spirit in His name (John 14:26), then that He Himself will send the Spirit from the Father (John 15:26), and finally, plainly, "I will send Him to you" (John 16:7). The Spirit takes what belongs to the Son and makes it known, and Jesus adds that everything the Father has is His (John 16:14-15). After His resurrection, Jesus breathed on His disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit" (John 20:22). The breath was not the Spirit Himself, but it was a vivid sign that the Spirit is the breath of the Son too.

From all this, a large part of the church has confessed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Even so, the Father remains the first source. Everything the Son has, He has from the Father, including this. In begetting the Son, the Father gives Him everything, so the Spirit comes from both at once, not first into the Son and then out again. When Jesus says the Spirit goes out "from the Father," He is not denying His own part. He regularly points what is His back to the Father, as when He said His teaching was not His own but the Father's who sent Him (John 7:16).

Another large part of the church disagrees, sincerely and with real concern. They point out that Jesus Himself said only "from the Father," and that the church's ancient creed said the same before words were later added to it in some places. They worry that naming two sources could blur the Father's unique role as the one fountain of the Godhead, or could make the Spirit seem less than the other two. Many on this side are glad to say that the Spirit comes from the Father through the Son, or rests on the Son and shines out through Him. On the core matters both sides fully agree. The Spirit is truly God. He comes eternally from the Father. He is not a created thing or a tool the Father used to make Him, and He is truly the Spirit of Christ. The disagreement is real, but it is narrower than it is sometimes made to sound.

One last misunderstanding. "Proceed," "come," and "be sent" do not mean the Spirit travels from one place to another, as if He left heaven empty to arrive at Pentecost. God is everywhere. David asks where he could go to get away from God's Spirit, and the answer is nowhere (Psalm 139:7). When the Spirit "comes," it means He begins to be present in a new way and to do a new work, dwelling in believers, giving life, and making Christ known. When we say He proceeds eternally, we mean not movement but relationship: who comes from whom.

So when you pray in the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father, you are not dealing with three separate gods or with a vague force. You are being drawn into the very love that the Father and the Son have shared forever. That love has now been poured into your heart, crying "Abba, Father!" (Galatians 4:6).

topics.title: Is the Holy Spirit properly named Love and Gift within the Trinity?
topics.cmp: Augustine of Hippo is the chief advocate of naming the Holy Spirit Love and Gift: he argues that the Spirit is the consubstantial communion and mutual love of Father and Son, is specially called by what both share in common ('Spirit', 'holy', love), and is relational as Gift, so that he is not a Son because he comes forth as given rather than born. He grounds this in Scripture (the Spirit 'of both', 1 John 4, Colossians 1:13), in analogies such as the Law and the Prophets and mind, knowledge and love, and in divine simplicity, while insisting that each Person is love and all three are one love. Jonathan Edwards reaches a similar conclusion by a different route, identifying the Son with God's understanding and the Spirit with God's will, affection, joy and delight, and arguing from the biblical images of water, breath, fire and pouring out, from the title Comforter, and from the saints' communion as a sharing in the Spirit. Ambrose and Hilary do not take up the Love-and-Gift naming; like Augustine they note that Father and Son are also called 'Spirit' (Hilary warning that this must not be used to deny the Spirit's distinct Name), but their stress falls on the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ being one Spirit and on unity of operation proving unity of Godhead. John Owen plainly diverges from Augustine on 1 John 4:8, which Augustine refers to the Holy Spirit and Owen refers personally to the Father; Owen treats the Spirit economically and devotionally, as the one sent from the Father and by Christ to shed abroad and assure believers of the Father's love, rather than as the love within the Trinity.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Holy Spirit Also is Equal to the Father and the Son…
refs.quote: Therefore the Holy Spirit, whatever it is, is something common both to the Father and Son. But that communion itself is consubstantial and co-eternal

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For our knowledge proceeds from one Spirit, through one Son to one Father; and from one Father through one Son to one Holy Spirit is delivered goodness and sanctification and the sovereign right of eternal power.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: But if this one Spirit of one Divinity, one in both God and Lord through the mystery of the birth, does not please thee, then point out to me what Spirit both works and distributes these diverse gifts to us

ans.text:
Yes, Christians have good reason to call the Holy Spirit both Love and Gift. These are not his only names, and they do not mean he alone is loving. They are fitting names because of how the Bible speaks of him. Let me explain what that means and what it does not mean.

Start with Gift, since the Bible uses this word for the Spirit most plainly. On the day of Pentecost Peter told the crowd, "Repent and be baptized... and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38). Jesus promised that the Father in heaven will "give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him" (Luke 11:13). Again and again the Spirit is the one who is sent, poured out and given. We never read of the Father being given to us in this way. The Son is given too, for God gave His one and only Son (John 3:16). But the Son is first of all the Son, born of the Father. The Spirit is the one Scripture keeps presenting as God's gift.

A gift is always someone's gift to someone. So this name shows how the Spirit is related to the others. He is the gift of the Father, from whom he comes (John 15:26). He is also the gift of the Son, which is why Paul calls him "the Spirit of His Son" (Galatians 4:6). This explains something curious in the Bible's language. Jesus is the Son of the Father, and never "our Son." But the Spirit is called the Spirit of God and also the Spirit given to us, dwelling in us and belonging to us. A child belongs to the parent who gave it life. A gift belongs both to the giver and to the one who receives it.

This does not mean the Spirit only became a gift when the church received him, or that he is a thing handed over. From all eternity he comes forth from the Father as the one who is to be given. In time he is freely given to us, and he gives himself, for he is a Person, God himself. He distributes his gifts "just as He determines" (1 Corinthians 12:11). God never gives us anything less than God.

This also answers a question people often ask. If the Spirit comes from the Father, why isn't he called a second Son? The Son comes forth by being begotten, which simply means born or fathered. That is why he is the Son and his name is Son. The Spirit comes forth in a different way. The Bible says he "proceeds," or goes out, from the Father. He comes forth as breath and as gift, not as a child. So it would be wrong to call him the Son of the Father, or a grandson, or the Son of both.

Why is he called the Holy Spirit in particular, when the Father is holy and spirit ("God is Spirit," John 4:24), and so is the Son? A thoughtful answer is that the third Person carries as his own name what the Father and the Son share. He is the Spirit of both, the one they have in common. So he fittingly bears the name that belongs to both of them.

Now to Love. Paul writes that "God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us" (Romans 5:5). He speaks of "the love of the Spirit" (Romans 15:30). The first fruit of the Spirit is love (Galatians 5:22). In 1 John 4, right after saying "God is love," John says, "By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit" (1 John 4:13). Everywhere the Spirit goes, God's love is brought home to people's hearts.

Many Christians have reasoned one step further. Scripture tells us that the Father has loved the Son eternally. Jesus prays, "You loved Me before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). Paul calls Jesus the Son God loves, which older translations render "the Son of His love" (Colossians 1:13). The Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. So he may rightly be thought of as the living love and joy between them. He is the bond of their unity, their shared delight. Think of the warmth between a father and a son who truly love each other, a fellowship that is more than either of them alone. In God this fellowship is not a mood or a force. It is a Person, fully God, as eternal as the Father and the Son. And the Father and Son are not united by borrowing this unity from someone higher. They are one by their very nature. When the Spirit is poured into us, we are drawn into that same love, crying "Abba, Father!" with the Son's own voice.

A few cautions keep this teaching healthy. First, the Spirit is not the only Person in God who loves or who is love. The Father loves, the Son loves, and the Spirit loves. They share one being and one love. We call the Spirit Love in a special sense for the same reason we call him Holy and Spirit in a special sense: he is what the Father and the Son share. Second, "God is love" in 1 John 4:8 is first a statement about God himself, the whole God. Sincere readers have noticed different emphases in the passage. Verse 9 speaks of the Father sending His Son, and verse 13 speaks of the Spirit. Both are true, and neither cancels the plain point that love is what God is. It is not just something he occasionally does. In fact the Trinity helps us see how this can be. Before the world existed, God was not lonely. The Father, Son and Spirit were already living in love. Third, calling the Spirit a bond must never make him sound like an impersonal link or a feeling. Scripture shows him teaching, speaking, interceding and grieving (John 14:26; Romans 8:26; Ephesians 4:30). He is a "Him," not an "it."

You should also know that Christians differ somewhat on how far to press the idea of the Spirit as the mutual love of Father and Son. Many find it a rich and fitting way to speak, rooted in the passages above. They tie it to the belief that the Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son. Others are more cautious. They stress that Jesus says the Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26). They worry that calling him the love between the other two can make him seem less of a Person in his own right. They prefer to speak of the Spirit coming from the Father and resting on the Son, as he did at Jesus' baptism. Both sides confess the same core truth. The Holy Spirit is fully God, a true Person, the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. He is given to us freely, and through him God's own love fills our hearts.

So when you call the Holy Spirit God's Gift and God's Love, you are speaking the Bible's language. You are not saying he is a thing God hands over, or the only loving Person in God. You are confessing that God has given us nothing less than himself, and that the love the Father has for the Son has been poured into us.

topics.title: What do the Spirit's scriptural titles and images reveal about him?
topics.cmp: Ambrose and Augustine mostly take up different titles, so there is little direct overlap. Where they meet, on the 'living water' and 'rivers' of John 7:38-39, they agree that the water is the Holy Spirit, and both rest this on the evangelist's own gloss. Ambrose uses it to show that the river from the throne in Revelation is the Spirit, and so that the Spirit is in God's throne. Augustine uses it to identify the water of John 4 with the Spirit, citing Paul's 'made to drink into one Spirit.' Ambrose's focus is on bodily and natural images ('Finger,' 'hands,' 'river'), which he reads by comparing Scripture with Scripture (Luke 11:20 with 'by the Spirit of God') and guards against carnal readings, insisting they show unity of power and Godhead rather than any inferiority or partition; his argument is that what diminishes the Spirit would equally diminish the Son as 'Right Hand.' Augustine instead concentrates on the Spirit as Christ's 'Gift' in Ephesians 4 and on reconciling Paul's 'gave gifts' with the Psalm's 'received gifts,' using the head-and-members relation and the one Gift distributing many gifts; one of his three answers is marked 'No,' but its reasoning agrees with the other two that the one Gift is the Spirit, and the 'No' appears to deny only that the plural 'gifts' tells against this.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: the Spirit is also called the Finger of God, because there is an indivisible and inseparable communion between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the…
refs.quote: For that which is in the one passage, “Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water,” is in the other, “shall be in him a fountain of water springing up unto eternal life.”

ans.text:
The Bible's names and pictures for the Holy Spirit show that he is God himself, present and at work, and not some lesser power God sends from a distance. Each title shows a different side of who he is and what he does. None of them makes him smaller than the Father or the Son.

Start with one of the most striking: the "finger of God." In Luke 11:20 Jesus says, "But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." Matthew tells the same moment, and there Jesus says "by the Spirit of God" (Matthew 12:28). So the Bible explains its own picture: the finger of God is the Holy Spirit.

Some people hear "finger" and think of something small, a minor part of God. But think how the Old Testament uses the phrase. When Pharaoh's magicians could not copy the plagues, they admitted, "This is the finger of God" (Exodus 8:19). The Ten Commandments were written "by the finger of God" (Exodus 31:18). In both places the point is that God himself acted, directly and unmistakably. When you sign your name with your own finger, nobody says a small part of you did it. You did it. In the same way, the Bible calls the Son the "arm of the LORD" (Isaiah 53:1), and nobody concludes that Jesus is only a fraction of God. God is not a body made of parts. These are pictures of his one power at work. The Father, Son and Spirit do not share out God's work in pieces. They work as one.

Then there is water. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the water he gives would become a spring inside a person, welling up to eternal life (John 4:10-14). Later he called out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink," and promised that streams of living water would flow from within the believer. John then explains: "He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him were later to receive" (John 7:37-39). Living water means fresh, flowing water, not a stagnant pool. The picture tells us the Spirit gives life, refreshes the thirsty soul, and keeps flowing rather than running dry. Paul uses the same image when he says we "were all given one Spirit to drink" (1 Corinthians 12:13).

The image reaches its height at the end of the Bible. John sees "the river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Revelation 22:1). Many Christians have read this river as a picture of the Spirit, since Jesus has already taught us that living water means the Spirit. If so, notice where the river comes from. It does not come from somewhere below the throne, like a servant waiting outside. It flows out of the throne itself, the place of God's rule, shared by the Father and the Lamb.

Jesus also gives the Spirit personal titles. He calls him the Advocate, sometimes translated Comforter or Helper. The word means someone called to your side to help, speak for you and strengthen you. Jesus says, "I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth" (John 14:16-17). The word "another" matters. The Spirit is another helper of the same kind as Jesus, not a lesser stand-in. He is called the Spirit of truth because he guides us "into all truth" (John 16:13) and opens our eyes to Christ. Paul calls him "the Spirit of life" (Romans 8:2), because he frees us from sin and death and makes us alive. These are not different spirits. They are many names for the one Holy Spirit, whom Jesus breathed on his disciples with the words "Receive the Holy Spirit" (John 20:22).

Finally, the Spirit is called God's gift. Peter promised that those who repent would "receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38). In Ephesians 4:7-8 Paul speaks of grace given "according to the measure of the gift of Christ," and quotes a psalm about the Lord who ascended on high and "gave gifts to men." Many Christians have understood "the gift of Christ" here as the Spirit himself. After rising and ascending, Jesus poured out the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The psalm says "gifts" in the plural, and Paul keeps that wording. It fits well, because the one Spirit brings many gifts and hands them out among the members of Christ's body. Not everyone has every gift, but every believer has the Spirit. Other careful readers think Paul here means more generally the grace and gifts Christ gives, rather than naming the Spirit directly. Either way, the passage links the risen Christ's giving with the Spirit's work in the church.

Does being a "gift" make the Spirit less than the giver? Not at all. When God gives the Spirit, he is not handing over some object. He is giving himself to live in us. And this Gift is not passive. Paul says the Spirit gives gifts "to each one as He determines" (1 Corinthians 12:11). He gives freely, by his own will, as only God can.

So every image points the same way. The finger shows God's own direct power. The living water shows God's own life poured into us. The river from the throne shows the Spirit sharing God's rule. The Advocate and Spirit of truth show a personal helper, equal to Jesus, who teaches and comforts. The Gift shows God giving himself. None of these pictures ranks the Spirit below the Father and the Son. Together they invite us to trust him, drink from him, and worship him as fully God.

topics.title: How is the Holy Spirit sent, and what does he do in believers and the Church?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Spirit is truly given to believers and that what he does in them is a divine work, and they ground this mainly in Scripture, especially John 14–16, Romans 5:5 and Romans 8. Several also argue from his works back to his deity: Basil from deification and the angels' dependence on him, Ambrose from his being given at once to scattered apostles and from regeneration, Hilary from the incomprehensibility of his coming, Novatian from his ordering of the Church, and Owen from the power of his inward witness. Their emphases differ markedly. John Owen, who supplies most of the answers, builds a detailed scheme around two ends, sanctification and consolation: the Spirit is sent by Christ as his 'substitute', in an order matching his eternal procession, and he works effectually and freely in prayer, conviction, unction and assurance, which Owen reads in Romans 8:16 as a judicial testimony. Augustine instead centres on the Spirit as the Gift and as Love, supported by an admittedly limited analogy from the mind. Irenaeus stresses the Spirit's giving of the likeness of God and quickening of the flesh; Novatian and Basil stress his ordering of the Church's gifts and offices; Edwards reads Scripture's images typologically to make the Spirit the sum of all good things; and Bickersteth argues that some prayers are addressed to the Spirit. There are also some differences in detail. Gregory of Nyssa reads 'witness with our spirit' simply as the Spirit dwelling in the mind, unlike Owen's courtroom reading. Athanasius says the Spirit departs from one who falls away and does not repent, as with Saul, whereas Owen stresses that the Comforter abides for ever and never leaves a believer wholly without consolation.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Holy Spirit is Called the Gift of God in the…
refs.quote: Because this living water, then, as the evangelist has explained to us, is the Holy Spirit, without doubt the Spirit is the gift of God

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: that this Spirit were altogether an inferior, created spirit, a mere servant, as some have blasphemed, nor yet merely and principally, as to his personality, the virtue of God, as some have fancied

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: how, then, do men deny that the Spirit can rebuke the world concerning judgment, Who removes doubt from judgment, and grants the successful issue?

ans.text:
The Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son to live in everyone who belongs to Christ. Once there, he makes everything Jesus won for us really ours: he joins us to Christ, makes us holy, comforts us, teaches us, and binds believers together into one Church.

Jesus spoke of this sending on the night before he died. He told his disciples that he would ask the Father, and the Father would give them another Advocate to be with them forever (John 14:16). He also said he himself would send the Spirit from the Father (John 15:26). He even said his leaving was for their good, because unless he went away the Advocate would not come (John 16:7). The words "Advocate" or "Comforter" describe someone called alongside to help, defend and encourage. Fifty days after the resurrection, at Pentecost, that promise was kept. Ever since, the same Spirit has been given to all who turn to Christ. Peter told the crowd, "you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38).

It helps to separate two ideas. One is the Spirit's eternal relationship within God, which Scripture describes by saying he comes from the Father. The other is his being sent into the world in time to do his saving work. All Christians agree that the Father sends the Spirit and that the risen Son sends him too. They have disagreed about whether, in that eternal relationship, the Spirit comes from the Son as well as from the Father. Some say yes, because the Spirit is called "the Spirit of His Son" (Galatians 4:6) and receives from what is Christ's. Others say Scripture speaks only of his coming from the Father, and that the Son's sending belongs to his mission in time. Both sides confess the Spirit as fully God, equal with the Father and the Son.

Being "sent" does not make the Spirit a junior servant or a mere errand-runner. When a father sends his grown son to run the family business, the son does not become less his father's equal. And the Spirit is not reluctant. Scripture says he gives his gifts "just as He determines" (1 Corinthians 12:11). He comes freely and in love, knowing full well that we will often grieve him. That is why Paul pleads, "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" (Ephesians 4:30). You can only grieve a person who loves you.

The Bible calls the Spirit the gift of God. That means more than that he hands out gifts. He is himself the gift. Jesus promised rivers of living water flowing from within those who believe, and John explains that he meant the Spirit (John 7:38-39). When Jesus says the Father will give good things to those who ask, Luke records it as the Father giving "the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him" (Luke 11:13). In other words, the Spirit is the sum of every good thing God gives. To have him is to have God himself living with us, and he is the down payment on our whole future inheritance (Ephesians 1:13-14).

What does he do once he comes? First, he gives new life. Paul says God saved us "through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit" (Titus 3:5). We cannot make ourselves alive to God. The Spirit opens dead hearts so that we can believe, and no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).

Second, he unites us to Christ. Everything Jesus has—forgiveness, righteousness, sonship, strength—is stored up in him like water in a spring. The Spirit is the one who draws from that spring and pours it into us. This is why Jesus says, "He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you" (John 16:14). The Spirit does not draw attention to himself. He acts like a floodlight that shines on a building, not into your eyes. He makes Christ look beautiful and precious to us.

Third, he pours God's love into our hearts. "God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us" (Romans 5:5). This is not only knowing in our heads that God loves us. The Spirit makes us feel it and enjoy it, and he enables us to love God and one another in return. Love is the first fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), and without love every other gift is worth nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1-3).

Fourth, he makes us God's children and teaches us to pray. God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out, "Abba, Father!" (Galatians 4:6). The Spirit replaces fear with a child's confidence. And because we often do not know what to pray for, Paul says the Spirit helps us in our weakness and intercedes for us (Romans 8:26-27). Real prayer is never something we manage on our own strength. It is the Spirit at work in us.

Fifth, he makes us holy and keeps us in the truth. He is called the Holy Spirit not only because he is holy but because he makes us holy. Day by day he weakens sin's grip and grows Christ's character in us. He is also "the Spirit of truth" who guides believers into truth (John 16:13). He does this partly by making the truth sweet. A person who has truly tasted the joy of the gospel is not easily talked into a counterfeit, because a counterfeit simply tastes worse.

Sixth, he builds the Church. The same Spirit who inspired the prophets and apostles to write Scripture (2 Peter 1:21) now opens our minds to understand it. He gives each believer gifts for the good of the whole body (1 Corinthians 12:4-7), so that no Christian is merely a spectator. He binds believers of every background into one people, the dwelling place of God (Ephesians 2:22).

This also tells us how to recognize the true Spirit when someone claims a special spiritual experience. The true Spirit always points to Jesus—the Jesus who was crucified and raised, the Jesus of Scripture. He never contradicts the Bible he inspired, and he never lifts anyone "beyond" needing Christ, prayer or the Word. His work brings love, peace, humility and a childlike trust in God, not pride, cruelty or slavish fear (1 John 4:1-3).

Two common misunderstandings are worth clearing up gently. The Spirit is not an impersonal force or a kind of spiritual energy. He is a person who teaches, intercedes, chooses and can be grieved. And the Spirit does not replace Jesus as though Christ were now absent and someone else had taken over. Jesus said, "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you" (John 14:18). Through the Spirit, Christ himself is truly present with his people.

So the Father gives his Son for us, the Son gives himself for us, and then together they give the Spirit to us. In the Spirit, God does not merely help us from a distance. He comes to live with us and in us, until the day we see him face to face.

topics.title: How does the Holy Spirit dwell in believers as anointing, seal and earnest?
topics.cmp: John Owen supplies nearly all the answers on this topic, so most of it reflects his single, closely argued position. He distinguishes the indwelling person of the Spirit from created habitual grace. He takes the earnest to be the Spirit himself, a first portion of the inheritance rather than a separate pledge, arguing from the grammar of Ephesians 1:14 and from Galatians 4:6. He treats sealing chiefly as the stamping of God's image that gives assurance, and the anointing chiefly as teaching, appealing to 1 John 2 and Isaiah 11. Irenaeus agrees that the earnest is a real portion of the Spirit given now that tends toward the fullness to come, but his emphasis falls elsewhere. For him the Spirit gradually accustoms man to bear God, matures the flesh for incorruption, and changes the quality of a person's works rather than the substance of the flesh, as in his image of the engrafted olive; Owen instead stresses assurance, holiness and communion with the Trinity. Basil's answer stands in some tension with both: he speaks of the Spirit being "in" creatures through grace that "naturally comes and goes" and is abiding only in those firmly disposed to good, whereas Owen insists the Spirit's earnest is abiding and cannot dwell anywhere without making that person holy, and Irenaeus says the Spirit, once he pervades a man, never leaves him.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: If the Spirit dwell not in you, if he be not your Comforter, neither is God your Father, nor the Son your Advocate, nor have you any portion in the gospel.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For what other visible fruit is there of the invisible Spirit, than the rendering of the flesh mature and capable of incorruption?

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: That the word “in,” in as many senses as it bears, is…
refs.quote: Where on the other hand the grace flowing from the Spirit naturally comes and goes, it is properly and truly said to exist in, even if on account of the firmness of the recipients’ disposition to good the grace abides with them continually.

ans.text:
The Holy Spirit lives in every true Christian personally, and the Bible uses three pictures to show what his presence means. He is an anointing who teaches us. He is a seal who marks us as God's own. And he is a down payment, the first part of the inheritance God has promised. Paul puts all three together in 2 Corinthians 1:21-22: God "anointed us, placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come."

First, notice who is given. It is not just a power, a feeling, or a set of good habits the Spirit produces. It is the Spirit himself. Galatians 4:6 says God "sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts," and only a person can be the Spirit of the Son. The new life, love and holiness that grow in us are the Spirit's work, and they can grow stronger or weaker. The Spirit is not the same thing as that work. He is the living God, dwelling in us as in a temple (1 Corinthians 6:19), and he is the one doing the work.

The anointing comes from 1 John 2. John tells ordinary believers, "you have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth" (2:20), and that this anointing remains in them and teaches them about all things (2:27). In the Old Testament, kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil for their task. Jesus is the Anointed One, the Christ, and Isaiah 11:2 says the Spirit would rest on him as the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel and knowledge. Believers share in his anointing. Its main work is teaching. This does not mean Christians need no pastors or Bible study. John himself is teaching them as he writes. It means the Spirit opens our eyes so that God's truth becomes our own conviction and not just information. Jesus promised that the Spirit "will guide you into all truth" (John 16:13). This is why the promises of Scripture can lie flat on the page for us one day and come alive the next. The words have not changed, but the Spirit has applied them to our hearts. So we read the Bible looking to him and asking for his light.

The seal comes from Ephesians 1:13: having believed the gospel, "you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit." In the ancient world a seal pressed into wax did two things. It left the owner's image on the thing sealed, and it showed whose property it was and kept it safe. Both ideas fit. The Spirit stamps God's likeness on us. He makes us more like Christ in love, purity and truth, and that family likeness gives us a growing, settled sense that God has truly accepted us. He also marks us as belonging to God and keeps us for him "for the day of redemption" (Ephesians 4:30). Sincere Christians differ on one point here. Some see this sealing as part of what happens to every believer at conversion, because Paul ties it simply to hearing and believing. Others see it also as a deeper experience of assurance that the Spirit may give later, because some believers clearly come to a fuller certainty of God's love over time. Both agree that every Christian belongs to God and that the Spirit is the one who makes us sure of it.

The third picture is the "earnest," as older Bibles put it, or the "pledge" in Ephesians 1:14: the Spirit "is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession." The idea is a down payment. A pawned watch left as security is a different thing from the money owed, and you get it back when the debt is paid. A down payment is different. It is part of the very thing promised, handed over now as a guarantee that the rest is coming. That is what the Spirit is. Heaven is not something other than the Spirit, given in exchange for him. The full inheritance is enjoying God completely, by the Spirit, without anything in the way. What we have now is a real first share of that same life. When the Spirit moves us to cry "Abba, Father," when he gives us joy in God, love for his people, and a hatred of sin, we are tasting heaven's own food. Romans 8:23 calls this "the firstfruits of the Spirit." He is also slowly getting us used to God, fitting us to bear the full glory to come.

Someone might ask about Hebrews 6:4-5, which speaks of people who have "tasted the powers of the coming age" and yet fall away. Can someone have the down payment and then lose the inheritance? The difference is real. A person can be stirred by the gospel, enjoy the life of a church, and feel the attraction of heavenly things for a while, without the Spirit ever making his home in them. That kind of taste passes. The down payment God gives his children stays. Jesus said the Spirit "abides with you and will be in you" (John 14:17). God does not put down a deposit and then walk away from the deal.

What changes in people who receive the Spirit? We do not stop being human. We do not become a different kind of being or get absorbed into God. Think of a wild branch grafted into a good tree. It is still wood, but it now bears different fruit. A Spirit-filled person is still flesh and blood, but the direction of their life changes. The Spirit cannot live in someone and leave them unholy, because his temple is holy. Wherever he dwells, the fruit of love, joy, peace, patience and self-control begins to grow (Galatians 5:22-23). Even our bodies are included. The same Spirit who raised Jesus "will also give life to your mortal bodies" (Romans 8:11). He does not always give us feelings of comfort; he gives those as he chooses. But he always makes holy those he lives in. Without him there is no Christian life at all. As Romans 8:9 says, "if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ." No one has God as Father and Christ as Savior while lacking the Spirit.

Do we receive the Spirit actively or passively? In one sense we are entirely passive. A dead heart cannot bring itself to life, any more than an empty jar fills itself. The Spirit gives new birth by his own power, and we contribute nothing (John 3:5-8). But once he has given us life, we welcome him by faith. We trust his promises, listen for his teaching, and rely on his comfort. Jesus said the world cannot receive him "because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him" (John 14:17). Believers know him, and so they can welcome him and enjoy him.

This is why Paul's warning matters so much: "And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" (Ephesians 4:30). Grieving is something only a person who loves can feel. You cannot grieve a force. In the verses around this warning, Paul names what grieves him: lies, bitter anger, theft, filthy talk, malice. In other words, living as though we were not united to Christ. This is serious because of who the Spirit is and why he came. He is God himself. And he has not come on his own errand. The Father and the Son sent him, carrying their love to us and making their grace real in us. To treat him carelessly is like slamming the door on a guest who came in the name of your Father and your dearest friend, bringing gifts from both. The other side of the warning is a warm encouragement. We can live in a way that pleases him. Choosing holiness out of love for the Spirit, because he delights in it, is one of the plainest ways to walk in fellowship with him.

So the Spirit in us is God's teacher in our hearts, God's mark of ownership and likeness on our lives, and God's first installment of heaven. He is given freely, he stays faithfully, and he deserves to be welcomed gladly.

topics.title: What is the Holy Spirit's work in Christ?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that the Spirit is fully and inseparably at work in Christ, but they frame this differently. Basil and Novatian stress the Spirit's presence in Christ's incarnate life: Basil cites the baptism, anointing, temptation, exorcisms and post-resurrection breathing to show that every operation of Christ was done with the Spirit's co-operation, while Novatian (twice) argues from Isaiah, David and the dove at the baptism that the Spirit dwelt in Christ entire, not in measure as in the prophets, making Christ the source of the Spirit's gifts to others. Ambrose and Gregory of Nyssa give the theme a more explicitly Trinitarian reading: Ambrose denies that Christ's slaying 'with the Spirit of His mouth' is a grace received from outside, calling it the undivided unity of the divine nature, and Gregory treats 'by the Spirit of God' as showing that the Persons' action is one and that the Son perfects every power through the Spirit. Irenaeus instead emphasizes the economy of salvation, holding that the Spirit was active in all God's dispensations, that he descended on the incarnate Son to grow accustomed to dwelling in humanity, and that his full gift at the resurrection will form us after God's image, while Owen applies the theme to believers, reading 2 Corinthians 3:17 as Christ's gift of the Spirit of adoption freeing them from the law's terror. Irenaeus and Ambrose share a typological reading of Gideon's fleece as the Spirit passing from Israel to the nations, though Ambrose speaks of the grace of faith and of the Jews losing their prophets, and he alone finds Christ's foot-washing prefigured in the wrung-out dew.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: That the Holy Spirit is in every conception inseparable…
refs.quote: In the first place He was made an unction, and being inseparably present was with the very flesh of the Lord

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Yet here is not a grace received, but the unity remains undivided, since neither can Christ be without the Spirit, nor the Spirit without Christ. For the unity of the divine nature cannot be divided.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: wherefore He did also descend upon the Son of God, made the Son of man, becoming accustomed in fellowship with Him to dwell in the human race, to rest with human beings, and to dwell in the workmanship of God

ans.text:
The Holy Spirit was with Jesus at every step of his earthly life. He formed his human body in Mary's womb, came down on him at his baptism, filled him without limit, empowered his ministry, and was with him in his death and resurrection. Then the risen Christ poured that same Spirit out on his people.

The Spirit's work begins at the very start. The angel tells Mary in Luke 1:35, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God." The eternal Son did not begin to exist in Bethlehem. But his human life, his body and soul, was brought into being by the Spirit's creative work. It was the same Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation.

At his baptism the Spirit came down on Jesus in bodily form like a dove (Luke 3:22). John the Baptist says the Spirit did not just touch him and leave; he "remained" on him (John 1:32-33). This fulfilled Isaiah's promise about the coming King: "The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him—the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength" (Isaiah 11:2). That is why Jesus is called the Christ, which means "the Anointed One." In Nazareth he read Isaiah 61 aloud and applied it to himself: "The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor" (Luke 4:18).

From then on the Gospels show the Spirit at work in all he did. Jesus, full of the Spirit, was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to face the devil (Luke 4:1). He said, "If I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (Matthew 12:28). Peter sums up his ministry this way: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, and he went about doing good and healing (Acts 10:38). Even the cross was not done apart from the Spirit. Hebrews 9:14 says Christ "through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God." Scripture also links the Spirit with raising him from the dead (Romans 8:11).

This is very different from how the Spirit came on the prophets. In the Old Testament the Spirit came on people for a task or a season. He gave a word to a prophet or strength to a judge, and that was a portion of the Spirit for a particular work. With Jesus it is not like that. John 3:34 says that "God gives the Spirit without limit." The Spirit rests on him fully and permanently. Jesus is not one more Spirit-filled man in a long line. He is the one in whom the Spirit lives in all his fullness, and from whom the Spirit flows out to others.

This raises a fair question. If Jesus is God the Son, why would he need the Spirit at all? Does it make him lesser, like a prophet receiving a gift from outside? The answer lies in who Jesus is. As the eternal Son, he has never been without the Spirit, and the Spirit has never been without him. Father, Son, and Spirit are one God, and they always act together. So when Jesus heals "by the Spirit," this is not a weaker person borrowing strength. It is the one God at work, with the Son and the Spirit acting as one. Paul can even call the Spirit "the Spirit of Christ" (Romans 8:9).

At the same time, the Son truly became a man. In his human nature he lived as we are meant to live: dependent on the Father and led by the Spirit, praying, trusting, and obeying. The Spirit's anointing of Jesus was real, and it concerned his humanity. It was not that Jesus was an ordinary man who became God's Son when the dove came down. The Gospels make clear he was the Son before his baptism, and the Father's voice there names him rather than promotes him. The Spirit's anointing showed him openly to Israel and equipped his human life for the work he came to do.

There is also a beautiful reason why this matters for us. The Spirit came to rest on a human being, Jesus, so that through him the Spirit might come to dwell in human beings everywhere. God had promised through Joel to pour out his Spirit on all people in the last days. That promise was fulfilled through Christ. After his resurrection Jesus breathed on his disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit" (John 20:22). At Pentecost Peter explained that the exalted Jesus had received the promised Spirit from the Father and "has poured out what you now see and hear" (Acts 2:33).

You could picture Jesus as the spring and believers as the streams. The Spirit who filled him without measure is the same Spirit who now lives in everyone who belongs to him. He was once given mainly to Israel, and now he is given to people of every nation. He makes us like Christ, frees us from fear, and teaches us to cry "Abba, Father" as God's children (Romans 8:15).

So the Spirit's work in Christ is not a side detail. It is the pattern and source of the Spirit's work in us. The life Jesus lived by the Spirit is the life he now shares with his people by the same Spirit.

topics.title: What do the Spirit's visible appearances as a dove and as tongues of fire show?
topics.cmp: Ambrose and Augustine agree that the dove at Christ's baptism (and, for Augustine, the tongues of fire at Pentecost) was not an incarnation of the Holy Spirit but a visible appearance given for the sake of human senses. They ground this differently. Ambrose works from the wording of Scripture: the Spirit came 'as' a dove, and Luke's 'bodily form' names an appearance. Augustine argues more philosophically and at greater length, holding that what appeared was a creature formed and changed at the Creator's command while the Spirit's immutable substance stayed unchanged. Augustine also develops points Ambrose does not address. Only the Spirit, not the whole Trinity, appeared in these forms. The forms were never united to the Spirit in one person, as the flesh was united to the Word, but passed away after signifying him. For that reason, unlike the Son's form of a servant, they imply no inferiority of the Spirit to the Father. On purpose their emphases converge, since Ambrose stresses that the sign was given so that those who could not see the Spirit might believe, and Augustine that it manifested him in a way fit for mortal men.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine…
refs.quote: it was not the Word of God Himself by His own substance, in which He is equal and eternal with the Father, nor the Spirit of the Father and of the Son by His own substance

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Luke, however, added that the Holy Spirit descended in a bodily form as a dove; you must not think that this was an incarnation, but an appearance.

ans.text:
The dove at Jesus' baptism and the tongues of fire at Pentecost were real, visible signs. God made them for a moment so that people could see that the Holy Spirit had truly come. But they were not the Spirit taking on a body, and they were not the Spirit himself changing shape. They were like a signal fire on a hill: the fire is real and you can see it, but it points to something beyond itself.

Look at how the Bible describes the dove. Luke 3:22 says the Holy Spirit "descended on Him in a bodily form like a dove." John the Baptist says, "I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him" (John 1:32). The Spirit did not become a bird, and no bird became the Spirit. The Spirit came, and a dove-like form showed people that he had come. At Pentecost, Luke also says the disciples saw something like tongues of fire resting on each of them (Acts 2:3). The words "like" and "as" matter. These were appearances given for people's sake, because we cannot see the Spirit with our eyes.

This is very different from what happened when the Son of God became man. John 1:14 says, "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us." The Son joined a real human nature to himself for ever. The man Jesus is God the Son. He was born, ate, wept, died and rose, and he is still man today at the Father's right hand. Nothing like that happened with the dove or the fire. The Spirit did not join them to himself. They did not become part of who he is. They appeared for a short time to do their job, and then they were gone. No one would say the dove is the Holy Spirit in the way we rightly say the man Jesus is the Son of God.

It also helps to remember that God, in his own being, cannot be seen. John 1:18 says no one has ever seen God. When the Spirit is shown to us, what our eyes see is something created, shaped for that purpose by God. The Spirit himself did not change, the way water turns into ice. God does not change. It was the created sign that was formed and then passed away, while the Spirit stayed exactly who he always is.

So what do these signs teach us? First, they show that the Spirit is a distinct person, not just a force or a mood. At Jesus' baptism, all three persons of the Trinity are present at once (Matthew 3:16-17). The Son stands in the water. The Spirit comes down as a dove. The Father speaks from heaven: "This is My beloved Son." The one God is not taking turns wearing three masks. Father, Son and Spirit are there together. It was the Spirit alone, not the Father or the Son, who came as the dove and rested on the disciples as fire. Yet the three always act together in perfect agreement, so the Spirit's coming is the work of the whole Godhead.

Second, the signs fit what the Spirit came to do. The dove recalls the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), and the dove that brought Noah an olive leaf after the flood. It speaks of new creation, peace and gentleness, resting on the Messiah who would bring them. The fire recalls God's presence in the burning bush and on Mount Sinai. It speaks of his holiness, of cleansing, and of hearts set alight. And the tongues, followed by the disciples speaking in many languages, show that the good news is for every nation.

Some people wonder whether being "sent" makes the Spirit less than the Father. Jesus does speak of the Spirit as sent. In John 14:26 he says the Father will send the Spirit in his name, and elsewhere he says that he himself will send the Spirit. But being sent does not mean being lower. When the Bible says the Son is "less" than the Father, it is speaking of him as a servant, in the human nature he took on (John 14:28; Philippians 2:7). The Spirit took on no such nature. The dove and the fire were never part of him, so they cannot make him smaller. Being sent tells us about the order of love among the three persons and their mission to us. It is not about rank. The Spirit who came as a dove and as fire is fully God, equal with the Father and the Son.

So when you picture the dove or the flames, don't think of the Spirit as a bird or a flame. Think of them as God's kind way of letting weak, earthbound people see that the invisible Spirit had truly come. He rested on Jesus, and he has been poured out on his people.

topics.title: Is the same Holy Spirit given in the Old Testament, to the disciples and at Pentecost?
topics.cmp: Ambrose, Irenaeus, Novatian and Hilary all affirm that the Spirit who spoke in the Old Testament prophets is the same Spirit given to the apostles, and Augustine likewise insists that the Spirit Christ breathed on the disciples is not different from the Spirit sent after the ascension, calling the twofold giving an economy rather than a sign of two Spirits. Their grounds differ. Ambrose argues by parallel with the one Father and the one Son acting in both covenants, and he uses this against heretics who divide the God of the Old Testament from the God of the New. Irenaeus makes a similar anti-dualist point from the Spirit's continuous prophetic and apostolic proclamation and from the Church suffering persecution as the prophets did. Hilary stresses the Spirit's oneness everywhere, from the patriarchs to John in the womb to believers. Novatian alone draws an explicit contrast in the manner of presence, occasional and sparing in the prophets but abiding and full in the apostles, citing Paul's 'having the same Spirit'; Irenaeus, on a different question, ties the outpouring of the life-giving Spirit to the Word's incarnate life and death.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: so, too, the Holy Spirit is one, who energized in the prophets, was breathed upon the apostles, and was joined to the Father and the Son in the sacrament of baptism.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: He Next Teaches Us that the Authority of the Faith…
refs.quote: He is therefore one and the same Spirit who was in the prophets and apostles, except that in the former He was occasional, in the latter always.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For the one and the same Spirit of God, who proclaimed by the prophets what and of what sort the advent of the Lord should be, did by these elders give a just interpretation of what had been truly prophesied

ans.text:
Yes. There is only one Holy Spirit, and he is the same in every age. The Spirit who spoke through Moses and the prophets is the Spirit Jesus breathed on his disciples on the evening of Easter, and the Spirit poured out on the church at Pentecost. What changed over time was not who the Spirit is, but how fully and how widely he was given.

Start with the prophets. Peter says that no true prophecy came from human will, but "men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21). He even calls this Spirit "the Spirit of Christ" at work in the prophets, telling ahead of time about Christ's sufferings and the glory that would follow (1 Peter 1:10-11). So the Spirit who foretold Jesus is the same Spirit who later came to live in his followers. That is one reason the Old and New Testaments fit together as one story. The same God speaks in both, by the same Spirit. Paul makes the link plain when he quotes a psalm and says that believers today have "the same spirit of faith" as the psalmist (2 Corinthians 4:13).

A common misunderstanding is that the Holy Spirit is a New Testament newcomer, or that he was absent before Pentecost. Not so. He hovered over the waters at creation. He filled craftsmen, judges, kings and prophets. David prayed, "Do not cast me from Your presence or take Your Holy Spirit from me" (Psalm 51:11). Before Jesus was born, John the Baptist was filled with the Spirit in his mother's womb.

Yet something really was new. In the Old Testament the Spirit usually came on particular people for particular tasks, often for a time, and often to a few. Moses wished that all the Lord's people could be prophets with the Spirit upon them (Numbers 11:29). The prophets looked ahead to a day when God would put his Spirit within his people to change their hearts (Ezekiel 36:27) and pour him out on everyone, young and old, men and women (Joel 2:28-29). Jesus pointed to this change when he told the disciples that the Spirit "abides with you and will be in you" (John 14:17). Think of a river. Before, it had been glimpsed in pools and springs here and there. Now it floods its banks. It is the same water, but far more of it, reaching far more people, and it stays.

What about the two givings to the disciples? In John 20:22, after rising from the dead, Jesus "breathed on them and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.'" Fifty days later, at Pentecost, the Spirit came with wind and fire (Acts 2). These are not two different Spirits. Scripture is clear that there is "one body and one Spirit" (Ephesians 4:4), and that all the gifts are the work of "one and the same Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:11). The same Spirit was given in two stages, and each stage teaches something. When Jesus breathes on the disciples, he shows that the Spirit comes from him. It echoes God breathing life into Adam, so this is the start of a new creation. At Pentecost the Spirit is poured out in power on the whole gathered church and sends them out to the nations. The first was a personal, quiet gift to a few. The second was a public outpouring for the mission of the whole church.

When and how, then, did the Son pour out the Spirit on the human race? The Bible ties it to the whole work of Jesus. John notes that the Spirit had not yet been given in this full way "because Jesus had not yet been glorified" (John 7:39). The Son of God became a real man. He lived among us, ate and drank with sinners, died for our sins and rose again. By doing this he opened the way for God's life-giving Spirit to dwell in sinful people, bringing forgiveness and new life. Then, as Peter preached at Pentecost, Jesus was raised to the Father's right hand, "received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit," and "poured out what you now see and hear" (Acts 2:33). The Spirit who once came on prophets now comes to every believer, because Christ has made us clean and joined us to himself.

So when you read of the Spirit in the prophets, at the empty tomb, at Pentecost, or in your own life of faith, you are meeting the same Person. He is God the Holy Spirit, one with the Father and the Son, always faithful, now given generously to all who belong to Christ.

topics.title: How are the Holy Spirit, water and baptism related?
topics.cmp: Basil of Caesarea and Ambrose of Milan agree fully in their conclusions: in baptism the water figures death and the burial of the body of sin, while the Spirit gives the earnest or pledge of life and renews and regenerates the soul. Both hold that whatever grace is in the water comes not from its nature but from the Spirit's presence, so water shares neither the Spirit's nature nor his honour. They differ somewhat in argument. Ambrose reasons from the difference of offices to a difference of natures, concluding that the Spirit is far superior to the water. Basil adds scriptural and historical grounds: John's baptism with water unto repentance contrasted with Christ's baptism with the Holy Ghost, and martyrs saved by their own blood without water. With these he charges that those who use the water to lower the Spirit compare what admits of no comparison.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Reply to the suggested objection that we are baptized…
refs.quote: the water fulfils the image of death, and the Spirit gives us the earnest of life.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: If, then, there be any grace in the water, it is not from the nature of water, but from the presence of the Holy Spirit.

ans.text:
Water and the Spirit belong together in baptism, but they are not equals. The water is the visible sign. The Holy Spirit is the living God who does the real work the sign points to. The water shows us a washing and a burial. The Spirit gives the new life.

Jesus joins the two when he tells Nicodemus in John 3:5 that "no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit." Paul does something similar in Titus 3:5, saying God saved us "through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit." Because the Bible puts them side by side, someone might ask whether the water is somehow on the same level as the Spirit. It is not.

Think about what each one does. In Romans 6:4 Paul says we were "buried with Him through baptism into death." Going under the water is like being laid in a grave. It pictures the end of the old life ruled by sin. But a picture of death cannot raise anyone. Life comes from the Spirit. He makes us children of God and joins us to the risen Christ. Ephesians 1:13–14 calls him the seal on believers and the pledge, or down payment, of the inheritance still to come. So baptism has two sides, dying and rising. The water shows the dying. The Spirit gives the rising.

So any blessing connected with baptism does not come from the water as water. Water is an ordinary created thing. It washes the body and cannot renew a soul. When God uses it, the power belongs to the Spirit who is present and at work. A wedding ring is a fair comparison. The ring matters, and you would not toss it aside. But the ring does not create the marriage. The love and the vows behind it do. In the same way, the water is a God-given sign and instrument, and it deserves respect because Christ commanded it. The Spirit is God himself, and he deserves worship. The water never does.

The Bible's own examples show this. The thief on the cross was promised paradise by Jesus without ever being baptized. In Acts 10 the Spirit fell on Cornelius and his household before they were baptized, and they were then baptized with water. The Spirit is free and sovereign. The water serves him, not the other way round.

Christians have disagreed about how closely God ties the Spirit's work to the act of baptism. Some believe God normally gives new birth through baptism itself, since passages like Titus 3:5 and Acts 2:38 speak so directly. Others believe baptism is a sign and seal of a new birth the Spirit gives through faith, sometimes before baptism and sometimes after. They point to the thief and to Cornelius. Both sides agree on what matters most for this question: the life comes from the Spirit, not from the water.

John the Baptist drew the same line in Matthew 3:11: "I baptize you with water for repentance... He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire." John could only apply water, an outward call to turn from sin. Jesus gives the Spirit himself, and only God can give God. That is one strong reason Christians confess that the Spirit is divine.

What about the fire? Many readers take it as judgment, because the next verse speaks of Christ burning up the chaff "with unquenchable fire." Paul likewise says in 1 Corinthians 3:13 that fire will test each person's work on the last day. Others see fire as purifying, burning away sin the way fire refines metal. Still others link it to the tongues of fire when the Spirit came at Pentecost in Acts 2. These readings can fit together. The same Christ who pours out the Spirit to cleanse his people will also judge, and nothing false will survive his fire.

Acts 19 offers a related lesson. At Ephesus, Paul met disciples who had received only John's baptism and had not even heard that the Holy Spirit had been given. They were then baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, and the Spirit came on them. This was not baptism repeated. John's washing was a preparation that looked forward to Jesus. Christian baptism, into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), is the one baptism Paul speaks of in Ephesians 4:5.

Finally, 1 John 5:6–8 says Jesus "came by water and blood," and that "there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood—and these three are in agreement." The water most likely points to Jesus' baptism, where the Father declared him his Son. The blood points to his death on the cross. Many Christians also hear in it the water of baptism and the cup of the Lord's Supper. The Spirit is the living witness who makes this truth known in our hearts and assures us that it is true.

These three are one in what they say, not in what they are. Water and blood are created things. The Spirit is God. Each witnesses in its own way. The water speaks of washing and burial, the blood of redemption through Christ's death, and the Spirit of new life. Their witness is not equal in kind, since the Spirit gives life and the other two point to it. Yet all three tell the same story: Jesus is the Son of God, and in him there is life.

One more note. Some older Bibles add words to this passage about three witnesses in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Spirit. Those words are not found in the earliest manuscripts, so most modern translations leave them out. The Bible's teaching on the Trinity does not depend on them, and it stands firmly on many other passages.

topics.title: How is the true Spirit discerned, and can anyone confer him by his own authority?
topics.cmp: The authors take up different halves of the topic rather than the same questions. John Owen alone addresses how the true Spirit is discerned. His test is the effects Christ promised: the true Spirit opens and brings to remembrance Christ's words as written in Scripture, and glorifies the Christ who came in the flesh and suffered. By contrast, a spirit that decries the written word, offers new revelations, or speaks of Christ only 'in the Spirit' is false. Irenaeus of Lyons and Ambrose of Milan instead address whether anyone can confer the Spirit, and they agree that no human can do so by his own power or authority. Their grounds differ somewhat: Irenaeus, using Simon Magus and Peter's rebuke, stresses that the Spirit is God's gift, not magic or anything that can be bought, given to those who believe through Christ Jesus; Ambrose, citing Paul's prayer and Peter's confession, stresses that God alone gives the Spirit while the priest only invokes and ministers.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: he shall bring to our remembrance, and give us understanding of the words of Christ in the Scripture, for our guidance and consolation. Is this, now, the work of the spirit which is abroad in the world, and perverteth many? Nothing less.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: supposing that the apostles themselves performed their cures by the art of magic, and not by the power of God; and with respect to their filling with the Holy Ghost, through the imposition of hands

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For this is no work of man, nor gift of man; but He Who is invoked by the priest is given by God, wherein is the gift of God and the ministry of the priest.

ans.text:
The true Holy Spirit is recognized by what he does: he always points to the real Jesus, who came in the flesh, and he always agrees with the words God has already given in Scripture. And no, no one can hand out the Spirit on his own authority. The Spirit is God's gift, given by God alone.

Start with the warning the Bible itself gives. John writes, "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God" (1 John 4:1). Christians are not meant to accept every inner voice, impressive experience or confident preacher. That is not a call to be cynical. It is how we show love for the truth. The Holy Spirit is not a vague force we can tap into. He is God himself, and God does not contradict himself. So there are real tests.

The first test is about Jesus. John goes on: "By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God" (1 John 4:2). Paul says that no one can truly say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). Jesus told his disciples that the Spirit "will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you" (John 16:14). The Spirit is like a floodlight on a great building. You don't stare at the light. You look at what it shows you. So when someone talks about a "spiritual Christ" or a "Christ within" but plays down the Jesus who was born, truly suffered, died for our sins and rose bodily, that is a warning sign. The same goes for any spirit that draws attention to itself, or to a leader, more than to the crucified and risen Lord.

The second test is about God's word. Jesus promised that the Spirit would "remind you of everything I have told you" (John 14:26). He did this first for the apostles. He brought Christ's words back to their minds so that they could pass them on and write them down for us. He goes on doing the same kind of work in believers today. He does not hand out a new gospel. He opens our eyes to understand, believe and take comfort in what is already written. So a spirit that belittles the Bible, or claims revelations that add to it or overrule it, is not the Spirit Jesus promised. The Spirit who inspired Scripture will not argue against it.

A third, gentler test is the kind of life he produces. The Spirit is holy, and his fruit is "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness" and the rest (Galatians 5:22–23). Pride, confusion, division and a craving for spectacle do not show that he is at work.

Now the second part of the question: can an apostle, pastor or priest give someone the Holy Spirit? In Acts 8, Peter and John prayed for new believers in Samaria and laid hands on them, and they received the Spirit. A man named Simon, who had practiced magic, saw this. He assumed the apostles simply had stronger magic than he did, and he offered them money for the same power. Peter rebuked him sharply, saying in effect, "May your money perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God!" (Acts 8:20). Buying spiritual power or church office has been called "simony" ever since, after this Simon.

That story teaches two things. First, the Spirit is a gift, not a product or a technique. He cannot be bought, earned or switched on by the right words or gestures. Second, even the apostles did not control him. Notice that before laying on hands they prayed that the believers would receive the Spirit (Acts 8:15). When Peter later saw the Spirit poured out on Gentiles, he did not claim credit. He said, in effect, "Who was I to stand in God's way?" (Acts 11:17). Paul too prayed that God would fill believers with joy and peace "by the power of the Holy Spirit" (Romans 15:13). He asked God. He did not presume to give the Spirit himself. Jesus put it simply: the Father will "give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him" (Luke 11:13).

So what is the laying on of hands? It is a prayer made visible. A minister places hands on someone and asks God to act, and God, who is free and generous, gives. The minister serves and prays. God is the giver. And the gift comes to those who trust in God through Jesus Christ, not to those with money, status or secret knowledge.

Sincere Christians do differ on how closely God ties his gift to these church actions.
