Some believe that in rites such as confirmation or ordination God has promised to work through the prayer and laying on of hands. They point to passages like Acts 8 and 2 Timothy 1:6. Others see these acts mainly as signs and prayers that confirm what God gives directly through faith. They point out that in Acts 10 the Spirit came before any hands were laid on anyone. Both sides agree on the main point: the power belongs to God, not to the minister, and the Spirit cannot be commanded or purchased.

In short, you can recognize the true Spirit because he exalts the real Jesus and opens up the Bible rather than replacing it. And you receive him not from anyone's private authority but from the hand of God, as a free gift to those who believe.

title: Inseparable Works and Distinct Roles
desc: How the three Persons act as one in creation, salvation and grace while each has a distinct, ordered role, including appropriation of common works.

topics.title: Do the Father, Son and Holy Spirit act inseparably as one?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Father, Son and Holy Spirit act as one in their outward works. Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Owen and Athanasius explicitly deny that these works are divided among the Persons, and all treat creation, life-giving and grace as the work of the whole Trinity. They argue for this differently. Ambrose relies most heavily on collating Scripture, showing that the same acts (grace, rebuking, appointing apostles, gifts, quickening) are ascribed to each Person, and infers one power and substance, even 'identity' (ταυτότης). Gregory of Nyssa argues more philosophically from the incomprehensible, bodiless nature and the identical manner of working, and Athanasius grounds the unity in the Son being the Father's own Word and Image. Augustine stresses that the Persons are indivisible in operation as in substance, so that they are 'one Beginning' toward creation, and he even applies this to the Son's being sent by both Father and Son. Within this unity the authors differ in how much ordered distinction they emphasize: Basil (original, creative and perfecting cause), Gregory (from the Father, through the Son, perfected in the Spirit), Irenaeus and Hilary (the Father commands, the Son executes, the Spirit nourishes) and Owen (authoritative, mediatorial and immediate concurrence, grounding distinct communion with each Person) foreground distinct roles. Waterland cautions against pressing such distinctions too rigorously, and Augustine marks off what is proper to one Person, such as the incarnation, conformity to the Son's risen body, and justification in Christ's blood.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: So grace comes also of the Holy Spirit as of the Father and the Son. For how can there be grace without the Spirit, since all divine grace is in the Spirit?

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The seven Spirits before the throne, are the Holy Spirit of God, considered as the perfect fountain of every perfect gift and dispensation. All are here joined together, and yet all mentioned as distinguished in their communication of grace and peace unto the saints.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: issuing from the Father as from a spring, brought into operation by the Son, and perfecting its grace by the power of the Spirit

ans.text:
Yes. Whenever God acts toward the world, whether creating, sustaining, saving or giving gifts, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit act together as one. They do not split the job into three parts, take turns, or simply cooperate the way three people might on a team project. There is one divine power at work and one action, carried out by all three at once. Yet each Person shares in that one work in a way that fits who he is.

Start with creation. In Isaiah 44:24 the LORD says he made all things and stretched out the heavens alone, by himself. No helper, no assistant. Yet John 1:3 says of the Son, the Word, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Genesis 1:2 shows the Spirit of God hovering over the waters, and Psalm 33:6 says the heavens were made by the word of the LORD and their host by the breath of his mouth. If God created alone, and the Son and the Spirit both created, then the Son and the Spirit are not helpers standing outside God. They are the one God who made everything. That is why Christians speak of one Creator, not three, and one source of all things, not three sources.

Jesus himself teaches this oneness of working. In John 5:19 he says, "the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does." This does not mean the Son is weak or only copying. It means the Son never acts apart from the Father, and the Father never acts apart from the Son. In John 14:10 Jesus says the Father dwelling in him is the one doing his works. What the Son does, the Father does, because they share one life and one nature.

The same is true of the Spirit. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 that there are different gifts but the same Spirit, different ministries but the same Lord, and different ways of working but the same God who works all things in all people. Spirit, Lord and God are named side by side, and the gifts come from all three. Elsewhere the Father appoints apostles and gives gifts, Christ sends the apostles and promises signs, and the Spirit hands out healings and tongues. These are not three supplies of gifts. They are one giving from one God.

Why does this matter? Because the way someone acts shows what they are. If the three had different powers, they would be different beings, and we would have three gods. But Scripture shows one grace, one peace, one power and one work coming from Father, Son and Spirit together. Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 joins the grace of Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit as one blessing. Where the working is one, the power is one, and where the power is one, the being is one. Their shared work is one of the clearest windows we have into their unity.

This does not blur the three Persons into one. There is an order in how they act together. A helpful pattern in Scripture is "from, through, and in." In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul says there is one God, the Father, "from whom all things came," and one Lord, Jesus Christ, "through whom all things came." And the Spirit is the one in whom God's work is brought to completion and made alive in us. So we can say: every work of God begins with the Father, is carried out through the Son, and is perfected by the Spirit. Think of a single act of speaking. A thought, the word that expresses it, and the breath that carries it are not three separate events. They are one act with an inner shape. That comparison is imperfect, but it shows how one action can have a real order within it.

Some wonder whether the Father acting "through" the Son means the Father needs help, or whether the Spirit "completing" the work means the Son's part fell short. No. The Father lacks nothing and could act by his will alone. He freely chooses to act through the Son, and the Son freely acts by the Spirit, because that is how the three live together in perfect agreement. It shows shared will, not weakness.

There are also things that belong to one Person in a special way. Only the Son became a man, was born, died on the cross and rose again. We are "justified by His blood," as Romans 5:9 says, meaning Christ's blood in particular. At Jesus' baptism the Father's voice spoke from heaven and the Spirit came down like a dove. Yet even here the three are not working apart. Luke 1:35 shows the Father's power and the Holy Spirit at work in the Son's coming in the flesh. The Father sent the Son, the Son came willingly, and he offered himself through the eternal Spirit, as Hebrews 9:14 puts it. So the whole Trinity brought about the incarnation, but only the Son took on flesh. One work, and one Person at the center of it.

That also helps explain why the Bible sometimes links a work with one Person: creation with the Father, redemption with the Son, making us holy with the Spirit. This is a true and helpful way of speaking, because it highlights each Person's place in the shared work. But it never means that Person works alone. When you are blessed in Christ, you are blessed by the Father and the Spirit too, since you are baptized into one Name of all three (Matthew 28:19).

This teaching is deeply practical. Your faith, for example, is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8), it comes from Christ who prays for you and grows it, and it is worked in you by the Spirit's mighty power. You never get a part of God, or deal with one Person who is out of step with the others. When the Spirit comforts you, the Father is loving you and the Son is caring for you in that same comfort. When you pray to the Father through the Son by the Spirit, you are not dividing God. You are meeting the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who always acts as one.

topics.title: Do the shared works and attributes of the three Persons show they are one God?
topics.cmp: All four authors conclude that Father, Son and Spirit are one God and not unequal or alien beings, but they reach this by different routes. Bickersteth argues most directly from Scripture's ascription of the same attributes, names and works to all three, for example the law of the Lord, of Christ and of the Spirit set against James's 'one lawgiver.' He also adds that the three are personally distinct in mind, will and heart while acting in harmony. Basil and Ambrose focus on unity of power and operation. Basil reasons philosophically that identity of essence entails equal power and therefore equal operations. Ambrose works exegetically from John 10, identifying the Spirit as the Father's Hand so that one Hand belongs to Father and Son. Gregory of Nyssa differs in approach: he argues polemically against Eunomius, contending that an unbroken relation is impossible between beings of unlike essence and rejecting as profane any ranking of the Son and Spirit as more or less honourable 'works.'

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: have the same Divine attributes, concur with a mind, and will, and heart personally independent, but unitedly harmonious in the same Divine acts, and are addressed by the same Divine names

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what…
refs.quote: For if in essence He is without variation, so also is He without variation in power. And of those whose power is equal, the operation also is in all ways equal.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: the same is certainly the Hand of the Father which is the Hand of the Son, since the Same is the Spirit of the Father Who is the Spirit of the Son.

ans.text:
Yes. When the Bible gives the same divine works, the same divine qualities, the same divine names and the same divine power to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, it is showing us that the three are not three gods but one God.

Start with the bedrock of the Bible's faith: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). God also says he will not share his glory with another (Isaiah 42:8). Some things only God can do, and some things only God can be. He alone creates out of nothing, gives eternal life, forgives sins, raises the dead, and is everywhere, all-knowing and eternal. So when Scripture says these things of the Son and of the Spirit as well as the Father, it is not adding two more gods. It is telling us who the one God is.

Look at creation. Genesis tells us God created the heavens and the earth, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters. John says of the Son, the Word, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Psalm 33:6 puts it together: the heavens were made by the word of the LORD and by the breath of his mouth. One work, one Creator, with the Father, the Son and the Spirit all present in it.

Look at salvation. Jesus says no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand, and then that no one can snatch them out of his Father's hand, and then, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:28-30). He does not mean two hands holding on, one stronger than the other. He means one grip, one power. And since the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son, it is that same Spirit who seals and keeps believers. A person who belongs to God is not held by the Father but loosely held by the Son, or kept by the Spirit but not the Father. He is held by the one God.

Or think about the resurrection of Jesus. The Bible says the Father raised him (Galatians 1:1). Jesus says he will raise up the temple of his own body (John 2:19). Paul speaks of the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 8:11). These are not three rival claims. They are one divine act, done by the three together.

Even God's law shows this. Scripture speaks of the law of the Lord, the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2) and the law of the Spirit of life (Romans 8:2). The prophets spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). Yet James says, "There is only one Lawgiver and Judge" (James 4:12). If there is only one Lawgiver, and the law belongs to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, then the three are that one Lawgiver.

The same goes for names and qualities. The Son is called God (John 1:1; John 20:28). Lying to the Holy Spirit is called lying to God (Acts 5:3-4). The Spirit is called eternal (Hebrews 9:14), and the Son is the same yesterday, today and forever. And Jesus told his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice it is one name, not three names.

Here is the simple reasoning behind all this. What something can do shows what it is. A bird flies and a fish swims because of the kind of creature each one is. If the Son and the Spirit do what only God does, with the same power and not a lesser copy of it, then they share what God is. Theologians use the word "essence" or "nature" for this: the "what" of God, as opposed to the "who." The three Persons are three "whos" sharing one undivided "what." Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). God's power and wisdom are not something outside God or less than God.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, this does not mean the Father, Son and Spirit are like a team of three people who agree to work on a project together. Human teammates have three separate wills and three separate supplies of strength. In God there is one will and one power. Jesus says, "The Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does" (John 5:19). That is not weakness. It means the Son never acts apart from the Father, because they are one God.

Second, this does not erase the differences between the Persons. They act together, but each in his own way. The Father sends the Son. The Son, not the Father, becomes a man and dies on the cross. The Spirit is poured out at Pentecost. Every work of God is from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. It is one work, and each Person has his own part in it. The Persons are distinct; the work is not divided.

Some have argued that the Son and Spirit are real but lesser, as though they were products of God's activity, ranked lower like a second-best creation. Scripture closes that door. The Son is not something God made. He is the one through whom everything was made. The Bible calls him "begotten," which means he comes from the Father the way a son shares his father's nature, not the way a table comes from a carpenter. And it makes no sense to speak of a "less honorable" part of God. Whatever is God is fully God. If the Son or Spirit were of a lower and different nature, they could not share one unbroken life and work with the Father at all. They would be strangers to him, not one with him. But the Bible shows them acting as one at every turn.

What about Jesus saying, "My Father ... is greater than all" or "the Father is greater than I"? Jesus said these things as the Son who came in humility, sent by the Father and living as a man. They speak of his role and his humble state, not of a lower divine nature. In the very same breath he says, "I and the Father are one."

So the shared works of the three are not a coincidence. They are God showing us himself. When the Father, the Son and the Spirit create, save, keep, raise and rule as one, we are seeing one God, and we can trust that the grip holding us is the full and undivided power of God.

topics.title: What distinct, ordered roles do the Father, Son and Spirit have in creation, salvation and prayer?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that the three Persons act together yet in a distinct order, with the Father as source, the Son as mediator and agent, and the Spirit as the one who applies, confirms or brings near. Irenaeus, Athanasius, Basil and Ambrose stress the Son and Spirit as true divine agents of creation against Gnostic and Arian intermediaries. On the return to God, Irenaeus (citing the presbyters), Gregory of Nyssa, Basil and Owen all trace the ascent from the Spirit through the Son to the Father. They differ in emphasis and grounds: the Fathers argue mainly from Scripture texts like Psalm 33:6 and from polemic against heretics, and Gregory and Owen read Proverbs' Wisdom differently (the Lord's flesh from the Virgin versus Christ building his church). Owen and Edwards develop a detailed economy of redemption (the Father designs, the Son purchases, the Spirit applies, with Edwards distinctively making the Spirit himself the thing purchased and grounding creation's being 'for the Son' in God's reflexive self-knowledge), while Warfield frames the order as subordination in modes of operation shown by Paul's incidental triadic language, and Waterland explains the distinct titles as a way of securing each Person's due honour.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: There Was No Other More Suitable Way of Freeing Man from…
refs.quote: And He was then given, when Jesus was glorified by the resurrection. For then He promised that He Himself would send Him, and He sent Him

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: And the grace given is one, given from the Father in the Son, as Paul writes in every Epistle, ‘Grace unto you, and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.’

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: establishing all things by His Word, and binding them together by His Wisdom— this is He who is the only true God

ans.text:
Every work of God is done by all three Persons together, and each Person does it in his own way: everything comes from the Father, through the Son, and is brought to completion by the Holy Spirit. That simple pattern runs from the first day of creation to the prayer you will pray tonight.

Start with what this does not mean. The Father, Son and Spirit are not three departments of a company, each handling a separate task while the others wait. There is one God with one will and one power. So when God creates, saves or answers prayer, the whole Godhead is at work. Jesus says in John 5:19 that whatever the Father does, the Son does too. Yet Scripture also speaks of each Person acting in a distinct way. Think of a single sentence spoken aloud. There is the speaker, the word, and the breath that carries the word. It is one act of speaking, but the three are not the same thing.

Creation shows this pattern. Psalm 33:6 says the heavens were made by the word of the LORD, and their host by the breath of his mouth. The New Testament tells us who that Word is: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). And at the very start, "the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters" (Genesis 1:2), giving life and order. Paul puts it clearly in 1 Corinthians 8:6: there is one God, the Father, "from whom all things came," and one Lord, Jesus Christ, "through whom all things came." The Father is the source, the Son is the one through whom, and the Spirit is the life-giver who perfects. God did not need some lesser go-between to make the world. He made it by his own Word and his own Spirit.

Salvation follows the same order. The plan starts in the Father's love. He chose a people before the world began and, "when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son" (Galatians 4:4). The Son came willingly and gave himself to redeem us. On the cross he offered himself to God for our sins. Some people imagine an angry Father and a kind Son who talks him round. That is a misunderstanding. The Son's sacrifice is itself the Father's gift: "God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son" (John 3:16). The Father gives, the Son offers himself, and both act out of the same love. Then the Spirit applies what Christ has won. He joins us to Christ, makes us new and seals us as God's own. Peter sums it up when he describes believers as chosen according to the Father's foreknowledge, through the sanctifying work of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by his blood (1 Peter 1:2).

Adoption shows how the Persons work together. It springs from the Father's love. We receive it through the Son, because he is the Father's true Son, and when we are united to him, his Father becomes our Father. The Spirit makes it real in our hearts: "because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, 'Abba, Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). Holiness follows the same shape. The Father chose us to be holy. The Son died to make us a pure people. The Spirit works that holiness in us day by day. Grace, too, is one grace. That is why Paul greets churches with grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together, and why he can bless them with the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Spirit in one breath (2 Corinthians 13:14).

The sending did not stop at the cross. After rising and returning to the Father, Jesus himself poured out the Spirit he had promised (John 15:26, Acts 2:33). Christians have sincerely disagreed about what this tells us about God's eternal life. Some hold that the Spirit eternally comes from the Father and the Son, because the Son sends him in history and he is called the Spirit of the Son. Others hold that the Spirit eternally comes from the Father alone, pointing to Jesus' words that the Spirit "goes out from the Father," and they say the Son's sending belongs to his work of salvation. Both sides agree that the Spirit is fully God and is given to us through Christ.

This order shapes how we pray. "Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit" (Ephesians 2:18). Normally we pray to the Father, in the name of the Son, by the help of the Spirit. Jesus taught us to ask the Father in his name (John 16:23). Christ is our high priest who always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). The Spirit helps us when we do not know what to pray (Romans 8:26). This does not mean it is wrong to speak to the Son or the Spirit directly. Stephen prayed, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). Since each Person is fully God, each may rightly be worshiped and called upon. The pattern is a road the Father has opened for us, not a fence.

Does this order mean the Father is greater, the Son second and the Spirit third? No. The order reflects how the Persons relate to one another, not a difference in rank or worth. The Father is Father, the Son is eternally his Son (that is what "begotten" means: he shares the Father's very being, not made but from him), and the Spirit eternally comes from God. So it fits that the Father sends the Son and the Spirit, and not the other way round. Being sent says nothing about being lesser. Among people, a father may send his grown son on an errand, and the son is no less human for it. Jesus could be sent and still say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). We are baptized into the one name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), not three names of different sizes. Sincere Christians also discuss whether the Son's obedience to the Father belongs only to his life as a man, or also reflects something eternal in how he relates to the Father. Those on both sides who hold the historic faith agree that the Son is in every way equal to the Father in power, glory and nature (Philippians 2:6).

So when you consider creation, the cross or your own prayers, you are seeing the one God at work in three ways at once. The Father loves and plans. The Son comes and accomplishes. The Spirit brings us in and makes it ours. All of it is one work of grace, so that we might know the Father through the Son by the Spirit.

topics.title: How can common works be attributed or proper to one Person?
topics.cmp: All four authors hold that the outward works of the Trinity are undivided while particular works or manifestations are still rightly tied to one Person. They explain this in different ways. John Owen gives the most systematic account. He distinguishes works common in every respect, such as providence, from works common in the act but distinguished by their immediate principle or order, as creation is appropriated to the Father, redemption to the Son, and sending to the Father. He grounds this in the one essential will shared by each Person. He also insists that the Persons are distinct fountains of dispensations to believers, such as grace from Christ, and not distinct sources of being. Augustine concentrates on visible manifestations: the voice, the dove, and Christ's flesh. He argues that the whole Trinity produces each one, but a bodily creature cannot show the inseparable Trinity inseparably, just as spoken words must name the Persons one after another. He also uses scriptural reasoning to settle which Person is meant: only the Father could say "my beloved Son," and only the Son and Spirit are said to be sent, so they best fit Lot's visitors. Ambrose and Gregory of Nyssa stress the unity side rather than appropriation. Ambrose collects scriptures in which Father, Son, and Spirit each sanctify, and concludes that the sanctification is one. Gregory argues that the Father shares in the thanksgiving for the Passion because he worked salvation through his own Power, Christ.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: being common in respect of their acts, they are distinguished in respect of that principle, or next and immediate rise in the manner of operation: so creation is appropriated to the Father, redemption to the Son

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Appearance to Lot is Examined.
refs.quote: The last, perhaps, is the more suitable; for they said of themselves that they were sent, which is that which we say of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For we find nowhere in the Scriptures that the Father was sent.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: So, then, the Father sanctifies, the Son also sanctifies, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies; but the sanctification is one, for baptism is one, and the grace of the sacrament is one.

ans.text:
A work of God can belong to all three Persons and still be spoken of as especially the Father's, the Son's, or the Spirit's, because each Person shares fully in the one act but takes part in it in his own way. The act is one. The way each Person stands within that act is not the same.

Start with what the Bible insists on. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), and he does not act in three separate pieces. Jesus says in John 5:19, "whatever the Father does, the Son also does." The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one divine nature, one power, and one will. So when God creates, saves, or makes holy, it is never one Person working while the others watch. All three act together, as the one God.

Yet Scripture also speaks of the Persons in distinct ways. Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 8:6 that there is "one God, the Father, from whom all things came," and "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came." Notice the small words: from the Father, through the Son. Elsewhere the Spirit is the one by whom God's work is brought to completion in us. This is not a division of labor, as if the Father did one part of creation and the Son another. It reflects the order within God himself. The Father is the source, with no one before him. The Son is from the Father. The Spirit is from the Father, and many Christians add through or from the Son as well. Every work of God carries that same pattern: from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.

That is why Christians have long linked certain works with certain Persons. Creation is often tied to the Father, because he is the source of all things. Redemption is tied to the Son, who came and died for us. Making us holy is tied to the Spirit, who lives in believers. Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 does something similar: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you." Grace, love, and fellowship all come from the whole Trinity. Still, each fits one Person in a special way, and Scripture names it that way so we can know and love each Person.

A good test case is holiness. The Bible says the Father sanctifies, which means makes us holy: Paul prays that "the God of peace Himself" would sanctify us completely (1 Thessalonians 5:23), and Jesus asks the Father to sanctify his disciples (John 17:17). It also says Christ has become our holiness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and it speaks of being made holy by the Spirit (2 Thessalonians 2:13). These are not three different holinesses. There is one work of making us holy, done by the one God, which each Person carries out in his own way.

So none of the Persons is ever left out. Sometimes people think of the Father as stern and distant, and of the Son as the kind one who rescued us from him. That gets it badly wrong. "For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son" (John 3:16). Our salvation is the Father's loving plan, carried out through the Son and applied by the Spirit. We owe thanks to all three.

There are also some cases where something truly belongs to one Person alone, even though all three brought it about. The clearest is the incarnation, meaning God the Son taking on a human nature. The whole Trinity was at work when Jesus was conceived. The angel tells Mary that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and the power of the Most High will overshadow her (Luke 1:35). Yet only the Son became man. The Father did not take flesh, and neither did the Spirit. The human body and soul of Jesus were formed by all three, but they belong to the Son alone. One act, done by all three, ends in one Person.

The voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism works the same way. "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!" (Matthew 3:17). The sound itself was something God made in the created world, and the whole Trinity made it. But the words can only be the Father's. Jesus is not the Spirit's son, and he is not his own son. Likewise in John 12:28 Jesus prays, "Father, glorify Your name!" and the voice answers, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The answer comes from the one he prayed to. In the same way, the dove at the baptism was made by all three, yet it shows us the Spirit.

Why would God show himself this way? Think about how we speak. When you say "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit," you have to say the names one after another. You cannot say all three at once, even though the three are never apart. Created things like a voice, a dove, or a human body are limited in the same kind of way. They cannot display the whole undivided Trinity in a single sign. So God uses them to point to one Person at a time, while all three are still at work behind each sign.

This also explains phrases that link one quality with one Person. Christians have sometimes connected eternity with the Father, beauty or form with the Son, who is the Image of God, and the enjoyment of God's goodness with the Spirit, who is God's Gift. These are not claims that only the Father is eternal. The Son and Spirit are just as eternal as the Father. The point is narrower. The Father has no one he comes from, while the Son, who is equally eternal, is from the Father.

Two mistakes are worth avoiding. One is to split God into three agents with three jobs, like a company with three departments. That would make three gods. The other is to say the names Father, Son, and Spirit are only labels for three roles one person plays at different times. That would deny the real distinction between them, which the baptism scene alone rules out, with the Son in the water, the Father speaking, and the Spirit descending. The Bible holds both truths together. God is one in all he does, and within that one work we really meet the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, each in his own way.

topics.title: How do the three Persons dwell and work as one in believers?
topics.cmp: All four authors agree that the indwelling and working of Father, Son and Spirit in believers is one and not divided: Hilary denies that two Spirits indwell, Augustine that the Spirit departs when Father and Son come, Ambrose that their presence, grace and baptismal working can be separated, and Bickersteth that there are three separate guests. Their grounds are largely scriptural but differently focused. Hilary reads Paul's identification of the Spirit of God with the Spirit of Christ and grounds the single indwelling in unity of nature. Augustine argues from the promise that the Spirit abides for ever, concluding that the three always come and dwell together. Ambrose reasons from baptism in the one Spirit and the one mystery and one death to an inseparable working, and from their joint coming to one presence and grace. Bickersteth, unlike the others, stresses that each Person truly dwells in the believer, citing separate texts for each, and then concludes that these are the one high and lofty One rather than three indwellers.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: This is no joint indwelling, it is one indwelling: yet an indwelling under the mysterious semblance of a joint indwelling, for it is not the case that two Spirits indwell, nor is one that indwells different from the other.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
refs.quote: He will not therefore depart when the Father and the Son come, but will be in the same abode with them eternally; because neither will He come without them, nor they without Him.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: The work is one, for the mystery is one; the baptism one, for there was one death on behalf of the world; there is, then, a oneness of working, a oneness of setting forth, which cannot be separated.

ans.text:
They dwell in believers as one God, not as three separate guests sharing a house. When God makes His home in a Christian, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are all truly present. Yet it is one presence, one grace and one life, because the three Persons are one God.

The Bible speaks of each Person living in believers. God the Father promises, "I will dwell with them and walk among them" (2 Corinthians 6:16). Paul prays "that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:17). Jesus says of the Holy Spirit, "He abides with you and will be in you" (John 14:17). Read on their own, these verses might sound like three visitors arriving one after another. Scripture does not let us think that way.

Look at how Paul moves between the names in Romans 8:9-10. He speaks of "the Spirit of God" living in you. In the same breath he calls Him "the Spirit of Christ." Then he says "Christ is in you." Paul is not counting up two or three different Spirits, or a Spirit plus a Christ. The Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are one and the same Spirit. To have the Spirit is to have Christ, and to have Christ is to have the Father. This is why Christians can say they have one divine guest, not a crowd.

Jesus teaches the same thing in John 14. He promises that the Spirit will be given "to be with you forever" (John 14:16). A few verses later He says, "If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him" (John 14:23). Someone might ask whether the Spirit steps aside when the Father and the Son arrive, as if He were only a placeholder until greater Persons came. Not at all. The Spirit stays forever, and the Father and the Son come to that very same home. The Spirit never comes without the Father and the Son, and they never come without Him. Where one is, all three are.

Why is this so? It is because the Father, Son and Spirit are not three beings who happen to agree. They share one divine nature, one being. When theologians call this the "essence" of God, they simply mean what God is. Since what God is cannot be divided into pieces, God cannot be present in pieces either. The Father does not supply one third of His grace, the Son another third, and the Spirit the rest. Each Person is fully present, and the presence is one. Human friends who visit you remain separate people, each with a life of their own. The divine Persons are not like that. Their coming together is not a partnership of strangers. It is the one God coming to live with you.

Baptism shows the same unity. Jesus commands His followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice that it is one name, not three names. Jesus also promised that His disciples would be baptized with the Holy Spirit. And Paul writes, "For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body" (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is one baptism because there is one saving work: Christ's one death and resurrection, into which we are joined. The Father, Son and Spirit do not do three separate things in baptism. They do one work of grace together.

This does not mean the three Persons are blurred into one, or that the names are just three labels for the same thing. The Persons remain truly distinct. The Father sends. The Son is sent and becomes man for us. The Spirit is given and pours God's love into our hearts. Their roles show the order and character of each Person, and the Bible keeps them clear. But the work they do in us is one undivided work. A helpful way to put it is that every work of God toward us comes from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. It is one act with a shape that shows all three.

This matters for ordinary Christian life. You do not need to wonder whether you have received all of God or only part of Him. If the Spirit lives in you, the whole Trinity has made a home in you. When you pray to the Father, trust in Christ, or ask for the Spirit's help, you are not dealing with competing guests who need to be kept happy one by one. You are dealing with the one God, who has come near in His fullness.

It is also a mystery meant to make us humble and glad, not anxious. Jesus thanked the Father for hiding these things from the proud and showing them to little children (Matthew 11:25). The simplest believer who loves Jesus and keeps His word already has this gift. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit live in that person as one God, and they have promised never to leave.

topics.title: How does the New Testament present the Father, Son and Spirit acting together?
topics.cmp: Each author answers a different question, so there is no direct disagreement, but all four read New Testament texts as presenting the Father, Son and Spirit as closely bound together in divine action and worship. Warfield argues that Jesus' teaching is Trinitarian in the Synoptics as well as in John, resting on his claim to unique Sonship and on his casting out demons by the Spirit of God. Augustine reads the plural of John 14:23 as naming Father and Son as relatives, with their unity of essence left unexpressed in that verse. Owen draws on Paul's interchangeable salutations to show that grace is peculiarly received from Christ. Irenaeus argues that offerings made through Jesus Christ are made to the Father's name, because the Son's name belongs to the Father, and he cites the Apocalypse for the incense as the saints' prayers. All rely on close reading of Scripture, though their emphases differ: Warfield on Jesus' self-understanding, Augustine on relational terms, Owen on the Son's distinct role in bestowing grace, and Irenaeus on worship directed to the Father through the Son.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: It is not merely in the Gospel of John that such representations occur in the teaching of Jesus. In the Synoptics, too, Jesus claims a Sonship to God which is unique

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and…
refs.quote: Sometimes also the unity of the essence is left unexpressed, and the relatives alone are mentioned in the plural number

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: he makes these two, “Grace be with you,” and, “The Lord Jesus be with you,” to be equivalent expressions; for whereas he affirmed the one to be the token in all his epistles

ans.text:
The New Testament never stops to give a formal definition of the Trinity, but on page after page it shows the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit acting together as the one God, each in his own way. Once you learn to look for this pattern, you see it in the Gospels, in Paul's letters, in baptism, in prayer and in the everyday blessings the apostles gave their churches.

Start with the Gospels. At Jesus' baptism all three appear at once. The Son stands in the water, the Spirit comes down on him like a dove, and the Father's voice says, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:16-17). This is one event, one act of God, yet each of the three has his own part in it. And this is not only in John's Gospel. In Matthew, Mark and Luke, Jesus speaks of God as his Father in a unique way, and he works by God's own power: "If I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (Matthew 12:28). The Son acts, the Spirit is the power at work, and the kingdom that arrives is the Father's.

John's Gospel makes the pattern especially close and personal. On the night before he died, Jesus said, "If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him" (John 14:23). Notice the word "We." Jesus does not say the Father will come, or that he alone will come. Father and Son come together. The plural shows they are truly two, not one person under two names. Yet they do not come as two separate visitors who happen to arrive together. They make one home, in one believer, by one act of love. In the same chapter Jesus says the Father will send the Spirit in his name (John 14:26), so the Spirit is part of this same coming. God moves into a believer's life as Father, Son and Spirit together.

Paul writes the same way, often without seeming to think about it, which shows how natural it was for the first Christians. In 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 he says, "There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. There are different ministries, but the same Lord. There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all men." Spirit, Lord (Jesus), and God (the Father) are all named as the source of the church's gifts. Paul is not describing three suppliers sharing out the work. He is describing one divine generosity, seen from three sides.

His best known blessing does the same: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you" (2 Corinthians 13:14). The Christian receives one salvation, but it comes to us as the Father's love, the Son's grace, and the Spirit's fellowship. Interestingly, Paul often closes his letters simply with "Grace be with you," and at other times with words like "The Lord be with your spirit." He treats these as two ways of saying the same thing. To have Christ's grace is to have Christ himself, and to have Christ is to have the Father who sent him and the Spirit he gives.

The same pattern shapes how Christians pray and worship. Paul says, "Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit" (Ephesians 2:18). And, "God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, 'Abba, Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). We pray to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. When the church offers praise and prayer through Jesus, it is offering it to the Father's own name, because the Son bears and reveals the Father's name. And when Jesus sends his disciples out, he tells them to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice it says "name," not "names." One name, shared by three.

Put simply, the New Testament teaches that all God's works toward us come from the Father, through the Son, and are brought home to us by the Spirit. And our response goes back the same road: by the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father. The three never work apart, because they are one God with one will and one power. Yet each acts in a way that fits who he is. The Father sends, the Son is sent and saves, the Spirit is poured out and dwells in us.

Two misunderstandings are worth avoiding. One is to picture the Father, Son and Spirit as three separate gods forming a team or a committee, each doing a different slice of the job. Scripture rules this out. There is only one God, and every work of God is the work of all three together. The other mistake is to think there is really only one person who wears three masks, sometimes appearing as Father, sometimes as Son, sometimes as Spirit. That does not fit passages like Jesus' baptism, where all three are present at once, or John 14:23, where the Father and the Son speak of themselves as "We."

A helpful way to hold this together is to remember that when God blesses you, you are never receiving a part of God. You are receiving the whole of God's love, and that love always has the shape of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. That is why the apostles could end a letter with a blessing naming all three, and why Christians still do.

topics.title: Do the prepositions 'of whom', 'through whom' and 'in whom' imply differences of nature or rank?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the question (Ambrose, Basil, Hilary, Waterland) agree that the prepositions 'of whom', 'through whom' and 'in whom' do not imply a difference of nature or rank. They allow at most a distinction of Persons without confusion, and Waterland alone adds 'a certain priority of order proper to the first Person.' Basil gives the fullest argument. He traces the scheme to Aetius and to heathen philosophy's classification of causes, and he catalogues scriptural passages where each preposition is used of Father, Son and Spirit and where 'from' and 'through' are interchanged. He also argues by contraries that identical language implies identical essence. Ambrose runs closely parallel, citing the same kind of examples ('through the will of God', 'I in the Father'), but he also gives each preposition a positive sense for the Son as Creator. Hilary instead reasons that 'from Whom' and 'through Whom' mark one Author of the same nature exercising the same power, and Waterland, explicitly following Basil, adds the grammatical point that dia with the genitive regularly denotes an efficient cause. On Romans 11:36 the authors diverge in emphasis. Ambrose and Basil refer it specially to the Son via Isaiah, Hilary and Augustine read it as showing one nature and one God (Augustine stressing the singular 'to whom be glory' and that the phrases are not indiscriminate), Novatian explains it of God's command, word and judgment without a Trinitarian division, and Edwards applies it to the three Persons in redemption.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: The origin of the heretics' close observation of syllables.
refs.quote: The object of all this is that the Creator of the universe may be regarded as of no higher dignity than an instrument, and that the Holy Spirit may appear to be adding to existing things nothing more than the contribution derived from place or time.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For the Apostle did not so say, All things are of God, and all things are through the Son, as to signify that the substance of the Father and the Son could be severed, but that he might teach that by a distinction without confusion the Father is one, the Son another.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: from Whom are all things and through Whom are all things must signify an Author of the same nature engaged in the same work

ans.text:
No. When the Bible says all things are "from" the Father, "through" the Son, and "in" the Spirit, it is showing that the three are distinct Persons who work together. It is not ranking them or saying they are different kinds of being. The best evidence is that the Bible itself freely swaps these little words between the Father, the Son and the Spirit.

Start with the verse most often raised. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul writes that there is "one God, the Father, from whom all things came," and "one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came." Some readers have reasoned this way: the Father is the real maker, and the Son is only the tool he works with, like a carpenter and his saw. If so, the Son would be a lesser being.

Paul's point runs the other way. He is writing to people surrounded by "many gods and many lords," and he places Jesus inside the one God's identity. He does not set Jesus among the created things. Jesus is the one through whom "all things" came, so he cannot himself be one of the things that came. A carpenter's saw is part of the world it helps to shape. The Son is not.

The little words were never kept in tidy boxes. Look at how the Bible actually uses them.

"Through him" is used of the Father too. Hebrews 2:10 speaks of God the Father "for whom and through whom all things exist." If "through" meant a lower servant, the Father would be serving someone above him, which is absurd.

"From him" is used of the Son and the Spirit. John says, "From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace" (John 1:16). Paul says the whole body of the church grows from Christ the head (Ephesians 4:16). The child in Mary's womb is from the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:20). Whoever sows to please the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit (Galatians 6:8).

"In" is used of all three. Paul writes to the church "in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thessalonians 1:1). Jesus says, "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me" (John 14:10).

The same freedom shows up with creation. Colossians 1:16 says of the Son: "in Him all things were created... All things were created through Him and for Him." In 1 Corinthians 8:6 we exist "for" the Father. Here all things are "for" the Son. Words that look like ranks in one verse are shared in another.

The clearest case is Romans 11:36: "For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever! Amen." Here all three phrases are said of one subject at once. So they cannot mark three different natures.

Christians have read this verse in slightly different ways. Some take it of the Father. Others note that Paul has just quoted Isaiah 40, which describes the Lord who measured the waters and weighed the mountains, and they see the Son as the Creator in view. Still others hear the three phrases as gently pointing to Father, Son and Spirit. Even on that last reading, Paul goes on in the singular: the wisdom and knowledge are "of God," and "to Him" be the glory. On every reading, the lesson holds. Either one Person is "from," "through" and "to" all at once, or three Persons are named and then praised as one God.

So what do the different words do when they are used side by side? They keep us from blurring the Persons together. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit. They also reflect a real order in how God acts. The Father is the source, the one who sends. The Son is the Word, through whom the Father acts and whom he sends. The Spirit brings God's work to completion within creation.

Think of a single act of speaking. There is the speaker, the word spoken, and the breath that carries it. These are distinct, yet it is one act, and the word is not a lesser thing than the speaker's own mind. In the same way, the Father, Son and Spirit do not do separate pieces of a job. All three do the whole work together, each in his own way. Order is not rank, and coming "from" the Father is not being less than the Father. The Son shares the Father's very nature, or "essence," which means everything that makes God God.

Romans 11 also adds a note of humility. Just before verse 36, Paul cries out at "the depth of the riches" of God's wisdom and knowledge, and he calls God's ways beyond tracing. That is a fitting warning. Grammar is a gift for reading Scripture well. But no one can take a few prepositions and use them to measure God or sort him into higher and lower parts. Paul's response to these words is not to rank the Persons. It is to worship the one God from whom, through whom and to whom are all things.

topics.title: When Scripture speaks of one Person alone, are the others excluded or outranked?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Ambrose, Bickersteth, Hilary and Waterland all agree that when Scripture names one divine Person alone, the others are neither excluded, divided, nor outranked. Augustine argues most broadly from the one substance working indivisibly, so that what is said of one Person is understood of all; he applies this to the sending of the Spirit, the Father's love, 1 Corinthians 2:11 and the title 'God of the fathers.' Ambrose reaches the same conclusions but stresses that exclusive statements are set against creatures rather than the other Persons. From this he draws the anti-subordinationist point that the Spirit is not a creature and that the Spirit's leading into truth does not rank him above Father and Son. On 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 Hilary and Ambrose agree there is no division, but they argue differently. Hilary reads Spirit, Lord and God as one Spirit of one Divinity through the mystery of the birth, while Ambrose speaks of diversities of offices with one shared operation of Father and Spirit. Bickersteth applies the principle practically to worship, and Waterland, unlike the others, rests his case on the testimony of the Ante-Nicene writers rather than on direct theological argument.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
refs.quote: in order to intimate the Trinity, some things are separately affirmed, the Persons being also each severally named; and yet are not to be understood as though the other Persons were excluded, on account of the unity of the same Trinity

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: While establishing the personal Godhead of the Spirit, we must not forget his essential unity with the Father and the Son. To those who believe this, every simple command “worship God” embraces the worship of the Holy Spirit

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Is, then, the Son of God excluded? Certainly not, since neither is the Spirit excluded, when it is said: “And none knoweth the Father, save the Son.”

ans.text:
No. When the Bible names one Person of the Trinity, it is not shutting the other two out or placing them lower. It is drawing our attention to one Person, while the other two remain present and at work.

The reason is simple. Christians believe in one God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The three are not three gods working side by side like partners in a business. They share one divine life, one power, one knowledge and one will. So whatever God does, the Father, the Son and the Spirit do together. Each does it in his own way, but never apart from the others. Jesus says in John 5:19 that whatever the Father does, the Son also does. In John 10:30 he says, "I and the Father are one."

That gives us a rule for reading the Bible. When a verse speaks of one Person alone, we ask what it is contrasting him with. Almost always the contrast is between God and creatures, not between one divine Person and another.

Take 1 Corinthians 2:11: "no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God." Does that mean the Son does not know God's thoughts? Surely not. In Matthew 11:27 Jesus says that no one knows the Father except the Son. If we read each verse as excluding the others, the two verses would cancel each other out. Worse, we would have the Spirit teaching the Son as a teacher instructs a pupil. The point of both verses is the same. No creature can search the depths of God on its own. Only God knows God, and the Spirit and the Son are both on the God side of that line.

The same is true of love. In John 16:27 Jesus says, "the Father Himself loves you." He is not saying, "but I don't," or "but the Spirit doesn't." He is the one who laid down his life for his friends. He is reassuring the disciples that they can come to the Father with confidence. The love of the Father is also the love of the Son and the Spirit.

Or think of sending. In John 14:26 Jesus says the Father will send the Spirit. In John 15:26 he says, "I will send to you from the Father." Neither statement contradicts the other. Both are true, because the Father and the Son act together.

The same pattern shows up in worship and in the names of God. When God calls himself "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6), we should not hand that title to the Father alone or to the Son alone. Only someone who is truly God can be the God of the patriarchs. Father, Son and Spirit are each fully God, and together they are the one God. So when the Bible simply tells us to worship God, that worship belongs to all three.

This does not blur the Persons into one. The Bible really does speak of each in a distinct way, and it does so on purpose. It is the Son, not the Father, who became man and died on the cross. It is the Spirit who is poured out at Pentecost. The Father sends the Son, and not the other way around. These distinct ways of naming them are how Scripture shows us that God is three Persons, not one Person wearing three masks. They act together, yet each acts in a way that fits who he is. One way to picture it is a single sentence. The whole sentence says one thing, yet each word does its own job.

A good example is 1 Corinthians 12:4-6. Paul speaks of different gifts but the same Spirit, different kinds of service but the same Lord, and different ways of working but the same God who works all things in everyone. That is not three separate departments run by three separate beings. It is one God giving his gifts to the church, with Paul naming the Spirit, the Son and the Father to show us the richness of who God is. Later in the chapter Paul says that one and the same Spirit works all these things (12:11). He can say that because the Spirit's work is also the Father's and the Son's.

What about ranking? It is natural to think that the one sent is lower than the one who sends, or that the one named first is the greatest. But in God there is order without rank. The Father is the source, the Son is from the Father, and the Spirit is from the Father, and many Christians add through or from the Son. Sincere believers have differed on how to state that last point. Some stress that Jesus says the Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26). Others stress that the Spirit is also called the Spirit of the Son and is sent by him (Galatians 4:6). Both sides agree that this order is about where each Person comes from, not about who is more divine. Each has the whole of the one divine nature, so none can have more of it than another.

So when Jesus promises that the Spirit will guide the disciples into all truth (John 16:13), he is not putting the Spirit above himself or the Father. In the same passage he says the Spirit will take what is his and declare it to them. The Spirit leads us into the truth of the Father and the Son. Growing up in faith means coming to know the one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

There are some harder sayings, such as Mark 13:32, where Jesus says that only the Father knows the day and hour. Christians have generally understood these to be about the Son as he lived among us as a true human being. He spoke as one who had taken a servant's form and a servant's role. They do not mean the Son is a lesser God.

The practical upshot is freeing. When you read that the Father loves you, the Son loves you too, and so does the Spirit. When you pray to one Person, you are not slighting the others. When the Bible speaks of one Person, read it with the whole Trinity in view. That one Person is never without the other two.

topics.title: How does Irenaeus present the Son and Spirit as the 'hands of God'?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus and Daniel Waterland agree that the Son and Spirit are the 'hands of God' by which the Father formed man in his image and likeness. Irenaeus also has these hands joining Adam's ancient substance in the incarnation to form a re-created living man, and he has God glorified by conforming his handiwork to the Son. Irenaeus's own answers are descriptive and economic: the Father speaks to and works through his hands in creation and incarnation, and the Son and Spirit act with him as the one Creator. Waterland takes the doctrinal question further, arguing from Irenaeus's wider usage that the image means more than instrumental agency. His grounds are that Irenaeus calls the Son uncreated and perfect, calls the Son and Spirit the Father's own offspring and figure whom angels serve, and treats 'hands' like dynamis, the power of God and God himself. On that basis Waterland concludes that the three Persons are one uncreated God and one Creator, and he explicitly rejects a reading in which the hands merely carry out the Father's will.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For never at any time did Adam escape the hands of God, to whom the Father speaking, said, “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness.”

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: the joint operations of the three divine Persons, concurring in the creation of man, are set forth in such a manner, as to intimate both the distinet personality and unity of essence.

ans.text:
One of the earliest Christian ways of describing the Trinity pictures the Son and the Holy Spirit as God's two hands: the Father makes, saves and perfects us through them, never at arm's length, and never by using them as mere tools.

The picture starts in the first pages of the Bible. In Genesis 1:26 God says, "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness." Who is God speaking to? Not angels, because angels did not make us and we are not made in their image. Early Christians read this as the Father speaking to his Word and his Spirit. Then Genesis 2:7 says the Lord God formed man from the dust and breathed the breath of life into him. God shapes the clay with his own hands and gives it life with his own breath. Elsewhere the Bible speaks the same way: "Your hands made me and fashioned me" (Psalm 119:73), and "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth" (Psalm 33:6). The Word is the Son (John 1:1-3), and the breath is the Spirit.

So the picture is this. The Father plans and wills. The Son carries the plan out, for "through Him all things were made" (John 1:3). The Spirit nourishes, strengthens and brings life to what is made: "The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life" (Job 33:4). It is one work done by one God. Yet each person has his own part in it. The Father works through the Son and by the Spirit. That pattern runs through the whole Bible: all things come from the Father, through the Son, and are brought to completion by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 8:6).

The same two hands that formed Adam come back to remake him. When the Son became man, the Spirit came upon Mary, and the Son took real human flesh, the same stuff Adam was made from (Luke 1:35). The Father did not start over with new material. He took up his original handiwork and repaired it from the inside. In Jesus there is finally a human being who fully shows the image and likeness of God. And the Father's goal is for all his people to be "conformed to the image of His Son" (Romans 8:29). The hands that made us are the hands that save us. That is why the whole person, body as well as soul, matters to God. He shaped the body with his own hands, and he means to raise it.

Does calling them "hands" make the Son and Spirit lesser beings, like servants or tools? No, and the comparison actually points the other way. A tool is something outside you. You can put down a hammer, lend it out, or replace it. Your hands are not like that. They are part of you. When your hand does something, you have done it. So when the Father works by his Son and his Spirit, God himself is at work. He does not hand the job to someone else. This is why it matters that God did not use angels or some go-between to make us. He made us personally. The Bible also treats the Son as far above any servant: "the Word was God" (John 1:1), and "Let all God's angels worship Him" (Hebrews 1:6). No one worships a tool.

Like every comparison, this one has limits. Hands are not persons, but the Son and the Spirit are. Each knows, loves and acts, and the Son can pray to the Father. Hands are also parts of a body, but God is not built out of parts. The Son and Spirit are not two pieces of God, each one a third of him. Each is fully God, sharing the one nature of the Father. So the image is not trying to explain everything. It makes two simple points. Whatever the Son and Spirit do, the one God is doing. And the Father never acts without them, because they are his own.

The comfort for ordinary believers is real. You were not made, and you are not being saved, by a distant God working through a stand-in. Isaiah says, "we are the clay, and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand" (Isaiah 64:8). The Father has kept his own hands on you from the beginning, through his Son and his Spirit. He will not let go until his work is finished.

topics.title: How did the Persons of the Trinity bring about Christ's incarnation, anointing and resurrection?
topics.cmp: The answers mostly treat different questions, so there is little direct disagreement. Where several authors speak, they agree that the saving events are the work of more than one divine Person, and each argues mainly from Scripture. Ambrose of Milan uses proof-texts ("The Lord created Me", "of the Holy Spirit", "Wisdom hath made herself a house") to make the Incarnation a common work of Father, Son and Spirit, and he contrasts the Spirit's permanent abiding on Christ with his intermittent action on the prophets. Hilary of Poitiers, by contrast, distinguishes the Spirit, who hallows the womb and joins himself to flesh, from the power of the Most High, which strengthens the Virgin to receive him. On the resurrection, Hippolytus of Rome and Hilary both refuse to set the Father's raising against Christ's own power, but with different emphasis: Hippolytus stresses that the Son, though himself the Resurrection, was raised by the Father, while Hilary, citing Colossians 2, stresses that the one Christ who died raised his own flesh by divine power. Hippolytus alone addresses whether the Father himself became incarnate and suffered; he rejects this on the authority of Scripture and the presbyters' confession that it was the Son who suffered and rose.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For as we read that the Father created the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, the Spirit too created it; and so too we read that Christ Himself created His own Body.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: it was the working of God which raised the dead Christ, and it was none other who raised Christ from the dead but Christ Himself, Who worked before His death, and put off His flesh to die.

refs.author: Hippolytus of Rome
refs.quote: the Father is Himself Christ, Himself the Son, Himself was born, Himself suffered, Himself raised Himself. But it is not so.

ans.text:
The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit were all at work in each of these great events, yet only the Son became a man, received the anointing, died and rose again. Holding both of those truths together is the key to this question.

Start with the incarnation, the moment God the Son took on human flesh. Scripture shows all three Persons involved. The Father is the one who sends: "when the time had fully come, God sent His Son, born of a woman" (Galatians 4:4). The Holy Spirit is the one through whom the conception happens. The angel tells Mary, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35). Matthew says she was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit. And the Son is not passive in this, as if something merely happened to him. He freely came. "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14), and Hebrews pictures him coming into the world and saying to the Father that a body has been prepared for him so that he may do God's will.

So the incarnation is one shared work of the one God. Yet the result belongs to the Son alone. The Father did not become a man, and neither did the Spirit. Think of three people working together to fit a coat on one of them. All three are busy with the task, but only one ends up wearing the coat. The comparison is imperfect, because the three divine Persons are not three separate beings, but it shows how a shared action can have an outcome that belongs to one person.

The same pattern appears at Jesus' anointing. "Christ" means "anointed one." At his baptism the Father speaks from heaven, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Son stands in the water (Matthew 3:16-17). Peter later sums it up: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38). Jesus himself reads Isaiah in the synagogue, "The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me" (Luke 4:18), and says it is fulfilled in him.

There is something special here. In the Old Testament the Spirit came upon prophets, judges and kings for particular tasks and particular times. With Jesus it was different. John the Baptist was told that the one on whom he saw the Spirit descend and remain would be the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit (John 1:33). The Spirit did not visit Jesus now and then. He rested on him fully and always. That is why Jesus can pour out the Spirit on his people. He is not one more prophet but the Anointed One himself, the Son of God living a fully human life in the power of the Spirit.

Now the resurrection. Who raised Jesus from the dead? The Bible gives more than one answer, and all of them are true. Very often it says the Father raised him: "God raised Him from the dead" (Acts 2:24), and Paul speaks of "God the Father, who raised Him from the dead" (Galatians 1:1). Paul also connects the resurrection with the Spirit, saying that the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to our mortal bodies (Romans 8:11). And Jesus says he will raise himself. "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again," he says, and John explains that he meant his body (John 2:19-21). Again he says, "I lay down My life in order to take it up again," and that he has authority both to lay it down and to take it up again (John 10:17-18).

These statements do not compete. The Father and the Son share one divine power, so when the Father raises the Son, the Son is not merely acted upon. As God, he shares fully in that same life-giving power. Jesus is the Resurrection and the Life. It was his human body that lay in the tomb, and it was the eternal Son, sharing the Father's power, who took that life up again. There is only one Christ. The one who died and the one who rose by divine power are the same person.

This also guards against a mistake some have made. They reasoned that if God is one, then the Father himself must have been born of Mary, suffered on the cross and raised himself. The Bible will not let us say that. The Father sends the Son. The Father speaks from heaven while the Son is baptized. The Son prays to the Father and cries out to him from the cross. The Father raises the Son and seats him at his right hand. None of this makes sense unless the Father and the Son are truly distinct Persons. It was the Son who was born, suffered, died and rose, not the Father in disguise.

So the picture is this. In everything God does, Father, Son and Spirit act together as the one God, never separately. Yet each acts in his own way. The Father sends and raises. The Spirit overshadows, anoints and gives life. The Son takes flesh, receives the anointing, lays down his life and takes it up again. That is good news for us. The whole Trinity was at work to bring us a Savior, and the Savior who came is truly God the Son, one of us and for us.

topics.title: How do the Father and the Son share in the final judgment?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa and Irenaeus of Lyons agree that final judgment is a single work in which the Father acts through the Son: the Son carries out judgment in accordance with the Father's will or command, so there are not two rival judges. They frame the point differently, though. Gregory is resolving an apparent scriptural contradiction between "God judges all the earth" and "the Father judges no man." He argues that the Father has committed all judgment to the Son, so the Father judges all through the Son while not judging directly, and neither person is excluded from judicial authority. Irenaeus instead describes a division of roles: the Father prepares both the kingdom and the furnace, while the Son, as the one Judge, receives the righteous and sends His angels to cast out the wicked. Irenaeus's emphasis is that the unity of the Son's judging work reveals the unity of the Father who sent Him, whereas Gregory's emphasis is on the shared authority of Father and Son to judge.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: one could not properly say either that They are two judges, or that one of Them is excluded from the authority and power implied in judgment

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: The Father, therefore, who has prepared the kingdom for the righteous, into which the Son has received those worthy of it, is He who has also prepared the furnace of fire, into which these angels commissioned by the Son of man shall send those persons

ans.text:
The Father and the Son share in the final judgment as one God giving one verdict. The Father judges the world through the Son, and the Son judges in perfect agreement with the Father. So there is one judgment and one Judge's will, not two judges sitting side by side.

At first the Bible can seem to pull in two directions. Abraham calls God "the Judge of all the earth" (Genesis 18:25), and many psalms say the Lord will judge the world. Yet Jesus says in John 5:22, "the Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son." Does the Father judge or not?

Both statements are true, and they fit together. The Father judges all the earth by means of the Son. Paul makes this clear. God "has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed" (Acts 17:31), and God "will judge men's secrets through Christ Jesus" (Romans 2:16). The Father is the Judge of all because the judgment is His. He "judges no one" in the sense that He does not step forward as a second, separate judge. The Son is the one who sits on the throne and speaks the verdict.

This does not make two judges who might reach different decisions. Jesus says in John 5:30, "I can do nothing by Myself; I judge only as I hear. And My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me." The Son is not a junior official carrying out orders he does not share. He is God the Son, sharing the Father's own nature, mind, and will. Whatever the Son decides, the Father decides, because their will is one. That is why the passage goes on to say that all should "honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). We cannot honor God as Judge while brushing aside the Son, and we cannot appeal to the Father against the Son's verdict.

Jesus' own picture of the last day in Matthew 25 shows this. The Son of Man sits on His glorious throne and separates the nations. To the righteous He says, in effect, "Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." To the wicked He speaks of the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. The Father has prepared the outcome. The Son receives some into the kingdom and sends His angels to carry out the sentence on others. It is one work from beginning to end, planned by the Father and carried out by the Son. The Holy Spirit takes part in it too. Even now He convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8). God does not split up His work into rival parts.

One common misunderstanding is to picture the Father as stern and the Son as soft, as if Jesus were pleading with an angry Father to go easy on us. Scripture gives no such picture. The Father loved the world and sent the Son. The Son judges with the Father's own justice. Mercy and justice belong to both of them equally. Another mistake is to think that because the Son judges, the Father has stepped back from the world. In fact, judging through the Son is how the Father shows He is fully involved and cares about every person and every deed.

So what does it reveal that the Son is the Judge? First, it reveals His glory. Only God can judge every human heart, so the Son's judging shows He is truly God. Second, Jesus says the Father gave Him authority to judge "because He is the Son of Man" (John 5:27). Our Judge is also one of us. He has lived a human life, been tempted, and suffered. No one will stand before a distant stranger. Third, the Judge is the same one who came to save. Jesus says God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17). Those who trust Him will meet as Judge the very one who died for them.

Finally, the Son's judging shows that God deals fairly with everyone. The same Christ is offered to all. The judgment separates people according to how they have responded to Him: whether they welcomed Him or turned away. God made people able to understand and to choose, and He takes those choices seriously. At the same time, nothing escapes His notice. The judgment shows that the Father has been watching over all things all along, and that in the end everything will be set right by His Son.

title: The Trinity in the Old Testament
desc: Old Testament intimations of the Persons, the Angel of the Lord and theophanies, Jehovah texts applied to Christ, and prophecies and types pointing to the Son.

topics.title: Is the Trinity revealed in the Old Testament?
topics.cmp: The patristic authors (Novatian, Hilary of Poitiers, Irenaeus, Ambrose, Gregory of Nyssa) agree that Old Testament texts such as Genesis 19:24 ('the Lord rained… from the Lord'), 'Let us make man,' the threefold 'Holy' of Isaiah 6, and Hosea 1:7 show distinct divine Persons, and that the Son is the Lord who appeared to Abraham and Moses.
