Hilary even says Moses and the prophets taught him that God is not to be worshipped as solitary. Their grounds differ: Novatian argues that the Lord who was seen and touched cannot be the invisible Father, and Augustine adds that the Word is not confined to a place. Waterland says the Person in the theophanies was not the Father because he acted ministerially, and that the Fathers did not argue from divine simplicity, while Hilary and Irenaeus stress the Father giving judgment to the Son. Waterland and Bickersteth, for their part, prove Christ is Jehovah by inspired New Testament applications of Jehovah-texts, though they split on Zechariah 12:10: Bickersteth uses it as proof, while Waterland calls one reading of it a 'fanciful turn' and rests Christ's title of Jehovah on his being the Father's express image. Warfield differs plainly from the earlier writers in holding that the Trinity is not broadly revealed in the Old Testament, since no one relying on it alone reached the doctrine; he finds only germs, chiefly the hypostatized Word and Spirit and the Angel of Jehovah, which are visible in the light of later revelation, and he explains the delay by revelation in word waiting on the redemptive sending of Son and Spirit rather than mainly by the need first to fix God's unity, a view closer to Gregory of Nyssa's 'through a glass darkly' and Irenaeus's types and parables than to Hilary's direct readings.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of…
refs.quote: Therefore the Lord overturned Sodom, that is, God overturned Sodom; but in the overturning of Sodom, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. And this Lord was the God seen by Abraham; and this God was the guest of Abraham, certainly seen because He was also touched.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: It is The Lord from the Lord; Scripture makes no distinction, by difference of name, between Their natures, but discriminates between Themselves.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.place: Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God
refs.quote: For it here points out that the Son, who had also been talking with Abraham, had received power to judge the Sodomites for their wickedness.

ans.text:
The Old Testament does not spell out the Trinity in so many words, but the God it reveals is the very same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and it holds real hints of this that come into full light once Jesus has come. Think of a room lit dimly, then brightly. The furniture was always there; the stronger light simply shows what was present all along.

Start with what the Old Testament says most loudly: there is one God. "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Israel lived among nations that worshiped many gods, and God was teaching his people, again and again, that he alone is God and there is no other. The Trinity does not soften this. Christians do not believe in three gods. We believe in one God, one divine being, who exists eternally as three Persons. So the Old Testament's stress on God's oneness is not a problem for the Trinity. It is the foundation the Trinity stands on.

Yet even while stressing that God is one, the Old Testament speaks of God in ways that suggest more than a single Person. In Genesis 1:26 God says, "Let Us make man in Our image." In Genesis 19:24 the LORD rains fire on Sodom "from the LORD out of the heavens," as though one who is LORD acts from another who is LORD. In Psalm 110:1 David writes, "The LORD said to my Lord," and Jesus himself uses this verse to show that the Messiah is more than David's descendant (Matthew 22:41-45). In Psalm 2:7 God says to his anointed King, "You are My Son." Isaiah 9:6 calls the promised child "Mighty God."

There is also the mysterious Angel of the LORD. He speaks as God, is called God, and receives honor due only to God, yet he is also sent by God. He appears to Hagar, to Abraham, and to Moses in the burning bush (Exodus 3:2-6). Many Christians from the earliest centuries have understood this figure as the Son, appearing before he took on human flesh. The Father is never seen, but the Son has always been the one who makes God known (John 1:18). Alongside these, the Old Testament speaks of God's Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), filling and guiding God's people, and of God's Word by which the heavens were made (Psalm 33:6).

It is fair to admit that sincere Christians weigh some of these texts differently. Some read "Let Us make man" as a clear hint of the Persons of the Godhead speaking together. Others think it may be God speaking in a royal way, or addressing his heavenly court, and they would not build much on it alone. The same goes for the angels' cry of "Holy, holy, holy" in Isaiah 6:3. Some hear in the threefold cry an echo of the three Persons; others see it mainly as Hebrew emphasis meaning "utterly holy." What matters is not any single verse taken on its own, but the whole pattern, and above all how the New Testament reads these Scriptures.

That is where the strongest evidence lies. The apostles take passages that speak plainly of the LORD, Israel's God, and apply them directly to Jesus. Isaiah 40:3 calls for a voice in the wilderness to prepare the way for the LORD, our God. The Gospels say that voice is John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus (Matthew 3:3). In Zechariah 12:10 the LORD says, "they will look on Me, the One they have pierced," and John applies it to Jesus on the cross (John 19:37). Psalm 102:25 praises the LORD who laid the foundations of the earth, and Hebrews 1:10 says these words are spoken of the Son. After describing Isaiah's vision of the LORD on his throne, John says, "Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him" (John 12:41). The LORD of the Old Testament refuses to share his glory with any creature (Isaiah 42:8). So when the apostles give that glory to Jesus, they are telling us he is not a creature, but the LORD himself, distinct from the Father yet one God with him.

This also answers whether the triune God is the God of Israel. Yes. Christians do not worship a new God. The Father, Son, and Spirit are the God who called Abraham, led Israel out of Egypt, and spoke through the prophets. Jesus told his followers that the Scriptures of Israel speak about him (Luke 24:27; John 5:39).

Why, then, did the full truth wait? Part of the reason is that Israel first needed to be firmly grounded in the truth that God is one, so that talk of Father, Son, and Spirit would never be mistaken for many gods. But the deeper reason is that God reveals himself not only by telling but by doing. The Trinity was made plain when the Father actually sent his Son to be born, live, die, and rise, and then poured out his Spirit on the church. Before those events, there was nothing yet to point to. It is like a family that speaks of a son living far away; you only truly understand when he walks through the door. Hebrews 1:1-2 says God spoke in many ways through the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son. The fuller revelation came when the time was right (Galatians 4:4-6).

So the honest answer is both yes and not yet. The Old Testament reveals the one true God who is, in fact, Father, Son, and Spirit, and it leaves clear footprints of this. But it was in Jesus, and in the gift of the Spirit, that God showed us plainly who he has always been.

topics.title: Was the Son known and revealed to the patriarchs and prophets?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Hilary, Waterland and Bickersteth agree that the Son was known and active before the incarnation. Irenaeus argues most fully, from Gospel texts such as "Abraham rejoiced to see my day" and the promise that many will recline with Abraham: one and the same Word chose and spoke to the patriarchs and prophets, revealed the Father to Abraham, and was later made visible in Christ. Hilary and Waterland read particular theophanies (to Hagar, Abraham, Jacob, and Moses at the bush in Justin's reading) as appearances of the Son, a distinct divine Person who is truly God. Bickersteth stresses instead that Old Testament promise and prophecy, from Genesis to Malachi, directed believers' saving faith toward the Son. Augustine differs plainly on how this happened: citing Stephen's speech and Hebrews' "word spoken by angels," he holds that the Old Testament words and appearances were produced by angels, which could foreshadow Christ but not take on his person, and that the Word was present in them only "in some wonderful and unspeakable manner" while announcing his coming. He explicitly sets aside the reading that the single "angel" of these texts is the Son, the reading on which Hilary and Waterland rely.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: since there is one and the same God the Father, and His Word, who has been always present with the human race, by means indeed of various dispensations, and has wrought out many things, and saved from the beginning those who are saved

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: that divine Person, who called himself God, and was God, was not the Person of the Father, (whose ordinary character is that of Maker of all things,) but another divine Person, viz. God the Son.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: on Him, from age to age the faith of every believer was fastened, by promise and by prophecy.

ans.text:
Yes. The Son of God was not a stranger to Abraham, Moses, David or Isaiah. The same eternal Word who later became a man in Jesus was already at work among God’s people from the beginning, speaking, guiding and promising. What changed at Christmas was not who God’s Word is, but how he came: once he spoke through visions, messengers and prophets, and then he came in our own flesh.

The New Testament makes this clear. Jesus told his opponents that Abraham rejoiced at the thought of seeing his day, and that he saw it and was glad (John 8:56). When they scoffed, he answered, “Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!” (John 8:58). He was not saying he had a good memory of old times. He was claiming to be the living God who had been with Abraham all along.

John also tells us that when Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up in the temple (Isaiah 6), Isaiah “saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him” (John 12:41). Paul says that Israel in the wilderness drank from a spiritual rock that went with them, “and that rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Peter says that the Spirit of Christ was in the prophets, pointing ahead to Christ’s sufferings and the glory that would follow (1 Peter 1:10–11). Jesus himself said that Moses wrote about him (John 5:46). After his resurrection he walked two disciples through Moses and all the Prophets, showing them what was written about himself (Luke 24:27).

So the Old Testament is not about a different God, or an earlier, harsher version of God. Hebrews 1:1–2 puts it this way: God spoke to our fathers through the prophets “in many different ways,” and in these last days “He has spoken to us by His Son.” It is one God speaking throughout, and the Son is the one through whom he has always made himself known. Think of a friend who wrote you letters for years and then finally came to your door. The person at the door is the same one who wrote the letters.

You can see hints of this in a mysterious figure in the Old Testament called “the angel of the LORD.” The word “angel” simply means messenger. Yet this messenger often speaks as God himself. He promises Hagar, “I will greatly multiply your offspring,” something only God can promise, and she calls him the God who sees her (Genesis 16:10–13). At the burning bush the angel of the LORD appears, and then God speaks from the bush: “I am the God of your father” (Exodus 3:2–6). This figure is sent by God and yet is God. Many Christians have seen here the Son, sent by the Father, appearing before he took on flesh.

There are other places where God seems to speak of God as someone else. God tells Jacob to build an altar “to God, who appeared to you” when he fled from Esau (Genesis 35:1). One divine person speaks of another, yet both are called God. These passages do not spell out the full teaching of the Trinity, but they prepare for it. They guard against the idea that God is a lonely, single person, while still holding firmly that there is only one God.

It is fair to say that Christians have not all read these appearances in exactly the same way. Many believe the Son himself appeared in these visible forms, as a kind of preview of his coming. They point to how the angel of the LORD speaks with God’s own authority and receives worship. Others are more cautious. They note that Scripture says the Law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). So they hold that God usually spoke through created angels, with the Son present and at work through them in a way we cannot fully explain. Both sides agree on what matters most. God himself, never seen in his own being, was truly making himself known. The Son was at the heart of that work, preparing the way for his own coming.

How, then, did Old Testament believers know the Father and the Son? Not as clearly as we do. They did not have the names “Father, Son and Holy Spirit” spelled out for them, and they did not yet know that the promised Savior would be named Jesus. But they truly knew the one God. They knew him through his Word, which created heaven and earth and called Abraham out of his homeland. And their faith looked forward to the Savior God had promised. That promise ran from the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15) to Isaiah’s child called “Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6). Job could say that he knew his Redeemer lives. David could hear the LORD say to his Lord, “Sit at My right hand” (Psalm 110:1). Their faith was real faith in the same Savior we trust. They looked forward to him, and we look back.

This is why Abraham could be called the friend of God. He followed God’s Word in trust, leaving everything behind. Jesus now says to his disciples, “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). The Word who befriended Abraham is the one who befriends us. He did not need Abraham, and he does not need us. He was complete in his life with the Father before Abraham was born. He offers his friendship out of pure goodness, to give eternal life.

So when you read the Old Testament, you are not reading about someone other than Jesus. You are watching the same Lord at work, speaking, rescuing and promising, until he came among us in person.

topics.title: Did the Son and the Holy Spirit act in Old Testament history?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Ambrose, Hippolytus, and Basil all affirm that the Son and the Spirit were really at work in Israel's history. Irenaeus centers this on the Word or Son, who gave the law and offerings, revealed Christ's coming to the prophets, brought the flood and Sodom's fire, and was the rock (1 Cor 10:4), and he uses this to argue that one God works through both covenants. Ambrose stresses the Spirit (guiding Israel in the wilderness, giving manna, at work in the Red Sea type of baptism) and argues from the single temptation of God, Christ, and the Spirit, and from the Song of Moses, to the joint work and unity of the whole Trinity, an emphasis Basil shares in reading the cloud as a shadow of the Spirit's gift. Hippolytus divides the roles: the Spirit made the prophets speak while the Word spoke of Himself through them. Augustine is more reserved: such appearances came through created bodily things, not God's invisible substance, and the text often does not show whether the Father, Son, Spirit, or the Trinity appeared, so he declines to assign them to one Person except where the context makes it clear. In contrast to Irenaeus's attribution of particular events to the Son, Gregory of Nyssa holds that singling out the Flood, Sodom, or the plagues adds nothing to the Son's glory and even implies a loss of it, since He governs all things, while Athanasius distinguishes God's commanding of creatures, which involves question and answer through the Word as Mediator, from the Father's working directly in the Word, which needs none.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: Since the Son of God is always one and the same, He gives to those who believe on Him a well of water[^4368] [springing up] to eternal life, but He causes the unfruitful fig-tree immediately to dry up

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Thou didst send Thy Spirit and the sea covered them, and the water was divided by the Spirit of Thine anger.” By which is signified the unity of the Godhead, not an inequality of the Trinity.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Of the Appearance in the Pillar of Cloud and of Fire.
refs.quote: But it is not similarly apparent whether the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself, the one God.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible teaches that the Son and the Holy Spirit were not idle until Bethlehem and Pentecost. They were present and at work all through Israel's history, because the one God who acted in the Old Testament has always been Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

This follows from who God is. Christians confess one God in three Persons. The Son and the Spirit did not come into being when Jesus was born or when the Spirit fell on the church; they are eternal, as the Father is. So when the Old Testament says "the LORD" acted, it is speaking of the same God we now know more fully. What changed in the New Testament was not who God is, but how clearly he made himself known.

The clearest witness is what the apostle Paul says about the exodus. In 1 Corinthians 10:1-4 he writes that the Israelites were all under the cloud and all passed through the sea, and that they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, "and that rock was Christ." Paul is not saying a stone was secretly Jesus. He means that the One who cared for Israel in the desert, who gave them water and food and went with them, was Christ himself. A few verses later he warns us not to test Christ the way some Israelites did, who were then killed by snakes (1 Corinthians 10:9). Some ancient copies of that verse read "the Lord" instead of "Christ," but either way Paul is drawing a straight line from Israel's God in the wilderness to the Lord Jesus. Jude 5 makes a similar point: it reminds readers that the Lord rescued his people out of Egypt and later destroyed those who did not believe, and a number of ancient copies name him there as Jesus.

The Holy Spirit was there too. Looking back on the exodus, Isaiah 63:10-14 says that the people rebelled and grieved God's Holy Spirit. It asks where is the One who set his Holy Spirit among them, and it says the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest, leading them like cattle going down into a quiet valley. The letter to the Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 about Israel testing God in the desert and introduces it with the words "as the Holy Spirit says" (Hebrews 3:7-9). Put these passages side by side and something striking appears. Scripture says Israel tested God, tested Christ, and grieved the Holy Spirit, all in the same wilderness rebellion. That was not three different sins against three different gods. It was one sin against the one God, who is Father, Son and Spirit.

Even the Song of Moses after the Red Sea hints at this. Moses sings that God's right hand shattered the enemy, and that by the blast of God's nostrils the waters piled up (Exodus 15:6-8). The Hebrew word for that breath or wind is the same word used for the Spirit. We should not press poetry too hard, but Christians have long noticed how naturally the song fits what we later learned: the Father acting through his Son, his strong right hand, and by his Spirit, his mighty breath.

Paul also treats the Red Sea and the cloud as a picture of baptism. He says Israel was "baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:2). Just as Pharaoh's army was drowned and Israel walked out free on the other side, baptism pictures our old slavery to sin being ended and our rising to new life. The cloud that covered and shaded the people is a fitting picture of the Holy Spirit, who comes over us and stays with us. If Christian baptism is the Spirit's work, it makes sense that its Old Testament picture was his work too.

The same is true of God's judgments. The flood, the fire on Sodom, and the plagues on Egypt were acts of the one God, and the Son shared in them fully. There is even a curious line in Genesis 19:24, where the LORD rains sulfur and fire on Sodom "from the LORD out of the heavens." Many Christians have seen in that double mention a quiet hint of more than one Person in God. We should be careful here, though. The point is not that the Son is only responsible for a few dramatic disasters. Scripture says all things were made through him and are held together in him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:17). Every work of God in history, gentle or severe, involves him.

The Spirit and the Son were also at work in the prophets. Peter says the prophets searched carefully to understand what time "the Spirit of Christ in them" was pointing to when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1 Peter 1:10-11). In other words, the Spirit moved the prophets to speak, and what they spoke about was the Son. That is why Jesus could say that many prophets and righteous people longed to see what his disciples saw (Matthew 13:17). They could only long for it because God had already shown them something of it. John even says that Isaiah saw Christ's glory and spoke about him (John 12:41).

A few cautions help us read all this well. First, the three Persons never work separately, as if the Father did some jobs, the Son others, and the Spirit the rest. Whatever God does, the whole Trinity does together, though each Person in his own way: from the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. So when Scripture highlights one Person in an event, it is not shutting the others out.

Second, when God showed himself in the pillar of cloud and fire, or in the glory that filled the tabernacle, people were not looking at God's own being. God is spirit and cannot be seen with ordinary eyes. He used created things, like cloud and fire, as signs of his presence, much as a voice carries a person's words without being the person.

Third, it is not always possible to say which Person is in view. Sincere Christians differ here. Many believe that when "the angel of the LORD" appears and speaks as God himself, or when God appears in human form, this was the Son, since he is the one who always makes the Father known (John 1:18). Others think the text often does not tell us, and that we should simply say the one God appeared, sometimes the Trinity together and sometimes one Person as the story makes clear. Both sides agree on the main thing: it was truly God, and the Son and Spirit were not absent.

Finally, none of this means that the Old Testament is secretly the New Testament, or that Israel understood everything we do. They saw in shadows; we see in the full light of Jesus. But it does mean that the God who led Israel out of Egypt is the same God who leads us out of sin. The Son who gave water from the rock is the one who now offers living water. The Spirit who guided Israel to rest is the one who now leads God's children home. One God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, has been at work in one story from the beginning.

topics.title: Was the Angel of the Lord the pre-incarnate Son of God?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Novatian, Hilary, Waterland and Bickersteth all answer yes: the Angel of the Lord who appeared to Hagar, Abraham, Jacob and Moses was the Son, truly God and not a created angel. Novatian, Hilary and Waterland argue that only God could promise to multiply Ishmael's seed or receive Jacob's vow, and that the Father cannot be called an angel. Novatian, Hilary and Bickersteth add that the Father is invisible, so the God who was seen must be the Son; Waterland further defends against Clarke the view that the Son spoke as God in his own Person, not merely as the Father's representative. Augustine differs sharply: he holds that God's substance is never seen and that the theophanies were wrought through created angels bearing God's person, as a crier speaks for a judge or a prophet for the Lord. He treats the angel at Isaac's sacrifice as a created angel, says the Person signified at the bush is uncertain, and warns that it is rash to deny that the Father ever appeared. Athanasius likewise says Moses saw an angel in whom God spoke through the Word. Yet all who address the title agree with Gregory of Nyssa that calling the Son 'Angel' names his office as the Father's messenger (the 'Angel of Great Counsel') and not an angelic nature, and Athanasius and Gregory both read Hebrews 1 as setting the Son above the angels in nature.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Thus God and the Angel of God are One; He Who is the Angel of God is also God the Son of God.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Well then, who could he be but God the Son? who being really God, might, in his own right, truly and justly assume those high titles

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine…
refs.quote: Does the Son of God say of the Father, “The Lord saith,” while He Himself is that Angel of the Father?

ans.text:
Many Christians, from the earliest centuries onward, have believed that the Angel of the Lord was indeed the Son of God, appearing ahead of time before he was born as a man in Bethlehem. Scripture does not spell this out in one verse, but it gives strong reasons for it. And calling him an "angel" does not make him a created being.

Start with the word itself. In both Hebrew and Greek, "angel" simply means "messenger." It describes a job, not what kind of being someone is. A man is called an ambassador because of what he does, not because ambassadors are a separate species. So when the Son is called an angel, Scripture is describing his work of being sent and making God known. That says nothing against his being fully God.

Now look at how this Angel behaves in the Old Testament. He is not like the ordinary angels. When he finds Hagar in the wilderness, he promises, "I will greatly multiply your offspring" (Genesis 16:10). Only God can make such a promise in his own name. Then the text says it was the Lord who had spoken to her, and Hagar names him: "You are the God who sees me" (Genesis 16:13).

At the burning bush, "the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire from within a bush" (Exodus 3:2). Yet the one who speaks from that same bush says, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6). Moses hides his face because he is afraid to look at God. The one seen and the one speaking are the same.

Jacob wrestles through the night with a man. Afterward he receives the name Israel because he has "struggled with God." He names the place Peniel, saying, "I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared" (Genesis 32:30). Hosea later calls that wrestler both an angel and God (Hosea 12:3-5).

When Jacob blesses Joseph's sons, he puts "the God who has been my shepherd" and "the Angel who has redeemed me from all harm" side by side as one source of blessing (Genesis 48:15-16). God says of this Angel, "My Name is in him" (Exodus 23:21).

Compare how true created angels act. When John falls down before an angel in Revelation, the angel stops him at once and tells him to worship God (Revelation 22:8-9). But the Angel of the Lord accepts worship. He speaks as God in the first person and makes promises only God can keep.

So this Angel is God. But he is also distinct from God, because he is sent by the Lord, and sometimes he even speaks to the Lord (Zechariah 1:12). He is God, and yet he is sent by God. That is exactly the pattern the New Testament shows us in the Father and the Son.

The New Testament makes this fit even more clearly. John says, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). The Son has always been the one who shows us the Father. John also says Isaiah "saw Jesus' glory" (John 12:41). Jesus says Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56-58). Malachi promised that "the Messenger of the covenant" would come to his temple (Malachi 3:1), which points to Christ. And an old Greek translation of Isaiah 9:6 calls the promised child the "Angel of great counsel."

A word of care is needed. These appearances were not the incarnation. The Son did not yet have a real human body or a human birth. He took on a visible form for a time, the way you might send a letter ahead before you arrive in person. The true and lasting union of God and man began only when "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14). The appearances were previews of that coming.

Sincere Christians have not all agreed on every detail. Some think the Angel of the Lord may have been a high created angel speaking for God, the way a herald speaks in the king's name. They point to Hebrews 1:1-2, which says God spoke through the prophets in the past but has spoken "in these last days" by his Son. They also note that the law was given through angels (Hebrews 2:2; Acts 7:53). Others reply that a mere messenger would never accept worship, would never call himself the God of Abraham, and would never be named God by those he met. Most Christians through the ages have found the second view more convincing. But the central truth does not depend on settling every passage.

That central truth is plain. Whoever spoke in these scenes, the Son of God is not an angel in nature. Hebrews 1 sets him apart from the angels entirely. To none of the angels did God ever say, "You are My Son." Instead God commands, "Let all God's angels worship Him" (Hebrews 1:6). He calls the Son "God" and says his throne lasts forever (Hebrews 1:8). The angels are servants; the Son is the Lord they serve.

So the Son can rightly be called the Messenger, because he is sent to make the Father known. He is always God, because he is the Father's own Son. The one who met Hagar in the desert, Moses at the bush, and Jacob in the night is very likely the same one who later came among us as Jesus. In every age, he has been showing us the God no one else could show us.

topics.title: Who appeared to Abraham at Mamre?
topics.cmp: Novatian and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the one who appeared at Mamre was God the Son. Novatian argues by elimination: the visible one called God cannot be the invisible Father, and cannot be a mere angel, since an angel is not called God. Hilary reads the text closely: the Man who promised is the Lord God who fulfilled the promise, and Abraham, though seeing three, worshipped one as Lord, foreshadowing the Incarnation. Hilary also holds that the other two were mere angels, because Lot addresses them in the plural ('my lords'). Augustine differs sharply. He denies that the title 'Lord' marks out the Son, since the Father and the Spirit are also called Lord, and he reads Lot's singular address to the two as ruling out a 'one God plus two angels' reading, so that Augustine and Hilary disagree on what Lot's address shows; for Augustine the three equal men, addressed as one Lord, intimate through a created form the equal Trinity of one substance, and since Abraham was awake, the episode tells against confining such appearances to the Son or Spirit. Waterland addresses a narrower point, arguing only that calling the Father the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob does not exclude the Son from being that God.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Whether God the Trinity Indiscriminately Appeared to the…
refs.quote: therefore, neither here does it appear plainly whether it was any person of the Trinity that appeared to Abraham, or God Himself the Trinity

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Moreover Also, from the Fact that He Who Was Seen of…
refs.quote: in order that His proper invisibility may be restored to the Father, and the proper inferiority be remitted to the angel, it was only God the Son, who also is God, who was seen by Abraham

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: The Man made the promise in the power of God; by the same power God fulfilled the promise. Thus God reveals Himself both in word and deed.

ans.text:
Genesis 18 says plainly that it was the LORD himself who came to Abraham at Mamre, and he came in the form of three men. The chapter opens, "Then the LORD appeared to Abraham by the Oaks of Mamre," and then tells us how. Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day, looked up and saw three men standing nearby. He ran to meet them, bowed low, washed their feet and fed them. Christians have long asked which of the three was the LORD, and what this meeting tells us about God.

Start with what is clear. This was not just a visit from messengers. The visitor speaks as God speaks. He promises that Sarah, long past the age of childbearing, will have a son within a year. When she laughs, he asks whether anything is too hard for the LORD. Then he tells Abraham what he is about to do to Sodom, and Abraham pleads with him as the Judge of all the earth. In Genesis 21 we read that the LORD visited Sarah and did for her just what he had promised. The one who made the promise at the tent is the same one who kept it: the LORD God. Abraham ate and talked with the living God.

Was one of the three the Son of God? Many Christians, from the earliest centuries, have answered yes. The story seems to point that way. Partway through, two of the men set off toward Sodom, while Abraham stays standing before the LORD (Genesis 18:22). Then Genesis 19:1 calls those two "angels." So it looks as though one visitor was the LORD and the other two were his angels. On this reading, the LORD who appeared was God the Son. This was before he was born of Mary, of course. He was not yet a man, but he took on a visible form for a time. It was a kind of preview of the day he would truly become one of us.

The main reason for this view comes from the New Testament. Scripture teaches that the Father is invisible. In John 1:18 we read, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known." Paul calls God the one whom no one has seen or can see (1 Timothy 6:16). It is the Son's role to make the unseen God known. So when God is seen, it seems fitting to think of the Son. Jesus himself links his own life with Abraham's. In John 8:56 he says, "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad." And he adds, "Before Abraham was born, I am!"

Other sincere Christians read the scene a little differently. They notice that the text gives no hint that one of the three looked greater or more glorious than the other two. Abraham speaks to the three as a group, but he also addresses them as one Lord. Some therefore see in the three visitors a picture of one God in three persons, not one God plus two angels. They also point out something about Lot. When the two came to Sodom, Lot too seemed to speak to them as one (Genesis 19:18-19). So addressing a visitor as "lord" does not by itself mark one as God and the rest as lesser beings. Those who hold this view take care not to say that the Father became visible in his own nature. They say only that God the Trinity chose to make himself known through created forms, as he could.

The two views share a great deal. Both agree that the LORD truly appeared and spoke. Both agree that God's own being is never seen with human eyes. What Abraham saw was a form God took to meet him. Both agree that whoever stood before Abraham was fully God, not a lesser god or a mere creature. The view that it was the Son is probably the more common one. If it is right, the passage is a strong witness to Christ's deity. The one Abraham called the Judge of all the earth would then be the Son.

A few common mix-ups are worth clearing up. The three men do not mean there are three gods. Abraham bowed to the LORD as one, and Scripture never stops saying that the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). Nor does the word "Lord" settle on its own which person appeared. The New Testament often calls Jesus "Lord," but the Father and the Holy Spirit are called Lord too. Some people point out that the Father is called "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." That does not mean the Son is not that God. Those verses tell us the Father is Abraham's God. They nowhere say the Son is not. Jesus shares the Father's name and glory.

What about Lot? He bowed to the ground when the two arrived, but that does not prove he knew they were angels. Bowing was an ordinary, respectful greeting in that culture. Lot also baked bread for them and pressed them to stay the night for safety. He seems to have treated them as honored human travelers, at least at first. Only as events unfolded did it become clear who they were. Hebrews 13:2 likely has these stories in mind. It tells us to show hospitality, because some have welcomed angels without knowing it.

The heart of the story is this. The God who cannot be seen came near enough to share a meal at a tent door. He did it to make a promise and to keep it. Christians see in that visit a glimpse of what God would one day do fully in Jesus. The Son of God came near to Abraham's children, ate at their tables, and made the invisible God known.

topics.title: How did God and the divine Persons appear in the Old Testament theophanies?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the question agree that the divine nature itself was not seen with bodily eyes in the Old Testament appearances. Augustine says God was shown through a creature subject to him; Hilary says the varied forms (angel, man, fire, the unconsumed bush) were an outward guise and not the Son's nature; Irenaeus says the prophets saw 'similitudes' and 'dispensations' rather than God's face, citing Ezekiel's own qualification; and Ambrose says Christ is seen only by the grace of the Spirit. They differ sharply on who appeared and through what: Hilary and Irenaeus hold that the Father is invisible and that the one seen (by Isaiah, in the furnace, foreshadowing the incarnation) was the Son, and Athanasius insists Scripture separates angel-visions (Zacharias, Manoah, Gideon) from seeing God (Isaiah, Moses, Abraham). Augustine, by contrast, argues that the appearances were wrought by angels, that Abraham at Mamre saw angels, and that the Son did not appear 'in fashion as a man' before the incarnation; he rejects the view that only the Father is invisible and even holds that the Father may be believed to have appeared in Daniel's Ancient of Days. Augustine argues from Hebrews, Wisdom and close reading of Genesis, uses the analogy of signs such as the eucharistic bread and God's name written in gold or ink, and repeatedly declines certainty about how angels work or which Person spoke (tentatively the Spirit at Sinai). Ambrose and Novatian instead read the theophanies typologically: for Ambrose, the bush, Gideon's fire and Ezekiel's wheels point to Christ, the Spirit and the two Testaments, and for Novatian the cherubim-chariot figures God presiding over creation.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Essence of God Never Appeared in Itself. Divine…
refs.quote: those words and bodily appearances which were given to these ancient fathers of ours before the incarnation of the Saviour, when God was said to appear, were wrought by angels

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: And if you, in your heresy, do not know that it was God the Only-begotten Whom the prophet saw in that glory, listen to the Evangelist:—These things said Esaias, when he saw His glory, and spake of Him

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: And neither he who saw God, beheld an Angel, nor he who saw an Angel, considered that he saw God; for greatly, or rather wholly, do things by nature originate differ from God the Creator.

ans.text:
When God showed himself to people in the Old Testament, they did not see God's own being with their eyes. They saw things God made or used for the moment, such as fire, cloud, a voice, a human-looking figure, or a vision, as signs of his real presence. The forms were created and temporary. The God behind them stayed exactly what he always is: invisible, unchanging, and beyond anything eyes can take in.

The Bible makes this point itself. Moses, who spoke with God "face to face" as a friend, still asked to see God's glory. God answered, "you cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live" (Exodus 33:20). He let Moses see only his "back" as he passed by. John says plainly, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). Paul describes God as living in light no one can approach, whom no human has seen or can see (1 Timothy 6:16). So when Genesis or Exodus says "the LORD appeared," it cannot mean that the divine nature itself became something you could look at. It means God truly made himself present and known, by means of something seen or heard.

The prophets were careful about this too. Ezekiel saw a blazing throne above a chariot of living creatures, and on it a figure "with the appearance of a man." Yet he sums it up this way: "This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD" (Ezekiel 1:28). Notice how he steps back three times: an appearance, of a likeness, of the glory. He wants no one to think he had seen God's very being. Daniel's vision of the "Ancient of Days," with white clothing and hair like wool, works the same way (Daniel 7:9). It is a picture of God's eternity, wisdom and authority as judge. It is not a portrait. God the Father is not an old man with white hair. He has no body and no age at all.

The same goes for other famous scenes. Adam and Eve heard "the LORD God walking in the garden" (Genesis 3:8). This tells us God came near to them in a way they could hear. It does not mean God has legs. At the burning bush, Exodus says "the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a blazing fire," and then God spoke from the bush and called himself the God of Abraham (Exodus 3:2–6). The fire was real, but it was not God's substance. Fittingly, it burned without destroying the bush. God's holy presence comes close to his weak people to rescue them, not to consume them. At Mamre, the LORD came to Abraham in the form of three men who ate a meal (Genesis 18). On Mount Sinai there were thunder, smoke, fire and thick cloud. No sensible believer thinks smoke and fire are what God is made of. They were created things serving their Creator, fitted to the moment and to human senses.

This also answers whether these appearances mean God can be seen or can change. They do not. The Lord says, "I, the LORD, do not change" (Malachi 3:6). Think of a voice heard over a radio. The sound is real and truly carries the speaker's words, but the speaker has not turned into radio waves. In the same way, God took up fire, cloud or a human-looking form to speak and act. The form came and went. God himself did not become fire and then stop being fire. Only once did God truly take a created nature as his own for good: when the Son became man, born of Mary (John 1:14; Galatians 4:4). That is different from every Old Testament appearance. In those, the forms were borrowed signs. In the incarnation, the Son really became one of us.

Who, then, appeared? Here Christians have read the texts in more than one way. The whole Trinity is always present and at work together, because the Father, Son and Spirit are one God. Many Christians, from early times until now, have held that the Son in particular was the one who appeared, especially as "the angel of the LORD." This angel speaks as God and is worshiped as God, yet is also sent by God (Genesis 16:13; Genesis 22:11–18; Exodus 3). It is the Son's role to make the invisible Father known (John 1:18). John also says Isaiah spoke of Jesus because he saw his glory, referring to the throne vision of Isaiah 6 (John 12:41). On this reading, these were previews of Christ before he came in the flesh.

Other Christians have urged caution. They point out that the New Testament says the law was delivered through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). They also note that Scripture places the Son's taking a servant's form at his birth, not before (Philippians 2:6–7). So they read many of these scenes as created angels speaking and acting in God's name, much as an ambassador speaks for a king. On this reading, "the angel of the LORD" can say "I am God" the way a herald reads out the king's own words. Both views agree on the main points. What people saw was never God's essence, the Son was not yet human, and the scenes still point forward to Christ. Some passages simply do not settle which Person is meant. Sinai is an example. Some have noted links to the Holy Spirit there: the law written by "the finger of God," and the fire and the fifty days that echo Pentecost. But it is wise not to press such guesses.

Why did God appear this way at all? Because he wanted to be truly known by creatures who cannot see him as he is. The fire, the cloud, the visions and the human-looking figures were gifts suited to their times. They taught Israel that God is holy, near, and faithful. They also prepared hearts for the day when the Son would come in the flesh and people could say, "we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). The New Testament promises a day when believers will see God more fully still (1 John 3:2; Matthew 5:8). That will not come through bodily eyes taking in his essence. It will come through God's own gift, when we are made like Christ.

topics.title: What does Moses seeing God's 'back parts' in Exodus 33 mean?
topics.cmp: Augustine supplies nearly all the answers on this topic, and he reads Exodus 33 christologically throughout. The 'face' is the form of God, equal with the Father, which no one can see and live. The 'back parts' are Christ's flesh, born, dead and risen. He adds that in the form of God the Word has no front or back at all, so both 'face' and 'back' appeared only in the form of a servant. He also reads the covering hand and the 'passing by' as figures: Israel's blindness before the passion, and its later faith in the resurrection as Christ's Passover to the Father. On how Moses could speak 'face to face' yet be refused God's face, Augustine and Irenaeus agree that God's own face cannot be seen by man, but they resolve the tension differently. Augustine says Moses saw God only through a created, corporeal appearance, so 'face to face' describes the friendly manner of speech rather than a vision of the divine substance. Irenaeus instead identifies the speaker as the Word and takes the refusal as a prophecy that man would see God 'in the depth of a rock,' that is, in the Word's coming as man. He holds this was fulfilled at the Transfiguration, where Moses truly spoke with the Lord face to face.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: that it is impossible for man to see God; and that, through the wisdom of God, man shall see Him in the last times, in the depth of a rock, that is, in His coming as a man

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How the Back Parts of God Were Seen. The Faith of the…
refs.quote: His “back parts” are to be taken to be His flesh, in which He was born of the Virgin, and died, and rose again

ans.text:
When God let Moses see His "back" but not His "face," He was giving Moses a real but partial glimpse of His glory. Moses received what a human being can bear, while the full blaze of who God is stayed hidden. It does not mean God has a body with a front and a back. It is picture language for the difference between seeing God truly and seeing Him completely.

The setting matters. After the golden calf, Moses pleads with God to keep going with His people. Then he asks for something bolder: "Please show me Your glory" (Exodus 33:18). God answers in two ways. He will cause all His goodness to pass before Moses and proclaim His name, the LORD. But He adds, "You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live" (33:20). So God hides Moses in a cleft of the rock and covers him with His hand while His glory passes by. Then He takes His hand away, and Moses sees His back. In the next chapter, what Moses mainly receives is words. God proclaims Himself compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness (34:6-7). The glimpse comes with a message about God's character.

God's "face" stands for God as He is in Himself: His very being, His infinite glory. A creature cannot take that in, any more than your eyes can stare into the sun up close. God is spirit (John 4:24). He has no body, so He has no literal front or back. The "back" stands for the trace God leaves as He passes: what we can see of Him after He has acted, in His deeds, His goodness, His spoken name. Think of seeing where a great ship has passed by the wake it leaves. The sight is real, but it is not the whole ship.

Many readers are puzzled because the same chapter says, "The LORD would speak with Moses face to face, as a man speaks with his friend" (33:11). This is not a contradiction. "Face to face" there describes the kind of relationship Moses had: direct, personal and warm, with nothing in between. Numbers 12:8 makes the same point by saying God spoke with Moses plainly, not in riddles. It is about closeness in conversation. It is not a claim that Moses gazed on God's very being. Even in their most intimate meetings, what Moses saw was a form God chose to show, such as the cloud or the fire. It was never the uncreated glory itself. We speak the same way when we call a talk "face to face" without meaning anything about seeing all there is to know about a person.

This is where the passage opens up toward the Trinity. The New Testament says, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). Many Christians from the earliest centuries have understood that the One who spoke with Moses as a friend was the eternal Son, the Word of God. He is the One who always makes the unseen Father known. He is truly God, equal with the Father. In His divine nature He is just as far beyond our sight as the Father is.

When the Son became man, God's glory came to us in a form we could look at. Paul says God has given us "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6), and Jesus could say, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). We still do not see the divine nature with our eyes. What we see is God the Son in real human flesh, living, dying and rising. In Him God has shown His face in the only way sinners could bear.

Some Christians have taken this further and read the scene as a picture of Christ. On this reading, the "face" is the Son's divine glory, which no one can see and live. The "back" is His human flesh, which came "later" in history and could be seen. Moses sees it only as God "passes by," and that points to the Passover, the Lord's passing from death to life in His resurrection. Many in Israel did not recognize Jesus until after He rose, as if a hand had been over their eyes and was then lifted. Other Christians prefer to stay closer to the plain sense of Exodus and treat this as a devotional picture rather than the passage's main meaning. Both agree on the heart of it: God is beyond our sight, and He has made Himself known through the Son.

There is a beautiful sequel. Centuries later Moses stood on a mountain again, this time with Jesus at the Transfiguration. He saw the Son's glory shining and talked with Him about the "departure" He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:30-31). The man who once saw only God's back finally saw the glory of God in the face of the incarnate Son.

The passage also holds out hope for every believer. For now, Paul says, we see only a dim reflection, but then we will see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). We are promised that God's servants "will see His face" (Revelation 22:4). What Moses longed for, and received only in part, God means to give His people in full, through Christ.

topics.title: Whom did Isaiah see enthroned in Isaiah 6?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that John 12:41 identifies the Lord of hosts whom Isaiah saw with the Son. Waterland, Bickersteth and Owen use it chiefly to prove Christ's deity, Bickersteth and Owen concluding that Christ is the Jehovah or Lord of hosts, and Waterland adding that Father and Son are thereby one holy Lord of hosts, showing both distinction of Persons and unity of Godhead. Gregory of Nyssa and Ambrose go further, combining the traditional reading (the Father), John (the Son) and Paul in Acts 28:25 (the Holy Spirit) to argue that the vision belongs to all three. For Gregory this becomes a general rule that every theophany is to be understood of the whole Trinity, while Ambrose grounds it in the one majesty and rule of the three, presses it to the point of saying the Spirit sent Isaiah and is the enthroned Lord of Sabaoth whom the Seraphim praise, and reconciles John and Paul as differing in words, not meaning (the Father is seen in the Son, the Son in the Spirit). Bickersteth, in a separate answer, likewise draws on Acts 28:25, the threefold 'Holy' and the plural 'us' to argue that the Spirit is worshipped with the Father and the Son, whereas Owen and Waterland's answers here do not take up the Spirit at all.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: the Prophet Isaiah, as may be inferred from 4 St. John, makes them both to be one holy, holy, Lord of hosts, therein signifying both the distinction of Persons and unity of Godhead

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: every specially divine vision, every theophany, every word uttered in the Person of God, is to be understood to refer to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: The message recorded determines the occasion to be the same. Therefore, Jesus Christ, of whom the inspired apostle is speaking, is Jehovah of hosts, before whom the seraphim veiled their faces in lowliest adoration.

ans.text:
Isaiah saw the one true God, the Lord of Hosts, on his throne. The New Testament shows that this one Lord is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together. It points to the Son and to the Spirit by name.

Start with what Isaiah tells us. "In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a high and lofty throne" (Isaiah 6:1). Mighty angelic beings called seraphim cover their faces and cry, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts." Isaiah is undone: "my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts" (Isaiah 6:5). Then he hears the Lord ask, "Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?" Isaiah answers, "Here am I. Send me!" He is told to go and give a hard message: the people will hear but not understand, and see but not perceive.

Now look at how the New Testament reads this scene. In John 12, John explains why many people refused to believe in Jesus despite his signs. He quotes Isaiah, then adds, "Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him" (John 12:41). John is pointing straight back to Isaiah 6. The glory Isaiah saw on the throne, the glory that made angels hide their faces, was the glory of Jesus. John is not saying Jesus is a lesser figure standing near God. He is saying that Jesus is the King, the LORD of Hosts. That fits what John says from the start: the Word who became flesh is God, and he is the one who makes the unseen God known (John 1:1, 14, 18).

Then turn to Acts 28. Paul quotes the very commission from Isaiah 6, "Go to this people and say...". He introduces it by saying that the Holy Spirit spoke rightly to their fathers through Isaiah the prophet (Acts 28:25-26). Isaiah heard the voice of the Lord on the throne. Paul says that voice was the Holy Spirit's. The Spirit is the one who sent Isaiah and spoke the words of the LORD of Hosts.

So do John and Paul contradict each other, one saying Isaiah saw the Son and the other saying the Spirit spoke? No. They would contradict each other only if the Son and the Spirit were two separate gods, or if one of them were not truly God. The Bible's teaching is that there is one God, and the Father, Son, and Spirit share one divine nature. They share one glory, one throne, and one rule. When you meet the one, you meet the whole God. Jesus says, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Paul says no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The Father is known in the Son, and the Son is known through the Spirit. That is why Christians have long read this vision as a vision of the Father too. It is not three different readings competing with each other. It is one God whose majesty belongs equally to all three.

A comparison may help, though every comparison falls short. Think of the sun's light, which you see by and are warmed by. You never meet one of these without the others. In a far deeper way, Isaiah did not see a third of God or one God among three. He saw the LORD, and that LORD is Father, Son, and Spirit.

The chapter also gives gentle hints that fit this truth, though they should not be pressed too hard. The Lord asks, "Who will go for Us?" He is one Lord, yet speaks with a plural "Us." The angels cry "holy" three times. In Hebrew, repeating a word stresses it to the highest degree, so the main point is God's utter holiness. Still, many Christians have seen in that threefold cry a fitting echo of the three Persons. The hints only become clear in the light of the New Testament, which names the Son and the Spirit in this very scene.

This also tells us something about worship. The seraphim fall before the one on the throne. John says that one is Jesus, and Paul says the voice from that throne is the Spirit's. So the worship of heaven is not given to the Father alone while the Son and Spirit stand aside. It is given to the one God, and so to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together. When we pray to the Father, honor the Son as Lord, and praise the Holy Spirit, we are not dividing our worship among three gods. We are joining the angels in Isaiah 6, bowing before the one thrice-holy Lord.

Finally, this vision should humble and comfort us. Isaiah cried, "Woe is me," because he was unclean before such holiness. Then a burning coal from the altar touched his lips, and he was told his guilt was taken away. The same Lord whose glory Isaiah saw later came near in Jesus. He took away our sin by his own sacrifice and sent his Spirit to make us his messengers.

topics.title: What does 'Let Us make man in our image' reveal about the Trinity?
topics.cmp: All the authors read Genesis 1:26 as pointing to a plurality of Persons within the one God. Where some answer "No," they are rejecting a rival reading. Warfield uses verse 27 to rule out the idea that God speaks to angels. Hilary rejects a solitary God. Augustine denies that gods made man after the image of gods. They differ on whom God addresses and what the text proves. Irenaeus, followed by Waterland, has the Father speaking to the Son and Spirit as his Word and Wisdom or "hands," and Irenaeus links that Word to his later healing of the blind man. Augustine and Waterland stress that man bears the image of the whole Trinity, since the image of one Person is the image of all. Hilary concentrates on Father and Son: from "Us/Our" he argues for a real Partner, from "likeness" for their being alike, and from the singular "image" for one shared nature. He then uses Genesis 1:27 and the command to Noah ("after the image of God") to prove that the Son is true God, reading "God made man after the image of God" as two Persons, God and God. Augustine explicitly denies that 1:27 proves the Son's divinity, saying other texts do that, and takes the singular "image of God" instead to guard against three Gods. Bickersteth argues on philological grounds, from the plural divine name Elohim used in strictly monotheistic Israel, and admits he gives the point no great prominence.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: But He, the very same who formed Adam at the beginning, with whom also the Father spake, [saying], “Let Us make man after Our image and likeness,”

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For an isolated being cannot be partner to himself; and again, the words, Let Us make, are inconsistent with solitude, while Our cannot be used except to a companion.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Why We Do Not in the Trinity Speak of One Person, and…
refs.quote: For it was not that gods might make, or make after the image and likeness of gods; but that the Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit might make after the image of the Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit

ans.text:
When God says "Let Us make man in Our image," He gives us an early glimpse that the one God is not a lonely, single person. There is fellowship within God Himself, and the image He stamps on us belongs to all who share that one divine life.

Look closely at Genesis 1:26-27. In verse 26 God says, "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness." The words "Us" and "Our" are plural. Then verse 27 says, "So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him." Now the words are singular. One God acts, yet He speaks as "Us." The image is "Our" image, yet it is one image, not several. Both truths sit side by side in two verses.

Think about how we talk. Someone who is truly alone says "I" and "my." He does not say "let us" to himself. When God says "Us" and "Our," it suggests someone is there with Him, sharing in the work. But the passage also does not say "Our images," as if there were several gods, each with its own likeness. There is one image of God, because there is one God. That is just what Christians mean by the Trinity: three Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who share one divine nature, or "essence," meaning what God is. They are not three gods. They are the one God.

Could God have been speaking to the angels? Many people have suggested so, and it is worth taking seriously. But the passage itself pushes against it. God says "Let Us make," so the ones addressed share in the making. Yet the Bible never presents angels as creators. Isaiah 44:24 has the Lord saying that He alone stretched out the heavens. And the next verse does not say man was made in the image of God and the angels. It says "in the image of God He created him." If the image is "Our" image, and that image is simply God's image, then those included in "Our" must share God's own nature. Angels are creatures. God does not share His image with them as partners in creation. He does not need advisers either. Isaiah 40:13-14 asks who ever counseled the Lord or taught Him, and the answer is no one.

Some have also suggested that God is speaking like a king who uses "we" for himself, or that He is talking to Himself to stress how serious the decision is. These ideas are possible readings of the grammar. But they do not explain why the plural is so quickly followed by a singular, as if the text wants to say both "Us" and "one" at the same time. The same thing happens elsewhere. In Genesis 3:22 God says man "has become like one of Us," and in Genesis 11:7 He says, "Come, let Us go down."

It is fair to say that sincere Christians weigh this passage differently. Some see it as a clear sign of more than one divine Person. Others think it is a quieter hint, one that would not prove the Trinity by itself. They point out that God revealed Himself step by step, and the full picture came only with Jesus. Both views agree that the passage fits what the rest of the Bible makes plain, and that it was never meant to suggest many gods.

When we read Genesis 1 with the whole Bible in hand, the hint comes into focus. Already in Genesis 1:2 "the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters." Then the New Testament tells us that the Son was at work in creation too. John 1:1-3 says the Word was with God and was God, and that through Him all things were made. Colossians 1:16 says that in Him all things were created. So when God says "Let Us make man," Christians hear the Father, the Son, and the Spirit working together as the one Creator.

This also tells us something about ourselves. We are made in the image of a God who has always lived in love and fellowship. It is no accident that the very next words are "male and female He created them." We were made for relationship because the God who made us is not alone. And in Christ, who is "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), that damaged image is being restored in us.

topics.title: Does the name Jehovah belong to Christ?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that the divine name belongs to the one true God alone and expresses his unique, eternal being. Daniel Waterland and Edward Henry Bickersteth both conclude that Christ bears this name and is therefore truly God. Bickersteth's answer is labelled 'No' on whether the name signifies necessary existence, but his explanation affirms that point and denies only that the name is ever given to a creature. On the meaning of 'I Am', the Fathers stress different aspects: Hilary of Poitiers reads it as absolute existence that guarantees God's eternity, Augustine as a sense of being proper to God and found in no creature, and Novatian as God's unchanging sameness, which any change would undo. Waterland argues most philosophically and polemically: he says the name is absolute rather than relative, and that its incommunicability and its meaning of eternal being confirm each other. He turns Dr. Clarke's and the Arians' own glosses against them to show that Christ is Jehovah in his own Person, the same substance and Being as the Father though not the same Person. Bickersteth instead draws on Scripture and devotion, citing the apostle's rendering of the name and arguing that Christ rightly receives the trust, worship and love due to Jehovah. Novatian reaches a similar conclusion by another route: he argues from the prophecies of God's coming that those who call Christ a mere man must call him God, without appealing to the name Jehovah itself.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: It neither is applied to any created being throughout the Scriptures, nor can be applied in reason, for it imports the necessary, independent, and eternal existence of the Most High.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the…
refs.quote: whether they call Him Father or Son, from his heresy, however unwillingly, they must needs withdraw if they are accustomed to say that Christ is merely man

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: “that Jehovah himself would save them, but not in his own Person.” Well then, it is by another Person, which Person the text expressly calls Jehovah.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible gives Jesus Christ the holy name of God, Jehovah, and with it the honour, worship and saving work that belong to God alone. It does this without making him the same person as the Father. He shares the Father's very being.

First, a word about the name. When God spoke to Moses from the burning bush, he said, "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14). He then gave Israel his personal name, four Hebrew letters often written YHWH. Older English Bibles spelled it "Jehovah." Most modern Bibles print it as "LORD" in small capital letters. It is closely tied to the verb "to be." It speaks of the God who simply is. He did not begin, he will not end, and he does not change. Everything else exists because he gives it life. He exists because he is God.

That is why this name is called "incommunicable." The word just means it cannot be handed on to anyone else. Kings, judges and even angels are sometimes called "gods" or "lords" in a loose sense. The personal name LORD is never given that way to a creature, because no creature exists in the way it describes. God makes this clear: "I am the LORD; that is My name! I will not give My glory to another" (Isaiah 42:8). If this name and its glory are given to someone, that someone must be the one true God.

The New Testament gives them to Jesus again and again. In John 8:58 Jesus says, "Truly, truly, I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!" He did not say "I was." He spoke of himself with the timeless "I am" of the burning bush. His hearers understood him. They picked up stones to stone him for blasphemy.

The apostles often take Old Testament verses about the LORD and apply them directly to Jesus. Isaiah 40:3 calls for a road to be prepared for the LORD. The Gospels say John the Baptist fulfilled this by preparing the way for Jesus (Mark 1:2-3). Joel 2:32 promises that whoever calls on the name of the LORD will be saved. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:13, right after saying we must confess that "Jesus is Lord" (Romans 10:9). The Lord we call on to be saved is Jesus.

In Isaiah 45 the LORD says there is no other God besides him and no other Saviour. He swears by himself that every knee will bow to him and every tongue will confess him. Paul takes that oath and applies it to Jesus: "at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:10-11). Paul is not putting a creature beside God. He is saying that the honour God swore he would never share is given to Jesus. And far from robbing the Father, this honour glorifies the Father.

The pattern runs through the whole Bible. In Isaiah 6 the prophet sees the LORD on his throne. John says Isaiah "saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him" (John 12:41). Psalm 130:8 promises that the LORD himself will redeem Israel from all their sins. Titus 2:13-14 speaks of "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ," who gave himself to redeem us from all lawlessness. The LORD is the Shepherd of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, who goes looking for his lost sheep. Jesus calls himself the good Shepherd (John 10:11) and says he came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). Jeremiah 23:6 even names the coming King from David's line "The LORD Our Righteousness."

One misunderstanding is that Jesus only carries God's name the way an ambassador carries a king's seal. On that view he would stand in for the LORD without being the LORD himself. The texts will not allow this. An ambassador is never worshipped as the king. Yet Jesus receives worship, is called on for salvation, and is confessed as Lord before every knee. No faithful servant of God in the Bible ever accepted that kind of honour. Angels and apostles refused it (Acts 10:25-26, Revelation 22:8-9). Jesus receives it as his right.

A second misunderstanding runs the other way. Some conclude that if Jesus is the LORD, then he must be the Father under another name. But Scripture keeps them distinct. Jesus prays to the Father, is sent by the Father, and is confessed as Lord to the Father's glory. So the conclusion is this. There is one LORD, one divine being. That one LORD is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Son is not the Father, but he is fully the same God.

This matters for ordinary faith. The Old Testament warns again and again against trusting anyone but the LORD. Yet the New Testament calls us to trust Jesus completely, love him above all, and call on his name. That would be idolatry if he were less than God. Because he bears the name above every name, resting on Christ is resting on God himself.

topics.title: What do Isaiah's prophecies teach about the Son's deity?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Isaiah's prophecies point to the Son as truly God. Irenaeus, Owen and Novatian each read Emmanuel as proof that the Virgin's child is God, but they ground it differently: Irenaeus contrasts divine and human tokens in the text to rule out both a mere man and a God without flesh, and also argues from divine prerogatives such as choosing the good and knowing the heart; Owen speaks of God taking our nature in the child; Novatian argues from Christ's promise to be 'with you' always. Owen and Bickersteth argue the same way from the New Testament's use of Isaiah's 'stone of stumbling' to identify Christ as the Lord or Jehovah of hosts. Hilary works most closely with the text: he defends the reading 'the true God' without 'Thee' against what he calls heretical tampering, and appeals to Paul, John and Isaiah's vision. His 'No' answers on these points share the substance of his 'Yes' answers and reach the same conclusion. On Isaiah 45:14-15, Hilary and Hippolytus both take the words as spoken of Christ, though they give opposite yes/no answers and stress different things: Hilary shows the Son's Godhead through Pauline parallels, while Hippolytus uses the economy of the Incarnation to show two persons rather than one. Ambrose alone addresses who gave the Son, answering the whole Trinity, and Owen alone treats Isaiah 54 as Christ's marriage to the church.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: God, then, was made man, and the Lord did Himself save us, giving us the token of the Virgin.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: Now, a child born to be “God with us,” is God in that child taking our nature upon him; and no otherwise can the words be understood.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: That Christ is God, is Proved by the Authority of the…
refs.quote: But because He is with us He was called Emmanuel, that is, God with us. God, therefore, because He is with us, was called God with us.

ans.text:
Isaiah teaches that the coming Messiah would be a real human child and also God himself, the LORD of Israel come to his people. The apostles saw this clearly, and when they applied Isaiah's words to Jesus they were not stretching them. They were reading them the way Isaiah meant them to be read.

Start with Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel." Matthew quotes this verse about Jesus' birth and tells us what the name means: "God with us" (Matthew 1:23). The child's everyday name was Jesus. Immanuel describes who he is. A name in the Bible often tells you what someone is. This child is not just a sign that God is on our side, the way any good king might be. He is God, present with us in our own flesh. Isaiah even holds both sides together. The child eats ordinary food and grows up like any boy (Isaiah 7:15), so he is truly human. Yet his name says he is God. He is not a mere man, and he is not God merely pretending to have a body.

Two chapters later Isaiah speaks of the same royal child: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given... And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6). The one who is born as a baby is the same one called "Mighty God." Some have tried to soften this to "mighty hero." But in the very next chapter Isaiah uses the same title for the LORD himself: "a remnant of Jacob, to the Mighty God" (Isaiah 10:21). Isaiah does not have two Mighty Gods.

Notice too the wording: a child is born, but a son is given. The child has a birthday. The Son already existed, and God gave him to us. That is the Christmas message in one line. Father, Son and Spirit all share in this gift. The Father sends, the Spirit brings about the conception, and the Son gives himself.

The title "Everlasting Father" sometimes puzzles people. It does not mean the Son is the same person as the Father. It describes the kind of king he is: one who cares for his people like a father, and does so forever.

Isaiah 8 gives an even sharper example. Isaiah says that "the LORD of Hosts" is the one Israel must treat as holy. That same LORD will become "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense" to many in Israel (Isaiah 8:13-14). The New Testament applies this stumbling stone to Jesus, the one rejected by many of his own people (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8). Peter goes further. He takes Isaiah's command to honor the LORD of Hosts as holy and writes, "in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord" (1 Peter 3:15). He takes words about the LORD himself and puts Christ in that place. Only someone who believed Jesus is the LORD could do that.

The same pattern runs all through Isaiah. Isaiah 40:3 calls for a voice to prepare the way for the LORD, and all four Gospels say John the Baptist prepared the way for Jesus. In Isaiah 45:23 the one true God swears that every knee will bow to him. Paul says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus (Philippians 2:10-11).

In Isaiah 6 the prophet sees the LORD on his throne and cries out that his eyes have seen the King. John tells us that Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus' glory and spoke of him (John 12:41). The glory Isaiah saw in the temple was the glory of the Son.

Isaiah also describes God as the husband of his people: "For your Maker is your husband—the LORD of Hosts is His name—and the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer" (Isaiah 54:5). In the New Testament, Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19), and Paul says Christ loved the church as a husband loves his wife (Ephesians 5:25). The divine husband of Isaiah is the Christ who gave himself for his bride.

Even Isaiah's description of the Messiah's wisdom points the same way. He will not judge by what his eyes see or decide by what his ears hear (Isaiah 11:3). John says Jesus needed no one to tell him about people, for he knew what was in them (John 2:25). Reading hearts belongs to God.

Some passages are less certain, and it is wise to say so. For example, in Isaiah 45:14 foreign peoples say "God is in you," and in Isaiah 65:16 people bless themselves by "the God of truth." Christians have often heard Christ in these verses. The case for his deity does not rest on them, though. It rests on the clearer texts above.

But did the apostles read Isaiah fairly? Some say they lifted verses out of context. Yet look at how the pieces fit. Isaiah 7, 9 and 11 belong together. They describe one coming son of David whose names, reign and wisdom are far too great for any ordinary king. The New Testament writers were not grabbing random lines. They saw that the child Isaiah longed for had come. Jesus himself taught them to read the Scriptures this way (Luke 24:27).

None of this means there are two Gods, or that the Father became a baby. Isaiah insists there is only one God. Within that one God, the Father gives and the Son is given. The Son is not a lesser god. He is the LORD of Hosts himself, who came near enough to be held in his mother's arms, and near enough to be stumbled over.

topics.title: What do the Messianic Psalms teach about the Father and the Son?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that the Messianic Psalms speak of the Father and the Son as two distinct Persons who are both truly Lord and God. Irenaeus, Owen, Hilary and Athanasius all read Psalms 110 and 45 this way, and Novatian, Hilary and Athanasius explain the passages that sound subordinating (David's son, 'thy God', the anointing, entering the gates) by distinguishing what is said of Christ as man from what is said of him as God. On Psalm 45:7 Athanasius and Hilary reject at length the reading that the Son was promoted to Godhead as a reward. They differ somewhat on the word 'wherefore': Athanasius denies that it signifies any reward and takes it as the reason the Word came down and was anointed for our sake.
