But He truly added a human nature to Himself. The fear, the tiredness, the thirst and the pain belong to Him as a man. They are real, and they are His. But they do not shrink or change His divine nature, any more than His being born as a baby meant God had begun to exist. Philippians 2:6-8 says that He, being in very nature God, "emptied Himself" by taking the nature of a servant and humbling Himself to death on a cross. He did not empty Himself by giving up being God. He did it by taking on what is lowly.

So when we see Him trembling in the garden, we are not seeing a lesser god. We are seeing God the Son humbling Himself all the way down to where we are.

The angel who strengthened Him in Gethsemane (Luke 22:43) fits the same pattern. As God, the Son made the angels and needs nothing from them. As a true man, He could be strengthened, just as He was once fed by His mother's hands. That is not a mark against His deity. It is the depth of His humility.

And this is good news for us. Hebrews 2:14-15 says He shared our flesh and blood so that by His death He might destroy the devil and free "those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death." He went through the fear so that we would not be ruled by it. When you are afraid, in pain, or weak, you are not facing anything your Lord refused to face. He has been there, and He has come out the other side.

topics.title: How can the Son, being God, advance, be exalted or be anointed?
topics.cmp: Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary agree on the core conclusion: the Word, being God and highest, cannot advance, be exalted or be anointed, so these things belong to the assumed human nature. Athanasius argues from God's being highest and the Son's likeness to the Father, from Luke's wording ('Jesus,' 'stature'), and from the absurdity that the flesh would perfect the Word. He also treats the advance as the progressive manifestation of the Godhead to observers and stresses that the flesh was truly the Word's own. Gregory of Nyssa applies the same reasoning that the Highest needs no exaltation to Acts, but he gives the Word an active role as the 'right hand' that raised the Humanity to its own height, making it Lord and Christ. Hilary places the anointing in time and argues that the Word needed no Spirit because he was himself the Spirit and power of God, emphasizing that our manhood was sanctified in Christ. John Owen addresses a different question, asserting from Scripture the eternity of Christ's kingdom, without discussing whether this concerns the divine or human nature.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: Where then could He be exalted higher, who is in the Father and like the Father in all things? Therefore He is beyond the need of any addition

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: the Right Hand of God, that made all things that are, (which is the Lord, by Whom all things were made, and without Whom nothing that is subsists,) Itself raised to Its own height the Man united with It, making Him also to be what It is by nature.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: It was then not the begotten Word, God with God in the beginning, Who was anointed, but that nature in God which came to Him through the dispensation later than His divinity

ans.text:
The Son never became more divine than he already was. When the Bible says he grew, was exalted, or was anointed, it is speaking about him as a man. These things happened to the humanity he took on for our sake. Yet they truly happened to him, because that humanity was his own.

Start with who the Son is. John's Gospel says the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made through him (John 1:1-3). God is already the highest and has all fullness. Nothing can be added to him. The Son cannot become wiser, because he is the Wisdom of God. He cannot be raised higher, because there is nowhere higher to go. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed, "glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). He was asking to return to a glory that had always been his.

But "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14). The eternal Son took a real human body and a real human mind and soul. He did not stop being God. He added a true human life to who he already was. Paul says that though he existed "in the form of God," he "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:6-7). Everything that is true of an ordinary human life became true of him, except sin. So we read things about him that could never be said of God as God.

Take his growth. Luke says, "Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man" (Luke 2:52). Notice that Luke says "Jesus," the name he was given as a baby, and that he mentions "stature," or height. God has no height. This is a boy growing up. His body grew. As a man he learned things the way children do, and Hebrews even says he "learned obedience from what He suffered" (Hebrews 5:8). As the years passed, who he really was also became clearer to the people around him, until his disciples confessed him as the Son of God. This growth was not play-acting. It was real, just as his hunger, tiredness, and suffering were real.

It helps to see why it cannot mean the Son himself grew in wisdom as God. If it did, the Son would have been lacking something before he became man, and his human body would have made God more complete. That turns things upside down. The Word did not need the flesh to perfect him. The flesh needed the Word. The Son brought his fullness to our humanity; our humanity added nothing to his Godhead.

The same is true of his exaltation. On the day of Pentecost Peter preached that Jesus was "exalted" to the right hand of God, and that "God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ" (Acts 2:33, 36). Some translations say "by" the right hand of God, since the original words can be read either way. Paul says that because Jesus humbled himself to death on a cross, "God exalted Him to the highest place" (Philippians 2:9). What was lifted up? It cannot be his divine nature, which was never low. It is the humanity that had been humbled, mocked, and crucified. The man Jesus, raised from the dead, was brought into the glory the Son had always had, and openly shown to be Lord of all. Being "made" Lord and Christ does not mean he became Lord for the first time. It means that, in his human nature and in the sight of the world, he was installed and declared to be what he always was.

His anointing works the same way. Peter tells how "God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power" (Acts 10:38). Jesus read the prophecy "The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me" (Luke 4:18, from Isaiah 61:1) and said it was fulfilled in him. As God, the Son needed no gift of the Spirit. The Spirit is his own Spirit, and they share one divine life. But as a man, Jesus lived, prayed, and worked in dependence on the Spirit, just as he calls us to do. The anointing happened at a point in time, at his baptism, not in eternity. What was anointed was his humanity, set apart and filled with the Spirit for his work as Prophet, Priest, and King.

A simple comparison may help. Imagine a king who leaves his palace and works among his people in disguise as a servant. When he is welcomed back and crowned before everyone, he does not become more royal. He always was the king. What changes is how he is seen and honored, and the servant's life he took up is now honored with him. The comparison falls short, because Christ's humanity was not a disguise. He really became one of us. But it shows how one person can be exalted without becoming more than he was.

There is good news in this for us. The Son did not need to grow, be raised, or be anointed. He went through these things in our nature, for our sake. Our humanity was made holy in him, lifted up in him, and filled with the Spirit in him. That is why he can pour out the Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33) and why we can share in his life. Our humanity now sits at the Father's right hand in Jesus.

Nor is this exaltation temporary. Hebrews applies Psalm 45 to him: "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever," and goes on to say that God has anointed him "with the oil of joy" (Hebrews 1:8-9). In one breath he is called God whose throne is eternal, and the man anointed by God. Isaiah promised there would be no end to the increase of his government (Isaiah 9:7). The crucified and risen Jesus reigns, as God and as man, forever.

topics.title: What do particular episodes of Christ's life reveal about his person?
topics.cmp: Most questions here have a single respondent, but where authors overlap they agree: Ambrose of Milan and John Owen both take the Transfiguration's brightness as a display of divine glory. Ambrose grounds this in the apostles' falling down in worship and Paul's teaching that the Godhead's glory belongs to the Trinity, while Owen grounds it in the described radiance and its parallel with the Ancient of days in Daniel. Hilary of Poitiers instead reads the Transfiguration as a preview of Christ's reigning body coming into his Kingdom. On the descent, Irenaeus of Lyons stresses a real descent to the realm of the dead, against those who read 'the lower parts' as this world, and gives its purpose as bringing salvation to the righteous dead, citing a saying he attributes to Jeremiah. Hilary is concerned instead with the identity of the one who descended and ascended, and with the indivisible divine nature that is present in Hades and Paradise at once; he explicitly holds that Christ's body lay in the grave and did not itself go into Hades. Irenaeus and Hilary both treat the Magi's gifts as acknowledging Christ's divinity and kingship, Irenaeus by symbolic reading of each gift and Hilary by prophetic fulfilment from Isaiah and Psalm 72, while Augustine alone takes up 'Touch me not', reading it spiritually as a call not to conceive of Christ after a fleshly manner but as equal to the Father.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: myrrh, because it was He who should die and be buried for the mortal human race; gold, because He was a King, “of whose kingdom is no end;” and frankincense, because He was God

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Whether, therefore, dead or buried, descended into Hades or ascended into Heaven, all is one and the same Christ

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Do not you think that they even, as they fell, worshipped, when they could not with their bodily eyes endure the brightness of the divine splendour

ans.text:
Each of these moments shows the same truth from a different angle: the one person Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, and he stays one and the same person in the manger, on the mountain, in death, and in heaven.

Start with the wise men. Matthew 2:11 says they came into the house, saw the Child with Mary his mother, "fell down and worshiped Him," and offered gold, frankincense and myrrh. The Bible does not spell out what each gift means. But Christians have long seen a picture in them. Gold is a gift for a king. Frankincense was burned in worship of God. Myrrh was used to prepare bodies for burial. So the gifts quietly point to who this baby is: a King whose kingdom will never end, God who is rightly worshiped, and a real man who would die for us. The worship is the clearest part. Faithful Jews of that time worshiped God alone, yet Matthew tells of these men bowing before a child without any hint that they were wrong to do so.

The visit also fulfils old promises. Psalm 72 and Isaiah 60 speak of kings and nations from far away bringing gold and incense to God's chosen King. The wise men were outsiders, not Jews. Their long journey was a first sign that the nations would come to worship the Son.

The Transfiguration lets us see behind the curtain. On the mountain, Matthew 17:2 says, Jesus' "face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light." This was not a borrowed glow, like Moses' face after he had been with God. It was Jesus' own glory showing through. The white clothing echoes Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days, whose clothing was white as snow. The Father's voice then says, "This is My beloved Son." The disciples fell on their faces in fear. That is the right reaction to the glory of God.

The Transfiguration was also a preview. Just before it, Jesus promised that some standing there would see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. On the mountain three of them did, for a moment. They glimpsed the risen and reigning Christ ahead of time. It reminds us that the humble Jesus walking toward the cross was the Lord of glory all along. He had laid aside the display of his glory, not the glory itself.

Then comes his death and what the Bible calls his descent "to the lower parts of the earth" (Ephesians 4:9). Jesus did not just seem to die. His body was laid in a tomb, and his human soul went where the souls of the dead go, called Hades in the New Testament. Peter applies Psalm 16 to him in Acts 2:27: God would not abandon him to Hades or let his Holy One see decay. Jesus really entered death as we do, so that he could be "the firstborn from among the dead" (Colossians 1:18) and break death's hold from the inside.

Christians have read this descent in more than one way. Many, from very early on, understand it as Jesus going among the dead to announce his victory and bring the faithful of old into his salvation. They point to passages like 1 Peter 3:18-19 and 4:6. Others read "the lower parts of the earth" as meaning simply the earth itself, or the grave. On that reading Paul is speaking of Christ coming down from heaven to be born and to be buried, and the 1 Peter passages are about something else. They note that these verses are hard to interpret and that Scripture does not give details. On either reading, the main point stands: Christ truly died and went all the way down.

At the cross Jesus told the dying thief, "Today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). How could he be among the dead and in Paradise at once? The answer lies in who he is. As a man, his body lay in the tomb and his soul was among the departed. As God, he is never shut up in one place. He fills all things. In the same way, while he walked the roads of Galilee as a man, he never stopped being the God who upholds the universe. He does not split into pieces, with one part in one place and another part somewhere else. He is one person, acting through two natures.

That is why Paul insists, "He who descended is the very One who ascended" (Ephesians 4:10). It was not a mere man who went down and a different, divine Christ who went up. The same Jesus who was laid in the grave rose in that same body and ascended. Acts 1:9-11 describes him taken up into heaven as the disciples watched. The angels promise that "this same Jesus" will return in the same way.

The ascension shows that the Son did not drop his humanity once his work was done. He took it with him. There is now a man, with real flesh, at the Father's right hand. He prays for us, rules over all things, and sends the Spirit. It fulfils Daniel 7, where one like a son of man comes on the clouds to the Ancient of Days and is given an everlasting kingdom.

Finally, there are the puzzling words to Mary Magdalene on Easter morning. In John 20:17 Jesus says, "Do not cling to Me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father." Yet in Luke 24:39 he tells the disciples, "Touch Me and see," and he invites Thomas to put his hand in his side. So the problem is not touching as such. Jesus wanted his followers to know his risen body was real flesh and bones, not a ghost. That gives us a pattern of our own bodily resurrection.

What Jesus refused was to be held on to as if things would simply go back to how they were. Mary, understandably, wanted the old friendship back on the old terms. Jesus points her forward. He was going to the Father. From then on his people would know him not mainly by sight and touch, but by faith, through the Spirit, as the exalted Lord who is equal with the Father. Paul says something similar in 2 Corinthians 5:16: we no longer know Christ merely in a human way. Notice also how Jesus words his message: "My Father and your Father, My God and your God." He is the Son by nature. We become children by grace through him. And as a man he can truly call the Father his God.

Taken together, these episodes tell one story. The child worshiped by foreigners, the Lord shining on the mountain, the man lying dead and entering the realm of the dead, and the King rising to heaven are all one person. He is the eternal Son of God, who became truly human for us and who remains both God and man forever.

title: Redemption, Atonement and Christ's Mediation
desc: Why the Son became incarnate and died, satisfaction and substitution, his victory over the devil, his priesthood and intercession, obedience, and the Trinity's part in salvation.

topics.title: Why did the Word of God become incarnate to redeem humanity?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Word had to become truly incarnate, because a mere man or a word of pardon given from outside human nature could not save fallen humanity. Novatian, Augustine and Owen each frame this in terms of a Mediator who shares both natures, and Athanasius and Irenaeus insist that the Saviour be the very creating Word who took the same flesh that fell. They differ markedly in how they picture what redemption achieves. Athanasius, Irenaeus and Gregory of Nyssa stress the healing and deification of nature: grace united to the body, passions abolished in the Impassible, life-giving power mingled with mortal nature, and incorruptibility conferred. Irenaeus grounds this especially in recapitulation and typology (Adam and Christ, Eve and Mary, tree and tree, every age of life sanctified). Augustine emphasizes the cleansing and illumination of darkened minds, humility as the remedy for pride, and a fitting sinless death that frees us from the devil's claim, even adding a numerical analogy between the sixth day and the sixth age. Hilary combines forgiveness, victory over evil powers and Christ's role as a credible witness, while Owen alone builds a juridical account of satisfaction of God's justice, penal sin-bearing (argued philologically from Hebrew nasa), propitiation and the rejection of any 'one drop' sufficiency, with little of the Fathers' language of deification or recapitulation.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: so did the latter, by an angelic communication, receive the glad tidings that she should sustain (portaret) God, being obedient to His word

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: the blood of Jesus Christ, being the blood of him that was God, though not the blood of him as God; for God is a spirit. And this undeniably testifies to the unity of his person as God and man.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: they could not become sons, being by nature creatures, otherwise than by receiving the Spirit of the natural and true Son. Wherefore, that this might be, ‘The Word became flesh,’ that He might make man capable of Godhead.

ans.text:
The eternal Son of God became a man because that was the only fitting way to bring us back to God: to stand between God and us as one of us, to die in our place, to undo what Adam did, and to share his own life with us. Humanity was lost, and the One who made us came in person, in our own flesh, to find us.

Start with the problem. God made people good and made them for himself. But through sin we turned away. We became guilty before God, our minds grew dark toward him, and death came into the world. We could not fix this from our side. A sinner cannot pay for his own sin, and a dying person cannot give himself life. The rescue had to come from God.

Yet the rescue also had to happen on our side, inside human life. Think of a bridge. It has to rest on both banks or it is no bridge at all. Paul writes, "For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). A mediator is a go-between who truly belongs to both parties. Jesus can bring God and people together because in his one person he is fully God and fully man. John says it simply: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). "The Word" is John's name for God's eternal Son, the one through whom all things were made.

The Son did not stop being God when he became man. He did not turn into something less, and he was not part God and part man like a mixture. He kept all that he is and took on all that we are, except sin. One person, the Son, now lives both a divine life and a fully human life.

Why did that matter? First, so that he could die for us. God in his own nature is spirit and cannot bleed or die. So the Son took a real body, a mortal one, so that he could give his life in our place. Hebrews says that since the children share in flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity, so that by his death he might break the power of the one who holds the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14). Because the one who died is truly God, Scripture can even speak of the church of God, "which He purchased with His own blood" (Acts 20:28). It was not his blood as God, but it was the blood of the person who is God. That is why his death has more than enough worth to pay for the sins of the world.

Second, so that he could carry our sin. Isaiah foretold the servant of the Lord: "He bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). In the Old Testament, when a person is said to bear his sin, it means he suffers its penalty. Jesus took that penalty on himself. He did not merely show us that God is willing to forgive. He dealt with the debt itself. Paul puts it this way: in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting people's trespasses against them (2 Corinthians 5:19). God's justice is honored and his mercy is set free, both at the cross.

Some people ask why God did not simply declare us forgiven with a word. He is all-powerful, after all. But the question is not only what God could do. It is also what would truly heal us. A pardon spoken from outside would leave us just as we were: weak, mortal, still bent toward sin, and needing to be pardoned again and again. By taking our nature into himself, the Son healed it from the inside. He joined God's life to human flesh for good. Forgiveness and new life now come to us in a person, not just a decree.

Third, so that he could reverse Adam's fall. Paul compares Jesus with Adam: "For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19). And again, "For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22). Jesus is the new head of the human race. Where Adam said no to God, Jesus said yes, all the way to the cross. He passed through every stage of human life, faced temptation and stayed faithful, so that a new humanity could begin in him.

This also helps explain why he was born of Mary rather than made fresh from the dust, as Adam was. God was not starting over with a different kind of creature. He came to save the very humanity that had fallen, Adam's own family. So the Son took his flesh from a daughter of Adam, "born of a woman," as Paul says (Galatians 4:4). Christians have long noticed a fitting echo here too. Eve listened to the wrong voice and disobeyed. Mary heard God's word through the angel and said yes. The child she bore was truly God, and through her trusting obedience the Savior came into the world.

Fourth, so that we might see and know God. Fallen people could not look on God's glory, and our hearts were too clouded to understand him. So God came close in a form we could see, hear and touch. John says that no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is himself God and is at the Father's side, has made him known (John 1:18). Jesus' gentleness, his teaching, his tears and his humility show us what God is like. His humility in being born in a stable and dying in shame is also the cure for our pride.

Fifth, so that we might become God's children. Paul says God sent his Son "to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:5). The Son of God became a son of man so that sons and daughters of men could become children of God. We do not become God, and we never stop being creatures. But we are joined to Christ by his Spirit and share in his life, his standing with the Father, and one day his resurrection and immortality. Peter even speaks of believers sharing in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). He took what was ours so that he could give us what is his.

It is worth seeing that the Redeemer is the same Word who made us in the beginning. The hand that formed Adam is the hand that came looking for the lost sheep. Our Maker did not send someone else to fix his broken work. He came himself. And this was not a hurried repair after things went wrong. Scripture says Christ was chosen before the foundation of the world and revealed in these last times for our sake (1 Peter 1:20). God foresaw our fall and, in love, had already purposed our rescue in his Son.

That same plan reaches beyond individual souls. Paul says God's purpose is to bring all things in heaven and on earth together under Christ as head (Ephesians 1:10). Jesus rose in a real human body, and that is a pledge that God will renew not only us but his whole creation. The risen Lord says, "Behold, I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5).

Even believers before Jesus' birth were saved through him. David, after his great sin, cast himself on God's mercy and looked forward to the cleansing God would provide. The forgiveness the Old Testament saints received rested on the same Savior and the same work that saves us. They looked ahead to it; we look back on it.

One honest note. Some sincere Christians have wondered whether the Son would have become man even if humanity had never sinned. Some think the incarnation was always God's plan to crown creation and unite it to himself. Others point out that the Bible always ties his coming to our salvation, such as "to seek and to save the lost." Either way, all agree on what Scripture plainly says: he did come, and he came for us and for our salvation.

So the answer to "why" is finally love. The Son did not need anything from us. He came down to where we were so that he could bring us up to where he is, home to the Father.

topics.title: Must the Saviour be truly God as well as truly man?
topics.cmp: Bickersteth, Athanasius, Irenaeus, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary agree that the Saviour must be God and not a creature. Bickersteth and Hilary add that denying the Son's divinity, or trusting Christ only as a creature, empties his work of saving power and leaves no hope of life. Their grounds differ. Irenaeus and Bickersteth rest mainly on Isaiah's prophecies that God himself, not an angel, an elder or a mere man, will save, and Irenaeus adds Paul's confession that no good dwells in his flesh. Gregory argues philosophically from the gulf between created and uncreated, which is the gulf between servitude and dominion: only the Master can free servants. Athanasius builds the most developed soteriological case. A creature could not unite man to the Spirit, and would remain external, like a teacher, so that sin stayed inherent in the flesh. Only the Word appropriating flesh deifies man and destroys corruption, whereas a created Word would fight the creaturely devil endlessly. Owen and Waterland come at the theme from different angles. Owen says satisfaction is still made to God's justice even though God appointed the remedy. He holds that Old Testament saints were saved by Christ's blood, that glory is the grace Christ purchased brought to perfection, and that sin's root dies only in Christ. Waterland argues more modestly and epistemically: we cannot know that anything less than infinite power would suffice for redemption, so the argument against Christ's divinity cannot be made.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: If then He was of nothing, He would not have been the Christ or Anointed, being one among others and having fellowship as the rest

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: “Neither an elder, nor angel, but the Lord Himself will save them because He loves them, and will spare them: He will Himself set them free.”

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: he who says that the created was saved by the uncreated God, or he who refers the cause of our salvation to the creature? Surely the judgment of pious men is not doubtful.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible teaches that the one who saves us must be truly God and truly man at the same time, and both halves of that matter. If he were only a man, or even the greatest of angels, he could not save us. If he were God but never truly became one of us, he could not stand in our place.

Start with the God side. Again and again the Old Testament says that saving people is something God keeps for himself. In Isaiah 45:21-22 the Lord says there is no other God besides him, "a righteous God and Savior", and then calls out, "Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God, and there is no other." The prophets did not promise that God would send a helper to do the job for him. They promised that God himself would come and save his people (Isaiah 35:4). So when the New Testament calls Jesus the only Saviour, and says in Acts 4:12 that "there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved," it is putting Jesus in the place the Old Testament keeps for God alone.

Why couldn't a very good man do it? Because every mere human being is part of the problem. Psalm 49:7-8 says, "No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice." Paul admits in Romans 7:18 that nothing good lives in his flesh. A drowning man cannot rescue other drowning men. Even the holiest people in the Bible still died. Death had a hold on them too.

Why not an angel, then? An angel is still a creature. It is greater than us in some ways, but it is still finite and still a servant of God, just as we are. Hebrews 1 takes great care to show that the Son is far above the angels. He made them, and they worship him. If our Saviour were only a creature, however exalted, salvation would be one servant visiting other servants. It would not be the Master himself coming down to set his servants free. A creature cannot give us God, because it does not own God's life to give.

This is the deepest reason. Salvation is more than having our debts cancelled. It is being brought back to God: forgiven, made new, filled with his Spirit, and given a share in his own life (2 Peter 1:4). Only someone who is God can join us to God. If Jesus were only a creature, he could at most be a teacher standing outside us and pointing the way. He could not take our nature into himself and heal it from the inside. He could not drive sin out at its root or give us his Spirit as his own. And he could not defeat death and the devil once and for all. If the devil, a creature, were fighting only another creature, the struggle could go on forever. But 1 John 3:8 says, "The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil." Only the Maker of all things can undo what has spoiled his creation.

The worth of what Jesus did also depends on who he is. One man's death might at most stand in for one other man. But Acts 20:28 speaks of "the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood." Because the one who suffered is God the Son, his sacrifice has infinite worth. It is enough for every sinner who comes to him, in every age. That includes the believers of the Old Testament, who looked forward to him in faith.

Now the human side. Being God was not enough on its own. God, as God, cannot die, and it was human beings who owed the debt and lay under death. So the Son became truly one of us, with a real body and a real human soul. He was not God wearing a human costume. Hebrews 2:14-17 says he shared our flesh and blood so that by his death he might break the power of the one who holds the power of death, and that he had to be made like his brothers in every way. That is how he could be our faithful high priest. 1 Timothy 2:5 calls him "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." A mediator has to belong fully to both sides. Jesus can lay one hand on God and the other on us, because he is both.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. Jesus is not half God and half man, like a mixture. He is one person who is fully God and fully man. Nor is the cross a kind and loving third party talking an angry God into forgiving us. The Father planned our rescue, the Son carried it out, and the Spirit applies it to us. As 2 Corinthians 5:19 puts it, God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ. God himself provided the sacrifice that his own justice required. Sincere Christians have sometimes wondered whether God could, in theory, have saved us some other way. But the Bible's own reasoning, and Christians everywhere, agree that the way God actually chose required a Saviour who is both God and man.

This is why the question is not a matter of fine print. If Jesus is admired as a great teacher or a high created being but not trusted as God, then what is left cannot save. It cannot take away sin, unite us with God, or overcome death. Faith rests on him because he is the Son of God. As Jesus says in John 17:3, eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. The comfort of the gospel is that the one who holds us is not a creature who might fail. It is God himself, who became our brother so that he could bring us home.

topics.title: Why must God's justice be satisfied, and how did Christ's satisfaction accomplish salvation?
topics.cmp: John Owen supplies nearly all the answers and argues one consistent position. God's holiness and justice as supreme Ruler, not as a private offended party, indispensably require that sin be punished. Christ, as God-man and voluntary substitute, bore the very penalty sinners deserved (the law relaxed only as to the person), and so made real satisfaction that is identical with propitiatory expiation, and this leaves pardon wholly free and magnifies God's love. Owen grounds this chiefly in Scripture (texts on not clearing the guilty, Romans 3:25, Isaiah 53, the redemption vocabulary of kopher, lutron and hilasmos) and in governmental and juridical reasoning, and he expressly rejects grounding satisfaction in God's free decree alone, the pecuniary-debt model, and the Socinian view that Christ merely revealed the way of salvation. Edward Henry Bickersteth agrees on vicarious atonement but argues more simply from Isaiah 53 that the Lord's bruising of an innocent servant implies substitution and a more-than-human bearer, and he stresses sin's fatality and humanity's inability to cure itself, without Owen's analysis of justice. Augustine frames redemption differently: humanity was justly handed over to the devil because of Adam's sin, and Christ overcame the devil's quasi-right because his innocent blood was unjustly shed; he also defines God's wrath as calm just retribution, not emotion, and says reconciliation is the ending of that wrath when sins are forgiven, adding that God loved sinners even as enemies. Irenaeus, Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius do not speak of satisfying justice at all and instead describe salvation as the Son assimilating humanity to himself and presenting it to the Father, with Athanasius insisting the Son must be true God for deification to be sure, so the patristic answers differ from Owen's mainly in their framework and emphasis rather than by contradicting him.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The love of the Father in sending of the Son was an act of his will; which being a natural and essential property of God, it was so far the act of the Son also, as he is partaker of the same nature

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For man had not been deified if joined to a creature, or unless the Son were very God; nor had man been brought into the Father’s presence, unless He had been His natural and true Word who had put on the body.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” There is a majestic condescension in these few words that nothing can equal. He was made man.

ans.text:
God's justice must be satisfied because God is not only loving but holy and righteous. Forgiving sin as if it did not matter would mean denying himself. In Christ, God himself met that demand, so that forgiveness could be both completely free and completely just.

Start with what sin is. It is not a small slip or a private matter between friends. It is a creature turning away from the God who made it and refusing his rightful rule. God is the Judge of all the earth and the author of a good law. If he simply shrugged at evil, he would be saying that evil is acceptable and that his own word means nothing. Scripture describes God as forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin, "yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" (Exodus 34:7). The prophet says to God, "Your eyes are too pure to look upon evil" (Habakkuk 1:13). Think of a judge who lets a guilty criminal walk free because he feels kindly that day. We would not call him merciful. We would call him corrupt.

Some people object that if God cannot just forgive without a cost, he must be weaker than we are, since we can forgive. But there are things God cannot do precisely because he is perfect. He cannot lie, cannot change, cannot deny himself. In the same way, the holy God will not pretend sin is not sin. That is not a limit on his power. It is the steadiness of his goodness.

So what did Christ do? The word "satisfaction" can sound cold. It simply means doing or suffering what is enough to answer the just charge against us. We could never do that. So God provided what he required. The eternal Son became a man, lived the obedient life we failed to live, and on the cross took on himself the judgment our sins deserved. Isaiah foresaw it: "He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him." Paul puts it in one sentence: "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21).

This is how God can forgive without becoming unjust. Paul says God presented Jesus as an atoning sacrifice "to demonstrate His righteousness," so that he would be "just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:25–26). At the cross, justice is not set aside and mercy is not held back. Both are shown in full at the same moment.

Doesn't this make forgiveness less free? Not at all. Free means free for us. We pay nothing, earn nothing, suffer nothing to gain it. The cost was real, but God paid it himself. Paul did something similar on a small scale. He asked Philemon to forgive the runaway Onesimus, and offered to cover any wrong himself. The forgiveness was still Philemon's gift, and Paul's offer made room for it. In the same way, the Old Testament sacrifices came before the words "he will be forgiven" (see Leviticus 4). Atonement does not compete with pardon. It opens the door to it.

A common misunderstanding pictures a kind Son persuading an angry Father to stop being harsh. Scripture says the opposite. The cross starts with the Father's love: "For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son" (John 3:16). Again, "love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins" (1 John 4:10). The Father, Son and Spirit are one God with one will to save. The Father sends. The Son gives himself willingly (John 10:18). Through the eternal Spirit he offers himself to God (Hebrews 9:14). So this is not God punishing some unwilling third party. It is God, in the person of his Son, bearing in our nature what we deserved.

Nor is it unfair that the innocent One suffered. He was innocent in himself. But he freely chose to stand in our place as our representative, the way a guarantor takes responsibility for another's obligation. Because he shares our human nature, he could truly act for us. Because he is God, his offering has infinite worth.

It also helps not to press the picture of a money debt too far. The Bible does speak of our sins as debts, and the image is useful. But sin is not really an unpaid bill that God could cancel with a stroke of the pen. It is rebellion against a holy King and his law. It deserves judgment, not just a payment. What Christ bore was that judgment.

Sincere Christians have differed on one finer point. Some hold that God's justice made the cross absolutely necessary: a holy God could not have forgiven in any other way. They point to texts like Exodus 34:7 and to the Father's not sparing his own beloved Son (Romans 8:32). Surely God would not have done that if an easier way had been open. Others hold that God, in his freedom, could have chosen another way, but that the cross was the wisest and most fitting way. It shows both his justice and his love most fully. Both sides agree on what matters most. God did in fact require atonement, and Christ's death really did satisfy his justice.

One more thing follows. We would never have known that God forgives at all apart from Christ. When Adam sinned, he did not run to God expecting mercy. He hid. Creation shows God's power, but the gospel shows his pardoning mercy. And it is not enough for that mercy simply to be announced to us. Christ also sends his Holy Spirit to bring us from spiritual death to life, so that we believe and receive what he won. From start to finish, salvation is the work of the one God: the Father who gives, the Son who offers himself, and the Spirit who brings us home.

topics.title: Did Christ die in our place as a substitute and public person?
topics.cmp: John Owen supplies nearly all the answers here and argues without qualification that Christ died in our stead, bearing the punishment due to our sins by the Father's appointment, and that denying this overturns the gospel. He grounds this in close philology (dying 'for' others in common usage, the Hebrew tachat and sabal, the Greek antí and antílytron, kopher in Numbers 35), classical examples of devoted persons such as the Decii, scriptural texts like Isaiah 53 and Caiaphas's counsel, and a covenant between Father and Son that makes Christ a public person and surety for the elect. Owen also stresses that this penal death glorifies God's vindictive justice and his truth in his threatenings while showing pure grace to the sinner. Augustine and Ambrose speak in noticeably different terms: Augustine denies that Christ's death was a punishment, since he died willingly and through righteousness rather than sin, and calls it a sacrifice for sin rather than a penalty. Ambrose says the Father gave the Son 'not to punishment but to grace', and both Fathers emphasize the Son's willing self-offering and the unity of Father and Son in the giving, where Owen's emphasis falls on penal substitution and satisfaction of justice.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The meaning and importance, we say, of these expressions is, that Christ died in our room, place, or stead, undergoing the death or punishment which we should have undergone

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Death of Christ Voluntary. How the Mediator of Life…
refs.quote: the spirit of the Mediator showed how it was through no punishment of sin that He came to the death of the flesh, because He did not leave it against His will, but because He willed, when He willed, as He willed.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: Now he says that the things which save are the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Spirit of our God.

ans.text:
Yes. When the Bible says that Christ died "for us," it means more than that he died for our good. It means he died in our place, taking on himself the judgment our sins deserved, and that he did this as our representative, the one who stood for us before God.

Think about how we use the word "for" in ordinary life. A soldier who throws himself on a grenade dies for his friends. He does not just help them; he takes what would have fallen on them, and they live. The Bible uses the word the same way. When the high priest Caiaphas said in John 11:50 that "it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish," he meant one man dying instead of many. He did not know it, but John tells us he was speaking a deeper truth than he understood. Jesus himself says in Mark 10:45 that he came "to give His life as a ransom for many." A ransom is a price paid in place of someone. The word translated "for" there is a word that means "in place of."

The Old Testament said this long before. Isaiah 53 describes the coming Servant this way: "He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him." And again: "the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all." In the Old Testament, to "bear" someone's sin means to carry its penalty. That is why Peter can say in 1 Peter 2:24 that Christ "Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree." Paul says the same thing in Galatians 3:13: Christ "redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." And in 2 Corinthians 5:21 he writes, "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." Jesus had no sin of his own. Our sin was counted to him, and his righteousness is counted to those who trust him.

This is also what it means to call Christ a "public person" or representative. Some people act only for themselves. Others act for a whole group, the way an ambassador signs a treaty for a nation. Paul explains in Romans 5 that Adam was a representative of this kind. When he fell, the human race fell with him. Christ is the second head of the race. He came to act for his people: "just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19). Hebrews 7:22 calls Jesus "the guarantee of a better covenant." Older translations say "surety." A surety is someone who signs for another person's debt and promises to pay it if they cannot. Christ stepped in to pay what we owed. He also stands as the guarantee that everything God promised in that covenant will be given to us.

Why was this needed? Couldn't God just forgive? God is love, but he is also just. A judge who simply waved away real wrongs would not be a good judge. At the cross, God does not pretend sin does not matter. He deals with it fully, and he does it by bearing the cost himself in the person of his Son. That is how Paul can say God is shown to be "just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). Toward us, salvation is pure grace; we pay nothing. Toward sin, God is perfectly just; nothing is swept under the rug. Nowhere does God's hatred of sin show more clearly than at the cross. There his beloved Son prayed in anguish, suffered and died, because our sins were laid on him. And nowhere does his love show more clearly either.

A careful point is worth making. Christ's death was not a punishment for any sin of his own, the way death came to us because of Adam's sin and our own. He was sinless. He walked into death freely, for others. Jesus says in John 10:18, "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord." So his death was a sacrifice offered for sin, not a sentence passed on a sinner. He bore the penalty that belonged to us, not one that belonged to him.

This leads to a question many people sincerely ask. Did the Father wrong the Son by handing him over to die? Isn't it unjust to punish an innocent person for the guilty? The Bible's answer is no, for several reasons. First, the Son was not an unwilling victim. Romans 8:32 says the Father "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all." Galatians 2:20 says the Son "loved me and gave Himself up for me." It is one act, seen from two sides. The Father gave the Son, and the Son gave himself. Hebrews 9:14 adds that Christ offered himself "through the eternal Spirit." Father, Son and Holy Spirit share one will and one love, and all three worked together in our rescue. This was not one person of the Trinity doing something to another against his wishes. The one God was freely bearing our sin in the person of the Son.

Second, a substitute is not unjust when he volunteers and has the right to do it. Christ has that right because he is both fully God and fully human. As a man, he could truly stand in for human beings. As God, his life is of infinite worth and could cover the debt of many. Third, the outcome was not loss for the Son but glory. He rose from the dead, he was exalted, and he received a people as his own. Hebrews 12:2 says he endured the cross "for the joy set before Him." The Father's giving of the Son is the greatest proof of the Father's love, not a contradiction of it.

It is fair to note that Christians have described the cross in many ways. It is a victory over the devil, a ransom, a sacrifice, an example of love, and a reconciliation. All of these are biblical. Some sincere believers are uneasy with the language of punishment. They prefer to stress Christ's victory or his self-giving love, and they worry that talk of punishment makes God seem harsh. Others answer that the other pictures depend on this one. Christ defeats the powers of evil precisely by removing our guilt, which was what gave those powers their hold on us. Scripture's own words, like "punishment," "curse" and "bore our sins," do point to substitution. Believers have also differed on a related question. Some hold that Christ died with the specific intention of saving those the Father gave him, "his sheep" in John 10. They point to the personal way Scripture speaks of his laying down his life for them. Others stress verses that say he gave himself "for all." They hold that his death is sufficient for and offered to everyone. Both sides agree that Christ truly stood in the place of sinners and that whoever trusts him is fully forgiven.

So the heart of the gospel is this. You owed a debt you could never pay. Christ, out of love and in perfect agreement with the Father and the Spirit, stepped into your place and paid it. When you trust him, his death counts as yours and his righteousness counts as yours. That is why the cross is such good news.

topics.title: Was Christ's death a true sacrifice and ransom?
topics.cmp: John Owen supplies most of the answers. Grounding his case in Scripture texts, the Levitical types and the common meaning of 'dying for another', he argues that Christ was properly a priest whose death was a real propitiatory sacrifice: a penal substitution and ransom that bore the curse on the cross, satisfied the law and reconciled God, though a positive righteousness must also be reckoned to sinners. Augustine and Ambrose agree with Owen that Christ offered for others and not for any sin of his own. Augustine grounds this in Christ's being alone perfectly righteous and holy, while Ambrose, reading the coal of Isaiah 6 as a figure of the passion, says that in Christ's flesh the whole human race is loosed from sin. On how Christ is both priest and victim, Augustine stresses that he stays one with the God to whom he offers and makes those he offers for one in himself, whereas Owen distinguishes the whole divine-human person as offerer from the human nature as what is offered. On the ransom they differ in framing: Augustine says Christ's blood was given 'as it were' as a price, but the devil was bound rather than enriched by accepting it, while Owen insists the price was paid to God as judge and lawgiver, who holds sinners captive under the law's sentence.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Christ the Most Perfect Victim for Cleansing Our Faults.…
refs.quote: might remain one with Him to whom He offered, might make those one in Himself for whom He offered, Himself might be in one both the offerer and the offering.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: And it is nowhere intimated, much less expressed, that these things are not spoken properly, but metaphorically only.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: all men should be cleansed by the passion of Christ, Who as a coal according to the flesh burnt up our sins

ans.text:
Yes. When Jesus died on the cross he was not only a good man dying bravely or an example of love. He was offering a real sacrifice for sin, and he was paying a real ransom to set captives free.

Start with the word "ransom." Jesus used it himself. He said that he came "to give His life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). A ransom is the price paid to release someone held captive. Peter tells believers that they were redeemed "not with perishable things such as silver or gold" but "with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Peter 1:18-19). Paul says simply, "you were bought at a price" (1 Corinthians 6:20). Scripture does not treat this language as a loose figure of speech. Something was truly owed, and something was truly paid.

That raises a natural question: paid to whom? Some early Christians spoke as if the price went to the devil, as though Satan held us hostage and God bought us back from him. Most Christians have seen that this cannot be quite right. The devil has no rightful claim on anyone. He is a rebel and a thief, not a lawful owner. What holds us captive is our guilt before God. Our sins are offences against him, and his holy law rightly condemns us. So the debt is owed to God's justice, and Christ's life is given to God. Paul says Christ "redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). The devil does lose his grip on us through the cross. Hebrews 2:14 says Christ died to break the power of the one who held the power of death. But Satan is defeated by the cross, not paid off.

We should also guard against a picture in which a loving Son pays off a reluctant, angry Father. That gets the story backwards. The Father is the one who "so loved the world that He gave His only Son" (John 3:16). Romans 5:8 says that God proves his love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. The Father sends, the Son freely offers himself, and Hebrews 9:14 says he did it "through the eternal Spirit." The whole Trinity is at work in our rescue. God himself provides the payment that his own justice requires.

Now the word "sacrifice." For centuries Israel brought animals to the altar. On the Day of Atonement, described in Leviticus 16, the high priest took two goats. One was killed as a sin offering. Over the other he confessed the people's sins, laying them on its head, and then it was sent away into the wilderness, carrying their guilt far off. The two goats together give one picture. Sin is placed on a substitute, the penalty falls on the substitute, and the guilt is removed. No single animal could show it all, which is why two were needed. At Passover a lamb died so that the firstborn of the house would live.

These were real sacrifices, but they could never take away sin for good (Hebrews 10:4). They were signposts pointing to the one sacrifice that could. That is why John the Baptist, seeing Jesus, cried, "Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29). It would be strange if real sacrifices were shadows of something that was only a sacrifice in a poetic sense. The shadows were real because the thing casting them is even more real. And if Christ's sacrifice were only a metaphor, our forgiveness would be only a metaphor too.

At the heart of every sin offering was the idea of substitution, one dying in the place of another. Isaiah foresaw this of the coming Servant: "the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). Paul writes, "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Peter says, "He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree" (1 Peter 2:24). This happened at the cross, in his suffering and death. "Bearing sin" in the Bible means bearing the penalty for sin. Jesus stood where we should have stood and took what we deserved, so that we could go free.

What is unusual about this sacrifice is that Jesus is both the priest who offers and the offering itself. In the old system the priest and the animal were different. Here they are one. Hebrews 9:14 says Christ "offered Himself unblemished to God." He is the one doing the offering, as the whole person, God and man. What he offers is himself, his own human life, body and soul. That is why Scripture can even speak of the church being bought with God's own blood (Acts 20:28). The one who died was not a mere man. He is the eternal Son, who took on our flesh so that he had a life to give.

He is also the only fitting priest. The high priests of Israel had to offer sacrifices for their own sins first, and only then for the people's. Jesus had no sin of his own to cover (Hebrews 7:26-27). Everything he suffered, he suffered for others. A spotless priest offering a spotless sacrifice: nothing less could make full atonement. And because he remains one with the Father, he can bring us to God without ever being cut off from God himself.

The result is reconciliation. Our sin had made us enemies of God and placed us under his just anger. Through Christ's death that barrier is taken away. Romans 3:25-26 says God put Christ forward as an atoning sacrifice. In doing so God showed that he is righteous even as he forgives. He does not overlook sin. He deals with it fully in his Son. Christ's death also does not stand alone. His perfectly obedient life gives us a righteousness we never had, so we are not only pardoned but welcomed as children.

Finally, a question that troubles some believers. When we bring our sins to Christ day after day and lay them on him by faith, are we making him suffer again? No. Hebrews is emphatic that he offered "one sacrifice for sins" for all time and then sat down at God's right hand (Hebrews 10:12). The work is finished. His suffering is over. Faith does not repeat the cross. It reaches back to it and takes hold of it. The believers of the Old Testament looked forward in faith to a sacrifice not yet made. We look back to one already complete. Each time we confess our sins and trust him, we are simply resting on what he did once and for all.

Like the person in Israel who fled to a city of refuge to be safe from the avenger (an image Hebrews 6:18 draws on), we run to Christ. And we find that the price has already been paid in full.

topics.title: How does Christ, the one Mediator, reconcile believers to God and intercede for them?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Christ mediates because he is one person who is truly God and truly man. Irenaeus, Bickersteth (with the image of Jacob's ladder), Augustine, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius and Owen each tie reconciliation to his sharing both natures. They differ in how they ground this. Irenaeus argues from the requirements of the work: a man must justly defeat the enemy, God must securely give salvation, and Christ's flesh must be of our very substance for the hostile flesh to be reconciled. Augustine stresses congruity and humility: Christ's likeness to us removes our unlikeness of unrighteousness and heals pride. He also reads Galatians 3:19 and John 17:23 of Christ, and holds that Christ's intercession as Priest will cease at the face-to-face vision. Gregory of Nyssa argues against Eunomius that Christ is mediator between God and humanity, not of doctrines or the Law, and not between divided Persons, since the Godhead is one. He develops a 'first-fruits' account in which the whole lump of humanity is united to God, which Athanasius parallels by locating the security of grace in the incarnate Word rather than in a mere man like Adam. Owen, by contrast, is more concerned with the believer's assurance and experience: only an infinite God supplies sufficient grace, the debt Christ paid is discharged and not transferred to the Son, his habitual righteousness made him a fit sacrifice, and practical counsel is given on seeking Christ's withdrawn presence. Irenaeus alone dwells on the indwelling Spirit as necessary to make flesh 'spiritual' without casting it off, and Hilary alone on human nature being transformed, not abolished, in its subjection to Christ.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: Take heed of them who would rob you of the Deity of Christ. If there were no more grace for me than what can be treasured up in a mere man, I should rejoice [if] my portion might be under rocks and mountains.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: God is one, not divided among the Persons in Whom we have been taught to believe (for the Godhead in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost is one)

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For unless man had overcome the enemy of man, the enemy would not have been legitimately vanquished. And again: unless it had been God who had freely given salvation, we could never have possessed it securely.

ans.text:
Christ brings us back to God by standing in the middle, fully God and fully human in one person. He laid down his life to remove what separated us from God, and he now lives in God's presence to speak for us, help us, and keep us. Paul puts it simply in 1 Timothy 2:5: "For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

A mediator is a go-between, someone who brings two estranged parties together. To do that well, he must belong fully to both sides. That is why it matters that Jesus is both God and man. Picture Jacob's ladder in Genesis 28, its foot resting on earth and its top reaching heaven. Christ is like that ladder. By the human nature he took on, he is truly one of us. By his eternal divine nature, he is truly one with the Father. He does not stand halfway between, as some lesser being. He reaches all the way to both.

Each side of his person does something we need. As a man, he could stand in our place, obey where we disobeyed, and suffer and die for us. It was a human being who had sinned, so it was fitting that a human being should face sin and death and win. As God, he gives what no mere creature could give. His sacrifice has infinite worth. His forgiveness is God's own forgiveness. His grace is a supply that never runs out. A good man, however holy, could at best pay for himself. Only one who is also God could carry the sins of a multitude and make our salvation secure. Adam received good gifts and lost them. What Christ has won for us is held in his own person, and he does not lose it.

How does he reconcile us? Our problem was not only that we were weak but that we were guilty. Sin had made us enemies of a holy God, and the law rightly condemned us. Christ took that condemnation on himself at the cross. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 5:19 that "God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men's trespasses against them," and two verses later that God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. Romans 5:10 says we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son.

One misunderstanding is worth clearing up here. Some picture a kind Son persuading an angry, unwilling Father. That is not the Bible's picture. The Father so loved the world that he sent the Son (John 3:16). The plan of reconciliation began in the Father's love, and the Son came gladly to carry it out. Nor should we think the debt was simply moved, so that we now owe the Son what we once owed the Father. When someone pays a debt in another's place and the payment is accepted, the debtor is set free. What we owe Christ now is not a debt of guilt. It is the glad response of thanks, love, and obedience.

Because of what he has done, Christ is the one way to the Father. Jesus says in John 14:6, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me." The open fellowship humanity had with God at creation was shut by sin. Hebrews 12:29 calls our God "a consuming fire," and without a mediator, coming near a holy God would only mean judgment. But Hebrews 10:19-22 says we may enter the Most Holy Place with confidence by the blood of Jesus, by a "new and living way" opened through his flesh. Ephesians 2:18 shows the whole Trinity in this: "For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit."

This is where real boldness in prayer comes from. It does not come from our track record, our feelings, or how well we pray. It comes from the blood of Christ, which has taken away the guilt that made us afraid. Israel stood far off at Sinai, trembling. Believers are invited to draw near, because in Christ the Judge has become our reconciled Father. Our prayers and our service are acceptable to God not because they are flawless, but because they are offered through him.

Christ's work did not end at the cross. He rose, ascended, and now intercedes for us. Hebrews 7:25 says, "Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them." Romans 8:34 says he is at God's right hand interceding for us. 1 John 2:1 adds, "But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One." This does not mean he is pleading with a reluctant God, or offering his sacrifice again. His sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 9:24-28). His very presence before the Father, as the one who died and lives, is a constant claim on our behalf. And he actively asks for what we need, as he did for Peter when he prayed that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

His intercession is full of sympathy. Hebrews 4:15 says, "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin." He knows from the inside what it is to be hungry, tired, grieved, and tempted. So the next verse invites us: "Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need." Hebrews 2:18 says that because he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.

That help comes in many forms. Sometimes he takes a temptation away. Sometimes he lets it remain but gives fresh strength, as he told Paul, "My grace is sufficient for you" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Sometimes he strengthens a person over years against a particular sin, and sometimes he pulls someone back at the very edge. He teaches us to grow wiser through our trials. And when we do fall, he does not abandon us. He restores us with mercy and pardon, so that we are not swallowed up.

Christ's mediation also makes us holy, not only forgiven. What he won for us he gives through the Holy Spirit, whom he pours out on his people (Acts 2:33). Paul says in Romans 8:9 that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. The Spirit joins us to Christ, gives us new life, and will one day raise our bodies too (Romans 8:11). Being "spiritual" in the Bible's sense does not mean escaping our bodies. It means people of flesh and blood receiving God's own Spirit. Jesus prays in John 17:23, "I in them, and You in Me, that they may be perfectly united." Christ is in us, and the Father is in Christ. So we are brought into fellowship with God through the Son who shares our nature. This is a real union, though never the same as the Son's eternal oneness with the Father.

There are seasons when believers do not feel Christ near. Scripture does not tell us to despair then, but to keep seeking him. That means honestly asking whether some sin has grieved him, returning to his promises, and using the means he gives, especially his Word, prayer, and the worship of his people. In all of these, what we are really looking for is Christ himself. His intercession does not stop when our feelings fade.

Christians have asked whether Christ's work as Mediator and intercessor will continue forever. Some point to Jesus' words in John 16:26-27, where he says he will not need to ask the Father for them because the Father himself loves them. They also point to 1 Corinthians 15:24-28, where the Son hands over the kingdom to the Father. From these they suggest that when we see God face to face, his work of pleading for us will be complete. Others stress that he "always lives to intercede" (Hebrews 7:25) and is a priest forever (Psalm 110:4). They hold that he will remain forever the one through whom redeemed humanity knows and enjoys God. Both sides agree on the main point. We will never stand before God except as people joined to Christ, and he will never stop being both God and man.

So the heart of the matter is simple and deeply comforting. You do not come to God on your own merits, and you do not come alone. You come through Jesus, who died for you, who knows your weakness, and who lives right now in the Father's presence for you.

topics.title: How did Christ conquer the devil?
topics.cmp: Augustine and Irenaeus agree on the core claim: the devil was overcome justly, not by sheer force. Augustine says Christ conquered by righteousness, since the sinless one was unjustly slain and those held as debtors are therefore justly released. Irenaeus says the Word reclaimed humanity by persuasion rather than violence, so that justice was not infringed. They also agree that the victory had to come through man, but they ground this differently. Irenaeus reasons from recapitulation: the Son of man kept the commandment Adam broke and bound Satan with the same chains, though only the Son of God, greater than vanquished man, could do this. Augustine stresses that the victor must come from the captive race, that Christ won in humility as God and man where proud Adam fell, and that the devil was defeated at the very moment of Christ's death, with the resurrection a later victory of power. Their emphases also diverge. Augustine builds an elaborate contrast between the devil as mediator of death, who brings humanity's double death, and Christ as Mediator of life, and draws a moral lesson that believers should likewise conquer by righteousness. Irenaeus instead emphasizes the limits of the devil's power (he only deceives, has no genuine authority, is 'strong' only relative to us) and God's invincibility, which would be defeated if man were not restored. The other authors address related but distinct points: Owen treats Christ's vengeance on his people's enemies as part of his loveliness, Hilary distinguishes abolishing hostile powers from subjecting enemies, and Ambrose reads the brazen serpent as Christ bearing the likeness, not the reality, of sin.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Man Was to Be Rescued from the Power of the Devil, Not…
refs.quote: it pleased God, that in order to the rescuing of man from the grasp of the devil, the devil should be conquered, not by power, but by righteousness; and that so also men, imitating Christ, should seek to conquer the devil by righteousness, not by power.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: it was necessary that through man himself he should, when conquered, be bound with the same chains with which he had bound man, in order that man, being set free, might return to his Lord

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: In that he doth and will, in the winding up of the matter, so sorely revenge the quarrel of their sufferings upon their enemies. He avenges his elect that cry unto him; yea, he doth it speedily.

ans.text:
Christ defeated the devil not by simply overpowering him, though he easily could have, but by living a perfectly obedient human life and dying an innocent death on the cross. Then he rose from the dead, so that the devil's chief weapons, sin and death, were taken from him for good. The Bible sums up the purpose of Jesus' coming this way: "This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8).

To see how this works, start with how the devil got his grip on us. He never had real authority of his own. He is a created being, a fallen angel, and his only tool was deception. In the garden he lied to Adam and Eve and drew them into disobeying God. Once humanity sinned, it came under the sentence of death and under the devil's influence, like prisoners whose own guilt keeps them locked in. Hebrews 2:14-15 describes the devil as the one "who holds the power of death," and speaks of people held "in slavery by their fear of death." His hold on us was real, but it rested entirely on our sin.

That is why God chose to win by righteousness rather than by sheer force. The devil is the great lover of power and the great enemy of what is right. God could have crushed him in an instant. Instead, God beat him on the very ground he had corrupted: obedience, truth and justice. This shows God's character. It also teaches us that the way to resist the devil is not to grab for power ourselves but to walk in Christ's righteousness.

The victory also had to come through a man. A human being had been defeated, so it was fitting that a human being should win the rematch. Where Adam disobeyed, Jesus obeyed. When the devil tempted him in the wilderness, Jesus answered with God's word and did not give in. Paul draws the contrast in Romans 5:19: through one man's disobedience many were made sinners, and through one man's obedience many will be made righteous. Jesus is the "second Adam" who kept what the first Adam broke.

Yet a mere man could not have done it. The devil had already defeated humanity, so the rescuer had to be greater than humanity. Adam fell because he grasped at being like God. Jesus is truly God, and he won by humbling himself. The eternal Son took on our human nature and fought in it from within. So the victory is fully human, won by one of us, and fully divine, so that all the credit goes to God.

When was the victory won? The resurrection makes it easiest to see, but the decisive blow fell at the cross, at the very moment the devil thought he had won. Jesus had no sin, so death had no rightful claim on him. Before his arrest Jesus said, in effect, that the ruler of this world was coming but had nothing in him to lay hold of (John 14:30). The devil drove an innocent man to his death. In doing so he overreached and lost his grip on everyone who trusts in that innocent one. Christ's blood, which he did not owe, was poured out to cancel the debt of sinners who did owe. Colossians 2:15 says that Christ "disarmed the powers and authorities" and made "a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross." Then the resurrection showed openly that death could not hold him.

Here a misunderstanding sometimes creeps in. The Bible calls Christ's death a "ransom," and some Christians in the past pictured this as a payment handed over to the devil. Most Christians have rejected that picture. God never owed Satan anything. The debt was ours, owed to God's justice, and Christ paid it. The devil loses his captives because the charge he held over them has been settled. When sins are forgiven, the accuser has nothing left to accuse.

Scripture gives this victory a vivid image. Right after the fall, God promised that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head, while the serpent would strike his heel (Genesis 3:15). At the cross the serpent struck, and Christ was wounded unto death. But that blow crushed the serpent's head. Later, in the wilderness, Israelites bitten by snakes were healed by looking at a bronze snake that Moses lifted on a pole. Jesus applied this to himself: just as Moses lifted up the snake, "so the Son of Man must be lifted up" (John 3:14). Notice that the bronze snake was only a likeness of a snake. In the same way, Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh. He had a real body but no real sin, and under the appearance of weakness he undid the true serpent's cunning.

Another helpful way to see it is as two opposite go-betweens. The devil acted as a go-between of death. Through pride he led humanity by pride into death, both the death of the soul cut off from God and the death of the body. Christ is the Mediator of life. Through humility he leads us back by obedience into life. The devil could drag us down into his death, but he could never raise anyone up. Christ, the living one, raised his own body from the grave and gives that life to all who believe in him.

None of this makes the devil a rival equal to God. Jesus called him a "strong man" whose house must be broken into. But he is strong only compared with us. Jesus is the stronger one who ties him up and carries off his plunder (Matthew 12:29). There is no contest between creature and Creator.

Finally, the victory won at the cross is now being worked out and will one day be complete. The risen Christ reigns as King, and "He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet" (1 Corinthians 15:25). Believers still face temptation and attack. But they fight a defeated foe, standing on the blood of the Lamb and holding to the truth. Christ's judgment on the devil is not at odds with his tenderness toward his people. It is part of his love, because he defends and vindicates those who belong to him. Paul gives the church this promise: "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet" (Romans 16:20).

topics.title: How does the incarnate Mediator cleanse us and heal our double death?
topics.cmp: Augustine supplies nearly all the answers: the one cleansing is the blood of the Righteous One and God's humbling, and Christ's single, undue death and resurrection in the flesh answers to our double death of soul and body. It works as a mystery for the inner man and a type for the outer, and Augustine even grounds the single-to-double ratio in the perfect number six. Gregory of Nyssa agrees that Christ's death and resurrection heal human nature, but his account differs in emphasis. Rather than a sacrifice that cancels debts or Augustine's inner/outer scheme, he stresses that Christ is the first-fruits and example of resurrection, through whose union with God the mortal puts on immortality, citing Paul and Peter. On false routes to God, Augustine rejects seeking him through cosmic powers, angelic wonders or demonic rites, which he ties to pride, and Irenaeus similarly holds from Scripture (Moses and Jacob as the Lord's portion) that believers are under the Lord himself, not under angels. Daniel Waterland takes up the theme of pride from a different angle, arguing against Emlyn from the history of pagan, Jewish and heretical objections that the pride of reason shows itself as an aversion to mysteries like the Incarnation and Trinity, not as a love of them.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How We are Rendered Apt for the Perception of Truth…
refs.quote: the one cleansing of the unrighteous and of the proud is the blood of the Righteous One, and the humbling of God Himself;[^448] that we might be cleansed through Him, made as He was what we are by nature, and what we are not by sin

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
