refs.quote: but that people which believes in God is not now under the power of angels, but under the Lord’s [rule]. “For His people Jacob was made the portion of the Lord, Israel the cord of His inheritance.”

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: the very mystery of the Trinity, which is the “ rock of offence” to some even at this time, gave very early offence to the Pagan wits; and was much disrelished by them::+so averse were they to the receiving of mysteries

ans.text:
Jesus heals our two kinds of death with one death of His own, and He is the only one who can make us clean enough to stand before God.

Start with what the Bible means by our "double death." One kind is the death of the body. We grow old, get sick and die, and that decay came into the world through sin. The other kind is deeper and comes first: the death of the soul. Paul tells believers, "you were dead in your trespasses and sins" (Ephesians 2:1). He does not mean their hearts had stopped. He means they were cut off from God, who is the life of the soul, in the way a branch broken from the vine is dead even while its leaves are still green. So we need two cures. Our souls need to be brought back to life now, and our bodies need to be raised one day.

Jesus, by contrast, died only one death. He never sinned, so His soul was never separated from God. He was never dead in that inner way. What He took on was our mortal flesh, and on the cross He died a real bodily death. On the third day He rose bodily. Yet that one death and that one resurrection reach both of our deaths.

For the inner person, Christ's death and rising work as a pattern that becomes real in us. When we turn to Him in repentance and faith, we die to sin and are raised to new life. "We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). This first resurrection happens now. It is the soul coming back to life.

For the outer person, Christ's rising is the promise and preview of what will happen to our bodies. Paul calls Him the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). The firstfruits are the first sheaf of the harvest, a sign that the rest is coming. Jesus puts both resurrections side by side in John 5. First He says that "the hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live" (John 5:25). That is the soul being raised now. Then He speaks of a coming hour when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out (John 5:28-29). That is the body being raised later. So one death of Christ answers our two deaths, and one resurrection of Christ brings about two resurrections for us.

Why can His single death do so much? Because it was not owed. Our death is a penalty we have earned. His was not. Jesus says of His life, "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord" (John 10:18). He gave it freely, out of love. Picture a man with no debts who willingly pays the debts of a whole crowd. Because Christ died a death He did not deserve, He could cancel the debt of those who deserved to die. "Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God" (1 Peter 3:18). His death was the one true sacrifice. It removes the guilt that gave sin, death and the devil their hold over us (Hebrews 2:14-15). Christians still die in the body. But for those in Christ, death can no longer do them final harm. It has become a doorway rather than a prison.

This brings us to cleansing. Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). Sinful and proud people cannot make themselves pure. The cure for our pride is God's own humility. The eternal Son became what we are by nature, a human being. He did not become what we are by sin. He shared our flesh so that we might share His life and one day see God. "The blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7).

That is why Christ alone is the way. People have always looked for other go-betweens: angels, spirits, rituals, charms, secret knowledge, or impressive spiritual experiences. Scripture is clear that "there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). Angels are God's servants, not our saviors, and Paul warns against the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18). Occult practices and dealings with evil spirits do not lift the soul toward God. They feed pride and fear, and they leave a person more weighed down even while promising to raise them up. The devil is a false go-between. He offers a shortcut to power and leads to death. Christ is the true Mediator. He leads to life by the humble road of the cross.

There is also a gentle warning here for ordinary believers. We do not draw near to God by chasing the spectacular or by searching outwardly for some special power. What keeps us far from God is not distance in space but the pride and wrong loves of our hearts. We draw near by trusting the Son who came near to us. We receive His cleansing in repentance and faith, and we wait in hope for the day when the One who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to our mortal bodies through His Spirit (Romans 8:11).

topics.title: Does Christ's saving work include his active obedience to the law?
topics.cmp: Nearly every answer here comes from John Owen. He consistently holds that Christ's saving work includes his active obedience to the law, performed for believers rather than for himself and imputed to them as a positive righteousness beyond the pardon won by his death. His grounds are chiefly Scripture (Romans 5:19, Galatians 4:4-5, Romans 8:3-4, Matthew 5:17, Philippians 3) and conceptual distinctions: doing versus suffering, the voluntary subjection of the God-man to the law, and a special 'law of the mediator.' He also argues by analogy from Adam, who even without wrath still had to obey to gain life. One Owen answer on imputation is headed 'No,' but its content rejects a rival view that puts faith and new obedience in place of Christ's righteousness and affirms imputation, so it agrees with his other answers; elsewhere he insists that believers' holiness remains necessary as the way to life, though never the cause, matter or condition of justification. Augustine appears only on whether one can be righteous by one's own law-keeping apart from Christ, and he agrees with Owen's 'No,' but on different grounds: where Owen argues from the law's weakness and the impossibility of perfect conformity, Augustine focuses on the pride of such self-reliance and its defeat by the cross, using a figurative reading of Moses' outstretched hands against Amalek.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The fault was an active transgression of the law, and the obedience opposed to it must be an active accomplishment of it.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: They are Proud Who Think They are Able, by Their Own…
refs.quote: There are, however, some who think themselves capable of being cleansed by their own righteousness, so as to contemplate God, and to dwell in God; whom their very pride itself stains above all others.

ans.text:
Yes. Christ saves us by the whole of his obedience, not only by his death. The perfect life he lived under God's law was lived for us, and it belongs with his sufferings in winning eternal life for everyone who trusts in him.

It helps to think about what a sinner needs before God. We need two things. First, our guilt must be taken away, because the wages of sin is death. Second, we need a positive righteousness, a record of doing what God requires. Picture a person deep in debt. Cancelling the debt brings his account back to zero, which is a great mercy. But zero is not the same as wealth. Forgiveness clears the record. Righteousness fills it.

The Bible's way of putting this is the line "Do this and you will live" (Luke 10:28). Life with God was always promised to those who keep his law. Adam was not under God's anger before he fell, yet he was still called to obey. Being forgiven brings us back to peace with God. But who has kept the law? None of us. That is why Jesus came not only to die but also to obey. He said in Matthew 5:17 that he came not to abolish the Law but "to fulfill" it. At his baptism he said it was fitting "to fulfill all righteousness" (Matthew 3:15). He loved God with all his heart and his neighbor as himself, every day, in every thought and deed.

Did he do this for himself? Paul says God sent his Son, "born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:4-5). The Son of God did not need to be placed under the law for his own sake. He took that place for us, just as he took our human nature for us. So his obedience was done on our behalf, as our substitute, in the same way his death was.

Someone might ask whether his perfect life was simply what made him a spotless sacrifice. His sinlessness did make him a fit offering. But he was holy from the moment he was conceived. Had he died as an infant, he would still have been without sin, and his person would have been of infinite worth. The long years of faithful obedience, then, were not just preparation. They were part of the gift.

Romans 5:19 sets the two men side by side: "For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous." Adam's sin was a deed, a breaking of God's command. The remedy is a matching deed, a keeping of God's command. Christ's life and death are really one great obedience. He "became obedient to death—even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:8). His obedience runs through his whole life and reaches its peak at the cross. Nearly everything he did involved suffering, and his suffering was itself willing obedience. Hebrews 5:8 says that, "although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered." Still, we can tell the doing apart from the bearing. He bore the curse we deserved, and he did the righteousness we owed.

This is what the Bible means when it says righteousness is "credited" or "reckoned" to believers. Theologians use the word "imputed." It simply means counted to our account. "God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Our sin was counted to him. His righteousness is counted to us. Paul longed to "be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith" (Philippians 3:9).

Sincere Christians who agree that we are saved by grace through faith in Christ have still differed on this point. Some hold that what is counted to us is above all the forgiveness won at the cross. In their view, to be justified is to be pardoned and treated as righteous, and Christ's sinless life was needed mainly so that his sacrifice would be perfect. Others, as presented here, hold that his lifelong obedience is also credited to believers. Their reason is that Scripture speaks of a righteousness given to us, not just a debt removed, and that Christ was placed under the law for our sake. Both sides want to honor Christ alone as our Savior.

This teaching also shuts the door on every attempt to earn God's favor ourselves. The law is good and holy, but it speaks only condemnation to sinners. It can show us the standard. It cannot lift us up to it. Many in Israel pursued righteousness earnestly, yet they did not reach it, because they sought it by their own works instead of submitting to the righteousness God provides (Romans 9:31-10:3). Trusting our own goodness is not only hopeless. It is also a form of pride, and the cross humbles that pride.

Does this mean our own obedience no longer matters? Not at all. It means our obedience has a different job. Christ's righteousness is the ground on which we are accepted. Our holiness is the path we walk once we are accepted. "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith... not by works, so that no one can boast. For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works" (Ephesians 2:8-10).

Think of it this way. Christ's death frees us from death as a punishment, yet we still die. In the same way, his obedience frees us from obeying in order to earn life, yet we still obey. We obey as children who already belong to the family, not as hired workers trying to earn a place in it.

Holiness is still necessary. God is holy, and those he welcomes into his friendship are made holy. The new life he gives must grow. Holiness is the road God has appointed toward glory: "Pursue peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord" (Hebrews 12:14). It is also evidence that we really are his children, and it is how we say thank you. But it never takes Christ's place. Mixing the two would either rob Christ of his glory or rob us of our peace.

So the believer can rest completely in Christ's perfect life and atoning death, and then gladly spend his own life following him.

topics.title: What did Christ's death and risen life secure for believers?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that salvation comes from God's prior, gracious love rather than human merit: Augustine says the Father loved us before the Son died, so the cross did not turn a wrathful Father into a loving one; Irenaeus calls redemption gracious, since God needs nothing from us; and Owen likewise says God's love consisted in giving his Son, so thanks are owed to the Father too. Owen gives by far the most detailed and technical account, using Scripture to argue that Christ died only for the elect as a public person and second Adam. He treats Christ's death as price, sacrifice and penalty yielding redemption, reconciliation and satisfaction, holds that acquittal follows only on covenant terms, distinguishes the reconciling death from the saving righteousness of Christ's life, and insists that no believer can finally be lost. Irenaeus differs in emphasis and arguably in conclusion: he warns that Christ will not die again and that those who sin after knowing him may obtain no further forgiveness and be shut out of the kingdom, and he joins Novatian in grounding human free will in the image of God, adding the evidence of Scripture's exhortations and Christ's lament over Jerusalem. Athanasius, Waterland and Ambrose tie the benefits of Christ's work to the dignity of his Person: Athanasius says adoption and deification are possible only through the true Son, Waterland says a mere creature could probably not have been entrusted with redemption, and Ambrose says Christ's being 'made sanctification' implies no change in his divine nature. Owen's two answers on whether God may still command faith and obedience begin with opposite words ('No' and 'Yes'), but both make the same point: satisfaction does not release the creature from duty to God.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: for adoption there could not be apart from the real Son, who says, ‘No one knoweth the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal Him.’

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: Christ in his suffering and oblation, had his intention only upon the good of his elect, and their acceptation with God

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: A Difficulty, How We are Justified in the Blood of the…
refs.quote: But I see that the Father loved us also before, not only before the Son died for us, but before He created the world

ans.text:
Christ's death and risen life secured everything a lost sinner needs to be brought home to God and kept there: forgiveness and peace with God, a place in God's family, a new and holy life, and the sure hope of glory. The Father planned it, the Son accomplished it, and the Holy Spirit brings it into our lives.

Start with what we were. The Bible says plainly that we were God's enemies. Our sin had cut us off from him, and his justice rightly stood against us. So the first gift of the cross is reconciliation, which means being made friends again. Paul writes in Romans 5:10, "For if, while we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!"

How can a holy God simply forgive? He does not overlook sin. Scripture describes Christ's death in several ways. It is a ransom, a price paid to set captives free. It is a sacrifice, which removes the barrier between us and God. It is also the penalty for sin, borne by Christ in our place. In 2 Corinthians 5:21 Paul says that God made the sinless Christ to be sin on our behalf, "so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." Christ stood as our representative, much as Adam once stood for the whole human race. Because he truly bore what our sin deserved, God's justice is not set aside when he pardons us. It is honoured. God can be both just and merciful at the same time.

A common misunderstanding needs clearing up here. Some picture a loving Son persuading an angry Father to change his mind. That is not the Bible's picture. The Father's love came first. He chose us in Christ before the world began (Ephesians 1:4), and he is the one who "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). The cross did not make God love us. It is the proof that he already did. So our thanks belong to the Father who gave, to the Son who gave himself, and to the Spirit who opens our eyes to see it.

Notice too that Romans 5:10 speaks of Christ's life as well as his death. Jesus lived the perfectly obedient life we never lived, and that righteousness is counted to everyone who trusts him. He also rose and now lives forever. Hebrews 7:25 says he always lives to intercede for those who come to God through him. His risen life is the ongoing source of our salvation, not just a happy ending to the story.

The next gift is adoption. We are not only pardoned like a criminal let off by a judge. We are welcomed as sons and daughters. Galatians 4:4-5 says God sent his Son to redeem us, so "that we might receive our adoption as sons." Romans 8:17 calls us "heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ." Christ is the rightful heir of all things, and we share in his inheritance. This even changes how we hold ordinary things like food, home and the good gifts of creation. We receive them now as children from a Father's hand, through Christ.

Then comes a changed life. The Bible calls this sanctification, which simply means being made holy. Christ did not die only to cancel sin's guilt. He died to break sin's grip. Romans 6 teaches that believers are joined to Christ in his death and resurrection. As he died for sin, sin is put to death in us. As he was raised so that death has no power over him, we are raised to a new life so that sin no longer rules us. This is a lifelong battle, but the outcome is not in doubt.

This raises a fair question. If we are not saved by good works, why do they matter? Because God saves us for them, not by them. Ephesians 2:10 says, "For we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life." Christ's payment for sin did not cancel our duty to love and obey God. We owe God obedience simply because he is our Creator. What changed is that we now obey as forgiven children rather than as people trying to earn their way. And because even our best efforts are mixed with faults, we never rest our peace on them. We rest it on Christ, and God gladly accepts our imperfect obedience for his sake.

Does this make us puppets? No. God made human beings in his image, with real wills, and he deals with us as people who choose. That is why the Bible urges, warns and invites. Jesus wept over Jerusalem because they were "not willing" to be gathered to him. Yet the Bible also teaches that sin has bent our wills, and that grace sets them free. Philippians 2:12-13 holds both together: "work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose." God does not force us. He renews us, so that we come to want what he wants.

Christ's death also secured a sure hope. Believers still die in the body, but not the deeper death of being cut off from God forever. Jesus says in John 10:28, "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand." At the same time, Scripture warns us seriously not to drift away, and reminds us that Christ will not die again for those who turn their backs on him. Sincere Christians have weighed these passages differently. Many believe that everyone truly born again will be kept to the end, pointing to promises like John 10:28 and Romans 8:30. Others believe a real believer can finally fall away, pointing to warnings like Hebrews 6 and 10. Both agree that the warnings are meant to keep us close to Christ and that our confidence rests on him, not on ourselves.

Christians have also differed on whom Christ intended to save by his death. Some stress that he laid down his life for his people and that his death will certainly bring every one of them home, citing verses like Ephesians 5:25, where Christ "loved the church and gave Himself up for her." Others stress that he died for the whole world, so that the offer of mercy is truly open to all, citing verses like 1 John 2:2. All agree that Christ's death is more than enough for any sinner, and that anyone who comes to him will be received.

Finally, the risen Christ is the head of his church. He gave his people the means by which he feeds and strengthens us, such as the preaching of his word, baptism and the Lord's Supper. These are his appointments, not human inventions, and we keep them because he is Lord. Through them the Spirit keeps applying to us what Christ won.

None of this was owed to us. We brought God nothing, and he needs nothing from us. It was planned before the world began and freely given in Christ. As 1 Peter 3:18 puts it, Christ suffered "the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." That is the heart of it. His death and risen life bring us to God, and keep us there, until faith gives way to sight.

topics.title: Is Christ the only way of salvation for those before and after his coming?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Irenaeus and Basil each answer a different question here, but all three treat Christ as the one necessary means of reaching God and salvation. Augustine is the most exclusive in his wording: no one is freed from the devil's dominion or forgiven except through Christ, and those left in the devil's abode face an endless miserable life better called death. Irenaeus widens the scope across time rather than limiting it. Christ came for all from the beginning who, according to their capacity, feared God, practised justice and desired to see Him; the same one God who guided the patriarchs justifies Jews and Gentiles by faith; and the patriarchs, who prefigured the Church, receive their reward within it. Basil differs in emphasis rather than conclusion: he reads Christ as 'the Way' in a higher, spiritual sense, an orderly ascent through works of righteousness and illumination of knowledge to the essentially good Father, and he stresses the soul's progress 'through the Son' rather than rescue from the devil or the fate of those before Christ.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: What Has Been Treated of in This Book. How We Have…
refs.quote: no one is freed from the dominion of the devil, through the forgiveness of sins, save by Him

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For it was not merely for those who believed on Him in the time of Tiberius Cæsar that Christ came, nor did the Father exercise His providence for the men only who are now alive, but for all men altogether

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what…
refs.quote: For our Lord is an essentially good Way, where erring and straying are unknown, to that which is essentially good, to the Father.

ans.text:
Yes. Christians have always confessed that Jesus Christ is the one and only Savior, and that this is true for everyone who has ever been saved, whether they lived before his coming or after it, and whether they were Jews or Gentiles.

The New Testament makes this clear. Jesus says in John 14:6, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me." Peter tells the leaders in Jerusalem in Acts 4:12, "Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved." And Paul writes in 1 Timothy 2:5, "For there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." A mediator is a go-between, someone who brings two estranged parties together. Scripture names only one.

Why only one? Because of what our problem is. Sin is not just a bad habit. It is guilt before a holy God, and it leaves us under the power of evil and death. Only someone who is fully God can pay a debt that large and break a power that strong. Only someone who is fully human can stand in our place and pay it for us. Jesus is both. He died for sins, rose bodily from the dead, and will never die again. No other person, practice or religion can do what he did, because no one else is who he is.

Notice too what "the way" means. Jesus is not only a teacher who points toward God, the way a signpost points down a road. He is himself the road. He brings us home to the Father, and he never leads anyone astray. That fits how God works throughout the Bible: we come to the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit.

That raises a natural question. What about Abraham, Moses, David and all the faithful people who lived centuries before Jesus was born? Were they saved some other way, perhaps by keeping the law or by offering animal sacrifices? The Bible says no. Hebrews 10:4 states that "it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins." Those sacrifices were real acts of obedience and worship, but they were pictures. They pointed ahead to the one sacrifice that would actually take sins away.

The faithful in the Old Testament were saved the same way we are: by God's grace, received through faith in his promise. Paul makes Abraham his main example. In Romans 4 he reminds us that "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." Abraham did not know the name Jesus. But he trusted the God who had promised that through his offspring all nations would be blessed. Galatians 3:8 says that God "foretold the gospel to Abraham" in that promise. Jesus himself says in John 8:56, "Your father Abraham rejoiced to see My day. He saw it and was glad." Hebrews 11 describes the faithful of old as people who saw the promises from far off and welcomed them.

Think of it like this. We look back to the cross, and they looked forward to it. The light is the same; only the angle differs. They saw dimly what we see clearly. Romans 3:25 even explains that God had patiently "passed over" the sins committed beforehand, because he was going to deal with them fully at the cross. So the death of Christ reaches backward in time as well as forward. Hebrews 13:8 says Jesus Christ is "the same yesterday and today and forever."

This is also why the God of the Old Testament and the God of the New are not two different gods, one stern and one kind. It is the one God who called Abraham, led Israel, spoke through the prophets, and now sent his Son. Paul argues in Romans 3:29–30 that because God is one, he is God of Gentiles as well as Jews, and he puts both right with himself in the same way, by faith. Even in Old Testament times there were outsiders, such as Rahab and Ruth, who turned to Israel's God and were welcomed. The faithful of Israel are not a separate group. They belong to the same family of faith as the church. Jesus speaks of many coming from east and west to sit at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11).

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, saying Christ is the only way does not mean God was careless about everyone before Jesus. God's care has always reached people in every generation, and Christ came for all of them, not just for the people alive in his own lifetime. Second, it does not mean Old Testament believers were saved by earning it. No one in any age has been saved by being good enough. All have been saved by grace, and that grace always comes through Christ.

There is one related question where sincere Christians have reached different conclusions. What about people who never heard the gospel at all? All agree that anyone who is saved is saved only through Christ and his cross, never through another religion or through their own goodness. Some believe that salvation also requires hearing of Christ and consciously trusting him, and they point to Romans 10:14: how can people believe in one they have never heard of? Others believe that God, in his mercy, may apply Christ's work to some who never heard his name but who respond in faith to the light God gives them, much as Abraham trusted a promise he did not fully understand. Both sides affirm that Christ alone saves. They differ on how much a person must know. Both also agree on what matters most for us: the command to make the gospel known to every nation.

So the answer is a confident yes. From Abel to the last person who will believe before Christ returns, every saved person is saved by the same Lord, through the same cross, by the same grace, received by faith. The whole Bible is one story with one Savior at its center.

topics.title: How is the whole Trinity involved in the work of salvation?
topics.cmp: Owen, Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius and Warfield agree that salvation is the work of the whole Trinity and depends on Christ's full Deity, but they address different questions with different arguments. Owen gives the most detailed account of distinct roles: the Father's love is free and grounded in himself alone, the Son purchases salvation (including the gift of the Spirit) and intercedes, and the Spirit works effectually, so that each Person is glorified in his own work. He argues mainly from Scripture (Ephesians 2, Hebrews 9:24) and from covenant and devotional reasoning about the believer's communion with God. Gregory of Nyssa makes a narrower exegetical point, that calling God 'Saviour' in 1 Timothy 4:10 does not exclude the Son and Spirit, yet Scripture does not speak of three Saviours. Athanasius argues from creation that the Redeemer must be Lord by nature, since redemption by a creature would lead us to serve the creature, while Warfield argues historically and from experience: the Trinity was revealed through redemption, stands or falls with it, is echoed in every redeemed consciousness, and was formulated under the guidance of Christ's Deity and the baptismal formula. Owen and Warfield both tie the Trinity to another doctrine as standing or falling together, but Owen links it to the person of Christ and Warfield to redemption.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: The doctrine of the Trinity, in other words, is simply the modification wrought in the conception of the one only God by His complete revelation of Himself in the redemptive process.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: it was fitting that the redemption should take place through none other than Him who is the Lord by nature, lest, though created by the Son, we should name another Lord

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: Now the Spirit, as unto us a Spirit of grace, holiness, and consolation, is of the purchase of Christ. It is upon the matter, the great promise of the new covenant

ans.text:
Salvation is not the work of one divine Person while the other two look on. From beginning to end it is the work of the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, acting together, with each Person doing his own part and receiving his own glory.

Paul lays this out in one long breath in Ephesians 1. The Father "chose us in Him before the foundation of the world." In the Son "we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses." And when we believed, we were "sealed with the promised Holy Spirit," who guarantees our inheritance. Peter says the same in a single sentence (1 Peter 1:2): we are chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit, and sprinkled with the blood of Jesus Christ. Put simply, the Father plans and sends, the Son comes and accomplishes, and the Spirit applies and completes.

Start with the Father. Salvation begins in his heart, not in ours. "For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son" (John 3:16). His love was not drawn out by anything he saw in us. There was nothing in one sinner that made him more lovable than another. God told Israel he did not choose them because they were greater than other nations, but simply because he loved them (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). That is good news. If his love depended on us, we could lose it. Because it springs from himself, anyone who comes to him through Christ will find that he really is love.

This also corrects a common misunderstanding. Some picture the cross as a loving Son calming down an angry Father, as if the two wanted different things. Scripture never puts it that way. The Father is the one who sent the Son. God's holy anger at sin is real, but the plan to rescue sinners from it came from the Father's love in the first place.

Then the Son. He took on our flesh, lived the obedient life we failed to live, died in our place, and rose again. Even now he appears in God's presence on our behalf (Hebrews 9:24), like a high priest who has brought the blood of the sacrifice into the holy place. He pleads for us everything his death won. And Scripture says he did all this out of love. He "loved me and gave Himself up for me" (Galatians 2:20).

Here the Trinity and the deity of Christ stand or fall together. If Jesus were only a creature, however exalted, then the God who made us would not be the one who saved us. We would owe our deepest worship and thanks to a created being, and that is idolatry. Scripture says instead that the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, became flesh to redeem us (John 1:1-3, 14). Only one who is truly God could carry the weight of our sin and bring us back to God. Deny that the Son is God and you lose the Trinity. Deny the Trinity and you lose a divine Savior.

Then the Holy Spirit. What the Son won, the Spirit brings home to us. Left to ourselves we would never believe. The Spirit opens blind eyes and gives new birth. Paul says God saved us "through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. This Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior" (Titus 3:5-6). Notice that the Spirit himself is given through Christ. The gift of the Spirit is one of the treasures Jesus bought with his blood.

The Spirit unites us to Christ, assures us that we are God's children, and teaches us to cry "Abba, Father!" (Galatians 4:6). He goes on making us holy until the day of redemption. Even our good works are his doing. Paul says we are saved by grace, "not by works," and then adds that "we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works" (Ephesians 2:8-10). So we cannot boast even of the good we do after we believe, because God produces it in us.

We should not picture three separate agents splitting up a job, as if there were three Saviors. Scripture calls God "the Savior of all men, and especially of those who believe" (1 Timothy 4:10). There is one God, so there is one saving work. Yet within that one work the Persons act in a real order: from the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. Each is honored in his own way. The Father is glorified for his free love, the Son for his finished work, and the Spirit for his power that makes it ours. Hebrews 9:14 shows all three in a single verse: Christ "through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God."

The same order runs back the other way when we come to God. "Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit" (Ephesians 2:18). We pray to the Father, through the Son, in the power of the Spirit. That is why Christians are baptized "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). The God who saves us is the God we belong to.

This shows why the Trinity is not a puzzle tacked onto the gospel. God made himself known as Father, Son and Spirit chiefly by saving us. The first believers knew the Father who gave his Son, the Son who gave himself for them, and the Spirit who came to live in them. After that they could not think of God any other way.

The same is true for us. Every Christian already lives by the Father's love, the Son's sacrifice, and the Spirit's presence. Take away any one Person and the gospel falls apart: there is no love behind it, no Savior at its center, or no power to make it ours. Knowing the triune God is simply knowing the God who saved you.

topics.title: How does Christ's redemptive work relate to the Father, and was he exalted for it?
topics.cmp: Owen and Basil agree that redemption both comes from the Father and is the Son's own act. Owen frames this in covenant terms: the work proceeded from the Father's will and love and from the Son's voluntary consent to stand in sinners' place. Basil instead reads texts like "delivered him up" as meaning the Son has his saving work from the Father, and he cites Scripture ascribing redemption to Christ himself to deny that the Son is a passive subordinate. On what redemption achieves, Owen stresses Christ bearing God's wrath, his exaltation to universal lordship, and adoption as a forensic, judicial act, all argued from Scripture. Augustine instead focuses on the devil being cast out and the predestinated being preserved, and Hilary on the Father glorifying Christ's assumed flesh into the unity of the Father's nature, arguing that God cannot be powerless to do for himself what he does for us.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: according to the will of the Father, and by his own counsel and choice, was substituted, and did substitute himself, as the mediator of the covenant

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: In how many ways “Through whom” is used; and in what…
refs.quote: It is meant that the Son has it of the Father that He works in goodness on behalf of men.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Remains of Death and the Evil Things of the World…
refs.quote: is only so far permitted to be an adversary according to the condition of this mortality, as God knows to be expedient for them

ans.text:
Christ's work of saving us was the Father's loving plan and the Son's own free choice at the same time, and after it was finished the Father did exalt him to the highest place. Both halves of that answer matter, and the Bible holds them together.

Start with the Father. The cross was not something the Son had to talk a reluctant Father into. "For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son" (John 3:16). Paul says the Father "did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). Our rescue begins in the Father's heart.

But the Son was not a passive tool in that plan, like a soldier sent where he would rather not go. Jesus is very clear about this: "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord" (John 10:18). The same Paul who says the Father gave him up also says the Son of God "loved me and gave Himself up for me" (Galatians 2:20). Scripture credits our redemption directly to Christ himself: he redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). So he was both sent in our place and chose to stand in our place. Hebrews even adds that he offered himself to God through the eternal Spirit (Hebrews 9:14), so the whole Trinity is at work in one saving act.

This is possible because the Father and the Son are not two gods with two separate agendas who happen to agree. They share one divine nature, and so one will and one love. When the Father sends and the Son goes, it is like one heart moving in two persons. The Son receives his mission from the Father, because he is the Son and everything he has comes from the Father. That is an order of relationship, not a difference in rank or worth.

What about verses that say the Son "obeyed" or was "subject"? Philippians 2 says he humbled himself and "became obedient to death—even death on a cross." Notice that he humbled himself; no one forced it. His obedience belongs to the role he freely took on when he became a man and a servant for our sake. A good comparison is a king's son who voluntarily takes the place of a servant to rescue his father's people. He really serves and obeys, but he does so as a choice of love, and he is no less royal for it. The Son's obedience shows his humility, not his inferiority.

Now the second question: was he exalted for this? Yes. Right after describing the cross, Paul writes, "Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names" (Philippians 2:9). Hebrews says that after he had provided purification for sins, "He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high" (Hebrews 1:3). The risen Jesus says, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me" (Matthew 28:18), and he tells John that he who was dead is alive forever and holds the keys of Death and of Hades (Revelation 1:18). Jesus himself said it was necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter his glory (Luke 24:26).

A common misunderstanding is to think Jesus was promoted to being God as a prize for good work. That is not the Bible's meaning. As God, the Son always had full glory. Before the cross he prayed, "Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). What changed at the exaltation is that the Son, now also truly human, was raised and honored in that humanity. A man who had died in shame now sits on the throne of the universe. The flesh he took for us now shares in his glory, and the hidden glory he always had is now openly shown.

Sincere Christians have put the "therefore" of Philippians 2 in slightly different ways. Some speak of the exaltation as a true reward the Father promised and gave, pointing to passages like Isaiah 53:12, where God says he will give his suffering servant a portion with the great because he poured out his life. Others prefer to say it was the natural result of his work rather than wages earned, since the Son is God and cannot earn what is already his. Both agree on the main point: Christ was exalted because of his suffering, and his glory was the goal set before him. Hebrews 12:2 says that for the joy set before him he endured the cross.

Why does this matter for us? Because Jesus uses his exalted power for his people. The one who now holds all authority is the same one who took God's judgment in our place. He stands between us and condemnation, gives eternal life, and guards us so that the enemy cannot finally have us. His glory is also a promise. If God raised the humanity of his Son into glory, he will one day transform our weak bodies to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The path he walked, from the cross to the crown, is the path he opens for everyone who belongs to him.

topics.title: How should the timing of Christ's death, burial and resurrection be understood?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus and Augustine each answer different questions here, so they never directly agree or disagree on a single point, though both treat the three days between Christ's death and resurrection as real and significant. Irenaeus is concerned with where Christ was. He argues that Christ descended to the place of the dead for three days before rising and ascending. He grounds this entirely in Scripture: the Jonah saying, Paul's 'lower parts of the earth', David's prophecy of deliverance from the nethermost hell, and the risen Lord's words to Mary that he had not yet ascended. Augustine is concerned instead with how the time is reckoned and what it means. He explains the 'three days and three nights' by counting part-days as whole days, reads the night-to-light order of the passion days against the light-to-night order of creation as signs of man's fall and restoration, and finds mystical meaning in the forty and thirty-six hours. This leans more on numerical and allegorical reasoning, though still anchored in Scripture, and he allows that others may explain the numbers differently.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: But the case was, that for three days He dwelt in the place where the dead were, as the prophet says concerning Him

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Three Days of the Resurrection, in Which Also the…
refs.quote: the first day is counted as a whole from its last part, and the third day is itself also counted as a whole from its first part; but the intervening day, i.e. the second day, was absolutely a whole with its twenty-four hours

ans.text:
Christ truly died on a Friday, lay in the grave through the Sabbath, and rose early on Sunday. During that time his body rested in the tomb while he himself went where the dead go. The Bible counts this as three days, and the day he died was chosen with purpose.

Start with what happened at his death. When Jesus died, he did not only seem to die. His body was laid in a tomb, and his human soul, the living self that thinks and wills, left his body the way ours will. In Luke 23:46 he says, "Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit." The New Testament speaks of him going down to the realm of the dead. Peter, preaching in Acts 2:27-31, applies Psalm 16 to Jesus: God would not abandon his soul to Hades, the place of the dead, nor let his body see decay. Paul, in Ephesians 4:9, says that before he ascended he first descended to the lower parts of the earth.

So Christ did not go straight up to the Father's throne the moment he died. After he rose he told Mary, "I have not yet ascended to the Father" (John 20:17). This is what the old creed means by "he descended to the dead." It does not mean Jesus suffered in hell as a lost sinner. His suffering for sin was finished on the cross, where he cried, "It is finished." It also does not contradict his promise to the thief: "today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). Among the dead, Jesus was with the faithful in rest, not in torment. He went there as the conqueror who holds "the keys of Death and of Hades" (Revelation 1:18), sharing our death all the way so that death would have no corner left where he had not been.

Christians have understood this descent in somewhat different ways. Many believe Christ actually went among the departed and announced his victory, pointing to 1 Peter 3:18-20, where he "preached to the spirits in prison." Others read that passage differently. They take the descent mainly as a vivid way of saying he truly died, was buried, and stayed under death's power for a time. All agree on the heart of it. Jesus really died, and he did not stay dead.

Next, the "three days and three nights." In Matthew 12:40 Jesus says the Son of Man will be "three days and three nights in the heart of the earth," just as Jonah was in the fish. Yet he was buried late Friday and rose before dawn on Sunday. That is nowhere near seventy-two hours. The answer lies in how people of that time counted. Any part of a day was counted as a day. Friday counts because he was buried at its end. Saturday was a full day and night in the grave. Sunday counts because he rose at its very beginning. We do something similar when we say a hotel stay was "three days" though we arrived Friday evening and left Sunday morning. The Old Testament counts this way too. In Esther 4:16-5:1, three days of fasting "night or day" end "on the third day." That is why the New Testament usually says Jesus rose "on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:4). The disciples on the road to Emmaus, speaking on Sunday, said it was the third day since these things happened (Luke 24:21).

Some sincere believers have wanted a full seventy-two hours. So they place the crucifixion on Wednesday or Thursday, taking Jesus' words about Jonah as an exact count of hours. Most Christians have held to Friday. The Gospels say plainly that he died on the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42). The "third day" wording also fits the Friday-to-Sunday reckoning naturally.

Notice too the movement of those days. They run from darkness to light. Jesus died as the land lay under darkness and was buried as night came on. He rose at dawn on the first day of the week. That is a picture of what he does for us. Paul says the God who said "Let light shine out of darkness" has shone in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6), and that we "were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord" (Ephesians 5:8).

Why did he die on the sixth day? In Genesis 1, God made man on the sixth day. Jesus is the new Adam, the one who starts humanity over again (Romans 5:12-19; 1 Corinthians 15:22). The first Adam disobeyed and brought death. Christ obeyed the Father to the point of death on the very day of the week when humanity was first made. Then, as God rested on the seventh day when creation was finished, Christ's body rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, his saving work complete. On the first day of the week, the day creation began, he rose as the start of a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). That is why Christians have gathered for worship on Sunday ever since.

The Bible's numbers and timings are not random. For example, the risen Jesus appeared to his followers over forty days (Acts 1:3), a number that echoes other times of testing and preparation in Scripture. Still, it is wise not to build doctrine on clever number patterns that Scripture itself does not explain. The plain meaning is enough. Jesus died a real death and went where the dead go. He kept the Sabbath rest in the grave and rose on the third day, just as he said. Because of that, no believer goes into death alone, and death is not the end of the story.

title: Worship, Glory and Baptism in the Triune Name
desc: The divine worship and honour due to the Son and Spirit, doxologies, the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19, and whether saving faith requires confessing the Trinity.

topics.title: Is religious worship due to God alone?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that religious worship belongs to God alone. Bickersteth grounds this in Scripture's claim on the creature's supreme love and service, Augustine notes that demons covet sacrifice precisely because it is owed to the one true God, and Waterland argues it at length from the Law (Exod. 20, 22:20; Deut. 6:13), Christ's "him only shalt thou serve," the angel's "Worship God," the Lycaonian episode, and the testimony of Justin, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Tatian and Tertullian. Waterland's distinctive emphasis, which no other author addresses, is his polemic against the Arian (and Romanist) division of worship into sovereign and inferior or relative kinds. He insists that God, not the worshipper's intention, fixes the meaning of worship, and that no human reasons or creaturely ability to help can override the plain command. Owen and Ambrose bring this exclusivity to bear on the Godhead itself and on Christ's humanity: Owen holds that worship occasioned by one Person's work is directed to the whole Godhead, and Ambrose explains the "footstool" of Ps. 99:5 as Christ's flesh, adored because Christ is not divided. Waterland similarly reconciles the worship of Christ with God-only worship by the Son's deity. The authors differ mainly in focus. Owen alone extends the principle to the manner of worship, reading the second commandment as forbidding humanly invented rites and calling false worship spiritual adultery. Augustine instead locates worship in love of God and traces pagan idolatry to philosophizing without the Mediator.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: miracles could not be sufficient to give credit to any one who should pretend to introduce another object of worship, or to set up another god, beside the one supreme God. All creatures whatever are hereby effectually precluded from receiving any religious homage and adoration.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: when any work of the Holy Ghost (or any other person), which is appropriated to him (we never exclude the concurrence of other persons), draws us to the worship of him, yet he is not worshipped exclusively, but the whole Godhead is worshipped.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: Further, He claims the supreme dependence, love, worship, and service of his creatures.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible teaches from beginning to end that worship belongs to the one true God and to no one else. This is not a minor rule. It sits at the very top of the Ten Commandments: "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Exodus 20:3). When Satan offered Jesus the kingdoms of the world in exchange for one act of worship, Jesus answered from Deuteronomy: "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only" (Matthew 4:10). Notice the word "only." Jesus did not say "serve Him most" or "serve Him first." He said only.

Scripture also explains why. God is not one great being among many. He is the Creator of everything, the One who holds all things in being, the One with no rival before Him or after Him. Through Isaiah He says, "Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come" (Isaiah 43:10), and, "I will not give My glory to another" (Isaiah 42:8). Worship is how creatures confess that someone is their Maker and their final Lord. To give it to anything that was made is to tell a lie about that thing and about God. That is why Paul says the root of human ruin is that people worshiped and served created things instead of the Creator (Romans 1:25).

Some have tried to soften the rule. They suggest worship comes in grades: top-level worship for God and a lower, lesser kind that may go to angels, heroes of faith, or other exalted beings. The Bible gives no room for this. Look at what happens when someone tries it. In Lystra the crowds wanted to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas (Acts 14). The apostles did not say, "That's fine, as long as you only mean a small honor." They tore their clothes and stopped it, insisting they were only men. In Revelation, John falls down before a glorious angel, and the angel says at once, "Do not do that!... Worship God!" (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). He did not say "worship God with the highest worship." He said simply, worship God.

The Law worked the same way. It did not forbid only the most serious kind of sacrifice to other gods while allowing a milder kind. All sacrifice belonged to the Lord (Exodus 22:20). If what you privately meant could make worship acceptable, then any idolater in Israel could have excused himself by saying he only intended a little respect. The early Christian martyrs understood this well. Many died rather than offer a pinch of incense to a pagan god or the emperor. They didn't believe in those gods at all. But they knew that the act itself said something, whatever was in their hearts. God, not the worshipper, decides what worship means. Out of kindness to us, He has kept all of it for Himself, so there is no confusion about whom we belong to.

This does not mean every kind of respect is forbidden. The Bible tells us to honor our parents, respect those in authority, and give thanks for faithful believers who have gone before us. Bowing to a king or standing for a judge is ordinary courtesy, not religious worship. The line is crossed when we offer to a creature what belongs to God: prayer as to the One who hears and rules, sacrifice, the trust of our whole soul, and adoration of someone as our Lord and the source of our life.

Christians have not all drawn that line in the same place. Some churches give a kind of honor to the saints and to holy images. They say it is a different kind of thing from worship, not a lower grade of worship, and that the honor passes on to God, who made the saints holy. Other Christians fear that this distinction is hard to keep in practice. They point out that Scripture never shows believers praying to departed saints and that the apostles and angels refused even outward signs of reverence. Both sides agree on the main point, though: worship in the true sense is for God alone.

That brings us to the most striking fact. The same New Testament that guards this rule so carefully shows Jesus being worshiped, and He welcomes it. His disciples worship Him after He calms the storm and after He rises (Matthew 14:33; 28:9, 17). Thomas falls before Him and says, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28), and Jesus does not correct him. Compare that with Paul and the angel, who refused worship at once. God the Father Himself commands, "Let all God's angels worship Him" (Hebrews 1:6). In heaven, every creature gives the same praise "to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb" (Revelation 5:13). Jesus says the Father's purpose is "that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). He means just as, not slightly less.

How can both be true? There is only one way. The Son is not a creature given a special exemption. He is God, sharing the one divine nature with the Father. That is why the first Christians could say without contradiction that God alone is to be worshiped and also that they worshiped Father, Son and Holy Spirit. They were not adding a second object of worship next to God. They were worshiping the one God, now made known as three Persons. Jesus Himself puts the three together under one name in baptism (Matthew 28:19).

The same reasoning explains how we worship the Persons of the Trinity. When we thank the Spirit for giving us new life, or adore the Son for dying for us, we are not splitting our devotion among three gods or leaving the others out. The Father, Son and Spirit are one God and always work together. To worship any one of them as God is to worship the whole Godhead.

So the rule stands without exceptions: worship God, and God only. Far from bending that rule, the worship of Jesus is one of the clearest proofs in the Bible of who He really is.

topics.title: What does Scripture's pattern of worship reveal about the deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the worship Scripture directs to the Son (and, where addressed, the Spirit) shows his true deity, and most build on the same premise that God alone may be worshipped. Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa and Waterland argue from that rule by dilemma: a worshipped creature would be idolatry, so the worshipped Son cannot be a creature. Waterland presses it furthest, rejecting any 'supreme versus inferior' worship, charging the Arians with paganizing idolatry, appealing at length to the Ante-Nicene Fathers, and adding that it is safer to over-honour the Son than to under-honour him. Bickersteth relies more on detailed scriptural and philological evidence (Old Testament worship of the Angel of Jehovah, counts of proskuneo, epikaleomai, Stephen's prayer, identical doxologies), and alone extends the argument to supreme trust in the Spirit and the whole Trinity. Owen grounds Christ's worship in his divine excellencies and also in his mediatorial work as man, while Ambrose and Basil focus on narrative examples and the Spirit's dignity: Ambrose notes the Spirit is never said to worship and reads Philippians 3:3 as 'serve the Spirit,' and Basil denies that praise of the Spirit can be excessive.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: That this Christ, God and man, is, because he is God, and on the account of what he has done for us as man, to be believed in, worshipped with worship religious and divine

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: For Mary worshipped Christ, and therefore is appointed to be the messenger of the Resurrection to the apostles

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: Scripture sanctions prayer to Christ, and commands the highest adoration and worship to be paid to him.

ans.text:
The way the Bible directs worship shows that the Son and the Holy Spirit are truly God. Scripture reserves worship for God alone, yet it gives that same worship and trust to Jesus, and places the Spirit beside the Father and the Son in the one divine name.

Start with the rule that runs through the whole Bible. The first commandment says, “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3). When Satan tempted Jesus to bow down to him, Jesus answered with Scripture: “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (Matthew 4:10). Worship is not a sliding scale, with top-level worship for God and a smaller portion for great creatures. It is the bowing of the whole person before the One who made us and on whom we depend for everything. In the Bible that belongs to God and to no one else.

The Bible shows this rule being kept carefully. When Cornelius fell at Peter's feet to worship him, Peter pulled him up and said, “Stand up, I am only a man myself” (Acts 10:26). When John fell down before a glorious angel, the angel stopped him at once: “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you,” and told him to worship God (Revelation 22:9). Good men and holy angels refuse worship, because they know they are creatures.

Now set Jesus beside that. He accepts worship again and again and never refuses it. The wise men worship him. The disciples in the boat worship him and confess that he is the Son of God (Matthew 14:33). After the resurrection the women take hold of his feet and worship him, and the eleven do the same on the mountain (Matthew 28:9, 17). Thomas falls before him and says, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Jesus does not correct him. He blesses those who will believe the same without seeing.

Some have said this was only the bow people gave to kings or great teachers. The word used can mean that in ordinary Greek. But in the New Testament it is used almost always for the worship of God, or for false worship that is condemned. And the people who bowed to Jesus were not just being polite. They were asking him for what only God can give: cleansing from leprosy, life for a dead child, forgiveness of sins. If Jesus were only a man, a faithful teacher would have stopped them, as Peter did. Jesus instead welcomed their faith.

The pattern goes beyond earth. Hebrews 1:6 says of the Son, “Let all God’s angels worship Him.” In Revelation 5 every creature in heaven and on earth sings “to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb.” Praise, honour, glory and power are given to both together. The Lamb is not one of the creatures giving praise. He receives it with the One on the throne.

The first Christians also prayed to Jesus. Stephen, as he died, cried out, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59), and asked him not to hold the sin against his killers. In the Old Testament, believers committed their spirits into God's hands. Stephen gives that same last trust to Jesus. Paul describes Christians everywhere as those who “call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:2). In the Old Testament, to “call on the name of the LORD” meant to pray to God for salvation. The New Testament uses the same language for calling on Jesus (Romans 10:9-13).

This is why the reasoning is so simple. If Jesus is a creature, however exalted, then worshipping him is idolatry, and the apostles, the angels and the whole church have been idolaters. If worshipping him is right, as Scripture plainly says it is, then he is not a creature. He is God. You cannot have a worshipped Jesus who is less than God without breaking the first commandment.

That is also why the early church held its ground when some teachers claimed the Son was the highest created being, made before the world. Those teachers still wanted to worship him. But the church saw that this would mean bowing to a being who once did not exist, a “new god,” which the Bible forbids. The argument was not about fine words for their own sake. It was about whether Christian worship was faithful to God or idolatrous.

What about the Holy Spirit? The Bible says less about worship offered directly to the Spirit, and we should be honest about that. The Spirit's work is often to point away from himself to Jesus and to lead us in prayer to the Father. Even so, Scripture treats him as fully God and gives him the same honour. Jesus sends his followers to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). That is one name, not three, and no creature could be listed in it. Paul's blessing joins “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (2 Corinthians 13:14). When Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, Peter told him, “You have not lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:3-4). Our bodies are temples because the Spirit lives in us, and temples are dwellings for God (1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19). Sinning against him is treated with the utmost seriousness (Matthew 12:31-32).

In Philippians 3:3 Paul describes Christians as those who worship by the Spirit of God. Old copies of the letter differ slightly here. Most English Bibles, ours included, follow the reading that has us worshipping by the Spirit. A few copies read “worship God in the Spirit,” and the Greek has also been understood to mean serving the Spirit of God. The teaching does not rest on this one verse. Either way, the Spirit is the one in whom true worship happens. Only God can be the source and place of our worship of God. So Christians have rightly worshipped and glorified the Spirit together with the Father and the Son, and have prayed, “Come, Holy Spirit.”

Worship also means trust. Scripture calls us to trust God with our whole hearts and warns against relying on mere man (Jeremiah 17:5). Yet we are told to believe in the Son just as we believe in the Father (John 14:1). He made all things, holds all things together, and will judge the world (Colossians 1:16-17; John 5:22). Someone who does what only God does deserves the full trust, love and adoration we owe only to God.

Someone might ask whether it is safer to honour the Son a little less, just in case. The Bible points the other way. Jesus says the Father has given judgment to the Son “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him” (John 5:23). Scripture warns many times against failing to honour the Son. It never warns against honouring him too much. Nor does it ever suggest the Father is jealous of the glory given to his Son. Paul says every knee will bow to Jesus and every tongue confess him as Lord “to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10-11). Still, the real answer is not to hedge our bets. The Son is to be honoured as God because he is God.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. Worshipping the Son and the Spirit does not mean worshipping three gods. We worship one God, who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Honour given to the Son flows to the Father, and we worship in the Spirit. Nor does it take anything away from the Father. The Father delights to have his Son honoured, and the Spirit delights to glorify the Son.

So the shape of Christian worship is itself a confession of faith. When we pray to Jesus, sing his praise, trust him with our lives, are baptised into the one name, and rely on the Spirit as God dwelling in us, we are saying with the whole Bible that the Son and the Spirit share fully in the glory that belongs to God alone.

topics.title: Should Christ receive divine worship, and on what ground?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Christ rightly receives divine worship and that this is because he is truly God, not a creature or mere man: Owen and Waterland insist that worship given to one who is not God by nature is idolatry and cannot be split into 'relative' or inferior kinds, Novatian and Bickersteth argue that prayer, hope, service and the bowing of every knee (Philippians 2) would be impossible toward a mere man, and Athanasius and Ambrose ground adoration in Christ being the one Word, with his flesh adored together with him (though not Mary). They also agree that his mediatorial exaltation does not supply his title to worship. Owen says worship is owed to him as Son, not as Mediator, and Waterland argues at length that the right rests on his personal dignity, creative power and essential perfections, existed before the resurrection, and was only more clearly declared afterward. Athanasius and Waterland both appeal to pre-incarnate worship by patriarchs and angels, Waterland drawing on Irenaeus, Eusebius and the Ante-Nicene consensus. Emphases differ, however. Owen reads the Lamb's worship in Revelation 5 as given on account of redemption, and Gregory of Nyssa refers Hebrews 1:6 to the second coming, with angels worshipping the 'First-born', a title taken for our sakes, out of joy at humanity's restoration, whereas Athanasius cites the same command as proof of worship before the incarnation. Meanwhile Irenaeus is concerned mainly that the God glorified in the Gospels is the Creator, the Father of the law and prophets, and Augustine supplies the douleuein/latreuein distinction reserving latreia to God alone.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: For they are divine, essential excellencies that are the formal reason and object of worship, religious and divine; and to ascribe it unto any one that is not God by nature, is idolatry.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: The Author Prosecutes the Same Argument.
refs.quote: If Christ is only man, why is hope rested upon Him, when hope in man is declared to be accursed?

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: how did He receive that Name for worship, who is always worshipped by His Name? Nay, certainly before He became man, the sacred writers invoke Him

ans.text:
Yes. Jesus Christ is rightly worshipped as God, by angels and by people, and the deepest reason is simply who he is: the eternal Son of God, one in being with the Father. He did not become worthy of worship partway through history. He always was.

To see why this matters, start with how jealously the Bible guards worship. When Satan tempted Jesus, Jesus answered from the Old Testament: "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only" (Matthew 4:10). God says in Isaiah 42:8, "I will not give My glory to another." So when Peter's visitor Cornelius fell at his feet, Peter made him stand up, because he was only a man (Acts 10:25-26). When John bowed before a glorious angel, the angel stopped him at once and said, "Worship God!" (Revelation 22:8-9). Good creatures, human or angelic, refuse worship.

Jesus did not refuse it. After he calmed the storm, the disciples worshipped him (Matthew 14:33). After the resurrection the women took hold of his feet and worshipped him (Matthew 28:9). Thomas called him "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28), and Jesus accepted it. When children shouted "Hosanna" in the temple and the leaders objected, Jesus defended their praise from the Psalms. Jesus even said the Father has given all judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). Note the words "just as." That is not a lesser, second-tier honor. It is the same honor.

Heaven agrees. Hebrews 1:6 says that when God brings his Son into the world, "Let all God's angels worship Him." In Revelation 5 the countless angels, and then every creature, give praise, honor, glory and power to the Lamb together with the One who sits on the throne. If the Son were only a creature, however exalted, all of heaven would be breaking the first commandment.

Some people try to soften this by saying Christians only give Jesus great "honour" or respect, the way we honor parents or leaders. But the Bible's language goes much further. Christians pray to him (Acts 7:59), put their hope and trust in him, love him above everyone, and serve him as their one Master: "It is the Lord Christ you are serving" (Colossians 3:24). Scripture warns against trusting in mere mortals for salvation. Yet trusting Christ is exactly what the gospel asks. This is the kind of devotion owed to God alone.

Now the second part of the question. Does Christ deserve worship only because God later gave him a high office, as our Mediator, King or Judge? Philippians 2:9-11 can seem to suggest that: "Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow."

Read the whole passage, though. It begins by saying Christ already existed "in very nature God" before he humbled himself and became a servant (Philippians 2:6-7). He did not climb up to deity. He came down from it. What God exalted was the Son who had humbled himself. That includes his human nature, which was raised from the shame of the cross to the throne. The words about every knee bowing come from Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD says every knee will bow to him alone. Paul applies them to Jesus, and adds that this is "to the glory of God the Father." Worshipping the Son does not rob the Father. It honors him.

Think of it this way. A rightful heir to a throne might live hidden among ordinary people for a time and then be publicly crowned. The coronation does not make him royal. It openly declares what was already true, and it adds the honor of what he has accomplished. In the same way, Christ's resurrection and ascension did not give him a right to worship he lacked. They showed it openly and crowned his saving work. The prophet Isaiah saw the Lord's glory on his throne, and John 12:41 says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory. Jesus himself prayed, "glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5).

So we can hold two things together. In his divine nature the Son has always deserved the same worship as the Father, because he is God. As our Redeemer, he is also praised for what he did. The angels sing, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain." His office and his work give us fresh reasons to adore him. They are not the foundation of his right to be adored. In fact, if Jesus were God only by appointment and not by nature, worshipping him would be idolatry, the very thing the Bible forbids most strongly.

One more point helps avoid confusion. We do not worship Jesus' human nature as something separate from him, as if we were worshipping a body or a man alongside God. We worship one Person, the eternal Son, who has taken our humanity to himself and never laid it aside. When we bow before the risen Jesus, we are bowing before God the Son made flesh.

That is why Christians from the beginning have prayed to Christ, sung hymns to him, and confessed him as Lord. We do not worship a second God beside the Father. We worship the one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and we gladly join the angels in giving the Son the glory that has always been his.

topics.title: Should prayer be directed to the Son as well as the Father?
topics.cmp: Owen, Bickersteth and Waterland all affirm that prayer and worship are rightly directed to the Father and to the Son as distinct persons, and all draw chiefly on Pauline and New Testament practice. Owen alone addresses the Father as a distinct object of prayer, grounding it in the Father's role as fountain of the Deity and of all good in Christ. He then argues from the conjoined yet distinguished address that each is God, since divine worship given to one not God by nature would be idolatry. Bickersteth stresses that Paul names the Father and Christ in either order without regard to rank. He adds a philological argument that 'call upon the name' is the Septuagint's ordinary term for invoking God. Waterland emphasizes the breadth of Christ's worship, by men, angels and the whole creation, and the ascription of eternal glory to him as to the Father. Unlike the others, he also appeals to the practice of the earliest Christian writers.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The workings, then, of the Spirit of grace in that duty are distinctly directed to the Father as such, as the fountain of the Deity, and of all good things in Christ

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: Here is express and direct supplication, so that we need not marvel this was one distinctive name of Christian believers

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: He is to be worshipped and adored, as well as the Father, by men, by dangels, by the ¢whole creation. Gloryand dominion for ever and ‘ever are fascribed to him, as well as to the Father.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible's ordinary pattern is to pray to the Father, through the Son, by the help of the Holy Spirit. But Scripture also shows believers praying directly to Jesus and trusting him exactly as they trust God. That is right and good, because the Son is truly God.

Start with the Father. Jesus taught his disciples to pray, "Our Father in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). He told them that whatever they ask the Father in his name, the Father will give them (John 16:23). Paul describes himself kneeling before the Father as he prays for the church (Ephesians 3:14). So praying to the Father is not a lesser or older habit we have outgrown. It is the main road of Christian prayer, and the Father is rightly thought of as the source from whom every good gift comes to us in Christ.

Yet the New Testament does not stop there. Paul sometimes addresses his prayers to the Father and the Son together. In 1 Thessalonians 3:11 he asks that "our God and Father Himself and our Lord Jesus" would open the way for him to visit the church. In 2 Thessalonians 2:16-17 he names them in the reverse order, "our Lord Jesus Christ Himself and God our Father," and asks them to encourage and strengthen the believers. Notice two things. First, he keeps them distinct. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father. Second, he asks the same thing of both, as one source of help, and he is happy to put either name first. No one would write that way about God and a mere creature.

There are plain prayers to Jesus himself as well. As Stephen was being stoned, he cried out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). He entrusted his very soul to Christ at the moment of death. Paul says he pleaded with the Lord three times to take away his thorn in the flesh. The Lord answered that his grace was sufficient and that his power is made perfect in weakness. The context shows Paul means Christ (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). The early church's cry, "Come, Lord Jesus!" (Revelation 22:20), is itself a prayer. Paul even describes Christians simply as people "who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 1:2). In the Old Testament, "calling on the name of the Lord" means praying to God. Paul applies that very phrase to Jesus in Romans 10:13: "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."

Jesus himself invited this. He told the Samaritan woman that if she knew who he was, she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water (John 4:10). He called, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). No prophet ever said that about himself. To come to Jesus for rest of soul is to lean on him in the way we lean on God in prayer.
