On the night before he died he told his disciples, in effect, that they trusted in God and should trust in him in the same way (John 14:1). He even said, "If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it" (John 14:14).

This matters because the Bible is fierce about worship. God alone is to be worshiped and served (Matthew 4:10), and he will not share his glory with another. Asking someone for forgiveness, for eternal life, or to receive your spirit at death is not a small favor between friends. It is to rely on a love, wisdom and power that only God has. If Jesus were not God, praying to him like this would be idolatry. The apostles knew this well. When crowds tried to treat them as divine, they were horrified and refused (Acts 14:14-15). When they healed people, they insisted it was not by their own power but in the name of Jesus (Acts 3:6, 12-16). Asking Jesus for help is therefore not like asking Peter or Paul for help. Jesus acted in his own right. The apostles acted only in his name. In heaven, the whole creation gives blessing, honor, glory and power "to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb" alike (Revelation 5:13).

What about closing our prayers "in Jesus' name"? Some people wonder whether that means Jesus is only a go-between, a kind of messenger who carries our prayers to the real God. Not at all. Praying in his name means coming on the strength of who he is and what he has done for us, not on our own merit. Jesus is our mediator because he became a man and gave himself for us. But he is not a go-between standing outside of God. When we pray to God, we are speaking to the one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Even when our words are addressed to the Father, the Son is not left out. He is honored as God, and he is the one through whom we have access. Think of how a child might speak to "Mom and Dad" by addressing only one of them. The other is not shut out of the conversation.

So is it right to pray "Lord Jesus, help me" as well as "Father, help me"? Yes. It is also fitting to call on the Holy Spirit, since he too is God. Christians have differed somewhat in their habits here. Some keep their regular prayers addressed to the Father, because that is how Jesus taught us to pray and how most New Testament prayers are framed. Others pray freely to Christ, because the apostles and martyrs did so and because he invites us to come to him. These are differences of emphasis, not of faith. Both agree that the Son may rightly be called upon and worshiped, and that he is never a rival to the Father. As Jesus said, the Father has given all judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). To pray to the Son is not to turn away from the Father. It is to honor the Father in the way he himself desires.

topics.title: Is the Son honoured and glorified equally with the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors who address the question agree that the Son is to be honoured and worshipped equally with the Father, and several (Hilary, Basil, Athanasius, Novatian) add that honour withheld from the Son is withheld from the Father as well. They argue in different ways. Waterland answers the claim of a lesser worship by holding that all religious worship carries the same import, and he rests John 5:23's 'even as' on the context of the chapter rather than on the particle alone. Athanasius and Basil use the analogy of image and prototype (the honour paid to the emperor's image passes to the emperor), and Basil also appeals to the fathers and to the liturgical wording of the doxology, arguing that 'with whom' expresses the Son's equal dignity while 'through whom' expresses his mediation and grace and does not imply subordination. Gregory of Nyssa argues from the Son's titles and works and by reductio: to deny the Son the Father's nature either insults him or turns worship of him into idolatry. Hilary relies mainly on Christ's own sayings, and Novatian on the Son's role in creation; Owen's single answer, which reads Titus 3:4 as referring to the Father as distinct from Christ the mediator, concerns exegesis and does not take up the question of equal honour.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: worship, religious worship, greater or smaller, longer or shorter, has the same import and significancy; and speaks the Person addressed to, to be divine

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: And Indeed that Christ Was Not Only Man, But God Also;…
refs.quote: For this contempt of the heretics will recoil also upon God the Father, if God the Father could not beget God the Son.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent Him[^774], be setting themselves to honour the Father, through honour paid to the Son.

ans.text:
Yes. The Son receives the very same honour, worship and glory as the Father. He does not get a smaller, second-tier version. Jesus himself makes this clear in John 5:23: God has arranged things "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him."

Some have tried to soften the words "just as," as if Jesus meant only that the Son deserves honour of a roughly similar kind. The setting of the verse rules that out. Earlier in the same chapter, people wanted to kill Jesus because he was "making Himself equal with God" (John 5:18). Jesus does not back away from that charge. He goes on to say that whatever the Father does, the Son does too. The Son gives life to whom he wishes, and all judgment has been handed to him. Then he draws the conclusion: because the Son shares the Father's work, he shares the Father's honour. In that context, "just as" means "to the same degree."

This matters because the Bible allows no middle category of worship. God says in Isaiah 42:8, "I will not give My glory to another." Worship is either given to God, or it is idolatry. A small offering and a large one both say the same thing: you are God. So it makes no sense to worship Jesus with a "lesser" worship. If he is not truly God, we should not worship him at all. If he is truly God, sharing the Father's own being, then he deserves everything the Father deserves. Scripture clearly takes the second view. The angels are commanded to worship him (Hebrews 1:6). In heaven, praise rises "to Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb," one song of "praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!" (Revelation 5:13).

You might worry that honouring the Son takes something away from the Father. It does the opposite. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." You cannot have the sun without its light. You cannot praise the light without praising the sun. In the same way, the glory of the Son is the Father's own glory, shining out. That is why Philippians 2:10-11 can say that every knee bows at the name of Jesus and confesses him as Lord, "to the glory of God the Father." The honour given to the Son flows back to the Father. It is one worship of one God, not two worships competing with each other. The reverse is also true. Whoever refuses the Son his honour insults the Father who sent him and who gladly shares his glory with him (John 17:5).

This leads to a question about how Christians word their praise. Should we give glory to the Father only "through" the Son, or may we also say "with" the Son? Both are biblical, and each says something true. "Through" him speaks of what Jesus has done for us. He is our Mediator, the Way and the Door. "Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit" (Ephesians 2:18). So it is fitting to give thanks to the Father through Christ. "With" him speaks of who Jesus is in himself: the eternal Son, equal in dignity with the Father. So it is just as fitting to give glory to the Father with the Son and the Spirit, or to give glory straight to Christ. The apostles did this themselves: "To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity" (2 Peter 3:18).

The only error would be to use "through" as a way of pushing the Son down, as if he were a lower being who merely passes our praise along. He is not. He came after the Father neither in time nor in rank. He was with the Father before the world began.

None of this denies that the Father and the Son are distinct. The Father sends and the Son is sent. In becoming man, the Son humbly obeyed. But being sent and obeying are about the roles the Son took on for our salvation, not about lesser worth. A son who obeys his father is not less human than his father. The eternal Son who carried out his Father's plan is not less divine. So when we worship, we can bow before Jesus with the same adoration we give the Father, knowing that this is exactly what the Father desires.

topics.title: What does it mean to glorify God, and how is the Son glorified with the Father?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that glorifying God adds nothing to him and that the Son shares the Father's glory rather than lacking it, but they come at the topic from different angles. Basil defines glorifying as recounting the wonders proper to the one glorified, applied equally to Father, Son and Spirit. Hilary, who supplies most of the answers, likewise holds that God's glory cannot be increased, and that the Father is glorified by being made known to humanity through the Son. Hilary's distinctive argument is exegetical and christological: Christ's prayers to be glorified (John 12, 13, 17) concern the human nature he assumed, not his Godhead, which never lost its glory. That flesh is raised into the divine glory through the cross, the Resurrection and a future taking into God, and he argues that 'God is glorified in Him' and 'glorified Him in Himself' prove Christ's Godhead and his unity with the Father; Hilary also concedes the Father is 'greater' as Unbegotten and Sender while insisting on a mutual giving of glory grasped by faith rather than syllogism. Waterland reaches a similar conclusion from John 17 (the honour of each redounds to both), Athanasius argues from Old Testament texts that the Son was already Lord and King before the Incarnation, Owen reads 'name' in John 12 as God's attributes made supremely glorious in redemption, and Augustine stresses instead the soteriological lesson of the Son's obedience unto death and its reward in the risen flesh.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: He had not lost His former being, but He had become what He was not before; He had not abdicated His own position, yet He had taken ours; He prays that the nature which He had assumed may be promoted to the glory which He had never renounced.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: it is plain that even before He became man, He was King and Lord everlasting, being Image and Word of the Father.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: The glorifying of the enumeration of His attributes.
refs.quote: For not even in the case of the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Only begotten Son, are we capable of giving Them glory otherwise than by recounting, to the extent of our powers, all the wonders that belong to Them.

ans.text:
To glorify God is not to give him something he lacks. It is to recognise, praise and make known the greatness he already has. God cannot grow or shrink. His glory was perfect before the world began and will be perfect forever. So when we glorify him, nothing is added to God. What changes is us, and the world around us. His greatness becomes seen, known and honoured where it was hidden or ignored.

Think of the sun on a cloudy day. When the clouds part, the sun does not become brighter. It becomes visible. In the same way, the Bible calls us to "ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name" (Psalm 29:2). We are not lending God brightness. We are saying out loud what is true about him. That is why praise so often takes the form of telling what God is like and what he has done. When we recount his holiness, his mercy and his mighty works, we are glorifying him.

This matters for how we think about the Son. God says in Isaiah 42:8 that he will not give his glory to another. Yet the New Testament gives the Son the very same glory. Jesus says the Father has given judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). In Revelation 5:13 all creation sings, "To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!" If God will not share his glory with anyone outside himself, and yet the Son receives it in full, then the Son is not outside God. He is God the Son, sharing one divine life and glory with the Father. Hebrews 1:3 calls him "the radiance of God's glory." Light shining from a lamp is not a lesser thing added later. It is the lamp's own brightness, there as long as the lamp is.

But then a question arises. If the Son already has divine glory, why does he pray for it? In John 17:5 Jesus prays, "And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed." Some people take this to mean the Son was lesser, or had lost something. A careful reading points the other way.

First, notice what Jesus asks for. It is the glory he already "had" with the Father before creation. A mere creature could not say that. The prayer itself shows he shared the Father's glory from eternity.

Second, remember what happened when the Son became man. He did not stop being God. He took on something he had not been before: a real human body and soul. His divine glory was not lost, but for a time it was veiled in ordinary flesh, in weakness, hunger and suffering. Philippians 2 says he "humbled Himself and became obedient to death—even death on a cross." So when he prays to be glorified, he is asking that the humanity he took on be brought into the glory that, as God, he never gave up. The man Jesus, born in time, is to share the everlasting glory of the eternal Son. This is very good news for us. Human nature, in Christ, is lifted into the presence of God.

Third, look at the shape of the prayer in John 17:1: "Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You." This is not a servant begging from a master. It is a mutual giving. The Father glorifies the Son, and the Son glorifies the Father. The honour of one is the honour of the other. Neither is in need. Each delights to make the other known.

How does the Son glorify the Father? By making him known. Jesus says, "Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). Humanity had fallen into darkness about God. The Son came to show us who the Father truly is. When people come to know the Father through the Son, the Father is glorified, not because he gained anything, but because he is at last seen for who he is.

The Gospel of John also shows that Christ's glorification comes in stages. It begins, surprisingly, at the cross. Again and again Jesus calls his coming death "the hour" of his glory. In John 12:28 he prays, "Father, glorify Your name!" and a voice from heaven answers, "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." God's name means God's very character: his love, justice, faithfulness and power. Nowhere are these shown more fully than at the cross, where God's justice and mercy meet. Jesus even tells the crowd that this voice came for their sake, not his (John 12:30). The Son did not need reassurance. The people needed to hear it. At his death the sky darkened, the earth shook, and a Roman soldier confessed that this man was truly the Son of God (Matthew 27:54). Even in his deepest humiliation, his glory was breaking through.

In John 13:31-32, as Judas goes out to betray him, Jesus says, "Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him. If God is glorified in Him, God will glorify the Son in Himself." There are two movements here. First, God is glorified in the Son of Man: in a real human life, in obedience to the point of death, the glory of God is seen. Second, God will glorify the Son "in Himself": raising him from the dead, taking him up to heaven, and seating him at his right hand. The crucified man is received into the very glory of God. And notice that the Father glorifies the Son "in Himself." The Son is not glorified as someone outside of God, but within the life of God.

This also explains why the Son's obedience is not a sign of a lower nature. Humanity was ruined by disobedience. The Son, out of love, entered our human condition and obeyed perfectly, even to the cross. That obedience heals our disobedience. And its reward is shown in his own resurrected body. That is why Philippians 2 goes on to say that God exalted him, so that every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, "to the glory of God the Father." When the Son is honoured, the Father is honoured. There is no rivalry.

It is worth adding that the exaltation after the cross did not make the Son Lord for the first time. He was Lord before he ever became man. David speaks of "my Lord" seated at God's right hand (Psalm 110:1), and Hebrews 1:8 applies to the Son the words, "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever." What is new at the resurrection and ascension is that he now reigns as one of us, the God-man, with our nature raised and glorified.

Sincere Christians do sometimes read passages like "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28) a little differently. Many understand them as referring to the Son in his humble human state. Others also see in them the fact that the Father is the source from whom the Son eternally comes, while insisting the Son is fully equal in being and glory. Both readings agree on the main point: the Son is true God, and his glory is the Father's own glory.

So what does this mean for us? When we worship, we join this exchange of glory. We glorify the Father through the Son, by the Spirit, telling the wonders of each, and we can do it without fear of taking glory from one by giving it to another. To honour the Son is to honour the Father. And because the Son has carried our humanity into the glory of God, we have hope that we too will one day see and share that glory (John 17:24).

topics.title: Is the Holy Spirit glorified with the Father and the Son, and how should doxologies be read?
topics.cmp: Basil, Ambrose, Gregory of Nyssa, Hilary and Waterland all agree that the Spirit is to be glorified with the Father and the Son and that no doxological form implies His inferiority. On the creation texts, Gregory, Ambrose and Hilary concur that the Spirit is not among the "all things" made through the Son, but on different grounds: Gregory reads Paul's list of creatures and the Spirit's sovereign working, Ambrose appeals to Psalm 33, the Spirit's knowledge of the Father and the lack of any text calling Him made, while Hilary counsels saying only that He is God's Spirit. On the prepositions, Ambrose treats "in" and "with" as interchangeable conjunctive particles that cannot divide, whereas Basil, while likewise noting Scripture's interchangeable usage and making "in" itself honour the Spirit, also distinguishes them: "with" expresses the Spirit's fellowship and dignity with God, "in" the grace in us and our own weakness. Basil uniquely rests much of his case on unwritten apostolic tradition and a catalogue of Fathers and liturgical witnesses (even the unsound Origen), and Waterland similarly reads the ancient doxologies by primitive doctrine against Arian misuse, while both Basil and Ambrose argue a fortiori that if believers are "with Christ" and reign with Him, so must the Spirit, Ambrose adding that the Spirit does so by nature rather than grace. John Owen differs in emphasis, treating glory as an ordered economy in which the Spirit is sent to glorify the Son rather than Himself, and speaking of the Spirit's consolation rather than of doxological forms.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Proof of the absurdity of the refusal to glorify the…
refs.quote: While then so many things are glorified, do you wish the Spirit alone of all things to be unglorified? Yet the Apostle says “the ministration of the Spirit is glorious.” How then can He Himself be unworthy of glory?

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: But of the Holy Spirit, as being above the nature of things that have come into being, Paul said not a word in his enumeration of existing things, not indicating to us by his words either His subordination or His coming into being

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: Does he, then, include the Holy Spirit here amongst creatures? Or when he says that the Son of God is before all things, is he to be supposed to have said that He is before the Father? Certainly not

ans.text:
Yes. The Holy Spirit is rightly worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, because He is not a lesser being or a created force but God, sharing one divine nature with them. Whether a prayer of praise says glory "to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit," or glory to the Father and the Son "with" the Holy Spirit, or glory to the Father through the Son "in" the Holy Spirit, a careful Christian can say all three and mean the same faith.

Start with why the Spirit deserves glory at all. The Bible gives honor to many created things. It speaks of the glory of the sun and the stars, the glory of Israel, even the glory of human beings made in God's image. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 3 that the ministry of the Spirit is far more glorious than the old covenant that came with such splendor. It would be strange if everything the Spirit touches were glorious and the Spirit Himself were not.

But the deeper reason is who the Spirit is. When Ananias lies to the Holy Spirit in Acts 5, Peter tells him, "You have not lied to men, but to God." Paul says in 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 that the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. He compares it to how only a person's own spirit knows that person's thoughts. No creature can know God from the inside like that. Hebrews 9:14 calls Him the eternal Spirit. In 1 Corinthians 12:11 Paul says the Spirit hands out gifts to each one "as He determines." That is the freedom of a Lord, not the duty of a servant. And Jesus Himself warns in Matthew 12 that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. No one could speak that way about a mere instrument.

Some have asked whether the Spirit is one of the "all things" made through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). The answer is no. When Paul lists what was created, he names things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, thrones and powers. He never puts the Spirit on that list. Psalm 33:6 even links the Spirit with the making of the heavens. Scripture nowhere says the Spirit was made. So the Spirit belongs on the Creator's side of the line, not the creature's.

The clearest sign of all is the name into which every Christian is baptized. Jesus tells us in Matthew 28:19 to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Notice that it says one name, not three. The three are placed side by side with the simple word "and," with no hint that one is a lesser partner. Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 does the same, joining the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Spirit. If we are baptized into the Spirit's name as truly as into the Father's and the Son's, we can glorify Him as truly too. Our worship should match our baptism.

Now to the small words in our prayers of praise, which are often called doxologies. A doxology is simply a short sentence giving glory to God, like "Glory be to the Father." Christians have used a few patterns, and people have sometimes argued over them.

The form "to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit" simply follows the pattern of the baptism command. The form "with the Holy Spirit" means the same thing. Saying "Paul and Silas and Timothy" is no different from saying "Paul with Silas and Timothy." Either way, all three are named together and honored together. "With" stresses that the Spirit shares in God's glory and stands alongside the Father and the Son.

The form "in the Holy Spirit" has sometimes been pushed by people who wanted to make the Spirit sound smaller, as if He were only the place or tool of worship, not its object. But the word "in" does not lower Him at all. Scripture uses "in" of Christ too. We are "in Christ," and we pray in His name, and no one thinks that makes Christ less than God. "In the Spirit" mostly tells us something about ourselves. We cannot praise God rightly on our own. We are too weak and too distracted. So the Spirit lives in us and makes our praise possible. Paul says in Ephesians 2:18 that through Christ we have access to the Father by one Spirit. In Philippians 3:3 he speaks of believers as those who worship by God's Spirit. Think of a musician whose skill lives in her hands. The music happens "in" that skill, and the skill is the very thing that makes the music beautiful. Saying the Spirit is "in" us is a way of saying He is the living power of God at work within us.

So "in" and "with" are not rivals. They are two sides of one truth. "In the Spirit" speaks of the grace God gives us, with the Spirit dwelling in His people and lifting their praise to God. "With the Spirit" speaks of who the Spirit is: one in glory with the Father and the Son. A healthy church can use both.

Some have objected that the exact phrase "glory to the Father and the Son with the Spirit" does not appear word for word in the Bible. That is true. But neither does the word "Trinity," and the truth behind the phrase is plainly biblical. The words come straight from the pattern of Matthew 28:19. Christians have also praised the Spirit together with the Father and the Son from very early times, in ordinary evening hymns and in the prayers of martyrs. This is not a late invention. It is the church saying out loud what it learned at the font.

What about the order, with the Father first, the Son second, and the Spirit third? That order is not a ranking of greatness, as if the Spirit got a bronze medal. It reflects how the three relate to one another and how God comes to us. Every good gift comes from the Father, through the Son, and is brought home to us by the Spirit. Then our thanks rises back the same way: by the Spirit, through the Son, to the Father. Jesus says in John 16:14 that the Spirit "will glorify Me," and the Son in turn glorifies the Father. Yet the three share one glory, not three portions of it. Scripture itself is free with the order. Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 names the Son first, and in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 the Spirit comes first, then the Lord, then God. That freedom shows that none of the three outranks the others in being God.

This matters for everyday faith. Jesus says in John 17:3 that eternal life is knowing the only true God and the One He sent. The Spirit is the One who makes that knowing real in us, and He brings strong, lasting comfort because He is Himself eternal. When you sing "Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit," you are not honoring two persons and adding a footnote. You are giving glory to the one God who loved you, redeemed you, and now lives in you.

topics.title: How is the Trinity worshipped: the essence or each Person?
topics.cmp: All four authors agree that the worship and glory given to God belong jointly to Father, Son, and Spirit, though they come at the question from different sides. John Owen speaks most broadly and most precisely about distinct direction: Scripture assigns faith, love, prayer, and praise to each Person respectively, so the saints address each Person in both moral and instituted worship. Basil and Ambrose focus on the Spirit's co-glorification, and they argue differently. Basil grounds it in the Lord's own ordering, chiefly the baptismal formula and the warning against blasphemy of the Spirit, and in the Spirit's inseparable association with the Godhead in confession, miracles, indwelling, and every gift; he also says the Spirit's honour exceeds any adequate measure. Ambrose instead argues from the economy of salvation: if we are glorified with Christ through the Spirit, the Spirit himself cannot be denied glory with Christ. Hippolytus, briefly and in doxological form rather than argument, affirms that the incarnate Son receives glory with the Father and the Spirit in the Church.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: That the Scripture doth distinctly assign all these unto the Father, Son, and Spirit, — manifesting that the saints do, in all of them, both as they are purely and nakedly moral, and as farther clothed with instituted worship, respect each person respectively

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Establishment of the natural communion of the Spirit…
refs.quote: What then ought to be thought of Him whom the world cannot receive, and Whom saints alone can contemplate through pureness of heart? What kind of honours can be deemed adequate to Him?

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: If we then shall be glorified together with Christ through the Spirit, how do we refuse to admit that the Spirit Himself is glorified together with Christ?

ans.text:
We worship one God, and that one God is never a faceless "something" behind the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. So the answer is both, rightly understood. When we worship, we worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, each with the same honor and glory. The reason each is worthy of that worship is the same for all three: each is fully God.

It helps to explain one word. The "essence" of God simply means what God is: his one divine being, with all its power, wisdom, holiness and love. The Father, Son and Spirit do not each have a separate share of this. Each is the whole of it. There are not three Gods standing side by side, and there is not a fourth thing called "the Godhead" hiding behind them. The one divine being exists as Father, Son and Spirit.

That is why worship does not split three ways. Scripture is firm that worship belongs to God alone. Jesus says in Matthew 4:10, "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only." Yet the same New Testament plainly gives divine worship to the Son and honors the Spirit as God. Jesus says the Father has given him judgment "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). Notice the words "just as": the same honor, not a lesser one. In Revelation 5:13 every creature in heaven and on earth gives praise, honor, glory and power both to the One on the throne and to the Lamb. The Spirit is not left out either. Jesus warns that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (Matthew 12:31-32). You cannot blaspheme a mere force or a creature in that way. And when Jesus sends his followers to baptize, he puts the Spirit's name right alongside his own and the Father's: "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). It is one name, not three, and the Spirit shares it equally.

So what exactly makes each Person worthy of worship? Not what sets him apart from the others. The Father is not worshipped because he is "the one who is not the Son," and the Son is not worshipped because he is "the one born of the Father." Each is worshipped because he is God: infinite in majesty, the source of all things, the One to whom we owe our very lives. That greatness is shared fully by all three. This has a lovely result. When you worship any one of them, you are never ignoring the other two. Love Jesus, and you are loving the God who is Father, Son and Spirit. Pray to the Father, and the Son and Spirit are not left outside the door. Jesus said, "Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him." The reverse is also true: to honor one truly is to honor all.

This does not mean the Persons blur together in our devotion. The Bible invites us to know and respond to each of them personally. Jesus tells his disciples, "You believe in God; believe in Me as well" (John 14:1). We trust the Father, who loved the world and gave his Son. We trust and love the Son, who gave himself for us. We rely on the Spirit, who lives in us, comforts us and makes us holy. Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 names all three: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you." Grace, love and fellowship come to us from the one God, yet we meet each Person in his own way.

The usual pattern of Christian prayer follows Ephesians 2:18: "through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit." We most often pray to the Father, through the Son, in the power of the Spirit. But this is not the only right way. Stephen prayed directly to Jesus as he died: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). Christians have long sung hymns and prayed prayers to the Holy Spirit as well. Speaking to any of the three is speaking to God.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. Some people quietly assume the Spirit deserves a little less honor than the Father and Son, as if he were a helper rather than God. Scripture does not allow that. The Spirit is glorified together with the Father and the Son. Others worry that if they pray mostly to Jesus, the Father might feel overlooked, or the reverse. There is no rivalry or jealousy within God. The Father delights when the Son is honored, and the Spirit's joy is to point us to Jesus. Still others imagine that worshipping "the essence" means worshipping a cold abstraction. It does not. It simply means we worship the Persons as the one true God, not as three separate deities.

Sincere Christians have differed a little over one practice: praying the same request to the Father, then to the Son, then to the Spirit, one after another. Some find this a rich way to confess that each Person is truly God and worthy to be addressed. Others hesitate, because it can suggest that we are making three separate requests and expecting three separate answers. Yet God acts toward us as one. Both sides agree on the main point. The three are one God, each is worthy of the same worship, and every blessing comes to us from Father, Son and Spirit working together.

So when you lift your heart in worship, you can do it with confidence. You may call on the Father, the Son or the Spirit, and you are worshipping the one God. Each receives the same glory, now and forever.

topics.title: What does the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 reveal about the Trinity?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Matthew 28:19 teaches the Trinity: one God in three distinct Persons, with the Son and Spirit fully divine and not creatures. Where Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius answer 'No' on the Son's divinity, they are rejecting the creaturely reading, not denying his divinity. Their grounds differ. Ambrose, Gregory of Nyssa and Warfield argue from the grammar of the text, the singular 'Name' (not 'Names') signifying one Godhead, with Warfield and Gregory adding that the repeated article or the naming of three subsistences marks distinct Persons. Basil and Owen argue from the Spirit's co-ordinate rank in one series, Basil rejecting any 'sub-numeration' or first-second-third counting and Owen showing the Socinian 'virtue of the Father' reading to be absurd. Athanasius, Owen and Bickersteth reason from what baptism does: it binds us to worship and joins us to God, so a creature or an abstraction named in it would mean idolatry, uselessness or confusion. Emphases also vary: Basil and Ambrose draw out the consequence that the Spirit must be glorified with the Father and Son. Owen, Hilary and Gregory of Nyssa treat the formula as the foundational and unalterable confession, Gregory turning it against Eunomius's renaming. Irenaeus ties it to regeneration. Warfield alone defends its authenticity on critical grounds and holds that it does not originate the doctrine but authoritatively announces a Trinity already presupposed.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Conclusion of the Book with a Prayer, and an Apology…
refs.quote: For the Truth would not say, Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, unless Thou wast a Trinity.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: This is a direct ascription to Jehovah the God of Israel, of a threefold personality, and is therewith the direct enunciation of the doctrine of the Trinity.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: He said, “in the Name,” not “in the Names.” So, then, the Name of the Father is not one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, for God is one

ans.text:
In one short command, Jesus names the God of the Christian faith, and that God is one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Just before he returned to heaven, he told his followers, “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). These are among his last and most solemn words. In them he does not invent a new idea. He puts into a single phrase what his whole ministry had already shown.

Start with what baptism means. To be baptized “in” or “into” someone’s name means to be handed over to that person, to belong to them and to serve them. Paul makes this point in 1 Corinthians 1:13, when he asks the Corinthians whether they were baptized into the name of Paul. Of course not. Being baptized into his name would have made them his followers. So whoever is named in baptism is the one we belong to and worship. In the Old Testament, God’s people bore the name of the LORD and no other (Numbers 6:27). Jesus now tells us whose name Christians bear.

Notice first that Jesus says “the name,” not “the names.” There is one name, because there is one God. The Bible never stops saying this: “The LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). If the Father, Son and Spirit were three separate gods, baptism would bind us to worship three gods, and that is exactly what Scripture forbids.

Yet within that one name Jesus lists three: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. He does not say “in the name of the Father-Son-Spirit,” as if these were three labels for one person. He names each one separately, side by side. And “the Son” here is Jesus himself, the one speaking. He is clearly a real person, distinct from the Father he prays to. Placed alongside him, the Father and the Spirit are just as clearly persons in their own right. We saw all three at Jesus’ own baptism. The Son stood in the water, the Spirit came down like a dove, and the Father spoke from heaven (Matthew 3:16–17). So the single “name” shows that God is one. The three titles show that within the one God there are three persons. Christians use the word “person” for each of these, and “essence” or “being” for the one divine life they share. Unity and distinction are both there in one sentence.

The command also shows that the Son and the Spirit are fully God, not created beings. Think how strange it would be to baptize people “in the name of God and of an angel.” No creature could share the name of the Creator in the act that makes us God’s children. Only God can make us his own. Jesus puts himself and the Spirit in the very same line as the Father, with nothing to set one above another. The Spirit is not a power or influence tacked on at the end. You would not baptize someone in the name of two persons and a force. He stands with the Son just as the Son stands with the Father. All three are equal.

This has a practical result. If we are baptized into the name of the Father, Son and Spirit, then we should believe in all three and worship all three. That is why Christians have always praised the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together. Paul blesses the church in the same threefold way: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14).

Why “Father, Son and Spirit” rather than other titles for God, such as Almighty or Creator? These names tell us who God is in himself, not just what he does for us. “Father” and “Son” belong together. You cannot be a father without a child. So if the Father has always been Father, the Son has always been with him. God did not become loving or relational when he made the world. He has always been a living fellowship of Father, Son and Spirit.

Two questions often come up. First, in Acts people are baptized “in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38). Does that contradict Matthew? Most Christians read Acts as describing what kind of baptism this was. It was baptism belonging to Jesus, distinct from John the Baptist’s baptism. Acts is not giving the exact words spoken. Some sincere believers take Acts to mean that the one “name” is Jesus, and that Father and Spirit are titles for him. But the Gospels show Jesus speaking to the Father and promising to send the Spirit as someone other than himself. So the historic church has held that the three are distinct, though never separate.

Second, some have questioned whether Jesus really said these words, suggesting a later church added them. Yet every ancient Greek manuscript of Matthew and every early translation contains the verse as we have it. A Christian manual of church life from around the end of the first century already tells believers to baptize in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. One early writer sometimes quoted the verse in a shortened form, but writers often abbreviated when they quoted. There is good reason to trust that these are Jesus’ own words.

So every Christian baptism is a small confession of the Trinity. When the water is poured and the threefold name is spoken, the one being baptized is claimed by the one God. That God is the Father who adopts us, the Son who saved us, and the Spirit who gives us new life. Jesus promised to be with us always (Matthew 28:20).

topics.title: Why must baptism invoke all three Persons, and when is it valid?
topics.cmp: Basil, Ambrose, Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius agree that baptism belongs to faith in Father, Son and Holy Spirit together. Basil ties the baptismal names to the same confession of faith. Gregory rejects Eunomius' substitute formula 'the one and only true God' because the Gospel command names the three. Ambrose and Athanasius both hold that naming the three is worthless if one Person is denied or lessened, and Athanasius applies this to declare Arian baptism, which names a created Son, empty. The authors differ plainly over partial formulas. Ambrose holds that baptism in Christ's name alone, or even in the Spirit's name alone, is complete when all three are believed, arguing from Scripture (Acts, 'baptized into one Spirit') and the unity of the divine work. Basil denies that a baptism invoking only the Spirit is perfect and insists that nothing be added to or taken from the handed-down tradition, though he too reads Paul's 'into Christ' as implicitly confessing the whole Trinity through the meaning of 'Anointed.' Basil alone discusses the martyrs' baptism in blood without water, the threefold immersion, and the legitimacy of joining the names with 'and.' Warfield, working instead from a survey of New Testament usage, adds that the order Father, Son, Spirit was apparently not regarded as essential, since the writers vary it freely.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Against those who assert that the baptism in the name of…
refs.quote: For as we believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, so are we also baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: although you name the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and lessen the power of either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, the whole mystery is made empty

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: But the order is very variable; and in the most formal enumeration of the three Persons, that of II Cor. xiii. 14, it stands thus: Lord, God, Spirit.

ans.text:
Baptism names the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit because Jesus himself told his church to baptize that way, and because the God we are baptized into really is Father, Son and Spirit. In Matthew 28:19 the risen Lord says, "go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Christians did not invent this wording. They received it as a command from Christ.

Notice that Jesus says "the name," not "the names." There is one God, so there is one name. Yet that one name belongs to three: Father, Son and Spirit. In a single sentence the verse teaches both the oneness of God and the reality of the three Persons. Baptism places a person into that name. It is a little like being taken into a family and given its name. You are not joined to a vague higher power. You are joined to the living God as he has shown himself to be.

This is why faith and baptism belong together. What we believe and what is done to us in baptism should match. We trust the Father, we trust the Son, and we trust the Spirit, and then we are baptized into the same three. The confession of faith comes first, and baptism seals it. If baptism named only one Person, it would not fit the faith it is meant to seal.

The Bible shows the three Persons at work together from the start. When Jesus was baptized, the Spirit came down on him like a dove, and the Father's voice spoke from heaven (Matthew 3:16-17). Paul says that "in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body" (1 Corinthians 12:13). In Romans 6:4 he says we were "buried with Him through baptism into death," so that, just as Christ was raised "through the glory of the Father," we too may walk in new life. Father, Son and Spirit act together in every saving work. Their work cannot be divided, so baptism does not divide them either.

But doesn't the book of Acts speak of baptism "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38)? It does. Most Christians have understood these words to mean baptism by Jesus' authority and into belonging to him. They mark it off from the baptism of John the Baptist. They are not a different formula that replaces the one Jesus gave.

The name "Christ" itself points to all three Persons. It means "the Anointed One." Peter says that "God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power" (Acts 10:38). So to confess Christ is to confess the Father who anointed, the Son who was anointed, and the Spirit with whom he was anointed.

Christians in the early centuries did not fully agree on one point. Some held that a baptism in Jesus' name could still be complete, as long as the person truly believed in all three Persons. Others insisted that the words Jesus gave must be used exactly, with nothing added and nothing taken away. Over time, the church as a whole settled firmly on using the words of Matthew 28:19. That is the safe and faithful path, because it is the one the Lord himself commanded.

So when is a baptism genuine? The historic answer is simple. Water is used, and the person is baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as the church intends to do what Christ commanded. Because of this, many churches gladly recognize baptisms done in other Christian churches, even when they disagree on other matters. A baptism does not depend on the personal holiness of the minister. It depends on Christ's promise.

There is one important limit. Saying the right words is not enough if they are emptied of their meaning. Suppose a group says "Father, Son and Spirit" but teaches that the Son is a created being, made from nothing, or that the Spirit is only an impersonal force. Then they are not really baptizing into the God of the Bible. They are using his names for a different god. In the early church, people who denied that the Son is truly God used the same words, and the church judged that their baptism was empty. The reasoning is plain. To deny any one of the three, or to make one of them less than fully God, is to overthrow the whole. For this reason most churches today do not accept baptisms from groups that reject the Trinity.

What about the order Father, Son, Spirit? It is the order Jesus gave, and it fits how God has acted. The Father sends, the Son comes, and the Spirit applies the Son's work to us. So it is fitting to keep it in baptism. Still, the order does not mean that one Person is more God than another. Elsewhere the New Testament feels free to vary it. Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 runs, "May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all." There the Son comes first.

The same is true in worship. When we sing "Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit," the word "and" puts all three side by side as equals. It comes straight from the pattern of Jesus' baptismal command. Some prayers say "with" instead, glorifying the Father together with the Son and the Spirit. Both forms are faithful. Each gives the Spirit the same honor as the Father and the Son.

Many churches baptize with three immersions, one for each Person, and others with a single immersion or by pouring. Christians differ on which way is best. Going under the water pictures being buried with Christ and rising with him, as Romans 6 describes. Doing it three times makes the one name of the three Persons visible. Churches that use one immersion or pouring stress that God is one, and that the words, not the number of dippings, carry the meaning. On both sides, the threefold name itself is not optional.

Finally, the water matters because Christ commanded it. But the power of baptism comes from God, not from the water. The Spirit gives new life. The church has long held that someone who truly believes but is killed for Christ before being baptized is not lost. Such a believer has, in a sense, been baptized in their own blood. This does not make baptism unimportant. It reminds us whose gift baptism is: the gift of the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit.

topics.title: What must one believe about the Son and the Spirit to be saved?
topics.cmp: The authors agree that saving faith cannot stop at the Father: Hilary of Poitiers insists one must confess Christ as truly the Son of God and as both very God and very man. Irenaeus makes faith in the Son the first part of the greater righteousness, and Ambrose sees confession of the Son's oneness with the Father as what separated Peter from Judas. Bickersteth likewise calls Christ's deity a foundation truth on which eternal life or death depends. Ambrose and Basil extend this to the Spirit, though on different grounds: Ambrose argues from the Spirit being one and the same Spirit of God and of Christ, while Basil argues from the Spirit's necessary role in confessing Jesus as Lord and from the baptismal covenant in the threefold Name. That baptismal emphasis is shared by Gregory of Nyssa, who holds that salvation is ratified by confessing the Names and partaking of the sacraments, not by doctrine alone. Warfield, for his part, reads the threefold Name of the great commission as the new Name of Jehovah. There is real tension, however, over how much precision is required: Owen says exact grasp of generation, procession and mutual in-being is not necessary for saving faith, and Gregory holds that sound thought matters more than wording, whereas Basil defends close scrutiny of syllables and prepositions as part of the path to likeness to God.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: what faith is it, pray, to deny Him to be true God, and to call Him a creature, when it is no faith to believe in the only true God without Christ?

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: this could not possibly have meant to His disciples anything else than that Jehovah was now to be known to them by the new Name, of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: every one, when the words father and son are spoken, at once recognizes the proper and natural relationship to one another which they imply. This relationship is conveyed at once by the appellations themselves.

ans.text:
To be saved, a person must trust Jesus as he truly is: the Son of God who shares the Father's own life and comes to us with the Father's own Spirit. Faith does not need a theology degree or a command of technical terms. But it does need to rest on the real Jesus, and the real Jesus is God the Son.

It helps to separate two things that are easy to blur. One is the faith that saves. The other is the full and careful explanation of that faith. A child who prays to Jesus, a new believer who has never heard the word "Trinity," and the dying thief who simply asked Jesus to remember him all had saving faith. None of them could have explained how the Son is eternally from the Father or how the Spirit relates to both. The Bible never makes those fine explanations the entrance exam for heaven. They are true and worth learning, because they protect and deepen our faith. But we are saved by trusting the Lord, not by passing a test on how to describe him.

At the same time, faith is not a blank feeling that can attach itself to anything. It always has an object, and its worth depends on that object. Leaning your full weight on a rotten beam will not hold you up, however sincere you are. This is why the Bible keeps pointing to who Jesus is. John wrote his Gospel "so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name" (John 20:31). In John 3:18 Jesus says that whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God's one and only Son. Notice what he says. The unbeliever is not condemned by some new sentence. He stands apart from God because he has turned away from the one through whom God draws near. The believer is joined to God through the Son and so is no longer under condemnation.

Why does it matter that the Son is truly God and not a creature? Because of what we are trusting him to do. In Philippians 3:9 Paul longs to be found in Christ, not having his own righteousness from the law, but the righteousness that comes from God through faith in Christ. Only God can give God's own righteousness. Only God can forgive sins against God, and only God can be the one we worship and rely on completely. If Jesus were merely the greatest of creatures, putting our whole hope in him would be putting our hope in something less than God. Jesus himself joins faith in God and faith in himself as one act. "Believe in God; believe also in Me" (John 14:1). And John says plainly, "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well" (1 John 2:23). You cannot keep the Father while pushing the Son away. The Father has made himself known in the Son.

The same is true of the Holy Spirit. Saving faith is not something we produce and then hand to God. It is the Spirit's work in us. "No one can say, 'Jesus is Lord,' except by the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:3). So a person who truly trusts Christ already has the Spirit at work in him, even before he can explain who the Spirit is. To knowingly reject the Spirit would be to reject the very one who brings us to the Son, just as rejecting the Son shuts us off from the Father. This is why Jesus sent his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). He speaks of one name, not three. The God of Israel was now to be known and confessed as Father, Son and Spirit. Coming to Christ means coming into the life of this one God.

So what is required? At its heart, what Paul says in Romans 10:9: if you confess with your mouth, "Jesus is Lord," and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. To call Jesus "Lord" in the Bible's sense is to give him the honor that belongs to God. A simple believer who does this has the substance of the whole faith, even if the words come later. The danger lies elsewhere. It lies with someone who has heard who Jesus is and deliberately rejects it, insisting he is only a man, a lesser god, or a created being. That person is not stumbling in understanding. He is turning from the Jesus the Bible presents. Jesus warned, "if you do not believe that I am He, you will die in your sins" (John 8:24).

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. Some people fear they must get every word exactly right or be lost. God looks at the heart, and he hears even our clumsy prayers. Still, words matter, because they carry our thoughts and shape how we teach others. That is why Christians have cared about saying things carefully. It is also why we keep the Bible's own names, Father, Son and Spirit. Those names tell us at once that the Son truly comes from the Father and shares his nature, as any son shares his father's. Others imagine that sound doctrine alone saves, as though agreeing to correct statements were enough. But even the demons believe there is one God and shudder (James 2:19). Saving faith is trust and surrender to the living God, not just correct opinions about him.

Sincere Christians have differed on some related questions. One is how much a person must explicitly know. Some stress that faith must include a clear grasp of Christ's deity, because faith must know whom it trusts. Others stress that God receives the smallest real trust in the true Christ, and that understanding grows afterward. Most agree on what matters most: real faith clings to the real Christ, and it will not finally reject him once it sees him clearly. Christians have also differed on how closely baptism and the Lord's Supper are tied to salvation. Some see them as means God uses to give and confirm his grace, pointing to Jesus' words about being born of water and the Spirit. Others see them as signs that follow and display a faith already given, pointing to the many verses that tie salvation to believing. Both sides agree that Christ commanded them and that no one should treat them lightly.

If you trust Jesus as your Lord and Savior, you are trusting the Son of God, by the work of the Spirit, and through him you have the Father. You may not yet be able to explain it all. Like the father in the Gospel, you can pray, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24). Learning more about the Trinity is not a hoop to jump through before God accepts you. It is a way of coming to know better the God who has already welcomed you.

topics.title: What follows for those who deny the Son's true Godhead?
topics.cmp: Bickersteth, Ambrose, Hilary and Gregory of Nyssa agree that denying the Son's true and eternal Godhead is no minor error: it puts one outside genuine Christian faith. They draw different consequences from it. Bickersteth argues from Scripture's witness that the Son shares the Father's essence, and he stresses doctrinal fallout: such denial is the 'denial of the Son' Scripture condemns, it empties the atonement, it charges the Church with idolatry, and it disbelieves God's record of his Son. Ambrose and Hilary focus on whether the deniers belong to Christ and his Church at all. Ambrose holds that Christ does not recognize his Name where it is cut off from the Father and the Spirit, and that the denier's own soul is broken and loses its coherence. Hilary holds that anyone preaching a Christ who is not Son by generation and God by nature preaches another Christ and falls outside the one faith of the one baptism. Gregory alone argues by philosophical reductio, backed by the historical example of the heathen: worshipping a created Son, as Eunomius' view implies, removes any principled stopping point, so deification spreads through all creation into polytheism and idolatry.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: what can denial of the Son be, if to deny his Godhead be not this negation?

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: I do not recognize My Name where My eternal Godhead is not. That is not My Name which is divided from the Father, and separated from the Spirit

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: the Divine element, once recognized in creation, will become a stepping-stone to the like conception in the case of that which is next contemplated, and that again for the next in order

ans.text:
Scripture treats this as a very serious matter: to deny that the Son is truly God is not a small difference of opinion but a denial of who Jesus actually is, and it changes the faith, the worship, and the baptism that rest on Him. That does not mean we may write off any particular person. But we should be clear about what the teaching itself leads to.

Start with the Bible's own warning. John writes, "Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well" (1 John 2:22-23). Some people say, "I don't deny the Son. I believe in Jesus. I just don't believe He is God." But denying the Son is not only refusing to say the word "Son." It is refusing what God has said about His Son. And God has said a great deal. The Son was with God in the beginning and was God (John 1:1). Through Him all things were made. Thomas falls before the risen Jesus and calls Him "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28), and Jesus accepts it. To keep the name "Son" while emptying it of what the Father has revealed about Him is still to deny the Son. John even says that whoever does not believe God's testimony about His Son has made God out to be a liar (1 John 5:10).

Notice too what John says follows: such a person "does not have the Father." We cannot keep the Father while lowering the Son. Jesus says the Father wants "all" to "honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him" (John 5:23). The Father is honored when His Son is honored as He is, and dishonored when the Son is made less than He is.

This brings up worship. The Bible draws one sharp line through all reality: on one side the Creator, on the other everything He made. Worship belongs only on the Creator's side. Jesus Himself says, "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only" (Matthew 4:10). When John falls at the feet of a glorious angel, the angel stops him at once and tells him to worship God (Revelation 22:8-9). Paul describes the root of human idolatry as worshiping and serving created things in place of the Creator (Romans 1:25).

Yet the Son is worshiped. God says of Him, "Let all God's angels worship Him" (Hebrews 1:6). The disciples worshiped Him. Every knee will bow to Him (Philippians 2:10-11). So there are only two choices. Either the Son is truly God, and worshiping Him is right, or He is a creature, and worshiping Him is idolatry. There is no safe middle ground where Jesus is a very high creature who is still worshiped.

Think about where that middle ground leads. If we may worship one creature because he is great and powerful, what stops us from worshiping the next greatest, and the next? Angels are mighty. The sun gives life to the earth. This is exactly how the nations around Israel fell into worshiping many gods. They admired the great things in creation, honored them one after another, and ended up worshiping the sun, moon, stars, and powers of nature. Once the line between Creator and creature is crossed even once, there is no principled place to stop. So the teaching that the Son is a created being, yet worthy of worship, does not protect belief in one God. It quietly undermines it. The only way to worship Jesus and still worship one God is to confess that He shares the one true nature of God with the Father.

It also touches the gospel itself. If Jesus is a creature, then God did not come Himself to save us. He sent someone else. The wonder of the cross is that God "purchased" the church "with His own blood" (Acts 20:28). The worth of Christ's sacrifice rests on who He is. Make Him less than God, and His saving work is made less too.

Then there is baptism. Jesus told His followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice it says one name, not three names of very different ranks. The Son stands alongside the Father and the Spirit, sharing the one divine name. Paul speaks of "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all" (Ephesians 4:5-6). The one faith is a faith in a particular Lord, the One the apostles preached. Paul warns about those who preach "another Jesus" (2 Corinthians 11:4). Someone can use the name of Jesus and still mean a different Jesus. To confess Christ while denying that He is truly God's Son and truly God is not the same faith in different words. It is a different faith. Faith is not only how sincerely we believe. It is also who we believe in.

Because of this, sincere Christians have had to decide how to regard baptisms performed by groups that openly deny the Son's deity. Many churches do not recognize such baptisms. Their reason is that the words of Matthew 28:19 were used with a different meaning, so the one faith was not really confessed. Others are more cautious about judging a baptism by the mistaken beliefs of whoever performed it. Yet nearly all agree on the main point. The faith into which Christians are baptized confesses the Son as truly God.

What does all this mean for how we treat people? First, we must keep the line between a teaching and a person. Many people raised in groups that deny Christ's deity have never really heard the Bible's case. Others are honestly confused or still learning. Judgment of hearts belongs to God, not to us. Second, we should not be careless. John warns that anyone who goes beyond the teaching of Christ, and does not remain in it, does not have God (2 John 9). Calling Jesus "Lord, Lord" is not enough if we refuse who He really is (Matthew 7:21). It is not loving to pretend that this difference does not matter. Third, our response should be patient, gentle persuasion from Scripture, with the hope that the person will come to say with Thomas, "My Lord and my God!"

For believers, this is also an encouragement. When you worship Jesus, pray to Him, and trust Him with your life, you are not giving a creature what belongs to God. You are honoring the Son just as you honor the Father, and in doing so you have the Father as well.

title: Communion with the Father, Son and Spirit
desc: Believers' communion with each divine Person, the Father's love, union and delight in Christ, adoption, and allegorical readings of the Song of Songs.

topics.title: What is communion with God, and how can sinful people have it?
topics.cmp: John Owen dominates this topic, and his answers form one connected account. Communion is a mutual communication of good things grounded on a prior union, as with Jonathan and David. Sinners have such fellowship with God only through Christ, who is himself the way and the medium of all traffic between God and believers. Owen argues mainly from Scripture (John 14:6, Hebrews on the veil and new way, Revelation 3:20 read alongside the Song of Songs, 1 John 4:10, Rom. 5:8). He sets this against Aristotle's verdict that the disparity between God and man rules out friendship, holding that corrupt nature alone yields only terror. He also distinguishes the real but veiled communion of Old Testament saints from the boldness given in the gospel. Augustine agrees with Owen that God's love comes first, but he grounds it differently: Owen argues from human enmity and Christ dying for sinners, while Augustine reasons from God's timelessness and predestination, so that it is the convert, not God, who changes. Gregory of Nyssa and Novatian address neighbouring questions rather than communion itself. Gregory explains how humanity lost its filial relation to God by losing the Father's image through sin and becoming kin to the devil by likeness of will. Novatian treats God's anger and threats as medicinal acts of wisdom, not passion, meant to recall people to virtue.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: By Jesus Christ alone, then, on all considerations as to being and full manifestation, is this distance taken away.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: And the name of Godhead itself, whether it indicates the authority of oversight or of foresight, imports a certain relation to humanity. For He Who bestowed on all things that are, the power of being, is the God and overseer of what He has Himself produced.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: What is Said of God in Time, is Said Relatively, Not…
refs.quote: far be it from us to say, that God loves any one in time with as it were a new love, which was not in Him before, with whom things gone by have not passed away and things future have been already done.

ans.text:
Communion with God is a shared life with him: God gives himself to us in love, and we answer him with trust, love and obedience, with delight on both sides. Sinful people can have it only because God himself has opened the way through Jesus Christ.

Think first about what communion means between people. It is more than knowing about someone or living near them. It is a two-way sharing of good things between people who are already bound together and who enjoy each other. The Bible gives a picture in David and Jonathan. Their hearts were knit together in love, and from that bond flowed everything else: gifts, loyalty, protection, open hearts. First the bond, then the sharing.

Communion with God works the same way, only far higher. The bond is the union God makes between himself and his people. What is shared is God's own love, grace, comfort and life, and in return our faith, praise and grateful obedience. John writes that he proclaimed the gospel so his readers could share in a fellowship that "is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ" (1 John 1:3). That is the goal of the whole Christian message.

This is not the same as God's general care for everything he made. God sends rain on everyone and keeps every creature alive. But communion is personal friendship. It is being welcomed into God's own household as his children.

Why is that so hard to come by? Not mainly because God is great and we are small. That gap is real, but God made us for himself, in his image, to know him. The real problem is sin. When Adam and Eve sinned, their first response to God's presence was to hide. Isaiah tells Israel that their wrongdoing has put a barrier between them and their God. Left to ourselves, a sinful conscience does not draw us toward God. It makes us afraid of him, or makes us invent smaller gods we can manage. On our own we cannot cross that distance, and we do not even want to.

This is where Jesus Christ comes in, and he is the only way. He says in John 14:6, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me." Notice that he does not say he shows us a way. He is the way. He took our sin on himself and died for it, so the barrier is removed and pardon is real. He rose and entered God's presence as our high priest. Hebrews says we now have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place "by the blood of Jesus," by "a new and living way" opened through his own body (Hebrews 10:19-20). Every kindness of God comes down to us through Christ, and every prayer, praise and act of love goes up to God through him.

The whole Trinity is at work here. Paul puts it in a single line: "through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit" (Ephesians 2:18). We come to the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit. The Spirit opens our blind eyes to see Christ, joins us to him by faith, and gives us the confidence to call God "Father." People who refuse Christ usually do so because they have never truly seen him. Paul says those who crucified him would not have done it had they understood who he was. When the Spirit shows us Christ's glory, we come gladly.

The believers of the Old Testament, like Abraham, Enoch and David, really did walk with God. Their communion was real, and it rested on the same promised Savior. But they had it as if through a curtain, with less freedom and boldness. The way into the holiest place was not yet fully open. Now that Christ has come and finished his work, believers can draw near with a confidence that even those great saints longed for.

This communion runs both ways. Jesus says in Revelation 3:20, "If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me." A shared meal is a picture of friendship. Christ feeds us with his grace, his word and his presence. Amazingly, he also takes pleasure in us, in the faith and love his own Spirit has grown in our hearts.

Above all, this communion begins with God's love, not ours. "We love because He first loved us" (1 John 4:19). John says love consists in this: "not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins" (1 John 4:10). God did not wait until we became lovely. "While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). He loves us not because we are better than others, but because he is good.

That clears up a common misunderstanding. When someone turns to God, God does not suddenly start feeling a new love he never had before. God does not change. We are the ones who change. His love for his people goes back before the world was made (Ephesians 1:4), and conversion is the moment that love reaches us and we wake up to it. Even God's warnings and anger against sin are not the opposite of that love. Like strong medicine, they are meant to call us back from ruin to himself.

Another misunderstanding is that communion with God belongs only to a few spiritual experts, or that it must be earned by intense feelings or effort. It is the ordinary birthright of every believer in Christ. It is enjoyed in plain ways: hearing and trusting God's word, praying to the Father in Jesus' name, coming to the Lord's Table, obeying from a grateful heart, and resting in his love when we feel weak. Feelings rise and fall, but the open door Christ made stays open.

So the answer is both humbling and wonderful. On our own, sinners can only hide from God. In Christ, the Father welcomes us, the Son brings us near, and the Spirit makes that nearness real in our hearts.

topics.title: How do believers have communion with each Person of the Trinity, and especially with Christ?
topics.cmp: John Owen supplies nearly all the answers. He holds, mainly from Scripture (1 John 1:3, 1 Cor. 1:9, 2 Cor. 13:14, Rom. 5 and 8, the Song of Songs), that believers have distinct communion with each Person: with the Father chiefly in love, with the Son in grace under the image of marriage, and with the Spirit as Comforter, whom they meet in his works and must not grieve, quench or resist. He qualifies this by saying such ascriptions are 'principally and by way of eminency' and do not exclude the other Persons, and his preface appeals to Clarke, Stuckley and the early church against the charge of novelty. Basil and Irenaeus agree with Owen that access to the Father and Son comes through the Spirit, but their emphasis differs: Basil argues that worship without the Spirit is impossible, so denying the Spirit forfeits true worship, while Irenaeus uses the analogies of Adam's breath and of water binding dough into one loaf to tie the Spirit's uniting work to the Church and baptism rather than to the individual soul's affections. Hilary differs plainly from Owen: he says Christ dwells in believers 'naturally' through truly receiving his flesh in the Eucharist, whereas Owen says communion with God is voluntary and by consent, not natural, and that Christ dwells in his people by his Spirit. Augustine's answers touch the topic only at its edges. He asks whether the Spirit is properly 'love' or whether love belongs to the Father, the Son or the Trinity, while Owen ascribes love peculiarly to the Father. Augustine also denies that faith depends on imagining Christ's bodily appearance, which fits Owen's view that Christ's personal grace is not the outward look of his humanity.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: That the saints have distinct communion with the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit (that is, distinctly with the Father, and distinctly with the Son, and distinctly with the Holy Spirit)

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: That they who deny the Spirit are transgressors.
refs.quote: it is impossible to worship the Son, save by the Holy Ghost; impossible to call upon the Father, save by the Spirit of adoption.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In What Way We Must Inquire Concerning the Trinity.
refs.quote: our wish is to see whether the Holy Spirit is properly that love which is most excellent which if He is not, either the Father is love, or the Son, or the Trinity itself

ans.text:
Believers have real fellowship with God, and that fellowship is with each Person: we receive and return the Father's love, we live on the Son's grace, and we enjoy the Spirit's comfort and presence. This is not three separate relationships with three gods. It is one fellowship with the one God, who meets us as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

First, what is communion? It is not just having right ideas about God. It is a living exchange. God gives himself to us, and we give back to him the trust, love and obedience he delights in. Think of a close friendship or a good marriage. There is giving and receiving on both sides. That exchange is possible only because we have been joined to God through Jesus Christ. John puts it boldly in 1 John 1:3: "And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ."

The Bible treats this fellowship as personal with each of the three. Paul's familiar blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14 shows this: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you." Grace is linked with the Son, love with the Father, and fellowship with the Spirit. We pray to the Father, we trust and honour the Son, and we are told not to grieve the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30). Each of these is directed to a Person. So our communion with God has a distinct shape toward each.

With the Father, the heart of it is his love. It is free, undeserved and eternal. It came before anything we did. In fact, it is why the Son was sent at all: "In this is love: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son" (1 John 4:10). Fellowship with the Father means looking at that love, believing it is really aimed at you, resting in it, and loving him back. Many Christians quietly picture the Father as stern and Jesus as the kind one who talks him round. Scripture says the opposite. The Father's love is the source of the whole rescue.

With the Son, the heart of it is grace. Paul says God "has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:9). This fellowship has several sides.

There is union. Jesus says, "I am the vine and you are the branches" (John 15:5). A branch does not just admire the vine. It is joined to it and lives by its sap. By faith, and through the Spirit, we are joined to Christ. So Paul can say, "Christ lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). Christ is not only beside us or ahead of us. He dwells in his people.

There are the benefits of his death. Because we are united to him, what he won becomes ours. His death counts as our death to sin's penalty. His righteousness covers us.
