His resurrection life begins in us. Communion with Christ means coming to him again and again to receive these things. We bring him our sins and he gives us his pardon. We bring our emptiness and he gives his fullness.

There is his presence and friendship. In Revelation 3:20 the risen Lord says, "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me." Sharing a meal is the Bible's picture of warm, unhurried closeness. Christ means to be known as a friend, not just a doctrine.

There is strength. Apart from him we can do nothing (John 15:5). Yet with him Paul can say, "I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength" (Philippians 4:13). When Paul begged to be rid of his weakness, Christ answered, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Fellowship with Christ often happens right at the point where we feel weakest.

And there is sympathy in suffering. The risen Christ is not distant from his people's pain. When Saul was hunting down Christians, Jesus asked him, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?" (Acts 9:4). What is done to his people, he takes as done to him. Hebrews tells us our High Priest is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). So in trouble we do not only receive help from Christ. We also share our trouble with one who feels it with us.

The Lord's Supper is one of the main places where this communion with Christ is enjoyed. Jesus says that whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood remains in him, and he in them (John 6:56). Paul calls the cup and the bread a sharing in Christ's blood and body (1 Corinthians 10:16). All Christians agree that Christ really meets his people at his table. Sincere believers differ on how. Some hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present in or with the bread and wine, and they take Jesus' words very directly. Others hold that Christ is truly present by his Spirit and received by faith, stressing that his risen body is now in heaven. Either way, the Supper is meant to deepen real union with Christ, not just to jog our memory.

With the Holy Spirit, the heart of it is comfort and life. Jesus promised "another Advocate," often translated Comforter or Helper (John 14:16). The Spirit is the one who actually brings God's promises home to us. When a verse you have read a hundred times suddenly warms and steadies you, that is the Spirit at work. It is good to recognise him in that moment and thank him. He pours God's love into our hearts (Romans 5:5). He makes us cry, "Abba, Father!" (Romans 8:15). He shows us the things of Christ (John 16:14). Scripture also describes our side of this fellowship mostly as warnings, and each one implies a duty. We are not to grieve him, for he lives in us as a Person. We are not to quench him, but to welcome his promptings. We are not to resist him as he works through God's Word and the gifts he gives the church.

The Spirit is also the bond of all the rest. We cannot truly call God Father except by the Spirit, and no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). He is the one who unites us to Christ and makes many believers one body, the church. So fellowship with the Spirit always leads into fellowship with the Father and the Son.

This raises a fair question. If love belongs to the Father, does that mean the Son and Spirit do not love us? Not at all. God is one, and the three Persons never act apart. When we enjoy the Father's love, the Son and Spirit are present in it too. The point is only that each Person is especially and most directly connected with certain gifts, as Scripture itself presents them. We worship one God, not a committee. But we know that one God more fully when we notice how each Person comes to us.

Two more things keep this from becoming mere sentiment. First, fellowship is tied to holiness. John says that if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship (1 John 1:7). Clinging to sin does not bring nearness, only darkness and confusion. Second, our fellowship now is real but partial. It is the first light of dawn, not yet full day. One day "we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2), and communion with Father, Son and Spirit will be complete.

In practice, this can shape ordinary devotion. When you pray, you can come to the Father as a dearly loved child. You can lean on the Son for pardon, strength and company. And you can ask the Spirit to make these things real in your heart, thanking him when he does.

topics.title: How do believers have communion with the Father in his love?
topics.cmp: Nearly all answers on this topic come from John Owen, and his answers are consistent. The Father has a peculiar love, eternal, free, unchangeable and distinguishing. It is the fountain of Christ's purchase, not its fruit. Believers receive it by faith, the Spirit reveals it, and it is communicated and returned only through Christ. Owen grounds these points chiefly in Scripture (Zeph. 3:17, 1 John 4:9-10, John 14:23, Titus 3:4-6, Rom. 5:8, Eph. 1:3-4) and in images such as Aaron's anointing oil and the fountain, with some philosophical reasoning about God's immutable will and the commensurability of his power and will. Hilary of Poitiers agrees with Owen's insistence on mediation through Christ, holding from 1 John that no one loves the Father except through faith in the Son, though he argues only from Scripture and with nothing like Owen's elaboration. Augustine of Hippo addresses a different point: God loves us now, as shown in his not sparing his Son, but loves us as we shall be rather than as we are, which marks a difference in emphasis from Owen. For Owen the Father's love is a love of rest and delight (complacency) in believers, not merely a love of willing them good, whereas Augustine's answer frames it as directed toward what they will become through faith leading to sight.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: There is love in the person of the Father peculiarly held out unto the saints, as wherein he will and doth hold communion with them.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For we have no love within us towards God the Father except through faith in the Son.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to…
refs.quote: not that He does not now love us, who spared not His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all; but God loves us, such as we shall be, not such as we are

ans.text:
Believers have communion with the Father in his love by receiving that love through faith in Jesus Christ, resting in it, and answering it with love of their own: trust, delight, reverence and obedience. Communion simply means shared life, a real giving and receiving between two persons. Here the Father gives his love, and we take it and return what love we can.

The Bible speaks of the whole Trinity loving us. Yet it often presents love as the Father's own special gift. Paul's blessing speaks of "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Corinthians 13:14). There "God" means the Father. Jesus says in John 16:27, "For the Father Himself loves you." He said this partly to correct a mistake his disciples might make, and one we still make. We can picture the Father as stern and distant, and the Son as the kind one who talks him round. Scripture says the opposite. The Father did not start loving us because Jesus died. Jesus died because the Father loved us. "For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son" (John 3:16). "Love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins" (1 John 4:10). The Father's love is the spring. The cross is the channel through which that love reaches sinners. This is also why Jesus says he will ask the Father to send the Spirit, but never says he will ask the Father to love his disciples (John 14:16; 16:26-27). The Spirit is a gift Christ won for us. The Father's love is where the whole plan of salvation came from in the first place.

This love has three marks that every believer should know. First, it is eternal. The Father "chose us in Him before the foundation of the world" (Ephesians 1:4). He loved his people before they existed, before they had done anything good or bad. Second, it is free. Nothing lovely in us drew it out. "God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). He loves because he is good, not because we are. That is exactly what makes the love so precious. Third, it is unchanging. Our feelings rise and fall, and our faithfulness wavers. Peter swore loyalty and then denied Jesus the same night. But the Father's love is as steady as God himself. If our failures could cancel it, it would have been cancelled long ago. What does change is how much we sense it and enjoy it. A child who disobeys may lose the warmth of a father's smile for a while and feel his discipline (Hebrews 12:6), but he is still his father's child.

This love comes to us only through Christ, and our love goes back only through him. Jesus says, "No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6). Every blessing the Father means for us is first given to the Son and then shared from him: "From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace" (John 1:16). Think of the anointing oil poured on the high priest's head that ran down onto his robes (Psalm 133:2). Love is poured on Christ and flows down to those joined to him. In the same way, our prayers and praise are imperfect, but they reach the Father through Jesus our high priest, who makes them acceptable. So faith usually comes to Christ first, as the one who saves. But it does not stop there. Through him it reaches the Father and rests in the Father's own heart.

How do we receive this love? By believing it. That sounds too simple, but it is the heart of the matter. It is not enough to admire the idea that God is loving. We must take the Father at his word that he loves us. We let that truth settle our minds and win our wills, and we let it fill our hearts. The Holy Spirit helps us do this. "God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Romans 5:5). The Spirit moves us to cry "Abba, Father!" (Galatians 4:6). Many Christians believe in Jesus yet still half fear the Father. Communion with the Father begins when we let ourselves believe that he himself is for us.

Our love back is different from his, and that is fine. His love comes down, like rain, and creates good where there was none. Ours rises up, like a grateful child's. It adds nothing to God; we cannot make him richer. Yet he delights in it. Our love looks like resting in him, enjoying him, honoring him, and obeying him. Remarkably, God takes pleasure in his people too. "He will rejoice over you with gladness... He will rejoice over you with singing" (Zephaniah 3:17). The Father does not merely wish us well from a distance. He delights in his children. "We love because He first loved us" (1 John 4:19). His love always comes first and never wavers, and ours always follows and often wavers.

This is also why real communion with the Father cannot exist alongside a careless, worldly life. "If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie" (1 John 1:6). This does not mean only perfect people know God's love. It means that his love, once truly believed, changes us. It is the strongest reason there is to want to please him.

Christians have disagreed on one related point: whether the Father's saving love is set on particular people he has chosen, or offered equally to all. Those who hold the first view point to passages about God's choice, such as Romans 9:13 and Ephesians 1:4-5. Those who hold the second point to God's desire that all be saved (1 Timothy 2:4) and to John 3:16. Both sides agree that the Father's love is free and not earned, and that it is fully trustworthy for everyone who comes to him through Christ. Whoever believes in the Son may rest without fear in the love of the Father.

topics.title: What is the mutual love and delight between Christ and believers?
topics.cmp: Christ's love for and delight in his people, the beauty he sees in them, the marriage covenant between Christ and the soul, and how he regards believers in their sin and suffering.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: Now, there is not any thing more grievous to the Lord, nor more subservient to the design of Satan upon the soul, than such thoughts as these.

ans.text:
Christ truly loves and enjoys his people, and they in turn come to love and enjoy him. It is a real relationship of mutual delight, which the Bible most often pictures as a marriage between a bridegroom and his bride.

Many Christians find this hard to believe. They may accept that Jesus died for them. But they imagine that he now looks at them with tired patience or quiet disappointment, putting up with them rather than enjoying them. The Bible paints a very different picture. Zephaniah 3:17 says, "The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing." Notice the gladness, the rest and the singing. Isaiah 62:5 says that "as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you." Think of the happiest moment at a wedding, when the groom first sees his bride. Scripture uses that very picture for how Christ regards his people.

To delight in someone means more than being kind to them. It means your love overflows into joy. Your heart is at rest and glad in their company. That is what Christ feels toward those who belong to him. One clear sign of it is that he opens his heart to them. People share their deepest thoughts only with close friends. Jesus says in John 15:15 that he no longer calls his disciples servants but friends, because he has made known to them what he heard from his Father. He also invites them to pour out their own hearts to him in prayer.

An honest believer will ask how a holy Lord can delight in people who still sin. The answer is that Christ himself makes his people lovely. Ephesians 5:25-27 says that Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. He did this to make her clean and holy, and to present her to himself without stain or wrinkle. He washed away our guilt with his own blood, because nothing else could. He clothes us with his own perfect righteousness. By his Spirit he is steadily changing us from the inside. So when Christ calls his people beautiful, he is not pretending they are better than they are. He is admiring the beauty he has put on them. It is like a groom who has paid for, sewn and fitted his bride's wedding dress himself, and then rejoices to see her wearing it.

This love cost him dearly. Philippians 2 describes the eternal Son emptying himself. He took the form of a servant and became obedient even to death on a cross. His whole earthly life of prayer, tears, obedience and suffering was undertaken for his people's sake. He did it willingly. He said that doing his Father's will was his food.

What does Christ ask of a sinner before he gives himself to them like this? Nothing but that they receive him. In the gospel he offers himself freely, as Saviour, Lord and husband. He does not wait for us to make ourselves attractive first. When a person trusts him and says yes to him, he binds himself to them for ever. Everything that is his becomes theirs: his righteousness, his grace, his life.

That raises the question of our sin after we belong to him. God does not stop loving his children when they fail, though he never loves the sin itself. A loving father may correct his child, speak sternly, or for a time withhold some of the warmth the child is used to. He does all this because he loves the child, not because the love has ended. Hebrews 12 says that the Lord disciplines the one he loves. In the same way, hardship in a believer's life is not proof that Christ has turned away. It is a mark of being his child. Through it he shapes us to be more like himself, and he is present with us in it.

Sometimes believers lose the feeling of his love altogether. The Holy Spirit never leaves God's people. But he does not always give the same sense of comfort. David, who still had the Spirit, prayed in Psalm 51:12, "Restore to me the joy of Your salvation." Feelings rise and fall. Christ's commitment does not. Often comfort is being offered in his promises, and our troubled hearts are slow to take it.

It is also worth knowing that when we pray to know more of his love, we are not asking Christ to love us more than he already does. His love is already full and cannot be increased. What grows is our grasp of it. Paul prays in Ephesians 3:18-19 that believers would understand how wide and long and high and deep Christ's love is, and know a love that goes beyond knowledge.

The delight runs both ways. As we see how Christ regards us, we begin to treasure him. 1 John 4:19 says, "We love because He first loved us." Loving someone also means loving what is dear to them. So believers come to delight in Christ's people, the church, even with all its flaws. They delight too in the ways he meets us: his Word, prayer, worship, baptism and the Lord's Supper. These can look ordinary or even foolish to the world. To those who love him, they are where the Bridegroom is found.

Christians have read the Song of Songs in different ways. Some see it chiefly as a picture of Christ and his church. Others read it first as a celebration of human married love, which points beyond itself. Either way, the wider Bible clearly teaches the marriage between Christ and his people. Revelation looks forward to the wedding supper of the Lamb.

So the heart of the matter is simple. Hard thoughts of God, which picture him as cold, grudging or impossible to please, are not humility. They are a lie, as old as the serpent's whisper in Eden. Christ is glad over his people. Believers grow by learning to rest in that gladness and to answer it with love of their own.

topics.title: What does communion with Christ accomplish in cleansing believers from sin?
topics.cmp: Whether Christ's blood sanctifies as well as justifies, how it is applied by the Spirit, and whether believers can be purified apart from communion with Christ.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: He doth not only justify his saints from the guilt of sin, but also sanctify and wash them from the filth of sin.

ans.text:
Communion with Christ does more than clear our record before God. It also begins to wash us clean on the inside. The blood that pays for our sins is the same blood that purifies us from their stain.

It helps to see that sin does two kinds of damage. It makes us guilty, like a debt we owe and cannot pay. It also makes us unclean, like a stain that soaks into the heart and spoils our desires, thoughts and even our best efforts. The Bible says Christ deals with both. To be justified means God declares us forgiven and right with him because of what Christ has done. To be sanctified means we are actually being made holy. Christ does not only make us accepted. He also makes us fit to be accepted, people who truly begin to reflect his goodness.

Scripture often ties this cleansing directly to Christ's blood. John writes in 1 John 1:7 that "the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin." Hebrews 9:14 says the blood of Christ will "purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God." That is not only about a verdict in heaven. It is about a conscience set free and a life turned toward God. Paul says in Titus 2:14 that Christ gave himself both to redeem us from lawlessness and to purify a people for himself who are eager to do good. Long before, the prophet Zechariah promised a fountain that would be opened to cleanse God's people from sin and impurity (Zechariah 13:1). In the Old Testament, the blood of sacrifices was used both to make atonement and to make unclean things clean. Christ's sacrifice fulfills both pictures at once.

How does this cleansing actually reach us? Here the Bible draws a helpful distinction. Christ's blood was shed once, on the cross, and that is where the cleansing was won and paid for. But it must also be applied to each person, just as in the Old Testament the blood was not only poured out at the altar but sprinkled on the people and things to be made clean. Peter speaks of believers as set apart by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and for sprinkling with his blood (1 Peter 1:2). Think of a medicine that has been fully prepared and paid for. It does nothing for the patient until it is given to him.

The Holy Spirit is the one who applies it. Christ gained the gift of the Spirit for us by his death, and he sends the Spirit to live in us. Through Ezekiel God promised to sprinkle clean water on his people, give them a new heart, and put his Spirit within them so they would walk in his ways (Ezekiel 36:25-27). Paul joins the whole work together in 1 Corinthians 6:11: "But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God." The Father plans our cleansing. The Son pays for it with his blood. The Spirit brings it home to our hearts. This is one reason the Trinity matters so much for ordinary Christian life.

Can we clean ourselves without Christ? No. God told Israel through Jeremiah that even if they scrubbed with strong soap, the stain of their guilt would remain before him (Jeremiah 2:22). Willpower, religious routine and self-improvement can tidy up the outside. They cannot reach the root. Jesus says plainly in John 15:5, "apart from Me you can do nothing." Real holiness grows the way a branch bears fruit, by staying joined to the vine. So when Christians struggle with sin, the first step is not simply to try harder on their own. It is to come back to Christ by faith, trusting what his blood has done and asking the Spirit to apply it. That kind of looking to him does more to change the heart than any amount of effort without him.

This does not mean effort has no place. The Spirit works in us so that we really do fight sin, pray, obey and grow. But our effort is the fruit of his cleansing, not the cause of it.

Some worry that if Christ takes our sins and gives us his righteousness, we will stop caring about sin or no longer need to repent. The opposite is true. Fellowship with Christ does drive out a fearful, slavish kind of sorrow, the kind that only dreads punishment and is mostly about protecting ourselves. But it deepens true repentance. The closer we come to Christ, the more clearly we see how ugly sin is and how much it cost him. That produces honest grief over sin and a real desire to turn from it, out of love rather than terror. And it comes with a promise: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

This cleansing is ongoing now and will be complete one day. Paul says Christ gave himself for his church to make her holy and to present her to himself without stain or blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27). Every believer who keeps coming to him is being prepared for that day.

topics.title: What is adoption, and what rights and inheritance does it bring?
topics.cmp: Owen supplies most of the answers here, and they hang together. Adoption is a legal translation, by Christ's authority, from the family of Satan into God's family. Fallen humans have no natural right to that family, so the right to the inheritance comes only by adoption. Owen grounds this mainly in Scripture: the expulsion of Adam, Paul's "if children, then heirs," and John 1:12. From it he draws ecclesiological and practical conclusions that the other authors do not address: only adopted children have a true title to the church's privileges, and adoption gives no civil claim to earthly goods. Hilary agrees that sonship is not natural, calling it a birth of faith rather than of the flesh, but he frames it as a prize offered to all and won by free choice, a voluntarist emphasis Owen's answers here do not share. Hilary also limits believers' brotherhood with Christ to his assumed flesh, so as to protect the Word's divinity. Irenaeus differs from Owen most plainly: he holds that all people are God's sons by creation and only believers are sons by obedience, and that the disobedient remain God's offspring and can regain sonship by repentance, whereas Owen denies fallen humanity any family relation to God by nature. Basil approaches the topic from another angle altogether, arguing that because the Spirit makes us free and adopts us as sons, he must be akin to God by nature and cannot be a creature.

refs.author: Basil of Caesarea
refs.place: Statement of the reason why in the writings of Paul the…
refs.quote: For how can we be made kin with God by one who is an alien? How can we be freed by one who is himself under the yoke of slavery?

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: adoption is the authoritative translation of a believer, by Jesus Christ, from the family of the world and Satan into the family of God, with his investiture in all the privileges and advantages of that family.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: No one is fellow to the Only-begotten Christ, God the Word: but we know that we are His fellows by the assumption which made Him flesh.

ans.text:
Adoption is God's act of taking people who did not belong to his family and making them his own children, with every right and privilege that true children have. The New Testament uses a word from family law of its day. In the Roman world a man could legally adopt someone, usually an adult, as his son and heir. The adopted person left his old family. His old debts and duties no longer bound him, and he took the new father's name with the same standing as a son born in the house. Paul uses that picture to describe what God does for us in Christ.

To see why adoption is such a gift, we have to be honest about where we start. In one sense every person is God's offspring, because God made us all (Acts 17:28). But since the fall we are not at home in his house. Paul says that we "were by nature children of wrath" (Ephesians 2:3). We belonged, so to speak, to another household, the household of sin and of the evil one. We had no claim on God's family at all. When Adam was sent out of the garden and the way back was guarded, it showed that humanity had lost any right to walk into God's presence as family. Adoption is therefore not God noticing children who already belonged to him. It is God reaching into a foreign household and bringing strangers home.

How does this happen? Paul puts it in Galatians 4:4-5: "God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons." The Son of God became one of us. He paid the debt that held us in our old family, and so he made us free to be transferred into his. John says the same from the human side: "to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God" (John 1:12). Notice the word "right." Adoption is not a vague feeling of closeness. It is a real standing, granted by the highest authority there is. We do not earn it, and we are not born into it. It comes as a gift, received by trusting Christ. And receiving him is not only a single moment at the start. It is an ongoing welcome of Christ, day by day, on his terms and by his grace alone.

It matters that the Bible says "sons." In the ancient world sons were the heirs. Paul is not leaving women out. He is saying that every believer, man or woman, gets the full heir's share. Elsewhere God promises, "you will be My sons and daughters" (2 Corinthians 6:18).

We should also be clear about how our sonship differs from Christ's. Jesus is the Son of God by nature. He has always been the Son, sharing fully in the Father's being. We become children by grace. After his resurrection Jesus told Mary to say to his followers, "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God" (John 20:17). He calls us brothers and sisters because he took on our flesh and joined our family (Hebrews 2:11). But he still says "My Father and your Father," not "our Father," as if we stood on the same footing. Adoption does not make us divine. It makes us beloved children in the house of the God who made us. That is wonder enough.

What rights does adoption bring? First, a new relationship. We may come to God as Father, with confidence rather than fear. "You did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (Romans 8:15). Second, a new family. The church is the household of God, and its life belongs to his children: the word, prayer, the Lord's table, and the care of brothers and sisters. The gospel is preached to everyone, inviting all to come home. But the privileges of the house are food meant for living children, not for those who only stand near the door. Third, a Father's care. That includes his loving discipline, which Hebrews 12 says is proof that we are true children and not outsiders.

Then there is the inheritance. Paul reasons simply: "if we are children, then we are heirs: heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ" (Romans 8:17). What do we inherit? Everything Christ won for us. We inherit the promise God made in Christ and sealed with his oath, which frees us from the guilt of sin and the grip of the evil one. We inherit righteousness and holiness, the means by which God makes us fit for his presence. We inherit eternal glory, a resurrected life in a renewed creation, "an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you" (1 Peter 1:4). Above all, we inherit God himself. The Lord becomes our portion, and we become his treasured possession.

One caution belongs here. This inheritance is spiritual and eternal, not a claim on earthly goods. Being God's child does not entitle a believer to someone else's house, land, or money, or to wealth we do not now have. What God gives us in this life through ordinary means, our adoption makes holy, to be used with thanks. But it does not create new earthly titles.

Finally, notice that the whole Trinity is at work in adoption. The Father chose us "for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 1:5). The Son redeemed us and shares his family with us. The Spirit is sent "into our hearts, crying out, 'Abba, Father!'" (Galatians 4:6), and "testifies with our spirit that we are God's children" (Romans 8:16). This tells us something important about who the Spirit is. No creature, however exalted, could make us children of God. An angel is a fellow servant. It can bear witness, but it cannot bring anyone into God's family. Someone who is outside God's own life cannot share that life with others, and someone who is himself a servant cannot set slaves free. Only one who truly belongs to God's own being can make us kin to God. Because the Son and the Spirit do exactly this, they are not created helpers but God himself.

So adoption is far more than a nice image. It is a real change of family, name, standing, and future. As John marvels, "See how great a love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are!" (1 John 3:1).

topics.title: How do God's adopted children live and obey?
topics.cmp: The filial spirit of obedience in adopted children contrasted with servile bondage, and the true meaning of their liberty.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: From an apprehension of love, they are effectually carried out by love to give up themselves unto him who is love.

ans.text:
God's adopted children obey him as sons and daughters obey a father they love and trust. They do not obey as slaves who work under the threat of a whip. The commands are the same ones a slave might hear, but the heart behind the obedience is completely different.

The Bible draws this contrast clearly. Paul writes in Romans 8:15, "For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" To be adopted means God takes people who were outsiders, even enemies, and makes them truly his children, with a child's name, place and inheritance. Notice that the whole Trinity is at work in this. The Father sets his love on us. The Son came "to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons" (Galatians 4:5). And the Father sends "the Spirit of His Son into our hearts" (Galatians 4:6), so that we really feel and speak like children. Adoption is not only a change in our legal standing. The Spirit also changes our hearts so we can live as children.

So what makes a child's obedience different? First, it comes from love answering love. John says, "We love because He first loved us" (1 John 4:19). When a believer begins to grasp how much the Father loves them in Christ, that love draws them. They want to give themselves to him. That is why Paul, after laying out God's mercy, urges believers to offer their bodies "as living sacrifices" (Romans 12:1). It is a gift freely given, not a tax extracted. Jesus puts it simply: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15).

Second, it is willing and cheerful rather than forced. Think of two people mowing the same lawn. One is a hired worker afraid of being fired. The other is a grown son helping the father he adores. The work looks identical from the street, but one is a burden and the other is a joy. John says that God's commands "are not burdensome" (1 John 5:3). That is not because they are easy. It is because love makes them light. A psalm speaks of running in the path of God's commands because he has enlarged the heart (Psalm 119:32). The Spirit gives a kind of roominess of heart that makes obedience natural.

Third, it rests on a law that no longer condemns. A slave obeys hoping to avoid punishment or to earn a place. A child already has a place. Christ's death has taken away the curse and condemnation of the law for those who trust him (Romans 8:1). So the child obeys from acceptance, not for acceptance. Failures are still serious and grieve a loving Father. But they do not undo the adoption. God disciplines his children the way a good father does, for their good (Hebrews 12:5-11), and does not drive them away.

Fourth, the child sees God differently. Jesus tells of a servant who buried his master's money because he thought the master was harsh and was afraid (Matthew 25:24-25). Fear of a stern master freezes people and makes them do as little as possible. God's children see God in Christ as a Father worth obeying. They also see him as the one who can truly satisfy their souls. Obeying him is not giving up their happiness. It is moving toward it.

This does not mean all fear disappears. Scripture still calls believers to reverent fear (1 Peter 1:17). But that is the awe and respect a child has for a great and holy Father. It is not the terror of a slave who expects punishment. "There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear" (1 John 4:18), meaning the fear of being rejected and condemned.

This brings us to a common misunderstanding about Christian freedom. Some think that because we are free in Christ, we may pick and choose which duties to keep. On this view prayer, worship, holiness and serving others become optional extras. The Bible rejects this. Paul says, "For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but serve one another in love" (Galatians 5:13). Freedom from duty is the kind of liberty a slave steals when the master isn't looking. The freedom the Spirit gives is something better: freedom in duty. The heart is set loose to go gladly toward God, the way a bird is free not when it is out of the air but when it can fly. "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom" (2 Corinthians 3:17). That is the freedom to love God and do his will with a whole heart.

So the adopted child's life is not lawless, and it is not anxious. It is obedience shaped by love, carried by the Spirit, resting on Christ's finished work, and aimed at a Father the child is glad to belong to.

topics.title: Does teaching God's unchangeable love encourage sin?
topics.cmp: Answers the objection that the immutability of God's love leads to moral license.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: He never tasted of the love of God that can seriously make this objection. The doctrine of grace may be turned into wantonness; the principle cannot.

ans.text:
No. When it is rightly understood, the truth that God's love never changes is one of the strongest reasons a Christian has to turn away from sin, not an excuse to keep on sinning.

The worry is understandable. If God has set his love on me and nothing I do can undo it, why not do as I please? The apostle Paul heard this same objection when he preached free grace. He answers it head on in Romans 6:1-2: "Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer?" He does not soften his message about grace to stop people from misusing it. Instead he shows that the objection misunderstands what grace is and what it does.

It helps to separate two things: the teaching about grace, and grace itself. Any good teaching can be twisted. Jude 4 warns of people who "turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality." Words about God's love can be bent that way by someone who wants an excuse. But the love of God itself, when it actually takes hold of a person, does not produce that result. Grace is not only a pardon handed over. It is God's own power at work in us. Titus 2:11-12 says the grace of God that brings salvation also "instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives." The same love that forgives also trains.

Think of a child who knows beyond doubt that her parents love her and will never stop. That security does not make her want to hurt them. It frees her to love them back. It is the child who fears that love can be lost who often lives anxious, resentful or rebellious. Scripture says the same about us: "We love because He first loved us" (1 John 4:19). Paul says Christ's love "compels us" to live no longer for ourselves but for him (2 Corinthians 5:14-15). Settled love is the soil in which grateful obedience grows.

This is why someone who has truly tasted God's love cannot seriously say, "Then I may sin freely." To say that is to treat God's love as a loophole rather than as the love of a holy Father. If the thought of God's unchanging kindness makes a person eager to sin, that is a warning sign. It suggests they have heard about his love without yet knowing it. It is not a sign that the teaching is dangerous.

It is also important to see that God's love never changing does not mean God stops caring about our sin. He can welcome a person fully and still hate the sin in that person's life. A loving parent hates a habit that is harming their child precisely because they love the child. So Hebrews 12:6 tells us that "the Lord disciplines the one He loves." God's steady love is exactly why he will not leave his children comfortable in what destroys them. He may correct us, bring us to grief over our sin, and take away the peace and joy we would otherwise enjoy, all without ever withdrawing his love. Unchanging love is not indifferent love. It is love that will not give up until we are made holy.

Finally, consider the alternative. If God's love rose and fell with our performance, we would be driven by fear. We would try to buy his favour, or despair when we fail. Neither leads to real holiness. But when we know with Paul that nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39), we are free to confess our sins honestly, to get up again after we fall, and to serve God out of love rather than dread. So teaching the unchanging love of God does not loosen the Christian life. Received with faith, it is what holds the Christian life together.

topics.title: How does the Song of Songs portray Christ, his church, and the believer's love for him?
topics.cmp: John Owen supplies almost all the answers here. He reads the Song as a picture of Christ's person and his love toward the church and the believer: the two natures appear in 'white and ruddy', his affections in the 'belly' and 'bowels', and his protecting love in the banner. He also takes it as a map of the soul's communion with Christ, covering love-sickness, Christ's absence as 'night', seeking him in the church's ordinances, and holding him fast by faith. Owen argues mainly from Scripture cross-references, the natural qualities of the images (rose, lily, doves, gold, myrrh) and occasionally the Hebrew or Greek wording. He treats the Chaldee paraphrase selectively, citing it in support of 'white and ruddy' but rejecting its reading of the cheeks as the tables of the law as strained. Ambrose of Milan addresses a different verse (1:3) for a different purpose: he uses 'ointment poured forth' to argue that such overflowing belongs to the Godhead, and he identifies the Holy Spirit as the oil with which Christ was anointed, citing the Psalm, Peter in Acts and Christ's words in Luke. Because the two authors do not take up the same passages, they never directly disagree. Ambrose's two answers on the anointing open with opposite words ('Yes' and 'No'), but in substance both affirm that the Spirit is called Christ's ointment, even if the 'ointment poured forth' is taken to mean Christ's Name.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The two eminencies of flowers, sweetness of savour and beauty of colour, are divided between these. The rose for sweetness, and the lily for beauty

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: In like manner that you may believe that that which is shed abroad cannot be common to the creatures but peculiar to the Godhead, the name of the Son is also poured forth

ans.text:
The Song of Songs is first a love poem between a bride and her beloved. For most of the church's history, though, Christians have also read it as a picture of the love between Christ and his people, and that reading can warm and deepen a believer's love for him.

It helps to be honest about what kind of book this is. On its surface the Song celebrates the love of a man and a woman, and many sincere Christians today read it mainly that way, as God's blessing on married love. That is a real and good meaning. Through most of church history, however, believers also heard in it a deeper love song. They had good reason. The Bible itself uses marriage to describe God and his people. The prophets call the Lord Israel's husband. John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom (John 3:29). Paul, after speaking of husband and wife becoming one flesh, says in Ephesians 5:32 that this mystery is profound, "but I am speaking about Christ and the church." The Bible ends with the wedding supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7). So reading the Song as a picture of Christ and his bride is not a strange invention. It follows a pattern Scripture itself sets. The wise way is to hold both readings together, without forcing every detail into a hidden code. Human married love is good, and it also points beyond itself to a greater love.

Read this way, the Song first shows us who Christ is. The bride says her beloved's "name is like perfume poured out" (Song 1:3). A jar of perfume kept sealed blesses no one, but once it is poured out the whole house fills with its scent. So it was when Christ came. His name, once known mostly in Israel, has spread its fragrance through all the world. Behind the image of perfume or ointment also stands the Holy Spirit. The Messiah is "the Anointed One." Jesus says in Luke 4:18, "The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me," and Peter says that God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power (Acts 10:38). So in this love song the whole Trinity is quietly present. The Father anoints the Son with the Spirit, and the Son comes to win his bride.

The beloved says, "I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valley" (Song 2:1). A rose is prized for its sweet scent and a lily for its beauty. Christ has both. His love, his goodness and his righteousness are a fragrance that draws people to him and refreshes them, and his person is beautiful and without flaw. When the bride later describes him from head to foot, she ends by saying he is "altogether lovely" (Song 5:16). That is the heart of it. There is nothing in Christ that is not lovely. He is truly God, with all God's fullness, and truly man, pure and without sin. He took on our flesh, lived a holy life, died for sinners and now reigns at the Father's right hand. Christians have taken the details of her description, such as his gentle dove-like eyes or lips that drip with fragrant myrrh, as pictures of his tender care for his people and the sweetness of his words. We should hold such details lightly, but the main point is plain. The more you look at him, the more there is to love.

The Song also shows how Christ sees his church. He calls her "a lily among the thorns" (Song 2:2). Notice that he uses the same word, lily, for himself and for her. That is because his people share his life. The same Spirit who rests on him lives in them, and God is shaping them to be like his Son (Romans 8:29). The picture has two sides. In his eyes his people are lovely and precious, standing out like a lily in a briar patch. Yet a lily among thorns also gets scratched. The church lives in a world that often wounds her.

The Song shows what Christ gives his bride, too. She sits in his shade and tastes his fruit, which nourishes her (Song 2:3). No angel and no great teacher can be that for a weary soul. Only Christ gives both food and rest. He brings her into "the house of wine," and "his banner over me is love" (Song 2:4). A banner flew over an army's camp to show whose people they were and who protected them. Over Christ's people flies the banner of his love. Nothing can reach them without first passing under it. The house of wine is the rich feast of grace he spreads for his people in the gospel, in his Word, in worship and in the comfort of the Spirit. No wonder the bride says she is faint with love (Song 2:5). She is not fearful or unloved. She has tasted so much of his goodness that she longs for more.

Finally, the Song shows the believer's love for Christ, including its struggles. In chapter 3 the bride lies on her bed at night and cannot find the one she loves. Nothing else is wrong, but his absence makes it dark. Many Christians know this experience. Life may be comfortable, yet Christ seems distant and the heart feels cold. The bride does not give up. She rises and searches the streets of the city. Christians have often seen in this a picture of seeking Christ in all the ways he has promised to meet us, in private prayer and also among his people, in worship, preaching, the Lord's Supper and fellowship. When she finds him, she says, "I held him and would not let him go" (Song 3:4). Faith takes hold of Christ, and love refuses to let go.

Near the end she asks him to set her as a seal over his heart and as a seal on his arm (Song 8:6). The heart is where love lives hidden, and the arm is where love acts with strength. She wants to be always in his heart and always kept by his power. She adds that love is as strong as death. Death never says "enough," and a heart that truly loves Christ is not content with a little of him. It wants him wholly.

The comfort in all this is that our love is only an answer. Before the bride ever sought him, he had already loved her, and the New Testament says Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). We love because he first loved us. The Song of Songs invites ordinary believers to know that they are loved and delighted in by Christ, and to love him back with warm, persistent and wholehearted devotion.

title: The Image of the Trinity in the Human Mind
desc: Augustine's mental and outer trinities, memory, understanding and will, the mind's self-knowledge, and the image of God in man, its defacement and renewal.

topics.title: In what sense is man made in the image of the Trinity, and where is that image found?
topics.cmp: Augustine of Hippo supplies almost all the answers on this topic. He holds that man is made in the image of the whole Trinity, citing the plural "our image" of Genesis, and he rejects the family triad of father, mother and child on scriptural grounds. He locates the image in the individual rational mind, not the body, as the triad of mind, self-knowledge and self-love, or more clearly memory, understanding and will. He insists this is properly the image only when the mind turns to remember, understand and love God and contemplates eternal things, not in transient trinities such as faith or knowledge of temporal things. Jonathan Edwards agrees that the image lies in the soul's inner structure, but he frames it as mind, idea or understanding, and will or affection, matched to the Father, the Son as God's idea, and the Spirit as God's love; this is close to Augustine's word-and-love analogy but stated without his stress on the turn toward God. Athanasius of Alexandria, on how the Son's being the image differs from ours, agrees with Augustine that humans are only "after" the image while the Son alone is the Image by nature, but he grounds this in the indwelling of the incarnate Word as a derived grace, where Augustine stresses that the likeness is unequal because man is created rather than born. Irenaeus of Lyons and John Owen do not address the image of the Trinity directly: Irenaeus stresses the creature's distance from the uncreated God and the unity of the mind's activities, and Owen the unity of habitual grace.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: John is Rather to Be Understood of Our Perfect Likeness…
refs.quote: we believe,—and, after the utmost search we have been able to make, understand,—that man was made after the image of the Trinity, because it is not said, After my, or After thy image.

refs.author: Jonathan Edwards
refs.quote: The one is in the spiritual creation, the soul of man. There is the mind, and the understanding or idea, and the spirit of the mind as it is called in Scripture, i.e., the disposition, the will or affection.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: yet not on our own account still, but for that Image and true Glory of God inhabiting us, which is His Word, who was for us afterwards made flesh, have we this grace of our designation

ans.text:
Human beings are made in the image of the whole Trinity, the one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and that image is found above all in the mind: our God-given ability to know, remember and love, and most fully when we know and love God himself.

Start with the Bible's first word on the subject. In Genesis 1:26 God says, "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness." The very next verse says, "So God created man in His own image." Notice the plural and the singular side by side: "Our image," yet "His image." There is one image because there is one God, but the God who speaks is not a lonely individual. So we are not made in the image of the Son alone, as if the Father and the Spirit stood off to the side. We bear the likeness of the one God who is three.

Yet there is a real difference between how the Son is God's image and how we are. Paul says in Colossians 1:15 that the Son "is the image of the invisible God." He is the image in the fullest sense: not made but begotten, which means he comes from the Father and shares the Father's own being, the way a son shares his father's nature. He is equal to the Father in every way, a perfect likeness with nothing missing. We, by contrast, are created. We are made after the image, a copy that resembles the original without being equal to it. Think of the difference between a son and a portrait. A son shares his father's life. A portrait only resembles him, however well it is painted. Christ is the true Image, and we are images by grace, shaped on his pattern. That is why God's plan is for us to be "conformed to the image of His Son" (Romans 8:29).

Where in us, then, does the image lie? Not in the shape of our bodies. Jesus says that "God is Spirit" (John 4:24). He has no arms, eyes or height for our bodies to copy, and it would shrink God to imagine otherwise. What sets us apart from the animals is that we can reason, know truth, tell right from wrong, and above all know God and love him. That is where Scripture points when it speaks of renewal. Paul describes the new self "being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator" (Colossians 3:10), and in Ephesians 4:23 he speaks of being made new in our minds. The image is restored where knowledge of God grows, and that happens in the inner person.

This does not make the body unimportant. God made it, Christ took a body, and he will raise ours. Many sincere Christians also see the image more broadly: in the whole person, body included, and in our calling to rule over creation as God's representatives, since Genesis 1:26 joins the image to that task. Others answer that ruling well is a result of the image rather than the image itself, because we can only govern wisely as beings who can know God and his will. Both sides agree that the heart of the matter is our capacity for knowing and loving God, which no animal shares.

How does a mind reflect a God who is three? Christians have long noticed a small echo of the Trinity in how a mind works. A mind can remember itself, understand itself and love itself. These are three, yet they are not three minds. They make one life and one person. They also depend on each other. You cannot love what you do not know, so love needs understanding. You cannot understand what is not held before you, so understanding needs memory. When the mind looks at itself, it is a little like bringing forth an inner word about itself, and love joins the knower and what is known. This gives a faint picture of the Father, the Son who is called the Word, and the Spirit who is often spoken of as the bond of love.

The picture is useful but very limited. In you, memory, understanding and love are three activities of one person. In God, Father, Son and Spirit are three persons, each fully God, not three parts or functions of one person. So the comparison helps us see that three-in-one is not nonsense, but it does not explain God. Paul says that for now "we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror" (1 Corinthians 13:12).

One more point matters a great deal. The mind images God most truly not when it is wrapped up in itself but when it turns to him. A mind that remembers God, understands him and loves him is reflecting its Maker the way a mirror does when it actually faces the light. Sin did not erase the image, but it turned the mirror away and clouded it. Salvation turns it back. As 2 Corinthians 3:18 puts it, we are "being transformed into His image" by the Spirit.

This also explains why the image is found in what lasts. Faith, for instance, is precious, but it is meant for this life. One day faith will give way to sight. So the image cannot rest on something that passes. It rests on the soul God made to live forever and to know him forever. The image is not something we gain and lose with our moods or seasons. It is part of what we are, waiting to be fully restored.

Does all this include women? Absolutely. Genesis 1:27 says plainly, "in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them." Some readers stumble over 1 Corinthians 11:7, where Paul says a man "is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man." But Paul is talking about order and symbols in worship, not denying what Genesis teaches. A few verses later he stresses that man and woman depend on each other and that "everything comes from God" (1 Corinthians 11:11-12). Christians differ on how to apply Paul's teaching about headship today, but they agree that women bear God's image fully. The image lives in the mind's ability to know God, and in Christ "there is... neither male nor female" (Galatians 3:28). Women are fellow heirs of grace, renewed in knowledge just as men are.

Finally, some people suggest that the image of the Trinity is a family: father, mother and child. It is easy to see the appeal, and family love can truly reflect the love of God. But it does not work as an account of the image. Genesis says Adam was made in God's image the moment he was created, before Eve existed and long before any child was born. If the image needed three people, Adam alone could not have been God's image, and neither could any single or childless person. Every human being, alone or in company, married or not, carries the image of the triune God within. That is the dignity of each person, and the hope of each believer is that the image will one day shine clearly when we see God face to face.

topics.title: How do the mind's memory, knowledge, love and inner word image the Trinity?
topics.cmp: Augustine supplies nearly all the answers. He holds that the mind's memory, understanding (or inner word) and love, and the triad of lover, beloved and love, are a true but very unequal image of the Trinity: memory resembles the Father, the inner word born of loved knowledge resembles the Son, and love, which proceeds rather than is begotten, resembles the Spirit. He argues this from Scripture (man made in God's image, 'God is love', the 'mouth of the heart', Rom. 1:20) and from close introspection. He also insists on the unlikeness: the three belong to one person and are not three persons, the human word is made and temporal rather than begotten and eternal, and the image is changeable and imperfect in this life. He adds that such inquiry needs divine aid and that the Trinity is believed more than seen through it. Hilary agrees that understanding depends on God's revelation rather than on reason's preconceptions, and he rejects physical analogies (spring and stream, tree and branch, fire and heat) as inadequate to the Son's real subsistence, though he does not address the mental image directly. Edwards goes further than Augustine in the other direction: he holds that the whole visible creation is ordered by God, as Scripture shows, to typify spiritual things, and he takes the sun as an image of Father, Son and Spirit. Warfield differs sharply from both Augustine and Edwards: he denies that any analogy in nature or even in the soul can prove or help comprehend the Trinity, and he argues that self-consciousness constructions, including Edwards's idea-and-love argument, fail because God's acts are not further Persons with objective reality and because the Spirit can be reached only artificially.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: That It is Not Easy to Discover the Trinity that is God…
refs.quote: and the Three Persons are of one essence, not as each individual man is one person.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: In His trinitarian mode of being, God is unique; and, as there is nothing in the universe like Him in this respect, so there is nothing which can help us to comprehend Him.

refs.author: Jonathan Edwards
refs.quote: The Spirit as it is God's Infinite love to Himself and happiness in Himself, is as the internal heat of the Sun, but as it is that by which God communicates Himself, it is as the emanation of the sun's action, or the emitted beams of the sun.

ans.text:
They give us a small, cracked mirror in which we can catch a glimpse of how one God can be Father, Son and Holy Spirit. They are not a photograph of God. The Bible says God made us in His image. In Genesis 1:26 God says, "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness." So it is natural to look inside ourselves, especially at the mind and heart, for some faint reflection of the God who made us.

Start with something simple. Your mind holds a great deal you are not thinking about right now: your mother's face, the way home, the words of a favorite hymn. Call that store your memory. When you actually bring something to mind, your mind forms a thought of it, a kind of silent word spoken inside you. This inner word is not English or Spanish or any language. It is the understanding itself, before you put it into speech. Then there is love. When you know something good, you take delight in it, and that delight joins together what you remember and what you now understand.

Memory, understanding and love are three distinct things, and you can tell them apart. Yet they are not three minds. They are one mind at work. Each is bound up with the others: you remember that you understand and love, you understand that you remember and love, and you love your remembering and understanding.

Here Christians have seen a hint of the Trinity. The Father is like the deep source, the one from whom all comes. The Son is like the inner word that comes from that source and fully expresses it. That is why John's Gospel calls Him the Word: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). When the Bible and the creeds say the Son is "begotten" of the Father, they mean He comes from the Father and shares the Father's very nature, the way a child shares a parent's nature, though without any beginning in time. Our inner word, which comes from what we know and mirrors it, gives us a small picture of this. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the exact representation of His nature." The Holy Spirit is like the love that unites the knower and what is known. He belongs to both and binds them together, yet He is neither one of them.

A second picture comes from the plain words "God is love" (1 John 4:8). Love is never just a feeling floating in the air. It is always someone loving someone. So love brings three things with it: the one who loves, the one who is loved, and the love that joins them. When Jesus speaks of the Father loving Him "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24), we see that God did not need to create anything in order to love. Love was already alive within God: the Father loving the Son, the Son loving the Father, and the Spirit as that love shared between them.

These pictures help, but we have to be honest about where they fall short. In fact the differences teach us as much as the likenesses.

First, and most important, your memory, understanding and love are not three persons. They all belong to one person, you. You have them, but you are not them, and it is you who remembers, understands and loves through them. God is not like that. God is not one person with three abilities. The Father, the Son and the Spirit are each truly a person. They are really distinct, and each is fully God, yet they are one God, sharing one divine nature or "essence," which means what God is. If we pushed the mind picture too far, we would end up with one God wearing three masks or using three faculties. The church has always rejected that idea. At Jesus' baptism the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks from heaven (Matthew 3:16-17). These are three, not one person in three moods.

Second, our inner word comes and goes. You know many things you are not thinking of at this moment. A musician still knows music while he is cooking dinner, but he is not "speaking" music in his mind right then. Our inner words are born in time and pass away. God's Word is eternal. There was never a time when the Father was without His Son. God's mind does not drift from one thought to the next.

Third, our word is a copy of a copy. We are images made by God. The Son is not made at all. He is born of the Father and equal to Him in every way. Our best and truest thoughts are like the Father's Word only from a great distance.

Fourth, our minds are fallen and changeable. Sin has bent the image. We forget, misunderstand and love the wrong things. That is why the New Testament speaks of believers putting on the new self, "which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator" (Colossians 3:10). The image in us is being restored in Christ. In God nothing needs restoring.

There is also a point where sincere Christians have differed. The picture of the Spirit as the love shared between Father and Son fits the belief, held by many churches in the West, that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son together. Jesus says He will send the Spirit (John 16:7), and the Spirit is called "the Spirit of His Son" (Galatians 4:6). Many churches in the East hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. They point to Jesus' words that the Spirit "proceeds from the Father" (John 15:26), and they want to keep the Father as the single source within God. They would also caution against treating the Spirit as a mere bond rather than a person in His own right. Both sides agree that the Spirit is fully God and a true person, equal with the Father and the Son.

So how should we use these images? As helps, not as proofs. We believe in the Trinity because God has shown Himself in Scripture as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, not because we discovered it by looking inward. But having believed it, we may find that our own minds and our own loving point, however dimly, toward the God who made them. Paul reminds us that for now we see only a dim reflection, but one day we will see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Until then, every time we know something truly and love it rightly, we are living out a small echo of the life of the God who is Knowledge, Word and Love.

topics.title: How are mind, its knowledge and its love one and yet three?
topics.cmp: Nearly every answer here comes from Augustine of Hippo, and his answers agree with one another. Mind, its self-knowledge and its self-love are three yet one essence. They are not parts of a whole, since each pervades the whole mind. They are not mixed like wine, water and honey, which would destroy their threeness. They are inseparable, unlike friends. They are equal when perfect, and each indwells the others without confusion. His parallel answers differ only in the grounds they stress. On why the three share one essence, one rests on the mind being known and loved by nothing outside itself, while another says love and mind are one spirit when the mind wills itself to be just as much as it is. On why the begotten word equals the mind, one says self-knowledge is neither of a lower essence (as with bodies) nor a higher one (as with God), while the other says the mind alone is the parent, being both knower and known. On love and the word, one answer says the word is itself conceived by love, while others present love as the bond joining mind and word in a way that mirrors the Spirit, or as mutually indwelling with the word. The only other author, Irenaeus of Lyons, answers a different question but sounds a cautionary note in tension with this whole approach: he denies that corruptible, compound, bounded created things can be images of spiritual, incomprehensible beings, because a true image requires an archetype with definite figure and limits. His answer does not directly address an incorporeal mind such as Augustine describes.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Three are One, and Also Equal, Viz. The Mind Itself,…
refs.quote: Therefore the mind itself, and the love of it, and the knowledge of it, are three things (tria quædam), and these three are one; and when they are perfect they are equal.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: how can those things which are possessed of figure, and confined within certain limits, be the images of such as are destitute of figure and incomprehensible?

ans.text:
When your mind knows itself and loves itself, you have three real things that are still one mind: the mind, its knowledge of itself, and its love for itself. This is one of the most helpful pictures Christians have found for thinking about how God can be one God and yet Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It is only a picture, and we will come to its limits. But it is worth walking through slowly, because it shows that 'one and three' is not a contradiction.

Start with something you already do. You are aware of yourself. You know that you exist, that you think, that you remember. That self-knowledge is not someone else's report about you. It comes from your own mind. And you also care about yourself. Paul takes this for granted when he says that no one hates his own body but feeds and looks after it (Ephesians 5:29). So in every person there is the mind, the knowledge the mind has of itself, and the love the mind has for itself.

Why call these three? Because they are not simply the same thing under different labels. Knowing is not loving. You can know something without loving it, and the mind itself is the one doing both. The knowledge comes from the mind, the way a thought is 'conceived' or brought to birth in us. The love also comes from the mind and reaches out to what it knows. So there is an order: mind, then the knowledge it produces, then the love that joins the mind to that knowledge.

Why call them one? Because nothing outside the mind supplies the knowing or the loving. The mind is the knower and also the thing known. The mind is the lover and also the thing loved. The knowledge and the love are not extra things added on from outside. They are the mind's own life. They share one nature, or what older writers called one 'essence', meaning simply what something is. You do not have three minds. You have one mind that knows and loves itself.

Are the three equal? They can be. If the mind knows itself truly, as it really is, its knowledge matches it exactly: no smaller, no larger. If it loves itself rightly, its love matches it too. We fall short here. We can think too little of ourselves, treating ourselves as no more than a body. Or we can think too much, loving ourselves as though we were God. Both are distorted. But a mind that sees itself truly and loves itself rightly has a knowledge and a love equal to itself.

Are they parts of a whole, like slices of a pie? No. A part never takes in the whole thing it belongs to. A slice does not contain the whole pie. But when the mind knows itself, its knowledge reaches through the whole mind, not one corner of it. When it loves itself, its love embraces the whole mind. So knowledge and love are not pieces of the mind. Each is, in its own way, the whole.

Are they blended together, like wine, water and honey stirred into one drink? Again, no. In a drink, three different substances are mixed and lose their separate identities. Here the three are of one nature from the start, and they stay distinct. If they were blended into a single soup, there would no longer be three.

Instead, they live inside one another. The mind is in its love, because it is what the love embraces. The love is in the knowledge, because the mind knows that it loves. The knowledge is in the mind, because it is the mind's own knowing. And the mind loves its knowledge and knows its love. Each is in the others, and all are in all, yet none is lost in the others.

Can they be pulled apart? Not the way friends can drift apart, or even the way a head can be cut off. If the mind's love for itself stopped, the mind would simply no longer love itself. The love and the lover cannot exist separately. The same is true of knowing.

You may ask why you do not feel this self-love all the time. Love is most noticeable when we lack something we want. Your mind is always present to itself, so there is no sense of lack to make you notice the love. It is like the air you breathe. It is always there, so you rarely think about it.

Now, why does any of this matter for the Trinity? The Bible says we were made in God's image: 'Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness' (Genesis 1:26). If God is Father, Son and Spirit, we might expect some trace of that in the deepest part of us. And Scripture uses exactly this language of mind, word and spirit. The Son is called the Word: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). A word is what a mind expresses when it knows. The Father eternally 'begets' the Son, which means the Son comes from the Father as his perfect self-expression, sharing his very nature, not made like a creature. That matches the way your mind's self-knowledge comes from your mind and is equal to it. Paul compares the Spirit of God to a person's own spirit: 'who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God' (1 Corinthians 2:11). And the Spirit is closely tied to love, for God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5). Many Christians have seen the Spirit as the bond of love between the Father and the Son, much as love joins the mind and its knowledge.

The mutual indwelling also echoes Jesus' words: 'I am in the Father and the Father is in Me' (John 14:11). The Father, Son and Spirit are not three parts of God. Each is wholly God. They are not mixed into one blur. They are not three gods who might part company. They are one God, each in the others.

But here we must be careful, because every picture of God falls short. Your knowledge and your love are not persons. They are activities of you, the one person. In God, the Father, the Son and the Spirit are each truly someone, each able to say 'I' and to speak to the others. Also, your mind changes. It can know itself badly and love itself wrongly. God's knowledge and love are perfect and never change. And you are one person who has a mind, while God is one God who is three persons. So the analogy does not explain God. It shows that being one and three at once is not nonsense, because we find a faint reflection of it in ourselves.

Sincere Christians weigh this picture differently. Some find it the best way into the mystery, because it shows the oneness of God so clearly and fits the Bible's language of Word and Spirit. Others worry that, used alone, it can make the Son and Spirit sound like mere powers inside God rather than real persons, and they prefer to lean also on pictures drawn from love between persons, like a family. Both concerns are fair. Used together, with humility, the pictures guard each other.

There is also a practical side. The image of God in us has been damaged by sin, but Paul says believers are being 'renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator' (Colossians 3:10). The image is clearest not when we only know and love ourselves, but when our minds remember, know and love God. The mind that turns toward God, knows him in Christ, and loves him by the Spirit becomes the truest likeness of the Trinity it was made to reflect.

topics.title: How are memory, understanding and will one and yet three?
topics.cmp: Augustine of Hippo supplies nearly all the answers here. He argues by introspection on the mind that memory, understanding and will are one substance, one life, mind and essence, which are terms said of each absolutely and of all together in the singular, while they are three in their mutual relations. He holds that they are equal because each contains the others whole, that they are coeval with no temporal priority, and that each name, though it refers to one faculty, is uttered by all three, as an image of the Trinity's inseparable operation. Augustine also limits the analogy: the Father is not the memory, the Son the understanding and the Spirit the love, since in God each Person has all three as one thing, and his examples of temporal succession are only teaching aids. Gregory of Nyssa reaches a conclusion that parallels Augustine's absolute/relative distinction, namely one being with distinct personal characteristics, but he grounds it in a different analogy: three individual men, Peter, James and John, rather than three faculties within one mind. Hilary of Poitiers does not discuss the mental triad at all; he defends using bodily analogies as aids to faith rather than measures of God, on the ground that God himself uses them in revelation, a cautionary stance that agrees with Augustine's own restrictions on his image.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In Memory, Understanding [or Intelligence], and Will, We…
refs.quote: But they are three, in that wherein they are mutually referred to each other

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: things that are identical on the score of being will not all agree equally in definition on the score of personality. For instance, Peter, James, and John are the same viewed as beings, each was a man

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: These illustrations, I repeat, must only be used as aids to apprehension of the faith, not as standards of comparison for the Divine majesty. Our method is that of using bodily instances as a clue to the invisible.

ans.text:
Memory, understanding and will are one because together they make up a single mind, a single life. They are three because each one stands in a different relation to the others. That is the short answer. To see why Christians have found this a helpful picture of the Trinity, it is worth walking through it slowly.

The Bible says God made us in his image. In Genesis 1:26 God says, "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness." If we bear God's image, it makes sense to look inside ourselves for some faint reflection of who he is. Paul says in Romans 1:20 that God's invisible qualities can be understood from what he has made. The human mind, with its power to remember, to understand and to love, is one of the most remarkable things he has made.

Start with how the three are one. Your memory is not a separate person living inside your head. Neither is your understanding or your will. You do not have three minds or three lives. You have one mind, and all three belong to it completely. So if we ask what each of them is in itself, the answer is the same every time: it is your mind, your life, your very self at work. When we add them up we still say "one mind," not "three minds."

Now see how they are three. The words "memory," "understanding" and "will" do not describe what the mind is in itself. They describe how it relates to something. Memory is memory of something. Understanding is understanding of something. Will is the will reaching toward something and taking hold of it. In those relations they are really distinct. Remembering a friend's face is not the same as understanding why she is upset, and neither is the same as wanting to comfort her. So there are words that fit all three together in the singular (one mind, one life), and words that mark them out from each other (memory, understanding, will). This is a small-scale picture of how Christians speak about God. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are each fully God, yet there is one God, not three. They are distinct in how they relate to one another: the Father is Father of the Son, the Son is Son of the Father, and the Spirit is the Spirit of both.

The three are also equal, and you can test this from your own experience. Each one holds the other two entirely. Everything you understand, you know that you understand, and what you know you remember. So your memory holds the whole of your understanding and the whole of your will.
