Your understanding grasps all three as well, since you can think about what memory is, what understanding is and what willing is. Your will takes in the other two whenever you choose to remember something or to think something through. Thought only returns to something because memory keeps it, and it only bothers to return because the will cares about it. Love, for its part, cannot love well without knowing what it loves. If one were smaller than the others, it could not contain them whole like this. This mutual indwelling echoes what Jesus says in John 14:10: "I am in the Father and the Father is in Me."

Notice too that when the mind considers itself, none of the three comes first in time. With outside things there is a sequence. You see a tree, store it in memory, later call it back to mind, and then decide to dwell on it. But the mind is never a stranger to itself. From the moment it exists it is present to itself, knowing itself and loving itself. Memory and understanding of itself are so tightly joined that they can almost seem like one thing with two names. This matters, because the Father did not exist for a while and then later have a Son. The Son and the Spirit are eternal with the Father. Sometimes we explain the mind with examples that unfold over time, like recalling a memory and forming a thought from it, because steps are easier to see. But the deeper picture is three that have always been together.

There is one more feature of the mind that Scripture invites us to notice. When you truly understand something, you form a kind of inner word. Before you say anything aloud, the thought is already spoken inside you. Your mind brings this word forth, almost gives birth to it, yet the word does not leave you. It stays within the mind that formed it. This is a picture of what the creed means when it calls the Son "begotten" of the Father. "Begotten" means brought forth from the Father's own being, not made from something outside. John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Like our inner word, the Son comes forth from the Father without ever being separated from him. He is with God and is God.

The mind also helps us understand how the three Persons always work together. Think about saying the word "memory." That word names only one of the three. Yet to say it you must remember it, understand it and want to say it. All three powers of your one mind produce the word that names just one of them. Something similar happens in God's dealings with us. The Bible links certain works especially to one Person. The Son became flesh. The Spirit came down like a dove and at Pentecost like tongues of fire. Yet the whole Trinity acts in each of these works, because God is one and does not act in pieces. Jesus says in John 5:19 that the Son does whatever he sees the Father doing. What God does is one undivided work, even when it shows one Person in particular.

Now some cautions, because every picture of God has limits. First, the mind is an image, not a blueprint. Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 13:12 that for now we see only dimly, as in a mirror. Using everyday pictures to grasp God is not irreverent. God himself speaks of himself as Father, as Word, as light. But such pictures help us understand. They do not measure God.

Second, do not take the picture too literally by saying the Father is God's memory, the Son is God's understanding, and the Spirit is God's love, as if each Person did only one job for the others. The Father does not need the Son in order to understand, or the Spirit in order to love. Each Person fully knows, fully remembers and fully loves, because each is fully God. In us, memory, understanding and will are different powers. In God, knowing and loving are not separate parts. They are simply who God is, just as he does not merely have wisdom but is wise.

Third, and most important, there is a real difference between us and God here. Memory, understanding and will are three powers of one human person. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are not three powers of one divine person. They are three Persons who share one divine being. That is why some sincere Christians prefer to stress pictures drawn from relationships of love between persons, warning that the mind picture can make God sound like one person with three functions. Others value the mind picture highly, since Scripture calls the Son the Word and the Wisdom of God, and since it guards so well against the opposite error of three separate gods. Both concerns are fair, and the best use of the picture keeps both in view.

Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 2:11, "For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him? So too, no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God." Our own minds are a mystery even to us. It should not surprise us that God is far deeper still. Yet each time you remember, understand and love, you carry in yourself a small reminder of the God who is one, who is three, and who made you to know and love him.

topics.title: How does the mind know, remember and love itself?
topics.cmp: Nearly every answer here comes from Augustine of Hippo, and his answers form one consistent position. The mind always knows, remembers and loves itself, even when it is not thinking of itself. He separates self-knowledge (notitia) from self-thought (cogitatio) with analogies from learned skills: the musician thinking of geometry, the grammarian thinking of medicine. He argues the rest philosophically. Nothing can be loved unless it is known, so the mind seeking itself already knows itself. The mind knows itself whole and through itself, by inward presence rather than by bodily images. The doubter cannot coherently doubt that he lives, remembers, understands and wills, and the skeptics' arguments from dreaming and madness cannot touch this. Because the mind is certain of itself but uncertain whether it is air, fire or brain, it is none of these. His few apparent disagreements come from how the questions are worded, not from any change of view. On whether the skeptics can cast doubt on the knowledge that one is alive, one answer opens 'Yes' but then argues that this knowledge cannot be deceived. The other answers on that question say 'No' in the same sense. Augustine draws on Scripture only lightly (fallen man still 'walketh in an image'), on Virgil to justify calling self-presence 'memory', and on the command to 'know thyself' read morally: the mind is to take its place under God and above what it should rule. Jonathan Edwards appears once, on a different matter: God's knowledge of Himself. He argues from God's delight in Himself that God must become His own object, so there is 'a duplicity in God', God and the idea of God, answering to our reflection without its imperfection. This sits in some tension with Augustine's emphasis that in the human mind's self-knowledge the same mind both knows and is known, with no doubling of itself. The two authors, however, are answering different questions.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: A Brief Recapitulation of All the Previous Books.
refs.quote: the mind could never be in such a case as not to remember, understand, and love itself, although it did not always think of itself

refs.author: Jonathan Edwards
refs.quote: However, if God beholds Himself so as thence to have delight and joy in Himself He must become his own object. There must be a duplicity. There is God and the idea of God

ans.text:
Your mind knows, remembers and loves itself in a way it knows nothing else: from the inside, directly, all the time, even when you are not thinking about yourself at all. Many Christians have found in this a small, faint reflection of the God who made us in His image. It is never a proof of the Trinity, but it is a picture that can help us think about Him.

Start with something simple. You cannot love what you know nothing about. That sounds wrong at first, because curious people seem to love things they do not yet know. A student longs to learn a language she cannot yet speak. But look closer. She already knows something about it: what speaking another language makes possible, how good it is to understand and be understood. She loves that known good, and it drives her to search for what she lacks. Love always leans on some knowledge, however small.

Now turn that toward yourself. When you ask, "Who am I, really?" you are seeking yourself. Does that mean you were a stranger to yourself? No. In the very act of asking, you know that you are the one asking. You know that you are searching, and that you do not yet see clearly. So even your search for self-knowledge shows that you already know yourself more than you are ignorant of yourself. Paul points to this inward knowing in 1 Corinthians 2:11: "For who among men knows the thoughts of man except his own spirit within him?" No one else has this inside view of you. You have it of yourself.

This self-knowledge does not switch off when your attention moves elsewhere. Think of a skilled pianist busy doing her taxes. She is not thinking about music, but she has not stopped knowing or loving it. It is all there, ready, and the moment she sits at the keyboard it comes forward. In the same way, your mind is always present to itself. You do not lose yourself when you think about lunch or the weather. When you turn your thoughts inward, you find you were there all along.

We can call this "memory," even though memory usually means holding on to the past. Memory is really what keeps something at hand, ready to be brought to mind. In that sense the mind remembers itself all the time. We already talk this way when we say someone "forgot himself" in anger. We mean he lost hold of who he is, though of course he was right there.

So three things are always going on together in one mind: it remembers itself, it understands itself, and it loves itself. They are not three minds, and none is bigger than the others. Your knowledge of yourself is not greater than you, because the one knowing and the one known are the same mind. Your love of yourself reaches just as far as you know yourself. And you cannot love yourself without first remembering and understanding yourself. Three distinct activities, one mind, each bound up with the others. This is where many Christians have seen a dim likeness of one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, made in His image as Genesis 1:27 says: "So God created man in His own image."

This inward knowledge is also the surest thing we have. Our eyes can be fooled, and we can be dreaming without knowing it. Someone may say, "How do you know you are not dreaming right now?" Perhaps we cannot always be sure. But whether I am awake, asleep or mistaken, I know that I am alive and thinking. Only a living, thinking person can be fooled at all. Doubt itself proves that there is someone doing the doubting. God has given us a foothold of certainty that no trick of the senses can take away.

It also says something about what the mind is. The mind is certain that it exists, that it lives, that it thinks and wills. It is not at all certain, from the inside, that it is made of blood, nerve or brain tissue. People who picture the soul as some fine physical stuff are not ignorant of their minds. They are simply adding a picture of matter, because they find it hard to imagine anything that is not. Scripture agrees that we are more than our bodies, though the mind works in close union with the body God gave it. Jesus says in Matthew 10:28 not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.

If we always know ourselves, why does the Bible keep calling us to self-examination? Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 13:5, "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves." The answer is sin. Our minds get so caught up in grasping at things, comfort, praise and possessions, that we live as though we had forgotten who we are. We forget that we stand under God, who rightly rules us, and above the things we were meant to care for, not serve. The prodigal son in Luke 15:17 is said to have come to his senses. That is the kind of self-knowledge God calls us to: not new facts, but remembering our true place before Him.

This also shows why the image is only an image. Our minds change. We grow, forget, wander and are renewed. God does not change. The mind's knowing, remembering and loving are three activities of one created person. The Father, Son and Spirit are three persons, each fully God, sharing one unchanging divine being. The comparison helps us see that "three" and "one" need not contradict each other. It does not explain God fully, and we only know that God is triune because He has revealed it in Scripture, not because we looked inside ourselves.

Finally, this image reaches its true purpose when it turns toward God. A mind that rightly knows and loves itself will see that it is not its own source. It will see that it was made to remember, know and love the God whose image it bears. Colossians 3:10 describes believers as having put on the new self, "which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator." Sin has smudged the image, but it was never erased. In Christ, God is restoring it, so that one day we will know Him, and ourselves, as we are fully known.

topics.title: How are knowledge, desire and love related, and can we love what we do not know?
topics.cmp: Whether the unknown, including the Trinity, can be loved, how the desire to know relates to love, and the nature of knowledge and of willing.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How the Trinity May Be Loved Though Unknown.
refs.quote: What then do we know, whether specially or generally, of that most excellent Trinity, as if there were many such trinities, some of which we had learned by experience

ans.text:
No one can love something they know nothing at all about, but we can love what we know only in part, and we can long to know it better. Love always leans on some knowledge, even a small or borrowed piece of it. Love in turn drives us to know more. Applied to God, this means we do not need to understand the Trinity fully before we can love Him. We do need to know Him truly, as far as He has shown Himself.

Think about how love usually starts. You hear a friend describe someone kind, brave and generous, and you find yourself warming to that person before you ever meet them. Do you love a stranger? Not quite. You already know what kindness, courage and generosity are, because you have met them in other people. Your mind builds a picture from those known pieces, and that picture is what you love. If you later meet the person and they really are like the picture, your love was not aimed at nothing. If they turn out to be different, you begin to love the real person only once you get to know them. Either way, love follows knowledge.

It helps to separate two things that sound alike: loving something unknown, and loving to know something. A student eager to learn a subject he has not yet studied does not love the unknown facts themselves. He loves the knowing of them. Even that desire depends on some first impression. He has heard enough to sense that the subject is worth learning. The word "know" in "I want to know" matters. What we love is the knowing we hope for, and that is a good we already have some grasp of.

So desire and love are not two separate forces. They are the same will in two stages. While we are still seeking, our will reaches out in desire and searching. When we find what we sought, that same will settles into love. It holds on to what we now know and joins it to us. Desire is love on the road, and love is desire that has arrived. This is why Scripture so often joins seeking with loving. "One thing I have asked of the LORD," says the psalmist, "this I will seek" (Psalm 27:4). He longs to see God's beauty because he has already tasted it.

Hope matters too. We long most eagerly for what we think we can actually reach. Most people work hard at their own language but feel only a faint wish to master every language on earth. They admire the goal, but it seems out of reach, so their love for it stays lukewarm. That is part of why the gospel's promise matters so much. Jesus does not only show us something glorious. He promises that we will truly know God: "Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). Real hope makes real longing possible.

Now the hard case: how can we love the Trinity? With other things, we form a picture from similar things we know. We have never met the Apostle Paul, but we know what a human being is, so we can picture him truly enough. With God there is no such shortcut. There are not many trinities around us that we could study and compare. We have no general category, like "human being", that God belongs to. So we cannot love the triune God by imagining Him from other examples. If we try, we will love an idol of our own making.

How, then? First, we know God truly because He has made Himself known. We know Him by what He says about Himself in Scripture and above all in Jesus Christ. Jesus says that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father (John 14:9). He promises the Spirit, who will lead us into the truth. We believe the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God because God has told us so. Faith is a real kind of knowing. It is like being certain a distant city exists because trustworthy witnesses have told you, even though you have never been there. Peter writes to believers who never saw Jesus in the flesh: "Though you have not seen Him, you love Him" (1 Peter 1:8). They had not seen Him, but they knew Him through the apostles' witness, and that was enough to love Him.

Second, God has not left us strangers to what He is like. Scripture says plainly, "Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love" (1 John 4:8). We cannot picture the Trinity. But we do know what love is, what goodness is, what justice and truth are. These are not foreign to us. When we love goodness and truth, we are reaching toward the One who is goodness and truth. John even says that loving the brother we can see is bound up with loving the God we cannot see (1 John 4:20). Real love for others trains our hearts to recognise and love God, who is love itself. And the Father, Son and Spirit loving one another from all eternity is the deepest love there is.

This also shows something about us. Everyone wants to be happy and not miserable. Every person can find that wish in their own heart and knows it lives in everyone else. People chase it in a thousand wrong directions. But that deep longing is a sign that we were made for something, and Someone, we do not yet fully see. The longing itself is a kind of dim knowledge. It is a sense that there is a good worth having, even before we know its name.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. Some think faith means loving God blindly, with no knowledge at all. That is not how Scripture speaks. In Athens, Paul did not leave people worshipping "an unknown god". He told them who that God is (Acts 17:23). Others think they must fully understand the Trinity before they can love God. That is not true either. We know only in part, but what we know is true. Paul admits that now we see dimly, as in a mirror, and later we will see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Partial knowledge can still be true knowledge. A child truly knows and loves a parent long before understanding everything about them.

One more point: we can only truly know what is true. If we "know" something false, all we really know is that it is false. So love that rests on a false picture of God is not love of God. It is love of a mistake. That is why the church has cared so much about speaking rightly about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Getting God right is not a matter of cleverness. It matters because we want to love the real God and not a figment.

Putting it together: knowledge, even partial, gives love something to hold. Love, in turn, makes us long to know more. Hope that we will one day know fully makes the longing burn brighter. With God, we start from what He has revealed in His Word and in His Son. We love Him truly now, and we keep seeking to know Him better, until faith gives way to sight.

topics.title: What trinities are found in the outer man's sight, memory and imagination?
topics.cmp: Almost every answer here comes from Augustine of Hippo. He consistently finds trinities in the outer man: in sight (the visible object, the vision formed in the sense, and the will or attention joining them) and in recollection (the memory-image, the inner vision, and the uniting will). His grounds are mainly philosophical reasoning and analogy: the ring pressed into a fluid, afterimages and double vision, the walker who forgets his route, and the black swan composed from memory. In both trinities the will is cast as neither parent nor offspring, though his answers justify this differently: as the combiner of begetter and begotten, as proceeding from what memory retains without being simply generated, and as existing before the vision without forming it. His answers differ in wording on whether the trinity of sight is an image of God: most say no, while one says yes, it is a kind of trinity. All of them agree it is only a trace, because its members are unequal and not of one substance. Even the inner trinity of recollection, though of one substance, is denied the status of image because it is drawn from bodies and belongs to the outer man. Irenaeus of Lyons appears only on a side question, using Scripture (Paul on the first and second Adam) to explain why the animal precedes the spiritual; he does not address the trinities of sight or memory, so no direct comparison with Augustine is possible.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Species is Produced by Species in Succession.
refs.quote: Yet in all cases the will does not appear unless as the combiner as it were of parent and offspring; and so, proceed from whence it may, it can be called neither parent nor offspring.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For there had been a necessity that, in the first place, a human being should be fashioned, and that what was fashioned should receive the soul; afterwards that it should thus receive the communion of the Spirit.

ans.text:
Even in our most ordinary acts of seeing, remembering and imagining, we can spot a faint pattern of three things working as one. These patterns are not pictures of God. They are more like footprints in the sand that tell you someone has passed by. Christians have found them helpful for one reason: they show that "three distinct, yet one" is not a strange idea. Our own everyday experience is full of it.

Start with sight. When you look at a tree, three things are involved. First, there is the tree itself, which was there before you looked. Second, there is the seeing: the shape and color of the tree taking hold in your eye. Third, there is your attention, the choice to turn your eyes toward the tree and keep them there. Without the tree there is nothing to see. Without the eye there is no seeing. Without your attention, your eyes slide past and you never really see it. Yet in the moment of looking, these three come together in one act.

The seeing really is something distinct from the tree. Stare at a bright window and then shut your eyes. For a moment you still "see" the glowing shape of the panes. Or press a finger gently against the side of one eye, and a single candle flame turns into two. The thing itself has not changed. What you are noticing is the impression it made in you. Your power of sight also exists before and after you look at anything. With your eyes closed you are still not blind. The tree does not give you the ability to see; it only shapes that ability into seeing this tree.

Now move to memory. Later, at home, you call the tree to mind. Again there are three. There is the picture of the tree stored in your memory, which stays there even when you are not thinking of it. There is the inner "view" of it that your mind forms when you recall it. And there is your will, which turns your mind toward that memory. The stored picture and the inner view feel like one thing, because they are so alike. But they are two. The memory stays put when you think of something else, while the inner view lasts only as long as you are looking at it.

Imagination shows the difference even more clearly. You can only remember the sun as you have seen it: one, round, a certain size. But you can imagine two suns, or a square green one. The mind takes what memory supplies and reshapes it freely. So what you remember and what you are picturing are not the same thing, and it is your will that brings them together.

The will plays the same part every time. It joins the eye to the object, the memory to what the eye received, and the mind's inner gaze to the memory. The same will can also pull them apart. You can shut your eyes, turn your thoughts elsewhere, or simply stop thinking about something.

This is where the comparison becomes most interesting. In each of these patterns, one thing gives rise to another. The tree gives its form to your sight, and the memory gives its picture to your inner gaze, a bit like a parent and child. But the will is neither the source nor the product. It is the third thing that binds the two together. Christians have seen in this a small hint of how the Holy Spirit is related to the Father and the Son. Scripture calls the Son the Father's "only begotten" Son, meaning one who comes from the Father as a son comes from a father, sharing his very nature (John 1:14, 18). The Spirit, by contrast, is never called begotten. Jesus says He "proceeds from the Father" (John 15:26). The Spirit is fully God, but He comes from God in a different way than the Son does.

We must be honest about how far these comparisons go, which is not very far. The tree, the seeing and the will are not equal. They are not even the same kind of thing. The tree is wood and leaves. The seeing happens in body and soul together. The will belongs to the soul alone. In God, the Father, the Son and the Spirit are completely equal and share one and the same divine nature. Nothing in our senses is like that. Also, these patterns depend on things lower than us, such as trees, light and stones, and animals share our senses. A dog sees and remembers too.

That is why Christians have looked deeper for the true image of God. Scripture speaks of an "outer self" that is wasting away and an "inner self" that is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16). The outer self is the life of the body and senses, much of which we share with the animals. The inner self is the mind that can know truth, love God, and be "renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator" (Colossians 3:10). Even when we use what our senses give us in a reasoning, thoughtful way, that reasoning belongs to the inner self, not to anything we share with animals. This is where we were made in God's image (Genesis 1:26-27), and it is there, not in the eyes, that we should look for clearer likenesses of the Trinity.

One last lesson comes from all this. When your will turns your eyes to something, it finds a kind of rest in seeing it, but only a small, passing rest. Seeing the tree does not satisfy you for good. You soon want something else. The deepest longing of the will is not for any one thing we can see. It is for God Himself. The God who "formed the eye" (Psalm 94:9) made our seeing, remembering and imagining so that they would point beyond themselves to Him, and finally lead us to the joy of knowing Him.

topics.title: Does the image of God survive sin, and how is it renewed and perfected?
topics.cmp: Nearly all the answers come from Augustine, and they hang together: the image survives sin because the mind remains rational and capable of God, but it is defaced. It is kept and renewed only by turning to and partaking of God, and the soul cannot re-form itself without grace. Augustine also says renewal is gradual: baptism forgives at once, but healing proceeds day by day (Psalm 103), and the image is perfected only in the face-to-face vision after judgment, which is how he reads 1 John 3:2. Augustine's several answers differ only in emphasis. One frames renewal as loving, remembering and understanding God, while others frame it as progress in knowledge, righteousness and holiness or as transferring love from temporal to eternal things. One even places perfection in renewed knowledge of eternal wisdom rather than explicitly in the final vision. John Owen agrees that the image was lost by sin and is restored, but he grounds this differently, locating restoration in holiness alone and appealing to the command to be holy and to putting on the new man. He says nothing of Augustine's distinctive themes: the image's persistence in reason, its gradual healing, and its eschatological completion in sight.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: John is Rather to Be Understood of Our Perfect Likeness…
refs.quote: But the image which is renewed in the spirit of the mind in the knowledge of God, not outwardly, but inwardly, from day to day, shall be perfected by that sight itself; which then after the judgment shall be face to face

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: To this honour, of conformity to God, of bearing his image, are we exalted again by holiness alone.

ans.text:
Yes, the image of God survives sin, though it is badly damaged, and God himself restores it: he begins the work when he brings us to faith in Christ, carries it on day by day through his Spirit, and completes it when we finally see him face to face.

Start with what the Bible says after the fall. Long after Adam and Eve sinned, God tells Noah that murder is a terrible crime because "in His own image God has made mankind" (Genesis 9:6). James warns believers not to curse people, because they "have been made in God's likeness" (James 3:9). Neither passage is talking about especially holy people. They are talking about ordinary sinners. So the image is still there in every human being, believer or not. This is why every person, even the worst, deserves respect and protection.

What is this image? At its heart, God made us able to know him, love him, and live with him. We can think, remember, understand, and choose. No other creature on earth can turn toward its Maker that way. Many Christians have noticed a faint echo of the Trinity in this. When the mind remembers God, understands him, and loves him, these are three distinct acts of one mind, each bound up with the others. This is only a picture. Our minds are not God, and the comparison is limited. But it suggests that we were made for a relationship with the God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Think of a coin stamped with a king's face, then dropped in the mud and scratched. It is still the king's coin, and the face is still there, but you can hardly make it out. Sin works like that. We did not stop being human, or stop being made to know God. What we lost was the right use of those gifts. Our minds became darkened. Our love got bent toward ourselves and toward lesser things. Ephesians 4:24 and Colossians 3:10 show what went missing, because they describe what must be restored: "true righteousness and holiness" and a new self "being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator."

It helps to see how the fall happened. The serpent's promise was "you will be like God" (Genesis 3:5). Being like God was not the problem. We were made to be like him. The sin was grasping at it on our own terms, apart from him, instead of receiving it as his gift. Even today, people chasing power, pleasure or independence are often reaching, in a twisted way, for something only God can give. And the drift away from God usually happens bit by bit, not all at once. Small neglects add up. The Bible calls this forgetting God. When we forget God, we forget the source of our own life. When he reminds us and we turn back, it is like coming alive again.

Can we repair the image ourselves? No. A smudged coin cannot re-stamp itself. Only the one who made the image can form it again. Jesus says plainly, "apart from Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). God does this through Christ, who is himself "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). God's goal is that we be "conformed to the image of His Son" (Romans 8:29). By faith we are joined to Christ, and the Holy Spirit begins reshaping us from within. Paul says that as we look to the Lord's glory, we "are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit" (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Notice the words "being transformed." Renewal is not finished in a moment. When we come to Christ, our sins are forgiven all at once. The healing of the damage sin has done takes a lifetime. Psalm 103:3 puts these side by side: God "forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases." Think of a fever that breaks overnight. The patient still needs weeks to get his strength back. Paul says that "our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). In this life the renewal happens through faith. We hold on to God's truth, keep it in memory, try to understand it, and grow in love for it. These are steps toward what we were made for. That is why the slow habits of the Christian life matter: hearing Scripture, prayer, worship, and loving our neighbor.

In this life we never hold God steadily in view. Our attention slips, and our clearest moments pass. Paul admits, "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12). The image will be made complete when that day comes. John writes, "We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2). Seeing God fully is what will make us fully like him. Our minds will then know him without confusion, and our love will rest in him without wandering. That is also when we will receive our resurrection bodies. Christians have read this verse with different emphases. Some stress our bodies being made like Christ's risen body. Others stress the inner likeness of a soul that at last knows and loves God perfectly. The two belong together, since God will renew the whole person.

Sincere Christians have described these points in somewhat different ways. Some distinguish the image, which remains in everyone, from the likeness, meaning a true closeness to God, which was lost and must be given back. Others say the image survives in a broad sense, as our human nature with mind and will, but was lost in a narrow sense, as true knowledge, righteousness and holiness. Those on the first side point to Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9, which show the image still present in sinners. Those on the second point to Ephesians 4:24 and Colossians 3:10, which speak of the image needing to be created anew. Both agree on the main things. Sin has not erased our humanity. It has ruined our relationship with God. And only God can restore it, through Christ and by the Spirit.

So you are not a lost cause, and neither is anyone you meet. You bear the mark of your Maker. If you belong to Christ, that mark is being cleaned and restored right now, more each day. One day, when you see him as he is, it will shine as it was always meant to.

topics.title: What do Paul's texts teach about renewal and transformation into God's image?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Hilary, Gregory of Nyssa and Bickersteth all read Paul's renewal texts as describing a real transformation of believers toward God's image, and all tie it to God's action in Christ or the Spirit rather than to human achievement. They differ in focus. Gregory uses 'the new man which after God is created' Christologically: the created new man is Christ himself, so his 'creation' refers to his humanity and its wondrous birth. Hilary instead reads Colossians 3:10 of redeemed humanity, conformed to Christ's glorified body and restored to the first man's pattern and to immortality. Augustine works mainly through close textual and grammatical analysis: 'after the image' means 'in the image,' that is, in the mind; the Latin 'speculantes' should be settled by the Greek as 'mirror'; and 'from glory to glory' chiefly means from creation to justification, given by grace through the Spirit. Bickersteth alone uses 2 Corinthians 3:18 to guard Christ's deity, arguing from Hebrews 1:3 that believers' likeness is derived and never equality with the Son who is the express image.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For if the garment of salvation is one, and that is Christ, one cannot say that “the new man, which after God is created,” is any other than Christ

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How the Image of God is Formed Anew in Man.
refs.quote: Let us not therefore so understand the words, “After the image of Him that created him,” as though it were a different image after which he is renewed, and not the very same which is itself renewed.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Leaving sin and the old man behind, he is made a new man unto the knowledge of God, and arrives at the perfection of his constitution, since through the knowledge of his God he becomes the perfect image of God.

ans.text:
Paul teaches that in Christ, God is restoring in us the likeness to himself that sin defaced. He does this by making us more and more like his Son, through the work of the Holy Spirit, beginning now in our minds and hearts and finished when we see Christ face to face.

Start with where the idea comes from. In Genesis 1:27 God made humanity “in His own image.” That means we were made to reflect God: to know him, love him, and show his character in the world, much as a mirror shows the face turned toward it. Sin did not erase that image, but it bent and dimmed it. Our minds turned away from God, and the reflection grew distorted.

Paul's good news is that God has not given up on his first plan. In Ephesians 4:22-24 he describes the Christian life as taking off old clothes and putting on new ones. We are to put off “your old self” and “be renewed in the spirit of your minds,” and “put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.” Notice the word “created.” This is not touching up the old person. It is God's own new creation, as fresh as the first one. And the pattern is God himself, not some admirable human hero or moral ideal.

Colossians 3:9-10 says much the same. Believers have “put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator.” Two details matter here. First, the renewal is ongoing: it “is being renewed.” Second, it happens “in knowledge.” It reaches the place where the image of God most clearly lives in us, our mind and inner self, the part of us that can know God, remember him, and love him. Paul is not describing a new image added from outside. The very image God first placed in us is being repaired and brought back to its true shape.

Whose image is it, exactly? Here the Trinity comes into view. Paul says plainly that Christ himself is “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son “the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature.” The Son is the perfect image of the Father because he shares the Father's very being. So when God renews his image in us, he shapes us after his Son. Romans 8:29 says God predestined his people “to be conformed to the image of His Son.” That is why Paul can also say, “clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14). Putting on the new self and putting on Christ come to the same thing. The new humanity is modeled on Jesus, the eternal Son who became truly human and shows us what a person fully alive to God looks like.

Second Corinthians 3:18 shows how this happens: “And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.” The Greek word behind “reflect” can mean either to reflect like a mirror or to gaze at something as in a mirror. Both ideas fit. We look at the glory of God where he has shown it, “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and as we keep looking, we begin to reflect what we see. We become like what we behold. This is why reading Scripture, worship, prayer, and the Lord's Supper matter so much. They are the places where we fix our eyes on Christ.

“Intensifying glory,” or “from glory to glory” in older translations, means the change is gradual and growing. Christians have heard several true things in it. We move from the glory of being God's creatures to the greater glory of being forgiven and made right with him. We move from the glory of faith, seeing Christ dimly, to the glory of sight. And we move from being God's children now to being fully like Christ at the end. As 1 John 3:2 puts it, “when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is.” Now, Paul admits elsewhere, we see only “a dim reflection as in a mirror” (1 Corinthians 13:12). One day we will see face to face.

All of this “comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.” That guards against a common misunderstanding. Transformation into God's image is not a self-improvement project. We are called to put off and put on, and we really do act. But the power that changes us is God's grace, given by the Holy Spirit. So the whole Trinity is at work in our renewal. The Father is the one whose image is restored. The Son is that image, the pattern we are shaped after. The Spirit does the shaping.

A second misunderstanding is that being “transformed into His image” makes us equal to Christ or turns us into God. It does not. Christ is the image of God by nature. He is the eternal Son, sharing fully in the Father's being. We become images of God by grace, as reflections. A mirror can shine brightly with the sun's light, but it never becomes the sun. Our likeness to God is real and growing, but it is always received, never our own.

A third point is worth a word. When Paul says the new self is “created,” he is speaking of us, the redeemed people of God. Some careful Christian readers have also seen in “the new man” a glance at Christ's own human nature, since he is the true new man and we are made new by being joined to him. That reading can be helpful, but it never means the eternal Son himself was created. As God, the Son has always been. What was new was his taking on our humanity, so that our humanity could be made new in him.

So Paul's message is deeply hopeful. If you belong to Christ, God is at work in you right now, in your thinking, your loves, and your character. The change is often slow, and you may notice it least of all. But the one who began it is faithful. As you keep looking to Jesus, the Spirit is quietly making you more like him, until the image God intended from the beginning shines fully in the day when you see him as he is.

topics.title: Where does the analogy between the mind's trinity and the divine Trinity fall short?
topics.cmp: Why the divine Trinity is the one God and not faculties in God, whether the Trinity can be seen through its image in this life, and how far the mind can know and resemble God.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Augustin Dwells Still Further on the Disparity Between…
refs.quote: in that, there both is said to be and is one God, nor is that Trinity in one God, but it is one God.

ans.text:
The comparison between the mind and the Trinity is a real help, but it breaks down at the most important points: the three in God are not powers inside God but are God himself, they are three persons rather than one, and in this life we see God through this likeness only dimly, never face to face.

First, what the comparison is. The Bible says we were made in God's image (Genesis 1:26-27). Many Christians have noticed something in the human mind that faintly echoes the Trinity. Your mind can remember itself, understand itself, and love itself. That is three activities, yet they are not three minds. There is one you. They are bound together: you cannot love what you do not know, and you cannot know what you do not in some way hold in memory. This gives us a small picture of how something can be truly three and truly one at the same time. It is worth having. But it is a picture, and every picture leaves things out.

Here is the first big difference. Your memory, understanding and love belong to you, but they are not you. They are things you have, like abilities or powers. You are more than them. You also have a body, feelings, a history. If you lost some of your memory, you would still be you. God is not like that. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not three abilities that God has, or three parts that God is made of. The Trinity is not something inside God. The Trinity is God. There is nothing in God that stands behind or beyond the Father, Son and Spirit. When Scripture says, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and when Jesus sends his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), it is speaking of the same one God, not of a God who owns three faculties.

The second difference runs the other way. In your mind there are three activities but only one person. In God there are three persons. The Father loves the Son, the Son prays to the Father, the Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son. These are not three moods or three functions of one individual. They truly relate to one another. So if we pushed the mind comparison too hard, we would end up picturing God as one person who simply remembers, thinks and loves, with "Father," "Son" and "Spirit" as labels for those powers. That would lose the real Father and the real Son we meet in the Gospels.

Put those two differences together and you see how strange and wonderful God's oneness is. Three human beings, however close, are three men, never one man. But the Father, Son and Spirit are three persons and yet are, and are rightly called, one God. Their unity is deeper than anything in creation, deeper even than the unity of your own mind. That is why no creaturely example can fully capture it.

A third limit has to do with seeing. Paul says that now we see as in a mirror, dimly, but then we shall see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). The image of God in us is that kind of mirror. It can point us toward God, but it is blurred by our smallness and by sin, and it is hard to read. In fact, a person can notice the threefold pattern in their own mind and never think of God at all. That is like staring at a mirror without realizing it is a mirror. The likeness only helps when we recognize it as an image of Someone, and then let it turn our attention to him. Even then, what we see is partial and provisional. The clear sight is promised for later: "we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2).

A fourth limit is the gap between Creator and creature. Knowing God and loving him does make us more like him. Paul speaks of believers being transformed into his image as they behold the Lord's glory (2 Corinthians 3:18). But becoming like God never means becoming equal to God. Our knowledge of him is real, but it is the knowledge of a creature, held in a created mind. He knows himself fully; we know him only in part. A reflection of the sun in a puddle is truly light from the sun, but it is not the sun.

Finally, even our own minds are a mystery to us. Think how you can recite a familiar song: memory somehow lets you anticipate the next line before you reach it. You do it easily, yet you cannot really explain how remembering and looking ahead fit together. If we cannot fully understand that about ourselves, we should not expect to figure out how knowing, remembering and foreseeing are one in God, who does not learn things one after another but sees everything at once in a single, eternal knowing. Here the right response is the psalmist's: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain" (Psalm 139:6).

So use the comparison gratefully, but hold it loosely. It shows that "three and one" is not nonsense, and it reminds us that we were made to reflect God. But God is not a larger version of a human mind. He is the one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and the faint likeness in us is meant to make us long for the day when we will see him face to face.

title: Key New Testament Texts on Father and Son
desc: Exegesis of central passages such as John 1:1, John 10:30, John 14, Philippians 2, Hebrews 1, Colossians 2:9 and 1 Corinthians 15:28 on the Son's relation to the Father.

topics.title: Who is the Word of John's prologue, and what does John 1:1 teach about his relation to God?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Word of John's prologue is the Son, Jesus Christ, truly God and distinct from the Father, but they reach this by different routes. Athanasius argues mainly from the correlative names Father and Son: what is from the Father is a Son, so Word and Son must be one Person, or else the Son would be greater than the Word. Irenaeus argues against Gnostic splitting of Monogenes, Logos and Christ. Owen and Bickersteth argue exegetically: Owen reads 'in the beginning' as the beginning of all things against Socinian readings, while Bickersteth appeals to John's own usage in Revelation and to Philo's Logos. On 'with God', Owen, Hilary and Waterland read 'God' as the Father and see a real personal distinction, with Hilary stressing that the Word was 'with', not 'in', God and Waterland that the Father is eminently styled God as first in order; Augustine, by contrast, allows that 'God' may mean Father and Son together and uses the analogy of the human inner word to explain creation through the Word. Gregory of Nyssa adds a pastoral reason: John wrote 'Beginning', 'was' and 'Word' rather than 'Father', 'begotten' and 'Son' to keep untrained hearers from carnal ideas of generation, and he holds that the name 'God' belongs equally to the Word.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: For if not Son, neither is He Word; and if not Word, neither is He Son. For that which is from the father is a son;

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.place: Chapter XI—Proofs in continuation, extracted from St
refs.quote: that the Son of the Creator was, forsooth, one, but the Christ from above another, who also continued impassible, descending upon Jesus, the Son of the Creator, and flew back again into His Pleroma; and that Monogenes was the beginning, but Logos was the true son of Monogenes

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: the name “God” belongs equally to the Beginning in which the Word was, and to the Word Who was in the Beginning. For the Evangelist tells us that “the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

ans.text:
The Word of John's prologue is the eternal Son of God, the same person who later became a man and was named Jesus Christ. John 1:1 teaches three things about him: he already existed before anything was made, he was distinct from God the Father, and he was himself fully God.

We do not have to guess who the Word is, because John tells us as the chapter goes on. The Word comes into the world, is rejected by his own people, and then "the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). In the same verse John calls him "the one and only Son from the Father," and a few lines later he names him Jesus Christ (John 1:17). In Revelation, John describes the returning Christ and says, "His name is The Word of God" (Revelation 19:13). So "Word" and "Son" are not two different beings. They are two names for one person. Everything John says about the Word belongs to the Son, and everything Jesus says about himself as the Son, such as "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), belongs to the Word.

Why does John start with "Word" rather than "Son"? Think about what a word is. Your words come from your mind and show what is in it. Others know you through them. In the same way, the Son comes from the Father and makes him known. As John puts it, "No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known" (John 1:18). The name also echoes the Old Testament, where God creates by speaking. "And God said, 'Let there be light'" (Genesis 1:3). Psalm 33:6 says the heavens were made by the word of the Lord. Before anything is built, it is first thought and spoken, and John says, "Through Him all things were made" (John 1:3).

There may also be a gentle wisdom in John's choice. Words like "Son" and "born" can make us think of human births, which happen at a point in time and involve change. A word coming from a mind carries none of that. John lets "Word" prepare us before he speaks plainly of Father and Son. When Christians say the Son is "begotten" of the Father, they mean that he truly comes from the Father and shares his nature, the way a son shares his father's nature. They do not mean he had a starting point.

"In the beginning" deliberately echoes the first words of the Bible: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). John is taking us back before creation. Notice that he says the Word "was," not that the Word "came to be." When the beginning began, the Word already existed. Some have suggested this only means the beginning of gospel preaching. But that would make the verse say almost nothing, and the next verses speak of the Word making all things, which plainly points to creation. Jesus himself prays about "the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5).

"The Word was with God" shows that the Word is a real person, distinct from the one he was with. You are not "with" yourself. You are with someone else. John repeats the point in verse 2, "He was with God in the beginning." Since nothing else existed yet, this was a living, personal relationship within God himself. In the other places John uses this kind of language, the one the Son was with is the Father (John 1:18; 1 John 1:2). Some have read "God" here a little more broadly, as the one Godhead the Word shares in. Either way, the Word is distinct from the Father. The verse does not mean merely that the Word was known to God before John the Baptist preached. That would be true of countless things, so it would hardly be worth saying.

Then comes the striking line: "and the Word was God." John does not say the Word was like God or was a lesser divine being. Scripture is firm that there is only one God (Isaiah 45:5), so John cannot mean a second, junior god. He means the Word shares the one divine nature fully. Some translations render this "a god," but that reading clashes with the rest of the Bible's teaching that there is only one God. It also clashes with John's own words, since he soon calls the Son "Himself God" (John 1:18) and later records Thomas saying to Jesus, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). Notice, too, that the things by which we know God, his name, his eternity and his work of creation, are all given here to the Word.

Put together, John 1:1 holds two truths side by side. The Word is distinct from the Father, because he was with God. The Word is one with him in being, because he was God. This is not three gods, and it is not one person wearing different masks. It is the one God, eternally Father and Son, joined by the Holy Spirit, as the rest of the New Testament shows. It also means the Father did not become flesh. The Word, the Son, did.

One last verse is sometimes brought in. In some older translations of John 8:25, when Jesus is asked who he is, he seems to call himself "the Beginning." The Greek of that verse is hard to translate. Many modern versions, including the one this site uses, read it as Jesus saying he is just what he has been telling them from the beginning. Where it was read the older way, it was not taken to mean that Jesus is the source of the Father. That would turn John 1 upside down. It was understood the way Colossians 1:18 calls Christ "the beginning": he is the source and origin of creation, the one through whom all things were made. The Father is the source of the Son. The Son, with the Father, is the source of everything else.

So when you read "In the beginning was the Word," you are reading about Jesus himself. He is the eternal Son who was with the Father before the world began, who is truly God, and who came near to us in the flesh so that we might see and know God.

topics.title: In what sense is the Word called God in John 1:1?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that John 1:1 calls the Word God in the proper, full sense and not merely by office, dignity or later exaltation, but they argue it on different grounds. Athanasius grounds the Word's deity in his being from God, the Beginning. Gregory of Nyssa explains only the order of titles, saying John put 'Word' first so readers would not think at once of the Father. Waterland gives the most extended and technical case: the same word is used of the Father in the same verse; it must first be divided into proper and improper senses; dominion was impossible before creatures existed; the Septuagint uses Θεὸς for Jehovah; and the missing article proves nothing. Owen and Hilary argue more directly. Owen stresses that 'in the beginning' rules out a deity by exaltation and calls the idea of being 'made God' incoherent, citing Thomas and Paul. Hilary argues from the unqualified name, which describes a nature, in contrast to Moses' qualified title 'a god to Pharaoh.' Bickersteth, like Waterland, appeals to the surrounding context of John 1 and grants that John 10:35 allows a lower official sense for men, but sets this against the Word's essential deity as Creator.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: The first and most general distinction of the senses of the word God, should be into proper and improper; after which it will be soon enough to come to your famed distinction of supreme and subordinate.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.place: The Doctrine of the Holy Trinity Explained and Vindicated
refs.quote: not a god by office, one exalted to that dignity (which cannot well be pretended before the creation of the world), but as Thomas confessed him, “Our Lord and our God,”

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Here is no loophole for any such conjecture as that He has received this name as a favour or taken it upon Himself, so possessing a titular Godhead which is not His by nature.

ans.text:
John means that the Word is truly God, God in exactly the same full sense as the Father, and not a lesser being who merely carries the title. The verse reads: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1).

It helps to see the verse as three short statements. First, the Word already existed "in the beginning." When everything else began, he was already there. Second, the Word "was with God." He is not the same person as the one he was with. There is a real relationship, a face-to-face fellowship. Third, the Word "was God." Whatever God is, the Word is. Put together, John is telling us that the Word is distinct from the Father but shares the Father's very nature, his "essence," meaning everything that makes God God. A few verses later we learn who this Word is: "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). The Word is Jesus.

Some people suggest that John calls the Word "God" only in a lower sense. Perhaps it is a title of honor or office, the way a king or judge might be called mighty, or a reward given to Jesus after his resurrection. The text itself rules this out in several ways.

First, look at the same verse. John has just used the word "God" for the Father, in the highest possible sense. It would be strange for him to use the very same word in the very next breath with a weaker meaning, and give the reader no hint. Imagine a friend saying, "I went with my father, and my brother is a father too," and then telling you he meant only that his brother acts fatherly at work. You would rightly feel misled. John is a careful writer, and he gives no signal of a shift.

Second, notice when the Word was God: "in the beginning," before anything was made. A title of office or rule only makes sense when there is something to rule over. Before creation there were no creatures. So there was nothing over which the Word could be "God" by office. He could only be God by nature. And John goes straight on to say that he is the Creator: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Making all things out of nothing is something only the true God does. The Old Testament insists on this again and again (see Isaiah 44:24). That is also why, when the Word came into the world, John says "He came to His own" (John 1:11). The world was his because he made it.

Third, John does not speak of the Word "becoming" God or being "made" God. Being truly God is not something anyone can be promoted into. Either one is God or one is not. John says the Word simply was God, from the start. And what he was, he still is.

What about Jesus' words in John 10:34–35? There he quotes Psalm 82, where human judges are called "gods." Doesn't that show the word can be used loosely? It does show that Scripture sometimes uses the word in a borrowed, figurative way. In a similar way, God told Moses he would be like God to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1). But in those cases the context makes the limited sense obvious. The judges are mortal men who will "die like men," and Moses is given a qualified role for a particular task. Someone called "god" in that borrowed way is not actually God at all. That is different from being God in a real but lower degree. Jesus' point in John 10 is an argument from the lesser to the greater. If Scripture could use the word for mere men to whom God's word came, how much less can you accuse of blasphemy the one the Father set apart and sent, who calls himself God's Son? Jesus is not placing himself on their level. He is contrasting himself with them. And John 1:1 has none of those limiting marks. The Word is called God plainly, before creation, as the Creator.

You may also hear an argument from the original Greek. In "the Word was with God," the Greek has "the" before "God": literally "with the God." In "the Word was God," it does not. Some conclude this means "a god," a lesser divine being. But this argument proves too much. In the same chapter John uses "God" without "the" several more times, for example "a man sent from God" (v. 6), "children of God" (v. 12), "born of God" (v. 13), and "no one has ever seen God" (v. 18). Nobody thinks those verses mean some lesser god. They plainly mean the one true God. In Greek, leaving out "the" often does not weaken a word at all. Here it serves a careful purpose. If John had written "the Word was the God," he would have seemed to say the Word is the very same person as the Father. That would erase the distinction he has just made with "the Word was with God." Without "the," John tells us what the Word is, which is God in nature, while keeping clear that he is not the Father. In English, "the Word was God" captures this exactly.

There is a deeper point too. When John's Jewish readers heard "God," they heard the one God of Israel, the LORD, who says there is no other (Isaiah 45:5). John uses the word that way throughout his Gospel. He gives no reason to think he meant a second, smaller god beside the LORD. That would contradict everything the Bible teaches about there being one God.

The rest of John's Gospel confirms this reading. Verse 18 calls Jesus "the one and only Son, who is Himself God." At the end of the Gospel, Thomas falls before the risen Jesus and says, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). Jesus accepts this worship rather than correcting it. Paul likewise speaks of Christ as "God over all, forever worthy of praise" (Romans 9:5). John opens and closes his Gospel with the same confession, and it is no accident.

It is also worth noticing that John calls him "the Word" before he calls him "God." This order keeps us from simply thinking of the Father when we hear "God." It introduces a distinct person first, and only then tells us that this person is God. A word comes from a mind and expresses it perfectly. So the Son comes from the Father, perfectly reveals him, and shares his nature, without being a creature made after him.

So when we read John 1:1, we are not meeting a lofty angel or an honored creature. We are meeting the eternal God himself, who is with the Father, shares his nature, made all things, and then became flesh for our salvation. That is why Christians worship Jesus, and why we can trust that in seeing him we truly see God.

topics.title: What does John 5:18 show about Christ's equality with God?
topics.cmp: All four authors agree that John 5:18 truly reports Christ's claim to equality with God, not a misunderstanding or slander by the Jews. Hilary and Warfield both locate the point in Jesus calling God his "own" Father. For Hilary this signifies a birth of nature from nature, and so equality of nature. Warfield contrasts this real sonship with the figurative sense in which Israel was called God's son, concluding that to be God's own Son is to be all that God is. Waterland argues most fully, drawing on the evidence of the text, the Fathers, and the opponent: the other parts of the charge (sabbath-working, calling God his Father in a peculiar sense) were true, so the rest should be. He adds that the Evangelist would have flagged a false charge, as he does elsewhere, cites Hilary, notes that even Socinus conceded the point, and reads "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" and v.19 as implying equal right or intimate union with the Father. Bickersteth instead argues from Jesus' own response: rather than protesting, as a mere man would have done with indignation, he went on to assert his essential supremacy as God. Bickersteth alone qualifies this with an acknowledged subordination of Christ's mission as man.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: Was not His clearly a birth of nature from nature, when He published the equality of His nature by speaking of God, by name, as His own Father?

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: To be the Son of God in any sense was to be like God in that sense; to be God’s own Son was to be exactly like God, to be “equal with God.”

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: It is not to be denied that he had really wrought on the sabbath, and had really called God his Father, and in a sense peculiar ; and why should not the rest of the charge be as true as the other?

ans.text:
John 5:18 shows that Jesus really did claim to be equal with God, and that John wants us to see this as the truth about Him, not as a slander made up by His enemies.

Here is the setting. Jesus healed a man on the Sabbath and told him to pick up his mat and walk. When religious leaders challenged Him, He did not say, "The healing was God's doing, not mine." Instead He said that His Father is always at work, even now, and that He Himself is working too (John 5:17). Then John explains their reaction: "Because of this, the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him. Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God" (John 5:18).

The key word is "own." Israel as a nation was sometimes called God's son, and believers can call God "our Father." No one in Jesus' audience would have wanted to kill Him for saying that. What shocked them was that Jesus spoke of God as His Father in a unique way, as if He shared the Father's very life and nature. A human son has the same nature as his father. He is fully human because his father is human. So when Jesus called God His own Father in this special sense, His hearers understood Him to mean that He is what God is. They also saw that He was claiming the same right to work on the Sabbath that only God has. God keeps the world going every day, Sabbath included, and Jesus put His own work right alongside the Father's.

Some readers suggest this was just a hostile misreading by Jesus' opponents. Three things in the passage point the other way.

First, verse 18 is not a quote from the crowd. It is John the narrator explaining why they wanted to kill Jesus. Elsewhere, when people misunderstand Jesus, John stops and corrects them. When Jesus spoke of destroying "this temple," John explains that He meant His body (John 2:19-21). John adds no such correction here.

Second, the other parts of the charge were true. Jesus really had worked on the Sabbath, and He really had called God His Father. It would be odd if only the last part were false.

Third, look at what Jesus says next. An ordinary godly man accused of making himself equal with God would have been horrified and denied it at once. Jesus does the opposite. He goes on to say that the Son does whatever the Father does (John 5:19). He says He gives life to whom He wishes, just as the Father does (5:21). He says all judgment has been given to Him (5:22). And He says this is "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (5:23). No mere creature could rightly ask for the same honor that belongs to God. Jesus does not back away from the claim. He makes it even stronger.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. One is that "equal with God" means Jesus is a second God, a rival working on His own. Jesus rules that out when He says the Son can do nothing by Himself, but only what He sees the Father doing (5:19). This is not weakness. It shows how close their unity is. Father and Son never act apart, because they share one divine life and will. What the Father does, the Son does too, in the same way. As Jesus says later, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30).

The other misunderstanding comes from the phrase "making Himself equal." It can sound as if Jesus reached for a status that was not His. His opponents thought of it that way. But the New Testament teaches that equality with God already belonged to the Son by nature. Paul says Christ existed in the form of God and did not cling to equality with God. Instead He humbled Himself and took on the nature of a servant (Philippians 2:6-7). This also explains why Jesus, in this same chapter, speaks of being sent by the Father and receiving from Him. As the eternal Son, He has the same divine nature as the Father. As the One sent to become man and save us, He gladly carries out the Father's will.

So John 5:18 is one of the clearest windows in the Gospels onto who Jesus is. His enemies understood His words correctly, even though they rejected Him for it. The Son is not a lesser god or a specially favored man. He is God's own Son, sharing fully in the Father's nature, and worthy of the same honor and worship as the Father.

topics.title: What do 'I and the Father are one' and 'He that hath seen Me hath seen the Father' teach about the Son's unity with the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors (Hilary, Athanasius, Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, Novatian, Hippolytus, Irenaeus, Owen, Waterland, Warfield) agree that these sayings teach both the Son's real distinction from the Father against Sabellius/Noetus and his true divinity against those who make him a creature or mere man. Most of them, especially Hilary, Athanasius, Augustine, Ambrose and Gregory, also read them against Arius. They mostly argue from the wording itself: the plural 'are', the conjunction 'and', the neuter 'one' (Hilary, Augustine, Ambrose, Novatian, Waterland, Basil on 'with'). They also appeal to the Jews' reaction (Hilary, Owen, Ambrose), to analogies of radiance and fountain (Athanasius), and, in Waterland's case, to the testimony of the Fathers. They differ on what kind of oneness 'one' asserts. Hilary, Athanasius, Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory and Warfield insist on unity of nature or essence and reject a mere unity of will, using reductio arguments that otherwise angels, prophets or saints would be equally 'one' with God (Athanasius, Gregory). By contrast, Novatian reads the neuter 'one' as concord and loving association, and Hippolytus as a oneness of power and disposition like the disciples' unity. Waterland mediates: the Fathers stressed consent against the Sabellians but founded it on unity of substance. Emphases also vary: Hilary and Athanasius ground the unity in the Son's birth and mutual indwelling. Gregory stresses the Father as cause and the order within coinherence. Basil holds that what is 'seen' in John 14:9 is the identical will that goes with the essence. Hilary insists the Father is seen by the understanding, not the eye of flesh, while Hippolytus and Novatian read that saying as the Son being the image or way through which the Father is known.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: through the truth of the birth and the unity of the nature, it is declared that whatever the Son did and said, the Father said and did in the Son?

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Again He Proves from the Gospel that Christ is God.
refs.quote: For how can it be that “I and the Father are one,” if He is not both God and the Son?

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: we are taught in that utterance the dependence of our Lord on a cause, and yet the absolute identity of the Son’s and the Father’s nature; we do not let our idea about them be melted down into One Person

ans.text:
These sayings teach that the Son shares the Father's own power and nature and lives in the Father, so that to know the Son is truly to know the Father. They also show that the Son is not the Father. Jesus speaks of two who are one, not one person wearing two names.

Start with the setting of John 10. Jesus says of His followers, His sheep, that He gives them eternal life and no one can snatch them out of His hand. In the next breath He says no one can snatch them out of His Father's hand. Then comes the summary: "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). The hand that holds believers safe is His hand and the Father's hand at once. Only God can give eternal life and guarantee it against every power in the universe. So the oneness here is not friendship or teamwork. It is one power, and behind that, one nature. Nature means what someone is. Jesus is saying that whatever the Father is as God, He is too.

The crowd understood Him that way. They picked up stones and said they were stoning Him for blasphemy, "because You, who are a man, declare Yourself to be God" (John 10:33). Jesus did not tell them they had misheard. He pointed to the works He did, which only God can do, and said these show "that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father" (John 10:38). Christians sometimes call this mutual indwelling. Father and Son are not two gods side by side. Each is wholly in the other, sharing one divine life.

Yet the same verse guards against the opposite mistake. Jesus does not say "I am the Father." He says "I and the Father," naming two, and "are," a plural verb. In the Greek the word "one" is not the form used for one person. It means one thing, one reality. Throughout John's Gospel the Son is sent by the Father, prays to the Father, and returns to the Father. A person does not send himself or pray to himself. So Father and Son are truly distinct persons. The Father is the Father and the Son is the Son, and the difference lies in how they relate: one begets and the other is begotten. "Begotten" means the Son comes from the Father eternally, the way light comes from a flame, sharing its nature rather than being made. Because the Son comes from the Father's own being, He can be both distinct from the Father and one with Him.

That is also why the other sayings follow. In John 12:45 Jesus says, "whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me." In John 14, Philip asks Jesus to show them the Father. Jesus answers, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Then He asks, "Don't you believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me?" (John 14:10).

This does not mean the Father has a human body, or that the Father is physically visible in Jesus' face. Nor does it mean Jesus is the Father in disguise. Notice that in the same breath He still speaks of "the One who sent Me." The point is that the Son is "the exact representation of His nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Think of a perfect image, not a painting that resembles someone but one that carries the very same reality. When we see by faith who Jesus is, His holiness, His love, His authority over sickness, sin and death, we are not seeing a lesser copy of God. We are seeing God Himself, because the same Godhead is in both. John 1:18 says no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God, has made Him known. Philip had been looking at the man in front of him. Jesus invited him to look through that humanity to the divine Son, and so to the Father.

Some readings of these texts fall short. One says Jesus only meant He and the Father agree, a unity of will. Of course their wills are perfectly united. But agreement alone cannot explain why the Son's hand is the Father's hand, or why the crowd heard a claim to be God. Some point to Jesus praying that His disciples "may be one as We are one" (John 17:22). That prayer asks believers to reflect the unity of God, as a mirror reflects the sun. It does not make the Son's oneness with the Father no deeper than ours. No disciple could say "whoever sees me sees the Father."

Another reading says the Son is a lesser, created being who is merely close to God. But nothing created can be "one" with the Creator in the way Jesus claims. A creature cannot hold souls with God's own power or show God's nature perfectly. Only one who comes from the Father's very being can.

Still another idea suggests that a divine Word living inside Jesus spoke these lines, distinct from the Son, who would then be only the man. But John says "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14). The Word is the Son. The one who says "I and the Father are one" also says plainly, "I am the Son of God" (John 10:36). There is one speaker, the eternal Son, now made man.

So these verses hold together the two sides of the faith Christians have always confessed. There is one God, so the Son is fully God, equal to the Father in power and nature. Within that one God the Father and the Son are truly distinct. For ordinary believers this is deeply comforting. When you look to Jesus, you are not looking at a go-between who might differ from God behind the scenes. You are seeing the Father's own heart, and you are held in a hand from which no one can snatch you.

topics.title: What does Christ's command to believe in Him (John 14:1, 11) teach about His deity?
topics.cmp: Hilary of Poitiers, Augustine, and John Owen all read 'Believe in God, believe also in Me' (John 14:1) as requiring the same faith toward the Son as toward the Father, and so as testifying to His deity. Their grounds differ. Hilary argues from the inseparability of the two beliefs to the inseparability of the two natures: since perfect life is given only to those who believe in both, Christ shares God's honour and nature. Augustine argues from the other direction, taking as given that Father and Son are one God and concluding that the same faith is therefore owed to both.
