Owen's emphasis is distinctive: the same divine, supernatural faith must be directed distinctly at the Son himself, which differs from merely believing on the Father's testimony that he is the Son of God. Only Hilary addresses John 14:11, which he reads as Christ's answer to 'Shew us the Father', teaching believers to contemplate the Father in the Son while remembering that the Son is in the Father.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: these words, uniting faith in Him with faith in God, unite His nature to God’s.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In What Manner the Son is Said Not to Know the Day and…
refs.quote: in the same way as you believe in God, so also believe in me; because I and the Father are One God.

ans.text:
When Jesus tells His troubled disciples to believe in Him just as they believe in God, He is claiming the kind of trust that belongs to God alone, and that shows He shares in the Father's deity.

The setting matters. It is the night before the cross. Jesus has just said He is leaving, and the disciples are frightened. His first words of comfort in John 14:1 are these: "Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well." He sets Himself right beside God as the One their hearts can rest on.

Think about what that means for a Jew in the first century. The Old Testament repeatedly warns against leaning your whole weight on any human being. Jeremiah 17 pronounces a curse on the person who trusts in man and turns his heart away from the LORD, and a blessing on the one whose trust is in the LORD. The prophets asked people to believe their message, but no prophet ever said, "Trust in me the way you trust in God." Moses pointed away from himself to the LORD. Jesus points to Himself. If He were only a great teacher, this would be a dangerous thing to say. Coming from Him, it is a quiet but clear claim to be God.

Notice too that Jesus does not ask for a lesser, second-tier faith, as if we trust God fully and Jesus a little. The words tie the two together: the same deep, heart-level reliance we give to the Father, we are to give to the Son. That fits what He says elsewhere, that all should "honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23), and that "whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me" (John 12:44). You cannot split the trust, because you cannot split the One you are trusting. The Father and the Son are distinct, yet they are one God, so the faith owed to God is owed to both.

There is also a difference between believing something about Jesus and believing in Jesus. A person can accept the fact that Jesus is the Son of God because the Father testified to it. That is good, but Jesus asks for more. To believe in Him is to rest on Him personally, to hand Him your fears, your future and your soul. That is the faith we give to God, now directed to the Son Himself.

This leads into verse 11. A few lines later Philip asks, "Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us" (John 14:8). Jesus answers, "Whoever has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Then He adds, "Believe Me that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me—or at least believe on account of the works themselves" (John 14:11). So the command to believe is His answer to the desire to see God. Philip wants a vision; Jesus gives him Himself. The way to see the Father is to look at the Son, and the way to see the Son rightly is by faith in His word.

What exactly are we to believe? That the Father is in Him and He is in the Father. This is not a picture of two separate beings working closely together, like two colleagues. Nor does it mean the Son is the Father under another name. The Son really is distinct from the Father, yet they dwell in one another so completely that to know the one is to know the other. When we look at Jesus, His kindness, His holiness, His words, His works, we are not seeing a copy or a rough sketch of God. We are seeing the Father truly, because the Father is in the Son, and we remember that the Son is always in the Father.

Jesus also mentions His works. He is gentle with weak faith. If the disciples struggle to take His word, they can look at what He has done: healing, forgiving, raising the dead. These are the works of God, and they point back to who He is.

So these two verses work together. In verse 1 Jesus asks for the trust that belongs only to God. In verse 11 He explains why that trust is fitting: He and the Father are in each other, so that seeing Him is seeing the Father. A common misunderstanding is to think that Christian faith has two objects competing for our hearts, God and Jesus. It does not. To believe in Jesus is to believe in God, and to believe in God fully is to believe in Jesus. For a troubled heart, that is the deepest comfort there is: the One we are asked to lean on is not merely a messenger from God, but God with us.

topics.title: What does Christ's prayer that believers 'may be one as We are' (John 17) show about the Son's unity with the Father?
topics.cmp: Athanasius, Hilary, Augustine and Bickersteth all reject the reading that the Son's unity with the Father is only the moral unity believers can have, and all treat the Son's unity as natural or essential while believers' unity is derived. They defend this in different ways. Athanasius relies mainly on grammar and analogy: 'as' signifies a pattern for imitation, not identity, as with Jonah and Christ, and 'in Us' rather than 'in Thee' marks a distance. He also reads the prayer as a request that the Spirit be given irrevocably, so that believers are in God by grace while the Son is in the Father by nature. Hilary argues that the words describe mutual indwelling rather than agreement of will, since Christ would have prayed for unity of will had he meant it. Augustine and Bickersteth, by contrast, readily say Father and Son are one in will as well as in substance; Bickersteth adds power and operation. Augustine stresses that Christ deliberately says the disciples are one among themselves, 'in their own kind,' and reserves 'we are one' for his consubstantial parity with the Father. He also says, more strongly than Athanasius, that believers share 'the same nature' and are united in love.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.quote: as the Father and Son are one, not only in equality of substance, but also in will, so those also may be one

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: if we too become one, as the Son in the Father, we shall not be as the Son, nor equal to Him; for He and we are but parallel.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For there would have been no lack of suitable words for our Lord, if it were will that made them one, to have prayed in this fashion,—Father, as We are one in will, so may they also be one in will

ans.text:
Christ's prayer does not shrink His unity with the Father down to the level of believers. It lifts believers up toward a pattern that only He and the Father truly fill. When Jesus prays in John 17:11 that His followers "may be one as We are one," He holds up His oneness with the Father as the model for theirs. A model is not the same as a copy.

The little word "as" does a lot of work here. In ordinary speech, and in the Bible, "as" often means "in a way that resembles," not "in exactly the same way." Jesus tells us to be merciful just as our Father is merciful (Luke 6:36), and to be perfect as our heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). No one thinks this makes us equal to God in mercy or perfection. He is the standard, and we reflect it in our small, creaturely way. Jesus also compared His three days in the grave to Jonah's three days inside the great fish (Matthew 12:40). The comparison is real, but it does not make Jonah equal to Christ. So when Jesus says "as We are one," He is pointing to a likeness, not claiming that the two kinds of unity are identical.

Some have argued the reverse. They say that if believers are one only by agreeing in heart and purpose, then the Father and the Son must be one only in that way too. On this view the Son is simply a perfectly obedient creature who agrees with God. But that reverses the direction of the prayer. Jesus does not start from our unity and measure His own by it. He starts from His own unity with the Father and asks that something of it be reflected in us.

The chapter itself shows how different His unity is from ours. In the same prayer Jesus asks the Father to glorify Him "with the glory I had with You before the world existed" (John 17:5). No disciple could pray that. He says to the Father that "all I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine" (John 17:10). That is the language of One who shares everything the Father is and has. He also says that eternal life is to know the only true God "and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). He places knowing Himself right beside knowing God. Earlier He said plainly, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). He said it right after promising that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand, and no one can snatch them out of the Father's hand. The same hand, the same power, keeps the flock safe. His hearers understood Him well enough to pick up stones, because they took Him to be making Himself God (John 10:33).

So in what way are the Father and the Son one? They are one in essence. "Essence" simply means what something fundamentally is. The Son is not a second, lesser being alongside God. He shares the one divine nature fully with the Father. Because of that, they are also one in power, in their works, in love, and in will. Their perfect agreement is real. But it grows out of something deeper than agreement: they are the one God.

Notice too how carefully Jesus words the prayer. He never says, "that they and I may be one the way the Father and I are one." He prays that believers may be one with each other, and that they may be "in Us" (John 17:21). We are not in the Father the way the Son is. The Son is in the Father by His very nature, from all eternity. We are brought in from outside, by grace. We are joined to the Son, and through Him we come to the Father. Jesus describes this order Himself: "I in them and You in Me" (John 17:23). He stands in the middle as the one Mediator. What He has by nature, He shares with us as a gift, chiefly by giving us His Spirit, so that His love and life dwell in us (John 17:26).

That gift is not a small thing. Believers are not merely asked to get along. We are drawn into a real, living fellowship with the Father and the Son, and so with one another. That is why the unity of the church matters so much to Jesus. He prays for it "so that the world may believe that You sent Me" (John 17:21). Our oneness is meant to be a visible echo of the oneness of God.

Two mistakes are worth avoiding. One is to think the Son's unity with the Father is only a close friendship or a shared purpose, like two people who see eye to eye. The other is to think that believers will one day become divine in the same way the Son is. Scripture teaches neither. The Son is one with the Father as God with God. We are one with each other, and united to God, as redeemed creatures who share by grace in His life.

So the prayer of John 17 actually highlights the Son's unique place. Only someone who is truly one with the Father could offer His own unity as the pattern for the whole church, and then give us the Spirit to make that pattern real in us.

topics.title: What does Philippians 2:6-7 teach about Christ's divine and human natures?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, John Owen, Daniel Waterland and Novatian all read 'in the form of God' as signifying true divinity, not a mere appearance or the status of a man or angel, but they argue for it differently. Gregory, Owen and Waterland reason from the antithesis with 'the form of a servant', which they take to mean true human essence or nature. Owen adds that only God can be equal to God. Waterland stresses agreement with Catholic antiquity, while Novatian argues from scriptural usage: men are made in God's 'image', not his 'form', and angels are never said to be in the form of God. On Philippians 2:7, Owen and Hilary of Poitiers agree that the form of a servant means a real human nature, but with different emphases. Owen shows this by comparing Scripture with Scripture (Romans 8:3). Hilary uses the phrases 'likeness' and 'fashion' to safeguard Christ's sinlessness. Waterland alone defends the divinity reading against the alternative translation 'did not assume to be honoured as God', granting it for argument's sake because the proof rests on 'being in the form of God' and on John 17:5. Gregory alone answers the charge that Basil's reading implies the servant-form existed before time, and he rejects it as calumny.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For as, “being made in the form of a servant,” He was formed in the essence of a servant, not taking upon Him the form merely, apart from the essence, but the essence is involved in the sense of “form,”

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: That the “form of God” is here the essence of the Deity, sundry things inevitably evince

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: “ Who being in the form of God,” that is, “ truly God, (which “ best answers to the antithesis following, the form of a servant “‘ signifying as much as ¢ru/y man,)

ans.text:
Philippians 2:6-7 teaches that Jesus Christ was truly God before he ever became a man, and that at his birth he took on a real human nature without ceasing to be God. In these two verses Paul shows us the whole shape of the gospel in a few lines. The one who was fully God became fully human, and he did it to serve.

Paul writes that Christ, "existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness." The key is in the two matching phrases: "the form of God" and "the form of a servant." Paul sets them side by side on purpose, so each helps us understand the other.

Start with the second one, because it is easier. When Jesus took "the form of a servant," he did not just look like a man or act out a part. He really became one. He was born, he grew, he got hungry and tired, he wept, and in the end he died on a cross, as verse 8 says. A pretend body cannot bleed and die. So "the form of a servant" means a true human nature, everything that makes us human.

Now apply the same meaning to the first phrase. If "the form of a servant" means really being human, then "the form of God" means really being God. In everyday words, "form" here points to what something truly is at its core, not just its outward shape. Theologians use the word "essence" for this: the basic nature that makes something what it is. Christ shared the very nature of God, not an imitation or a borrowed glory.

The rest of the verse confirms this. Paul speaks of Christ's "equality with God." But God himself says that no one is his equal. In Isaiah 46:9 the Lord declares that there is none like him. A creature, however great, can never be equal to the Creator. Only God is equal to God. So if Christ had equality with God, he must himself be God, sharing one nature with the Father.

Notice too that Paul does not say Christ was made in the "image" of God. That is the language Genesis uses for every human being. Adam was created in God's image. Paul says something higher: Christ existed in the very form of God. Nor does the Bible ever speak of angels this way. This is language reserved for the Son alone.

What, then, does it mean that he "emptied Himself"? This is where many people get confused. Some imagine that the Son set aside his divine nature, or stopped being God for a while, in order to become a man. But Paul explains the emptying by what follows: Christ emptied himself by "taking the form of a servant." He did not empty himself by subtracting his divinity. He emptied himself by adding our humanity. God cannot stop being God, any more than he can stop being holy or eternal.

Think of a king who lays aside his royal robes and puts on the clothes of a common laborer so he can work alongside his people. He is no less the king. But his majesty is hidden, and he chooses to live as a servant. In a similar way, the Son's glory was veiled during his earthly life. It was not lost. That is why Jesus could pray in John 17:5, "And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed." He was asking to have openly again the glory that had always been his.

The phrase "being made in human likeness" also sometimes troubles readers. Does "likeness" mean he only seemed human? No. Paul uses the same kind of language in Romans 8:3, where God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh. Jesus had real flesh, but not sinful flesh. The word "likeness" protects two truths at once. He was truly like us in every way, and yet he was without sin. Hebrews 4:15 says the same: he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. He shared our nature, not our faults.

You may notice that Bible translations word verse 6 a bit differently. Some say Christ did not consider equality with God "something to be grasped," others "something to cling to" or "something to exploit." One older suggestion even took it to mean he did not insist on being honored as God while on earth. These differences are real, and careful scholars have weighed them. But none of them weakens the main point. The heart of the verse is the opening phrase: he was "existing in the form of God." Whichever wording we choose, Paul is describing someone who truly was God and who chose not to use that status for his own advantage. Even if the verse means he did not demand divine honor during his humble life, that says nothing about lacking it beforehand. It describes a choice to set aside the honor he was due.

One more point clears up a common confusion. This passage tells us mainly about the incarnation, that is, about what the Son did when he became man. It is not a full description of how God exists in eternity. But that does not mean a mere man existed beforehand and then emptied himself to become a man, which would make no sense. Nor does it mean his human nature existed before he was born of Mary. The one who emptied himself was the eternal Son. His human nature began in Mary's womb. The person is the same; the humanity is new.

So the passage gives us one person, Jesus Christ, with two natures. He is fully God, sharing the Father's nature from all eternity. He is fully man, having taken a real human body and soul. He did not trade one for the other. He holds both together.

Finally, remember why Paul wrote this. He was not giving a theology lecture for its own sake. In verse 5 he tells the Philippians to have the same attitude that was in Christ Jesus. The one who had every right to glory chose to serve, and to serve all the way to the cross. Verses 9 to 11 then tell us that God has highly exalted him, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. The God who became a servant is the Lord we worship, and his humility is the pattern for ours.

topics.title: What do Christ's exaltation and the 'Name above every name' in Philippians 2:9-11 mean for the Son's divinity?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that Philippians 2:9-11 does not mean the divine Word was promoted or given anything he lacked by nature. Athanasius, Augustine, Waterland (following Hippolytus) and Gregory of Nyssa all refer the exaltation to Christ's humanity or 'form of a servant', and Athanasius and Gregory share the argument that nothing can be higher than the divine height. They differ in how they develop the point. Athanasius gives several readings: the exaltation is 'for our sake', so that we are exalted in him; it is the resurrection, with 'wherefore' giving its cause, as in Acts 2:24; it is the deification of his manhood; and a reward-of-virtue reading would make him Son only by grace. Waterland, citing John 17:5, and Hilary, by contrast, speak of the exaltation as a return or restoration to the glory and equality of form he had before, while Gregory describes the assumed Man being assimilated to the Divine Nature. On the 'Name above every name', Novatian argues directly that it is the name of God and so proves Christ is God, whereas Hilary uses Philippians 2:11 ('in the glory of God the Father') to show that the Son is all that the Father is and no longer abides in fleshly weakness.

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: If He was exalted and received grace, on a ‘wherefore,’ and on a ‘wherefore’ He was anointed, He received a reward of His purpose; but having acted from purpose, He is altogether of an alterable nature.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: He is said to be exalted, as having “ wanted it before ; but in respect only of his humanity

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: That the Same Divine Majesty is in Christ, He Once More…
refs.quote: For He has “received a name which is above every name,” which assuredly we understand to be none other than the name of God. For since it belongs to God alone to be above all things

ans.text:
The exaltation in Philippians 2:9-11 does not mean that the eternal Son was promoted to a rank he lacked, or that he stands below the Father. It means that the one who was always God, having stooped down to become a man and die, was raised and enthroned in the very human nature in which he had been humbled. The name he receives is God's own name, and the honor given to him is the honor that belongs to God alone.

Look at the shape of the whole passage. Paul says that Christ Jesus was "existing in the form of God" and "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped," but "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness" (Philippians 2:6-7). He then "humbled Himself and became obedient to death—even death on a cross" (2:8). Only after that downward journey do we read, "Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names" (2:9).

The story begins with the Son already equal with God. The movement is first a descent, and then a return. Nobody starts out equal with God and then works his way up to something higher. Nothing is higher than God. So the exaltation cannot be the Son climbing to a divine status he did not have before.

What, then, was lifted up? The answer is his humanity, the real human life, body and soul, that the Son took to himself. As God, the Son never stopped being the Most High. But as a man, he was born in weakness, grew tired, suffered, and was laid in a tomb. That same human nature, which was truly his own, was raised from the dead, taken into heaven, and seated at the Father's right hand. Peter says in Acts 2:24 that God raised Jesus because it was impossible for death to keep its hold on him. The one who died was the Lord of life, so the grave could not keep him.

Think of a king who leaves his palace, puts on the clothes of a laborer, and works among the poorest of his people. When he returns to the throne, he has not been promoted. He has come home. Yet the laborer's clothes he wore, his humanity, are now brought into the throne room with him. Jesus prays in John 17:5, "And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed." He is asking for a glory he already shared with the Father before creation. Now it shines in and through the human nature he took on.

What about the word "therefore"? Doesn't that sound like a reward for good behavior? It does tell us that the exaltation follows from his humble obedience. But it is not the reward a student earns by passing a test, as if the Son had to prove himself worthy of being God. If his divine status were a prize he earned, he would be God only by grant. Something granted could in principle be lost. Scripture never speaks of the Son that way. He is the Son by nature, as light shines from the sun simply by being what it is.

The "therefore" shows the right and fitting outcome of his saving work. Because he humbled himself for us, he was raised for us as well. When the Son was exalted as a man, our human nature was lifted up in him. Paul says elsewhere that God "raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms" (Ephesians 2:6). The exaltation is good news for us. Where our Head has gone, his people will follow.

What is "the name above all names"? Christians have read this in two ways. Some take it to be the name "Jesus" itself, now honored everywhere because of what he has done. Many others note that verse 11 points to the title "Lord." In the Greek Old Testament that the first Christians read, "Lord" stood for God's own personal name, the LORD. Either way, the point is the same. A name above every name can only be the name of God, for only God is above all things.

Paul makes this unmistakable by echoing Isaiah 45:23. There the LORD swears that every knee will bow before him and every tongue will confess him. In that same part of Isaiah, God insists that he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). Yet Paul applies these words directly to Jesus: "at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord." If Jesus were a lesser being, this would be idolatry. Instead, it shows that the honor God keeps for himself rightly belongs to the Son.

It also helps to remember that Jesus was not worshiped for the first time after Easter. Hebrews 1:6 says that when God brings his firstborn into the world, all God's angels are to worship him. What he "receives" as a man at his exaltation, he always had as God. The new thing is that this glory is now openly given to him as the crucified and risen man, Jesus of Nazareth, so that its blessing reaches us.

Finally, the confession that Jesus is Lord brings "glory to God the Father." Some readers think this puts the Son in second place. In fact it shows how fully the Father and the Son share one glory. Honoring the Son does not take anything away from the Father. It is one of the ways the Father is honored. Jesus says in John 5:23 that all should "honor the Son just as they honor the Father." The Son is not given some outside glory of his own. He is glorified with the Father's own glory, the glory he had with the Father before the world began.

This also means that the risen Jesus no longer lives in the weakness he took on for our sake. He is still truly human, and he always will be. But his humanity now lives in heavenly glory, and the whole universe is called to bow before him.

So Philippians 2 does not teach a lesser god who earned a promotion. It teaches the eternal Son, fully equal with the Father, who came down to serve and die. He was then raised and enthroned as a man, so that every creature might confess him as the LORD, to the glory of the Father with whom he is one.

topics.title: What does Colossians 2:9 mean by 'all the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily'?
topics.cmp: Hilary of Poitiers and Edward Henry Bickersteth agree that Colossians 2:9 affirms Christ's full and true Deity, but they read 'bodily' differently and use the verse for different purposes. Hilary treats it mainly as a statement about the Son's relation to the Father. The indwelling fulness is the Father's own Godhead, present in the Son wholly and by birth, not by condescension or will. So the Son is 'God in God, whole of whole', in natural unity with the Father yet personally distinct from him. On this basis Hilary rejects two readings: that the Father is confined in the Son as a person, and that their unity is mere agreement or harmony of will. Bickersteth instead reads 'bodily' in terms of the incarnation: the essential being of God now dwells corporeally in Christ's glorified body, whereas before the incarnation it dwelt in him as the Word without flesh, but not bodily. Hilary grounds his reading in the Apostle's wider language about God's 'everlasting power and divinity' and in arguments about generation, while Bickersteth's emphasis falls on the contrast between the pre-incarnate and the incarnate Word rather than on the Father–Son relation.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: prove Him true and perfect God of His Father’s nature, neither severing Him from, nor identifying Him with, the Father

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: “The Godhead, i.e. Deity, the essential being of God – bodily, i.e. manifested corporeally in his present glorified body.

ans.text:
Colossians 2:9 means that everything it is to be God, nothing held back and nothing watered down, lives in Jesus Christ, and that it lives in him in a real human body. Paul writes, "For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form." That one sentence says two huge things. Jesus is fully God, and Jesus is truly human, and these are not two Christs but one.

It helps to know why Paul wrote it. The Christians in Colossae were being pulled toward a spiritual "philosophy" (Colossians 2:8) that promised more: secret knowledge, angelic powers, special rules. The message was that Christ was a good start, but you needed something extra to reach God. Paul answers that there is nothing extra to reach. God has not spread himself out among many spiritual beings, with a share here and a share there. All of God is found in Christ. He already said this in 1:19: "For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him."

The word translated "Deity" matters. Paul does not say that Christ has some godlike qualities, the way a good person might reflect God's kindness. He uses a word that means God's very being: what makes God God. In Romans 1:20 Paul says creation shows God's "divine nature", meaning signs of God that can be seen in the world. Here he goes much further. In Christ is not a sign of God but God himself, in full. The word "dwells" also matters. It is not a brief visit, like the Spirit coming on a prophet for a season. It means to live somewhere as at home, permanently.

Whose Godhead is this? There is only one God, so it can only be the one divine nature that belongs to the Father. Scripture never suggests that the Son has a second, smaller kind of deity of his own. If it did, Paul, who preached one God, would be bringing in a second god. The Son has the Father's own nature, whole and not in part, because he is the Son. When the Bible calls him "begotten", it means he comes from the Father the way a son comes from a father and shares his nature. But this begetting is eternal. It is not a moment in time when he began to exist. So the fullness in Christ is not a gift the Father chose to lend him, the way he gives gifts to us. It is his by nature, as the Son. That is why Jesus can say, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). When the Son speaks, the Father speaks in him. When the Son acts, the Father acts in him.

This does not mean the Father has been squeezed into Jesus, or that Jesus is the Father in disguise. The verse says God's fullness dwells in Christ, and for that to be true there has to be a real, distinct Someone in whom it dwells. The Father stays the Father. He was not shut up in a body in Galilee. He still sent his Son and spoke from heaven over him. The Son is a distinct person from the Father, yet he has the very same Godhead. They are not two gods who happen to agree, and they are not one person wearing two masks. They are one God: Father and Son, with the Spirit.

What about "bodily"? This is where the Son is unique. The Father did not become human. The Son did. "The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). Before he was born of Mary, the Son was already fully God, but not in a body. At the incarnation, meaning his "taking flesh", the eternal Son took a real human nature, body and soul. Since then the fullness of God dwells in him in bodily form. He did not stop being God when he became man, and he did not stop being man when he rose. Notice that Paul says "dwells", not "dwelt." The risen Jesus still has his body, now raised and glorified, and the whole fullness of God lives in him today.

Some readers also hear in "bodily" the sense of "really" or "in substance." A few verses later Paul says the old rules were "a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ" (2:17). On that reading, Christ is the solid reality of which the old system was only a shadow. Both ideas can sit together. God's fullness is in Christ really and in a real human body.

The next verse brings this home to us: "And you have been made complete in Christ, who is the head over every ruler and authority" (2:10). In the original the word "complete" is close to "fullness". It is easy to misread this as if believers get the same thing Christ has. They do not. The fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ by nature. We are made full in him. We have no fullness of our own, but by being joined to him we lack nothing we need for life with God. That is why we do not need the extras the false teachers offered. If you have Christ, you have everything. And because he took our flesh, there is now a human body in which God fully dwells, and we are made part of that body by faith. One day he will finish the work. He "will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body" (Philippians 3:21).

A similar point answers Ephesians 3:19. There Paul prays that believers would know Christ's love "that you may be filled with all the fullness of God." This is a wonderful prayer, but it does not mean Christians become God or share in Godhead the way Christ does. Paul means that God fills us with his life, love and goodness, each believer as far as a creature can be filled, like vessels of different sizes all filled to the brim. And this filling comes through knowing Christ's love. A cup can be full of the ocean's water without being the ocean. Christ, though, is not a cup holding some of God. He is God, now also man. As John puts it, "From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace" (John 1:16). He is the source and we are the receivers.

So Colossians 2:9 guards against two opposite mistakes. One makes Jesus less than fully God: a great teacher or a highly blessed man with a large portion of the divine. The other makes him less than truly human, or blurs him into the Father. Paul's answer is that all of God dwells in the Son, in a real body, for us. That is why we can trust him completely and look nowhere else.

topics.title: What does Hebrews 1–2 teach about the Son's divinity and relation to the Father?
topics.cmp: All the authors read Hebrews 1–2 as teaching the Son's true divinity. Waterland and Gregory of Nyssa both take the 'brightness of glory' in 1:3 to prove the Son's eternity and inseparability from the Father, but on different grounds: Waterland appeals mainly to the Fathers (Origen, Dionysius, Alexander) and the analogy of eternal light, while Gregory argues from the text itself, from the participle 'being' and from the order of brightness to glory, which he also uses to show the Son is not Ungenerate. On 'express image' the emphases differ. Gregory takes it to mean the Father's greatness is fully expressed in the Son's power; Hilary uses it against any difference of nature, holding that the phrase marks only distinct existence; Waterland, following Eusebius against the Sabellians, stresses that it shows a real distinction of Persons, which he insists does not divide the substance. Owen and Bickersteth argue from the passage's structure: Owen says only one of such divine dignity could purge sins, and Bickersteth says divine titles in a passage about Christ's superiority to angels prove deity, while the humiliation of chapter 2 belongs to the nature he took. Athanasius alone stresses that 1:4's 'better than the angels' refers to the Incarnation and the Economy rather than to the Son's essence, yet he holds that 'better' signifies a difference in nature because the Son is above created things. Waterland alone treats 1:10, which he applies to the Son on grounds of context and the consensus of antiquity.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: since God is light, and Christ the ἀπαύγασμα, or shining forth of that light, quoting this text, that they could never have been separate one from the other, but must have been coeternal.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For the word “being” is a witness that interprets to us the Son’s continuity and eternity and superiority to all marks of time.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: discriminate between Christ and Him from Whom He is, but only to establish Their distinct existence, not to teach a difference of nature

ans.text:
Hebrews 1–2 teaches that the Son is fully God, sharing the Father's very nature while remaining a distinct person, and that he humbly became a real man to rescue us. Both truths sit side by side in these two chapters, and the letter needs both.

The letter opens by saying that God once spoke through prophets, "but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe" (Hebrews 1:2). Then comes one of the richest sentences in the Bible: "The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word" (1:3).

Think about the first picture, radiance. Sunlight comes from the sun. It is not a second thing the sun builds later. As long as there is a sun, there is shining. If God's glory is eternal, its radiance is eternal too. There was never a moment when God was without his shining. The Son did not begin to exist. He is from the Father, as light is from its source, but never after the Father. Notice too that the verse says the Son "is" the radiance, not that he became it. It describes what he always is.

The second picture, "exact representation," first meant the stamp a seal leaves in wax, which matches the seal line for line. "Nature" means what God is, the very reality of God. So the Son matches the Father's being exactly. Nothing in the Father is missing from the Son. Whatever greatness we see in the Son, the Father has the same. That is why Jesus could say, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).

This verse guards against two mistakes. One is to think the Son is a lesser, created copy of God. But no creature could exactly match the nature of the Creator. A perfect image of God has to share God's nature. The other mistake is to think Father and Son are just one person wearing two masks. But an image and the one it images are not the same. A stamp is not the seal that made it. So the Father is not the Son. They are two distinct persons, yet one God with one nature. This is exactly what Christians mean by the Trinity: real distinction of persons, no division of God's being.

The rest of chapter 1 piles up proof. Hebrews is comparing the Son with angels, the highest creatures people could imagine. If the writer only meant that Jesus was a top-ranking creature, this was the place to say so. Instead he says things no creature could share. Angels are told to worship him: "Let all God's angels worship Him" (1:6). Yet Scripture forbids worship of anyone but God. The Father addresses the Son, "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever" (1:8). Angels are servants. The Son is the King on the eternal throne.

Then verse 10 continues: "In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands." These words come from Psalm 102, a prayer to the LORD, the God of Israel. Some readers ask whether Hebrews means them for the Father rather than the Son. The flow of the passage answers that. Verse 8 begins, "But about the Son He says," and verse 10 simply adds, "And," carrying on the same address. The whole chapter is about showing the Son is greater than angels, and nothing shows that better than being the Creator. It also echoes verse 2, which already said that God made the universe through the Son. So Hebrews takes a psalm about the LORD himself and says it speaks of Jesus. The heavens will wear out like old clothes, "But You remain the same, and Your years will never end" (1:12). The Son does not change and does not end. Later the same letter says, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (13:8).

Why does verse 3 list all this glory before mentioning that he "provided purification for sins"? Because only someone this great could do that work. The one who washed away our sins is the same one who made the world and holds it together. A mere creature could not carry the weight of the world's sin. The Son could.

That helps with a phrase that puzzles many readers. Verse 4 says, "So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs." How can God "become" superior to angels? Wasn't he always above them? He was. Look at the setting. The verse comes right after he purified sins and sat down at God's right hand. It speaks of "these last days," the time when the Son came as a man. The point is not that the Son was once an ordinary creature who got promoted. The point is that the Son, having become human, was raised in his human nature to the highest place, and his work now outshines all that came before. Angels and prophets delivered God's messages. The Son brings the real salvation they pointed to. In a parable Jesus told, servants come to collect fruit from a vineyard, but the son is the heir (Mark 12:1–8). A son is a different kind of being from a servant, not just a better servant.

The same is true of the many "better" things Hebrews describes: a better covenant, a better hope, better promises, a better sacrifice. These are not just a little better, the way a large house is better than a small one. They are better in kind, because the one who brings them is not a creature at all.

Then chapter 2 seems to turn things upside down: "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death, so that by the grace of God He might taste death for everyone" (2:9). He shared our "flesh and blood" (2:14). He "had to be made like His brothers in every way" (2:17). He suffered and was tempted (2:18). Does that clash with chapter 1? Not at all. The same writer wrote both chapters, one right after the other, on purpose. The eternal Son did not stop being God when he became man. He added a human nature to himself. As God he cannot die. So he took a body and a human life so that he could die for us. His lowliness is something he took on out of love, not a sign that he was less than God.

In fact, we need both chapters. If Jesus were only a man, his death could not save the world. If he were only God and never truly human, he could not stand in our place, suffer as we do, or be a priest who understands our weakness. Hebrews shows us one person who is both: the Creator on the eternal throne, and the brother who "is not ashamed to call them brothers" (2:11).

So when you read these chapters, see the whole picture. The Son is the shining of the Father's glory, sharing everything the Father is, distinct from him yet one God with him. Out of love he came down lower than the angels, tasted death for us, and was raised and crowned. The one who made the stars is the one who died for your sins.

topics.title: In what sense is the Son subject to the Father so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28)?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa and Hilary of Poitiers all deny that the subjection of 1 Corinthians 15:28 makes the Son inferior in divine nature, but they explain it differently. Augustine grounds it in the two-forms distinction: the Son is subject as Priest in the form of a servant, the human nature he assumed, while in the form of God he is equal to the Father; he supports this by John's "My Father is greater than I" and reads the delivering up of the kingdom as bringing the just to the vision of God. Gregory of Nyssa takes the subjection to be that of the believers in whom the Son dwells, united as his body, whose adoration redounds to the Father. Hilary's several answers tie it to the dispensation in time and the glorifying of Christ's assumed body, which is promoted so that the God-Man becomes wholly God; he argues that 'then' marks a temporal event rather than natural subordination, since Christ's obedience is eternal, and he goes further than the others in calling the subjection a sign of true divinity. Irenaeus, by contrast, speaks plainly of the Son handing over his completed work to the Father after reigning and subduing death, without raising the question of inferiority, while Hippolytus uses the passage chiefly to show that the Son is distinct from the Father, who is Lord of the Son, and that through this order the one God is manifested.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: in due time the Son will yield up His work to the Father, even as it is said by the apostle, “For He must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.”

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: In What Manner Christ Shall Deliver Up the Kingdom to…
refs.quote: so that, in so far as He is God, He with Him will have put us under Himself; in so far as He is a Priest, He with us will be put under Him.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: the mighty wisdom of Paul affirms that the Son, Who is in all, is subject to the Father by virtue of the subjection of those in whom He is

ans.text:
Paul does not mean that the Son is a lesser God. He means that Jesus, as the man who came to rescue us and rules as our King, will finish his work and hand it back to the Father. Then the whole universe will rest under God's rule with nothing left in rebellion.

It helps to follow Paul's story in 1 Corinthians 15. Christ has been raised as the "firstfruits" of the resurrection. Now he reigns, and he "must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet" (15:25). The last enemy to be destroyed is death. When that work is done, "the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father" (15:24). Then comes our verse: when all things have been put under the Son, "the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all" (15:28).

The key is to remember who Jesus is. He is fully God and fully man. As God, he shares everything the Father is. Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one," and Philippians 2:6 says he existed "in the form of God." But he also "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7). He became a real man, our representative, our priest, and our King on God's behalf.

The Bible speaks of Jesus in both ways. Some things are true of him as God and some as the man who serves. When he says, "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), he speaks as the servant who has come to do the Father's will. The subjection in 1 Corinthians 15 belongs to that same side of who he is. It is about his role as the Messiah, the one sent to win back a rebel world. It is not a ranking of divine natures.

Think of a trusted general whom the king has sent to free the land. The general is the king's own son, of royal blood. When the war is won, he comes home and lays the victory at his father's feet. That act does not make him less royal. It shows that the whole campaign was always the father's purpose and that the son carried it out faithfully. Jesus says the same of himself: "I always do what pleases Him" (John 8:29). So this future subjection is not a new obedience, as if the Son had been holding back until then. It is the open, final display of a faithfulness that was always there.

Nor does handing over the kingdom mean Christ stops reigning. The angel promised Mary that "His kingdom will never end" (Luke 1:33). In the last chapter of the Bible, the throne in the new creation is called "the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Revelation 22:3). It is one shared throne. The handing over marks the end of the campaign against sin and death, not the end of the Son's rule.

This passage does show clearly that the Father and the Son are distinct persons. Paul notes that when everything is put under the Son, this "clearly does not include the One who subjected everything to Him" (15:27). One person gives and the other receives. One person hands over and the other is handed to. The Son is not just another name for the Father. Yet there is still only one God, and in the end every creature is gathered under that one God, together with Christ.

Sincere Christians have weighed one further question. Does this verse only describe Christ's role as the incarnate Savior? Or does it also reflect something eternal in how the Son relates to the Father? Most have read it as being about Jesus' mission and his human nature, for the reasons above. Others add that the Son's willing obedience fits the fact that he eternally comes from the Father as Son. They hold this without making him any less God. Both sides agree on the main point: the Son is equal to the Father in godhood, and this verse does not teach otherwise.

Some readers wonder whether "God may be all in all" means Jesus' human nature will finally melt into God and disappear. A few early Christians spoke as if his humanity would be so filled with glory that it was swept up into the divine. But the Bible's steady teaching is that Jesus remains a man forever. His manhood is glorified, but it is not dissolved or turned into something else. He is "the man Christ Jesus" who is our one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5). He holds his priesthood "permanently" because he lives forever (Hebrews 7:24). This is good news for us. The one who sits on the throne will always be one of us, with a real, risen human body, and he is the pattern of what we will become.

Finally, "all in all" does not mean God will gain something he lacked, as if he will at last become complete. God is already perfect and needs nothing. He says, "I, the LORD, do not change" (Malachi 3:6), and all things are "from Him and through Him and to Him" (Romans 11:36). What changes is creation, not God. Today the world is full of rebellion, sin and death, and God's rule is resisted and hidden. On that day no enemy will remain. Every heart will gladly own him. God's presence and goodness will fill everything without any rival. The phrase describes a creation finally set right, not a God finally made whole.

So 1 Corinthians 15:28 is not a verse that shrinks the Son. It is a picture of the finish line. The Son, who is fully God, became man and fought our battle. He defeats death, lays the completed victory before his Father, and goes on reigning with him. Then the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is gladly known and loved in everything and by everyone.

topics.title: How does Christ's reign relate to the Father's Kingdom, and what does it mean that he delivers up the kingdom?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Hilary of Poitiers and Bickersteth all deny that Christ's delivering up the kingdom (1 Cor 15:24-28) means he loses, resigns or ceases his reign. They agree that the 'kingdom' handed over is the redeemed themselves, whom Christ presents to the Father. Augustine treats the delivering up chiefly as Christ the Mediator bringing believers from faith to face-to-face contemplation of God. He insists that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not excluded from that God, since they are one God with the Father, and he answers the objection from 'until' with the parallel of Psalm 112:8. Hilary argues more from the wording of the text: Paul says 'the Kingdom', not 'his Kingdom'; 'the end' means perfection, not dissolution, as Christ is the 'end of the law'; and the passage forms a chain of causes ordered to 'God all in all'. Distinctively, Hilary reads the subjection as the glorified body's further glorification, a 'promotion into the Godhead' grounded in John 13:31-32, whereas Augustine stresses the end of an economy of similitudes and the Father being revealed by the Son. Bickersteth instead refers the subjection to Christ as the second Man and federal Head of the church: his mediatorial pleading will cease, yet he keeps a shared, undivided supremacy with the Father, and Scripture says his kingdom shall have no end. Irenaeus touches the topic only by tying the general resurrection to Christ's resurrection as first-fruits.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: He shall deliver the Kingdom to God the Father, not in the sense that He resigns His power by the delivering, but that we, being conformed to the glory of His body, shall form the Kingdom of God.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: All are Sometimes Understood in One Person.
refs.quote: when He shall bring believers to the contemplation of God, even the Father, doubtless He will bring them to the contemplation of Himself, who has said, “And I will manifest myself to him.”

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: a time will come when He will no longer exercise his mediatorial office, by pleading the virtue of his blood for penitent sinners (seeing that sin and death are forever abolished)

ans.text:
When Paul says Christ will hand over the kingdom to the Father, he is not describing a king who gives up his throne. He is describing the finish line of Christ's saving work: the moment when he presents his rescued people, complete and glorious, to God the Father, so that they may see God face to face.

The key passage is 1 Corinthians 15:24-28. Paul writes, "Then the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power. For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet." He goes on to say that the Son himself will be made subject to the Father, "so that God may be all in all." Read quickly, this can sound as if Jesus rules for a while and then steps aside. A careful reading shows otherwise.

Start with what the kingdom is. In the Bible, a kingdom is not only a territory but a people under a king. Christ's kingdom is the people he bought with his blood. Notice that Paul says "the kingdom," not "his kingdom." Christ does not hand away his authority. He hands over us. Think of a shepherd who has led his flock through a long, dangerous journey and finally brings every sheep safely home to the owner's house. The shepherd has not lost anything. His task has reached its goal. That is what Jesus does at the last day. Right now we live by faith. We trust a God we cannot see. Paul says elsewhere, "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12). Handing over the kingdom is that passage from faith to sight.

And Christ is not left outside the God to whom the kingdom is given. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God. When Jesus brings us to see the Father, he brings us to see himself as well, for he said, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). We will not be handed from Jesus to someone else. We will be brought by Jesus into the full life of the one God he shares with the Father and the Spirit.

Does Christ's reign stop? No. The angel told Mary, "His kingdom will never end!" (Luke 1:33). In Revelation the heavenly voices say that he "will reign forever and ever" (Revelation 11:15). In the new creation the city is lit by "the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Revelation 22:3). It is one throne, shared forever.

So what about the words "until" and "the end"? In the Bible, "until" often marks a point that is reached without saying anything changes afterward. Psalm 112 says the righteous man does not fear until he sees his enemies defeated. Nobody thinks he starts being afraid after that. In the same way, Christ reigns until every enemy is beaten, and then he goes on reigning, only now with no opposition left. Likewise "the end" means the goal or completion, not destruction. Paul calls Christ the end of the law (Romans 10:4), yet Jesus said he came to fulfill the law, not abolish it. The end of a journey is arriving, not disappearing.

What about the Son being "made subject" to the Father? Here we need to remember who Jesus is. He is fully God, equal with the Father, and he also became fully man. As man, and as the Mediator who stands for his people, he gladly submits to the Father, just as he did on earth when he prayed, "not My will, but Yours be done." Many Christians understand 1 Corinthians 15:28 mainly in this way. At the end, the risen Man who leads redeemed humanity offers the whole finished work to the Father. His work of pleading for us against sin and death is complete, because sin and death are gone. But he remains our King and our Head forever. Other Christians add that the passage also reflects a real order among the persons of God: the Son is from the Father and always delights to honor him. That order does not make the Son less divine. Both views agree that this subjection is not a demotion. It is a loving son bringing the fruit of his labor home. Its purpose, Paul says, is "that God may be all in all." That means God himself will fill everything, and we will need nothing else to know and enjoy him.

This is not only Paul's idea. Jesus taught it too. After explaining that he will clear out of his kingdom everything that causes sin, he said, "Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father" (Matthew 13:43). Notice the movement: his kingdom becomes the setting where his people shine in their Father's kingdom. It is one kingdom, seen from two sides. On the mountain of the Transfiguration, the disciples glimpsed that shining glory in Jesus' own body. One day his people will share it. Before the cross Jesus also spoke of being glorified, and of God glorifying him in himself (John 13:31-32). His path runs through humility to glory, and he takes us along that path.

Who will judge at the end? Jesus himself, and as a man. He said the Son of Man will come in his glory with all nations gathered before him (Matthew 25:31-32). The Father "has given Him authority to execute judgment, because He is the Son of Man" (John 5:27). This is a great comfort. Our judge is one who shared our flesh and knows our weakness. Yet the power by which he judges is God's own power. Only God can see every heart and give perfect justice. The one person, Jesus, does it all. The judge we will see has a human face, and he judges with divine authority.

Finally, all of this hangs on the resurrection. Paul's whole argument in 1 Corinthians 15 begins there. "Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, the guarantee that the rest was coming. As death came through one man, Adam, so resurrection comes through one man, Christ. If the dead are not raised, Paul says, then Christ is not raised and our faith is useless. But he is raised. Because his body came out of the grave, ours will too. The kingdom he hands over is a kingdom of raised, renewed people, made like his glorious body.

So Christ's reign does not compete with the Father's kingdom, and it does not run out. He reigns now to defeat every enemy and gather his people. At the end he brings them home, whole and shining, to the Father. Then we will see God face to face, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and the Lamb will still be on the throne.

topics.title: How should other New Testament texts and writers be read on the Father and the Son?
topics.cmp: Owen and Warfield answer different questions here, so their positions never directly meet. Owen works exegetically on single verses. He takes 'God' in Ephesians 2:10 as the Father personally, distinct from Christ, who appears there as mediator. He reads 'the love of the Father' in 1 John 2:15 as our love directed to the Father as its object, set against the world, rather than the Father's love for us, and ties this to Malachi's language of the Father's honour. Warfield argues more broadly, surveying Peter, Jude, Hebrews and Revelation (citing 1 Peter 1:2, Jude 20-21 and Revelation 1:4-5) to show a shared threefold grounding of redemption in Father, Son and Spirit, which he calls a fixed Trinitarian consciousness universal in apostolic circles. Both rely on Scripture alone. Owen's emphasis falls on distinguishing the Father as a person within particular texts, while Warfield's falls on the consistent Trinitarian pattern across the New Testament writers.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: Clearly these writers, too, write out of a fixed Trinitarian consciousness and bear their testimony to the universal understanding current in apostolical circles.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: The Father is spoken of personally, Christ being mentioned as mediator.

ans.text:
Read them the same way you read Paul. Across the New Testament, the word "God" very often points to the Father in particular, while Jesus is set beside him as the Son and Lord, and the Holy Spirit is named with them both. That habit runs through Peter, Jude, Hebrews and Revelation just as it does through Paul's letters.

Start with a simple pattern. When the apostles say "God" with no other description, they usually mean the Father. They call Jesus "Lord" or "Christ" or "the Son." This does not mean the Son is less than God. The same writers plainly call him God elsewhere (John 1:1; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8). It is a way of keeping the persons distinct while worshiping one God. Think of a family where everyone shares one surname, but in daily talk each is called by a first name. "God" names what the three share, yet in ordinary speech it often lands on the Father, the one from whom the Son and Spirit come.

Ephesians 2:10 shows this. Paul says, "For we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life." Here "God" most naturally means the Father. Christ is named as the one in whom we are made new, the go-between who brings us to God. So the picture is personal. The Father planned our good works ahead of time and made us new in his Son. This does not shut the Son or the Spirit out of the work. Whatever God does toward us, all three persons do together. But the verse invites us to see the Father's own care behind our daily obedience.

First John 2:15 raises a different question. John writes, "Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him." Does "the love of the Father" mean his love for us, or our love for him? The words can be read either way. Most readers take it as our love for the Father, and the setting supports this. John is contrasting two things we might love: the world or the Father. A heart cannot give itself fully to both. Others point out that John elsewhere stresses that God's love comes first and lives in us (1 John 4:19). The two readings are close in the end. Our love for the Father is a response to his love, and where his love has truly taken root, love for the world loses its grip. Either way, John speaks of a real relationship with the Father as a person, someone who can be loved, not just a force.

Now the wider question: do the other writers think about God the way Paul does? They do. They rarely stop to explain the Trinity. They simply take for granted that our salvation comes from the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit.

Peter opens his first letter by greeting believers chosen "according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and the sanctifying work of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling with His blood" (1 Peter 1:2). In one breath he names all three. The Father chooses, the Spirit makes holy, and the Son's blood cleanses.

Jude does the same near the end of his short letter. He urges believers to build themselves up in the faith and to pray in the Holy Spirit. They are to keep themselves in the love of God while they wait for the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ, which brings eternal life (Jude 20-21). Again: Spirit, God the Father, and the Lord Jesus, each with his own part in the Christian life.

Hebrews tells us that Christ, "through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God" (Hebrews 9:14). The Son offers, the Spirit empowers, and the offering is made to God the Father. The same letter calls the Son the radiance of God's glory and the exact expression of his nature (Hebrews 1:3). So he is truly God, yet distinct from the Father.

Revelation opens with a greeting: "Grace and peace to you from Him who is and was and is to come, and from the seven Spirits before His throne, and from Jesus Christ" (Revelation 1:4-5). Grace comes from the eternal Father and from Jesus Christ. Between them stand "the seven Spirits." Many Christians understand this as the Holy Spirit pictured in his fullness, since seven in Revelation is a number of completeness. Who else could be a source of divine grace alongside the Father and the Son? Some readers instead think the seven are high angels. But it would be strange to place created beings in the middle of a blessing that flows from God himself.

Taken together, these passages show something important. The Trinity was not one apostle's private idea. Peter, Jude, the writer of Hebrews and John share the same outlook as Paul. Their letters come from different people writing to different churches, yet they speak this way without explaining it. That suggests it was already the shared faith of all the early believers. They knew one God and worshiped him as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

The practical lesson for reading the Bible is this. When you see "God" and "Christ" side by side, don't conclude that Christ is not God. Usually the writer is speaking of the Father and the Son as two persons. And when the Spirit appears alongside them, notice that salvation is always the work of all three. The Father plans and sends, the Son redeems, and the Spirit applies that work and makes us holy.

title: Arian Controversy and Patristic Witness
desc: Arian, Eunomian and Clarkean alternatives to orthodoxy and the testimony of the Ante-Nicene and Nicene Fathers to the Son's unity and coeternity with the Father.

topics.title: Is Arian or subordinationist teaching a credible alternative to Nicene orthodoxy?
topics.cmp: All the authors reject Arian and subordinationist teaching as a credible alternative, and they converge on one core argument: a created or inferior "God" beside the supreme God means either two Gods or a Son who is not God at all. Athanasius frames this as a choice between polytheism and atheism, Gregory of Nyssa holds that "created God" is a contradiction in terms, Hilary says true and lesser Gods cannot be joined under one Godhead, and Daniel Waterland, at greatest length, presses dilemmas about two Gods, two Creators and two objects of worship. They differ in grounds and emphasis. Athanasius also argues from novelty against the fathers' tradition and from the devil's misuse of Scripture. Gregory of Nyssa adds that the Eunomian scheme is worse than Manichaeism. Irenaeus, Ambrose and Owen argue from Scripture's naming of the Father and Son alone as God and Lord and from the honour due to Christ. Waterland relies mainly on logical analysis, testing Samuel Clarke's king-and-son analogy and the definition of God as "Author and Governor" against Isaiah's monotheistic texts, while also charging Clarke with begging the question and putting conjecture in place of demonstration. Waterland adds one qualification: whether Arianism implies a plurality of Gods depends on whether "God" is taken strictly or loosely. There is also a real difference on subordination itself: Waterland grants that the Son is in some sense subordinate and the Father eminently the one God, and Owen reads the Father as the Son's "God" only by the covenant of redemption, whereas Warfield endorses Calvin's affirmation that the Son is autotheos, self-existent rather than deriving his deity from the Father.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: Thus the Doctor's scheme is liable to the same difficulties with the other.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: so neither is Godhead discoverable in the creature, nor the attribute of being created in the Godhead: but if He be God He is certainly not created, and if He be created He is not God

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: the prophets and the apostles confessing the Father and the Son; but naming no other as God, and confessing no other as Lord

ans.text:
No. Once you think it through, the idea that Jesus is a lesser, created "god" under the one true God does not hold together, and it does not fit what the Bible says.

First, what is this teaching? It says the Son is the first and greatest thing God ever made. Through him God made everything else. Because he is so exalted, he may be called "God" and even worshipped, but only in a lower sense. The Father alone is God in the full sense. Some later forms of the idea speak of a "supreme God" (the Father) and a "subordinate God" (the Son). The aim is usually sincere: people want to protect the truth that there is only one God. But the teaching ends up undoing the very thing it set out to protect.

The simplest problem is this. A great king and a little king are still two kings. In the same way, a supreme God and a lesser God are two Gods. The only way out is to say the lesser one is not really God at all. Then the Son is "God" in name only, the way you might give a horse a man's name without making it a man. So the scheme must choose. Either it keeps two Gods, or it keeps one God and leaves the Son outside. It cannot have both. Either a being is God, and so was never made, or it was made, and so is not God. There is no halfway point between Creator and creature.

The Bible does not leave room for a lesser god either. When God declares in Isaiah 43:10, "Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come," He is not only ruling out rival gods of equal rank. He is ruling out any god that was made. In Isaiah 45:5 He says, "I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me." The pagan nations around Israel did not believe in two equal supreme gods. They usually had one high god and many lower ones. That is exactly what Scripture calls idolatry. Adding the word "supreme" to "one God" does not get around these texts. It changes what they say.

Yet the New Testament plainly calls the Son God and gives him what belongs to God alone. Take creation. John 1:1 says, "the Word was God," and John 1:3 says, "Through Him all things were made." Colossians 1:16 says all things were created through him and for him. If the Son is a creature, we now have two creators, and one of them is himself a creature. That is a contradiction. Or take worship. Jesus himself says in Matthew 4:10, "Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only." When John falls down before an angel in Revelation 22, the angel stops him and tells him to worship God. Yet Hebrews 1:6 says, "Let all God's angels worship Him," speaking of the Son. And Jesus says in John 5:23 that all should "honor the Son just as they honor the Father." If the Son is a creature, then this is worship of a creature, which the Bible forbids. If the Son is not to be worshipped, the New Testament is wrong. Only the church's historic faith makes sense of it all. There is one God, and the Son shares fully in that one Godhead with the Father and the Spirit.

Some people say the subordinate view is at least easier to understand. It is not. It too calls the Father God and the Son God, and it too insists God is one. So it faces the same question as everyone else: how are they one? It cannot give an answer that does not slide either into three gods or into blurring the persons together. The historic teaching admits honestly that God is beyond our full grasp. But it does not contradict itself. It says God is one in his being, meaning what God is. And it says God is three in persons, meaning who God is: Father, Son and Spirit.

What about the verses that seem to rank the Son below the Father? In John 14:28 Jesus says, "the Father is greater than I." The Son truly became a man and took a servant's place (Philippians 2:6-8). As a man he prays, obeys, and grows tired. There is also a real order within God. The Father sends and the Son is sent. The Son is "begotten," meaning he is eternally from the Father, as a son shares his father's nature. He is not made, as a craftsman makes a table. Being from the Father is not the same as being less than the Father. Christians who fully confess the Son's deity still discuss how far that order goes. Some see an eternal pattern in which the Son gladly does the Father's will. Others think talk of authority and submission belongs only to his earthly mission. But all of them agree that the Son is equal to the Father in being, glory and power.

Two other points are worth knowing. The idea that the Son is a creature was new when it spread in the early fourth century. Christians at the time were shocked by it, because it was not what they had always believed and prayed. And quoting Bible verses does not by itself make a teaching biblical. The devil quoted Scripture to Jesus in the wilderness. The question is always whether the teaching does justice to the whole of Scripture. A lesser, created God does not. It is too high for the verses that say God alone is God, and too low for the verses that call the Son God, Creator and Lord.

So the choice is not between the church's faith and a reasonable alternative. A Jesus who is "God" but not truly God would leave us either with two Gods or with a Savior who is only a creature. The Bible gives us something far better. In Jesus we meet God himself, come to save us.

topics.title: Can the Son be truly God if the Father alone is self-existent and the source of the Son's perfections?
topics.cmp: Most of the answers here come from Daniel Waterland, writing against Dr. Clarke. He holds that the Son receives everything belonging to the Father except what is personal: being first in order and being unoriginate. On that reading, excepting supremacy and independence does not strip the Son of infinite perfections, and the real question is whether the Son is a creature. His arguments are philosophical and polemical rather than scriptural. He shows that the maxim 'nothing individual can be communicated' is ambiguous and decides nothing, and he turns Clarke's own account of divine omnipresence against him as no more intelligible than communication among the Persons. He also charges Clarke with inconsistency for calling the Son truly God while denying him self-existence, which Clarke treats as God's most essential character. Hilary of Poitiers answers only the narrower question of the Father's self-existence, describing the Father as unbegotten, eternal, possessing being from and in Himself, and the origin of all things acting in and through Christ. His answer does not take up the dispute over whether the Son shares that self-existence, so the two authors address different parts of the topic rather than directly agreeing or disagreeing.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: that to the Son are communicated all things belonging to the Father, excepting only what is personal; that is, excepting that he is not the first im order; not supreme, in that sense, nor wnoriginate.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: In contrast to all else He is self-existent. He does not draw His being from without, but possesses it from Himself and in Himself.

ans.text:
Yes, the Son is fully and truly God, even though the Father is the one from whom the Son eternally comes. Being "from" the Father describes how the Son relates to the Father. It does not measure how much of God he is.

The Bible clearly gives the Father a kind of first place. The Son is sent by the Father, speaks of the Father as the one who "granted" him things, and is called the Father's only Son. Christians have rightly said that the Father is unbegotten: he comes from no one. The Son is "begotten," which simply means he is born of the Father. He is not made, and he did not start at some moment. He eternally comes from the Father the way a son shares his father's very nature.

Some have reasoned like this: if the Father alone exists of himself, and the Son receives everything from him, then the Son must be a lesser, borrowed sort of God. That sounds tidy, but it mixes up two different things.

The first is the divine nature itself, everything that makes God God. That includes being eternal, all-knowing, all-powerful, and depending on nothing outside himself. The second is the personal relationships within God: Father, Son and Spirit, each related to the others in a particular way. Being unbegotten is the Father's personal mark, just as being begotten is the Son's. It is not an extra piece of divinity that the Father has and the Son lacks.

Jesus puts it this way in John 5:26: "For as the Father has life in Himself, so also He has granted the Son to have life in Himself." Notice what the Son receives. He does not get a smaller life that hangs on the Father's from outside. He receives life "in Himself," the very same self-sustaining life the Father has. The giving is real, but what is given is complete. That is why Jesus can say, "Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine" (John 16:15), and "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). The only things the Father does not share with the Son are the things that make the Father the Father rather than the Son: being first in order and being from no one.

This also helps with the word "self-existent." If it means "depending on nothing outside of God, never caused or created," then the Son is self-existent. He depends on nothing in creation, and he made all things (John 1:3). If it means "not begotten of anyone," then only the Father is that, and it is simply another way of saying he is the Father.

An everyday picture can help, as long as we don't push it too far. Sunlight comes from the sun, yet there was never a sun without its light. The light is not a weaker copy; it is the sun's own brightness. Hebrews 1:3 uses this very image: the Son is "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." Radiance is as old as the source it shines from, and an exact representation lacks nothing.

So the real question underneath this debate is simple. Is the Son a creature or not? There is no middle ground between God and creation. Infinite perfections cannot be handed to a creature; something limited cannot hold the unlimited. So if the Son truly has all divine power, knowledge and glory, as Scripture says, he cannot be a creature. If he were a creature, then calling his powers "divine" would be an empty compliment. Colossians 2:9 settles it: all the fullness of the Deity lives in Christ in bodily form. Not a share, but all of it.

There is a consistency problem too. Some have wanted to call the Son God "by nature" while denying him what they themselves called the most essential mark of God. That cannot work. Nothing is truly human without what makes something human, and nothing is truly God without what makes God God. Paul warns in Galatians 4:8 against serving beings that "by nature are not gods." Yet the church has always worshiped Christ. That worship is right only because the Son is God by nature, not a high creature given a divine title.
