Another objection says that something belonging to one being cannot be shared at all. It sounds weighty, but it only says that what can't be shared can't be shared. It doesn't tell us what God has actually done. The divine nature is not divided into pieces and parceled out, as if the Father kept some and gave the Son the rest. The one undivided divine life is wholly the Father's and wholly the Son's. That is beyond our full understanding, but it is not a contradiction. Even the simple belief that God is wholly present everywhere, without being split up, stretches our minds in the same way.

Sincere Christians who agree on all of this have differed somewhat on wording. Some like to say the Son is "God of himself." They mean that his divine nature is not borrowed or lesser, and they want to guard his full equality. Others prefer to say he is "God from God," because the Bible stresses that the Son receives everything from the Father, and they want to keep that order clear. Both sides confess the same thing in the end. The Son is not God in a secondhand way. As a person he is from the Father, and in his nature he is everything the Father is.

So the Father's being the source does not lower the Son. The Father has always been Father, which means he has always had the Son, sharing with him the fullness of his own life and glory.

topics.title: Did the early Church believe in the Trinity and the Son's divinity?
topics.cmp: Warfield and Waterland both answer yes: the Trinitarian faith, including Christ's divinity, belongs to the apostolic and early Church and is not a later invention. They work on different evidence, though, and answer different questions. Warfield reads Paul's letters directly. He argues that from 1 Thessalonians to 2 Timothy Paul refers redemption to a threefold divine causation, and that Paul's intense monotheism sits alongside treating the Father, Christ, and the Spirit as equally God, through a distinction of Persons within one Being. He adds a philosophical-religious claim that only Trinitarian theism can keep a lasting hold on the mind and heart. Waterland makes no direct appeal to Scripture or to that kind of reasoning. He argues from the Fathers, defending Bishop Bull's case against Whitby that the second-century Fathers grounded the Godhead's unity on the same principle as Nicaea and genuinely upheld Christ's divinity, and he treats Whitby's objection about the term 'individual' as an evasion.

refs.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
refs.quote: Everywhere, throughout their pages, God the Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit appear as the joint objects of all religious adoration, and the conjunct source of all Divine operations.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: we have very clear and full proof that the Catholic Church did all along profess a Trinity of consubstantial, coeternal Persons, in unity of nature, substance, and Godhead.

ans.text:
Yes. From the very beginning Christians worshiped one God and confessed Jesus as truly divine, and they spoke of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together as the one God they served. The later creeds sharpened the wording, but they did not invent the belief. They put into careful words what the church had prayed, sung, and baptized into from the start.

The earliest evidence is in the New Testament itself. Paul's letters are some of the oldest Christian writings we have, written within about twenty to thirty years of Jesus' death and resurrection. Paul was a devout Jew. For him there was only one God, and he never let go of that. Yet in 1 Corinthians 8:6 he takes Israel's great confession that God is one and places Jesus inside it: "for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist." Jesus is not set beside God as a helper. He is named as the one through whom everything was made, which is something only the Creator can be.

This pattern runs through all of Paul's letters, from the earliest to the latest. Salvation and all its gifts come from the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. Sometimes Paul names one of them, often two, and quite often all three together. He closes 2 Corinthians by asking that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with his readers (2 Corinthians 13:14). Paul is not giving a lecture on the Trinity here. He is simply praying, and he assumes his readers already know whom he means. That is telling. Some of the best evidence for what people believe is what they take for granted.

The rest of the New Testament agrees. John opens his Gospel with "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). Thomas falls before the risen Jesus and says, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). Jesus does not correct him. And Jesus sends his followers to baptize "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Notice that it says one name, not three names, yet three are named.

That command shaped the life of the church after the apostles. New believers were baptized by confessing the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. The early creeds grew out of those baptismal questions. Christians closed their prayers by giving glory to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together. They sang hymns to Christ. One Roman official, writing early in the second century, reported to the emperor that Christians met before dawn to sing to Christ as to a god. These were not private theories held by a few scholars. They were the public, everyday worship of ordinary believers. When teachers came along who said the Son was less than God, or only a creature, the churches treated this as a departure from what they had always believed.

It is worth asking how likely it would be for the church to get this wrong so quickly. The apostles founded churches and taught them in person for years. Those congregations had the apostles' letters and remembered the apostles' preaching. Many of their leaders had known the apostles or their close companions. Many of them were later willing to die rather than deny Christ. It is very hard to believe that such churches misunderstood the apostles on the most basic question of all, which is who God is and whom we worship. It is harder still to believe they all drifted into the same mistake at once, across many lands.

There is also an interesting clue from the church's early opponents. Some teachers in the early centuries said that the Father, Son, and Spirit were really one person who simply appeared in three different roles or masks, like one actor playing three parts. These teachers accused the main body of the church of believing in three gods. That charge is a backhanded witness. Nobody would accuse you of believing in three gods unless you clearly taught that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are each truly God and truly distinct from one another. If the church had thought the Son was only divine in some loose or honorary sense, the charge would have made no sense. The church's answer was to hold both truths at once. There is one God, sharing one divine nature or "being," meaning what God is. And there are three persons, meaning who God is: the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. They are not three gods, and they are not one person wearing three masks.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. Some people say the Trinity was invented at the Council of Nicaea in 325, or by a Roman emperor. In fact the council was called because a teacher had begun saying the Son was a created being, and the church gathered to say plainly what it already believed. Others point out that the word "Trinity" is not in the Bible. That is true, but a word is only a label. The reality it names is everywhere in Scripture. It is also true that some writers before Nicaea used wording that sounds loose or awkward to us. They were working out how to say things carefully before the hard questions had been fully pressed. But in what they worshiped, confessed at baptism, and defended against unbelievers and false teachers, they held that Jesus is truly God.

This matters for more than history. The God the early Christians worshiped was not a distant, lonely unity. He is the living God, Father, Son, and Spirit, who has always lived in love and who has drawn us into that life through Christ. The faith we confess today is the same faith they confessed, because it is the faith the apostles handed down from Scripture.

topics.title: Did the Ante-Nicene Fathers teach the Nicene doctrine of the Son's eternity, consubstantiality and unity with the Father?
topics.cmp: Waterland supplies nearly all the answers here, and he consistently affirms that the early Fathers taught the Son's unity, consubstantiality and coeternity with the Father. He grounds this in patristic testimony: Irenaeus, Athenagoras, Tertullian, Clement, Origen, Hippolytus, Lactantius, Novatian and Eusebius, together with Bishop Bull's collected witnesses. He adds the argument that consubstantiality implies coeternity, and that its appearance in precise anti-heretical debate rules out a merely rhetorical sense. His emphasis is polemical against Dr. Clarke: Clarke's citations yield only inferences the Fathers themselves disowned, and Nicene homoousios meant numerical rather than merely generic unity, guarded by qualifying clauses against tritheism. Irenaeus and Augustine do not address the historical question directly. Irenaeus confesses the Father of Christ as the only true God of Abraham, and Augustine speaks of believers being made one in Christ through charity; neither contradicts Waterland, but both bear on the topic only obliquely.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: They thought that the divinity of the Son could not be otherwise secured, and Polytheism at the same time avoided, than by asserting Father and Son to be one God; and they thought right.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.place: Chapter VI—The Holy Ghost, throughout the Old Testament Scriptures, made mention of no other God or Lord, save him who is the true God
refs.quote: Lord God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob and Israel, who art the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ

ans.text:
Yes. In substance, the Christian writers before the year 325 taught what the creed of that year later put into precise words: the Son has always existed, he shares the Father's own divine being, and he and the Father are one God. They did not always use the later technical vocabulary, and some of their phrases can sound odd to us. But the faith behind the words was the same.

It helps to know why this question comes up at all. In the early 300s a teacher in Egypt argued that the Son was the first and greatest thing God made: glorious, but created, with a beginning. Church leaders met in 325 and answered that the Son is "of one being" (or "of one essence") with the Father. "Essence" simply means what something is. To say the Son has the same essence as the Father means he is God in exactly the same sense the Father is God, not a lesser kind of god. Ever since, some have claimed this was a new idea and that earlier Christians thought of the Son as a lower being. When we look at what those earlier believers actually said and did, that claim does not hold up.

Start with how they worshipped. The first Christians were fiercely committed to one God. They would die rather than offer a pinch of incense to a lesser deity. Yet from the beginning they prayed to Jesus, sang to him as God, and baptized in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). If they had thought of the Son as a created being, this would have been exactly the idolatry they refused to commit. They could only worship him because they believed he belonged within the one God, not outside him.

Then look at what they said about him. Again and again they called the Son eternal, uncreated, the Maker of all things, and all-powerful. Each of these is something only God can be. They took this straight from the Bible. John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and adds that through him all things were made. Paul says in Colossians 1:17, "He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together." Jesus prays in John 17:5 for the glory he had with the Father "before the world existed." Something that made all things cannot itself be one of the things made.

They also taught plainly that the Father and Son are one God. Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one." Some early writers took this verse mainly as a statement of perfect agreement and love between Father and Son. But they also said it would be absurd for a mere man to speak this way. They saw that oneness of love grows out of a deeper oneness of nature. A son shares his father's nature, and this Son shares the Father's very being.

One of the clearest pieces of evidence comes from the church's opponents. For two centuries, critics complained that the church's teaching seemed to split or divide God's being by saying the Son came from it. Nobody worries that God's being is divided when he creates an angel or a star. That complaint only makes sense if the church was teaching that the Son truly comes from the Father's own being, as light comes from the sun. Hebrews 1:3 uses just that picture: the Son is "the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature." The sun has never existed without its shining, and the Father has never existed without his Son.

That brings us to the word "begotten," which means fathered or born, as opposed to made. Early Christians held that the Son is begotten of the Father, not created. They seldom used the later phrase "eternal generation," meaning that the Father has always been the Father of the Son and the Son has always come from him. But they believed everything the phrase contains. The Son is eternal. He is distinct from the Father. He shares the Father's being. And the Father is his source. Put those together and you have eternal generation, even without the label.

Some early statements can sound troubling, so they deserve a closer look. Some writers said the Father "comes before" the Son. In context they meant order, not time, the way a source comes before what flows from it, or a speaker before the word he speaks. These same writers said the Son is before all time and was always with the Father. So the "before" cannot mean there was a moment when the Son was not.

Other writers spoke of the Word "going forth" from the Father at creation, or even being "born" when God made the world. They often explained this with the picture of a thought that is always in a person's mind and then is spoken aloud. The Word was always in the Father. At creation he came forward outwardly to make and reveal. That outward coming was something added to his eternal existence, not the start of it. When some said this happened by the Father's will, they did not mean the Son was optional or might never have existed. They meant the Father is not forced by anything outside himself.

Some writers also said the Son appeared in the Old Testament "in the name" or "by the authority" of the Father. They did not mean he was a mere stand-in. They meant he appeared as the Lord God himself, which he could do because he truly is God.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, saying the Son shares the Father's essence does not mean the Father and Son are the same person, as though God simply wore different masks. Early Christians rejected that idea just as firmly as they rejected the idea that the Son was created. One God, two distinct persons (and with the Spirit, three) is what they held. Second, saying the Son is "of one being" with the Father does not mean two separate beings of the same kind, the way two people share human nature. The creed of 325 added phrases such as "God from God, Light from Light" to make clear there is one undivided divine being, not two gods side by side.

It is fair to admit that some early writers expressed themselves loosely. They were working before the questions had been sharply posed, and sincere Christians today still differ on how precise particular writers were. Some think a few leaned toward making the Son lesser in a way later believers would not accept. Others think their wording was simply imperfect, while their worship and core beliefs were sound. But a stray phrase should not outweigh the steady pattern: worship of the Son, belief in one God, and confession of the Son as eternal Creator.

Did later believers change the doctrine, then? No. Both earlier and later Christians taught that the Father is the source and the Son comes from him. Both taught that the Son is a real person distinct from the Father. And both taught that he is uncreated, eternal, the Creator, and one God with the Father. What changed after 325 was the precision of the words, sharpened because someone had finally denied the Son's full divinity outright. The church did not invent a new faith. It found clearer language to guard the faith it had confessed from the start, the faith that was there in the pages of the New Testament all along.

topics.title: Is the Trinitarian or the Arian reading of Scripture correct?
topics.cmp: Waterland and Bickersteth both side with the Trinitarian reading against the Arian one, but they answer different questions and so never directly overlap. Waterland argues on several fronts. He puts the burden of proof on the Arian, who would have to demonstrate an impossibility in a nature of which we have no ideas. He charges Dr. Clarke with making Scripture yield to an unproved philosophical maxim that being and person are the same. He also appeals to Eusebius and the Ante- and Post-Nicene ancients to show that attributing creation primarily to the Father denies the Son only original, not proper, efficiency, and marks him as second Person rather than a lesser being. Bickersteth works purely at the level of exegesis, using Ezekiel's parallel vision to show that the living creatures 'in the midst of the throne' support it from beneath and fall down before the Lamb, so their position does not weaken the Lamb's claim to share the throne and receive worship. The difference is mainly one of method and emphasis: Waterland combines Scripture with polemic against philosophical assumptions and appeals to patristic testimony, while Bickersteth reasons from Scripture interpreted by Scripture.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: It lies upon you, in this case, to prove the negative, viz. that no union whatever can make two persons one Being, one τὸ Θεῖον, one God: you are to shew the supposition to be impossible, in the nature of the thing

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: That they did not occupy the throne and receive adoration is plain; for (ch. 5:6) the Lamb appears in the midst of the living creatures, as well as in the midst of the elders; and verse 8, they, with the elders, fall down before him.

ans.text:
The Trinitarian reading is the one that does justice to the whole Bible. When Scripture's statements about the Son are taken at face value, they show him to be fully God, sharing the one being of the Father, not a splendid creature standing just below God.

It helps to know what the other view says. In the fourth century a teaching spread that the Son of God was the first and greatest thing God ever made. On this view he was made before the world and then used by God to make everything else. He was exalted, even called "god" in a lesser sense, but he was not God as the Father is God. There was a time, it said, when the Son did not exist. The church weighed this against Scripture and rejected it. Christians have confessed ever since that the Son is "true God from true God," of one being with the Father.

The Bible says two things plainly and often. First, there is only one God: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Second, the Son is God: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The Word is "with God," so he is distinct from the Father. Yet he "was God," so he is not a second, lesser deity beside him. The doctrine of the Trinity simply holds both truths together. There is one divine being, or "essence," meaning what God is. There are three Persons, meaning who God is: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

An objection is often raised at this point: "One being cannot be more than one person. Since the Father and Son are two persons, they must be two beings, so the Son must be a lesser one." Notice where this argument comes from. It does not come from any verse. It is a rule borrowed from our experience of human beings, where one being is one person, and then laid over God. But God is not a creature, and we have no inside view of his nature. To prove that God could not possibly be one being in more than one Person, someone would have to know God's inner life thoroughly enough to rule it out. No one does. So the burden of proof lies with the person who says it is impossible, not with the person who believes what Scripture reveals. We should let God tell us what he is like, rather than tell him what he can be.

This matters because that borrowed rule is the main tool used to explain away the strongest texts. Take John 1:1. The plain sense is that the Word is God. To make it mean "a god" or "godlike," one must already assume the Son cannot share the Father's being. Take John 8:58: "Truly, truly, I tell you," Jesus declared, "before Abraham was born, I am!" He does not say "I was," as if he were merely older than Abraham. He uses the timeless "I am" that echoes God's name in Exodus 3:14. His hearers understood him, which is why they picked up stones. Take Acts 20:28, where Paul speaks of "the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood." God's own blood can only be said if the One who died, the Son, is truly God. A tool that can empty texts as clear as these could empty any text at all. When an idea has to be brought in from outside to overrule what Scripture says, it is Scripture that should win.

The book of Revelation gives a striking picture. John sees "a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne" (Revelation 5:6). The throne in Revelation is God's own throne. The Lamb is not standing before it like a servant. He stands at its center, and then he receives worship. The living creatures and elders fall down before him. Every creature in heaven and on earth cries out, "To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be praise and honor and glory and power forever and ever!" (Revelation 5:13). In this same book, when John bows before an angel, he is told sharply not to, because worship belongs to God alone (Revelation 19:10; 22:8-9). Yet the Lamb receives the very worship given to the One on the throne.

Some reply that the four living creatures are also described as "in the midst" of the throne and around it (Revelation 4:6), so the Lamb's position proves nothing. But compare the parallel vision in Ezekiel 1. There the living creatures are beneath the throne, holding up the platform on which it rests. They are around it and under it, as its bearers. They never sit on it and never receive worship. Instead they fall down before the Lamb. The contrast actually strengthens the point. Creatures support the throne and worship. The Lamb shares the throne and is worshiped.

Then there is creation. The Bible insists that the LORD alone made the heavens and the earth, with no helper (Isaiah 44:24). Yet the New Testament says of the Son, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Paul writes that in him "all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible," and that "all things were created through Him and for Him" (Colossians 1:16). Notice the word "all." If the Son were himself a created thing, he would have had to make himself, which is nonsense. So he stands on the Creator's side of the line, not the creature's. Hebrews 1:10 even takes a psalm addressed to the LORD and applies it to the Son: in the beginning, Lord, you laid the foundations of the earth.

It is true that the Bible often speaks of creation as coming from the Father through the Son. Christians have long said that the Father plans and the Son carries out. But this describes an order among the Persons, not a difference in rank of being. A father and his son are equally human, even though one comes from the other. In the same way the Son is "begotten" of the Father. That word means he comes from the Father's own being, not that he was made. He is God from God, the way light shines from light without ever being less than light. When Jesus says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), he speaks as the one who has come from the Father, and who has humbled himself to become man. He is not denying what he says elsewhere: "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30).

So which reading is correct? The one that lets every text speak. The view that the Son is a creature must strain against John 1, John 8, Acts 20, Colossians 1 and Revelation 5, and it does so only by leaning on a human assumption about what God can be. The Trinitarian reading receives all these passages as they stand. It also keeps faith with the oneness of God that the whole Bible guards so jealously. That is why Christians worship the Son with the Father and the Spirit. They are not honoring a great creature. They are worshiping the one true God.

topics.title: Must the term 'homoousios' be kept in the Creed?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa and Daniel Waterland both defend keeping 'homoousios', but they answer different challenges to it. Gregory, recounting Basil's stand before the emperor, makes a practical and principled case: the confession of faith may not be added to, subtracted from, or even reordered, even for peace with the emperor and concern for his soul. Waterland meets a historical objection instead. He argues that the Council of Antioch's condemnation of the word was aimed only at Paul of Samosata's Sabellian misuse of it, and that Antioch actually taught the same doctrine as Nicaea, citing Hilary's remark that the word was misunderstood at first and rightly received later. Gregory thus rests on the inviolability of the received Creed, while Waterland relies on historical and patristic interpretation to show the term's orthodoxy.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: but a diminution of or addition to the Faith was so far from his (Basil’s) thoughts, that he would not change even the order of the written words.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: They condemned the word, as it had been misunderstood and misapplied by Paul of Samosata; but established the very same doctrine with the Nicene Fathers.

ans.text:
Yes. The phrase 'of one substance with the Father' should stay in the Creed. It is not a decoration that can be traded away for good relations. It is the guard rail that protects what the Bible says about who Jesus is.

Start with what the word means. The Greek word behind the phrase is homoousios. 'Homo' means 'same,' and 'ousia' means 'being' or 'substance,' the basic reality of what something is. So the Creed is saying that the Son is the same kind of being as the Father. Whatever it means to be God, the Father is that, and the Son is that too, fully and equally. Some modern versions of the Creed say 'of one being with the Father' or 'of the same essence.' Those are different English words for the same claim, and that is fine. What matters is that the meaning is kept.

Why use a word that is not found in the Bible? Because a word was needed to say clearly what the Bible says. In the early fourth century, some teachers argued that the Son was the first and greatest thing God ever made. He was glorious, but he was a creature, and there was a time when he did not exist. The trouble was that these teachers were happy to repeat Bible phrases. They would call Jesus 'Son of God,' 'the Word,' even 'God' in a loose sense, while meaning something quite different. Church leaders found that every biblical phrase they offered could be agreed to and quietly emptied. So they chose a word that could not be slipped around. You cannot say the Son is the same being as the Father and also say he is a creature.

The word is a short summary of what Scripture teaches. John 1:1 says, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' The Word was not made at the beginning. He already was. Jesus says in John 10:30, 'I and the Father are one.' Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son 'the radiance of God's glory and the exact representation of His nature.' Colossians 2:9 says that 'in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form.' None of these could be said of even the highest angel. 'Of one substance' simply gathers them up into one plain statement.

So why not drop it for the sake of peace? In the early church, powerful rulers sometimes pressed bishops to soften the wording so that everyone could sign on. That pressure has its modern versions too: the wish to get along, to avoid a word that sounds technical or divisive. The desire for unity is good. Jesus prayed that his people would be one. But the unity he prayed for is unity in the truth. In John 17:17 he asks the Father to sanctify them by the truth, and says, 'Your word is truth.' A peace bought by blurring who Jesus is would not be real peace. It would be agreeing to stop asking the question that matters most.

Think of it like a wedding vow. Two people could make a vow vaguer so that nobody feels uncomfortable. But if the words that actually bind them are taken out, the ceremony may be smoother, and the marriage is weaker. The Creed is the church's vow about who its Lord is. Jude urges believers to contend for the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all. A faithful pastor might gladly welcome a ruler, or anyone else, into the church for the good of their soul. He would still not change the confession in order to do it. If the words are removed, it is no longer the same confession.

There is another reason. In 1 John 2:23, John says that whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either. How we speak about the Son is not a side issue. If Jesus is less than fully God, then God has not truly come to us himself. He has sent someone else. The good news is that God himself came to save us. The phrase 'of one substance' protects that good news.

Some people point out that, decades before the Creed, a church council in Antioch actually rejected this same word. Doesn't that undercut it? The answer is no, once you see what was being rejected. In the third century, a bishop of Antioch taught that Jesus was merely a man indwelt by God's power. In that debate the word was being used in a confused sense. It was taken either to mean that the Father and the Son were one and the same person, simply wearing different titles, or to suggest that they were two pieces cut from some common divine material. The council rightly refused those meanings. And that same council firmly taught that the Son is truly divine and existed before all things, against the bishop's view that Jesus was only a man.

In other words, the earlier council and the later Creed were defending the same truth from different directions. The earlier council rejected a misuse of the word that would have erased the difference between Father and Son. The later Creed used the word, carefully explained, to deny that the Son is a creature. Words take their meaning from how they are used. A word that was badly understood in one setting can be rightly understood in another. The Creed's own wording makes the right sense clear, because it also calls the Son 'begotten,' meaning that he comes from the Father as a son from a father, not made as a builder makes a house. That word keeps Father and Son distinct, while 'of one substance' keeps them equal.

Two misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, 'one substance' does not mean the Father and the Son are the same person. They are truly distinct. The Father sends, the Son is sent, and they speak to and love one another. Second, 'substance' does not mean some physical stuff, as if God were made of material. It means what God is: his very being and nature. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not three gods sharing a supply of divinity. They are one God, each fully possessing the one divine life.

So the word stays. It is a fence around a treasure, and the treasure is this: the Jesus who was born, died and rose again is not a messenger from God but God the Son himself, equal with the Father in every way. The church may explain the word in plainer language, as long as it keeps the meaning. But it should not let go of what the word protects, whether for peace, convenience or the approval of anyone.

topics.title: Do Eunomius's arguments from the divine energies prove the Son and Spirit inferior?
topics.cmp: Critique of Eunomius's ranking of divine energies and works and his circular reasoning between energies and beings.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: it starts from data that are not granted, and then it constructs by mere logic a blasphemy upon them. It attempts no demonstration that could attract towards such a conception of the doctrine

ans.text:
No. The argument fails, both because of what it assumes at the start and because its reasoning runs in a circle. The Bible points the other way: the Father, Son and Holy Spirit do one shared work, which shows they share one divine nature.

In the fourth century, some teachers who denied the full divinity of the Son and Spirit offered an argument that sounded careful. It ran like this. We know what a being is like by what it does. The Greek word for those doings was "energies," which simply means activities or workings. The Father's works are of the first rank. The Son's are of a second, lesser rank, and the Spirit's are lesser still. So, the argument concluded, the Son and the Spirit must be lesser beings than the Father.

The first problem is that the argument quietly assumes what it sets out to prove. Before any reasoning starts, it treats Father, Son and Spirit as three separate beings, each with a different level of dignity, each producing works of a different grade. But that is the very point in dispute. Christians confess one God, not three beings ranked like officers in an army. Begin by assuming they are unequal, and you will of course conclude they are unequal. That is not a proof. And nowhere does the Bible teach that the Son's works are second-class or the Spirit's third-class. The ranking is simply asserted, and a claim with no support from Scripture or sound reason proves nothing.

The second problem is that the reasoning goes in a circle. Its defenders said that if we are unsure about the works, we can settle the question by knowing the beings. They also said we come to know the beings through their works. Think about how proof works in daily life. You explain something uncertain by pointing to something already clear, the way you use a known landmark to find an unfamiliar street. Here, though, both the nature of God and the ranking of his works are uncertain. If we already understood the being, we would not need the works to show it. If we do not understand it, it cannot clear up our doubts about the works. Each side leans on the other, and nothing holds either one up.

Now turn to what Scripture actually says about the works of God. Far from ranking them, it shows Father, Son and Spirit acting together in everything God does. Jesus says in John 5:19, "whatever the Father does, the Son also does." He does not say the Son does a smaller version, or a second-grade copy. He says the Son does the same works. In creation, the greatest work of all, John 1:3 says of the Son, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Psalm 104:30 gives the Spirit the same role: "When You send Your Spirit, they are created." Paul ties the three together in 1 Corinthians 12:4–6. There are different gifts but the same Spirit, different ministries but the same Lord, and different kinds of working but the same God who works them all.

The principle in the original argument was partly right. Works do reveal something about the one who does them. But followed honestly, it leads to the opposite conclusion. Only God can create from nothing, raise the dead, forgive sins and give new life. Scripture credits the Son and the Spirit with all of these. So their works show them to be truly God. When Jesus says in John 10:30, "I and the Father are one," he is claiming a oneness that his works back up (John 10:37–38).

Some readers may wonder about verses where the Son is sent, obeys, or says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). These are real, and they matter. Within the one God there is an order: the Father sends, the Son is sent, and the Spirit is sent by the Father, and Christians have differed over whether the Spirit is sent by the Son as well. Order is not the same as rank in nature, though. A son who obeys his father is not less human than his father. And when the eternal Son became a man, he truly took a lowly place for our sake (Philippians 2:6–8). His humble obedience on earth shows his love, not a lower kind of divinity.

So the argument from the divine works does not prove the Son and Spirit inferior. Rightly read, God's works show one God in three persons. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together create, save and give life, and they are worthy of the same worship.

topics.title: How should particular Ante-Nicene Fathers' statements about the Son be read?
topics.cmp: Examines disputed language in Justin Martyr, Ignatius, Origen and Eusebius on the Son's generation by the Father's will, creaturely titles, worship, creation, and the use of 'agennetos'.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: These considerations convince me, that Justin as well as Athenagoras taught the strict cocternity of the Son; which is equally true of all the other writers.

ans.text:
Read them the way you would read a letter from a trusted friend written before a family argument broke out: patiently, in context, and with the whole of their thinking in view, not by pulling out a single phrase. The writers of the first three centuries after the apostles loved Christ and worshiped him. But they wrote before the great fourth-century dispute over whether the Son is truly God or a very exalted creature. Because of that, they sometimes used words loosely that later had to be used with great care. When we read them fairly, the phrases that seem to make the Son a creature usually turn out to mean something quite different.

One example is a single word. In Greek there were two very similar words. One meant "unbegotten," not born of anyone. The other meant "unmade," not created. They differ by only one letter and were often used interchangeably in the early centuries. So when an early writer says that God alone is "unbegotten," we have to ask which sense he means. Often the context settles it. He sets the word beside "eternal" and "incorruptible," and against things that are made and perish. Or he contrasts "made man" with "unmade God." In such places he is drawing the line between Creator and creature, not between the Father and the Son. The Son falls on God's side of that line. John 1:3 says, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made." Whoever made everything that was made cannot himself be one of the things made.

A second example is the way people speak of rank and age. Some early writers call the Son the "eldest" or "first" of God's works. That can sound as if he is the first creature. But people often use superlatives this way to mean "older than all of them," without counting the one described as part of the group. We might call someone "the best of the bunch" when they were never really in the bunch at all. Scripture speaks similarly. Colossians 1:15 calls the Son "the firstborn over all creation." The very next verse explains why: "For in Him all things were created." "Firstborn" here means first in rank and rightful heir over creation. It does not mean the first thing created. The same writers who use this language also take care to separate the Son from God's works and call him uncreated and unchanging.

A third example is language about the Father's "will." Some early writers say the Son was begotten, or is Son, "by the will" of the Father. Does that mean the Father simply chose to produce him, as he chose to make the world? Read in context, usually not. Sometimes the writer means the Son's mission rather than his being. It was the Father's good pleasure that the Son should come as his messenger, act as Creator, or become man. Sometimes the writer simply means the Son comes from God, as "God from God." The Father has never been without his Son, and he has never wished to be. His will is in full and eternal agreement with the Son's existence. That is very different from saying the Son exists only because the Father happened to choose it.

In the same way, one early writer says the Son bears titles such as Word, Wisdom, Lord, Messenger and God for two reasons together. One is that he is begotten of the Father. The other is that he serves the Father's purposes. Some titles describe who he is. Others describe what he does for us. Mixing the two leads to false conclusions.

A fourth example is talk of the Son being "begotten" or "put forth" at the time of creation. Some early writers speak this way while also saying, in the same breath, that the Son was with the Father before the world. What they are describing is his coming forth to act, to create and reveal. They are not describing his beginning to exist. Jesus himself speaks of "the glory I had with You before the world existed" in John 17:5.

The same care helps with a phrase like "Son of God according to the will and power of God." When it is set beside "of David according to the flesh," it points to a higher sonship than his human birth. Paul makes the same pairing in Romans 1:3-4. There the Son is "a descendant of David according to the flesh" and is also declared with power to be the Son of God.

It also helps to notice what these writers did, not only what they said. They worshiped the Son. Some taught plainly that only the Creator may be worshiped, then called the Son that Creator and spoke of honoring Father and Son together as one God. Others gave the Son the highest title, "Maker of all things." Many read God's words in Genesis 1:26, "Let Us make man in Our image," as the Father speaking with the Son. Hebrews 1:10 applies to the Son the words, "In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth." People do not worship a creature they believe the Creator has forbidden them to worship. Their practice shows what they believed, even where their vocabulary was still unsettled.

In fairness, not every early phrase can be smoothed over. Some of these writers did use expressions that later Christians judged unclear or unhelpful. Some modern readers think a few of them really held a lower view of the Son. Others think their wording was simply imprecise and their faith sound. Sincere people weigh the evidence differently. That honesty is healthy.

It also points to the most important principle. These writers are valued witnesses, but they are not our foundation. The church's confession that the Son is true God, eternally begotten and not made, rests on Scripture. Jesus says the Father has given judgment to the Son "so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father" (John 5:23). We read the early writers charitably and learn from them. But we measure everything, their words and ours, by the Bible.

topics.title: What did the Cappadocians and Chrysostom mean by the Son's unity with the Father?
topics.cmp: Only Daniel Waterland and Gregory of Nyssa answer here, and they answer different questions, so there is no direct disagreement. Waterland's answers all argue against Dr. Clarke's reading of Chrysostom and Basil. He holds that their unity 'in power' (κατὰ δύναμιν) means an essential equality and identity of power, and therefore of essence. His grounds are textual: Chrysostom's next words say that the same power implies the same essence, and Clarke drops 'equal' when translating Basil. He adds a philosophical point, that infinite and finite power cannot properly be called one. He also argues that Basil rejected only unity of Person (Sabellianism), not unity of essence. Gregory of Nyssa, in his own voice, addresses a related point: he affirms that the Father is ungenerate and the Son generated, but denies that these terms reveal what either Person is in his nature.

refs.author: Daniel Waterland
refs.quote: One having infinite and the other only finite power, could not, according to Chrysostom, be properly said to be one, κατὰ δύναμιν, in power.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: we do not intend to deny that the Father exists without generation, and we have no intention of refusing to agree to the statement that the Only-begotten God is generated;—on the contrary the latter has been generated, the former has not been generated.

ans.text:
They meant that the Son shares the very same power as the Father, and therefore the very same divine being. They did not mean that the Son merely agrees with the Father or acts on his behalf. The early preachers and teachers who spoke of the Son being one with the Father "in power" were explaining Jesus' own words. Some later readers have taken them to mean something weaker, so it helps to look carefully at what they were saying and why.

Start with the verse at the center of it all. In John 10:30 Jesus says, "I and the Father are one." Look at what comes just before. Jesus says of His sheep, "No one can snatch them out of My hand," and then, "No one can snatch them out of My Father's hand" (John 10:28-29). The same safekeeping is credited to both hands. That is why early Christian teachers said this oneness is first of all a oneness of power. The Son's hand holds the sheep with the same strength as the Father's hand.

Some have argued that "one in power" means only a lesser unity. On that view the Father has all power and lends some of it to the Son, the way a king gives authority to an ambassador. Or the Father and Son are simply of one mind, the way two friends agree. But that is not what these teachers meant. Being one in power means being equal in power. Imagine one person with unlimited power and another with only limited power. You could not honestly call their power "one." At most you could say the weaker one was working for the stronger.

These teachers also took a further step, and it is the heart of the matter. God's power is not something separate from God, like a tool He picks up. His almighty power belongs to what He is. So if the Son has the very same almighty power as the Father, then the Son has the very same divine nature as the Father. Same power means same essence. "Essence" here simply means what something is at its core. The Son is not a lesser being given great authority. He is God in the same full sense that the Father is God.

The Bible points the same way. Jesus says in John 5:19 that whatever the Father does, the Son also does. He does not mean some of the Father's works or smaller versions of them. He means the same works, done in the same way. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son "the exact representation of His nature," who upholds all things by His powerful word. Holding the whole universe in being is not something you can hand off to a creature. Paul even calls Christ "the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). Jesus' hearers in John 10 understood Him this way too. They picked up stones because, as they said, He, a man, was claiming to be God (John 10:33).

A second misunderstanding concerns what these teachers denied. They did insist that the Father and the Son are not one and the same Person. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father. That is why Jesus can speak to the Father, be sent by Him, and pray to Him. Some later readers took this denial and stretched it to mean these teachers rejected a shared divine essence. That confuses two different things. To say the Father and Son are two distinct Persons is not to say they are two different kinds of being. The church has always held both truths together: one God, one divine nature, and yet the Father and the Son are truly distinct.

A third point concerns the Son being "begotten." To be begotten means to come from someone and share their nature, as a child shares the humanity of a parent. It is not like a carpenter making a table. These teachers firmly held that the Father is unbegotten, coming from no one, and that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father. They did not deny this at all. What they denied was that the words "unbegotten" and "begotten" tell us what God's nature is, as if being unbegotten were the definition of true divinity and the Son, being begotten, must therefore be less. These words describe how the Persons are related to each other. The Father is Father because He has the Son, and the Son is Son because He is from the Father. They do not describe two different natures. A human son is no less human than his father, and the eternal Son is no less God than His.

So when these early teachers spoke of the Son's unity with the Father, they meant three things together. The Son has the same almighty power as the Father. Because of that, He shares the same divine being. And He remains a distinct Person, eternally begotten of the Father. That is the faith the church has confessed from the early creeds onward. It is why Christians can trust Jesus with their very lives. The hand that holds them is as strong as the Father's, because it is the hand of God Himself.

title: One Creator God against Gnostics and Marcion
desc: Defence of the Creator and God of the Old Testament as the Father of Christ, against Demiurge, Aeon and emanation systems, Gnostic numerology and secret traditions.

topics.title: Is the Creator of the world the one supreme God and Father of Christ, rather than a lesser or ignorant Demiurge?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that the Creator is the one supreme God and the Father of Christ, and that the Gnostic or Marcionite idea of a higher God above a lesser or ignorant Demiurge is false. Irenaeus supplies nearly all the answers, and he argues from many directions. He appeals to Scripture: Christ calling his Father 'Lord of heaven and earth', the parables of the vineyard and the wedding feast, Paul at Athens and Lystra, Peter to Cornelius, and Mark's opening. He also appeals to apostolic tradition (Clement's letter, the Jerusalem Church's prayer), to the Eucharist and the Church's offering of creation's fruits, and to philosophical reasoning: God as Pleroma must contain all, so there is no void or higher being; Marcion's two gods would bound each other; goodness and judgment cannot be divided. On a few points he simply declines to speculate, saying how God produced matter is not revealed. Novatian reaches the same conclusion more briefly, from Scripture's 'God is one' texts, the argument that God contains all things, and the claim that the Christ promised in the Old Testament is fulfilled in the New. Hippolytus adds that even the heretics' many principles reduce to one cause. Gregory of Nyssa, Athanasius, Owen, Hilary and Warfield take the anti-Gnostic conclusion for granted and turn it toward Trinitarian debates: Gregory says Eunomius is worse than Marcion, Athanasius traces the Arian 'will before the Word' to the Valentinian Ptolemy, Owen roots the Marcionite error in denying the Son's eternity, Hilary says the new name the Son revealed is 'Father', and Warfield says the New Testament writers saw their Trinity as the Old Testament Jehovah himself rather than new gods beside him.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: there is no one besides Him, or above Him, neither has He any mother, as they falsely ascribe to Him; nor is there a second God, as Marcion has imagined

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: In Fine, Notwithstanding the Said Heretics Have Gathered…
refs.quote: For we both know, and read, and believe, and maintain that God is one, who made the heaven as well as the earth, since we neither know any other, nor shall we at any time know such, seeing that there is none.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For no man knows God unless He confess Him as Father, Father of the Only-begotten Son

ans.text:
Yes. The God who made the heavens and the earth is the one true and highest God, and he is the very same God whom Jesus called "Father." There is no greater, hidden God standing behind him, and no lesser god who botched the job of making the world.

This may seem obvious to most churchgoers, but in the first centuries some teachers taught otherwise. One group claimed that the physical world was made by a lower being, sometimes called the "Demiurge" (a Greek word for a craftsman or builder). In their story, this builder was weak, ignorant or even proud, and our world of bodies and matter was the result of a mistake. Jesus, they said, came from a higher, unknown God to rescue a few enlightened souls out of this flawed creation. Another teacher taught that there were two gods: a stern, judging God of the Old Testament who made the world, and a kind, loving God revealed by Jesus. Ideas like these still turn up today, whenever people speak of the "angry God of the Old Testament" against the "gentle God of Jesus," or treat the body and the material world as a trap to escape.

The Bible answers these ideas from its first line to its last. "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). No helpers, no angels, no lesser craftsman share the work. Through the prophet Isaiah the Lord insists that he made all things and stretched out the heavens by himself alone (Isaiah 44:24). And when God looks at what he has made, he does not see a mistake: "God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31).

Most important, Jesus himself names the Creator as his Father. He prays, "I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth" (Matthew 11:25). He tells us that our heavenly Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies (Matthew 6:26-30). He says the Father makes his sun rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous (Matthew 5:45). When asked about marriage, he points back to creation and says God made them male and female from the beginning (Mark 10:6). Jesus never hints at a second, higher God. The God who runs the weather, feeds the sparrows and made the first man and woman is the one he calls Father.

The apostles say the same. Paul writes, "for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came" (1 Corinthians 8:6). He speaks of "one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all" (Ephesians 4:6). Long before, the prophet Malachi had asked, "Do we not all have one Father? Did not one God create us?" (Malachi 2:10). In Scripture, "Father" and "Creator" are not two different people. They are the same God.

Notice too that the Son is not a stranger to creation. John's Gospel opens by telling us that the Word, who was with God and was God, is the one through whom the world was made: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Colossians 1:16 adds that in him all things were created, visible and invisible. So Jesus did not come into someone else's world to raid it. He came into his own world, the world he had made with the Father. John makes this clear: "He came to His own" (John 1:11). The One who creates and the One who saves belong to the one God. Even in the creation story we glimpse this: God speaks his Word, and his Spirit hovers over the waters (Genesis 1:2). Father, Son and Spirit act together as one Creator.

This matters for how we understand salvation. If the world belonged to a lesser god, then Jesus taking on a real human body would make no sense, nor would his rising bodily from the grave. When Jesus took ordinary bread and wine, things grown from the earth, and gave them to his disciples as his body and blood, he was treating creation as his Father's good gift, not as enemy property. When he forgave sins, he forgave debts we owe to the God who made us, which only makes sense if his Father is our Maker. And Christians look forward not to escaping the material world but to its renewal: a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1).

What about the claim that the Old Testament God is harsh while the God of Jesus is kind? Jesus' parable of the tenants answers this (Mark 12:1-6). The owner of the vineyard sends servant after servant, the prophets, and finally sends his beloved son. It is one owner from start to finish. The God who gave the law through Moses is the same God who sent his Son full of grace. The covenants differ because they suit different stages of God's plan, not because two different gods wrote them. And the Old Testament is full of God's mercy, just as the New Testament speaks of his judgment.

In fact, splitting goodness from justice ruins both. A judge who is not good would be cruel, not divine. A "good" god who never judges evil would be weak and careless, letting wrong go unchecked. The living God is both perfectly good and perfectly just, and that is why he can be trusted. A so-called good god who quietly steals people away from the One who made them would not be good at all. He would be a thief.

Plain reasoning points the same way. God, by definition, is the highest reality, the source of everything else. Nothing can exist beyond him or outside him, because he holds all things in being and nothing holds him. If there were two ultimate gods, each would limit the other. Each would lack what the other had, and neither would truly be almighty. Then why stop at two? You would end up with a crowd of rival powers, and no real God at all. Scripture's answer is simpler and deeper: there is one first cause of all things. "The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth" (Acts 17:24).

So when Christians confess, "I believe in God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth," we are saying something precious. The God who made you is not a distant or clumsy craftsman, and the God who loves you in Christ is not a stranger to your world. They are one and the same. Your body, the food on your table, the sky above you and the Savior who died and rose for you all come from the same faithful Father.

topics.title: How did God create the world, and does rejecting created things deny the Creator?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus of Lyons, Gregory of Nyssa and Athanasius of Alexandria agree that God created by his own will and power alone, without pre-existent matter, instruments or helpers. Irenaeus alone addresses creation out of nothing directly, affirming it on the rule of truth, contrasting it with human making from existing matter, and dismissing the Valentinian appeal to pre-existent matter as borrowed from Anaxagoras, Empedocles and Plato. Gregory reaches the same conclusion from how Scripture speaks: 'generation' is language stooping to human capacity, and God's will itself supplied matter, place, time and instrument ('He spake and they were made'). Athanasius likewise argues from Scripture ('He hath done whatsoever pleased Him') that God's will alone suffices, using this to show that a created mediator in creation would be superfluous. The main difference is emphasis: Irenaeus stresses most strongly that God made all things freely, by himself and through his Word, and only he names the Son and the Spirit as God's own 'hands', the Word and Wisdom whom he addresses in 'Let Us make man' and whom the angels serve, whereas Gregory's and Athanasius's answers here centre on the sufficiency of the divine will.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: He the Creator, who made those things by Himself, that is, through His Word and His Wisdom— heaven and earth, and the seas, and all things that are in them

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: neither place nor time nor preparation of material, nor the co-operation of instruments, nor the purpose in the things produced, but it leaves these out of sight, and greatly and loftily claims for God the generation of the things that are

refs.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
refs.quote: why, when He would create us, does He seek for a mediator at all, as if His will did not suffice to constitute whatever seemed good to Him?

ans.text:
God made the world out of nothing, simply by willing it and speaking it into being through His own Word and Spirit. He did not need any helpers, tools, or raw materials. And yes: to treat the good things He made, like marriage or food, as evil in themselves is, in the end, to find fault with the One who made them.

Start with the opening words of the Bible: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." Genesis 1 never mentions a lump of material God was working with, or assistants who did part of the job. Again and again it simply says, "And God said... and it was so." The psalmist sums it up: "For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm" (Psalm 33:9). Hebrews 11:3 adds that the universe was formed by God's command, so that what we see was not made out of what was already visible.

This is the difference between God and us. A carpenter needs wood, a workshop, tools and time. Everything we make, we make out of something that already existed. God is not like that. When He wills something, His will is enough. It does the work that matter, tools and workshop do for us. Paul speaks of God as the One who calls into being what does not yet exist (Romans 4:17). That is what "creation out of nothing" means. It does not mean "nothing" was some strange stuff God used. It means there was God, and nothing else, until He freely brought the world into existence.

The Bible sometimes describes God's creating in very human language, as if He fathers or gives birth to the world. These are pictures that stoop to our level so we can grasp something. They do not mean God needed a place, a stretch of time, or materials, as a human parent or craftsman does.

God did not create through lesser beings either. Some early teachers claimed the world was made by angels or by a lower, clumsy god, so that the true God would not get His hands dirty with matter. Scripture says the opposite. John tells us that the Word, who is the Son, was with God and was God, and "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Paul says all things were created through Christ and for Him, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, including angels (Colossians 1:16). The Spirit was hovering over the waters at the start (Genesis 1:2). So when God says "Let Us make man in Our image" (Genesis 1:26), He is not consulting angels. The Father, Son and Spirit are the one God at work. You could say the Son and the Spirit are God's own "hands." They are not hired help. They are God Himself acting. Angels are not co-creators. They are creatures who serve.

God also created freely. He was not forced by anything outside Himself, and He was not lonely or lacking something. He made the world because He was pleased to, out of sheer goodness. The heavenly worship in Revelation 4:11 praises Him: "for You created all things; by Your will they exist, and were created." This means the world is a gift, not an accident or a necessity.

That brings us to the second part of the question. If the one good God made everything, then the material world is not a prison or a mistake. At the end of the creation week, "God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). He made us male and female and blessed their union (Genesis 1:27–28; 2:24). Jesus pointed back to this when He defended marriage (Matthew 19:4–6).

So when people teach that marriage is unclean, or that eating meat is sinful in itself, they are quietly accusing the Creator of making something bad. Paul warns about exactly this. He describes false teachers who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods "that God has created to be received with thanksgiving." Then he gives the reason: "For every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected" (1 Timothy 4:3–4). Hebrews 13:4 says marriage should be honored by all.

It matters why someone holds back, though. Choosing not to marry in order to serve the Lord is something Paul himself commends (1 Corinthians 7:7–8, 32–35). Fasting is a long-standing Christian practice. Someone may skip meat for health, conscience, or love of a weaker brother or sister, and Paul tells us not to judge one another over such things (Romans 14:1–6). None of that rejects the Creator. The problem comes only when a good gift is condemned as evil in itself, or when holding back is made a rule for being truly spiritual. The first is a sacrifice offered to God. The second is a complaint against Him.

The heart of it is this: the God who saves us in Christ is the same God who made the world through Christ. We do not grow holier by despising His creation. We grow holier by receiving it with thanks and using it as He intended.

topics.title: Is the God of the Old Testament, the Law and the prophets the same God as the Father of Jesus Christ?
topics.cmp: Nearly every answer on this topic comes from Irenaeus of Lyons, who answers with one conclusion throughout: the God of the law and the prophets is the Father of Jesus Christ and the Maker of all things, and there is no higher Father above the Creator. His grounds are mainly scriptural and exegetical: Christ's use of the law against Satan, his renewal of the great commandment, his calling the Temple his house and Moses' writings his own words, the testimony of Simeon, Anna, Gabriel, Stephen and Philip, and the apostles' continued keeping of the Mosaic observances. To these he adds arguments of providential order (the law as a temporary pedagogue suited to Israel's condition, given for man's benefit rather than God's need) and polemical reasoning against the Gnostics: their mutual disagreements, the failure of the tabernacle's measurements to match their Aeons, and the impossibility of one being conceiving the world while another makes it. He also argues that the same justice, displayed more moderately in the Old Testament and more severely in the New, rules out a separate Old Testament God, and that free will rather than divine weakness explains Israel's disobedience. Gregory of Nyssa adds only a brief agreeing point from a different angle: Moses and David share one Teacher, the Holy Spirit, so the Psalms may interpret Moses. John Owen's single answer does not address whether the two Gods are the same but explains persecution as ignorance of the Father and the Son, so the authors do not openly disagree, though their emphases and concerns are quite different.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: for Him whom the law proclaimed as God, the same did Christ point out as the Father, whom also it behoves the disciples of Christ alone to serve.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: know that their blind and desperate ignorance is the cause of their fury and persuasion

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: since both Moses and David have one and the same Teacher, I mean the Holy Spirit, Who says that the fiat went before the creation

ans.text:
Yes. The God who called Abraham, spoke to Moses, gave the Law at Sinai and sent the prophets is the very same God whom Jesus called His Father. Christians do not worship a new God who replaced an older one. They worship the one God of Israel, now made fully known in His Son.

Jesus Himself settles the matter. When He was asked about the resurrection, He pointed back to the burning bush and said, "have you not read what God said to you: 'I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'?" (Matthew 22:31-32). He did not say, "That was the God your ancestors knew, but I have come from someone higher." He spoke of that God as the living God, the one He knew and served. In John's Gospel He goes even further. He says, "If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me" (John 5:46). Moses and Jesus are not rivals. The same voice runs through both.

Look at how Jesus used the Old Testament. When Satan tempted Him in the wilderness, He answered every time with words from Deuteronomy, the book of the Law (Matthew 4:1-11). When asked for the greatest commandment, He did not bring some new, higher rule from heaven. He quoted the Law of Moses: "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (Matthew 22:37). When He rebuked the religious leaders, He blamed them for setting aside "the commandment of God" to honor father and mother for the sake of their own traditions (Mark 7:8-13). In every case He treated the Law as His Father's word. When He drove the traders out of the Temple, He called it His Father's house (John 2:16). His anger was with those who misused it, not with the God who gave it.

Jesus also said plainly that He had not come to tear down what came before: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them" (Matthew 5:17). Fulfilling something is not the same as rejecting it. A promise is fulfilled when the thing promised arrives. Much of the Law, such as the sacrifices and the Temple rituals, was like a signpost or a shadow pointing ahead. Once Christ came, the signpost had done its job. Paul puts it this way: "the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ" (Galatians 3:24). Think of a tutor who prepares a child for adulthood. When the child grows up, the tutor's work is finished, but nobody concludes that the tutor worked for a different family.

The apostles preached the same way. Peter told the crowds in Jerusalem that "The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified His servant Jesus" (Acts 3:13). When Philip met the Ethiopian official reading Isaiah 53, about the lamb led to the slaughter, he began right there and told him about Jesus (Acts 8:26-35). The letter to the Hebrews opens by saying that the God who "spoke to our fathers through the prophets" has now "spoken to us by His Son" (Hebrews 1:1-2). It is one God speaking, first in many partial ways and then fully in His Son. Even the early church's big argument about circumcision (Acts 15) only makes sense if the God of the Law and the God of the gospel are the same. Nobody argues about how to keep a law that came from a false god.

The Gospels make the same point from the very beginning. Mary and Joseph bring the baby Jesus to the Temple to do what the Law of the Lord required. There, old Simeon takes Him in his arms and praises God for letting him see His salvation (Luke 2:22-32). The angels announce His birth "in the city of David," because God had promised David a King from his own family whose kingdom would never end. The God who made that promise is the God who kept it.

This also fits what Christians believe about the Trinity. The one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and He has always been so. That means the Son and the Spirit were not absent from the Old Testament. Peter says the prophets spoke by "the Spirit of Christ" when they foretold His sufferings (1 Peter 1:10-11). And Jesus, after His resurrection, walked through Moses and all the Prophets to show His disciples what was written about Himself (Luke 24:27). The whole Bible is one story told by one God.

Many people sincerely wonder about this because the Old Testament can seem harsh while Jesus seems gentle. It is worth looking more closely. The God of the Old Testament describes Himself to Moses as "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). He forgives, pleads with His people, and promises a new heart. And Jesus, for all His gentleness, speaks more about final judgment than anyone else in Scripture. He warns of a day when the unrepentant will be sent away. The New Testament still says, "our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews 12:29). Paul even says that the judgments on Israel in the wilderness were written down as warnings for us (1 Corinthians 10:11). That only makes sense if it is the same God then and now. His holiness and His mercy are both on display in both Testaments. What changes is not God's character but how fully He has shown it. In the cross we see both at once: sin taken with deadly seriousness, and sinners loved at unthinkable cost.

Some have also claimed that one being thought up the world while a lesser being actually built it. But the Bible knows of only one Creator, who simply speaks and it is done (Psalm 33:9). Paul admits that people worship many so-called gods, "yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came" (1 Corinthians 8:6), and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came. The Maker of heaven and earth in Genesis is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

So when you read the Old Testament, you are not reading about a stranger. You are reading about your Father, the God who was preparing, step by step, to send His Son. The Law, the prophets and the gospel are chapters of one story, written by one faithful God.

topics.title: Did one and the same God give both the Old and the New Covenants?
topics.cmp: Nearly all the answers here come from Irenaeus of Lyons, who consistently holds, against those positing two gods, that one and the same God, acting through his Word, gave both covenants. He grounds this in apostolic and presbyteral tradition, in Scripture and its types (Jacob's two wives, Abraham prefiguring both covenants, the householder bringing out things new and old, sower and reaper), and in philosophical reasoning that 'greater' and 'less' apply only to things of the same substance. He accounts for the differences between the covenants as progressive grace from an unchanging God: shared precepts begun among the Jews and completed among Christians, similar concessions to human weakness in both, and Christ's advent pouring out a greater gift of the same paternal grace rather than revealing an unknown Father. John Owen addresses a narrower question, not the identity of God, and names the chief difference between the covenants as the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit by the ascended Christ, the basis of the church's gifts and graces. The two are compatible but differ in emphasis: Irenaeus speaks of the Spirit only in passing, as the same life-giving gift given to all of Christ's sons, and stresses continuity and growth of grace, while Owen makes the Spirit's eminent outpouring the decisive mark of the new administration.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: all things had ever been revealed and shown to believers by one and the same God through the Word; He at one time conferring with His creature, and at another propounding His law

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: that he had received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, Act ii. 33; and that in such an eminent manner as thereby to make the greatest and most glorious difference between the administration of the new covenant and old

ans.text:
Yes. The God who made a covenant with Abraham, gave the law through Moses, and spoke by the prophets is the very same God who made the new covenant in the blood of Jesus. There are two covenants but only one God behind them both. The New Testament makes no sense without this.

Start with how the Bible itself tells the story. Hebrews opens like this: "On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son" (Hebrews 1:1–2). Notice that it is the same God speaking both times. Only the way he speaks has changed, from prophets to his own Son. The writer is not announcing a new God. He is telling us that the God of Israel has now said his final and fullest word.

The new covenant was in fact promised in the old. Through Jeremiah the Lord said that the days were coming when he would make a new covenant with Israel and Judah, writing his law on their hearts and forgiving their sins (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus picked up that very promise at the Last Supper when he spoke of "the new covenant in My blood" (Luke 22:20). A promise and its keeping belong to the same person. If someone else showed up to fulfil it, it would not be fulfilment at all.

This is why the apostles keep saying that the gospel is old news made new. Paul calls it the gospel God "promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures" (Romans 1:2). He says Scripture "foretold the gospel to Abraham" (Galatians 3:8). He also says that "all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ" (2 Corinthians 1:20). Jesus himself said he did not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them (Matthew 5:17). Think of a seed and the tree that grows from it. They look very different, but nobody thinks they come from different gardeners.

The two covenants also share the same heart. When Jesus was asked for the greatest commandment, he did not invent something new. He quoted the Old Testament: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind (Deuteronomy 6:5), and love your neighbour as yourself (Leviticus 19:18). Trusting God, following his word, loving him above all, and turning from evil are found in both covenants. They first took root in Israel and came to full growth in the church.

So why is the new covenant so much greater? Because the same God gives more. He has not turned into someone else. Picture a good father who gives his child more freedom and responsibility as the child grows. The father has not changed, but what he gives has. Believers under the old covenant heard that the King would come. We have seen him come. The biggest difference is the Holy Spirit. Before, the Spirit came upon particular people for particular tasks. Now the risen Christ has poured out the Spirit on all his people, just as Joel had foretold (Acts 2:16–18, 33). And because we have been given more, more is expected of us (Luke 12:48).

Jesus once said that "something greater than the temple is here" (Matthew 12:6). Some have taken this to mean he stood against the God of the temple. But you only call one thing "greater" than another when the two are the same kind of thing. A river is greater than a stream, and a sunrise is brighter than a candle. You would never compare a candle and a stone that way. Jesus was saying that what the temple pointed to, God dwelling with his people, had now arrived in fullness in himself. Elsewhere he compared a teacher of the kingdom to a homeowner who brings out treasures both new and old from the same storeroom (Matthew 13:52). It is one house and one owner, with both kinds of treasure.

This also fits what Christians believe about the Trinity. The Son and the Spirit were not absent in the Old Testament, waiting to be introduced later.
