Jesus said Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56). Paul says the rock that gave Israel water in the wilderness was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Peter says it was "the Spirit of Christ" in the prophets who foretold his sufferings (1 Peter 1:10–11). The one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, was at work throughout the whole story. In the new covenant that same God has shown himself most fully, by the Son taking on our flesh and the Spirit being poured out.

A common misunderstanding is that the Old Testament God is harsh and the New Testament God is gentle. But the Old Testament is full of mercy. When God revealed his name to Moses, he described himself as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion (Exodus 34:6). The New Testament is also full of warnings. Jesus spoke more about judgment than almost anyone in Scripture, and he said that towns which rejected him would fare worse than Sodom (Matthew 11:23–24). The same Christ is life to those who believe and judgment to those who refuse him (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). Mercy and justice run through both Testaments because both belong to one God.

It is true that some things have changed. The sacrifices, the food laws, and the temple worship have passed away now that Christ has come, as Hebrews explains at length. But they pass away the way scaffolding comes down once the building is finished. The builder has not changed. The work is complete.

So when you read the Old Testament, you are not reading about some other God whom Jesus came to replace. You are reading the earlier chapters of your own family story. The God who called Abraham, rescued Israel, and spoke through the prophets is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the one who has now kept every promise in his Son.

topics.title: Does Matthew 11:27 mean the Father was an unknown God, different from the Creator?
topics.cmp: Answers the Gnostic and Marcionite reading of 'No man knoweth the Father, but the Son' as revealing a previously unknown God. It replies that the Father was known before the incarnation through the same Word.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: they explain it as if the true God were known to none prior to our Lord’s advent; and that God who was announced by the prophets, they allege not to be the Father of Christ.

ans.text:
No. When Jesus says that no one knows the Father except the Son, He is not unveiling a brand-new God whom the Old Testament never knew. He is saying that He Himself is the one through whom the Father has always been made known, to Abraham, to Moses, to the prophets, and now fully in His own coming.

Some early teachers did read the verse the other way. They thought the God of the Old Testament, the one who made the world and gave the law, was a lesser or harsher being, and that Jesus came to announce a higher, kinder God nobody had heard of before. Matthew 11:27 looked to them like proof: if no one knew the Father until the Son, then the God of Israel could not be the Father. The idea still turns up today whenever people set the "Old Testament God" against the God Jesus shows us. But it does not fit the verse or the rest of the Bible.

Start with the verse itself. Jesus says, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him." Notice that He speaks in the present tense: no one knows. He does not say no one ever knew until now. He is describing a lasting truth about who He is. Knowing the Father always comes through the Son. That has been true from the beginning, not only since Bethlehem. Likewise, "those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him" is not limited to people after His birth. It covers everyone, in every age, to whom the Son has made the Father known.

Look also at the words just before it. Two verses earlier Jesus prays, "I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth" (Matthew 11:25). The Father He is about to say only He truly knows is the Lord of heaven and earth, the Maker of all things. In the same breath, Jesus names His Father as the Creator. There is no room for a second, unknown God.

The Bible also tells us the Son was at work long before He was born of Mary. John 1:3 says that through Him all things were made. He is the Word, God speaking and acting. So whenever God made Himself known to His people in the Old Testament, the Word was already the one making the Father known. That is why Jesus could say, "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day" (John 8:56), and why He told His critics that Moses "wrote about Me" (John 5:46). Abraham and Moses were not worshiping a different God. They knew the true God, through the same Son who later stood before them in the flesh.

Jesus is blunt about this when He argues with the religious leaders. He tells them that the One who honors Him is His Father, the very one they call their God (John 8:54). His complaint was not that they served the wrong God. It was that they claimed to know the God of Abraham but did not recognize His Son when He came. In context, then, Matthew 11:27 is partly a rebuke. The "wise and learned" had the Scriptures, yet missed the one the Scriptures pointed to. Knowing the Father is not a matter of cleverness. It is a gift the Son gives, and He was giving it to humble "little children" while the experts turned away.

So what is new in Jesus' coming? Not a new God, but a fuller and clearer showing of the same God. Hebrews 1:1-2 puts it this way: long ago God spoke to our fathers through the prophets in many ways, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son. Same God, same speaking, now in person. Think of a friend who wrote you letters for years and then finally came to your door. You meet him face to face for the first time, but he is the same friend. You now know him far better, yet the letters were really from him all along.

This is also why the verse matters for the Trinity. Only the Son knows the Father fully, as the Father fully knows the Son. That kind of complete, mutual knowing belongs to God alone. Jesus is not a messenger who learned about God from outside. He shares the Father's own life, and so He alone can open that life to us. John 1:18 says the same: no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father's side, has made Him known.

So when you read Matthew 11:27, hear it as good news, not as a split in God. The Father Jesus reveals is the Creator of heaven and earth, the God who called Abraham and spoke through Moses and the prophets. He has always been known through His Son, and in Jesus we see Him most clearly of all.

topics.title: Are justice and goodness, mercy and judgment, compatible in the one God?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus of Lyons and Edward Henry Bickersteth agree that justice and goodness are not opposed in the one God, and both reject a God of pure benevolence without judgment. Irenaeus argues the point at greater length against the idea of two gods. Goodness and justice coexist without diminishing each other, with goodness taking precedence. Judicial power belongs to the Father's wisdom. The one Creator of wheat and chaff is the same Judge who separates them. Man's rational free will, not God, makes him chaff and justly condemned. Bickersteth frames the matter in Trinitarian and pastoral terms: the true God is named Father, Son and Holy Ghost, whose love includes righteousness. He also adds a point Irenaeus does not raise here, that the present day of grace is limited and pardon will one day close, though Irenaeus likewise says the bountiful God will judge those who abuse His bounty.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: nor does goodness desert Him in the exercise of justice, nor is His wisdom lessened; for He saves those whom He should save, and judges those worthy of judgment.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: you may beautify the name of the Father whom you adore with every trait of benevolence, and tenderness, and grace, but it is not the name of the one living and true God, for that is the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.

ans.text:
Yes. Justice and goodness, mercy and judgment, belong together in the one God, and they never pull against each other. The God who made the world, who forgives sinners, and who will judge the world is one and the same God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Some early teachers split God in two. They said the God of the Old Testament was a stern lawgiver and judge, while the Father revealed by Jesus was purely kind and never angry. Many people still feel something like this today. They picture an angry God in the Old Testament and a gentle one in the New. The Bible does not allow that split.

Look at how God describes Himself to Moses in Exodus 34:6-7. He is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in loving devotion. He forgives iniquity, transgression, and sin. Yet in the same breath He says He will not leave the guilty unpunished. Mercy and justice are named together, by the same God, in the same sentence.

The New Testament speaks the same way. Jesus tells us that our Father in heaven "causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous" (Matthew 5:45). That is pure, undeserved kindness. Yet the same Jesus speaks more about final judgment than anyone else in Scripture. Paul puts it simply: "Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God" (Romans 11:22). He does not mean two gods. He means one God seen from two sides.

Why do these go together? Think of a good judge in a courtroom. If he shrugged at cruelty and let abusers walk free, we would not call him kind. We would call him careless, even wicked. Real goodness cares about what is right. It takes the harm done to victims seriously. A love that does not mind evil is not a deeper love. It is a smaller one. So God's justice is not a stain on His goodness. It is part of what makes His goodness real.

The same is true of correction. Some think it is beneath a loving Father to rebuke or discipline. Scripture says the opposite: "the Lord disciplines the one He loves" (Hebrews 12:6). A wise parent must sometimes test, warn, and correct, and that is part of wisdom, not a lapse from it. God is wise above all, and so He is rightly Lord and Judge over all.

This is true of each person of the Trinity. The Father has entrusted judgment to the Son (John 5:22). The Son, who welcomed sinners and wept over Jerusalem, will also separate the wheat from the chaff (Matthew 3:12). The Holy Spirit, the Comforter, also convicts the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8). There is no soft member of the Trinity and no harsh one. The one God is both loving and just in all that He does.

At the same time, God's goodness comes first. He is patient long before He judges, and He gives good gifts to people who ignore Him. Paul says God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4). God waits, calls, and pleads. Through the prophet Ezekiel He says He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but wants them to turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11).

The clearest place to see mercy and justice meet is the cross. God did not pretend our sin did not matter. He dealt with it fully in His Son, who bore it in our place. In this way, Paul says, God shows Himself "to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). Justice is not set aside so that mercy can win. Justice is satisfied, and mercy flows freely.

This patience is real, but it is not endless. Scripture calls the present "the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2). Jesus warns that a time will come when the master of the house rises and shuts the door, and those outside knock too late (Luke 13:25). God's kindness now is an invitation to come in, not a promise that the door will stay open forever.

Is God to blame, then, when someone is condemned? No. Jesus pictures judgment as separating wheat from chaff. But people are not like grain, which simply is what it grows into. God made human beings in His image, able to think, choose, and answer Him. When someone hardens their heart against God and against what is right, the fault is theirs, not God's. God judges no one unfairly. He gives light, patience, and warning, and He offers Christ freely. Those who are lost are lost because they turned away from the good God who was calling them.

So we do not need to choose between a kind God and a just God. The one true God is both. That is good news. His justice means evil will not have the last word. His mercy means sinners like us can be forgiven. Both meet in Jesus Christ.

topics.title: Do the hard deeds of the Old Testament God prove he is a different God?
topics.cmp: Replies to objections drawn from the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, the taking of the Egyptians' goods, and Paul's language of God blinding unbelievers. It shows these acts belong to the one just and good God.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For one and the same God [that blesses others] inflicts blindness upon those who do not believe, but who set Him at naught; just as the sun, which is a creature of His, [acts with regard] to those who, by reason of any weakness of the eyes cannot behold his light

ans.text:
No. The hard deeds of the Old Testament are not the work of a harsher, lesser god. They are the acts of the same just and good God whom Jesus calls Father, and the New Testament shows him acting the same way.

Some people have read stories like the plagues of Egypt and concluded that the God of Israel must be a different being from the loving God of the Gospel. The idea surfaces in every age, often as a feeling that the 'Old Testament God' is angry and the 'New Testament God' is kind. Jesus never speaks that way. He calls himself the Son of the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 22:32), and the apostles preach that 'the God of our fathers has glorified His servant Jesus' (Acts 3:13). If the Old Testament God were someone else, Jesus would be the son of the wrong God. So we should look closely at the hard passages themselves.

Take the hardening of Pharaoh's heart. Before any plague falls, God tells Moses that he already knows the king of Egypt will not let Israel go unless a mighty hand compels him (Exodus 3:19). God is not taking a man who wanted to obey and forcing him to refuse. He is dealing with a ruler he knows will resist. The story also says, again and again, that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 8:32). God's hardening is a judgment that confirms Pharaoh in the path he chose. God gives him over to the unbelief he insisted on, so that even plain miracles look to him like magic or chance. To 'harden' here means to stop holding back a person's own stubbornness and let it run its course.

Think of the sun. The same sunlight that lets a healthy eye see can dazzle an eye that is diseased or that has stayed in the dark too long. The sun is not two suns, one kind and one cruel. The difference lies in the eye. In the same way, God's truth brings light to those who welcome it and deeper darkness to those who push it away.

The New Testament shows this very pattern, which is why it cannot belong to some other god. Jesus explains that he speaks in parables because 'though seeing, they do not see; though hearing, they do not hear or understand,' and he says this fulfills Isaiah (Matthew 13:13-15). Paul writes that when people refused to acknowledge God, 'He gave them up to a depraved mind' (Romans 1:28). He warns that those who refuse to love the truth will be handed over by God to a powerful delusion (2 Thessalonians 2:10-11). Paul even uses Pharaoh as his example of how the one God works (Romans 9:17-18). The God who gives the Gospel is the God who hardened Pharaoh.

One verse is sometimes raised here: 2 Corinthians 4:4 says the minds of unbelievers have been blinded by 'the god of this age.' Christians have read this two ways. Most today take it to mean Satan, whom Jesus calls 'the prince of this world.' Some earlier readers took it as the one true God acting in judgment, as in the passages above. Neither reading supports a second God. Satan is a created and fallen being, not a rival creator. And if the phrase means God himself, it is the same God who judges in Romans 1.

None of this makes God arbitrary. He does not invent unbelief in people who would otherwise believe. He knows hearts ahead of time, and his judgments fit what people truly are and truly choose. That is justice, not cruelty. The same God shows endless patience: Pharaoh was warned many times before the final blow.

Now consider the Israelites taking goods from the Egyptians as they left (Exodus 12:35-36). Some have called this theft and blamed God for it. But look at what came before. Egypt owed its survival to Joseph, an Israelite, during the great famine. Then Egypt enslaved Joseph's people for generations, worked them brutally to build its cities, and tried to kill their baby boys. No wages were ever paid. The Israelites asked for silver, gold and clothing, and the Egyptians gave them. A few valuables were a small payment for years of unpaid, cruel labor. They left far poorer than justice would have allowed.

This matches God's own law. When an Israelite servant was set free, his master was not to send him away empty-handed but to supply him generously (Deuteronomy 15:13-14). Long before, God had promised Abraham that his descendants would come out of their bondage 'with many possessions' (Genesis 15:14). The God who did this is the God who cares for the oppressed worker, the same concern James voices when he condemns withheld wages (James 5:4).

There is a picture of the Gospel here too. Christians are rescued out of the world as Israel was rescued out of Egypt. Like Israel, we carry with us things we gained in the world, such as our homes, our work and our skills, and we put them to God's service. The Exodus is our story in shadow form, told by the same God.

So the hard passages do not reveal two Gods. They show one God who is both good and just: merciful to those who turn to him, and willing to give the stubborn over to the darkness they love. The cross itself holds both together. There God's love for sinners and his judgment on sin meet, and it is the one God of Israel who does it.

topics.title: Where does evil come from: God, or the devil as a rival power?
topics.cmp: Gregory of Nyssa, Irenaeus, Novatian and Augustine agree that God is not the author of evil and that the devil is no rival First Principle. They ground this differently. Gregory argues philosophically against Manes that neither God as fashioner of evil nor any second principle can be conceived. Novatian locates evil in man's willed departure from the good God, defines evil itself as departure from God, and denies that the forbidden fruit was evil; he says the command was given to restrain liberty from contempt of the Giver. Irenaeus works mainly from Scripture and moral judgment: the devil is an envious apostate creature who sowed the tares and created nothing, so his 'children' are such by imitation, not nature. Irenaeus also cites the actual pattern of who believed in Christ, with Paul, against claims of naturally superior souls. Augustine stresses a different side, that even the devil and evil angels live only by God's quickening power and remain under His power and goodness.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: it is impossible even to conceive of God as the fashioner of evil, or on the other hand, of any other First Principle besides Him

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: that God who reveals what is hidden [in the heart], but who worketh not evil

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: Moreover, He is Good, Always the Same, Immutable, One…
refs.quote: evil does not occur to man from any other cause than by his departure from the good God. Moreover, this very thing is specified in man, not because it was necessary, but because he himself so willed it.

ans.text:
Evil does not come from God, and it does not come from a second creator who rivals Him. It comes from good creatures, first angels and then human beings, who freely turned away from the good God who made them. To see why, it helps to ask what evil actually is.

The Bible opens with one Maker of everything. "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). When He had finished, "God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). The New Testament adds that this one Creator is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit working together. Of the Son, John says, "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). Paul says the same: in Christ all things were created, "things visible and invisible", including thrones, powers and rulers in the unseen world (Colossians 1:16). That leaves no room for a second creator. There is no corner of reality that the devil built for himself.

So where did the devil come from? He is a creature, an angel God made good, who rebelled. He made nothing. He can only spoil what God has made, the way rust can eat a car but can never build one. When the Bible calls some people "children of the devil" (1 John 3:10) or says, as Jesus does in John 8:44, that they belong to their father the devil, it does not mean the devil manufactured them. It means they have chosen to copy him and do his works. Nobody is evil by nature from the factory. Every person, and every angel, came from God's hand as something good.

This points to what evil is. Evil is not a substance or a thing alongside the good things God made. It is a twisting, a lack, a turning away. Sickness is not a second kind of body; it is a good body going wrong. In the same way, sin is good creatures with good gifts, such as will, desire and strength, aiming them away from God. That is why evil cannot have its own creator. There is nothing positive there to create, only good that has been bent.

Genesis 3 shows this clearly. The forbidden fruit was not poisonous or evil in itself. God's command was a loving boundary that kept freedom from turning into contempt for the Giver. The evil came when Adam and Eve, urged on by the serpent, chose to distrust God and disobey Him. The fault lay in the choice, not in the tree and not in God.

Jesus tells a parable about this. A farmer sows good seed, but weeds appear among the wheat. When the servants ask where they came from, he answers, "An enemy has done this" (Matthew 13:28). Jesus explains that the enemy is the devil (Matthew 13:39). Notice two things. The weeds are not the farmer's doing. And the enemy did not create the field, the soil or the seed. He crept into someone else's good work to spoil it. The farmer stays in charge throughout and decides when the harvest will come.

That is the other half of the answer. The devil is not God's equal opposite, like a dark god facing a light one. He is a rebel creature who still exists only because God keeps every creature in being, and he can go no further than God allows. In Job 1 and 2 Satan has to ask permission and is given limits. When we fall under the devil's sway we are still under God's hand, and God has already promised to defeat him. Right after the fall, God said that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15). Jesus, born of a woman, does exactly that. "The Son of God appeared for this purpose: to destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8).

Does God, then, cause evil in any way? No. James is direct: God cannot be tempted by evil, and He tempts no one (James 1:13). Some verses say God sends disaster or judgment, as in Isaiah 45:7. These speak of God's just punishment of sin and His rule over hard events, not of God making anyone wicked. A judge who sentences a criminal is not the author of the crime. God can also take what others intend for evil and turn it to good, as Joseph told his brothers in Genesis 50:20, and as God did supremely at the cross. Overruling evil is the opposite of authoring it.

Some have suggested something subtler: that because God is so great and so far above us, His greatness itself leaves lesser beings in a darkness and ignorance that leads to sin. The answer is that being smaller than God is not a fault. A child who cannot yet understand everything her father knows is not guilty of anything. Being a limited creature is part of the goodness of creation. Sin is not being less than God; it is refusing to trust and obey Him. If God's greatness were the cause of our evil, God would be the source of all evil. That is exactly what Scripture denies. God's greatness is where our help comes from, not our ruin.

One further point. God's way of dealing with evil does not follow human rank or status, as though some souls were born better. In the Gospels the powerful religious leaders and rulers mostly rejected Jesus, while beggars, the blind and the despised believed. Paul notes that God chose the lowly things of the world to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:27-28). Salvation is grace given to sinners, not a reward for a higher kind of nature.

So the Christian answer has two sides that belong together. There is one good God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who made everything and made it good, and who is in no way the author of evil. And evil is real, but it is a parasite: the free rebellion of creatures who were made good, first the devil and then ourselves. That is why the gospel does not tell us to escape the physical world as though a bad god made it. It tells us the good Creator has come in His Son to reclaim His own world, to judge evil, and to set it right.

topics.title: Is the Valentinian and Gnostic system of Aeons and emanations true?
topics.cmp: Nearly every answer here comes from Irenaeus of Lyons, who uniformly rejects the Valentinian and Gnostic Pleroma, its Aeons and emanations, and every attempt to prove it from scriptural or natural numbers. His grounds vary from question to question. He uses reductio and arguments from internal inconsistency: Logos and Sige cannot coexist, the Triacontad fails by excess or defect, and the healings or the apostles break the numerical pattern. He uses philosophical reasoning about God's simplicity, saying emission would make God compound and corporeal and that the unbegotten Father cannot be counted with produced Aeons. He exposes borrowings from pagan poets such as Antiphanes, Hesiod and Pindar. He appeals to Scripture read under the baptismal rule of truth, citing the vineyard parable, 'Seek and ye shall find', the three passovers in John, and Peter at Pentecost, together with the testimony of the elders who received it from John. Throughout, he contrasts the Gnostics' mutual discord with the Church's single, unchanging faith in one God the Creator, one Christ, and the Spirit. The only other author, Novatian, answers one related question, and does so independently of Irenaeus. He argues that a Christ who hated the body could not consistently take even its likeness. This shares Irenaeus's method of exposing inner contradiction, but it is directed against docetic Christology rather than the Aeon system itself.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: Our Lord, therefore, being the truth, did not speak lies; and whom He knew to have taken origin from a defect, He never would have acknowledged as God, even the God of all, the Supreme King, too, and His own Father

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as…
refs.quote: For thou oughtest to have hated the imitation of a body, if thou hatedst the reality; because, if thou art something else, thou oughtest to have come as something else

ans.text:
No, the old teaching about Aeons and emanations is not true. It is a made-up mythology, and it contradicts the plain message of the Bible about who God is, how the world came to be, and who Jesus Christ is.

It helps to know what these teachers claimed. They said that far above us was an unknowable highest God, surrounded by a 'Fullness' (in Greek, the Pleroma) of thirty spiritual beings called Aeons. The Aeons flowed out from him in pairs, one generation after another, like ripples spreading from a stone dropped in a pond. That outflowing is what 'emanation' means. The youngest Aeon, Wisdom, longed to grasp the Father, fell into passion and confusion, and gave birth to a flawed offspring. From her grief, fear and tears came the stuff of the physical world. A lesser, ignorant god then shaped that stuff into our universe. Christ and the Holy Spirit were produced later to repair the damage. Salvation meant secret knowledge that let a few 'spiritual' people escape back to the Fullness.

The Bible tells a completely different story, and it begins on its first page: 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth' (Genesis 1:1). There is one God, and he is the Maker of everything. Paul puts it simply: 'for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist' (1 Corinthians 8:6). There is no ladder of half-gods between God and the world, and no second, clumsy creator. The world exists because God freely willed it, not because a spiritual being had a breakdown. That is why God could look at all he had made and call it 'very good' (Genesis 1:31). Matter is not a mistake to escape from. It is God's good gift, and he will one day renew it.

This system also gets God himself wrong. It counts the Father as one more member in a set of thirty, as if he were the top rung of a ladder. But the true God is not one item in a list of beings. He is unmade and without beginning. Everything else is made by him and depends on him. You cannot put the potter in the same row as his pots.

It gets the Son and the Spirit wrong too. In this myth, Christ and the Spirit show up late, as a patch for a problem lower beings caused. Scripture says the opposite. 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1), and 'through Him all things were made' (John 1:3). The Spirit was there at creation, hovering over the waters (Genesis 1:2). The Son and the Spirit are not afterthoughts or repairmen. They share the one being of God and act with the Father in all he does. They are like God's own two hands, through whom he made us and through whom he saves us. Notice also that the Bible uses the very word these teachers loved, 'fullness,' but puts it in Christ: God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in him (Colossians 1:19). The fullness of God is not a crowd of Aeons somewhere far off. It came near to us in Jesus.

These teachers claimed the Bible supported them, but they read their ideas into it. They counted numbers and letters and turned them into secret codes. The thirty years before Jesus' baptism stood for thirty Aeons. The twelve apostles, or the woman healed after twelve years of bleeding, pointed to the twelfth Aeon who suffered. Judas, the apostle who fell away, was a picture of fallen Wisdom. The problem is that numbers can be bent to prove almost anything, and these readings don't even fit their own scheme. The woman suffered for twelve years and was healed, while their Aeon was the one who suffered. Judas was twelfth among the apostles, but their fallen Aeon was supposed to be thirtieth. The right order is to learn the truth from Scripture's plain teaching and then notice how details fit it, not to start with numbers and build a theology from them.

They also claimed that Jesus preached for only one year, because Isaiah speaks of 'the year of the Lord's favor' (Luke 4:19). That fit their scheme of twelve Aeons, one for each month. But John's Gospel mentions several Passovers during Jesus' ministry (John 2:13, 6:4, 11:55), so it lasted about three years. In any case, the 'year of the Lord's favor' is a prophetic picture. It describes the whole time of grace, from Christ's coming until the final judgment, the time in which we still live and hear the gospel.

Nor did the prophets speak partly for a higher god and partly for a lower one. Hebrews 1:1-2 tells us it was God who spoke through the prophets and who has now spoken by his Son. Jesus makes the same point in his parable of the vineyard (Mark 12:1-6). The same owner sends servant after servant and finally his beloved son. One God stands behind the whole Bible, Old Testament and New.

Finally, much of this system turns out to be old pagan storytelling with new names. Their Saviour, for example, was assembled from the best gifts of all the Aeons, much like a figure in Greek myth fashioned from gifts of all the gods. Paul warned against exactly this kind of thing: 'myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God's work, which is by faith' (1 Timothy 1:4).

The danger is real even today. Wherever people say the body and the physical world are evil, or that the God of the Old Testament differs from the Father of Jesus, or that salvation comes by secret knowledge for an elite, they are reviving these ideas. Against all of it, the Christian faith confesses something simpler and far better. There is one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth. There is his eternal Son, Jesus Christ, who truly became flesh. And there is the Holy Spirit, who gives life. This God made a good world and loves it enough to redeem it. And he has made himself known openly, to ordinary people, through his Word.

topics.title: Can Gnostic speculation on numbers, letters and names prove truths about God?
topics.cmp: Critiques Gnostic numerology, Marcus's derivations from letter values, and the selective rearranging of scriptural names and numbers. It also asks whether the supreme power can coherently be composed of letters.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: subdividing the Father, who cannot be contained, but contains all things, into a Tetrad, and an Ogdoad, and a Decad, and a Duodecad

ans.text:
No. Juggling the numbers, letters and names found in the Bible cannot prove anything about God, and when people try, they nearly always end up proving whatever they already wanted to believe.

In the early centuries some teachers built elaborate pictures of the heavenly world. They imagined God unfolding into groups of spiritual beings: a set of four, a set of eight, a set of ten, a set of twelve. To back this up they combed the Bible for those numbers. Jesus chose twelve apostles, so there must be twelve heavenly beings. Something happened in the thirtieth year, so there must be thirty. One teacher went further. He added up the values of Greek letters, since in Greek each letter also served as a number. He noted that the name Jesus adds up to 888, and claimed this revealed where Christ came from and what he was. Similar ideas are still around today in "Bible codes" and in number systems that promise hidden messages.

The first problem is simple. The Bible is a large book, and every number turns up in it many times. Take the number five. There are five loaves that fed the crowd, five wise and five foolish young women in Jesus' parable, and five books of Moses, and we have five senses besides. With a little effort you could gather hundreds of fives. Does that mean there are five secret divine beings? Of course not. But that is exactly the kind of reasoning the number systems use. If any number can be "found" everywhere, finding it proves nothing. You are only seeing your own pattern reflected back.

The second problem is how the pieces get chosen. Imagine cutting single words out of a family letter and pasting them into a new message. Every word is genuinely from the letter, yet the message says something the writer never meant. That is what happens when names and phrases are lifted from different parts of Scripture and rearranged into a system. A reader who knows the Bible will recognise the words but notice that each has been pulled out of its place. Put each word back where it belongs, in its own sentence and story, and the invented system falls apart. Paul warns Timothy about people who "devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation" instead of building up faith (1 Timothy 1:4).

The third problem concerns letters themselves. Alphabets are human inventions. People developed them at particular times and places, and they added and dropped letters over the centuries. God is eternal. He was there before any alphabet and before the world itself. As John 1:1 says, "In the beginning was the Word." If God's truth were made out of Greek letters, then truth would be younger than the people who invented the Greek alphabet. That is plainly absurd. Letters and numbers are tools God lets us use to speak about him. They are not the stuff he is made of.

The deepest problem is what these systems do to God himself. Scripture presents God as the one who holds all things, not one who is held or measured by them. Isaiah pictures him measuring the waters in the hollow of his hand (Isaiah 40:12). Paul says he "does not live in temples made by human hands" and is not in need of anything (Acts 17:24-25). God is not built out of parts. You cannot split him into a group of four plus a group of eight, or assemble him from vowels and consonants. The teachers who tried this even contradicted themselves. They called the highest power spiritual, undivided and beyond matter, then described it as made of many letters sorted into different kinds. Something made of pieces is not undivided.

This matters for how Christians understand the Trinity. When the church confesses one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, it is not saying God is a set of three parts or a number puzzle. The three are not fractions of God that add up to a whole. Each is fully God, and God remains one. We believe this because God has shown himself this way in Scripture: in the sending of the Son, the coming of the Spirit, and Jesus' command to baptise "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). We did not work it out from the shape of a number.

We should be fair here. The Bible does sometimes use numbers with meaning. Seven often suggests completeness, and twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Revelation even invites the reader to think about a number (Revelation 13:18). The difference is that these meanings come from the passage itself and its own setting, and they serve the plain message of the text. Noticing what an author is clearly doing is a very different thing from adding up letters to unlock secrets the author never mentions.

Jesus tells us that even the hairs of our head are all numbered (Matthew 10:30). The point is God's tender care for us. It is not an invitation to work out why the number is what it is and build a theology on it. Trying to uncover hidden causes behind every count in creation is wasted effort. Worse, it quietly puts our cleverness above God, as if we could get behind him and solve him. Paul's warning fits: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Corinthians 8:1).

So where should we look instead? Moses puts it simply: "The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever" (Deuteronomy 29:29). God has not hidden himself in codes for a clever few to crack. He has spoken openly, in the plain words of Scripture and above all in his Son. The path to knowing God is to read the Bible as it was written and believe what it says. That is open to every believer, not just the ones who are good with numbers.

topics.title: Did the apostles hand down the full and open knowledge of God, or secret traditions?
topics.cmp: Almost all the answers here come from Irenaeus of Lyons, who consistently holds that the apostles received perfect knowledge through the Spirit and handed it down openly to all, with no secret teaching held back and no accommodation to their hearers' errors. He supports this on several grounds: Scripture (Paul's speech at Miletus, Luke's eyewitness sources), the martyrdom of apostles like Stephen as proof they did not merely echo prevailing opinion, the analogy of the physician who prescribes what the cure requires, and above all the public succession of bishops, especially at Rome, as a visible guarantee of one unchanging faith. His repeated argument is that if hidden mysteries existed, the apostles would have given them to the bishops they appointed, yet those bishops knew nothing of the Gnostic doctrines; he also contrasts the Church's unity with the disagreements among heretical teachers. Hilary of Poitiers addresses a narrower question, the source of heresy in interpreting Scripture. He locates it in a distorted mind that bends the text to its own opinion, rather than in any appeal to secret tradition. His answer does not conflict with Irenaeus, but it rests on submitting one's opinion to Scripture itself, whereas Irenaeus leans chiefly on public apostolic tradition and episcopal succession.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: after our Lord rose from the dead, [the apostles] were invested with power from on high when the Holy Spirit came down [upon them], were filled from all [His gifts], and had perfect knowledge

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: these dissensions concerning the faith result from a distorted mind, which twists the words of Scripture into conformity with its opinion, instead of adjusting that opinion to the words of Scripture.

ans.text:
The apostles handed down the full and open truth about God, not a secret teaching for an inner circle. What they knew, they preached in public, wrote down, and gave freely to anyone who would listen.

This question matters because, in the early centuries, some groups claimed that the apostles had two kinds of teaching. There was the ordinary message for simple believers, they said, and then a hidden knowledge passed privately to the spiritually advanced. That hidden knowledge usually said that the God of the Old Testament, the Maker of the world, was a lesser being, and that above him stood a higher, unknown God. Only the initiated, often after paying for it and going through a special rite, could learn this. The Bible gives us good reason to reject all of this.

Start with how Jesus himself taught. When he was questioned at his trial, he said, "I have spoken openly to the world... I said nothing in secret" (John 18:20). He did explain things more fully to his disciples at times, but always so that they would go and proclaim it. He told them that what they heard in private they should shout from the rooftops (Matthew 10:27). A teacher who hides his real message from most of his hearers is not the Jesus of the Gospels.

The apostles followed the same pattern. When Paul said goodbye to the church leaders at Ephesus, he reminded them that he had taught them publicly and from house to house, and then he said, "I did not shrink back from declaring to you the whole will of God" (Acts 20:27). Notice: the whole will of God, not part of it with the rest held back. In the same speech he warned that false teachers would come later and twist things (Acts 20:29-30). He saw the danger coming and armed the church against it by having already given them everything.

Think about it in a plain, human way. If the apostles had secret teachings, who would they have given them to? Surely to the trusted leaders they appointed to care for the churches. Yet Paul tells Timothy to pass on "the things you have heard me say in the presence of many witnesses" to faithful people who can teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). The teaching was given in front of many witnesses, so that anyone could check it. And the churches the apostles founded taught the same faith they had received, with no trace of a hidden higher God.

The same goes for claims that Paul had private mysteries no one else knew. Luke traveled with Paul for years and wrote the book of Acts. Near the end of his life Paul wrote, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:11). Luke tells us he carefully passed on what came from eyewitnesses and servants of the word from the beginning (Luke 1:1-4). If Paul's closest companion learned nothing of a secret system, people who never knew Paul can hardly claim to have it from him.

But doesn't Paul talk about "mysteries"? He does, but he uses the word differently from how we might expect. In the Bible a mystery is something God kept hidden in the past and has now made known. Paul speaks of "the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints" (Colossians 1:26). The mystery is Christ himself, and God's plan to save Jews and Gentiles alike through him. It is a secret that has been told, not one still locked away. Of course God remains greater than our minds can grasp, and there are things he has not revealed (Deuteronomy 29:29). But that is very different from saying a few people possess a hidden gospel the rest of the church lacks.

Some also suggested the apostles did not fully understand, or that they softened their message to suit their hearers, leaving later teachers to discover the deeper truth. Both ideas fall apart. Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would guide his apostles into all truth (John 16:13), and at Pentecost the Spirit came upon them before they went out to preach (Acts 2). And these men did not tell people what they wanted to hear. They were beaten, jailed, and killed for preaching a crucified Jesus as Lord and calling people to turn from idols to the one living God who made heaven and earth (Acts 14:15). People who are only saying what is popular do not die for it. Like a good doctor, they gave the cure that was needed, not the one the patient preferred.

That public message, by the way, is exactly the faith Christians confess about God. There is one God, the Creator of all things, not a lesser maker under some higher hidden deity. This one God has made himself known as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Jesus is the Son of that same Creator, the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3). Nothing in the apostles' teaching sets the God of Israel against the Father of Jesus. They are one and the same.

What about special rites that promise a higher salvation? Some groups offered a ceremony they called "redemption," claiming that ordinary baptism only forgave sins while their rite made a person truly spiritual. Scripture knows of only one redemption: "In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses" (Ephesians 1:7). Baptism into Christ is not a beginner's step to be surpassed later; it unites us to him (Romans 6:3-4). A rite that changes with every teacher who performs it cannot be the one saving work of Christ.

And truth from God is never for sale. Jesus told his disciples, "Freely you have received; freely give" (Matthew 10:8). When a man named Simon tried to buy spiritual power from the apostles, Peter sharply rebuked him for thinking God's gift could be purchased with money (Acts 8:18-20). Any teaching about God that is kept for those who can pay is, by that very fact, unlike the teaching of Christ.

So how can an ordinary Christian know the genuine apostolic faith? The answer is refreshingly simple. It is the faith written openly in Scripture, preached openly in the churches from the beginning, and summed up in the early creeds that Christians everywhere have confessed. It does not depend on a private source or a special insider. It was "once for all entrusted" to God's people as a whole (Jude 3), and it is the same yesterday and today. Christians do differ on some related points. Some give great weight to the unbroken line of church leaders as a living witness to what the apostles taught, reasoning that Jesus promised to be with his church always. Others stress that Scripture alone is the final test, since leaders can err and only the Bible is God's own written word. But both agree that the true faith is public, not secret, and that the written word of the apostles is its sure foundation.

One last word of caution. Most false teaching does not come from reading a different Bible but from reading the same Bible with our own ideas already fixed, bending the words to fit. The faithful way is the opposite: to let Scripture shape our thinking, reading each passage in its plain sense and in light of the whole. Even a child can grasp the heart of the gospel. That is not a weakness of the Christian faith. It is a sign that the truth has nothing to hide.

title: Related Questions beyond the Trinity
desc: Questions on anthropology, sin, ethics, blessedness, providence, creation, resurrection, sacraments and particular texts that are not about the Trinity itself.

topics.title: How does God create the world, and what is creation for?
topics.cmp: The authors largely answer different questions here, so agreement is mostly implicit, but they converge on God as the sole and faithful source of creation's being and continuance. Augustine, arguing from philosophical reasoning and Scripture (1 Cor 3:6, Jacob's rods), insists that only God creates from within through the unchangeable reasons or 'life' in the Word, while parents, farmers, angels, souls and Jacob merely supply external occasions. Novatian likewise stresses God's ongoing presence, describing Him as a Mind that pervades, quickens and binds the elements, and he adds that the visible world is not God's only work but the latest among angels, heavens and underworld powers. On creation's purpose and end, Hilary appeals to unaided reason that God did not make rational beings from nothing only to perish, and Irenaeus, citing Paul and the Psalms, holds that only the 'fashion' of the world passes while its substance endures, with bodily resurrection of the same body and soul once God's predetermined number is complete. Athanasius alone takes up why creation is not eternal, answering that things made from nothing cannot coexist with the eternal God and that God created when it was good for them, while warning that prying into this is presumptuous.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: For, on the only rational theory of creation, its purpose was that things non-existent should come into being, not that things existing should cease to be.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: We are Made Perfect by Acknowledgement of Our Own…
refs.quote: even body, which is not life, would not have been made by Him, except it had been life in Him before it was made. For “that which was made was already life in Him;”

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For neither is the substance nor the essence of the creation annihilated (for faithful and true is He who has established it), but “the fashion of the world passeth away;”

ans.text:
God creates the world freely, out of nothing, by His word. The Father makes all things through the Son and by the Holy Spirit. He keeps everything in being moment by moment, and He made it all to share in His goodness and to bring Him glory. Its final end is not destruction but renewal.

The Bible opens with the plainest statement of all: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). God did not shape some raw material that was already lying around. Before He spoke, there was nothing but God. Hebrews 11:3 says the universe was formed at God's command, so that what we see was not made out of anything visible. That is what "creation out of nothing" means. God did not need anything outside Himself to make the world.

Creation is the work of the whole Trinity. John tells us that the Word, the eternal Son, was with God in the beginning, and "through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3). At the very start, the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters (Genesis 1:2). The Father does not work alone, and the Son and Spirit are not His tools. The one God creates, and each person shares in that one work.

John goes on to say that in the Word was life. One helpful way to think of it is this. Before anything existed, even a stone or a speck of dust, it was already fully known in God's own wisdom, like a design in the mind of an architect before the first brick is laid. That design is not a creature. It belongs to the living, unchanging wisdom of God Himself. Everything that exists comes from that wisdom and reflects it.

God did not just make the world and step back. He goes on holding it together. Hebrews 1:3 says the Son upholds all things by His powerful word, and Paul says that in God "we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:28). Think of a song rather than a clock. A clock, once wound, can run without its maker. A song exists only while the singer keeps singing. The world's order, its laws and seasons and the way one cause leads to another, all depend on God's steady care. The world will hold together until He Himself decides otherwise.

This helps answer a question people sometimes ask: who really makes new living things? Parents have children, farmers grow crops, animals breed. But none of them creates in the full sense. Built into creation from the beginning are hidden "seeds" of things, the inner patterns and powers by which a seed becomes wheat or a calf grows in its mother. God is the maker of those hidden seeds. Human beings and animals supply the outward occasions, and God works from within to bring about new life.

Paul says it well about his ministry: "I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow" (1 Corinthians 3:6). The farmer plows and waters, but he cannot make a single grain sprout. The preacher speaks, but only God changes a heart. What is true in the church is true in the field and the womb as well.

This is also why we should not call creatures "creators," even when they have real power. Your soul really does move and affect your body. Your mood can change your heartbeat, and your will can lift your arm. But your soul did not make your body, and it cannot give your body its shape, its order, or its life. Those come from God.

Scripture gives a curious example in Genesis 30. Jacob set peeled, striped branches in front of the flocks at the watering troughs, and the animals bore streaked and speckled young. Jacob did something outward. Perhaps what the mothers saw even had some effect. But Jacob did not create the colors in the lambs, and neither did the ewes. That sheep give birth to sheep at all, and that body and soul can affect each other at all, comes from the wisdom of God. Jacob himself later admits that it was God who took away Laban's livestock and gave them to him (Genesis 31:9).

Some wonder why God, who was always able to create, did not create from all eternity. Was He idle, or did He change His mind? The answer is that the problem lies not with God but with creatures. Something made out of nothing has a beginning by its very nature. Only God has no beginning. A creature that had always existed alongside God would no longer be a creature in the ordinary sense. God was never lonely or lacking, for Father, Son, and Spirit have shared perfect love forever. He created when He judged it good, in His wisdom and His time, just as He sent His Son "when the fullness of time had come." Beyond that, humility is wise. Paul asks, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" (Romans 11:34). We can trust God's timing without prying into it.

The world we can see is not the whole of God's creation. Paul says that in Christ "all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities" (Colossians 1:16). Angels and other spiritual powers are creatures too. Scripture also speaks of the dead awaiting judgment in a realm we cannot see. Our universe, vast as it is, may be only one part of God's handiwork. That should make us marvel at the greatness of the Maker. It should also keep us from worshiping anything He has made, however impressive, whether stars, spirits, or angels.

Why did God create at all? Not because He needed anything. He is complete in Himself. He created out of overflowing goodness, to give being to things that did not exist and to share His goodness with them. Colossians 1:16 says all things were created "through Him and for Him," that is, for Christ. Heaven's worship gives the reason: "You created all things; by Your will they exist, and came to be" (Revelation 4:11). Creation exists to display God's glory, and its creatures, above all human beings, are meant to enjoy Him.

This tells us something important about ourselves. God made us able to think, to know truth, and to know Him. It would make no sense for Him to give us a share in His wisdom only to let us vanish at death. It would be like a craftsman building something beautiful just to smash it. The point of creating is that things which were not should come to be, not that things which are should be lost. Scripture promises that the dead will be raised in their own bodies. Those who belong to Christ will rise to live with God forever.

What about the end of the world? Jesus says that heaven and earth will pass away, and Peter speaks of fire. Does that mean God will throw creation away and start from scratch? Scripture points the other way. Paul writes that "this world in its present form is passing away" (1 Corinthians 7:31). It is the form that passes, the broken, aging, sin-scarred condition of things, not creation itself. The psalmist says God will change the heavens like a garment (Psalm 102:26). A garment is changed, not the person wearing it.

Paul says creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God (Romans 8:21). The promise at the end of the Bible is not "I make all new things" but "Behold, I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5). God is faithful to what He has made. The story that began with "In the beginning God created" ends with a new heaven and a new earth, where God dwells with His people and nothing will ever decay again.

So the whole of creation, from the first word to the final renewal, comes from God, is held up by God, and returns to God. As Paul puts it, "from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory forever!" (Romans 11:36).

topics.title: How does God's providence govern nature, history and suffering?
topics.cmp: All the authors agree that God actively governs creation and that nothing, whether nature, the devil, or human affairs, lies outside His care. Hilary of Poitiers denies that God could neglect His world, Irenaeus of Lyons holds that creatures can know Him as ruler and Father, Novatian insists that providence reaches every individual thing and that no impersonal Nature drives day and night, and John Owen adds that God deliberately confounds the counsels of the worldly wise for His glory. Augustine of Hippo gives the most developed philosophical account: God's will is the first cause above all proximate bodily and spiritual causes, a hierarchy of spirits is ruled by God, and miracles differ from ordinary works only in their unusualness, not in their author. One of his answers on whether God's will is the first cause of natural phenomena is labelled "No" while the others say "Yes", but its substance affirms the same position. On evil and suffering, Irenaeus and Augustine agree that the devil has no independent power: Irenaeus argues mainly from Scripture that the devil lied about holding the kingdoms, while Augustine uses analogies, such as convicts in the mines and a judge punishing a crime, to show that evil powers act only by God's permission and that death is caused by sin. Irenaeus says suffering teaches humility and love of God, Augustine lists correction, the proving of righteousness and longing for the life to come, and Basil of Caesarea addresses a narrower question, explaining that the Spirit works miracles in the worthy only as need requires, as an art is present in an artist.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: God does, however, exercise a providence over all things, and therefore He also gives counsel; and when giving counsel, He is present with those who attend to moral discipline.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: It could not hold that neglect of a world created by Himself was worthily to be attributed to God

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.quote: when, for the admonition of men, they are thrust in by an unusual changeableness, then they are called miracles.

ans.text:
God's providence means that the God who made the world never lets go of it: he holds every part of it, from the weather to the rise of nations to the hardest days of our lives, and he steers it all toward the good he has planned.

Start with nature. We usually explain rain by clouds and air pressure, and a calf's birth by biology. Those explanations are true as far as they go. But they describe the nearer causes, the 'how' of things. Behind every one of them stands the will of God, the first cause on which all the others depend. Psalm 148 lists lightning and hail, snow and clouds, and then adds that the powerful wind is 'fulfilling His word.' Weather is not chance, and it is not an impersonal force called Nature. In Isaiah 45:7 God says, 'I form the light and create the darkness.' Day and night take turns because he orders them. The New Testament says the same of the Son: he upholds all things by his powerful word (Hebrews 1:3), and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:17). Father, Son and Spirit do not make the world and then leave it running alone like a wound-up clock. A God who made the world and then ignored it would not be the God of the Bible.

This care is not only for the big picture. Jesus says that not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father's will, and that the very hairs of your head are all numbered (Matthew 10:29-30). That only makes sense. The world is made up of small things, so a God who governs the whole must govern each part. Scripture shows this in surprising detail. Israel's clothes and sandals did not wear out in forty years in the desert (Deuteronomy 29:5). The three young men came out of the furnace without even the smell of smoke on them (Daniel 3:27).

What about miracles, then? If God is behind the ordinary course of things, a miracle is not a different God, or a different kind of power, breaking in from outside. It is the same God doing something unusual. Every autumn he turns rain and soil into grapes, and grapes into wine. At Cana he did it in a moment (John 2). Every day he gives life to children in the womb. On rare occasions he gave life back to the dead. When his works come in their regular rhythm we call them natural. When he does them suddenly, or against all expectation, to get our attention and show us something, we call them miracles. This also helps explain why miracles are not constant, even among faithful believers. The Holy Spirit is always present with God's people. But he works signs and healings as God's purposes require, the way a skilled craftsman always has his skill but uses it when the job calls for it. A miracle that happened every day would no longer stand out as a sign. And God's ordinary works are no less his than his rare ones.

Providence also rules history. Proverbs 21:1 says, 'The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases.' When the devil showed Jesus the kingdoms of the world and claimed they had been handed over to him (Luke 4:6), he was lying, as Jesus says he has done from the beginning (John 8:44). The devil is a creature. He has only as much power as God allows, only for as long as God allows, and he is always made to serve purposes he never intended. God also brings the clever plans of proud people to nothing. He 'will destroy the wisdom of the wise' (1 Corinthians 1:19), and the schemes of the powerful often end by defeating themselves (Psalm 2).

The clearest example is the cross. It was the worst crime in history, driven by human hatred and the devil's malice. Yet Peter says Jesus was handed over by God's set plan and foreknowledge, even though lawless people killed him (Acts 2:23). Joseph said something similar to his brothers: what they meant for evil, God meant for good, to save many lives (Genesis 50:20). This does not make God the author of evil. The people who sin are truly guilty, and their intentions are truly wicked. But God is wise enough to take even their evil and make it serve his good purposes, without being stained by it.

The same is true of death and suffering. God did not make the world for death. Death came in through sin (Romans 5:12). It is something like a judge passing sentence: the judge hands down the penalty, but the cause of the penalty is the crime. Yet even in a fallen world, God does not waste his children's pain. In God's hands suffering can do several things. Sometimes it corrects us, the way a loving father disciplines his children (Hebrews 12:5-11). Sometimes it tests and strengthens real faith, as gold is refined in fire (1 Peter 1:6-7). And sometimes it simply shows us how broken this life is, so that we long more deeply for the life to come.

Paul is a good example. He begged three times for his 'thorn in the flesh' to be taken away. God answered, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness' (2 Corinthians 12:9). Weakness taught Paul that he was mortal and God is mighty. It kept him from pride and drew him closer to Christ. So 'no' is sometimes God's kindest answer.

A few gentle cautions. Providence does not mean every hardship is punishment for a particular sin. Jesus rejected that idea about the man born blind (John 9:3). Nor is it fatalism. God works through means, so we still pray, see the doctor, plant crops and make wise choices, and our choices really matter. And Christians have not all explained God's rule in the same way. Some stress that God actively decides all that comes to pass, because Scripture speaks of his plan covering everything. Others stress that he permits much that he does not desire, because Scripture also shows him grieving over sin and pleading with people to turn. Both sides agree on the main thing: nothing slips out of God's hands, and evil never gets the last word.

That is the comfort providence gives. 'We know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose' (Romans 8:28). The storm, the evil plan and the hospital bed are not outside his care. The Father who numbers your hairs is shaping all of it toward the day when his children are made like his Son.

topics.title: What is human nature and the soul?
topics.cmp: The authors mostly take up different questions here, so there is little direct overlap. Irenaeus of Lyons and Augustine of Hippo both reject the transmigration of souls, but on different grounds. Irenaeus argues from the soul's lack of memory of former lives, from God's power to give each body its own proper soul, and from Scripture in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus. Augustine argues that reported memories like those of Pythagoras are false, like dream recollections, perhaps suggested by deceitful spirits, and that if they were genuine nearly everyone would have them. Irenaeus also stresses the soul's simplicity, unity and immortality against Gnostic claims, while Augustine reasons philosophically about the soul as a changeable 'great nature' that can partake of God, about pride as a fall into private and bodily concerns, and about why corporealists err; Gregory of Nyssa adds that moral choice changes a person's relationship-names but not human nature, and John Owen alone treats Adam, from Scripture, as created upright with full and spiritual knowledge and with all his posterity sinning in him.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For the intellect of man—his mind, thought, mental intention, and such like—is nothing else than his soul; but the emotions and operations of the soul itself have no substance apart from the soul.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: while their nature in each case remains the same, the differences of their purpose assume the names of their relationship, according as they become either children of God by virtue, or of the opposite by vice

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: That Adam, being made upright, sinned against God; and all mankind, all his posterity, in him

ans.text:
A human being is one person made of two parts woven together: a body formed from the earth, and a soul given by God. Scripture shows both at once in Genesis 2:7: "the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being." We are not souls trapped in bodies, and we are not just clever bodies. We are embodied souls, made by God and for God.

The soul is the inner you: the part that thinks, chooses, loves, remembers and prays. Your mind is not a separate thing sitting beside your soul. Your thoughts, feelings, intentions and understanding are simply your soul at work, the way running and walking are not extra parts of your legs but what your legs do. So there is no hidden "higher self" that could break away from you and drift off into some spiritual realm on its own. Whatever happens to your soul happens to you.

Some have thought the soul must be a kind of thin, invisible body, because they could not picture anything real that has no size or shape. But being hard to picture is not the same as being unreal. Your love for your children is real, yet it does not take up space or weigh anything. The soul is like that. It is not made of physical parts. Because it is not built out of pieces, it cannot come apart the way a body does at death. Jesus says in Matthew 10:28, "Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." People can harm the body, but they cannot reach in and destroy the soul.

This does not make the soul a little god. Only God has life in himself. The soul lives because God gives and keeps giving it life, and it answers to him (Matthew 10:28 goes on to say that God can destroy both soul and body in hell). Most Christians have held that every soul lives on after death and faces God's judgment. A smaller number of believers read passages like that one to mean that the lost are finally ended rather than kept forever. Both sides agree that the soul's life depends entirely on God.

What happens at death? The body returns to dust and the soul goes on. Ecclesiastes 12:7 says the dust returns to the ground "and the spirit returns to God who gave it." Paul speaks of being "away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8). In Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31), both men are still themselves after death. The rich man recognizes Lazarus and Abraham. He remembers his brothers and his own life. Each is already in a place fitting to how he lived. People do not dissolve into nothingness, and they do not become someone else.

That also answers the old idea of reincarnation, that souls are recycled from one body to the next. The Bible gives no room for it. "Man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment" (Hebrews 9:27). Common sense agrees. If we had all lived before, nearly everyone would remember it, yet almost no one does. The few who claim such memories are more likely mistaken, much as dreams give us vivid "memories" of things that never happened. And God is not short of souls. The same God who gives each person a unique face and fingerprints gives each person a soul of his or her own. You are not a used soul in a new body. You are a new creation of God, known by him from the womb (Psalm 139:13-16).

Christians have agreed that each soul is truly from God, but they have differed on how. Some believe God creates each soul directly when a person comes into being, because the Bible calls him the one who gives the spirit. Others believe the soul is passed on from parents along with the body, by God's ordinary working, because Adam's children are said to be born in his likeness and to share his sin. Either way, no one is an accident, and no one's soul is borrowed.

Why is the soul so precious? Because it was made for God. "God created man in His own image" (Genesis 1:27). The soul is not the highest thing there is, so it can be damaged, darkened and corrupted. But it is a great thing, because it is able to know God, love God and share in his life. Nothing else in the visible world can do that. The image of the Trinity shows itself here as well. God is the God of knowing and loving, and we were made able to know and love him back.

This also explains how the soul falls. Its great danger is pride. God made us to have our part in a world he rules wisely, and our joy is to live gladly under him. Pride wants more than its share. It wants to be its own law and run its own little kingdom. The strange result is that the proud soul does not grow bigger. It shrinks. Cut off from the whole that God governs, it turns in on a small private corner and becomes ruled by the very things it meant to master: possessions, pleasures, appetites, image. By grasping for more, it ends up with less. "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The same pattern appears in the devil, who was created good as one of God's angels. He fell through pride and envy, setting himself against God and against the humans God loved (see 1 Timothy 3:6, which warns about falling into "the condemnation of the devil" through conceit).

Adam did not begin in that fallen condition. "God made men upright" (Ecclesiastes 7:29). When Adam was created, his mind was clear, not clouded. He had everything he needed to know in order to live with God and care for the world. He did not know things that did not yet exist, like history or the many languages of later peoples. But he could see the creatures truly, which is why he could name them (Genesis 2:19-20). His knowledge was never merely practical either. It was given so that he could walk with God. Even his understanding of animals and plants served that purpose, which is why God gave him a command and a warning about life and death. Knowing the world and knowing God belonged together.

When Adam sinned, he did not sin only for himself. He stood at the head of the human race, and we fell with him. "Sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). "Through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners" (Romans 5:19). That is why every human heart is bent toward self, and why we all need a Savior.

Sin did not turn us into a different kind of creature, though. A sinner is still fully human, and a saint is still fully human. When Scripture calls some people "children of wrath" and others "children of God," it describes where their hearts are turned and how they stand with God, not a new species. That is good news. It means a fallen human being can be restored without ceasing to be human. Jesus took our very human nature, body and soul, so that in him the same human nature that fell in Adam is lifted up again: "so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19).

The Christian hope is therefore not that the soul escapes the body forever. It is that God will raise our bodies and reunite them with our souls, healed and made new, so that whole people can live forever with him. The soul is precious, but God's plan is to redeem the whole person he made.

topics.title: Why did God permit the Fall, and what did the first sin bring?
topics.cmp: Augustine, Irenaeus, Novatian, Gregory of Nyssa and Owen all deny that the Fall reflects malice or weakness in God: it was permitted, not commanded (Augustine), and God's dealings with fallen man were merciful. Novatian and Irenaeus both say God barred Adam from the tree of life not out of envy but to spare him an immortality of guilt or endless sin, and both point to the curse falling on the ground or labour rather than on Adam himself. Their reasons for why God permitted the Fall differ, however. Irenaeus gives a pedagogical and providential account: man as a newly made creature could not be perfect at once, he learns obedience by experiencing disobedience, and he was swallowed like Jonah so as to be saved and grateful. Augustine instead stresses God's justice in abandoning the sinner, the devil's false appearance of power, and an allegorical reading of Genesis as consent within one mind, and Owen alone states explicitly that all humans are brought into sin and enmity, arguing from Scripture that in Christ sin is made to serve the glory of pardoning grace. Gregory and Irenaeus agree that Adam died on the very day he ate, but Gregory means a death of the soul through alienation from God, while Irenaeus means becoming death's debtor and adds chronological arguments (the sixth day, the thousand-year day); Irenaeus also argues at length, against Tatian, that Adam himself is saved.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: All, on Account of the Sin of Adam, Were Delivered into…
refs.quote: ought not to be so understood as if God did this, or commanded it to be done; but that He only permitted it, yet that justly. For when He abandoned the sinner, the author of the sin immediately entered.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: so also, from the beginning, did God permit man to be swallowed up by the great whale, who was the author of transgression, not that he should perish altogether when so engulphed

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: For by the fact of his alienation from the true life, the sentence of death was ratified against him that self-same day: and after this, at a much later time, there followed also the bodily death of Adam.

ans.text:
God allowed the Fall not because He was unable to stop it or careless about it, but because He meant to make creatures who could truly love Him, and because He already planned to bring a far greater good out of the ruin through His Son. The first sin brought death, broken fellowship with God, and a damaged human nature passed down to all of us. It did not get the last word.

Start with the question many people ask: why didn't God just make people perfect, or unable to sin? Part of the answer is that something created is, by its nature, new and unfinished. Adam and Eve were good, but they were like children at the start of a life meant to grow into fuller glory with God. Being unfinished is not a flaw in God's power. It is simply what it means to be a creature and not the Creator. God could do anything that makes sense, but a creature made yesterday cannot already have the maturity that only comes with time and growth.

There is a deeper reason too. Think of a husband whose wife is programmed to say "I love you." Those words would mean nothing. Goodness that a creature cannot help having is not really its own. God wanted children who would know His goodness, delight in it, and choose it freely. That kind of love requires real freedom, and real freedom means the real possibility of saying no.

This does not make God the author of sin. James 1:13 says God tempts no one. God permitted the Fall. He did not push Adam into it. When people turned from Him, they put themselves under the influence of the tempter. Even then, God did not let go of them. He kept giving them life, breath, food and family, and He never stopped being their Lord.
