Scripture also shows that God was not caught off guard. Christ was chosen as Redeemer "before the foundation of the world" (1 Peter 1:20). Paul calls Adam "a pattern of the One to come" (Romans 5:14). From the beginning, God's plan for humanity was tied to His Son. He allowed people to be swallowed up by sin, a bit like Jonah swallowed by the fish, not so they would be lost, but so they would be rescued in a way no one could have hoped for. Rescued people know the bitterness of disobedience and the sweetness of grace, and they cling to God with a gratitude they could not otherwise have had.

What about the Genesis story itself? God told Adam that "in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die" (Genesis 2:17). Some wonder why Adam lived for centuries afterward. The answer is that death began that very day. Real life is fellowship with God, and the moment Adam turned away, he was cut off from that life. He hid from God, felt shame, and blamed others. His body's death came later, but the sentence took hold at once.

Notice how God handled the guilty. He questioned Adam and Eve, giving them room to own up, but He did not question the serpent. He cursed the serpent outright. He did not curse Adam himself. Instead He said, "Cursed is the ground because of you" (Genesis 3:17). Adam would face hard work, pain and finally death, but not destruction. In the middle of the judgment came the first promise of the gospel: the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15). Then God clothed them with garments of skin (Genesis 3:21), a quiet sign of His care.

God also sent them out of the garden so they would not eat from the tree of life and "live forever" (Genesis 3:22). This was not jealousy, as if God begrudged them immortality. It was mercy. To live forever in a fallen, sinful state would be endless misery, with no way out. Bodily death puts a limit on sin, so that through Christ a person can die to sin and be raised to a new life that sin cannot touch.

The effects reach all of us. Paul writes that "sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned" (Romans 5:12). Because of Adam, every person is born turned away from God, with a heart that leans toward self rather than toward Him. Christians agree on this much. They have differed on exactly how it works. Some hold that Adam acted as the head of the human race, so his guilt is counted to all his descendants. Others stress that what we inherit is a wounded, corrupted nature and the reality of death, and that we become guilty when we sin ourselves. Both sides take Romans 5 seriously. Both agree that we cannot fix ourselves and that only Christ can rescue us.

It also helps to know that hell was not God's original intention for human beings. Jesus speaks of "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matthew 25:41). People come under it only if they, like the devil, refuse to turn back.

Was Adam himself saved? Scripture does not say so in plain words, but there are strong reasons for hope. God dealt with Adam with mercy, gave him the promise of a coming Deliverer, and clothed him. Adam showed fear and shame rather than defiance. Christ came to undo what began with Adam, and "as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22). It would be strange if the first man the enemy captured were the one prisoner the Victor left behind. Through most of Christian history, believers have held that Adam is the lost sheep the Shepherd went out to find.

Finally, does sin serve any purpose? In itself, no. Sin only dishonors God and ruins people. But God is able to take what was meant for evil and turn it to good. Paul says, "where sin increased, grace increased all the more" (Romans 5:20). Without the Fall, we would never have known God as the One who forgives, who gives His own Son, and who loves enemies into children. That does not make sin good. It makes God's grace astonishing.

topics.title: What can fallen humanity do, and how does grace work?
topics.cmp: Augustine and John Owen both stress fallen humanity's helplessness: Augustine reads "by nature children of wrath" as nature depraved by sin, not as created, holds that release from the devil comes only through God's merciful remission of sins, and reads the "spontaneous rain" of Psalm 68 as grace given freely rather than for merit. Owen goes further in describing incapacity, denying that fallen people have any natural communion with God or any power to stop sinning or return to him. He argues from Scripture ("none righteous") and from the contrast between God as light, life and love and sinners as darkness, dead and at enmity. Owen also holds that neither nature nor the law can teach people their own impotence; that knowledge comes only in Christ. Irenaeus of Lyons puts the weight elsewhere: he insists that faith lies within a person's own power and that God compels no one, because humans were created free. He grounds this in the Lord's sayings ("according to thy faith," "ye would not") and the image of light, and he places the blame for unbelief and imperfection on human refusal rather than on any defect in God's calling. This is a real difference in emphasis and conclusion: Augustine and Owen emphasize what sin has disabled and what grace freely supplies, while Irenaeus emphasizes preserved free choice and human responsibility, and none of the answers given reconciles the two.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: All, on Account of the Sin of Adam, Were Delivered into…
refs.quote: viz. by nature as it has been depraved by sin, not as it was created upright from the beginning

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: Now all such expressions demonstrate that man is in his own power with respect to faith.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: He is life, we are dead, — he is love, and we are enmity; and what agreement can there be between us?

ans.text:
Left to ourselves, fallen people cannot turn to God or make themselves right with him. But that is not because God made human nature evil, and it is not because God forces anyone. Grace is God's free, undeserved kindness. It reaches us when we could not reach him, and it brings us to him without crushing who we are.

Start with how we were made. When God finished creation, "God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). That includes human beings, made in his image. So when Paul says in Ephesians 2:3 that "we were by nature children of wrath," he does not mean that being human is itself evil. He means human nature as it now is, bent and damaged by sin since Adam. It is a bit like a fine instrument that has been dropped and warped. The instrument is still good workmanship, but it no longer plays true. Sin is not part of what God designed us to be. It is a wound and a corruption that has come into it.

That wound goes deep. A few verses earlier Paul says, "you were dead in your trespasses and sins" (Ephesians 2:1). In Romans 3:10-11 he gathers the Old Testament's verdict: "There is no one righteous, not even one. There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God." Sin does more than give us a bad record. It turns our desires away from God, so that we do not truly want him for his own sake. God is light and life and love. Sinners are in darkness, spiritually dead, and at odds with him. We still make real choices every day, and we can do many decent things. But on our own we cannot break free from sin, stop loving it, or make our way back into friendship with God. Jesus puts it plainly: "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him" (John 6:44).

We do not even see this clearly by ourselves. Pride tells us we can do better if we try harder. God's law shows us what is right and exposes where we have gone wrong. But the law cannot give us the power to obey. Paul says, "what the law was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh, God did by sending His own Son" (Romans 8:3). It is in Christ that we finally learn both how helpless we are and how complete God's rescue is.

That rescue is grace. Grace is not a reward for people who have earned it, or for those who showed promise. "It is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). God shows his love in that "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). He gives grace not because we are worthy but because he is good and chooses to be generous. Sin had put us under guilt and under the power of evil. God sets us free by forgiving our sins and reconciling us to himself through Christ's death. He did not simply overpower the devil by force. He dealt with our guilt justly and mercifully at the cross.

Knowing this is humbling, and that is healthy. It stops us from trusting ourselves. The Lord told Paul, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). The people who receive grace are the ones who stop pretending to be strong.

Does grace then force people against their will? Christians agree that it does not. God does not treat people like puppets or drag them in kicking and screaming. Grace works on the will from the inside. It frees it, renews it, and makes it willing. God promises, "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you" (Ezekiel 36:26). Paul tells believers to work out their salvation, "For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose" (Philippians 2:12-13). Both are true at once. We really believe, choose, and obey. God is the one who makes that possible. Think of a sick person nursed back to health. When they finally get up and walk, it is truly they who walk, but they walk only because they were healed.

It also means that when people reject God, the fault is theirs, not his. Jesus wept over Jerusalem: "how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!" (Matthew 23:37). In his parable of the wedding feast, the invited guests who refused shut themselves out (Matthew 22:1-14). The sun does not fail because someone closes their eyes. God's call is sincere, and those who turn away are responsible for turning away.

Sincere Christians do differ on one point here. Some hold that when God sets out to save someone, his grace will surely succeed. In their view, God's work in the heart is what decides the matter, and they point to passages like John 6:44 and Ephesians 2. Others hold that God gives grace that truly enables everyone it reaches to respond, but that a person can still resist it. They point to Jesus' tears over those who "were unwilling" and to the many invitations to believe. Yet both sides agree on the essentials. Human nature was created good but is now fallen. No one can save themselves or earn grace. Salvation is God's free gift in Christ. God does not coerce anyone. And those who refuse him are to blame for their refusal.

So the honest answer to "What can we do?" is that, on our own, we cannot do what we most need. But that is exactly where the good news begins. God does for us what we could not do, and then gives us a new heart that gladly answers him.

topics.title: How is a sinner justified, and what is saving faith?
topics.cmp: The authors mostly answer different questions rather than the same ones, so their positions sit side by side rather than in direct agreement or conflict. John Owen deals with the mechanics of justification. He reads Zechariah 3 and Isaiah 61:10 as showing both the removal of guilt by Christ's death and the gift of righteousness by Christ's obedience. He distinguishes reconciliation (non-imputation of sin) from justification (imputation of righteousness) as conjoined but not identical. He excludes even believers' post-conversion works from justification on the basis of Ephesians 2:8-10, while holding that those works are made acceptable through Christ's priestly cleansing and that eternal life is a reward only by God's constitution. Augustine of Hippo addresses something different when he says no one is perfectly justified in this life, since justification is completed only at the end, measured against the righteousness of the angels; Owen's answers here do not speak to whether justification is complete in this life. Augustine's other answers analyze faith psychologically and philosophically rather than forensically. He distinguishes the faith by which one believes from what is believed, holds that faith is seen inwardly by its possessor but only inferred in others, and calls believers' faith one in kind, not in number, using analogies of a shared countenance and will. Irenaeus of Lyons alone takes up continuity across the covenants, arguing from Paul that Abraham's faith in God's promise of future things is the same faith Christians have.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: there is more also required, even a collation of righteousness, and thereby a right to life eternal. This is here called “Change of raiment;”

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The One Death and Resurrection of The Body of Christ…
refs.quote: in His sight shall no man living be justified,[^455] in comparison of the righteousness in which we shall be made equal with the angels

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: because his faith and ours are one and the same: for he believed in things future, as if they were already accomplished, because of the promise of God

ans.text:
A sinner is justified, that is, declared right with God, not by anything he does but by God's free grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and lived the obedient life we could not. Saving faith is the trust by which we take hold of Christ and rest on Him. It is not a good work that earns anything. It is more like an empty hand that receives a gift.

Start with the problem. Paul says that "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). We owe God a perfect love and obedience, and none of us has given it. If we are to stand before Him, two things must happen. Our guilt must be taken away, and we must be given a righteousness we do not have. The very next verse gives the answer: we "are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (Romans 3:24).

The Old Testament gives a vivid picture of this. In Zechariah 3, Joshua the high priest stands before the Lord in filthy clothes. God orders the dirty garments removed, says He has taken away his iniquity, and has him dressed in clean, fine robes. Both halves matter. Taking off the filth is forgiveness, the removal of guilt, which Christ won by His death. Putting on the new clothes is being counted righteous, which comes from Christ's whole life of obedience. Isaiah 61:10 speaks the same way of God clothing His people with "garments of salvation" and a "robe of righteousness." Paul puts it in one sentence: God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us, "so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Scripture uses related words for this. "Reconciliation" stresses that our sins are no longer counted against us, so that enemies become friends (2 Corinthians 5:19). "Justification" stresses that righteousness is counted to us. These are not quite the same idea, but they never come apart. Everyone who is forgiven is also accepted, and everyone accepted is forgiven.

How does this become ours? Through faith. "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (Romans 4:3). Faith does not earn the credit. It receives what God gives. That is why Paul can say, "it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9).

What about good works? The very next verse says we are "created in Christ Jesus to do good works" (Ephesians 2:10). So good works are not optional. God delights in them, and a living faith always produces them. Paul speaks of "faith, expressed through love" (Galatians 5:6), and James warns that faith with no works is dead (James 2:17). But notice what Ephesians 2 does. It shuts out works as the ground of our acceptance, and it does this even for the good works believers do after they come to Christ. Works done as a Christian earn our standing with God no more than works done before. Christ alone is our righteousness. To add our own record next to His, as if He were not enough, would quietly insult Him.

In fact, even our best deeds need Christ. Our prayers and acts of love are mixed with pride, distraction and weak faith. Like a high priest, Christ bears the guilt of what is faulty in them, washes them, and presents them to the Father, so that what is truly from the Spirit is received with pleasure. This is why a struggling believer can still serve God with joy rather than fear.

The Bible also speaks of reward. Hebrews 11:6 says God "rewards those who earnestly seek Him," and Jesus often speaks of treasure in heaven. Is eternal life then a gift or a wage? At its root it is a gift: "the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). Yet God has also chosen the path of faithful obedience as the way His people walk into that life. So He is pleased to call it a reward, the way a father might "reward" his child with an inheritance that was always freely his. The reward is real, but it rests on grace, not on merit.

Sincere Christians have differed on some of this. Many hold that justification is God's verdict, declaring us righteous because Christ's righteousness is counted to us, while our inner renewal is a separate, lifelong work that always follows. Others hold that justification also includes God actually making us righteous within, so that the good works grace produces in us have a real part in our final standing. The first group stresses that Scripture speaks of righteousness being "credited," like a legal ruling. The second stresses passages such as James 2 and the many promises tied to perseverance. Both agree that salvation begins and ends in God's grace, that no one can earn it, and that true faith bears fruit.

Are we perfectly righteous now? Before God's court, the believer is fully accepted in Christ; there is no half-forgiveness. But in our actual lives we are not yet what we will be. We still sin and still face temptation. Our full transformation waits for the day when, as John says, "we will see Him as He is" and be made like Him (1 John 3:2).

Now to faith itself. It helps to separate two things: what we believe and the believing. The content of the faith, that Christ died, rose, and will come again, is the same for every Christian, and it comes to us from outside, through the message we hear. "Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ" (Romans 10:17). The believing is something that happens in each person's heart. Hebrews 11:1 calls faith the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.

So is the faith of all believers one? In one sense, yes, and in another, no. Each person has his own faith. Jesus can praise one person for "great faith" (Matthew 8:10) and gently scold Peter, "You of little faith" (Matthew 14:31). But because all true believers trust the same Christ in the same way, we rightly speak of "one faith" (Ephesians 4:5), much as people who want the same thing are said to be of one mind. This unity reaches back across the ages. Abraham trusted God's promise about things still future as though they were already done. We trust the same God and the same promise, now fulfilled in Christ. That is why Paul calls Abraham the father of all who believe (Romans 4:11). His faith and ours are the same kind of faith.

How can you know you have faith? Faith is not something you can see with your eyes or touch. It lives in the heart. Yet it is not hidden from the one who has it. You know your own trust from the inside, much as you know you love someone without needing proof. Your conscience bears witness. Paul even tells us, "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith" (2 Corinthians 13:5). The question is not whether your faith is strong, but whether it is resting on Christ. Weak faith in a strong Savior still saves.

With others it is different. You cannot look into another person's heart. You can only believe their faith is real, and you believe it more firmly as you see its fruit: love, repentance, perseverance. Faith can be faked, and people can be mistaken about others or even about themselves. That is a reason for humility and charity, not suspicion. Judge by the fruit, leave the heart to God, and keep looking yourself not at your faith but at the Christ it trusts.

topics.title: How should believers live as members of Christ's kingdom?
topics.cmp: The questions here are mostly distinct, so the authors rarely address the same point. Where their concerns overlap, they share a picture of salvation that must be actively lived out. Irenaeus grounds this in effort and suffering: the kingdom is seized by strenuous free striving, not possessed by nature, and tribulation grinds believers like wheat into pure bread, an image he takes from a martyr's words. Owen also stresses a demanding discipleship, in which despising all things for Christ is the first lesson of the gospel and temptation can bring self-knowledge. Yet he places the decisive power outside the believer: comfort comes from the Holy Spirit's working rather than from circumstances or the heart, and temptation profits only with Christ's help. Augustine argues more from Scripture and definition: faith without love does not profit, which separates it from the devils' faith; prayer does not inform an all-foreknowing God; and Scripture's call to rebuke the wise shows that the wise are not sinless. Bickersteth uses an analogy to hold that trusting faith saves as truly as long investigation, a view that sits somewhat apart from Irenaeus's emphasis on strenuous effort, though neither addresses the other's question. Hilary alone makes right confession of Christ's divine sonship within the one God the condition for possessing the kingdom.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: They may not have so intelligent a knowledge of the way in which that elaborate key turns back one secret spring after another; that knowledge, whenever acquired, belongs to the patient painstaking investigator. But both alike possess the jewels.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: And for this cause tribulation is necessary for those who are saved, that having been after a manner broken up, and rendered fine, and sprinkled over by the patience of the Word of God

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: Still Further of the Difference Between the Knowledge…
refs.quote: For we too pray to Him, yet do not inform Him what our necessities are. “For your Father knoweth,” says His Word, “what things ye have need of, before you ask Him.”

ans.text:
Members of Christ's kingdom live by trusting him, belonging to him wholeheartedly, loving as he loved, and leaning on the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit through everything life brings, including trouble, temptation and failure. The kingdom is not a place we visit on Sundays. It is the rule of Jesus over people who have given themselves to him, and it shapes the whole of life.

It starts with faith, and faith does not have to be complicated to be real. Some people come to Christ after years of questions and study. Others hear the gospel and simply believe it, the way a child trusts a parent. Both are equally saved. Think of a key to a locked treasure chest. One person examines the key closely before trying it. Another just puts it in the lock and turns. The chest opens for both, and both have the treasure. The careful thinker may understand better how the key works, and that is a good thing. But what saves is not how much we have worked out. It is Christ himself, received by trust. Jesus said the kingdom belongs to those who receive it like little children (Mark 10:15).

True faith, though, is never just agreeing with facts. James points out that even the demons believe God is one, and it only makes them tremble (James 2:19). What separates saving faith from that is love. Paul says that in Christ what counts is faith that works itself out through love (Galatians 5:6). Faith joins us to Christ. Love is the life that flows from being joined to him. A faith that never loves God or neighbor is not the faith the Bible praises.

This faith is also faith in the true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. When a teacher of the law agreed with Jesus that God is one, and that loving God and neighbor matter more than sacrifices, Jesus told him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God" (Mark 12:34). Not far, but not yet inside. The man had much right. But the one God he confessed had come near in the Son standing in front of him, and he had not yet seen it. Entering the kingdom means coming to the Father through the Son.

Belonging to Christ also means he comes first. Jesus said, "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me" (Luke 9:23). This does not mean every Christian must give away every possession. It means nothing we own, want or love can sit on the throne that belongs to him. Paul pictures the church as a bride promised to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). A bride does not keep one eye on other lovers. The gospel invites us to give ourselves to a Savior who has already given himself for us. That is why following him is not grim duty but glad loyalty.

Jesus also spoke of people who lay hold of the kingdom with force (Matthew 11:12). Christians have read this saying in different ways. Some take it as a warning about opponents who attack the kingdom. Others see it as a picture of believers who seek it with eager, wholehearted effort. Either way, the wider New Testament is clear that we are not meant to drift. We are told to stay awake, to press on, and to strive. This effort does not earn salvation. It is how people act when they truly value what they have been given.

Life in the kingdom includes hardship. Jesus never promised his people an easy road. But God puts suffering to work. Paul writes that "suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope" (Romans 5:3-4). Think of wheat. It must be threshed, ground into flour, mixed with water and baked before it becomes bread. Trials grind away pride and self-reliance and make us more like Christ. They are not signs that God has abandoned us. They are part of how he prepares us for the joy of his presence.

Temptation can serve a good purpose too, though it is never something to seek. Often a temptation shows us sins hiding in our hearts that we never suspected. That is painful, like having a wound opened up. But a wound that is opened and cleaned can heal, while one left hidden can poison the whole body. We cannot turn temptation to good on our own strength. We need Christ, who was tempted in every way as we are yet without sin, and who helps those being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). God promises that he will not let us be tempted beyond what we can bear and will provide a way out (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Prayer is the breath of this life. Some wonder why we pray if God already knows everything. Jesus himself says your Father knows what you need before you ask him (Matthew 6:8), and then he teaches us to pray anyway. Prayer does not give God information. It is how children talk with their Father, depend on him, and come to want what he wants. God, who knew from all eternity what we would ask, has chosen to work through our prayers.

How can we know we are praying according to God's will? The Bible says, "If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us" (1 John 5:14). The surest guide is God's own promises. When we ask for what he has promised in Scripture, such as forgiveness, strength, wisdom, and the Spirit's help, we can pray with confidence. Two things keep such prayer honest. First, we ask for these gifts as things Christ has won for us, not things we deserve. Second, we ask for the reason God gives them, which is to make us holy, not to feed our selfish desires (James 4:3). And when we do not know what to pray, the Holy Spirit helps us in our weakness and prays for us (Romans 8:26). So Christian prayer is itself shaped by the Trinity: we pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.

Where does a believer's comfort come from? Not mainly from good circumstances, and not even from how steady our own feelings are. Real comfort comes from the Holy Spirit. Jesus promised that the Spirit, the Advocate, would remind his disciples of everything he had told them (John 14:26). When the Spirit brings Christ's promises home to the heart, comfort can reach people in prison cells, hospital beds and at gravesides. Circumstances cannot stop it, because it does not come from circumstances. That is why Christians through the ages have been able to sing in the dark.

Finally, none of this means a Christian must be perfect to be faithful or wise. Proverbs says, "rebuke a wise man, and he will love you" (Proverbs 9:8). You only rebuke someone who has done wrong. So the wise person in the Bible's sense is not sinless. He is someone who takes correction gladly. John says that if we claim to be without sin, we deceive ourselves, but if we confess our sins, God is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:8-9). Mature believers are not people who never fall. They are people who keep turning back to Christ, are quick to repent, and are ready to be taught.

So life in Christ's kingdom is simple at its heart, even if it lasts a lifetime. We trust Christ, love God and neighbor, put Jesus first, endure trials and temptations with his help, pray by his promises, take comfort from his Spirit, and humbly accept correction. We are living now as citizens of the kingdom we will one day see in full.

topics.title: How does Christ's coming relate to the Mosaic law?
topics.cmp: Irenaeus, Owen and Hilary agree that Christ's coming frees believers from the ceremonial requirements of the Mosaic law without making the law void. They argue this on different grounds and with different emphases. Irenaeus gives the fullest account, mostly from Scripture and salvation history: righteous men from Abraham to Enoch were justified before circumcision, so circumcision and the Sabbath were signs and types, not causes of righteousness. For him Christ fulfils rather than destroys the law, cancelling the laws of bondage while widening the natural law summed up in the Decalogue, and the same God's justice runs through both Testaments. Owen frames the question in terms of law, justice and the believer's liberty: God bound his truthfulness to punish sin, Christ nailed the ceremonial ordinances to the cross, and believers are freed from the moral law's terror, its role as an instrument of righteousness, and its curse, as well as from any human authority that would bind their conscience. On Christ's Sabbath healings the authors reach the same conclusion by different routes: Irenaeus argues from the law itself (it permitted priestly service, circumcision and acts of necessity on the Sabbath), while Hilary appeals to Christ's divine birth, by which the Father works with him in everything. Hilary also alone treats the 'circumcision of Christ' as baptismal rebirth into a new man.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: Abraham himself, without circumcision and without observance of Sabbaths, “believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness; and he was called the friend of God.”

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: That God, has also engaged his veracity and faithfulness in the sanction of the law, not to leave sin unpunished

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: the Father is working with Him in all that He does, will save us from supposing that the Lord of the Sabbath was doing wrong in working on the Sabbath

ans.text:
Jesus did not come to throw the law of Moses away. He came to fulfill it, to bring to completion everything it was pointing toward. He makes this clear: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them" (Matthew 5:17). To understand what that means, it helps to ask what the law was for in the first place, and what it could and could not do.

Start with what the law could not do. It could never make a sinner right with God. Paul makes this point by going back to Abraham, who lived centuries before Moses. Scripture says that "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (Romans 4:3). This happened before Abraham was circumcised and long before any Sabbath law was given. Noah, Enoch and others walked with God and pleased him without the law of Moses at all. So circumcision, the Sabbath and the other ceremonies were never the cause of a person's acceptance with God. They were signs. They marked Israel out as God's people and reminded them that it was the Lord who made them holy.

That does not mean these signs were empty. A wise God gave them, and they meant something. Circumcision of the body pictured a deeper need, a heart cut free from sin. The Sabbath rest pictured a life given over to God and pointed ahead to the final rest of his kingdom. Paul calls such things a shadow of what was coming, with the reality found in Christ (Colossians 2:16-17). A shadow is real, but you do not hold on to the shadow once the person who casts it has walked into the room.

The law also showed something important about God himself. He is just, and he does not pretend sin is nothing. From the warning to Adam that he would surely die, to the curse on everyone who does not keep the law, God put his own truthfulness on the line. He would not leave sin unpunished. Some people imagine that the God of the Old Testament is stern and the God of the New Testament is soft. But the New Testament speaks just as seriously about judgment. Paul writes that God's wrath is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness (Romans 1:18), and that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9). It is the same God in both Testaments, with the same holiness and the same love.

This is exactly why Christ's coming is such good news. God's justice was not set aside. It was satisfied. Jesus lived the perfect obedience the law required, which none of us has managed. Then he took the law's penalty on himself. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). So believers are not made right with God by their own law-keeping. They are counted righteous because of Christ's righteousness, received by faith. Paul says that this righteousness from God has now been revealed apart from the law, yet the Law and the Prophets themselves bear witness to it (Romans 3:21-22). The Old Testament was not a failed first attempt. It was the promise, and Jesus is the keeping of the promise. If he had not turned out to be just as the prophets described, they would have been shown to be false. But he matched their words exactly.

What, then, happens to the law's commands now? Christians have long found it helpful to see that the law of Moses contains different kinds of commands. Many were given to Israel as a nation: the sacrifices, the food laws, circumcision, the festivals and other ceremonies. These pointed to Christ, and now that he has come they have done their work. Paul says God canceled the record of debt that stood against us, setting it aside by nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14), and the early church decided not to place the yoke of circumcision and the ceremonial law on Gentile believers (Acts 15). Other commands express what God has always required of every human being: to love him with all our heart and to love our neighbor. These are summed up in the Ten Commandments. Jesus did not loosen them. He deepened them. In the Sermon on the Mount he shows that hatred breaks the command against murder and lust breaks the command against adultery (Matthew 5:21-28). Through the Holy Spirit, God now writes this law on his people's hearts, so that they obey from love as sons and daughters, not from fear as slaves.

This also explains Jesus' actions on the Sabbath. He was often accused of breaking it, by healing people and by letting his hungry disciples pick grain as they walked through a field. But he did not break the law. He broke the extra rules people had piled on top of it. The law itself allowed priests to serve in the temple on the Sabbath, allowed babies to be circumcised on that day, and allowed people to rescue an animal from a pit. What it forbade was ordinary work for gain. Jesus pointed to David eating the consecrated bread when he and his men were hungry, and he asked whether it was right to do good on the Sabbath or to do harm (Mark 2:23-28; 3:4). Healing a suffering person was exactly the kind of mercy the Sabbath was meant for. "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath," he said, and he added that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. When he healed, he was not acting alone or against God. As he said, "My Father is working until now, and I am working" (John 5:17). The Lord who gave the Sabbath was the one keeping it truly.

Christians have not all agreed on how the Sabbath command applies today. Some believe its pattern of one day in seven for rest and worship still stands, now kept on the Lord's Day, Sunday, because the command is among the Ten Commandments and is rooted in creation itself. Others believe the Sabbath was one of the signs given to Israel and is now fulfilled in the rest Christ gives, pointing to passages like Colossians 2:16 and Romans 14:5, while still gladly gathering for worship on the Lord's Day. Both sides agree that Jesus himself is our true rest. He calls, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28).

Paul also speaks of "the circumcision of Christ" (Colossians 2:11-12). He does not mean a physical operation. He means what Christ does inwardly: cutting away the old, sinful self. Paul connects this with baptism, in which we are buried with Christ and raised with him through faith in the power of God, who raised Jesus from the dead. What the old sign pictured, Christ actually accomplishes. A believer has died to the old life and now lives a new one belonging to him.

Finally, all of this brings real freedom. "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free," Paul writes. "Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). That freedom is not permission to sin, since we have been freed in order to love and serve. But it does mean no one may add rules of their own and tell believers that God requires them. Church leaders can give wise guidance and good order, but only God can bind the conscience. Children of God answer to their Father, and his commands, unlike human additions, are not burdensome.

So Christ's coming does not set the law aside as a mistake, and it does not leave it hanging over us as a curse. It shows what the law was always for. It revealed God's holiness, exposed our sin, and pointed ahead to a Savior. In Jesus, the shadows give way to the reality, the penalty is paid, and the heart of the law, love for God and neighbor, is written on the hearts of his people.

topics.title: How are love of God, self and neighbour related?
topics.cmp: Augustine supplies nearly all the answers on this topic, and they hang together. Love of God and love of neighbour cannot be had apart. We love God for his own sake and ourselves and our neighbour for God's sake, God incomparably more than ourselves and the neighbour as ourselves. We are to enjoy ourselves and our brethren in God, not in ourselves. His grounds are mainly scriptural, especially 1 John's "God is love," which lets him say that brotherly love is God and that whoever loves his brother knows God more surely than the brother. He also gives a philosophical account of love as a life coupling lover and beloved, which leads to the good itself, God, as what the soul must cleave to. John Owen and Gregory of Nyssa take up different questions and neither addresses how love of God, self and neighbour relate. Owen places God's love chiefly in his eternal purpose to relieve sinners and in his sending the Son as propitiation, a Christ-centred, soteriological emphasis absent from Augustine's answers here. Gregory argues from Job and from causation that human discoveries made through the faculty of conception are rightly ascribed to God as its Author.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: That He Who Loves His Brother, Loves God; Because He…
refs.quote: For since “God is love,” he who loves love certainly loves God; but he must needs love love, who loves his brother.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: In his holy eternal purpose of providing a relief for lost sinners.

refs.author: Gregory of Nyssa
refs.quote: And by the law of causation, whatever is discovered and established by conception must be ascribed to Him Who is the Author of that faculty.

ans.text:
Love of God, love of self and love of neighbour are not three separate loves pulling against each other. They are one love, flowing from God and returning to him, with God at the center and everything else loved in its proper place.

Start with what Jesus said. When asked which commandment was greatest, he answered, "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.' All the Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments" (Matthew 22:37-40). Notice the order. God comes first and receives everything: all the heart, all the soul, all the mind. The neighbour is loved "as yourself." So we are to love God incomparably more than anything, and our neighbour as much as ourselves.

Yet Jesus says the second commandment is "like" the first. They belong together. You cannot really keep one while ignoring the other. The apostle John puts it bluntly: "If anyone says, 'I love God,' but hates his brother, he is a liar" (1 John 4:20). And the other direction holds too. If you love God, you will do what he says, and what he says is to love your neighbour (1 John 4:21; 5:3). Love of God that never reaches people is not real love of God. Love of people that ignores God is missing its root.

Why are they so tied together? Because, as John says, "God is love" (1 John 4:8). Love is not something God simply happens to do. It is what he is. From all eternity the Father has loved the Son, and the Son the Father, in the Holy Spirit (John 17:24). God did not need to create anyone in order to have someone to love. When he made us, he made us to share in a love that was already there. So when we truly love a brother or sister, we are using a love that comes from God. "Love comes from God," John writes, and "everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God" (1 John 4:7). This is why John can sometimes talk about loving our brother and say nothing else. He assumes God is already present in that love. That does not mean every human feeling is God. It means that real, self-giving love is God's gift and bears his likeness, and the person who practises it is drawing near to God, even before understanding much.

It helps to ask what love is. At its simplest, love is delight in something good, and the desire to be joined to it. A friend loves a friend and wants to be with them. That is why the deepest love must be love for God himself. Everything else we love is good only because he made it good, and none of it can fully satisfy us. God is not one good thing among many. He is the source of every good. Other things we rightly enjoy, but God is the one we hold on to.

Where do we see God's love most clearly? Above all at the cross. "God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). John says love "consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins" (1 John 4:10). God's love was not a reaction to how lovable we were. He planned from eternity to rescue lost sinners, and he sent his own Son to do it. Our love always comes second: "We love because He first loved us" (1 John 4:19). That is very freeing. We do not have to generate love from our own resources. We pass on what we have received.

What about loving yourself? Jesus assumes we already care for ourselves; that is the measure he uses for the neighbour. But Christian self-love is not selfishness, and it is not the popular idea that you must first learn to love yourself before you can love God or anyone else. The truest way to love yourself is to love God. You were made for him, and you flourish only when you are joined to him. A person who chases their own pleasure apart from God is actually harming themselves. The more you love God, the more you really love yourself, because you are seeking your own deepest good.

So we enjoy ourselves and our neighbours "in God." Think of a family gathered around a fire. Each person warms the others, but the heat comes from the fire. We should delight in one another, truly and warmly, but not as if another person could be our god. When we try to make a spouse, a child or a friend the center of our life, we crush them with a weight only God can bear. When we love them in God, as his gifts and for his sake, we can love them more freely and more faithfully, not less.

This reaches into all of life, including our minds. Every skill people have, from medicine to music to building, comes from abilities God gave to human nature. Scripture speaks of craftsmen being filled by God's Spirit with skill (Exodus 31:3), and James tells us that "every good and perfect gift is from above" (James 1:17). So our learning and discoveries are also meant to be received with thanks and turned back toward him. "Whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Put simply: God loves us first, most clearly in giving his Son. We answer by loving him above everything. And in loving him, we learn to love ourselves rightly and our neighbours truly, with the same love, flowing from him and leading back to him.

topics.title: What is true blessedness?
topics.cmp: Almost all the answers on this topic come from Augustine, who builds a sustained philosophical account: blessedness requires both having what one wills and willing nothing evil. Where both cannot be had, a good will is preferable, though human depravity leads most people to choose the reverse. He rejects the philosophers' ideal of resigned willing (Terence's 'will that which thou canst'), as well as blessedness through hope alone and indifference to losing one's life. He identifies the final, unchangeable good as the Trinity itself, which the soul can reach because, unlike the immutable God, the soul is changeable and so can be restored. John Owen answers only one question, and his approach differs: rather than reasoning about the will, he works exegetically from Romans 5 and 1 Thessalonians 1:6. He attributes the believer's ability to glory in tribulation to the Holy Spirit's pouring out of God's love in the heart. The two do not contradict each other, but their emphases differ. Augustine stresses that present blessedness through hope is not yet true blessedness, while Owen stresses the present joy the Spirit gives even amid affliction.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: The Mind Loves God in Rightly Loving Itself; And If It…
refs.quote: “His desire will be satisfied with good things,” good things unchangeable,—the very Trinity itself, its own God, whose image it is.

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: He tells us, verse 5, it is from the “shedding abroad of the love of God in our hearts by the Holy Ghost.”

ans.text:
True blessedness is the complete and lasting joy of knowing God and being with Him, with every desire satisfied and nothing evil left to want. The Bible's word "blessed" is close to what we mean by deep happiness, but richer: it is the good life as God intended it, whole and secure.

Everyone wants to be blessed in this sense. No one wakes up hoping to be miserable. That desire is not a flaw. God built it into us. Yet people disagree wildly about what will make them happy. Some look for it in pleasure, some in success, some in being a good person, some in a mix of these. The disagreement does not come from anyone refusing happiness. It comes from not knowing what happiness really is. We tend to name as our happiness whatever delights us most at the moment.

A common answer is that being happy simply means living as you please. A little thought shows this cannot be right. If someone wants something wicked and gets it, he is not better off. He is worse off. It is sad to miss what you want, but it is sadder to want what you should not. So a good will, a heart that wants good things, is already a real good and a step toward blessedness, even when it does not yet have what it longs for. Full blessedness needs both: having what you want, and wanting nothing that is wrong.

Some people settle for a quieter answer: since you cannot have what you want, learn to want only what you can have. That is wise advice for getting through hard times. But it is not blessedness. It is a brave way of bearing what you would change if you could. The truly blessed person is not making do. He has what he loves.

Blessedness also has to last. If a person could lose his happiness at any moment and did not care, that would show he did not really love it. And a life you do not love is not a blessed life. So real blessedness must be secure, beyond the reach of death. That is why the Bible's hope is eternal life, where God "will wipe away every tear from their eyes" and death will be no more (Revelation 21:4).

What good could satisfy us like that? Nothing that changes or fades. Only God Himself. We were made in His image, and our hearts are shaped for Him. The psalmist says that in God's presence there is fullness of joy and pleasures forevermore (Psalm 16:11). Jesus describes eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent (John 17:3). To be blessed is to share, through the Son and by the Holy Spirit, in the life and love of the Father. Held close to God, we will be so filled with Him that sin will never again appeal to us.

This is where faith comes in. Wanting to be blessed is not enough to get there. Everyone wants it, but not everyone trusts God, and many give up hope of anything beyond this life. So they live in ways that lead away from it. Faith turns us toward God. It receives forgiveness through Christ, who gave His life to free us from sin and the power of evil. Faith also cleans the heart, and Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). Seeing God is the heart of blessedness, and faith is the road there. As Scripture puts it, "The righteous will live by faith" (Romans 1:17).

In this life, then, believers are blessed in hope rather than in full possession. We are on the way, waiting patiently for what we do not yet see (Romans 8:24-25). Yet even now there is real joy. Paul says believers can rejoice even in suffering, because "hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom He has given us" (Romans 5:5). The Spirit gives a foretaste of the joy to come. Without that hope, someone who bears suffering bravely is courageous but still unhappy. With it, he is on the way to joy.

What about the classic virtues of wisdom, courage, self-control and justice? Many people outside the faith practise them, and they are good things. But they reach their true purpose only when they serve love for God and trust in Him. Even then, in this life our virtue is never perfect, and we always need God's forgiveness.

Will these virtues disappear in heaven? Not really. They will be changed and completed. Justice, which at heart means living rightly under God's rule, will not end. It will be perfect. Wisdom will mean always preferring God to everything else. Courage will mean holding fast to Him without wavering. Self-control will mean taking no pleasure in anything wrong. What will end is only the part of each virtue that deals with evil: bearing hardship, resisting temptation, helping the suffering. There will be no evil left to face.

So true blessedness is not getting whatever we want, or simply putting up with what we cannot change. It is wanting what is good, receiving the greatest good, and never losing it. That good is God Himself. As John writes, when Christ appears, "we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2).

topics.title: Is God the final end of the will, seen and enjoyed by the saints?
topics.cmp: Augustine supplies nearly all the answers here, and they fit together into one account. God is the supreme good, already known as the standard behind our judgments of better and worse. Every act of will is referred to a final end of blessed life, so that resting with delight in a creature is not yet arriving at that end, and the right order is to use creatures and enjoy God (charity), not to love creatures for themselves (cupiditas). The contemplation of God is the final fullness of joy, yet because God is incomprehensible he is found in order to be sought ever more eagerly, and even in glory the creature never becomes equal to God's nature. Irenaeus agrees that the vision of God is the goal, and his point that love keeps growing the more we contemplate God fits Augustine's endless seeking, though Irenaeus rests it on Paul's faith, hope and love rather than on divine incomprehensibility. His distinct emphasis is that seeing God gives life and immortality, through the analogy of being inside light and sharing its brightness, whereas Augustine's arguments run through the analysis of the will and the use–enjoyment distinction. Ambrose's single answer takes a different angle: he identifies the 'living water' from the Fount of Life as the Holy Spirit, the divine grace that cleanses the mind, without addressing the will's final end directly.

refs.author: Augustine of Hippo
refs.place: How God May Be Known to Be the Chief Good. The Mind Does…
refs.quote: we could not say that one was better than another, when we judge truly, unless a conception of the good itself had been impressed upon us, such that according to it we might both approve some things as good, and prefer one good to another.

refs.author: Ambrose of Milan
refs.quote: we certainly do not understand a fount of that water which is created, but the Fount of that divine grace, that is, of the Holy Spirit, for He is the living water.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For we do never cease from loving God; but in proportion as we continue to contemplate Him, so much the more do we love Him.

ans.text:
Yes. God himself is the goal that every human desire is finally reaching for, and the Bible's great promise is that his people will one day see him and delight in him forever.

Start with something ordinary. All day long we judge some things to be better than others: a kind word over a cruel one, a true friend over a flatterer, a sunrise over a parking lot. To say one thing is better, we need some sense of what good is. We carry a measuring stick inside us, even if we rarely notice it. Christians believe that stick points beyond every created thing to the One who is goodness itself. Jesus says in Mark 10:18, "No one is good except God alone." Everything else is good because it comes from him and reflects a little of him.

Now think about how our wants are linked. I want to open the window to see who is passing by. I want my coffee so I can wake up. I want to work so I can feed my family. Each want has its own small goal, but if you keep asking "and why do you want that?" you eventually reach something you want for its own sake: to be truly happy, to live well, to be blessed. Every person wants that, even people who look for it in the wrong places. The Christian claim is that this deepest want has only one true answer, and it is God. As one psalm puts it, "Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You" (Psalm 73:25).

This helps us see the difference between using something and enjoying it. To use something is to take it up for the sake of something further. To enjoy something is to rest in it with delight as a goal in itself. We may and should enjoy many good things. Paul says God "richly provides us with all things to enjoy" (1 Timothy 6:17). But there is a right order. Food, money, work and possessions are gifts to be used well, with thanks, on the way to God. Other people are not tools. We love and delight in them, but we love them in God, wanting God's best for them. Only God can carry the full weight of our heart's rest.

This is where love goes right or wrong. Loving creation is not sin. The problem comes when we love a created thing as if it were our final home, asking it to be what only God can be. Then the love turns into grasping desire, and it bends us out of shape. A career, a romance, or even a family can become an idol in this way, and it always lets us down, because no created thing was built to bear that load. When the same love is aimed through the gift toward the Giver, it becomes healthy and free. That is why the direction of the will matters so much. If the final goal is God, our many small choices become like steps on a road leading home. If the final goal is something else, the same chain of choices becomes a chain that binds us.

An everyday picture helps. A traveler on a long road stops at an inn. He eats, rests and enjoys it, and that is fine. But the inn is not his country. He gets up and goes on. Many of the good things of this life are inns along the road. Hebrews 11 describes believers as people who admitted they were strangers on earth, longing for "a better country, a heavenly one" (Hebrews 11:16). The real rest is ahead.

This also explains why the inner life matters, not just outward actions. If the heart's aim is meant to be God, then gladly turning bad desires over in our minds, savoring what we know is wrong even without acting on it, is already a small turning away. It is far less serious than deciding to do the wrong, but it still needs forgiveness. That is part of why Jesus teaches us to pray daily, "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12).

So what is the final rest? Scripture says it is to see God. Jesus promises, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God" (Matthew 5:8). John writes, "We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is" (1 John 3:2). Paul says, "Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12). And the last chapter of the Bible says of God's servants, "They will see His face" (Revelation 22:4). Here and now, faith is the road. It cleans the heart and trains our eyes. The sight of God is the reward at the end of faith. When we see him, there will be nothing further to look for, because we will have the one thing all our looking was for. "You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand" (Psalm 16:11).

This seeing is not like glancing at a picture. In the Bible, to see God is to know him personally and to share his life. Jesus says, "Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent" (John 17:3). Think of stepping into sunlight. You do not just look at the light; you stand in it, and it warms and brightens you. In the same way, seeing God means being brought into his life and glory, and that is what makes us fully and endlessly alive.

It is also a vision of the triune God. Jesus says, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). The Son is the one in whom we see the Father's face. And the Holy Spirit is the one who brings us there. Jesus speaks of the Spirit as living water welling up inside believers (John 4:14; 7:38-39). The Spirit cleans our hearts and pours God's love into them, so that we can come to the Father through the Son. Our final joy is not a vague spiritual glow. It is being welcomed into the love the Father, Son and Spirit have always shared.

A few misunderstandings are worth clearing up. Some worry that heaven will be boring, like an endless church service. But God is not a small subject that can be used up. Even now, Scripture tells us to "seek His face always" (Psalm 105:4), though it also promises he can be found. Both are true because God is bigger than we can take in. Every time we find him, we discover more to seek. In the world to come, the seeking will no longer be painful or uncertain, but it will be full of fresh wonder. Love will not fade. Paul says that faith, hope and love remain, and "the greatest of these is love" (1 Corinthians 13:13). The more we see of God, the more we will love him.

Others worry that this makes the world and other people unimportant. It does not. Fixing our hearts on God is what frees us to love creation rightly, without crushing it under demands it cannot meet. The Bible's hope even includes a renewed earth.

Still others wonder whether seeing God means we will become God. No. We will be made like him, shining with his goodness, holy and free from all lies and confusion. But a creature always remains a creature. A mirror can be perfectly clean and bright and still not be the sun. God alone is the unmade source; we are his made and much-loved children, forever receiving from him.

Sincere Christians have described this hope with somewhat different emphases. Some put the stress on seeing and knowing God, since Scripture so often speaks of sight and face. Others put the stress on love and union, since the greatest commandment and the greatest gift is love. Most hold these together: we will know God in order to love him, and love him the more as we know him. Christians have also differed on how directly a creature can see God. Some say the saints will truly see God's very being, because 1 John 3:2 promises we will see him "as He is." Others say we will see God's glory and share his life without ever grasping his inner being, because Scripture also says God "lives in unapproachable light" (1 Timothy 6:16). Both sides agree that what we receive will be really God himself, not a substitute, and that it will fill us without ever being exhausted.

So the answer to the question is a joyful yes. Every honest longing in us is a signpost. God made us for himself, and he will not leave the longing empty. One psalm puts the whole Christian life in a sentence: "One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD" (Psalm 27:4).

topics.title: Will the dead rise in the body?
topics.cmp: All the authors who answer here affirm a real, bodily resurrection, and none dissents. Irenaeus supplies most of the material and builds the case from many directions. He argues from God's power over nature and the greater difficulty of creation from nothing. He argues from the Incarnation, Christ's healings, the Eucharist, and the Spirit's indwelling and 'inheriting' of the flesh. He also gives repeated exegesis of 1 Corinthians 15:50, reading 'flesh and blood' as flesh without the Spirit or as carnal works, not the body's substance. Novatian agrees on that verse, saying it rebukes the flesh's guilt rather than its God-built substance, and he points to Christ's wounds as proof He rose in the same body. Augustine adds a different emphasis: believers hope as members following their risen Head, the soul is raised now by faith while the body's resurrection waits for the end, and the chief good is the vision of God's substance rather than the bodily sight of the Son of man. Hilary grounds the hope partly in nature's teaching that life tends toward immortality and in the conquest of death as the last enemy. Gregory of Nyssa and Owen touch the topic only indirectly, on the senses of life and death and on eternal life promised to Christ as head.

refs.author: Novatian
refs.place: That Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Truly Man, as…
refs.quote: And that He was raised again in the same bodily substance in which He died, is proved by the wounds of that very body, and thus He showed the laws of our resurrection in His flesh

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For if it were not in the very same, then certainly those same individuals who had died did not rise again.

refs.author: Hilary of Poitiers
refs.quote: This victory over death is nothing else than the resurrection from the dead: for when the corruption of death is stayed, the quickened and now heavenly nature is made eternal

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible teaches that at the end of this age God will raise the dead in their own bodies. The very bodies that were buried will be brought back to life and made new, so that they can never again grow sick, decay, or die. This is not a picture or a figure of speech. It is a real event that God has promised, and Christ's own resurrection is the first instance of it.

The clearest place to start is Easter morning. When Jesus rose, His tomb was empty. The body that was laid there is the body that came out. When the frightened disciples thought they were seeing a ghost, He said, "Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have" (Luke 24:39). He ate fish in front of them. He showed Thomas the wounds in His hands and side. Those scars matter. They show that the risen Jesus was not handed a brand-new body in place of the old one. The same body that was crucified was raised and glorified.

Paul says this is the pattern for us. "Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits are the first sheaf of a harvest, and they promise that the rest of the crop is coming. The Head has risen, so the members of His body will follow. Jesus Himself said that the hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out (John 5:28-29). Even before Easter He gave previews. Lazarus and the widow's son at Nain were not given someone else's body. They got up in their own. That only makes sense, since otherwise it would not really be the same person who rose.

The whole work of the Trinity points the same way. The Father sent the Son. The Son did not take on a body for a while and then throw it away. He became truly human, flesh and blood like us, and He keeps His risen body forever. If our bodies could not be saved, there would have been no reason for God's Son to take one. Paul adds that if the Spirit of the One who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, He will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit (Romans 8:11). The Father raises the dead through the Son by the Spirit.

But won't the resurrection body be different? Yes, in its condition, though not in its identity. Paul compares it to a seed and a plant (1 Corinthians 15:36-44). What comes up from the ground looks far more glorious than the seed that was sown, yet it is the same living thing. "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." Our bodies now are weak and wear out. Then they will be strong, glorious, and immortal. Paul calls the new body a "spiritual body." That does not mean a body made of spirit, like a ghost. It means a body fully alive with God's Holy Spirit and ruled by Him. Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

Some people stumble over one verse: "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God" (1 Corinthians 15:50). Does that mean our physical bodies are left out? It cannot mean that, because three verses later Paul says, "For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:53). Notice the word "this" in the passage. This perishable body is what puts on imperishability. The body is not thrown away. It is clothed. In the Bible, "flesh and blood" often means human nature as it is now: weak, mortal, and on its own, without God's Spirit. Elsewhere Paul uses "the flesh" for a sinful way of life, and he lists its works, such as sexual immorality, idolatry and hatred (Galatians 5:19-21). Our bodies as they are now, dying and stained by sin, cannot enter God's kingdom unchanged. They must first be transformed. So the verse speaks of change, not of losing the body.

What happens to us between death and that final day? The Bible teaches that at death the soul and body are separated. The body goes to the grave. The believer's soul goes to be with Christ. Jesus told the dying thief, "Today you will be with Me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). Paul said he would rather be "away from the body and at home with the Lord" (2 Corinthians 5:8), and that to depart and be with Christ is "far better" (Philippians 1:23). This is a real comfort for those who grieve. Still, it is not the final goal. A soul without a body is not a whole human being, and Scripture never treats that state as the end. Some sincere Christians believe the dead rest without awareness until the resurrection, pointing to the Bible's frequent description of death as "sleep." Most Christians have understood "sleep" as a gentle way to speak of the body's rest, while the soul is consciously present with the Lord, because of verses like the ones above. Either way, all agree that the great hope is the resurrection of the body.

It also helps to see that the Bible speaks of two kinds of death. Bodily death happens when the soul leaves the body. A deeper death happens when a person is cut off from God, the source of all true life. That is why Paul can describe people as "dead in trespasses" while they are still walking around. The first death follows from the second. Sin separated us from God, and physical death came into the world as its result. Christ undoes both. He gives new life to the soul now through faith and the Spirit, and He will give new life to the body at His return. That is why Paul calls death "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26). Death is not fully defeated until the bodies it has held are raised out of its grip.

Why does God let our bodies die and decay at all, if He means to raise them? One answer the Bible suggests is humility. We learn by hard experience that we do not have life in ourselves. Life is a gift from God, and God's power is made perfect in weakness. A body raised from dust shows His power more plainly than a body that never fell. God formed the first human from the ground and breathed life into him. Raising us again is not harder for Him than making us in the first place.

This teaching shapes how Christians live now. Our bodies are not shells to be discarded. They belong to the Lord and are temples of the Holy Spirit, so what we do with them matters. It is why Christians have traditionally buried their dead with respect and hope. It also tells us that God's salvation is not an escape from the world He made. It is the renewal of that world, starting with our own flesh. Job, long ago, already hoped that in his flesh he would see God. In Christ that hope is sure. The same person who is laid in the grave will rise, will be known, and will live with God forever, body and soul.

topics.title: Will God's promises be fulfilled in a renewed creation?
topics.cmp: How types and unfulfilled promises, such as the land promised to Abraham, find fulfilment in a renewed earth after the resurrection.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: For a type and emblem is, no doubt, sometimes diverse from the truth [signified] as to matter and substance; but it ought, as to the general form and features, to maintain a likeness [to what is typified]

ans.text:
Yes. Every promise God has made will be kept in full, and the Bible teaches that many of them will finally be kept in a renewed creation, a real world made new, where God's people live in raised and glorified bodies. Paul puts it simply: "all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ" (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Take the promise to Abraham. God told him that he and his descendants would have the land of Canaan. Yet Abraham never owned it. He lived there as a foreigner, moving his tents from place to place. When his wife Sarah died he had to buy a field just to bury her. Stephen points this out in Acts 7:5: God gave Abraham no inheritance there, "not even a foot of ground." Hebrews 11:13 says of Abraham and his family: "All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised."

So was God's promise empty? Not at all. God is faithful, and he does not break his word. If Abraham did not receive the land in this life, he must receive it in the life to come. That is why Hebrews says Abraham was looking for "a better country" and for a city whose builder is God. It is also why Jesus could say, "Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5). That is a promise about the earth, not only about heaven.

The promise also grows larger as the Bible goes on. Paul says in Romans 4:13 that Abraham and his offspring were promised that he would be "heir of the world." The small strip of land in Canaan was a kind of preview, or "type," of something much bigger. A type is a real person, place or event that points ahead to a greater reality. It is not the same thing as what it points to. A coin's stamp is not the king, but it has his likeness. Still, the two must truly resemble each other. The promised land was a real place on the earth, given to a real people to live in under God's blessing. So what it points to is not a vague, ghostly existence. It is a real, renewed earth where God's people live with him for ever. And who are Abraham's offspring? Paul answers in Galatians 3:29: "if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise." Every believer, Jew or Gentile, shares in that inheritance.

The Bible shows the same pattern with other promises. When Isaac blessed his son Jacob, he promised him plenty and authority over others. But Jacob spent much of his life working hard for his uncle, bowing low before his brother, and finally going down to Egypt because of famine. The blessing was real, but its fullest meaning lay ahead. Many promises in Scripture are like a seed: planted in history, but only reaching full bloom at the end.

This is why the resurrection of the body matters so much. God does not plan to throw away his creation and save only our souls. Paul says in Romans 8:21 that "the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay" and share in the freedom of God's children. Peter writes that "we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells" (2 Peter 3:13). John saw it in a vision: "a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1), with God himself living among his people.

Jesus himself pointed this way at the Last Supper. He told his disciples he would not drink the fruit of the vine again "until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father's kingdom" (Matthew 26:29). Drinking wine at a shared table is something people with bodies do, in a world with vines and harvests. Jesus rose bodily from the grave. He ate fish with his friends afterward. His risen body is the first piece of the new creation, and ours will be like his.

What about prophecies like Isaiah's picture of the wolf and the lamb feeding together and the lion eating straw like the ox (Isaiah 65:25)? Already today these words come true in one sense, when people from hostile nations are made friends in Christ. But many Christians have also believed that they point to a real peace in the renewed world itself, with the harm and violence of a fallen creation healed. God is rich and generous; his renewal reaches every corner of what he made.

Sincere Christians have differed on some details. Some believe that when Christ returns he will reign on this earth with his raised people for a long age, often called the thousand years of Revelation 20, before the final new creation. They see this as the time when promises like Abraham's are visibly fulfilled. Others read that passage as a picture of Christ's present reign, and believe the promises will be fulfilled directly in the eternal new heavens and new earth. Christians also differ on how literally to take some prophetic images, such as the animals. But on the heart of the matter they agree: Christ will return, the dead will be raised in their bodies, and God will make all things new.

It can be easy to imagine eternity as floating on clouds, far from anything earthy. Scripture gives a richer hope. The Father who made the world will not abandon it. The Son, who took on a human body and rose in it, will share his inheritance with his brothers and sisters. The Spirit, who gives life, will raise our bodies and renew all things. Nothing God promised to Abraham, or to us, will be lost. We will receive more than we were promised, never less.

topics.title: Will God judge and punish eternally?
topics.cmp: All four authors affirm that judgment is real and that its punishment is eternal, but each comes at it from a different angle. Irenaeus is the one who most directly addresses how punishment comes about. He treats it as self-chosen separation from God, who is the source of all good, and argues by analogy (blindness, people shutting out sunlight) that God is not its immediate cause. Bickersteth instead rejects the inference that divine love rules out eternal condemnation. He grounds God's severity in creation, providence and Scripture, including Christ's warning, and he stresses righteousness and holy jealousy rather than the sinner's self-exclusion. Owen focuses on the certainty of a universal judgment, reasoning from Christ's resurrection, which appoints him judge, and from his death, a public condemnation of sin that prefigures the last judgment. Basil, interpreting the parable of the servant 'cut asunder', describes the punishment as the soul's complete and eternal separation from the Holy Spirit. This echoes Irenaeus's idea of separation, but Basil frames it as the Spirit being withdrawn from one who defiled grace rather than as the sinner's own flight.

refs.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
refs.quote: God, however, does not punish them immediately of Himself, but that punishment falls upon them because they are destitute of all that is good. Now, good things are eternal and without end with God, and therefore the loss of these is also eternal and never-ending.

refs.author: Edward Henry Bickersteth
refs.quote: God is love indeed – but love embraces all his attributes, not mercy only, but righteousness likewise

refs.author: John Owen
refs.quote: he hath given faith and assurance of this thing to all, by raising Christ from the dead, having appointed him to be the judge of all; in whom and by whom he will judge the world in righteousness.

ans.text:
Yes. The Bible teaches that God will one day judge every person through Jesus Christ, and that for those who finally reject him the result is a punishment that does not end.
